title: The Book Isn’t What Failed
html:
I’m self-publishing a novel right now, working with a book coach, Donna Knutson, who’s kept me honest about the production and rights decisions I didn’t know I needed to make. A few weeks ago I sat in a virtual workshop run by Molly Seabrook of Credible.Ink. Her line has been sitting with me since: don’t let your book land with a thud.

When a book lands in silence, Molly’s point is, it’s almost never because the writing was bad. It’s because no one had context for it. Never seen it. Never heard of the author. No reason to care yet. The book didn’t fail. There was nowhere for it to land.

I’ve watched the exact same failure mode in founder pitches for two decades, and I never had the language for it until Molly handed it to me.

The pitch isn’t the problem. The absence is.

A founder walks into a room with a strong deck, a real product, a defensible model – and gets a pass. The instinct is to rewrite the deck. Sharpen the ask. Cut two slides. Sometimes that’s the right call. More often, the deck was never the variable that mattered. The investor had no context for this founder, this category, this bet, before the meeting started. The pitch was the first touch, not the fortieth. It was asking a stranger to catch something they hadn’t been warming up to catch.

Self-publishing removes the gatekeeper but not the problem – it just moves it later. There’s no agent to reject you and no one to blame the silence on. The book goes up, and either there’s an audience already leaning toward it or there isn’t. Skipping audience-building because you skipped querying is the same mistake in a different sequence.

The fix isn’t a bigger launch. It’s a longer runway – showing up consistently, in public, long before there’s anything to sell. That’s slow, unglamorous, and it’s the part almost everyone skips, in a book launch or a company launch.

Three skills get conflated into one, and only one of them is optional.

Every first-time author is carrying three separate skill sets and pretending it’s one job: the expertise itself (which they usually have), the craft of putting it on the page (maybe), and everything else – positioning, production, distribution, the slow work of being findable before anyone’s looking. Most people budget time and money for the first two and assume the third will sort itself out on launch day.

It won’t. Launch day arrives, and the audience that was supposed to materialize on its own simply doesn’t, because “on its own” was never how it was going to happen.

Ownership is the question nobody asks until it’s too late.

Self-publishing doesn’t remove this risk; it just relocates it. Whose name is the KDP account under? Who’s listed as publisher of record on the ISBN? If a designer or formatter touches the files, who owns the source when the project’s done? None of it feels urgent while you’re building. All of it becomes the whole problem the day you need to update, move, or prove you own what you made.

Founders skip the identical question constantly – with platforms, with early co-founder agreements, with vendors who quietly become infrastructure. The account question is a control question wearing a boring disguise.

The wrong metric will make you feel like you’re failing when you aren’t.

Authority nonfiction – the kind of book that exists to open doors, not top bestseller lists – gets judged by writers on the wrong scoreboard. Sales numbers, royalty checks, launch-week rank. Almost none of that is the point. The book is a container for the thinking and a credential for the rooms it gets you into afterward. Judge it by that, and a “quiet” launch looks completely different.

Founders do this to themselves too – measuring a new initiative by a metric that was never actually the goal, then concluding the work failed when the goal was simply mismeasured.

It’s the same reason companies keep promoting people into roles nobody built a runway for, then wonder why the readiness gap shows up later as a crisis. Organizations grow people into leadership roles faster than they grow leadership capability. Same absence, different room.

I sometimes see the publishing version and the founder version in the same week. A client gets handed a VP title with no decision rights to go with it, and six months later everyone’s confused why nothing moves without the founder in the room. Nobody built the context for that person to be believed as a leader before they needed to act like one. It’s not a confidence problem. It’s not a skills problem. It’s the exact gap Molly’s describing, dressed up as an org chart instead of a book jacket.

None of this is really about books. It’s about what happens to anything – a product, a pitch, a person – that shows up expecting to be caught by a market that was never warmed up to catch it.

Build the place before the thing arrives. The thing was probably fine.

title: The Gear You Reach For Under Pressure
html:
You can learn more about a leader in the first ten seconds of a crisis than in a year of one-on-ones. Watch what they reach for before they think.

Do they zoom out and reframe? That’s Visionary. Take the wheel and start solving? Operator. Go silent and let it ride? Independent. Whatever fires before thought, that’s the default – and the default is almost always the gear that built the career.

A strength on a timer becomes a liability

VOICES gives you six gears: Visionary, Operator, Independent, Coach, Encourager, Sculptor. One for each kind of moment. But pressure shrinks the gearbox to one. The founder who built on vision keeps casting vision when the room needed a decision. The operator who scaled on execution keeps diving into tasks when the team needed to be developed. Neither gear is wrong. The reflex is.

What makes the default so hard to see is that it works, right up to the point it doesn’t. It got you promoted. It feels like competence. So you keep using it past its terrain, and the costs hide in plain sight: a team that brings you problems instead of solutions, an inbox that fills because you’re still the answer, a star performer who leaves for a place where they’ll get to drive.

The tell is usually fear, not preference

Here’s the part worth being honest about. Your default isn’t just what you’re good at. It’s what protects you. The operator dives into tasks partly because tasks are safer than the harder conversation. The visionary stays at altitude partly because thirty thousand feet is a comfortable place to avoid the messy specifics. The gear you grab under pressure is doing double duty – getting the work done, and keeping you away from the part of leadership you’d rather not feel.

Caption: Your default does double duty – it gets the work done, and it keeps you from what you’d rather not face.

That’s why the most valuable downshift for most leaders is into Coach, and also the one they resist hardest. The urge to grab the wheel and answer is usually the precise moment someone was ready to find the answer themselves. Coach is slower than telling, right until the week you’re out, and the place runs fine without you – which is the entire point of the job.

The work isn’t to abandon your default. It’s to feel it firing and ask one question before you move: what does this moment actually need? Sometimes the answer is your default, and you choose it on purpose instead of on reflex. Often it’s the gear you avoid. Either way, that half-second of noticing is the whole skill, and it can be trained.

Notice your hands this week, then ask:

  • What gear do you reach for in the first ten seconds of a hard moment?

  • What does that gear protect you from having to feel or face?

  • Who needed you in Coach this week, and what would have changed if they’d gotten it?

title: The Coach Gear
html:
Someone on your team brings you a problem. You see the answer immediately – you’ve solved this exact thing a hundred times – so you give it to them. Clean, fast, correct. They thank you and leave. It felt like help, and it was, a little.

It was also a small withdrawal from the one account you most need to keep growing: their ability to solve it themselves next time.

The urge to answer is the signal

Here’s the reframe that changes everything, once you can feel it: the urge to give the answer is the signal to ask a question. That pull to grab the wheel – oh, I know this one – almost always fires at the exact moment the person in front of you was about to find the answer themselves. Your certainty is the tell. The faster you know the answer, the more it’s probably their rep to take, not yours.

This is the Coach gear in VOICES – leading through questions instead of answers. Not therapy, not withholding for its own sake. Just the discipline of asking “What have you tried?” or “What do you think the move is?” before you reach for “Here’s what I’d do.” The question keeps the problem in their hands long enough for them to grow a grip on it.

What a question does that an answer can’t

An answer solves today’s problem. A question builds the person who’ll solve the next ten without you. When you tell, the solution is yours – borrowed, not owned – and they come back for the next one, because why wouldn’t they? You’re faster. When you ask, they do the cognitive work, and the judgment that work builds stays in their head after they leave your office. One exchange makes you indispensable. The other makes you replaceable, which is the entire goal.

Caption: Telling vs coaching – an answer solves today; a question builds the person who solves the next ten.

Slower this week, faster the week you’re out

There’s a reason high-control leaders skip this gear, and it isn’t that they don’t care. It’s that coaching is genuinely slower in the moment, and a busy leader optimizes for the moment. Asking takes longer than telling. Watching someone work toward an answer you already have is mildly excruciating. So you tell, and you tell, and you stay the fastest path to every answer – which is exactly why nothing moves when you’re gone.

The Coach gear is a trade: a little slower this week, in exchange for a team that doesn’t need you next quarter. You won’t always have time for it – a real crisis wants Command, not a coaching question. But on the ordinary Tuesday problems, the ones where there’s time and the stakes are survivable, the question is the highest-leverage thing you can do, because you’re not just solving a problem. You’re building someone who solves problems.

Worth sitting with this week:

  • Where did you give an answer this week that someone was one good question away from finding themselves?

  • What’s your tell – the feeling, right before you grab the wheel, that you could learn to read as “ask, don’t tell”?

  • Who would grow fastest if you spent a month asking them instead of answering them?

title: The Stage You Skipped
html:
I once watched a founder hand his best engineer a whole product line on a Friday, with a “you’ve got this,” and mean it as the highest compliment. By the next Friday, the engineer was underwater, the launch was slipping, and the founder was privately furious at someone he’d set up to fail.

He hadn’t given too much trust. He’d skipped a stage.

The middle is the part that builds the driver

Developing someone to run without you happens in three steps, and the order matters more than the speed. The Ride-Along: you drive, they watch, you think out loud. The Learner’s Permit: they drive, you ride along, asking questions instead of seizing the wheel. The Solo Drive: they own it, and you’ve stepped back to occasional passenger.

The mistake almost everyone makes is collapsing the middle. You show someone how it’s done once, jump them to solo, and brace for the crash. They didn’t lack talent. They lacked the Learner’s Permit – the only stretch where judgment is actually built, in the reps where they make the call and you’re near enough to coach but far enough to let it be real.

There are two ways to get the middle wrong, and both are everywhere. You can end it too early, mistaking one good week for mastery and pushing someone solo before they’re ready. Or you can never end it at all, hovering in the passenger seat so long that a capable adult is stuck on a permanent learner’s permit, asking permission for calls they could have owned a year ago.

Caption: Readiness × release – push too soon and they crash; hold too long and they stall.

The cost lands on both of you

The person stalls. They start to wonder whether they have a real future here, or whether they’ll be checking in with you forever. That’s when capable people leave – not in a blaze, but in a slow drift toward a job where they’ll be allowed to grow up.

And you stay the bottleneck. You tell yourself you’d delegate more if only they were ready, never clocking that you’re the reason they aren’t. The skipped stage doesn’t just cost you a stronger team member. It re-signs your own contract as the person everything routes through. Sitting in the discomfort of the Learner’s Permit, watching someone struggle and not rescuing them, is the price of ever getting to put the wheel down.

There’s a simple discipline that fixes both failures. Before you push someone to solo or hold them back, ask what specific decision they’ve now made well, on their own, more than once. If you can name it, give them more rope. If you can’t, they’re still on a permit, and the work is reps, not a verdict. Readiness is evidence, not a feeling you have about someone.

Walk your bench, one person at a time:

  • For each person you’re developing, which stage are they really in?

  • Who got pushed to Solo too soon, and who’s been left on a permit far too long?

  • Which of those is more about your comfort than their readiness?

title: The Mechanic’s Education:
subtitle: Why Classics Still Matter When Everything Moves Fast
html:
Late one night in 1925, a classics professor named Carol Wight came across a mechanic reading Thucydides on the grimy floor of his shop. When Wight asked the predictable question – “What good will that do you?” – the mechanic gave the answer that changes everything:

“With this,” he said, holding up his lathe, “I can shape steel. And with this,” holding out the book, “I can shape men.”

That sentence contains the entire argument about leadership. The mechanic already did. And it has been waiting a hundred years for your organization to notice.

The mechanic wasn’t studying philosophy to become more cultured. He was reading the ancients because they taught him how to read people – how to understand motivation, consequence, the way a decision moves through a system. He was learning judgment. Not the kind you certify in a workshop. The kind you build into how you see, that shows up under pressure, that lets you hold a difficult decision without collapsing into false clarity.

An Atlantic piece this week noticed something the business schools have been pretending isn’t true for twenty years. When AI labs hit the ceiling of what optimization alone could produce, they didn’t call the MBA programs. They called the philosophers. They didn’t hire more engineers to refine the machine. They hired people trained to read difficult texts and answer difficult questions. Daniel Greco at Yale, Daniel Korman at Stanford – sitting with frontier models, teaching them to think, grading reasoning the way a classics professor grades an essay. Because the thing the machine needed wasn’t another layer of calculation. It was judgment.

Click here to read the piece in The Atlantic.

That’s not a coincidence. That’s the whole story.

Three institutions spent a century manufacturing the opposite of what the AI labs just discovered they needed. School taught you to find the right answer. The MBA taught you to choose well between options. Your organization rewarded you for arriving with the answer already formed. Twelve years of reproduction, six years of optimization, and then a career of performing confidence – all of it practicing suppression of the exact thing the moment just revealed as scarce.

The mechanic in the shop got there differently. He was reading Thucydides in the margins of work that mattered – reading about power, consequence, how empires collapse under the weight of decisions made for the wrong reasons. He wasn’t acquiring a skill. He was being formed. And by the time the moment arrived when he needed to read a person instead of steel, the instrument was already built.

The Atlantic piece lands on something this whole series kept circling: the thing the mechanic had that your organization probably doesn’t.

A relationship with old thinking. Not as nostalgia. As infrastructure.

The classics don’t become important because you need to pass a test on Thucydides. They become important because you spent enough time inside someone else’s impossible decision that when yours arrives, you don’t experience it as unprecedented. You recognize the shape of it. You’ve watched empires fall to pride before. You’ve read about judgment corroding under pressure. You’ve encountered the moment when two good people disagree on something real and no framework resolves it cleanly.

You’ve been formed.

I work with founders and operators – people scaling from 25 to 150 people, the point where your personal judgment can no longer carry the organization. The work I do is build the infrastructure that distributes judgment before one person becomes the bottleneck. Load-test it deliberately. Grow people under weight instead of hoping they’ll absorb judgment they were never asked to practice.

That’s the mechanic’s move translated into an operating system – the way an organization builds people instead of just deploying them.

The mechanic had the Atlantic’s benefit: a hundred years of distance between him and Thucydides, enough perspective to see the pattern repeat. Most of us don’t have that luxury. We’re in the moment. The pressure is now. The decision is real, and the map is incomplete.

So what we can do instead: stop selecting for people who arrive with the answer already formed. Start watching who builds the frame under pressure. Stop measuring what shows up on command. Start observing what holds under load. Stop sending people to workshops. Start designing systems that deliberately shape them over time.

The AI labs already proved the point. They had the technology. It wasn’t enough. They needed philosophers. They needed people trained in the difficult discipline of reading something that didn’t immediately make sense, of sitting inside unresolved tension, of letting a question open rather than closing it too fast.

They needed people the classics had formed.

The mechanic’s move is the move you’re building right now, whether you know it or not. Not Thucydides on the shop floor – though you’d be lucky to have someone reading that way. But the understanding of what old thinking is actually for: not cultural credibility, not self-improvement, but the unglamorous, foundational work of building the interior architecture that lets a person read a situation accurately and respond to what’s actually there.

That’s what I do. That’s what every organization that will win the next decade is quietly building – not better tools, but better people, formed deliberately, under conditions that make judgment visible before the moment it actually matters.

Three questions for this week:

  • What judgment do you have in your organization that your hiring and promotion systems structurally overlook?

  • Who has been reading the hard texts – not in a classical sense, but living through complexity without the playbook – and what have they learned that your official frameworks never captured?

  • What changes if you stop trying to install judgment and start building the conditions that form it?

At this point I’ve written enough about leadership from the ancient Greeks that I’m convinced I should just publish the whole thing as a single book: Everything You Need to Know About Running Your Business from Dead Philosophers (The MBA Edition Never Covers This).

But in case ten essays on Plato, Homer, and Sophocles feels like too much investment, here’s an easier way in. Pick any of these. The argument doesn’t change – the Greeks just showed it from different angles.

Read the full series:

  1. The Humanities Were Never Soft – Five capacities the humanities build. Why they’re formation, not skills.

  2. The Philosopher-King Problem – Plato on why organizations promote the people least fit to lead.

  3. What Greek Tragedy Knew About Your Organization – Sophocles. Ajax, Oedipus, Creon: three failure modes still running in your org.

  4. The Oldest Management Failure on Record – Homer’s Iliad. The day Agamemnon’s authority and Achilles’ judgment stopped being the same thing.

  5. What Are You Practicing? – Marcus Aurelius. You don’t rise to the occasion; you fall to the level of your preparation.

  6. They Educated It Out – Creativity as the engine beneath everything. Why schools systematically suppress it.

  7. Skill Is the Wrong Word – Formation can’t be installed. It has to be built. Why the word matters for your budget.

  8. The Judgment Shortage – AI demand spiked; supply was driven to zero on purpose. The scissors closing.

  9. What Holds Under Load – Formation under load, not on command. Why tests miss it. The Showcase vs. the test.

  10. They Didn’t Send the Machines to Business School – AI labs called philosophers, not MBAs. The alliance, not the rivalry.

CLUTCH is the operating system I built for exactly this: the infrastructure that forms judgment the way judgment is actually formed – under weight, over time, with the handoff made on purpose. The mechanic just needed Thucydides and the pressure of real work. Your organization needs both: ancient wisdom and a deliberate system that keeps judgment distributed rather than hoarded.

title: The Difference Between the Title and the Keys
html:
Most leaders think they’re delegating. What they’re actually doing is one of two things, and both backfire.

The first is the toss. You hand someone the keys, say “good luck,” and disappear until the deadline. That’s not trust. It’s abandonment with a nicer name, and people crash in it.

The second is sneakier. You give someone the title but keep the keys. You call it their project, then sign off on every real decision yourself. The title says owner. The license says intern. People feel that gap on day one, and they stop stretching, because they’ve learned that the authority here is a costume.

The title is not the keys

The title is the role name and the accountability that never leaves you. The license is the operating authority to act without asking. Most “promoted” people get the first and not the second, and then everyone’s confused about why they aren’t stepping up. They aren’t stepping up because, in any way that counts, they were never actually handed the wheel.

Caption: The title vs the keys – real delegation hands over both, on purpose.

Real delegation hands over both, on purpose. DELEGATE is the structure that does it without dropping the handoff: Define the win, so “done” isn’t a picture that lives only in your head. Establish the way. List the guardrails, the red lines, and the open field. Expect the process, so the first stumble reads as learning, not failure. Give the right support. Agree on checkpoints, so syncing is planned, not panic. Transfer ownership, out loud. Encourage growth, so they know you’re betting on them.

You won’t run all eight on a quick task. But when the work matters and someone’s stretching, the full frame is what keeps good intentions from drifting into a mess you clean up later.

Why it pays

Real delegation, the kind where the keys actually change hands, does more than clear your plate. It builds someone who clears the next ten plates, and eventually teaches the person after them. That’s the difference between renting relief and owning it. The leader who only ever tosses or hovers stays the single point of failure forever. The one who transfers cleanly compounds their own time, because every genuine handoff is a small permanent reduction in how much the place needs them.

There’s a trust dividend underneath it. People who are given real authority and the support to use it don’t just perform better; they stay. The fastest way to lose your best person is to give them a title and treat them like an intern.

Want a fast read on whether the keys really changed hands? Watch what happens when you’re away. The title-only owner texts you for permission. The real owner makes the call, tells you after, and is right often enough that you stop bracing. One of those is delegation. The other is an expensive way to feel in control.

Look at your last real handoff, then sit with these:

  • Did you transfer the keys, or just the title?

  • Where is someone carrying the weight of a job you never gave them the authority to actually do?

  • What would you have to believe about them to hand over the keys for real?

title: You're Not Delegating. You're Teaching Them to Drive.
html:
I spent two decades in classrooms before I ever set foot in a boardroom, and the lesson that carried over cleanest was this: you cannot hand someone judgment in a single sitting.

You can hand them information. You can hand them a task. Judgment is different. It forms in the reps, in the stretch where they make the call and you’re close enough to catch the fall but far enough to let it be real. A teacher who lectures and then tests has taught nothing about how to think. The same is true of a leader who explains the job once and then expects ownership.

Delegation transfers a task. Development builds a driver.

You build a driver in stages

And you don’t build a driver by tossing a teenager the keys and a destination. You build one in stages, and the order isn’t optional.

The Ride-Along comes first. You drive, they watch, and the point is to make your thinking visible. You narrate the reasoning behind the call, not just the call. They learn how you read the road before they ever touch the wheel.

Then the Learner’s Permit. Now they drive, you’re in the passenger seat, and this is where most of the real growth happens. You ask instead of grab. You let them work the problem while you sit on your hands, which is harder than it sounds. The 6C Compass becomes a teaching tool here: “This one’s yours to call. Here’s why I’m not making it for you.”

Last is the Solo Drive. They own it. You’ve moved from instructor to occasional passenger, close enough to coach, far enough to let it become theirs.

Caption: You build a driver in three stages – and the middle is the one most leaders skip.

The skipped stage is the expensive one

Most leaders compress this. They go from Ride-Along straight to Solo and call it trust, then wonder why their people freeze or crash. The missing middle is where it costs you, because the Learner’s Permit is the only place judgment is built, and judgment is the one thing you can’t cover for when you’re out.

Think about what a single real driver is worth to you. Not a competent task-doer – a driver, someone who can take the next decision off your desk and the one after that, and grow the person beneath them. One of those is worth more than a year of you working weekends, because they multiply while you only ever add. Development is the only line of work where the payoff is your own freedom.

A caution worth holding: development is slow on purpose, and slow is exactly what an overloaded leader can’t stand. So you grab the wheel “just this once,” and just this once becomes the pattern, and a year on you’re still the only driver. The investment feels like a tax in the moment. It’s the only thing that ever actually lightens the load.

Look at the people you’re growing, and ask:

  • Which stage is each of them actually in, and which stage are you treating them as if they’re in?

  • Where have you jumped someone to Solo and called it empowerment?

  • What becomes possible for you in a year if even one of them becomes a true driver?

title: The Spanx Learning Curve
html:
You hand a stretch project to someone with real promise. They’re a level below the work, but they’re ready to grow into it – that’s the point. Two weeks in, they hit the first real stumble. A deliverable comes back rough. A call they made needs to be walked back.

Everything turns on how you read that stumble. Most leaders read it as evidence – proof the person wasn’t ready – and quietly pull the work back to do it themselves. They think they’re being responsible. They’re actually ending the development right where it was supposed to start.

The first stumble is data, not a verdict

When you hand someone work that stretches them, a stumble isn’t a failure. It’s the curve. Skill doesn’t arrive on day one; it’s built through exactly the rough drafts and wrong turns you’re tempted to rescue them from. The problem is almost never that the person can’t do it. It’s that you didn’t name the curve out loud – to them or to yourself – so the first wobble landed as failure instead of as the expected first rep.

This is one of the eight elements of DELEGATE, and the one leaders skip most under pressure: Expect the Process. Say it at the handoff: “This will be bumpy at first. The first version won’t be right, and that’s not a problem – it’s the plan. Here’s where I’ll be when you hit the wall.” Name the curve, and a stumble becomes a checkpoint. Skip it, and the same stumble becomes a verdict.

What pulling it back teaches

The cost of grabbing the work back isn’t just the hours you spend redoing it. It’s the lesson you teach. Pull a stretch project back at the first wobble and the person learns, fast, not to stretch – because stretching got the work taken away and their competence quietly questioned. So next time they play it safe, hand you the hard parts, and stop reaching. You’ve trained the exact passivity you were frustrated by, and the work boomerangs permanently back to your desk.

Caption: Name the learning curve, or the first stumble reads as failure.

Sara Blakely expected the curve

Sara Blakely built Spanx into a billion-dollar company with no business training and no background in fashion. She didn’t know how to write a patent, so she read a textbook and drafted one herself. She didn’t know how to manufacture hosiery, so she cold-called mills until one said yes. By any conventional measure, she was unqualified at the start of nearly everything she did – and she treated each stumble as tuition, not as a sign to stop.

That’s the posture to extend to the people you’re developing: not the expectation that they arrive expert, but the expectation that they’ll learn in public, wobble early, and get good through the reps. Your job isn’t to protect them from the curve. It’s to name it, stay close while they climb it, and resist the urge to rescue them off it. The stumble you let them work through this quarter is the reason you can hand them something bigger next quarter – and the reason it won’t come back to you.

Worth sitting with this week:

  • Where did you pull a stretch project back at the first stumble – and what did that teach the person?

  • On your next handoff, what would it sound like to name the learning curve out loud, up front?

  • Whose growth are you cutting short by mistaking the curve for a verdict?

title: A Birthday Worth Giving Away
subtitle: Some thoughts on the Fourth and the 250th
html:
Today is my birthday. I’ve never made much of it.

There’s a quiet gift in sharing your birthday with the country’s: there’s always something bigger than you, and the day was never yours to own. You learn to hand it over – to not take over the picnic, to be one part of something larger. It’s one of the more useful lessons of my life.

The frame I’m holding is the best birthday gift I’ve ever received. My father gave it to me on my 21st – a framed Declaration of Independence. He’s a disabled veteran, and it’s hung in every bedroom and every office I’ve ever had. It is a flawed document, written by flawed men – but it is also a promise to become something better than the people who made it. That’s the only kind of leadership worth studying: the kind that builds something designed to outgrow you.

Because that’s what the Fourth actually marks. Not a war won – the war hadn’t been fought yet. Not a king beaten – he wouldn’t concede for years. A promise announced before it was true. A handful of men signed their names to a sentence they could not yet honor – all men are created equal – and a country spent two and a half centuries fighting over whether it meant what it said. That’s the audacity of the day. We didn’t celebrate what we’d built. We celebrated what we’d sworn to become.

Chuck Todd caught the failure this week: the 250th should have been a moment to take the country seriously – a republic born in contradiction, visionary and hypocritical, dragged again and again toward the thing it said it wanted to be – and instead we shrank it into a cartoon of 1776, afraid of its own hard chapters. But the failure runs deeper than a bad party. Every time we make the day about a person – a founder on a pedestal, a president at a podium – we get the idea exactly backwards. The whole point is that it belongs to no one. The real job isn’t to claim the day. It’s to make room for everyone else’s patriotism, to rise above yourself long enough to let the country have it.

Because America is an idea. Reagan said it best in what he called his last speech as president, reading a letter from a stranger: you can live in France, Germany, or Japan and never become French, German, or Japanese – but anyone, from any corner of the earth, can come to America and become an American. Not a bloodline. Not a birthplace. An idea – and an idea is the one thing you can hand to a stranger without losing your own share of it.

Walter Isaacson calls the Declaration’s second sentence the greatest ever written – all men are created equal – and he’s right about why: the words arrived before the reality, and America has spent 250 years being dragged toward them. Frederick Douglass understood this better than the men who signed it. On July 5th, 1852 – the day after, chosen on purpose – he stood before a country that still held millions in bondage and called its founding a glorious liberty document. Not because it was true yet. Because the promise was real even where the country wasn’t. That’s the whole American wager: a more perfect union. Not perfect. More perfect. The gap between the sentence and the fact isn’t the country’s failure. It’s the country’s assignment.

I’ve stood on both sides of that idea. I spent my childhood on military bases scattered across the world, which is a particular way to learn that freedom isn’t free. You learn it young, from the people around you who are paying for it. My father gave his life’s work to that cause. Other kids’ fathers gave the last full measure. Years later I went back out on my own. Traveled, studied, lived abroad – over seventy countries by now. Going to school abroad, I was often the first American my classmates had ever really known – not a tourist or a character on a screen, but a kid willing to sit in our contradictions rather than explain them away. Same lesson from the other side of adulthood: to a lot of the world, America isn’t a policy or a flag. It’s whichever American happens to be standing in front of you. Later still, I understood it while working at USAID – that for much of the world, the only America they’ll ever meet is a person arriving at their most vulnerable moment: food after a flood, clean water after a war, a vaccine, a shelter. When you are someone’s first American, you are the whole country to them. And it runs the other way too. Someone’s first American isn’t always met across an ocean. Sometimes they’ve just arrived, and the whole country is whoever happens to greet them. Sometimes that’s you, on your own street, without ever leaving it. “From the American People” was stitched over my heart. One year ago this week, the agency that stitched it there closed for good.

But you cannot close an idea. It is bigger than the agency that carried it, bigger than the president who moved against it, bigger than a trillionaire welding a chainsaw on stage at a rally, bigger than the founders who wrote it down and didn’t live to see it kept. My father understood the terms. A page like that isn’t a possession. It’s a debt. He didn’t hand me the Declaration so I could hang it and feel something on the Fourth. He handed it to me because it was my turn to owe what he’d owed – to be, for someone, the first American they ever meet. To leave the union more perfect than I found it, or at least to spend myself trying.

That’s the part no one tells you about inheriting an idea: you don’t get to keep it. You hold it for a while, you pay what you can against it, and you pass it on still unfinished – because unfinished is the only form it comes in.

But the debt is paid in small coin. That’s the mercy of it. Not in grand gestures or foreign postings or anyone’s idea of sacrifice – in the ordinary decency you offer someone who just arrived and doesn’t yet know how things work here. The neighbor whose name you take the time to learn. The family at the edge of the potluck no one has walked over to yet. The stranger you give the benefit of the doubt, because someone once gave it to all of us. You pay it by being, on an ordinary Tuesday, the American who acts as if the promise is already true.

So this one isn’t really mine to close either. You’re holding your own version of it today, whatever it is – the flag on the porch, the argument at the cookout, the quiet vote you cast that no one thanked you for. That’s the debt. You don’t have to cross an ocean to pay it. Somewhere near you, someone is still waiting to meet their first American. Let it be you.

title: The Decision That Belonged to the Expert
html:
I picked this one thinking I had a case study in CLUTCH most people wouldn't know. Then I learned there's a film coming about the D-Day weatherman. Less dramatic than Saving Private Ryan, but make no mistake – far more Allied troops would have died if Eisenhower hadn't listened to his Core Expert. Kudos to the studio for finding the rare war story where the hero is quiet, technical, and right.

June 1944. The largest invasion in history is staged and waiting – a hundred and fifty thousand troops, thousands of ships, a weather window measured in hours. And the most consequential judgment in the entire operation, whether the skies would hold, rests with one man in the room. He was not the Supreme Commander. He was a Scottish meteorologist named James Stagg.

The most important call on D-Day

Eisenhower carried the authority and, ultimately, the accountability. But he could not read a North Atlantic weather system, and he was wise enough to know it. When Stagg identified a narrow break in a vicious storm – a thin window opening on June 6 – Eisenhower’s job was not to second-guess the science. It was to decide what to do with the expert’s read. He took it. The invasion went. Stagg was right.

The lesson isn’t simply that Eisenhower deferred. It’s that he knew exactly which part of the decision was his and which part wasn’t. The forecast belonged to the meteorologist. The go/no-go belonged to the commander. Confusing the two – overruling the expert on his own turf, or dodging the command call because it was heavy – would have been the failure.

Core Expert mode

This is Core Expert, one of the six modes on the 6C Compass: the call goes to the person closest to the problem, because proximity beats rank when the question is technical. The leader’s job in this mode isn’t to make the decision. It’s to name that someone else owns it, give them the authority to own it, and back the call they make.

It sounds obvious. It’s the mode leaders skip most.

Caption: Decide by rank vs decide by proximity – on D-Day, the call belonged to the meteorologist.

Why leaders hold calls that aren’t theirs

Because seniority feels like it should come with answers. You got the corner office by being good at decisions, so handing one off can feel like dodging the job. But rank is not expertise, and the higher you rise, the wider the gap between the two. The person three levels down often knows the actual terrain – the customer, the codebase, the classroom – far better than you do, and your “input” on their turf is frequently just confident noise that overrides someone who’s right.

The cost of holding those calls is double. You make worse decisions, because you’re deciding above your knowledge. And you tell your expert, in the clearest possible language, that their expertise stops at your door – which is exactly how you lose the people who actually know things. The leader who can say “this one’s yours, you know it better than I do” doesn’t look weaker. They look like Eisenhower.

Worth sitting with this week:

  • Which decision on your plate actually belongs to someone who knows the terrain better than you?

  • Where has your “input” on an expert’s turf really just been an override?

  • Who on your team would step up if you named, out loud, that the call was theirs?

Subscribe now

title: When Seconds Matter: The Case for Command
html:
Picture the worst ninety seconds of your year. The outage is live, the customer is on the line, the room turns to you – and you say, “What does everyone think?”

It’s a reasonable instinct. It’s also, in that moment, the wrong one. A crisis is the one situation where gathering opinions doesn’t feel like leadership; it feels like the absence of it. The room didn’t turn to you for a discussion. It turned to you for a direction.

What a crisis actually asks for

Under acute stress, something physical happens to a team. Attention narrows. Working memory shrinks. People stop generating options and start scanning for instructions they can execute right now. In that state, a wide-open “what should we do?” doesn’t unlock the room’s intelligence – it floods it. What steadies people isn’t more input. It’s certainty: a clear call, clearly owned, so everyone can stop deliberating and start moving. In a crisis, teams don’t need consensus. They need certainty.

The case for Command

This is Command, the first mode on the 6C Compass: you make the call, fast, and you direct the response. It has a bad reputation in modern leadership, and most of the time it earns it. But there’s a reason it exists. When seconds matter, and hesitation costs more than a wrong guess, Command isn’t heavy-handed – it’s the most humane thing you can do, because it ends the paralysis and gives people something to do with their fear.

Apollo 13 is the cleanest example I know. When the spacecraft was crippled, Mission Control didn’t hold a vote. Gene Kranz took the room: here’s the situation, here’s who’s working what, here’s the sequence. He didn’t have the answer – nobody did – but he owned the call about how the room would find it. Command isn’t pretending to be certain. It’s taking responsibility for the next move, so the people around you aren’t frozen waiting for permission.

Image: When Seconds Matter - The Case for Command - graph 1.png Caption: Consensus vs Command – when seconds matter, the room needs certainty, not a vote.

When Command becomes a trap

Here’s the catch, and it’s the reason Command earns its bad name. The same mode that saves a crisis wrecks an ordinary Tuesday. Run Command when there’s no fire and you teach a capable team to stop thinking, wait for orders, and bring you every call – which manufactures the exact dependence the rest of this book is trying to dissolve. Command is a fire extinguisher: indispensable in a fire, absurd as a daily tool.

So the skill isn’t being decisive, and it isn’t being collaborative. It’s reading which situation you’re actually in – and naming the mode out loud, so the team knows whether this is a moment to execute your call or to make their own.

Worth sitting with this week:

  • When a real crisis hit recently, did you reach for certainty or for consensus – and which did the moment need?

  • Where are you running Command on decisions that aren’t fires, and training your team to wait?

  • Could your team tell the difference between “this one’s mine to direct” and “this one’s yours”?

title: A Captain Doesn’t Swim the Fastest
html:
My friend Jennifer wrote about what swimming taught her about culture. It sent me back to a line I buried in my own acknowledgments – and to the average swimmer I used to be.

My friend Jennifer Smith wrote an essay last week about what swimming taught her about building culture. She swam for fifteen years and competed in college, and one passage stopped me. Click here to read her work.

You cannot win a swim meet on a single great swimmer, she points out. Put Michael Phelps on your roster, and you still lose if the rest of the team doesn’t show up. Winning a meet takes a collection of winners – sometimes a swimmer touching the wall in fourth place is the margin. Which is why, at the best meets, the loudest cheer in the building is often for the slowest swimmer in the pool.

That sent me looking for a line I’d buried in the acknowledgments at the end of CLUTCH.

Here it is:

Before any of the other roles, I was a college team captain. I learned that a captain is not the best player on the team. A captain is the player whose presence makes the rest of the team better. Everything since has been a variation on that lesson – and on an adage a mentor of mine repeated until it stuck: hire people smarter than you, enable them, then get out of the way.

It’s a cryptic thing to leave sitting in the front of a book about building leadership systems, and I never explained it. Jennifer’s essay is a good excuse to.

I was, by any fair measure, an average swimmer. I walked on to the team and eventually earned a scholarship. In my whole college career, I won only a handful of individual events. However, what I could be counted on for was a steady second or third – I scored points, just never the kind anyone remembers. What I loved were the relays. And whatever I brought to that team beyond a dependable third place, it wasn’t speed. It was the fledgling leadership of a teenager still working out what the word meant.

The conviction underneath that line didn’t come from my own captaincy. It came from a book that never appears in mine: Sam Walker’s The Captain Class. Walker spent a decade studying the most dominant teams in sports history, expecting the pattern to live in the stars, the coaches, or the budgets. He found it in the captains – and almost none of them were the best player on the roster. The captain of the dominant U.S. women’s soccer team wasn’t Mia Hamm or Brandi Chastain. It was Carla Overbeck, a defender one coach called average at best, who carried her teammates’ bags to their hotel rooms and passed the ball to better players the instant she got it. That humility gave her the standing to get in anyone’s face when the team needed it. Walker’s research shaped how I think about leadership more than almost anything else I read while writing, and it earned exactly zero footnotes in the final manuscript. So consider this the footnote.

Somebody builds that structure – the one where a fourth-place finish counts and the slowest swimmer is worth screaming for. On Walker’s teams, it was the captain. In Jennifer’s pools it was the culture the swimmers reinforced every grinding afternoon.

That somebody is rarely the star. And that is the part most leaders get backwards. We assume the person out front should be the most talented one in the room – the best engineer running engineering, the best closer running sales. But the captain’s job was never to swim the fastest. It was to make the team faster than the sum of its swimmers. Those are different jobs, and they call on completely different skills.

This is the whole argument of CLUTCH. Leadership is infrastructure, not performance. The work is building the conditions under which other people do their best work – and then, the hardest part, stepping back so the structure holds without you standing in the middle of it.

Get out of the way is the line leaders can’t execute. It feels like the team will sink the moment you stop holding it up. Walker’s dynasties say the opposite. The captains who built something lasting made themselves essential to the structure and invisible in the spotlight. They built teams that kept winning whether or not anyone was watching them lead.

So the line was never about being a captain. It was about building the kind of team that no longer needs one out front – the kind where the loudest cheer in the building goes to the slowest swimmer, and no one can quite tell you who taught them to cheer like that.

title: They Didn’t Send the Machines to Business School
html:
The essay series was supposed to be AI against the humanities. But the AI labs quietly put them on the same side of the table. The credential that loses is the one in the middle.

Here is a fact that should reorganize how you think about what a mind is worth.

The companies building the most advanced artificial intelligence on earth have been quietly paying philosophers to teach their models how to reason. Not to write the marketing copy. To think. Daniel Greco, a professor of philosophy at Yale, described the work in the Chronicle of Higher Education this month: he sits with a frontier model, hands it questions hard enough to find the edge of its reasoning, and grades what comes back, so the next version can be trained on the difference. He is one of many. Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and OpenAI have all brought philosophers inside, some on staff, some on the side. OpenAI’s Sam Altman has said the company consulted hundreds of moral philosophers while deciding how its model should behave.

One AI adviser told Wired it may be the best time to be a philosopher since Aristotle tutored Alexander. He was half joking. He was not wrong about the demand.

The tell is in who they didn’t call.

These are the most sophisticated buyers of cognition who have ever existed. Near-unlimited capital, one defining problem: build something that can think. When they reached the edge of what the machine could do on its own, they did not phone the business school. They went to the philosophy department.

That should tell you which capacity is actually scarce.

Watch what the machine was already good at before the philosophers arrived. It could summarize anything. It could optimize inside a defined problem, run the analysis, produce fluent output at volume, and pick the efficient path among the options on the table. That is not a small thing. It is also, almost exactly, the skills the MBA spends two years and six figures learning. Optimize the given frame. Choose well among the options. Execute.

The machine does that now. Faster, cheaper, no signing bonus.

What the machine could not do, the thing the AI labs are paying Greco and people like him to build into it, is reason its way to an answer that was never in the material. His questions are built to find the limit, hard enough that the model cannot retrieve a stored answer and has to generate one. That is the whole line. The difference between looking something up and thinking. Between the answer in the back of the book and the question no one has asked yet.

I have spent this series arguing that this line is the entire game.

That the capacities good leadership runs on are not skills you install, but a formation you build into how a person sees. I made the case through Plato on who gets promoted, Sophocles on the truth a court cannot hear, Homer on the day a title and the judgment under it stopped being the same thing. Then, through two philosophers fighting in public over how to save the humanities, Jennifer Frey and N. Ángel Pinillos, in the same Chronicle that just ran Greco.

The whole way through, I wrote it as a rivalry. The humanities against the machine. The generator against the optimizer. Human judgment as the thing AI was coming for, and the thing we had to defend.

I had the contest wrong. Watch what AI the labs actually did and the sides redraw. They did not set the machine against the humanities. They sat them down together. Greco does not compete with the model. He sits beside it and teaches it to think. The most advanced technology we have ever built hit its ceiling, and the breakthrough came from fusing it with the oldest training in judgment we have. The machine and the philosopher are on the same side of the table.

The rivalry was never AI against the humanities. OK, maybe it was a little. But, in another frame, it was the two of them against the thing in the middle. And the thing in the middle is the move the MBA sells.

I was building an argument. The AI labs were running the experiment. It came back with more than my answer. It came back with the alliance; most of us have been too busy defending one side to see.

The Wall Street Journal reported this month that demand for the MBA is drifting down along with the pay. A survey of more than 600 corporate recruiters by the Graduate Management Admission Council puts the projected median starting salary at $120,000, down from $125,000 a year ago, with fewer openings and a harder landing even for graduates of the top programs.

A slipping salary is not the story. The reason behind it is.

Part of it is cyclical and real: the post-pandemic hiring frenzy cooled, consulting pulled back, and the targets came down off record highs. McKinsey cut its intake from Chicago’s Booth School from 71 in one year to 33 the next; Amazon, Google, and Microsoft trimmed too. But the structural reason is the one that should hold your attention. MBA graduates funnel into a narrow band of destinations: finance, consulting, technology, and professional services. Gad Levanon, chief economist at the Burning Glass Institute, named the trap precisely: those are the sectors shedding jobs fastest right now, and the entry roles inside them go first. As he put it, “the bottom rungs young grads depend on are being pulled away.”

Sit with what is pulling them. The junior MBA job was, in plain terms, a ticket to entry-level optimization. Build the model, run the analysis, format the deck, and work on the defined problem under a partner. Repeat every year with new associates. That is the work the machine now does at volume. Andrew Yang saw a world where AI came for truck drivers; he may be proven correct, too. But AI is currently eating the lunch of many white-collar professions. The rung is not just contracting in a soft economy. It is being automated out from underneath, in the same sectors, by the same force. The degree was a credential into the exact tier of cognition the machine just absorbed.

And the market is already pricing the alternative. A February 2026 report from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that philosophy majors now have lower unemployment than computer science majors. Read it twice. The degree your uncle called useless is outperforming the one everyone stampeded to get.

The MBA sold a single promise: come here, and we will make you the person who optimizes well and judges well, the complete operating mind that a company pays a premium for. It only ever delivered the first half. It taught the optimization and assumed the judgment, which is the same assumption the machine makes when no one has built the judgment in. Now the machine does the optimization for free. The judgment the MBA never taught is being built by hand on both sides at once, into the AI model and into the student, the humanities form. That is the alliance, seen from the side that loses to it. AI took the floor the MBA stood on. The humanities hold the ceiling it could never reach.

I am not arguing that MBAs lack intelligence, or that the degree teaches nothing. Some of the sharpest operators I work with came up through it. I am arguing that it monetized half of cognition the machine just turned into a commodity, and never had the half that was the humanities’ to give.

The fair objection is that some of this is theater.

Edward Harcourt, a philosopher at Oxford who directs its Institute for Ethics in AI, has warned about ethics-washing: hire a few philosophers, and the public reads your product as wise and safe, whether or not anything changed. There is a real version of that worry. A philosopher on the payroll can be a credential a company wears rather than a conscience it consults.

Grant all of it. The point survives. You do not perform respectability with a degree nobody respects. If hiring philosophers signals seriousness to the market, that is the market telling you what it now takes seriously. And the work Greco describes is not a press release. It is hours of paid expert labor, writing questions and grading reasoning, because the model got measurably better when a trained mind sat across from it. Marketing does not move a benchmark. Judgment does.

Make it concrete. A self-driving car is bearing down on a choice no driver ever wants to make: protect the passenger, the old woman in the crosswalk, or the kid chasing a ball into the street. It cannot save all three, and someone has to decide whose life the software values before the car is ever built. Would you pay extra for the model that picks you? Plenty of people would. That is not a marketing question, and it is not one the optimizer can answer. There is no efficient path through it, no answer in the material to retrieve. It has to be reasoned by someone trained to reason about exactly that. Classical streetcar dilemma for the 21st century.

The AI labs did, at the level of the machine, exactly what most organizations refuse to do at the level of their people. They found the scarce input, named it plainly, and paired the tool with it. No workshop. No tool bought on hope. They put the optimizer and the judgment on the same team.

Your company has the same problem one layer down, and most leaders miss why. AI does not supply judgment. It multiplies whatever judgment is already in the building, upward if it is there, into confident error at volume if it is not.

That is the whole reason I named the book CLUTCH. An engine with no clutch can only do one thing: send all its power straight to the wheels, all the time, whether or not the road can take it. A car becomes drivable the moment you add the part that decides how much force reaches the ground, and when. Judgment is that part. In the book, that clutch is emotional intelligence, the capacity to read the moment and meter the power to it. The machine has no clutch. It assumes the judgment and scales whatever it finds, full power, every time.

Whether the labs actually built that clutch into the model is a separate question, and I am not convinced they have. The reasoning got sharper and the benchmark moved. But ethics, and judgment in the situation no one has seen before, the things I have spent this series arguing the humanities form, may not be the kind of thing you can install in a system trained only on what already exists. The labs are paying a fortune to find out, which tells you how rare the thing is.

Either way, your move is the same, and it runs through people, not licenses. Formation does not transfer by the seat. What you can do is build the infrastructure that forms it and finds it: systems that reward the person who questions the frame instead of screening them out, that move real weight onto someone in stages and watch what holds. Then put your tools in those hands.

That is the work. Not better tools. A clutch for the judgment you already have, and the judgment you still need to grow.

Step back far enough, and the whole arc collapses into one strange sentence.

We built schools on the logic of the factory and trained generations to reproduce the right answer. We built business schools on top of that and trained the survivors to optimize the given frame. Then we built machines that ran that optimization better than any of us, and to give them the judgment the business school skips, we sat them down with philosophers.

The machine is going to grad school for the formation we spent a century training out of the humans.

The labs already made the correction. They paired the most powerful tool ever built with the oldest discipline of judgment we have, and let the credential in the middle fall away.

Yours is sitting in your building right now, in the people your system was built to overlook. The labs found theirs and put it to work beside the machine.

Go find yours.

Subscribe now

Three questions to sit with this week:

  1. Where in your company are you still paying a premium for the optimization the machine now does for free?

  2. If you had to find the one person who can reason to an answer that isn’t in the playbook, would your hiring and promotion systems surface them, or screen them out?

  3. What changes if you treat judgment as something you grow under load, the way the labs treat it as something worth pairing with every tool they build?

CLUTCH is the operating system I built for this: the infrastructure that forms judgment the way judgment is really formed, under weight, over time, with the handoff made on purpose. The labs just spent a fortune proving where it comes from. Plato has been making the same point, unpaid, for 2,400 years.

title: Drowning in Decisions That Were Never Yours
html:
Three months into her job as VP of Product, Elena hit a wall she never saw coming. The team was strong. The strategy was sound. And every morning her inbox told a different story: a dozen threads waiting on her sign-off, six messages asking “is this mine to decide?”, a calendar packed with meetings that existed only because nobody knew who owned the call.

She wasn’t failing at strategy. She was drowning in decisions that were never hers.

Decision fog, and where it comes from

Michael Porter argued that the essence of strategy is choosing what not to do. Decision fog is what happens when no one ever made that choice about authority itself. The same call gets made three times by three people. Talented contributors stop taking initiative because the rules are invisible. Everything ambiguous routes back to the leader, not for lack of capability, but for lack of clarity.

The 6C Compass clears it. Six modes for any decision, each for different terrain. Command when seconds matter and hesitation costs more than a wrong guess. Consultative when you’ll decide, but you want the field of view first. Collaborative when the call is truly shared. Consensus when full buy-in is worth the time it takes. Core Expert when the person closest to the problem should own it. Choice when you hand the decision over completely, inside clear lines.

Caption: The 6C Compass – six decision modes, each for different terrain.

The common failure isn’t picking the wrong mode. It’s never naming one, and letting the room guess. Every decision is a message. It tells your team who matters, what’s expected, and whether they’re allowed to move or have to wait for you.

What the fog costs, and what clearing it buys

That waiting has a price, and it compounds. Every call that loops back to you is a day your roadmap doesn’t move. Multiply that across a quarter, and the fog isn’t an annoyance; it’s the reason you missed the window. When leaders get explicit about who decides and how, decision latency drops sharply, often close to half. Half. That’s features shipping in weeks instead of months, and a team that stops parking work on your desk because they finally know which calls are theirs to make.

There’s a human dividend, too. Ambiguity is exhausting in a way people rarely name. The relief on a team when ownership gets clear is visible in a single meeting – the moment someone realizes a decision they’d been dreading was theirs to make all along, and they were allowed to just make it.

And the relief, when it comes, is structural, not motivational. You don’t inspire a team out of decision fog. You clear it, by saying in advance which mode the next call is in. Try it once. Name the mode out loud before the discussion starts, and watch how fast the room stops performing for you and starts working the actual problem.

Some questions to hold this week:

  • Which decisions in your inbox right now actually belong to someone else?

  • Where have you asked for input and then let the head-count make the call for you?

  • Does your team know how the next big decision will be made, or are they reading your face for clues?

title: What Holds Under Load
html:
Formation doesn’t show up on a resume, survive an interview, or pass a test. That isn’t because it can’t be measured. It’s because you’re using the wrong instrument.

The last essay ended where this one has to begin. The judgment your organization needs is already inside it, sitting in people the system was built to overlook, and the instruments you’d use to find them can’t see them. So this is the essay about the instruments: why they’re broken, what a working one looks like, and a concession the philosopher N. Ángel Pinillos made along the way that he didn’t have to.

Here’s the concession. Pinillos splits the humanities into two cases and keeps only one. There’s the skills case, verifiable, material, backed by grading and standardized-test data, and the plain fact that philosophy majors outscore nearly everyone on the GRE verbal. And there’s the formative case, the intrinsic, soul-deep transformation the philosopher Jennifer Frey spent a whole New York Times interview defending. Pinillos believes in the second one. He says so directly: he has spent his life inside it. But he hands it back to faith. The intrinsic argument, he writes, tells you to take it on trust, and the data tells you that you don’t have to. So he builds his public case on the measurable half and lets the other half go, because he thinks it can’t be proven, and he’s tired of losing arguments that depend on it.

I understand why. But he gave away the most important thing in the room, and he gave it away because he accepted a premise he should have questioned. That formation is unverifiable.

It isn’t. It’s verifiable. Everyone in this argument, Frey, Pinillos, and the company running its promotion cycle next quarter, is trying to measure it with the wrong instrument.

The instrument they’re all reaching for is the test. A test – and grades – is a demonstration on command, great if you are measuring skills. You set a standard in advance, you ask the person to perform against it, and an evaluator who already holds the answer key scores the result. That’s what the GRE measures. That’s what a graded paper measures, mostly. And it works, for skill. Skill is precisely the thing that shows up on command, because skill is acquired and demonstrable, and a test is built to catch exactly that. Notice that all of Pinillos’s evidence is of this kind: test scores, graded essays, and LSAT placement. Of course it is. He’s writing from inside the academy, and the test is the instrument the academy owns. It’s the right tool for his room. It just doesn’t travel to yours.

Formation doesn’t show up on command. That’s not a flaw in it; it’s the definition of it. Formation, the slow remaking of how a person sees and responds, is the architecture that’s there when there’s no command: no standard set in advance, no answer key, no precedent, no time to rehearse the performance. It’s what the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius was circling when he wrote that you don’t rise to the occasion, you fall to the level of your preparation. I spent a whole essay on that line, on the interior architecture a leader builds in the ordinary moments. You can read it here. “What Are You Practicing?”

Formation is that architecture, and the thing available to you under pressure is whatever you built before it arrived. That isn’t a skill you perform. It’s a structure you stand on, and you only find out it’s there when the weight comes down. You can’t catch it with a test, for the same reason you can’t inspect a bridge by asking it to describe itself. You have to put weight on it.

Pinillos looked at the formation, saw that it didn’t survive a test, and concluded it can’t be measured. The right conclusion is that it can’t be tested. Those are different. A thing can be entirely real, entirely verifiable, and invisible to the one instrument you happened to bring.

There’s another instrument. I described it in the essay on creativity without flagging it as the answer to this. It’s the difference between a test and a Showcase. A test asks you to reproduce what’s already known. A Showcase asks you to make something that didn’t exist before you made it, in front of a real audience whose reactions you can’t script, where the frame has to be authored in the moment, and originality can’t be pre-scored because no one wrote the rubric in advance. The test verifies reproduction. The Showcase verifies generation. And generation, the capacity to build the frame before you optimize inside it, is formation made visible.

In the work I do, the Showcase has a less academic name. Solo Drive. It’s the last phase of a three-part progression, and the progression is the whole point. First, the Ride-Along, where the experienced person drives and the learner watches, and the work is to demystify the judgment, to say out loud the tacit calls a veteran makes without noticing they’re making them. Then the Learner’s Permit, where the learner drives and you coach from the passenger seat, close enough to catch a real mistake. Then Solo Drive: full license, real stakes, no one else in the car. That last phase isn’t a graduation ceremony. It’s the load test. You find out what someone is made of by watching what holds when you finally get out.

You already know what this looks like, because you’ve watched people reveal it and watched people fail to. It looks like how someone behaves when they’re wrong in public, whether they get curious or get defensive. It looks like what happens to the people around them over a year, whether those people grow or quietly shrink to fit. It looks like someone in the meeting questions the frame before everyone rushes to solve inside it. None of those are interview questions. You can’t ask them in thirty minutes. They’re observation questions, and they only answer themselves under load, over time, in conditions you have to deliberately build.

Which is exactly what most organizations refuse to build. This is the problem I named through Plato a few weeks back, and it’s worth naming plainly now. Plato’s philosopher-king problem is that the people most fit to lead are the least likely to be chosen, because the system rewards the appetite for the role over the capacity to hold it. Read about that here, “The Philosopher-King Problem.” It’s a description of your promotion process, and the reason it misfires is mechanical. Your promotion is a test: a thirty-minute interview, a calibration meeting, a performance review scored against a plan set in advance. Every one of those measures the demonstrable, the thing that shows up on command. So your system reliably verifies skill and reliably misses formation. It promotes the person who arrives with the answer, performs confidently, and signals ambition, because those are the legible signals, the ones that survive a calibration meeting.

Here’s the distinction that promotion blurs, and you’ve already watched it play out at full tragic scale. The Iliad, I argued a few weeks ago, is the oldest management failure on record, and the failure is this exact one. Agamemnon holds the title: the authority, the command, the standing. Achilles holds the capacity: he’s the one whose judgment changes the outcome. The army runs for ten years on the fiction that those are the same thing, that the person with the title is the person whose judgment matters most, and the whole poem is what happens when the fiction breaks. Read about that one here, “The Oldest Management Failure on Record.”

A promotion grants a Title, which is final accountability, handed over on command, in a meeting, on a Tuesday. It can’t grant the License, the operational ownership that only proves out in operation. You can give someone the title of VP and find out two quarters later that the license was never held, that the authority was real, but the judgment underneath it was never load-tested. Homer drew you the worst case. Patroclus puts on Achilles’ armor, the symbols of an authority the system never transferred to him, the Trojans see the armor and answer the title, and the gap between the title and the capacity is the exact place Hector kills him. That’s the underprepared promotion in its oldest form, the role without the transfer. The handoff that works moves real weight to a person in stages and watches what they do with it, long before the title is on the door. Not what they say in the room. What holds when the weight is theirs.

It gets sharper. The person most likely to question the frame before solving inside it is often the one the pipeline already flagged as difficult – the generative cognitive style, read one more time as a problem to manage rather than a capacity to find. Build the instrument to catch formation under load instead of performance on command, and you stop screening that person out. An instrument tuned to the mind your old one overlooked sees judgment better in everyone.

So the work is not another defense of the humanities, though this clearly is; sorry, not sorry. The humanities don’t need defending; they need an organization with a working instrument. And a working instrument is not a better test. It’s a different kind of thing: a leadership operating system that makes capacity visible the way it moves, through the decisions people make, the gears they shift, the way authority travels through the company over time. It designs the load-bearing moments on purpose, watches who holds and who doesn’t, and refuses to mistake the performance of confidence for the substance of judgment.

And here’s the part I’ve been holding back. I said formation can’t be installed. That’s true. The two-day offsite was never going to deliver it. But an organization, of all the institutions left standing, still has what formation requires: time, stakes, and load.

This is why the person you grew tends to outperform the person you bought. Not because internal candidates are smarter, or more loyal, or a safer bet. Because they have already been under your load, and held. An external hire arrives with a resume, which is a record of outcomes. The internal candidate arrives with a formation, which is a record of how they behave when the outcome is still in doubt. One of those is far harder to fake, and far more useful when the next hard thing lands.

So the investment that looks slow – growing your own bench, is the one compounding underneath everything else. Every stretch assignment, every owned failure, every decision made without you in the room is a deposit. You don’t see the return on the day you promote someone. You see it for the first time when they hold something you would have had to hold yourself.

You can’t send your people back to school for the formation they missed. Though I suspect you can nurture it by encouraging a learning culture. You can build the one environment still capable of forming it. That isn’t a training program. It’s infrastructure, and it’s the most valuable thing you can build in the decade the machine just handed us.

Three essays, one argument. The capacities the humanities build are not skills; they are formation, and the lever you hold is the infrastructure you build around and into your people. Formation is now the scarce input on every kind of knowledge work, because the institutions that should supply it were built to manufacture its opposite. The shortage feels unfixable only because you’ve been hunting for formation with an instrument built to find skill – measuring what shows up on command, missing what shows up under load.

Frey was right that education is formation. Pinillos was right that you can’t win the public on faith. They were both missing the same thing. Formation can be verified, and it can be built. Not on a resume. Not in an interview. Not on a test.

Under load. Over time.

That’s not soft. It’s the only place it was ever going to show.

Three questions to sit with this week:

  • Who in your organization holds the title without the license, and how would you know?

  • Where could you move real weight to someone in stages, and watch what holds?

  • What judgment are you screening out at the interview that would show itself under load?

Subscribe now

CLUTCH is the operating system I built for this, the infrastructure that forms judgment the way judgment is really formed: under weight, over time, with the handoff made on purpose. Marcus Aurelius wrote his way toward the same idea twenty centuries ago. You don’t rise to the occasion. You fall to the level of what you built before it.
