title: The Judgment Shortage
html:
AI made human judgment the most valuable thing a person brings to work. Three institutions spent twenty years making sure there’s almost none of it left.

N. Ángel Pinillos is an epistemologist. His subject is doubt itself: how it works, where it comes from, when we’re right to trust it, and when we aren’t. He ends his Chronicle of Higher Education case for the humanities (see yesterday’s essay) on a note of real optimism, reaching for David Hume to get there. We’re only entitled to project the past into the future, Hume said, if we have reason to believe the future will resemble the past. And the future, Pinillos argues, just stopped resembling it. Large language models aren’t a continuation of the trend that hollowed out the humanities for twenty years. They’re the wrench that jams the machinery and bends the line. The bottleneck on the whole revolution turns out to be human judgment, the careful kind, trained against hard texts and harder questions. This, he thinks, might be the century of the humanities, and of his own field, philosophy.

He’s right that the wrench landed. He’s right that demand for judgment just spiked, sharply, across nearly every kind of knowledge work, all at once. That part is real, and it’s new.

Here’s the question he closes the laptop without asking: If judgment is suddenly the most valuable thing a person can bring to work, how much of it is there?

I spent a whole essay on the answer, and it isn’t good news. We’ve spent the better part of a century running systems whose real function, not the stated one, the real one, is to manufacture the opposite of judgment.

School first. The factory model that public education was rebuilt around in the late 1800s was designed, deliberately and well, to produce what the industrial economy needed: punctual, compliant people who could reliably reproduce a standard. Rows, bells, batches, a correct answer in the back of the book, and a student whose whole job is to find it. Twelve years of that, and the lesson lands as reflex. Reproduce, don’t generate. Then the MBA, which takes that reproduction-trained mind and hands it a more refined version of the same instruction: optimize, choose well between the options on the table, pick the efficient path. All of it sits downstream of a prior act that the program never teaches, which is generating the options in the first place. Then the organization, which finishes the job by rewarding the person who arrives with the answer and quietly penalizing the one who questions the frame. Three institutions, one direction, twenty years per person spent practicing the suppression of the exact capacity the machines just made scarce.

An organization trained only to optimize is an organization stuck in one gear. I ended the “They Educated It Out” essay on the cleanest way to say it: the MBA teaches you what to do when the options are on the table, and the humanities teach you to question the table. Questioning the table is a different gear. In the work I do, it has a name, Visionary, the mode that authors the frame and asks whether you’re solving the right problem at all. The pipeline runs the other gear, Operator, the mode that ships the play, indispensable and only one of six, and it never teaches the shift. Most teams can’t find the clutch.

I gave you the designer Tom Wujec’s marshmallow in that essay. In his experiment, he hands teams some spaghetti and a marshmallow that has to sit on top. The kids usually win – except against the engineers. Kindergartners build taller towers than business school graduates, because the kindergartners prototype while the MBAs plan the perfect structure and build it once. Here’s the part that matters now. AI is the marshmallow. It’s the weight nobody’s plan accounted for, the thing that turns out heavier than the theory said, and it comes down on the structure at minute seventeen. The MBA team isn’t failing for lack of effort. It’s flooring the Operator gear inside a frame nobody thought to question.

If you think the supply problem can be fixed by deciding to fix it, by funding a program and declaring it rigorous, there’s a natural experiment running right now. A movement has spent the last few years and tens of millions of dollars trying to rebuild exactly this: classical, Great Books, formation-rich humanities education on public campuses. New centers, serious money, framed photographs of Oxford on the walls. The writer Ann Manov went to look at the flagship for Harper’s this summer, and what she found is the whole supply problem in one building. The programs built to restore rigor require less reading and writing than the ordinary departments they were created to shame: twenty-seven pages a week, where the regular course assigns a hundred and twenty, excerpts instead of books, a rap video for a final. Her conclusion is the line I’d put on the wall. To pull this off, “you would need a whole new ideal of the person.”

That’s the supply problem at its starkest. Pour money and conviction into it, brand it “Oxford,” and the customer-student economy reasserts itself anyway, because formation was never something you could conjure by relabeling the syllabus. It’s the educational version of sending three managers to a storytelling workshop and calling it narrative intelligence.

So put the three of them in a room. Pinillos says the demand for judgment just spiked; I agree. Manov shows that the supply can’t be summoned even by people pouring millions of conservative dollars into summoning it. I recall Allan Bloom’s work here, and also agree. And the conclusion that neither of them quite states is the one that matters to you. The gap doesn’t close on its own, and it doesn’t close by fiat. This is the scissors: demand climbing at the steepest rate of our working lives, supply driven down on purpose by institutions doing exactly what they were built to do, the two lines crossing at the same moment. That isn’t a shift in what the market wants. It’s a shortage. And a shortage is a far harder problem than a shift, because you can’t retrain people on the thing you spent twenty years training out of them.

Watch how most companies are meeting the moment, and you’ll see the shortage hiding in plain sight. The AI rollout becomes a procurement exercise. Buy the licenses, pick the vendor, set up the governance framework, the prompt library, and the center of excellence, build the perfect plan, and execute it once. Every dollar flows into the layer the machine already owns: the optimization, the speed, the fluent output at volume. Almost nothing flows into the only input that’s scarce, the judgment required to tell whether any of that output is worth shipping.

Here’s how it plays out, and you may have already watched it. The AI goes live. The dashboards light up, more drafts, more decks, more code, faster. And six months in, the work is quicker and quietly worse: more output, more confident errors, more polished documents that are wrong in ways nobody caught, because the people shipping them were trained for twenty years to reproduce a standard, not to read a confident paragraph and find the place it’s evading the question. The organization ran the MBA’s move at company-scale. It floored the optimization gear. And the marshmallow came in heavier than the deck accounted for.

Because that’s what AI is, underneath the demos. A multiplier. It takes whatever judgment is already in the gearbox and scales it, upward if the judgment is there, into slop at unprecedented volume if it isn’t. The machine doesn’t supply the judgment. It assumes it. The capacity to read a situation and shift modes under pressure, to feel when the frame is wrong and change it, has a name in the work I do, too. EQ, the clutch. It’s the thing that lets a leader move between gears without grinding them. AI has no clutch. It assumes that you and most organizations spent twenty years driving the thing it assumes toward zero.

There’s a second cost, quieter and more expensive. When the judgment that’s left lives in one person, the one everyone routes the hard calls to, the founder who still signs off on everything, or the senior lead the whole team quietly escalates to, AI doesn’t fix the bottleneck. It widens it. It scales everyone else’s drafts and leaves that one person reviewing more of them, faster. That person is the hero worker. I spend a lot of time writing about that phenomenon. And the whole company pays for the arrangement, a standing distributed readiness tax: the price of keeping the hard judgment in one set of hands while the work happens in everyone’s. AI raises that price. It doesn’t pay it down.

So the company that wins this transition will not be the one with the best tools. The tools are a commodity; everyone has the same ones by Thursday. It’ll be the one that still has people who can generate the frame, question the premise, and hear what the confident paragraph is evading, and that knew where those people were before it needed them. You can’t buy that capacity. It is formation, and repeat after me, formation can’t be acquired by the seat.

What you can do is two things. Stop running your own internal pipeline in the same suppress-the-generator direction the schools and the business programs already ran. And distribute the judgment you already have, deliberately, out of the hero worker and into the hands that do the work, because load-tested judgment in many hands is the one thing in this whole story that compounds.

That distribution is the harder of the two, and it’s where this goes next. The systems you’d use to find and spread judgment, your hiring screens, your promotion criteria, your performance reviews, were built by the same logic that produced the shortage. They measure the optimizer and miss the generator. They reward the person who arrives with the answer, which is the single move that tells you nothing about what someone does when there’s no answer and the weight is already on the structure.

The judgment is in the building. You just can’t see it yet, because every instrument you have was built to reward its opposite. That’s the last thing to fix.

Three questions to sit with this week:

  • Where in your organization does the judgment that matters sit in a single person?

  • What did your last technology rollout invest in, the tools, or the people who have to judge what the tools produce?

  • What becomes possible when readiness is distributed instead of hoarded in one set of hands?

CLUTCH is the operating system I built for distributing exactly this. EQ is its clutch, the capacity to shift gears that the machine will never have. We built our schools on the logic of the factory floor in 1890, and the machine just made that logic obsolete; the work now is to build people who can do what it can’t.

title: Why Leadership Training Doesn't Stick
html:
You’ve seen this movie. The offsite is great – an energizing speaker, a clean framework, sticky notes everywhere, and real insight in the room. People leave fired up. The binder goes on the shelf. And three weeks later, nothing has changed: the same manager is still avoiding the same hard conversation, still running the same meeting the same way.

It’s tempting to blame the content or the people. Usually, it’s neither. It’s the form.

Training is an event. Development is a practice.

A workshop is an event – a fixed block of time where information gets transferred. Development is a practice – reps, over time, with feedback, until a behavior becomes a default. We keep funding the first and calling it the second – a training line when the thing we want needs a capital plan: designed, maintained, never quite finished – then act surprised when capability doesn’t show up. Leadership isn’t something you can be told. It’s something you get better at by doing, badly at first, with someone close enough to coach the next attempt.

Why the event fades

There’s a reason the binder doesn’t stick, and it isn’t motivation. Memory decays fast without retrieval – Ebbinghaus mapped the forgetting curve more than a century ago, and a single exposure, however good, sits right on it. Worse, knowing a framework and being able to use one under pressure are different skills entirely. You can recite the steps of a hard conversation the afternoon of the workshop and still freeze in the real one on Thursday, because what you practiced was understanding, not doing.

<< insert image here >> Image: Why Leadership Training Doesn’t Stick - graph 1.png · Caption: Why training fades – what the evidence says about how skill actually forms.

What actually builds people

John Wooden, the most successful coach in the history of college basketball, almost never gave speeches about winning. He ran reps. Footwork, fundamentals, the same small things over and over, until they were automatic and his players could improvise on top of them under championship pressure. He built judgment the only way judgment gets built: in the doing, corrected in real time.

Marcus Aurelius named the law two thousand years before that gym existed: you don’t rise to the occasion, you fall to the level of your preparation. A workshop raises the ceiling of what someone understands. It never moves the floor they fall to – and the floor is the only part that shows up on Thursday.

That’s the shift for anyone serious about developing people. Frameworks don’t develop people. What you do inside them does. The framework – CREATE, VOICES, the 6C Compass, any of them – isn’t the lesson; it’s the field you practice on.

And the reps have an order. CLUTCH calls it the DELEGATE handoff, and it runs in three stages.

  • First, the Ride-Along: you make the call while they watch, and say the quiet part out loud – the judgment a veteran makes without noticing they’re making it.

  • Then the Learner’s Permit: they drive, and you coach from beside them, close enough to catch a real mistake.

  • Then Solo Drive: you get out of the car, the decision is theirs, the stakes are real, and you find out what they actually built. That’s where development lives – in the wobble, in the debrief that turns one decision into judgment they keep – not in the binder.

If you coach for a living, this is the line for the client who asks you for a workshop: I can give you the event, or I can build you the practice. One of them is over by Friday. The other one is still working a year from now.

That’s the case for the slow version. You can’t shortcut a skill into someone in an afternoon, and the afternoon doesn’t compound. The reps do – every coached decision is a deposit, and a year of them is a person who is measurably better, which is more than any binder has ever returned.

Worth sitting with this week:

  • What development are you funding as an event that only works as a practice?

  • Where could you turn a real decision this week into a coached rep instead of a quick answer?

  • A year from now, who on your team will be measurably better – and what reps will have gotten them there?

title: Skill Is the Wrong Word
html:
The best public defense of the humanities I’ve read gets one word wrong. That word decides everything that follows.

To read the piece that started my mind whirling on this post, click here.

For a week this spring, I argued that the capacities good leadership runs on aren’t skills. They are a formation: built into how a person sees, not installed by a workshop or certified by a competency model. I made that case through Plato, Sophocles, and Homer, basically the argument that the humanities are more important than ever.

Then two living philosophers picked up the same fight in public, in the Chronicle of Higher Education and the New York Times, and I want to carry it somewhere neither of them has ventured: Into the room where you run an organization.

Start in a studio at the New York Times this spring, where the columnist Ross Douthat sat across from Jennifer Frey, a philosopher at the University of Tulsa who built its honors college and then watched the university’s new administration cut its funding by more than ninety percent. Douthat played the skeptic, the parent who wants his kids employable and can’t see why they’d spend tuition on Plato. Is Shakespeare better than John Grisham? he asked. Frey said yes, and defended it well: Shakespeare’s language, the way great art calls you toward truth and beauty, the hierarchy of goods you can’t pretend away the moment you say “higher education.” Aristotle, she reminded him, thought the purpose of education was leisure, schole, the root of the word “school,” the space set aside to cultivate the highest parts of a person.

To read that piece, click here.

It’s a serious case made by a serious person. And it has one fatal property. It only works on people who already believe it.

That isn’t my objection. It’s the one N. Ángel Pinillos made a few weeks later, in the Chronicle of Higher Education, in the best public defense of the humanities I’ve read. A piece that opens by throwing Frey’s entire argument overboard. Pinillos chairs the philosophy department at Arizona State University, one of the largest in the country, and he has watched the enrollment charts go gray for twenty years. So he did the thing almost no defender of the humanities is willing to do. He gave up the argument his own side keeps reaching for. The intrinsic-value case, that Shakespeare is higher, that great art calls you to the transcendentals, that self-cultivation is its own reward – he calls impotent. Not wrong. Impotent. If you already recognize the value, the argument is unnecessary. If you don’t, you’re being told that your failure to see it is itself the proof of your deficiency. There’s no third path. The argument can’t reach across the divide it was built to cross.

Pinillos and I agree on nearly everything. Well, almost. The intrinsic case is a dead end. The humanities build something real and identifiable. AI makes that capacity more valuable, not less. Where we split is on a single word, on what to call the “thing” the humanities... build.

He calls it a skill.

I completely disagree. In fact, that week of essays made exactly that point.

“Skill” is the whole disagreement, and it isn’t semantics. It’s the difference between two completely different theories. If you’ve ever sat through a leadership offsite and wondered, six months later, why nothing changed, the answer lives in this one word.

Here’s why he reaches for it. Skill is legible. A skeptical parent understands a skill. A legislator can fund a skill. A donor can be shown the return on a skill. Pinillos picks the word on purpose because he’s trying to win an argument in daylight with people who don’t share his assumptions, and “skill” is the currency those people accept. I understand the move. It’s a good-faith translation of something precious into terms the market will price.

But the translation is the trap.

The moment you call what the humanities teach ... skills, you’ve told every organization on earth exactly how to mishandle them. A skill is something you acquire. It comes from a workshop, a certification, a two-day offsite, and a feedback form that asks whether the session met your expectations. Skills are installed. They have a vendor and a completion date. The capacities I ascribe to what the humanities teach: reading what isn’t said, holding a decision open when the information is incomplete, authoring coherence before it exists, can’t be installed in anyone. These get built over years, or they get done poorly by people who took a weekend course and posted the certification on LinkedIn.

You don’t inspect a skill. You demonstrate a skill. A skill lives inside a person and shows up on command – in the recital, the exam, the thirty-minute interview, where someone performs competence for an evaluator who already holds the answer key.

Infrastructure is different. By infrastructure, I mean what carries the weight when no one is consciously carrying it. You can’t see whether it was built well by watching it. You find out under load – when the situation has no precedent, the weight comes down, and the thing either holds or it doesn’t. There is no answer key.

The inspector in the basement isn’t checking a skill. He’s checking a structure – whether it was built right, whether it holds.

Listen to the inspector, and you’ll notice the words do double work. Built. Holds. They’re the same words we reach for when we describe a person who came through something hard and stayed intact. Two built things, described in the same language. But they’re built in different places, and only one of them stays.

What gets built into a person is formation – the humanities’ work. Judgment, character, what a classroom lays down inside someone over the years. It’s real, and it’s load-bearing, but it isn’t transferable. It walks out the door when the person does.

What gets built around people, by the organization, is infrastructure. Roles, decision rights, and the handoffs that hold whether or not any one person is having a strong day. It’s impersonal by design – that’s the point of it. It survives the person.

But survival isn’t the whole of it. The same infrastructure that outlasts a person is also the last thing left that can still form one – the organization doing the schools’ old job, under load this time. It survives the person, and it forms the person. Both. Hold that; it’s where these three essays end up.

Formation gets mislabeled as skill because both live inside the person. So when something fails, everyone looks inside the person – first for the missing skill, then the missing character. They almost never look at what was never built around the person.

Neither one is a skill. A skill shows on command; these only show under load. And the line between them isn’t just inside versus around – it’s what leaves when the person leaves.

This isn’t a semantic quarrel. It’s the reason your leadership development budget is shaped the way it is.

The word you use for a capacity decides which line it goes on. Skills get a training budget – a course, a vendor, a sign-in sheet, a number for how many people attended. Infrastructure gets a capital plan – designed, built, maintained, inspected, never quite finished. Those aren’t the same line, not the same money, and they don’t produce the same thing. Call narrative intelligence a skill, and you send three managers to a storytelling workshop and measure whether they enjoyed it.

Call it infrastructure, and you ask the two questions a workshop was never built to answer. First: what in our system makes coherent meaning possible, or impossible? Second: when that capacity degrades – and it always degrades – whose job is it to notice and rebuild?

The first is a design question. The second is a maintenance question, and it’s the one no one is assigned: which is why Sophocles can still show you, exactly, how it fails. In Oedipus, the prophet Tiresias brings the king the truth, is accused of conspiracy for it, and is sent away. After that one public punishment, the rest of the court runs the same quiet calculation and goes silent. The information existed. The structure couldn’t carry it. That’s a culture problem with a mechanical cause, and the fix is structural: a receiving culture, where the person who names the problem early isn’t the person who pays for it. Not a morale program. In CLUTCH, that’s Culture, Relationships, and Ethics doing load-bearing work – and it’s the first thing to go when you treat formation as a weekend-course.

One word produces an event. The other produces a structure. That’s the whole difference, and it’s the thing Pinillos got wrong while getting everything else right.

I want to say the next part carefully, because I admire the argument and the man making it.

Pinillos and I are writing for different rooms, and you can tell where his is by where the piece ran. The Chronicle of Higher Education is the trade paper of the academy. His case is built exactly right for that room: a real, identifiable competence, an invaluable skill with material consequences, proven by grades and test scores, and where philosophy majors land on the LSAT. To the parents and legislators and donors who decide whether the humanities survive the next budget, that’s the argument that wins, and I’m glad he’s making it.

Here’s the gentle irony. His critique of Frey was that her argument only persuades the already-persuaded. He’s right. But his own argument has the same shape, one room over. Outside higher ed, in the room you and I work in, full of founders and operators and the people who run things, “it raises your GRE verbal” is not the case that lands. You don’t need your next VP to test well. You need to know what that person does when the test is gone, when the information is incomplete, the stakes are real, and there’s no answer key. Under load. Pinillos diagnosed the boundary of Frey’s argument perfectly. He just couldn’t see the boundary of his own.

So I’ll take his argument and finish it, because it deserves finishing. He’s right that the humanities build something verifiable and material. He’s right that the intrinsic-value case can’t carry the weight, and right that AI made the whole question urgent in a way it wasn’t a decade ago. He’s one word short – and it’s the wrong word, in a way that costs you.

What the humanities build into a person is formation, and formation can’t be acquired in an afternoon, performed on command, or bought by the seat. That’s exactly why his own evidence kept betraying the word he chose. But formation isn’t where this ends. Most of the people in your organization never got twenty years of difficult texts, and you can’t send them back to school for it. What you can build is the infrastructure around them – a leadership operating system that makes coherence, dissent, and judgment structurally possible, and that, given enough time and real stakes, forms some of the judgment the schools never did. That part is still yours to design. The next two essays are about how.

If you missed that week, here’s the shape of it.

I opened with “The Humanities Were Never Soft”: Rolling Stone had named five of these capacities and called them skills too, narrative intelligence, moral imagination, tolerance for ambiguity, deep listening, systems thinking, and I argued each one was a formation instead.

“The Philosopher-King Problem,” on Plato’s Republic and the reason organizations keep promoting the people least fit to lead.

“What Greek Tragedy Knew,” on Sophocles and the three ways a good leader fails inside a system that can’t develop him, deliver truth to him, or let him receive it.

“The Oldest Management Failure on Record,” on Homer’s Iliad and the day a commander’s authority and a fighter’s judgment stopped being the same thing.

“What Are You Practicing?” on Marcus Aurelius’s Meditations and the one architecture no organization can build for you, the interior kind.

“They Educated It Out,” on the engine underneath all five, creativity, the capacity to generate the frame before you optimize inside it.

Three thousand years of material, all of it describing a Tuesday in your company. I’ve hyperlinked them for your perusal later if you’d like.

His case rested on grades – the most direct evidence imaginable, he said, generated millions of times a year. But a grade certifies. It doesn’t transfer, and it proves nothing about a situation no one saw coming. By that standard, his argument had only ever been graded: an A in the one room it was written for. So I transferred it – out of the Chronicle and into yours, where the answer key is gone, and the weight is real. It held. But only once I swapped the word it was resting on. That is the test a grade can’t run, and his argument passed it. The demonstration was never the test; the load was – the moment the playbook runs out and the thing either holds, or it doesn’t. A claim that works only in the room it was written for is a skill. A claim that holds when you carry it into a room it was never built for is infrastructure.

There’s a piece of this Pinillos gave away too easily, the part Frey was right about, and it’s where this goes next.

Three questions to sit with this week:

  • What capacity does your team keep calling a skill, and funding like one?

  • Where are you running a workshop to install something that only gets built over years?

  • What becomes possible if you put that capacity on a capital plan instead of a training line?

Subscribe now

CLUTCH is the operating system I built for this, the infrastructure that holds judgment when the situation has no precedent. Plato spent the Republic asking what it takes for something to function well. I’ve reread it for thirty years now, more times than is strictly healthy, and the one thing all that formation bought me is this: the ability to take a 2,400-year-old question and aim it at something Plato never imagined, your org chart. Which is rather the point. You can’t weekend-course your way to that. This is the buildable version of his question.

title: The Dashboard That Lies
html:
On paper, Jordan’s team looked flawless. Targets hit. Calendar full. Decks immaculate. Jordan herself was magnetic, composed, always on. Every signal you could measure read momentum.

Then a colleague said the quiet part out loud: “It’s like all the lights are green, but nobody’s actually driving.”

She wasn’t wrong. Turnover had started to climb. Meetings carried a low static of tension no one named. Jordan hadn’t checked out – she’d disconnected, holding the performance together while the thing underneath ran dry. The team felt it. They just didn’t feel safe saying it.

A dashboard can lie by telling the truth

Her dashboard wasn’t faking numbers. It was measuring the wrong ones. She was reading outputs – deliverables and deadlines and presence – and ignoring inputs, the reserves that made those outputs possible. Green light, empty tank.

Viktor Frankl, writing after the camps, located human freedom in a single gap: the space between what happens to us and how we respond. That gap is the most important mechanism a leader has, and the easiest to override. Emotional intelligence is the clutch that lives inside it. It’s what lets you shift gears without grinding, because it buys you the half-second between stimulus and reaction where the choice actually is. It’s also what lets you read the dashboard that matters – the one tracking whether your people’s capacity can sustain the pace – before something expensive breaks.

Outputs vs inputs – the dashboard most leaders watch, and the one that warns them in time.

And it does get expensive

Disengagement isn’t a mood. It’s a cost. Gallup has put the global productivity drag of it in the trillions, which is a number too big to feel. On your team it lands smaller and sharper: the A-player who stops offering ideas, the problem that stays buried until it’s a crisis, the resignation that blindsides you on a Tuesday. Every one of those was visible months earlier on the right dashboard. None of it was on the one Jordan was watching.

Here’s the uncomfortable part. The leaders most at risk of this are the high performers, because they’re the best at producing clean outputs while the inputs fail underneath. The dashboard rewards them right up until the engine seizes. Reading the real gauges isn’t softness. It’s the most practical thing a leader can do, because it’s the only version where you see the breakdown coming in time to prevent it.

For the skeptics: this isn’t feelings for their own sake. A resignation you didn’t see coming runs into six figures by the time you backfill and ramp, and the warning signs sat on the input gauges for months. EQ isn’t the soft corner of the dashboard. It’s the early-warning corner, and it’s the only one that buys you time to act before the cost is locked in.

Check the gauges you’ve been skipping:

  • When did your dashboard last show green while something underneath felt off?

  • What is someone on your team feeling right now that doesn’t feel safe to say to you?

  • Are you tracking your outputs or your reserves, and what would change if you started watching the second one?

title: Return to Office Is a Confession
html:
I’m writing this on the Acela. A few World Cup tourists drifting toward the café car, but mostly business travelers – laptops open, spreadsheets and decks, somewhere over Connecticut. Half this car is running a company from a tray table, calmly, between coffees. Nobody is being watched. Everyone is working.

Some of them, back home, require their own employees to be in an office five days a week.

Here’s a question I put to the owners among them: what would happen to your company if you went on vacation for two weeks and turned your phone off? Not silenced. Off. Most people go quiet when they picture it. A few admit the place would be on fire by day four.

Now flip it. What would happen to your company if your employees didn’t see an office for two weeks?

Most owners can’t come up with much. They reach for culture, or collaboration, or the new hire who needs supervision. But press for the concrete disaster – the thing that actually breaks – and it rarely arrives.

Sit with which of those two answers should worry you more?

We spend enormous energy on the second question, whether people can be trusted out of sight, and almost none on the first. Which is strange, because the first is where the real fragility lives. The danger in most companies isn’t the unwatched employee. It’s the one person who can’t be unwatched without the whole thing wobbling – and that person usually has a corner office and signs the mandate.

Adam Grant and his Wharton colleagues published an op-ed this Monday (6/22) in the New York Times (click here), which argued that the trait most reliably predicting opposition to remote work isn’t a concern for productivity. Once you control for trust and sociability, it’s narcissism. The appetite for an audience, imagine that?! Grant has a whole argument and the data to carry it: six years of surveys across thousands of managers and the Fortune 500 chief executives. His research used proxies for narcissism – the size of the pay package, the signature, the photo in the annual report. The bigger those ran, the more hostile the leader was to hybrid work. They even pinned the causation: prompt an executive to admire the role a bold ego played for Steve Jobs or Larry Ellison, and their taste for return-to-office mandates climbed. All probably true. But the sharper tell isn’t on the couch, it’s structural: the people who write these mandates are, more often than not, exactly the ones who’ve quietly exempted themselves from them.

None of which means presence never matters. Some work plainly needs the room, and a few jobs are nothing but the room. I taught for twenty years, and teaching over a screen was miserable – not inconvenient, miserable – because teaching runs on the attention moving between people in a space: the small corrections you make off a face that’s drifting, the question you only think to ask because you saw someone hesitate. None of that survives a grid of muted squares. The apprentice who learns the job by overhearing it, absorbing what nobody thought to write down, loses the same way. Pretending that work transfers cleanly through a screen costs you something real.

But notice what it has in common: it’s episodic and intense, not nine-to-five. Mentoring, the hard conversation you need a face for, the messy week when a team actually forms – these are moments, and they reward being deliberate about presence, gathering on purpose. A blanket five-day mandate does the reverse. It makes presence routine and ambient, and therefore cheap, and a thing that’s always happening stops being a thing anyone shows up for. The owner’s mistake isn’t believing presence can matter. It’s losing the ability to tell when it does – and reaching, instead, for the version that mostly soothes him.

In CLUTCH, I keep coming back to the difference between a title and a license. A title is the role and the accountability that rides with it. A license is the authority to act without asking. Both two-week questions are the same diagnostic pointed in opposite directions – they measure whether the license was ever granted. Give it, and the business runs while you’re on a beach and your people are at their kitchen tables. Withhold it, and the company is just you, wearing an org chart, and the mandate is how you keep everyone close enough to disguise that.

Which leaves the owner somewhere awkward. The thing he won’t tolerate in his employees – being trusted out of sight – is the exact thing he can’t do himself. He’s the one who can’t take the phone off. The only difference is that no one writes a policy for him. He’s the unwatched node, and he’s the one that would actually break.

So before the next mandate, run the test on yourself first. Two weeks, phone off. If the answer frightens you, the problem was never that your people might vanish from a building. It’s that you built a company that can’t survive anyone vanishing – and the first person it can’t survive is you.

A few questions worth sitting with:

  • What would keep working if you were unreachable for two weeks?

  • Who on your team is ready for more license than they currently hold?

  • What does presence give you that a system hasn’t yet?

title: The Hero Who Trained the Team to Wait
html:
The alarm goes off – a key deal about to collapse, a launch sliding, a customer threatening to walk – and you handle it. You step in, make the calls, pull the late night, and by morning, the crisis is gone. The team exhales. You’re the hero, and in that moment, it feels exactly like leadership.

And it is, the first time. Maybe the third. The problem is what it quietly teaches everyone watching.

The rescue that trains the waiting

Here’s what your team learns, without anyone deciding to teach it: when something gets hard, the move is to wait for you. Why wrestle a problem to the ground when the founder will swoop in and solve it cleaner and faster? So they bring you the problem instead of a solution. They escalate sooner. They stop reaching for the hard call because the hard call was always going to land on your desk anyway. Every time you swoop in to save the day, you train your team to wait for the next rescue.

Time-teller or clock-builder

Jim Collins and Jerry Porras spent six years at Stanford studying companies that lasted, and drew a line I’ve never been able to unsee. On one side is the time-teller: the brilliant individual who always has the answer, the person you ask because they always know. On the other is the clock-builder: the leader who builds something that can tell time without them – a system, a team, a set of habits that produces good answers whether or not the founder is in the room.

The hero is a time-teller. And a time-teller, however brilliant, is a ceiling. The organization can only ever be as good as the one person every answer routes through – and only ever as available as that person’s calendar.

Caption: Time-teller vs clock-builder – the hero has every answer; the clock-builder builds answers that outlast them.

Why can’t the hero scale?

The cost is quiet and compounding. Initiative fades. Your best people – the ones with the most options – get tired of waiting for the wheel and leave for somewhere they’ll get to drive. And the day you try to step back, into a Chair seat or a new venture or a real vacation, the thing you built sags, because it was never built to stand without you holding it up. I’ve watched a first CEO transition fail for exactly this reason: the founder had been the answer for so long that no one beneath him had ever been allowed to become one.

None of this means the rescue is always wrong. Some fires you do have to fight yourself. The shift is to notice the reflex and ask, before you swoop in: Is this a fire only I can fight, or a chance for someone else to learn to fight it? The clock-builder spends the same energy the hero does – just upstream, on the people and the systems – so that the next time the alarm sounds, it isn’t only your name being called.

Worth sitting with this week:

  • Where did you save the day this week – and who might have grown if you’d let them handle it instead?

  • What does your team bring you that they could decide themselves, if they trusted you’d back them?

  • If you stepped back for a season, what would sag – and what does that tell you about what you’ve built?

title: Most Leaders Drive in One Gear
html:
I know my default.

I know my default. Put me under pressure and I reach for Sculptor. Most leaders aim that gear at the people around them, sharpening everyone else's work until nothing leaves the room unpolished. I aimed it at myself. I sharpened my own work long past the point anyone needed it sharp, and called the delay a standard. It's the gear that made the work good, which is exactly why it took me years to see it as the thing keeping the work from ever being done.

Every leader has one of these. The gear you grab when the heat rises, the one that feels like leadership because it’s the one that got you here.

Six gears, one habit

VOICES is the gearbox: Visionary, Operator, Independent, Coach, Encourager, Sculptor. Six modes of presence, one for each kind of moment. Visionary zooms out and reframes. Operator gets into the work. Independent steps back so others carry the weight. Coach builds judgment through questions instead of answers. Encourager fuels belief. Sculptor sharpens the work until it’s sharp.

Caption: VOICES – six gears, one for each kind of moment.

The skill was never picking a favorite. It’s reading the grade and shifting before you redline. Stay in first on the open highway, and you smother a team with control they’ve outgrown. Drop into fifth on a steep climb, and you’re casting vision at people who needed you in the room, deciding one hard thing.

The trap is that under stress, the whole gearbox collapses into your default. The founder who built on a vision keeps casting vision to a team that needs a decision. The operator keeps diving into tasks when the team needs to be grown rather than directed. The gear isn’t the problem. The reflex is.

What does the stuck gear cost you

A team that waits. Stay in Operator, and people learn to bring you the problem instead of the solution, because you’ll take it anyway. You feel busy and indispensable. They feel small and a little bored. Boredom in a capable person isn’t harmless; it’s a countdown. Two years of that, and your best engineer is taking a recruiter’s call, looking for a job where they actually get to drive.

There’s a number under this, too. Gallup’s research keeps landing on the same finding: clear roles and real development drive engagement by about 20 to 30 percent, and engaged teams simply produce more, churn less, and cost less to keep. The leader stuck in one gear is leaving that on the table every week, and calling it dedication.

The single most useful shift for most leaders is the downshift into Coach. The urge to grab the wheel and answer is usually the exact moment someone in front of you was ready to find the answer themselves. It’s slower this week. It’s the only thing that pays off the week you’re out.

And the cost lands first on the people you can least afford to lose. Your most capable person has the most options and the least patience for being managed in a gear they outgrew two promotions ago. The leader who can’t shift out of their default doesn’t lose their weakest performer to it. They lose their strongest.

Catch yourself this week, then sit with these:

  • What gear do you reach for in the first ten seconds of a hard moment?

  • Who in front of you needed Coach this week and got your default instead?

  • Where might your strongest gear be the very thing capping the people you lead?

title: Build Guardrails, Not Gates
html:
“I just want them to use their judgment,” she told me – a founder who’d spent the last quarter approving expense reports, reviewing every client email, and signing off on calls three levels below her. She built the company on heroics, doing whatever it took, and when that stopped scaling, she did the natural thing: she added control. Approvals. Sign-offs. Run-it-by-me-first. And somehow every decision still landed on her desk, now with more steps in front of it.

She’d traded one trap for another. Heroics had made her the engine. Control made her the bottleneck. Both kept the whole operation running through her.

The two traps look like opposites

Most leaders cycle between them. Heroics feels like leadership – you’re in the work, saving the day – right up until you’re exhausted and nothing moves without you. So you swing the other way, into control: gates, approvals, sign-offs. That feels responsible. But it produces the same result by a slower road. Every move waits for you, and the team quietly learns to stop deciding.

The fix isn’t somewhere in the middle, looser or tighter. It’s a different axis entirely.

Gates or guardrails

A gate blocks. Nothing passes until you open it. Every decision becomes a request routed up to you, and your team idles at the barrier, waiting for a yes.

A guardrail does the opposite. It defines the edge of the road – here’s the budget, here’s the line you don’t cross, here’s what “good” looks like – and then it clears out of the way. Inside the lane, people move at full speed without checking over their shoulder, because they know exactly where the limits are and trust that you won’t second-guess a call that stayed in bounds.

Caption: Gates vs guardrails – both create order; only one creates speed.

Why guardrails are faster

Think about how a highway actually works. The reason you can drive seventy isn’t the absence of limits – it’s the presence of good ones. Lanes, shoulders, barriers. The structure is what makes the speed both safe and possible. Strip the guardrails out, and nobody goes faster; they slow to a crawl, because now every inch is a judgment call with no margin for error. Guardrails don’t restrict speed. They make it possible.

Teams run the same way. Gates feel safer, but they tax every decision with a wait. Guardrails feel riskier, but they’re the thing that lets a capable team move without you in the room. The leader who builds gates stays at the checkpoint forever. The one who builds guardrails becomes something better – the person who set the lane lines once, so everyone else could drive.

And here’s the quiet relief in it: guardrails are less work than gates, not more. A gate demands your attention every single time someone reaches it. A guardrail you build once, and it holds. You’re not approving, and you’re not absent. You set the edges, you back the calls made inside them, and you get your week back.

Worth sitting with this week:

  • Where have you installed a gate – an approval, a sign-off – that’s really just routing decisions back to you?

  • What’s one decision your team could own completely if they knew the guardrails?

  • Are you spending your week opening gates, or could you set the lane lines once and let them drive?

title: Your Decision Chart Answers the Wrong Question
html:
You have been in this meeting.

EVERYONE has been in this meeting. Yet they still exist. Why?

The decision was assigned. Someone owned it on paper. The roles were clear enough that nobody could claim confusion. And still, the room filled with people who had no real reason to be there, the conversation circled for an hour, and everyone walked out without a call being made.

The chart was not missing. The chart was fine.

What was missing was the mode.

Three researchers just published the definitive autopsy on why this happens. Lindy Greer and Maxim Sytch of Michigan’s Ross School and Jennifer Jordan of IMD examined decision-rights tools across more than a hundred companies and found they fail not because they are flawed, but because people misunderstand them, ignore them, or let them drift from how the team behaves. The line that traveled furthest in the coverage compares a decision chart to the position plan for a kids’ soccer game – a tidy diagram nobody understands or remembers.

Two pieces from the HBR that were the inspiration for this piece.

  1. What Companies Get Wrong About Decision Rights

  2. Why Decision-Making Frameworks Fail

I read that and stopped. Because underneath it sits a quiet surrender: the system is a nice idea on paper, and paper loses. I do not accept that. A well-built system does the opposite of lose. It makes decisions faster, it makes them clearer, and it makes them more trusted. The failure in that meeting is not evidence that systems do not work. It is evidence that this one was half-built.

A chart answers who. It never answers how, and how is the part that decides whether twelve people sit in the room or four, whether you are gathering input or building agreement, whether the meeting ends in a decision or a rematch. RACI, the most common of these tools, sorts people into responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed and hands you a seating chart: who holds the final say, who is in the room. Worth having. Not what breaks the meeting. What breaks the meeting is that nobody names how the call gets made before they walk in, so the room fills with people meant to be informed afterward and advisors who start arguing as if they hold the decision.

This is the question the 6C Decision Compass is built to answer. In CLUTCH it is the navigation system, the part that tells you which route a decision should take. It names six modes. Command, when one person must act now. Consultative, when the leader gathers input and then decides. Collaborative, when a stronger solution gets built together. Consensus, when shared agreement matters more than speed. Core Expert, when authority should flow to whoever knows most. And Choice, when the decision is handed off in full.

Each mode carries what a role on a chart cannot. It names how the call gets made – out loud, in the moment, for the decision in front of you.

Picture the same meeting run differently. A leader has to decide on a senior hire. Before anyone sits down, she says it plainly. “This is Consultative. I’m making the call. The three of you are here because you see angles I don’t, so push hard. Everyone else, I’ll walk you through it once it’s made.” Four people in the room instead of twelve. The conversation runs twenty minutes, not ninety. The three advisors argue freely because they know they are advising, not competing for the final say. She decides. She explains it to the rest the next morning.

Nothing about the org chart changed. One sentence changed. And look at what the one sentence bought. Speed, because the room emptied. Clarity, because everyone knew the mode. Trust, because the advisors could push hard without anyone reading it as a power grab. That is not the absence of a system. That is a system working, in the only place a system ever runs, which is the moment the decision arrives.

The authors’ own findings give the game away. Two of them break companies most often, and neither is a case for a better chart.

The first is that decision rights die in a file. A leader builds the chart, hands it down, and assumes people will play their parts because the document exists. They rarely do. The authors read this as a buy-in problem and prescribe co-creating the chart so people remember it. But a mode is not information you store. It is an instruction you speak. “This is a Core Expert call. You own it.” That sentence does work no document can do, because it reaches the person in the moment they need to act, not in a file they have already closed.

The second is the one I see most in founder-led companies. People get stuck in the same roles. The founder is always accountable. Everyone below is always responsible.

One founder I work with kept the renewal call with her largest account, the way she had since the company was eight people. Her head of customer success had flagged twice that the client’s new procurement lead was raising implementation questions the founder, four layers removed from the rollout, could not answer in the room. She ran the call anyway, gave a confident answer that proved wrong, and spent six weeks rebuilding a relationship her CS lead could have protected in one sentence. The account renewed, at a discount the client demanded as insurance against the gap they had just watched open.

That is Core Expert mode, missed. The chart did not fail her. She never named the decision as one where someone else should hold the call. The fix was not a cleaner spreadsheet. It was one question, asked before the call went on her calendar. Not who ranks highest. Who sees it clearest.

Which brings me back to the soccer field. The manager in the article is right that nobody remembered the chart. He is wrong about why. The lesson he draws, and the framing the coverage runs with, is that the players failed. People are undisciplined. People swarm the ball. People forget. But you cannot forget a mode the chart was never built to name. The advisors in that first meeting did not lose the plan. The plan never held the part that would have ended the meeting. Memory was never the problem. Design was.

The authors are right that decision tools fail. But a better chart will not save you. A chart answers who, and the meeting that runs long and produces nothing is rarely a who problem. It is a how problem. The answer is not less system. It is the part of the system these tools leave out: a single sentence, said before the meeting starts, that tells everyone how this call gets made.

Name the mode. Watch how much shorter the meeting gets.

THREE QUESTIONS BEFORE YOUR NEXT BIG DECISION

Before the next call that fills your calendar with a meeting, sit with these:

  1. Think back to the last decision that ate up a full meeting and still ended without a call. What got named before anyone sat down, and what got assumed?

  2. When you hand a decision to someone else, what do you say out loud – who owns it, or how the call gets made?

  3. Look at one decision on this week’s calendar. Which of the six modes does it call for, and who still needs to hear you say so?

Most of the organizations I work with – founders, leadership teams, schools, nonprofits, government agencies – arrive at the same place: clean charts of who decides, and no shared language for how. The work is building the infrastructure that closes that gap.

I take on a handful of clients at a time because this work doesn’t happen in a single session. If that sounds like what you need, let’s talk. If not, the book and the essays aren’t going anywhere.

Calendly | matt@thatsgoodedesign.com | LinkedIn

title: The Engine Most Leaders Never Tune
html:
Before I worked with companies, I spent time around humanitarian operations, the kind of work where the strain on a system is never theoretical. The crises aren’t what stayed with me. What stayed with me was watching good organizations, full of people who cared enormously, come apart under pressure they were never built to hold.

The talent was there. The mission was there. What gave way was the wiring underneath: who owned what, who had the authority to act, whether people trusted each other enough to move fast when there was no time to check. The caring never stopped. The structure beneath the caring was never engineered for a bad day.

The engine you forgot you had

That structure has a name in CLUTCH. CREATE is the engine your leadership runs on, and it has six cylinders.

Culture is the climate you set. Relationships is the trust you can actually draw on. Execution is whether work finishes or just moves. Agility is how fast you adapt when the plan breaks. Teaching is whether people are more capable because of how you lead them. Ethics is what holds when the easy call and the right call split.

Caption: CREATE’s six cylinders – the engine your leadership runs on.

Most leaders pour everything into the two or three cylinders they’re already good at and let the rest idle. The operator floors Execution and lets Relationships go cold. The visionary keeps Culture humming and never builds the systems Execution needs. The engine still turns. It just isn’t balanced, and an unbalanced engine grinds down the people riding in it.

The cold cylinder always sends an invoice

And it’s not a soft cost. A cold Relationships cylinder shows up as the manager you didn’t know was unhappy until the resignation lands, at something like $65,000 to recruit and ramp a replacement, plus the months of half-speed while the seat is warm but empty. A cold Teaching cylinder shows up as a bench too thin to cover for you, which is the actual reason you can’t take the two weeks. A cold Ethics cylinder shows up once, catastrophically, in a decision you wish you could take back.

The instinct, when something feels off, is to add horsepower to what you’re already good at, because that’s where it feels good to push. It’s the wrong move. The leverage is in the cylinder you stopped checking. Find that one, warm it up, and the whole engine smooths out.

The tell is usually a story you’ve stopped questioning. “Relationships sort themselves out.” “No time to teach right now.” “Ethics isn’t really an issue here.” Each one is a cylinder you decided to stop checking, and the decision is invisible to you precisely because you made it so long ago. The diagnostic works by making you say it out loud.

Worth asking, not answering quickly:

  • Which cylinder carries most of your leadership right now?

  • Which one have you let go cold, and what has that cost you that you never connected to it?

  • If you tuned one cylinder this quarter, which would the people around you feel first?

title: It’s Not You. It’s the System.
html:
“Best quarter we’ve ever had,” he told me. Then, almost in the same breath: “and I’ve never been more buried.”

He’s a CTO — builds hard, knows the product cold, sits in on every customer call because that’s how the difficult ones close. The growth was real. So was the exhaustion, and here’s the part that didn’t add up to him: it was getting worse, not better, in direct proportion to the wins.

A great quarter should buy you room. His bought him more calls he couldn’t miss, more decisions that routed through him, more nights spent catching up on the work he’d set aside to do the closing. Success was pouring more volume through the one part of the system that can’t be in two places at once — him.

You can’t hustle your way out of a bottleneck

Watch what he kept doing, because almost every capable builder does the same thing. He’d hit the edge of his capacity, feel the strain, and answer it by working harder. Earlier mornings. Tighter calendar. One more personal system to keep the plates spinning. And every time, the relief held for about a week before the load caught back up — because effort doesn’t change the architecture. It just runs the same design at higher RPM.

A bottleneck isn’t a measure of how hard you’re working. It’s a property of how the work is routed. When every call that matters flows through one person, that person becomes a constraint no amount of personal horsepower can fix — because the problem was never the horsepower. It was the single lane that everything had to merge into.

It’s not a character flaw. It’s a design state.

This is the reframe that actually lets a leader breathe, so let me be precise about it. The reason you’re the bottleneck is not that you’re disorganized, or undisciplined, or secretly not good enough for the job you built. That’s not a verdict on your character. It’s a design state, and the distinction matters enormously — because you can’t change your character on a Tuesday, but you can change a design. You don’t rise to the level of your effort; you fall to the level of your systems. The leaders who get free didn’t find more willpower than you have. They changed what had to route through them.

title: The Two Week Test
html:
Every framework in this book grew out of one question. Not a question about strategy, or vision, or the org chart. Something smaller, and far harder to sit with:

Could you leave for two weeks – phone off, laptop shut, unreachable – and trust the work to keep moving without you?

I’ve asked it for years, in boardrooms and on factory floors and across enough dinner tables to know the tell. The words rarely come first; the body answers before the mouth does – a flicker, a held breath, the quiet math of what falls over by Thursday. That flinch is the most honest thing a leader ever shows me. The day I understood what it was telling me is the day this book started.

The sentence that gave it away

A few months back, I sat across from the CEO of an engineering firm I admire. Sharp, well-liked, the kind of founder people follow into a fire. He told me, almost sheepishly, that he was finally taking his family to Italy. Two weeks. First real break in years.

“That’s overdue,” I said.

He nodded. Then, after a beat: “I’ll still be working most of it, though.” His laptop was already packed.

That sentence is the whole problem, and he didn’t hear himself say it. He wasn’t packing the laptop because he distrusts his team. He was packing it because the company had been built – quietly, over the years – to run through him. Italy wasn’t going to change that. It was just going to move his desk to a hotel balcony.

The test underneath the sigh

So picture your own two weeks. Phone off. Laptop shut. Now run the tape to day fourteen. When you walk back in, did the work move, or did it wait for you?

Most leaders can’t answer cleanly, and the flinch is the diagnosis. Noam Wasserman, who tracked nearly ten thousand founders at Harvard, named the trap. He called it the founder’s dilemma: the instincts that build a company – ownership, decisiveness, high standards – are the same ones that cap it. You move fast, so you do it yourself. The system grows around your judgment. One day, you look up, and you’re the tollbooth on your own highway, every car idling for you.

You can’t out-work this. No run of late nights fixes a problem baked into the design. Effort is finite; a well-built system scales. Until the design changes, the bottleneck stays – and so do you, laptop in the carry-on.

Caption: Owner-dependent vs. built-to-hold – across the vacation, the return, the sale, and what each runs on.

Why it’s worth fixing, in plain numbers

Here’s the part founders feel in their gut but rarely price out. The business that can’t run without you is worth less the day you try to sell it, because a buyer isn’t purchasing a company – they’re purchasing your calendar, and your calendar isn’t for sale. Acquirers discount owner-dependent firms hard, sometimes by a third or more, for exactly this reason. The same trap that ruins your vacation also caps your exit.

And the cost isn’t only financial. It’s the slow erosion of why you started. The engineer who headed to Italy didn’t build a company so he could answer Slack from a balcony while his kids swam without him. He built it for freedom, and somewhere along the way, the thing he built started owning him back. The always-on, last-to-leave story wears like a badge, right up until the day a body or a marriage sends the invoice the business never did.

The leaders who can disappear for two weeks are no less committed. They built something that holds. That’s not a personality difference; it’s a design difference, and design can be changed. That’s the whole bet of this book: the two-week test isn’t a verdict on you – it’s a readout on what you’ve built. And what’s built can be rebuilt.

So this is where we start, because it’s where I started: not with a framework, but with one uncomfortable question and the honest flinch that follows it. Everything after this is the answer.

Take these into your next quiet hour:

  • If you disappeared tomorrow for two weeks, what moves without you, and what stops?

  • For the things that stop, what about the design routes them through you?

  • What would taking that trip for real be worth to you?

title: The Fog of War Is in Your Third Quarter
subtitle: Fifteen minutes inside a simulated attack, and the two gears most leaders never shift out of.
html:
The fake blood was the detail that got me. Not the smoke, not the blast that knocked the plan out of my head – the fake blood. Hadn't expected that.

It was a simulation. A hostile-environment course built for a posting that never came. Smoke. A vehicle still rolling behind the noise. Extras trained to scream and bleed until they owned the scene. A call that there might be a second device. Men playing militia working the edges with rifles. And a ring of staff with clipboards, grading every move. Inside ninety seconds, I stopped seeing the clipboards. The people scoring me went invisible.

Leadership runs on a gearbox. Six gears, and almost every leader lives in two: Visionary, which paints the goal, and Operator, which drives the work. Both run on control, so under pressure we grip them harder and call it range. It isn't. It's two gears and four blind spots.

A good driver doesn't shift on a schedule. They read the tachometer, feel the engine strain, watch the road, and move the instant the car asks for it. The instrument that tells you when to shift is emotional intelligence – your read on your own state, your people's, and the conditions in front of all of you. Most leaders drive with that gauge covered.

Operator got me in. Off the X, you call it in, you two with me – then hands in the work, reading bodies because the words weren't in a language I had. When two of my people clustered on one casualty and left others bleeding, ten seconds of Visionary – here's where everyone goes – then back down. Those two came easily. They always do.

Then the scene stopped being a task.

A crowd had turned while my head was down. A woman reached me first – help my baby, in a language I didn't share, holding something I had to make myself look at. You can't command panic into calm or inspire it away. So I shifted into the gear with no task in it: dropped my voice, slowed my hands, gave her a face that wasn't panicking. Ninety seconds. It was the difference.

Then the medevac came in hot and every call was routing through me. The instinct is to grip tighter. I gave the calls away instead. You own the LZ. You own the count. You own her.

Then the whistle, and the two gears the scene had no room for, waiting in the debrief.

Operator and Visionary got me started. They couldn't have finished it. A leader with only those two is right for the first ninety seconds and wrong for everything after.

And here's what the gearbox metaphor almost hides: each shift wasn't only a different move, it was a different voice, each one pitched to the person in front of me. Same leader, six registers. That's why it isn't called gears. It's called VOICES.

Where each one came out, and the voice it took:

Visionary — The lifted, horizon-pointing voice. Ten seconds mid-scene when my people clustered on one casualty: here's where everyone goes.

Operator — The clipped, directive voice. The opening minutes and the hands-in triage, running the sequence out loud.

Independent — The releasing voice: you own this, decide. When the medevac came in and every call routed through me, I handed the decisions off instead of becoming the bottleneck.

Encourager — Almost no words at all. A lowered voice, slowed hands, a steady face. At the crowd, with the mother I couldn't speak to, because steadiness is the only thing that interrupts panic.

Coach — The questioning voice. In the debrief: what would each of us do differently?

Sculptor — The structural voice. The debrief again, when several of us hit the same wall – a system problem, not a people problem.

So what does any of that have to do with your third quarter?

Yours had no smoke. But it had a blast – the hire who quit, the deal that died, the number that took the plan with it. A crowd of stakeholders wanting answers while you worked the real problem. A second device under the visible one. And clipboards – your board, your team, the market – grading every move after you'd stopped noticing them. If the quarter went sideways, I'd bet it wasn't the wrong move. You stayed in two gears and couldn't hear the moment change.

You can't control the road. That's VUCA. What you control is how you respond – which gear, which voice, and whether you're reading the car and the road closely enough to know when to shift. The instrument that does the reading is EQ. The only real skill is hearing which gear the moment is already asking for, before it forces your hand.

That's the through-line of the book I'm writing, CLUTCH. You don't need the book to start, though. You need to notice, this week, which gear you keep reaching for – and which one the room has been quietly asking you to find.

The Leadership Lab is where I work these ideas out. If this is the lens you want on the next quarter, subscribe and the next one comes to you.

title: The System You Haven't Built Yet
html:
His company had just posted its best year on record, and it still couldn’t close the books without him in the room. Not because no one else could do the work. Because every exception, for five years, had routed to him – and the team had quietly learned to stop trying. He wasn’t indispensable. He’d built a trap, one helpful intervention at a time.

He didn’t have a talent problem. He had an architecture problem, and most leaders reading this have a version of the same one. The whole operation runs through one set of hands, and on a hard day, that person can feel exactly which ones.

When the work routes through you like that, the cause is rarely your work ethic. Decisions pile up at the top. Roles blur. Accountability gets implied instead of named. A good team starts to stall, not because no one cares, but because the structure makes the work harder than it should be.

Leadership is driving

That’s the idea at the center of CLUTCH. You don’t control the road. Conditions are volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous. What you control is the vehicle, and a well-built vehicle handles roads that wreck a cheap one.

Caption: The CLUTCH Leadership Operating System – seven systems, built in order.

The whole thing fits on one page. CREATE is the engine, the six cylinders your leadership runs on. VOICES is the gearbox, the modes you shift between to meet the moment. EQ is the clutch, the half-second between stimulus and response that keeps the shift smooth. The 6C Compass is the navigation: who decides, and how. DELEGATE is the handoff that moves real ownership across without dropping it. Development is how you build drivers. Results is the flywheel, where momentum finally compounds on its own.

Build it. Choose it. Bring it. Align it. Transfer it. Grow it. Compound it.

What it’s costing you right now

Founder dependency isn’t a personality quirk. It has a price, and you’re paying it today. You pay it in turnover when good people hit a ceiling that only you can move, and walk. You pay it in decisions that sit for three days because one signature is missing. You pay it on Sunday night, when the inbox is still yours and the holiday never quite happened.

The founder who couldn’t close his books was paying all three, and calling it dedication.

Jim Collins, after five years studying 1,435 companies for Good to Great, said you have to get the right people in the right seats on the right bus. True. And you can do all of that and still stall, if the route only works while one driver keeps both hands on the wheel.

So the real question isn’t whether you’ve hired well. It’s whether the bus moves when you step off it.

This series is built one system at a time, and every build starts with an honest look at the friction. So start there. Three questions to carry into the week, with no rush to answer them:

  • Where are you the slowest part of your own system right now?

  • What does the work route through you for that it no longer needs to?

  • What are you still holding that someone on your team is already ready to carry?
