title: Fogging Standards
subtitle: Arteta Removed His Two Best Players. That Was the Rebuild.
html:
A non-negotiable is only worth what you're willing to lose to keep it. Mikel Arteta lost his highest earner and his own captain to prove Arsenal's.

A captain booed off his own pitch by his own fans. Two eighth-place finishes. A dressing room full of expensive, comfortable men who had stopped believing in the thing they were paid to do. That was Arsenal in December 2019, the week Mikel Arteta took the job.

The talent hadn't gone anywhere, ok ok ok, yeah it kinda did. But so did the standards. So the first thing he did wasn't tactical. Before they practiced a single corner, he named three non-negotiables – respect, commitment, passion – and repeated them from his first press conference onward. The word did real work. A negotiable is something you trade when the price is right. He was telling a room full of millionaires that on these three, there was no price. The question every one of them was quietly asking is the only one that matters when a leader announces a standard: what happens to the person too valuable to hold to it?

Anyone who has watched All or Nothing, Amazon's documentary of the rebuild, knows he meant it at volume. The team talks run close to violent. "I don't want one fucking player complaining, one fucking player walking," he tells the changing room at half-time. It plays as theatre. It wasn't. The proof came in who he was willing to lose.

<iframe width="560" height="315" src="

And the non-negotiables were never only about attitude. They became a system. The model he brought to Arsenal asked the whole team to defend as one – a press that starts at the very front, every forward hunting the ball, every player tracking back the instant it's lost. There is no place in that system for a passenger, however gifted. And the two most gifted attackers at the club were exactly that. Neither Özil nor Aubameyang pressed with conviction. Neither of them tracked back. Özil practically never ran at all in fact, but his passes could break defensives, and make grown men cry. He even “invented” his own shot. Such was the prerogative of genius so it was said. In the era they came up in, the gifted attacker was excused from defending – that was for other, lesser players to do. Arteta's non-negotiable was that no one is excused.

Start with the man you could least afford to bench. Mesut Özil was the highest-paid player at the club, on a reported £350,000 a week, a fan icon, the closest thing Arsenal had to a marquee name. In the spring of 2020, when the squad was asked to take a pay cut to protect jobs through the pandemic, most of them agreed. Özil wanted assurances first, he wanted his money, nevermind the cooks, trainers, or the crew that cuts the grass. 

Arteta froze him out. He didn't play a competitive minute after March 2020, was left out of the Premier League and Europa League squads entirely, and by January 2021 his contract was torn up and he was gone to Fenerbahçe. The official line was "football reasons." It was also the literal one: there was no room in a pressing side for a player who would not press. That is what a standard with teeth looks like from the wrong side of it.

Then Arteta did the harder thing. He did it to his own man.

Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang was the mercurial footed captain Arteta inherited and chose to keep. More than that, he was Arteta's bet: the manager backed a new three-year contract in September 2020 that made him one of the highest earners at the club, and said openly that he wanted to build the team around him.

What ended it was lateness. In March 2021, Arteta left his own captain out of the squad for a North London derby – a derby – for arriving late to a team meeting on the morning of the game. Arsenal won 2-1 without him. Aubameyang kept the armband that time. Nine months later, after he returned late from a trip, Arteta took the armband for good and dropped him from the squad. He never played for Arteta again. Weeks later he left for Barcelona, his contract terminated, the sunk cost eaten in full.

The size of that is easy to miss. A manager benched his best forward for the biggest fixture of the season, then took the armband off him for good, over minutes on a clock. Lateness to a meeting doesn't look like a thing worth losing a player over – which is exactly why it's the truest test of a standard. It was never about the minutes. Turning up late says the quiet part out loud: my time is worth more than yours, the rule that binds the room binds me a little less, what we agreed was closer to a suggestion. Arteta treated a late arrival as a fact about the club, not a fact about the clock.

And the breach is cheapest to forgive in exactly the people you can least afford to lose. The replaceable player who rolls in late gets corrected without a thought. Your best one gets a reason it's fine – he's brilliant, he was probably working, the meeting could wait. The team clocks which you do, every time. So picture the last time someone wandered into your 9:00 five minutes late with a giant Starbucks latte in hand and you said nothing. That's the same behavior that cost a captain his armband. The only difference is whether you treat it as load-bearing or as a courtesy you keep quietly extending.

The easy version of "high standards" is a lie. It punishes the people you were glad to be rid of anyway – the marginal squad player, the attitude you'd already written off – and it costs you nothing. Every leader alive will tell you they hold a high bar while quietly only ever enforcing it downward. A real standard runs the other way. It's worth exactly what it costs you to apply it to the person you can least afford to lose. Arteta's became real the moment it cost him his most gifted player, then his own captain, then a season, then a pile of money paid to make both men disappear. The bill is the proof. If your standard has never cost you a star, you don't have a standard. You have a preference you enforce on the weak.

True story, as his swim coach, I once left my own son behind when he was late for departure to an away meet. Gasps ensued. No one was ever late again, and it became part of team lore handed down for years. Yo, coach left his own son behind: don't be late.

The most common exemption inside any company is talent. Picture the engineer who closes the hardest tickets and has left a junior shaken after code review for two years running – because the one time someone raised it, the answer was a shrug and "that's just how he is, and have you seen his output?" Everyone on the team can name him. The speed with which they can name him is the culture. The values page says one thing; the team runs on the version they have watched you permit. And he stays exempt for the same reason Arteta refused to accept: he's too good to lose.

His wager was that the standard was a more valuable asset than the player – that a dressing room watching their manager hold the line against the biggest name in the room would become something no individual talent could buy. It took years, and it was not clean. Three straight seasons ended in second place, close enough to feel like failure.

It's tempting to read this backward, now that there's a trophy at the end, as though the standard was always going to pay off. It wasn't. For three years this looked like a manager who had traded away match-winners for a principle and finished second with it, and for stretches it looked like it would cost him his job. The bet could have failed. Had it, these same decisions would read today as stubbornness. That is the actual nature of a standard – you hold the line before you know whether it works, because the moment you only enforce it when the payoff is guaranteed, it stops being a standard and goes back to being a preference.

Then, this spring, it paid. Arsenal won the Premier League – their first title in 22 years, built on the best defence in the division: the fewest goals conceded, a clean sheet in half their matches. The trophy was won by eleven players doing the exact work Özil and Aubameyang would not. The talent that won it came later. The standard that made the talent worth buying came first.

Culture is not the values you frame on the wall. It's the worst behavior you're willing to walk past – and the real test of it is never the person you were glad to lose. It's the one you weren't.

The frameworks underneath this – the engine that holds a culture together when the cost finally comes due – are what I write about here every week. If that's the work you're doing, subscribe. It's free, and it lands in your inbox instead of waiting on an algorithm.

title: I Have Loved You Since 1989
subtitle: A letter to Arsenal, on the occasion of becoming champions of England again.
html:
This isn’t my usual lane. The Leadership Lab is for founders, operators, and the people building organizations that grow people faster than they grow capability. This post is none of those things. This is a letter to a football club on the occasion of becoming champions of England again, written by someone who has loved them for thirty-seven years.

If you have zero interest, I understand entirely – skip it. I’ll be back to leadership and infrastructure next week.

Some things you just have to put into the universe. The Champions League final is in nine days. This one could not wait.

I have loved you since 1989. Thirty-seven years later, you are champions of England again.

I did not jump on a bandwagon. There was no bandwagon. Following Arsenal from the United States in 1989 was not a thing most Americans would have understood as possible. The NASL had collapsed five years earlier. MLS would not arrive until 1996. The 1990 World Cup was a year away and the 1994 one that finally gave American football its language was still half a decade out. ESPN treated soccer as a curio that aired at three in the morning if it aired at all.

The way you watched English football in 1989 was that you knew where the British pub was, or you got lucky with a syndicated highlights package on a low-channel cable station, or you waited for the FA Cup Final once a year on PBS. That was it. No streaming. No league pass. No app on a phone that did not yet exist. There was a kid in front of a television, late at night because of the time difference, watching whatever fragment of English football had crossed the ocean. A grainy broadcast. Michael Thomas charging through the midfield at Anfield, the title up for grabs, the last minute of the last game of the season, against the defending English champions and four-time European champions, at the fortress they had built that dynasty on, six weeks after Hillsborough in a fixture only rescheduled because of it, a city still in mourning, Brian Moore’s commentary cracking with disbelief.

If you want to understand the mania of that moment and what it does to a person, read Nick Hornby’s Fever Pitch, or watch the Colin Firth film if you must. The book ends on the Thomas goal – Hornby alone in his flat near Highbury, hearing the streets erupt, writing the closing sentence that every Arsenal supporter of a certain age can recite.

By the time I moved to London for graduate school you were already mine. I chose a hall in Marylebone because it was the closest to Islington. I was within walking distance of Highbury before Arsène Wenger was hired, which is to say, I was there for headlines: Who? I remember chestnuts roasting on the North Bank, the smell of them more than any goal, because that is how memory works. The big moments blur. The small ones stay.

Then I came home, and the internet slowly grew into a thing that could carry a football match across an ocean. By 2010 you could watch all of them, in HD, on a phone you carried in your pocket.

The same infrastructure that finally let me follow Arsenal from a Baltimore suburb let everyone else find them too. Supporters’ clubs in Lagos and Nairobi and Bangkok and São Paulo and Mumbai and Jakarta, packed pubs at four in the morning local time, kids in red and white in countries Wenger’s Arsenal had never visited. Football was the seed. The internet was the soil. By the time the streaming was clean enough to follow a match in real time across an ocean, there were already millions of us doing it. The congregation arrived right around the time the football had stopped being good, which meant most of them found us in the lean years, the trophyless years, the fourth-is-a-trophy years. They loved us anyway. That is a different kind of love than the love of the supporter who watched Michael Thomas at the time. It is no less real. It might in some ways be more honest, because nothing about the football was selling itself in 2014.

Supporting a club in England is a generational thing in a way Americans, with our mobility and our short attention spans, do not really understand. An English boy is born into a club the way he is born into a parish. His grandfather took his father to the ground; his father takes him. You do not pick a club because you saw a good goal on television. You inherit it. You stand where your father stood and your father’s father stood, in the same end, sometimes in the same seat the family has held for forty years. There is a continuity to it that American sport simulates but does not actually possess, because American fans move cities and switch loyalties and arrive in new markets ready to wear whatever colors the new market sells. The English do not move. The seats do not move. The clubs barely move either. When Arsenal relocated approximately 500 meters from Highbury to the Emirates in 2006, still in Islington, still in the N5 postcode, the supporters mourned for years and Wenger himself eventually said we left our soul at Highbury. When West Ham left the Boleyn Ground in 2016 for the London Stadium – three miles east, after 112 years on the same site, into a converted Olympic venue with a running track between the fans and the pitch – their supporters never accepted it. Half a kilometer is a betrayal. Three miles is sacrilege. American franchises move two thousand miles, change their names, change their colors, and the fans go with them. English fans do not. A kid who is born in Islington is born an Arsenal supporter the way another kid is born Catholic, and there is not really a moment of decision in it. Only a moment of recognition.

I am the wrong kind of supporter for that tradition. I picked Arsenal from a grainy broadcast in Maryland. There was no grandfather at the Clock End. There was no family seat. There was a kid and a television and a goal in injury time. So I gave the inheritance backwards. I took my dad to his first match. QPR on Boxing Day, when he came to visit. He played fullback in high school and taught me my love of the game. Some kids played catch with their dad; my dad took PKs with me in goal. Later I moved from goalie to striker, so I am equally happy keeping a clean sheet or scoring one, so I get 1-nil to the Arsenal. He understood the game before I did, but I think I gave him Arsenal. That is a thing a son can give a father. Not many. In England it would not have been mine to give. In America it was mine because nobody else had it. Sometimes the wrong kind of supporter finds the right kind of gift.

Then came the glory.

Wenger arrived in October 1996 from Japan, of all places. A French manager nobody had heard of, with a degree in economics and the bearing of a university lecturer. Pasta and chicken and stretching and the kind of nutrition science the rest of the league laughed at until it stopped laughing. He brought in Patrick Vieira and Emmanuel Petit from France. He kept Tony Adams and Martin Keown and the back four George Graham had built and put them behind a French midfield and a Dutch number ten in Bergkamp. And then he found Thierry Henry.

You cannot explain Henry to someone who did not watch him in his prime. The footage does not do it. Henry on a Saturday afternoon at Highbury, drifting in from the left, twenty yards out, opening his body half a step before the defender realised he was about to shoot – it was a category of football that the Premier League had not seen before and may not see again. He scored two hundred and twenty-eight goals for Arsenal across eight seasons. He played football the way certain pianists play Chopin. Like the instrument was invented for him.

Wenger won the double in his first full season. Won it again in 2002. By then the football had changed shape. Wengerball was not really a system; it was a temperament. The belief that you could win the league while playing better football than anyone else. That there was no contradiction between style and substance. That the most attractive team could also be the hardest team.

Then came the Invincibles.

Thirty-eight league games, May 2003 to May 2004. Not one defeat. Twenty-six wins. Twelve draws. The first English top-flight side to go unbeaten across an entire season since Preston North End in 1888-89, when the league had twenty-two games and most of the players also worked day jobs. We went to Old Trafford and drew nil-nil and Ruud van Nistelrooy missed a penalty in injury time that would have ended the run at seven games, and then we did not lose another league game for the rest of the season. We won the league at White Hart Lane, of all places. Vieira scored. Henry assisted. The Tottenham faithful stayed to watch us lift the title in their stadium because they had to. Some things in football are too rare to leave the building for.

Forty-nine games unbeaten in total, across two seasons. Twenty-two years later it is still the longest unbeaten run in the history of English top-flight football. Nobody has come within ten games of it. There is a 49 tattooed on my forearm. It sits in a grid with other numbers that matter to me. Birthdays, an anniversary, the dates that mark a life. The Invincibles are in there next to my children. That is what kind of fan I am.

We had been building a stadium the whole time. We had to. Highbury sat thirty-eight thousand. Old Trafford sat seventy-five. By the late nineties the gap between matchday revenue at a 38,000-seat ground and a 60,000-seat ground was the difference between competing for the league and not. Arsenal made the only decision a modern football club could make. We mortgaged ourselves to build the Emirates. Three hundred and ninety million pounds of debt, secured against ticket revenue we had not yet sold, paid down across the years we were supposed to be defending the title we had just won unbeaten. The Invincibles were not the start of a dynasty. They were the down payment.

What happened next was not a slump. It was a haunting.

Roman Abramovich bought Chelsea in the summer of 2003. By 2004 he had spent two hundred million pounds on players. By 2005 Chelsea had won the league. The market we had just mortgaged ourselves against had been replaced, almost overnight, by a market in which the price of a player was whatever a Russian oligarch felt like paying that morning. Wenger had a phrase for it. Financial doping – he said it out loud in 2004, while everyone else in the league was still pretending the money was clean. He was mocked for the phrase at the time. Every Financial Fair Play case since has been the league quietly conceding he was right.

It started with Ashley Cole. He was a Hale End boy, raised in our system, the best left-back in the world and in his prime, and we could not pay him what he was now worth because we were paying for our roof. Chelsea offered him ninety thousand a week. Arsenal offered fifty-five. In January 2005, José Mourinho and Chelsea’s chief executive met Cole and his agent in a London hotel without telling Arsenal. The Premier League fined all four parties for illegal tapping up. Cole left for Chelsea the following summer in a swap deal that, with admirable structural irony, sent William Gallas the other way.

We did not just lose a player. We lost the precedent. From that point forward, any of our best players could be tapped up by anyone with enough of Abramovich’s money to make it worth their while. And John Terry, Chelsea’s captain, stood in the middle of it all. Captain, leader, legend, the man whose entire public career was a tutorial in how to dress out self-interest as devotion to the badge. I have hangnails I have liked more than that man.

Everything that came next traces back to that summer. The football did not get worse. The money got dirtier.

And then it got dirtier still. If Abramovich was the first act, City was the second, and the second act was worse because the money was bigger and the laundering was state-sponsored. A nation-state bought a football club. Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, brother to the President of the United Arab Emirates, acquired Manchester City for around £200 million in September of that year, and then proceeded to spend more money on it than any owner has ever spent on any football club in history. The official transfer figure since the takeover is somewhere north of £2 billion. That is just what is on the books. The 115 charges – brought by the Premier League in February 2023, alleging financial misconduct across the 2009 to 2018 seasons – are still unresolved. The hearing finished in December 2024. The verdict has been expected soon for over a year. Whatever the commission eventually rules, the money that is alleged to have been moved is the money that built the team that beat us to three consecutive league titles. The football was downstream of the accounting.

And then, having built the platform, they went out and hired the best football coach of the modern era and handed him the biggest annual budget in the league for ten years running. Pep is a genius. Nobody is disputing that. But Pep with the resources of a petrostate behind him is not a sporting competition. It is a category error. We finished second to that machine three years in a row, and those second-place finishes were not failures. They were what it took to even be in the same conversation.

But after the Invincibles came the banter years.

I was there for those too. Twitter sucked. The leg breaks. The 8-2. Wenger sent to the stands at Old Trafford. Wenger memes of his sleeping bag coat zipped to the chin. He was a man whose religion had stopped working. Top four as a trophy. William Gallas wearing the number ten – the number Dennis wore, Dennis – and somehow we handed it to a man who sat down on the pitch in tears when we needed a captain.

Post-Invincibles, Wenger built his team around small, deft, technical footballers. Hleb, Cesc as a teenager, Rosický, Cazorla, Wilshere. Players who saw a pass other players did not see, players you could not catch unless you stopped them by other means. And the league did. Dan Smith broke Diaby’s ankle at Sunderland in 2006 – a giant, silky midfielder intended to replace Vieira, and we never got him back. Martin Taylor broke Eduardo’s leg at Birmingham in 2008. Do not google that video. Ryan Shawcross broke Ramsey’s leg at Stoke in 2010. Three career-altering injuries in four years to three of Wenger’s most gifted young players, all from challenges that should have ended in long bans and did not. The league was a hunting ground, and our players were the prey, and the men with the whistles looked the other way.

But the Invincibles were not soft. The Alan Davies podcast – It’s Up For Grabs Now, named after Brian Moore’s call from Anfield in 1989 – has a piece of received fan wisdom that says you need seven players in a squad who will rumble, or the league will eat you. The Invincibles had nine. Vieira would fight anyone. Petit would fight anyone. Keown would fight anyone, sometimes during games and once memorably after one. Cole would fight Gary Neville on principle. Henry would not fight you, but he would humiliate you in front of fifty thousand people, which was worse. The softness came later, after we had to sell those stalwarts to clubs we could not afford to match.

Cesc went home to Barcelona. Henry followed Cesc to Barcelona. Overmars before them. Van Persie went to United and won the title under Ferguson in his very first season in red, which is the kind of insult only football can devise. Nasri to City. Adebayor to City – and then, in his first game against us in sky blue, scoring at the Etihad and running the entire length of the pitch to celebrate in front of the Arsenal away end, knee-sliding to a stop in front of the supporters who had sung his name. Clichy to City. Touré to City. Sánchez to United. Song to Barcelona. Hleb to Barcelona.

We were a selling club because we were paying for our roof. The cruel joke is that the destinations have not aged well. Barcelona – more than a club – turned out to be less than solvent, technically bankrupt by their own audit in 2021, selling their stadium’s best seats thirty years into the future to register the players they could no longer afford. City are under investigation for financial irregularities. United are an ongoing tragedy. Chelsea are a hedge-fund experiment in real time. Twenty years on, the buyers look worse than the seller.

I was there in the early online days, when the community was small enough to feel like a pub. Arseblog before he was an institution – I was in the first couple hundred who followed. I drew the redhead logo for Gingers for Limpar. Twitter was still good then. The jokes were ours. The misery was ours. We made our own warmth because the football was not giving us any.

Arsenal essentially pioneered the modern football fan ecosystem online. The blogs and pods. The match-day Twitter accounts. The community of supporters who built something the club itself was too slow to build. Other clubs caught up. None of them had the head start. We were first because we needed it most.

Then the ecosystem turned. The same building blocks that gave us Arseblog gave us Arsenal Fan TV. Faces more famous than half the squad, monetised by being more upset than anyone else in the queue. Outrage paid better than analysis. We became the meme we used to be writing around.

talkSPORT figured out the radio version around 2010. An Arsenal fan calling in to cry about Wenger filled an afternoon. So they booked us. Every loss, every draw, every win that should have been by more. Claude from north London with the voice of a man who had not slept since Eduardo’s leg. The hosts laughed. The producers cued it up. The rest of the league learned to think of Arsenal as the club whose own supporters could be relied on to deliver the post-match indictment, free of charge, on a competitor’s airtime.

Don’t shitpost your club. Supporters are allowed to complain. They are not allowed to monetise the complaint.

The shirt is not a microphone. The badge is not content.

And now, after the win, the same supporter ecosystem has produced its mirror image: the celebration police. Twenty-two years without a title and there is a genre of content whose job for the week is telling us how to feel about the one we just won. Calm down, it’s only the league. Have you forgotten the Invincibles? This squad isn’t that good. You won by points, not style.

Predictably, the celebration police are mostly former United players and the occasional sycophantic journo. Wayne Rooney – the dive in match fifty that ended the Invincibles’ run at forty-nine – watched our players celebrate reaching the Champions League final with the fans on the pitch after the Atletico second leg and criticised them for it. Reaching the final. Arsenal legend Ian Wright had to publicly tell Arsenal fans to ignore the celebration police – his phrase, not mine. They should put a statue of Wrighty outside the Emirates already. Roy Keane – former United hardman, never met an Arsenal player he did not want to kick – has been at this for over a decade. In 2014, after we reached the FA Cup final, he said our players needed a reality check for daring to celebrate at the final whistle. Last season they celebrated finishing fourth and now they celebrate beating a Championship side on penalties – we are talking about Arsenal FC here. Jamie Carragher – Liverpool legend, never won a league, current Sky Sports moralist about teams that do – told Martin Ødegaard to “get down the tunnel” in 2024 for the crime of taking a photograph after we beat Liverpool. In March of this year, with us still top of the table, he wrote that neutrals were rooting against us and called our online presence hysterical. The week before the Etihad in April, he predicted that an Arsenal defeat would make Pep Guardiola champion in May. When neither his prediction nor his rooting interest landed, he wrote a follow-up explaining why everyone else dislikes Arsenal. The follow-up is always there. The follow-up is the job. Gary Neville – also of United, who spent the 2004 fixture at Old Trafford kicking José Antonio Reyes every time he touched the ball, has spent two full title races publishing variations on the same column: Arsenal are not good enough, the squad is not deep enough, the title will be City’s, the title will be Liverpool’s, the title will be anyone else’s. He was wrong every week and back on air every week. The job is not to be correct. The job is to keep the suspicion of Arsenal in the air.

You see this on no other club. You did not see it for City the first time, or the fifth. You did not see it for Liverpool in 2020. You did not see it for United for two decades. The genre exists only for Arsenal, because the genre that preceded it – the AFTV meltdown, the talkSPORT call-in – trained the rest of football to think of our joy as suspicious. The world learned to hold us to a standard it holds no one else to. We taught them how.

And then there is the manager.

Mikel Arteta came to Arsenal as a player in 2011 from Everton. He captained the side from 2014, lifted two FA Cups, retired in 2016, and the following summer was on the bench at Manchester City as Pep Guardiola’s assistant. He stayed three years. He won two Premier League titles on Pep’s bench. Pep noticed something his other assistants did not do – when City scored against everyone else, Mikel jumped; when they scored against Arsenal, he stayed seated. Pep said it out loud years later: that guy likes Arsenal.

In 2018, when Arsène finally left, Arsenal passed Mikel over and hired Unai Emery instead. Eighteen months later, with the club in tenth place and the wheels coming off, they finally called him. He left City. He came home.

His first season we finished eighth, our worst league position since 1995. He won the FA Cup in August anyway – the first Arsenal manager to win a major trophy in his first season since George Graham in 1987. The second season we finished eighth again. Three painful years of teardown followed. Aubameyang exiled. Özil exiled. Mustafi and Xhaka shipped out. The backline rebuilt from scratch. By the time he was done, Arsène’s last side had been entirely sold or retired and the new spine was eighteen, twenty, twenty-two years old. Saka. Saliba. Martinelli. Ødegaard. Rice.

And then the title races came. Every one of them, every spring for four years, against the same man. Pep on one touchline, Mikel on the other. The teacher who had taught the student, the student who had spent three years studying the teacher’s notebook from inside the classroom. Each season closer than the last. Each second-place finish to the same team that had once been Mikel’s classroom. The fourth time of asking, the apprentice got him.

And here is the part nobody outside the family understands.

February 2008. Five points clear at the top. Martin Taylor broke Eduardo’s leg at St Andrew’s, we drew that match conceding a 95th-minute penalty, William Gallas sat down on the pitch in tears at the final whistle, and we won three of our next twelve. We finished third. Eduardo never played for us at that level again. In 2018-19 Liverpool took ninety-seven points – still the highest second-place total in Premier League history – and lost the title to City by one. They lost only one match all season. Klopp said it on the way out: as long as City had the money, no team was passing them easily. And then there was the refereeing. The penalties that did not go to us against City and did go to them against us. The yellows that should have been reds. The two-point margin in 2024 was inside the margin of decisions a neutral observer could not have called the same way twice. We did not need a conspiracy. We needed an explanation, and the explanation was the same explanation Liverpool had been given, and Eduardo, and Diaby, and Ramsey. The machine finds a way. The universe pays the bill in a currency the table does not record.

So we did not say it. Not in February when we were level. Not in March when we went a point clear. Not in April when the maths started to bend our way. Amy Lawrence wrote about this unique Arsenal psychology (trauma) for The Athletic in the spring of 2023 – trukke trukke, a phrase she picked up from Roma supporters chasing a Scudetto in 2001. The point of trukke trukke is that you do not name the thing you want, because to name it is to risk it. You call it the run. You call it what is happening. You do not call it the league. Amy wrote that piece in April 2023, when we were top and the title looked ours and you could feel it slipping at the edges. City won twelve in a row from February. We knew the rules even then. We talked around the word. We lost it anyway. We talked around it for two more seasons after that, and lost those too.

So this year we did not talk about it at all.

The reason we did not is that we had all seen the same horror movie too many times. The machine in sky blue. The petrodollar infrastructure. The genius on the touchline. And the giant robot at the centre of it all – Haaland, six-foot-five and built in a factory we cannot afford, the late-game equaliser that always seemed to be coming. The Etihad, ninety-eighth minute, Stones rising to head in the goal that stole us two points and then Haaland in Arteta’s face at the final whistle – telling our manager to stay humble. BTW, Haaland has not won the league since.

Sitting on the Arsenal bench that night, unused, was an eighteen-year-old kid called Myles Lewis-Skelly. Hale End since he was eight. Raised in Islington, a stone’s throw from the Emirates, born into the parish. He was wearing the forty-nine on his back because when they offered him a first-team number he turned it down. He knew what forty-nine meant to Arsenal. He wanted to keep it. After the final whistle Haaland got in his face too – an unused substitute, a kid he had never heard of – and shouted who the fuck are you? The kid took the insult and said nothing.

But, the next time Arsenal played City, the kid was starting at left-back. Sixty-third minute, Arsenal already 3-1 up, the score on its way to becoming 5-1. Lewis-Skelly turned in the box, slotted past Ortega for his first senior Arsenal goal, ran to the corner flag, and sat down cross-legged in Haaland’s meditation pose with the entire Emirates rising behind him. Haaland saw it. Haaland did not like it. The Emirates already had a chant – forty-nine, forty-nine, undefeated – for the Invincibles run. After that goal they added a new verse. Forty-nine, forty-nine, Lewis-Skelly. He’s one of our own.

And then there was Bernardo Silva, with two games to go, with us two points clear, with the title we were about to win sitting on the table between them and us. Told The Athletic, on the record, that we needed to man up. About the team that had spent five months at the top of the table while his own had been chasing. The contempt was institutional. We were the soft team. The team that did not want it enough. The team that did not bottle it because we never had the bottle in the first place. There was a meme that did the rounds all year – a City supporter caught on camera drinking out of an Arsenal water bottle in his own stadium, drinking out of us, with the running joke underneath: bottlers, bridesmaids again, here comes another second place. They were so sure. We were so sure they were right.

You watch enough of those and you stop trusting the table. You stop trusting the lead. You stop trusting the maths. The fixture list looks fine and you do not believe it. The gap is six points and you do not believe it. Because somewhere out there is the machine, and the machine is going to find a way. It always finds a way. It found a way in 2022 when Aubameyang was put in a fridge and we collapsed in the final weeks. It found a way in 2023 when we went top in January and City won twelve straight to catch us. It found a way in 2024 when we put up the highest second-place total in Premier League history and still finished second. You learn, after enough seasons of that, that the table is a trick the league plays on you. The table is a thing the universe is preparing to take away. Do not name it. Do not look at it directly. Do not say the word.

The thing that surprised me about this season was not that we won it. It was that, somewhere around March, I noticed I had stopped flinching. The body learns to expect the wound. And then one week it does not come, and the next week it does not come, and you realise you are watching a team that is going to do this. But I still did not say it. Right up until the maths made it impossible to lose, I did not say it.

And then, somehow, the bill came due in our favour. The machine did not find a way. The giant robot stayed in his factory. Bernardo Silva flew home with no medal. The City supporter drinking out of our bottle watched us lift a different one. And Myles Lewis-Skelly – in the team room where the squad watched City drop points against Bournemouth to mathematically hand Arsenal the title – held up a magnum of champagne and said it to a camera: they called us bottlers, but now we have the bottles. The kid said it. The maths held.

Fourteenth league title. Champions of England.

Nobody outside England fully understands what that means in 2026. The Premier League plays through Christmas. Boxing Day. New Year’s Day. There is no winter break in any meaningful sense. PSG took two full weeks off in December and came back to a fifth-tier cup tie. Bayern took most of January. We played Wolves away on a cold, dark, wet Tuesday while PSG players were sunning themselves on a beach in Dubai.

PSG are another state-sponsored machine. Owned by the Qatari state, just as we were pushed by Abramovich’s roubles and Abu Dhabi’s petrodollars before. The difference is that PSG do not have to work as hard as City, because they have no domestic competition. Ligue 1 is a one-club league. PSG have won eleven of the last thirteen titles, and the team chasing them this year was Lens. Their reigning Ballon d’Or winner, Ousmane Dembélé, has started nine league matches all season. Nine. The best player in the world does not play every game because there is no game to play. Luis Enrique rotates because he can. Arteta rotates because somebody is injured.

Riccardo Calafiori – our gorgeous, oft-injured left-back – has logged nineteen hundred competitive minutes in the league and in Europe this season, and that is the version of him that keeps breaking. Dembélé has played a third of that time and is the best player in the world. The fixture list is not the same fixture list. The calendar is not the same calendar. We are not playing the same sport.

The league below us is the deepest in the world by every honest measure. The hardest top to bottom. Wolves at home is a fixture other top clubs in Europe simply do not have on the calendar. Brentford away in December is a fixture you can lose. We do not get to take our feet off the pedal. And then there are the London derbies. Tottenham twice. Chelsea twice. West Ham twice. Crystal Palace twice. Fulham twice. Brentford twice. London is a city of six top-flight clubs and the emotional weight of that calendar is something only London clubs carry. Manchester City have one rival in their own city and that rival has been a sub-Champions League team for over a decade. Ferguson left and United fell apart, slowly, then all at once. Arsène left and we wobbled. We tried two managers who could not hold it together. And then we built it again, properly, with Arteta and an actual football operation behind him, and we are about to walk into a Champions League final having played a calendar that PSG would not recognise.

PSG eliminated us in the semi-final last year. They are our opponent in nine days, in Budapest.

Nobody knows what will happen against PSG. That is not the point of the letter. The point is that for the first time in a long time the bill came due in our favour. And we did not have to name it for it to arrive.

One more thing.

Eberechi Eze grew up an Arsenal supporter. Boyhood Gooner – in his case the cliché was true. Released from Hale End at 14, he bounced around, before finally becoming Crystal Palace’s talisman and leading them to win the FC Cup last year. Tottenham tried to sign him last summer. He could have gone. The wages would have been there. The minutes would have been there. The route was open. He did not want to go. Famously he called Areta, then drove in circles around the Emirates Stadium until the deal was confirmed. BTW, he scored five against Spurs this year. The boy who loved Arsenal, from a family of Gooners, who was released from the club, eventually got to grow up and play for them and win the league with them, all in one career. That does not happen often. It almost never happens. Except this year.

If there is a moral to thirty-seven years of this, it is that one. Sometimes the wait is the whole of it.

Trust the process.

Jump on the fun boat.

Sometimes it works out.

title: What I’m Reading This Summer
html:
Apologies, reader. It’s been a busy few weeks since I got back from Boston. I haven’t had much time for writing, with business projects booming and (ironically) two books getting ready for release. Plus, my son is home briefly before starting his co-op…

My dad actually emailed me the other day to ask if I had fallen and couldn’t get up, because he hadn’t seen a Substack post in a while. OK, Dad, I get it, neglecting this forum.

So, here’s my first post in a while:

Every summer I build a stack. Seven to ten books. Not a TBR, not aspirational – the books I’m actually going to read between Memorial Day and Labor Day, in roughly the order I’ll read them.

The tradition started inside curriculum redesign. One year I switched grades and inherited an Ancient Egypt unit. I prefer thematic teaching to geographic teaching, and I brought that approach to life in year two. But in year one, I wanted to read everything about Egypt. Toby Wilkinson’s The Last Dynasty. Kara Cooney’s When Women Ruled the World. That set the pattern.

Other summers got their own obsessions. One was World War One – Tuchman’s Guns of August, which I’d already read in isolation. But that summer, rather than serially read one book at a time, I organized my list, jumping from book to book, chapter by chapter, building the war chronologically across writers. Another summer it was Iliad retellings: Madeline Miller’s Circe and The Song of Achilles, Natalie Haynes’s A Thousand Ships, Caroline Alexander’s The War That Killed Achilles.

Those two summers eventually fused into a book of my own, The Wrath of Archie Ellis, currently being proofread. I’m aiming for an autumn 2026 release for that book, my third. It’s a structural retelling of the Iliad set at the Third Battle of Ypres in 1917 – Achilles and Hector rewritten as a British captain and a German Hauptmann. Twenty-four chapters, one for each book of Homer. I wanted to know what the rage of Achilles looks like without the elegy – and what kleos looks like in the age of modern war.

2016 was election books, naturally. Mayer’s Dark Money. Cramer’s classic about the 1988 race, What It Takes. And some prophetic doom-reading: Roth’s The Plot Against America and Lewis’s It Can’t Happen Here back to back. Lessig’s Republic, Lost for the campaign finance rot underneath all of it.

The Covid summer, when no one was going anywhere, was travelogues only. William Heat-Moon’s Blue Highways, Mayle’s Provence, Theroux’s The Great Railway Bazaar, Troost’s The Sex Lives of Cannibals, Oxenreider’s At Home in the World. That one bled into a longer arc – Frankopan, Weatherford, Harl, Anthony’s The Horse, the Wheel, and Language – on how the Silk Road and the steppe quietly built the modern world while everyone was looking the other way.

This year’s stack is heavier on nonfiction than usual, lighter on fiction, and built around a single question that’s been sitting with me since February of last year: What does it mean to build something durable in a moment when so much is being dismantled?

I run a small leadership coaching and consulting practice. Before that, nearly two decades in independent school education, and a stint at USAID’s Bureau of Humanitarian Assistance before the 2025 RIF. The throughline across all three institutions is the same one – how they form people, how they fail people, how they get built and broken. Most of what’s on this list is, one way or another, about that.

Here’s the stack.

1. Into the Wood Chipper: A Whistleblower’s Account of How the Trump Administration Shredded USAID – Nicholas Enrich. I have to start here. Enrich was USAID’s acting assistant administrator for global health when he was placed on administrative leave in March 2025 for telling the truth about what was happening to the agency. I lived a version of this story from a different seat, and I owe it to my former colleagues to read the version that becomes the record. Atul Gawande wrote the foreword. This is the book I’ve been putting off because I’m not sure I want to reread a lived experience. I think I’m ready now. It goes first.

2. One Day, Everyone Will Have Always Been Against This – Omar El Akkad. El Akkad’s title is the whole argument: institutions – and the people inside them – tend to discover their moral courage retroactively. The gap between stated values and revealed values is where most of the damage happens. The book is built around Gaza, and around what El Akkad calls the gap between the West's lofty ideals and its bloodstained reality. He's writing for Western centrists and liberals who didn't speak. I read it from the other side of that gap. At the time of the RIF, USAID's humanitarian response was being constrained by the Biden administration for the sake of the alliance with Israel – meaning the agency I worked for was being dismantled at exactly the moment it was already being prevented from doing the work it existed to do. Two institutional failures running at the same time. Reading this after Enrich isn't a pairing I planned so much as one that became inevitable.

3. Crisis Engineering: Time-Tested Tools for Turning Chaos into Clarity – Marina Nitze, Matthew Weaver, and Mikey Dickerson. This is the constructive inverse of the first two. Dickerson founded USDS after the healthcare.gov rescue; Nitze was CTO of the VA. Between them, they've spent a decade teaching federal agencies how to function under pressure. The book's opening question is When the system breaks, what do you do? – which, frankly, is most of what I do in my business. If the first two books are about how government capacity gets destroyed, this one is about how it gets built. I expect to mark it up heavily – there's real material here for the consulting work I do with mission-driven organizations.

4. The Coming Storm: Power, Conflict, and Warnings from History – Odd Arne Westad. Westad is a serious historian writing at the height of his powers. Most of what I read about the current moment is hot-take journalism that ages badly within weeks. Westad operates at a different time-scale, and I want my sense of scale recalibrated before the fall. What captured my attention was his appearance on the podcast Hidden Forces, where he frames his argument around the premise that 2026 looks a lot like 1914. See my interest in WW1, and its similarities with the Bronze Age Collapse and the end of the Edwardian World.

5. How Great Ideas Happen: The Hidden Steps Behind Breakthrough Success – George Newman. A cognitive scientist on the empirical mechanics of breakthrough thinking. I’ve spent years building operational frameworks for clients – CREATE, VOICES, the 6C Decision Compass – and I want to read someone with research credentials writing seriously about how good ideas actually emerge. I’ll be reading this with a pen in hand and probably arguing with it on every other page.

6. Strong Ground: The Lessons of Daring Leadership, the Tenacity of Paradox, and the Wisdom of the Human Spirit – Brené Brown. Brown’s argument is that bluster and cruelty are increasingly being framed as strength. She’s writing into the same cultural moment I write into, with a much bigger platform. I want to read her not as a fan but as a colleague – to see where her packaging is sharper than mine, where mine is sharper than hers, and what she’s missing that I should be saying louder.

7. The Power of Mattering – Zach Mercurio. The premise: showing people they matter is the most underrated lever in leadership. This sits squarely inside my EQ-i 2.0 and CliftonStrengths work, and I suspect at least one client conversation and one essay will come out of it. Short, well-researched, and immediately applicable.

8. Primal Intelligence: You Are Smarter Than You Know – Angus Fletcher. Fletcher draws on case studies of visionary thinkers and U.S. Army Special Operators to argue there’s a trainable form of intelligence that outperforms AI under volatility and uncertainty. I’ve written publicly about AI as a tool rather than a shortcut, and I want to read someone making a serious, non-hyped argument for what humans still uniquely contribute. This is the wildcard on the list – the one I expect to surprise me.

9. Open Socrates – Agnes Callard. Callard is one of the few living philosophers writing real philosophy for general readers. Her argument is that the examined life – the actual, rigorous Socratic version – looks almost nothing like what most of us call self-reflection. The Socratic method is the spine of what I do as a coach. Callard is going to press on whether I’m really doing it or just gesturing at it. This is the book I expect to change how I work.

10. The Death of Ivan Ilyich – Leo Tolstoy. The one classic on the list, and the one I should have read years ago. A successful judge confronts the meaninglessness of a life spent climbing institutional ladders without ever asking what he actually valued. I’m reading this at exactly the right moment – post-RIF, mid-pivot, building something I hope is the answer to the question Ivan Ilyich never quite asked himself in time. Short enough for two evenings. I expect it’ll stay with me for years.

That’s the stack. Witness and world, practice and philosophy. I’ll report back in September.

If you’re putting together your own list, I’d love to hear what’s on it. Reply or drop me a line.

– MG

Two of my own, since you’re here.

If you’re looking to put together your own summer reading list…

Balance – out now. My debut novel. Ellie Beckett is a CRISPR scientist in Kendall Square, thirteen years into a relationship with Alex, when her CEO starts paying a different kind of attention. Four POVs, no villains, no easy answers. The Ethical Slut explains ethical non-monogamy. An Atlantic piece argues about it. Balance lets you feel it – chosen family, female mentorship in STEM, the slow honesty of loving more than one person well. Find it on Amazon or on my author website: www.mkirkwrites.com .

CLUTCH – July 2026. The nonfiction one. I’m looking for a few more advance readers. If you want a free copy of the manuscript in exchange for an honest review at launch, click here to sign up for the ARC team. The argument: organizations grow people into leadership roles faster than they grow leadership capability, and the gap is where most of the damage happens. CLUTCH is the system I built to close it – an engine, a gearbox, and a GPS for founders and operators trying to lead under volatility without burning out the humans around them. If you’ve ever inherited a team you didn’t build, promoted someone before they were ready because no one else was, or watched a “good” decision-making process produce a bad decision in slow motion, the book is for you.

title: Seventy-Four Years Later
html:
Along the old Battle Road that runs between Lexington and Concord, there is a small stone marker almost hidden in the hostas. You can drive past it for years without noticing. I did. Someone had not.

The stone marks the graves of British Regulars who died on April 19, 1775.

The inscription, a stanza from a poem by James Russell Lowell, reads:

They came three thousand miles, and died, To keep the past upon its throne; Unheard, beyond the ocean tide, Their English mother made her moan.

Consider what the stanza refuses to do. It does not call these men invaders. It does not call them oppressors. It does not gloat. It names what they left behind: a mother, an ocean, a country that would never know where they fell.

Nobody composed these inscriptions in 1775. Lowell wrote the poem in 1849, after visiting one of these roadside graves with Nathaniel Hawthorne. Seventy-four years after the battle. The stones were placed over the decades that followed, some as late as 1910. British soldiers are buried at sites scattered along the road their army took that day, and nearly all of them have been marked, tended, and cared for by towns that had every reason to forget them.

A single generous moment is a mood. A century and a half of sustained attention is an architecture.

Here is the thing nobody in 1775 specified.

The Sons of Liberty designed the militia. They designed the muster. They designed the signals, the redundancy, the Committees of Correspondence, and the parallel routes. They designed every piece of the receiving culture that held when Revere was captured, and Prescott finished the ride. They designed all of it patiently, for years, in rooms whose minutes survive.

None of them designed a culture that would tend the graves of the men who came to kill them.

That was not in the architecture. It is what the architecture produced.

This week, somebody left two small wooden crosses with paper poppies and a Union Jack on a stone marking men whose names are not even carved on it. None of that was specified. All of it is what the culture the Sons of Liberty built made possible, without instruction, long after the architects were gone.

The deepest evidence of what your culture has actually built is what it produces that nobody specified. Not the handoffs you designed. Not the onboarding deck. Not the all-hands slides. What the culture does, at scale, in the long tail, for people who cannot repay the attention, when no one is watching and no one is keeping score.

Most companies that call themselves families have built the opposite of Battle Road.

They have built a culture whose downstream output is that the moment someone leaves – for a competitor, for a new sector, for a different life, for any reason at all – they become persona non grata. Slack access revoked Friday afternoon. The farewell lunch is the last time the name is spoken. A culture does not announce this. It just produces it, for every person who exits. Every time. The reason does not matter. The architecture handles the rest.

That is the downstream. That is what was actually built.

The word family was the marketing. The erasure is the architecture.

I left a company once that called itself a family. I still have occasion to be in the building. When management sees me coming, they put their heads down, change direction, find a reason to move away. My former teammates, seeing me in the same room, walk over for handshakes and slaps on the back.

Two responses to the same arrival. Only one of them was trained.

I kinda wanna send them a copy of CLUTCH when it drops, lol.

The stone is still there.

Notice what the receiving culture at Battle Road produced that nobody in 1775 asked for. Not the muster. Not the Minuteman companies. Not the victory. A small stone, tended for more than a century, for men whose names are not carved on it, by the same towns that mustered the minutemen who killed them.

The Sons of Liberty did not live to see this. The towns that placed the markers had no relationship with the men buried beneath them. The poet who wrote the stanza had been born forty-four years after the war. Every person in the chain was acting without supervision and without credit, in quiet repetition, for reasons that were never written down.

That is the test.

Not whether your founding documents are generous. Not whether your values doc reads well. The test is what your culture produces, unprompted and uncredited, for the people it no longer needs.

A Friday afternoon of revoked access.

Or a century and a half of quiet decisions.

Both are what the architecture built. Only one of them is what anyone would admit to designing.

The question is what your organization is producing, right now, that you did not specify.

Would you be proud of it if it were carved in stone seventy-four years from now?

title: A 13.1 Is a Sprint. A 26.2 Is a System.
html:
Patriots Day in Boston. THE marathon was run this past Monday. I haven’t qualified.

My PR is 3:30. For the BQ I’m chasing, I need 3:15. 15 minutes to shave across 26.2 miles. 30 seconds a mile. On paper, modest.

It means moving from an 8:00 pace to a 7:30 pace. In practice, a different race.

The Marine Corps was my first marathon. I’ve run others since. My halves are fast. Once I doubled up, Baltimore on Saturday and then flew to Boston to run the BAA Half Marathon on Sunday, I ran both under 1:30. That’s under 7:00 pace. Twice in 24 hours. I smoked my brother-in-law.

So I can run a 7:00 pace. I’ve proved it. I just can’t hold 7:30 for twice as long.

That’s the gap I’ve been chasing for years. Not a speed gap. An architecture gap.

Finishing a marathon, though, isn’t a big deal. How do you know if someone has run a marathon? Don’t worry: They’ll tell you. 🙋 Guilty.

Oprah ran a marathon, no disrespect. Ashton Kutcher ran 3:54. Ryan Reynolds ran 3:50. I smoked them both. Then Harry Styles ran 3:24 and smoked me.

Finishing is fitness. Qualifying is architecture.

A half-marathon and a full marathon are not the same race doubled. They are physiologically different events. The half finishes before mile 20. Before your glycogen runs out. Before the point where your training either holds or it doesn’t.

You can win a half on fitness and grit. You cannot win a full without the engine underneath.

Mile 22 of a full isn’t mile 12 of a half with more grit. It’s a different event entirely. One is still a sprint. The other is past the horizon of what willpower reaches.

Arlington taught me the rest.

In the Marine Corps Marathon, the course takes you past Arlington National Cemetery in the last mile. You think a marathon is loud until you run past rows of white stones, each one marking a person who gave the last full measure of devotion.

I wasn’t going to slow down. I couldn’t.

That wasn’t physiology. That wasn’t architecture. That was meaning. Meaning can carry the last mile. It cannot build the twenty before it.

I think about this with every founder I work with. They’ve all got a weekend where they ran two halves back to back.

They can point to it. The launch that nearly killed them. The fundraiser. The quarter they pulled out of the fire with a whiteboard and a suitcase. That weekend is real. It’s also the most dangerous reference point they carry.

They look at that weekend and think it’s proof they can scale. It isn’t. A weekend is a sprint. Scale is a system.

Somewhere between 40 and 80 employees, founders try to run a 26.2 at half-marathon pace. The engine that handled 15 people does not handle 60. Meetings that used to decide things now consume them. Issues that were resolved in a Slack thread now need a standup. The standup that used to surface problems now reveals five people solving the same one. The founder works harder. The output grows more slowly.

Not a motivation problem. A physiology problem. Running another heroic weekend doesn’t put fuel back in.

A 13.1 is a sprint. A 26.2 is a system. Confuse them, and you spend a decade trying to outrun the architecture you never built.

This is why I still want to BQ. Not for the medal. Because I want to know I’ve built the engine. Not just the willpower. Not just the peak fitness. The architecture that holds across 26.2.

Boston isn’t a goal. It’s a diagnostic.

The halves prove I can run the pace. I don’t know yet whether I’ve built the system.

THREE QUESTIONS FOR THE FOUNDER AT MILE 20

Before your next leadership meeting, sit with these:

  1. What’s the weekend you point to as proof you can scale? How long ago was it, and what did it prove?

  2. Where in your company are you running 26.2 at half-marathon pace? Where is the effort trying to do what architecture should?

  3. If you removed yourself from the race tomorrow, what mile would the company fail to finish?

If those questions hit a nerve, you’re not alone. Most of the founders I work with arrive at the same place around 40 to 80 employees: their effort is no longer the asset moving the company forward, and nobody has said it out loud yet.

That’s the work. Building the architecture that lets you step back without the company breaking. If you’re the founder at mile 20, reach out.

title: The Night Nobody Waited for Orders
html:
Isaac Davis led his Acton company at the front of the advance on North Bridge. He was killed in the first volley.

His company kept advancing.

That is what distributed readiness looks like.

By the time the British Regulars reached the bridge on the morning of April 19, 1775, the Minutemen from Concord, Lincoln, Acton, and five other towns were already in position. Thirty-two companies. Roughly 1,380 men. They had mustered inside the window, the name implies – a minute’s notice, or close enough that it matters. Nobody had told them to converge on North Bridge. They had pre-decided where to go. They had drilled the rally points through the winter. When the alarm came, the question was not what do we do. It was how fast we could get there.

Now contrast that with how your organization moves when the bell rings.

A Slack message pings. It goes through a manager, who routes it to a VP, who routes it to the founder. Three days later, a decision lands. By then, the window has closed, the client has moved on, and the person closest to the problem has learned exactly what you did not want her to learn.

Most organizations I work with have built the opposite of distributed readiness. Central authority. Untrained edges. A culture that quietly punishes anyone who acts without permission, and then complains that nobody takes initiative. The founder wants his team to move fast. He has also, without realizing it, made sure that moving fast requires three approvals, a decision memo, and a meeting.

You know the textures.

The VP who tells the new hire to use her judgment on Monday, then overrules her in front of her peers on Wednesday.

The all-hands speech about ownership, delivered by the same founder who personally signed a vendor invoice at nine p.m. last Tuesday because the team was “still getting up to speed.”

The capable hire on day ninety who has stopped asking for permission and started waiting to be told, because she has learned which one gets her through the quarter without a fight.

By midmorning at Concord, Lieutenant Colonel Francis Smith was still sending officers back to Boston to ask for reinforcements he would not see for hours. His column was being fired on from stone walls by men who had never been introduced to each other and did not need to be. Smith brought the best-trained professional infantry in the world. He lost because he did not build the Minutemen. He brought Regulars.

If you are the Head of People or Operations reading this, you are probably the Minuteman of your own organization and have been for a while. You have drilled your team on the patterns they need. You have written the playbooks nobody reads until the night they break. You have built the receiving culture that the founder takes credit for when the save happens.

Here is the harder question.

The readiness your organization thinks it has – is it actually yours? Carried in your head, in your inbox, in the Slack threads you are on that nobody else reads? If you left tomorrow, would the muster pattern leave with you?

What you are watching is not a people problem. It is an engine running on three missing cylinders.

Teaching is what closes the competence gap – not the skills gap, the authority gap, the knowing-what-you-are-allowed-to-decide gap. Agility is what gives the edges permission to respond to conditions the center cannot see. Execution is the muscle memory that turns a situation into a response without waiting for instructions. Skip one, and you get an organization that looks busy and moves slowly.

The Minutemen had all three. The Provincial Congress had spent six months building Teaching into every town. Agility was pre-authorized by the Committee of Safety in October of 1774 – every competent militiaman had pre-cleared authority to alarm his own neighbors without asking Boston for permission. Execution lived in the weekly drills. When the bell rang, the question of who decides had already been answered. The company commanders did not need a Slack thread.

The capable person on day thirty who needs permission to act is not a training issue. She is a map of where your authority structure has not caught up with your growth.

Every time she escalates a decision she was hired to make, the organization pays a distributed readiness tax.

Nobody measures it. Everybody feels it. And the person who feels it most is usually the person who wrote the onboarding and has been quietly absorbing the gap ever since.

This week's move for you is not to build the whole system. You cannot. You do not own the authority lines that are the real problem.

The move is to pick one decision that currently routes through three people and name it to your leadership team as an example of what distributed readiness would cost. One call. Not a strategy memo. Not a culture initiative. One specific decision, one specific delay, one specific dollar figure. Make the tax visible.

Regulars wait for orders. Minutemen muster on the bell.

The question is which one you have been quietly building.

If you want the frameworks that structure this precisely, the CREATE engine names the three cylinders the Provincial Congress built into every Massachusetts town six months before the British marched — Teaching, Adaptability, Execution — the three that turn a capable hire into a trained Minuteman instead of a regular waiting for orders. The 6C Decision Compass maps the authority conversation the Committee of Safety had before the alarm ever rang, six decision modes and five delegation levels, one grid that tells you exactly where the line sits before you hand anything off. DELEGATE gives you the eight-step handoff architecture for moving a real decision from the center to the edges, not just writing a new job description and hoping the rest follows.
