title: Paul Revere Was the Failure
html:
Paul Revere was not supposed to matter.

Hi, welcome from Boston. Those are fighting words. I wasn’t planning on writing this week; I’m up here to visit my parents. We missed each other at Easter, so I decided to come visit them this week. While I was here tho… an idea popped into my head. Yesterday was Patriots’ Day — the running of the Boston Marathon - but also the anniversary of the shots heard round the world - the Battle of Lexington and Concord.

And of course, why did the colonists “win” the day — because of course, listen my children and you will hear of the midnight ride of Paul Revere.

But hold on a sec… hear me out.

The Sons of Liberty spent years engineering a system that was never supposed to depend on him. They built Committees of Correspondence in every town. They drilled militia captains weekly. They pre-positioned powder and pre-arranged rally points. They designed signal protocols so redundant that if the primary messenger went down, the message would still reach its destination. They sent three riders that night, not one. Dawes took the land route. Prescott joined in Lexington. The lanterns in the Old North Church were a backup in case no rider got through at all.

The whole architecture was designed to refuse a hero.

And yet.

What do we remember? Longfellow, 1860. Hoof beats. Lanterns. One man warns a sleeping country sounds great, right? Eighty-five years after the ride, a poet wrote the architecture out of the story and wrote a single rider in. Total myth. But a lot sexier than “systems” or “procedures.” The receiving culture, the redundancy, the drilled captains, the parallel routes, the sexton in the steeple. All of it collapsed into one silhouette on a horse.

That is the failure I want to talk about. It is not a failure of Revere. He did his job. The failure is that the system the Sons of Liberty built was good enough to win a war and bad enough to get remembered as one man’s midnight ride.

This is the hero worker problem.

In my work, I call someone a “hero worker” when the organization has come to depend on them in a way the original design never intended. You know the one. The person whose out-of-office email makes three VPs panic. The name that shows up in every postmortem as the reason the crisis did not become a catastrophe. The employee whose resignation letter triggers an emergency leadership meeting before the coffee is cold. They are not villains. They are often the most committed person in the building. The problem is structural. The organization runs through them, and when they are tired, unreachable, or gone, the system does not realize what it has lost until it tries to operate without them.

Every founder I work with has a Paul Revere. Sometimes two. Sometimes the founder is the Paul Revere.

Here is the part of the Revere story most of us did not learn.

Paul Revere never made it to Concord.

He was captured by a British patrol outside Lexington. Stopped on the road, questioned, and held for hours. I did not know this for most of my life. A few years ago, my brother-in-law took me running on the route. He pointed out the spot where Revere was arrested. I stood there, breathing hard, and said what most people say when they find out. What do you mean, he was arrested? How did the message get out then?!

Seventh-grade history did not cover that part. Not for me, probably not for you unless you grew up in Boston. The poem does not cover it either. Longfellow does not want you to know his hero never made the last leg. Because the moment you know that, the whole story changes.

The message reached Concord because Samuel Prescott did. A local doctor who joined the ride in Lexington, who knew the roads, who kept going when the other two riders were stopped or thrown. Prescott finished what Revere started. Take that, Malcolm Gladwell - stay with me here... *

The militia companies mustered on time. The redundancy held.

The system worked because Revere failed.

Read that sentence again. The system worked because Revere failed. If the Sons of Liberty had bet the revolution on him, the British patrol that stopped him on the road to Concord ends the story. But they did not bet on him. They built something that could survive his capture. Prescott was not a backup plan after the fact. He was the design. The redundancy is what saved the revolution.

That is what a receiving culture is. An engineered condition. In the CREATE framework, it is the intersection of three of the six cylinders: Culture, Teaching, and Execution, running in sync long before the message arrives. Culture is what makes the captain willing to get out of bed. Teaching is what gave him the drill patterns he executes without thinking. Execution is the muscle memory that turns a warning into a mustered company in forty minutes. One cylinder is missing, and the ride is a ghost story.

The Sons of Liberty built all three. They built them patiently, without credit, in towns whose names nobody wrote a poem about. The receiving culture won the day at Concord. The ride got remembered.

The 6C Decision Compass maps the authority conversation the Committee of Safety had before the British marched. Six decision modes – Command, Consultative, Collaborative, Consensus, Core Expert, Choice – crossed with five delegation levels, one grid that tells you exactly where the line sits before you hand anything off.

Sorry, the social studies teacher in me can’t resist; feel free to skip if this bores you, not offended:

The Massachusetts Provincial Congress did not improvise its authority structure on April 18th. Six months earlier, in October of 1774, it had voted Joseph Warren and the Committee of Safety formal power to alarm and muster the militia. It had directed every town to raise companies of minutemen. It had pre-positioned the stores at Concord and designated who held which call. By the time Warren sent Revere out the door on the night of April 18, the authority conversation had already happened. When Prescott picked up the warning in Lexington and carried it into Concord, he was not asking for permission from Boston. He was operating inside a decision architecture the Provincial Congress had built six months earlier, under which any competent militiaman in any town had pre-authorized authority to alarm his own neighbors. That is what the 6C does. It takes the conversation most organizations have in the middle of a crisis – who gets to decide this right now? – and moves it to a time when nobody is bleeding, and everyone is thinking clearly. Without that grid, every handoff becomes a negotiation in the dark.

DELEGATE is the eight-step handoff architecture for building the Prescott your organization needs, rather than promoting the person closest to ready and hoping the rest follows. Most leaders treat delegation as a single event. A title changes, an inbox gets forwarded, a Slack channel gets transferred, and the assumption is that ownership has moved with the paperwork. It has not. Ownership transfers through eight steps – including the Title versus License distinction most organizations collapse into one – and skipping any of them leaves the new owner holding the title without the license to act. Prescott did not finish Revere’s ride because he had been handed a business card. He finished it because the Provincial Congress had built the underlying competence, context, and authority into every minuteman company in Massachusetts, long before the night anyone needed it. That is the difference between a promotion and a handoff. A promotion is the announcement. A handoff is the architecture. DELEGATE is how you build the second, so you stop relying on the first.

The chairman of the Committee of Safety – Joseph Warren, the man who engineered the authority structure and dispatched Revere on the night of April 18 – died at Bunker Hill two months later. He did not live to see the system he built run at scale. It ran anyway. That is what a receiving culture is supposed to do.

Outlive the architect.

And we’re back…

Most of us in advisory work spend our days on the wrong end of this inversion. A client walks us through the save. The all-nighter. The call to the vendor. The founder who flew out at four in the morning to close the deal. We are supposed to be impressed. And the save was real. But the story the client is telling is a Longfellow story. One rider. One crisis. One legend. The receiving culture, if it exists, goes unnamed. If it does not exist, nobody notices because the ride is covered for its absence.

The question the client almost never asks is who was already awake.

Who had been organizing the downstream response before the crisis hit? Whose prior work made the midnight call possible? What receiving culture caught the message and ran with it while the founder got the credit for the ride? And the harder version. What happens the night the rider does not make it?

If your client cannot name the people who make the rider replaceable, you are working with an organization that has quietly organized itself around its Paul Revere. That is what needs to be named. Not the rider. The dependence.

* see: Malcolm Gladwell (a Canadian, lol) called Revere a “Connector” in The Tipping Point and used the ride to argue that certain people move ideas because of who they know. Gladwell’s Connector is the poem in a new suit. Total myth again. The real leadership question is not who the rider is or why his network is special. It is why the organization ever needed to depend on him in the first place, and whether the receiving culture would have held if the British Regulars had captured him earlier in the night.

Which, for the record, they did. And we won.

CLUTCH: How Leaders Build Systems That Run Without Them is a book about that question. CREATE is the engine that builds the receiving culture. The 6C Decision Compass is the grid that decides who holds which call before the crisis arrives. DELEGATE is the architecture that turns the Prescott in your organization into the person who finishes the ride when the named hero does not make it. The Sons of Liberty did all three. The poem erased all three. Most organizations repeat the erasure every quarter.

Here is the move for you this week.

The next time a client walks you through a late-night save, do not ask what they did. Do not ask how they handled it. Ask who was already awake when the message came in. Ask who had been building the room that could receive it. Ask what those people were doing six months earlier that nobody credited at the time. And then ask the question the client will not want to hear.

Who are you treating as a Paul Revere? And what happens on the night the rider does not make it?

The ride is a poem. The receiving culture is an organization. The failure is telling yourself you have built the second when what you have built is the first.

THREE QUESTIONS FOR ADVISORS AND COACHES

When a client walks you through their latest late-night save, sit with these:

  1. Who in the organization is being treated as a Paul Revere right now? What would it cost the company if that person did not make it to Concord?

  2. If the rider left tomorrow, would the receiving culture still be there? Or does it live in one person’s head and phone?

  3. What question could you ask your client this week that would surface the infrastructure they have been taking credit for, and the dependence they have been mistaking for strength?

If those questions hit a nerve, you’re not alone. Most of the organizations I work with – founders, leadership teams, schools, nonprofits, government agencies – arrive at the same place: the rider gets remembered, the receiving culture goes invisible, and the next crisis exposes the gap.

My work is building the infrastructure that closes it.

If you want the frameworks that structure this precisely, the 6C Decision Compass maps the authority conversation the Committee of Safety had six months before Revere ever mounted a horse – six decision modes, five delegation levels, one grid that tells you exactly where the line sits before you hand anything off. DELEGATE gives you the eight-step handoff architecture for building the Prescott your organization actually needs, not just promoting the person closest to ready and hoping the rest follows. CREATE is the engine underneath both – the six cylinders that build the receiving culture long before the night anyone needs it. All three are in CLUTCH.

title: The Succession Tax
html:
Your organization lost approximately 14 hours this week to decisions that were held, deferred, or made badly because there was no one authorized to make them well. That’s 28 decisions sitting in a holding pattern, thirty minutes of organizational friction each.

That’s before you count what left with your best person. Gallup’s research on employee turnover places the conservative replacement cost for a senior leader at 100 to 150% of annual salary, once you account for recruiting, onboarding, lost productivity, and the institutional knowledge that doesn’t transfer. As the Transition Tax established, external replacement runs three to five times the cost of developing from within. No one ran either number. No one will.

The Succession Tax doesn’t start when someone leaves.

It starts the moment the organization has no viable answer to a simple question: if the founder stepped back for ninety days, who runs this? Not who would try. Who actually could.

Most founders never ask it. Not because they don’t care – because the question feels like a trap. Naming a number two feels like rehearsing your own replacement. And the rationalization that holds the trap in place is usually this: the organization needs me fully present. That’s true, which is exactly what makes the trap effective. The more the organization needs you, the more logical it feels to stay, and the less space there is to build the infrastructure that would eventually make your constant presence unnecessary.

So the question doesn’t get asked. And the tax runs.

Here’s what it looks like before anyone leaves.

Jonathan has been at the company for four years. He’s the founder’s most trusted operator – the person who can read the room, make the call, hold the thread. In February, the founder takes two weeks off. Not catastrophically: a long-deferred vacation, a real one, phone mostly down.

By day three, Jonathan has a list of eleven decisions he’s holding. Not because he can’t make them. Because he doesn’t know which ones he’s supposed to make, and asking feels like admitting the founder left without a handoff. Two members of the team have quietly stopped bringing him problems – not out of disrespect, but because the informal authority map said every hard thing goes up. The org chart didn’t change. But something contracted.

By day ten, two proposals have missed their windows. One vendor has moved to a competitor – the same vendor Jonathan had spent eight months building a relationship with, the one who’d given the company favorable terms twice because he trusted Jonathan specifically. The founder comes back, clears the queue in a week, and calls it a good trip.

Jonathan puts his resume on LinkedIn six weeks later.

The founder doesn’t connect the two weeks to the six weeks. That’s the design of the tax. The departure reads as a retention problem, a compensation issue, a better offer somewhere else. What it actually was: a man who spent four years building real organizational capacity, discovered in two weeks that the capacity wasn’t structurally his, and drew the only rational conclusion available.

The Succession Tax runs on everything the accounting system can’t see. The eight months of relationship capital that walked out with Jonathan. The institutional memory of why that vendor deal was structured the way it was. Which nobody else fully understood, and which nobody thought to document, because Jonathan was always there.

The talent retention cost is the one nobody runs until it’s too late.

Your best people can see the ceiling from the moment they arrive. They’re not impatient. They’re accurate. When it becomes clear that the trajectory ends at the founder’s shoulder, they leave for somewhere with headroom.

This isn’t disloyalty. It’s arithmetic. And it compounds. The second-best person watches the best person leave, does the same calculation, and arrives at the same answer. The ceiling doesn’t just stop people from rising. It accelerates the rate at which the people most capable of raising it decide to go raise it somewhere else.

Succession isn’t retirement planning. It’s resilience infrastructure.

A number two isn’t a replacement. It’s a redundancy layer. You don’t configure a backup the week the primary fails. You configure it when everything is working, because that’s the only time you have the capacity to do it right.

Building that layer requires a designed progression – not a title change, not a mentorship conversation, but a deliberate expansion of authority in stages. Each stage requires the leader to release something real, and most organizations stall at the first one indefinitely.

The first stage moves the successor from executing your decisions to making their own. Most handoff failures stop here. The authority hasn’t moved – only the task. The successor is still routing every call upward because nobody established what they actually own.

The second stage moves them from consulting you to acting and informing. They make the call, then tell you. Not ask. The shift is small. The effect on organizational capacity is not. This is the stage that requires explicit decision rights – the kind the 6C Decision Compass maps precisely.

The third stage moves them from holding your framework to building theirs. This is where you give up something real: the assumption that your way of reading a situation is the only reliable one. Amy Edmondson’s research is instructive here – people don’t develop independent judgment in environments where exercising it feels risky. If the successor knows you’ll second-guess the call, they’ll keep asking before they make it. The Jonathan scenario is what happens when an organization never gets out of stage one.

Three signals the Succession Tax is running right now:

  1. The two-week test: if you stepped back tomorrow for two weeks – real absence, not checking in – would your team know which decisions to make and which to hold? If the answer requires you to brief anyone before you leave, the infrastructure isn’t there.

  2. The ceiling signal: when you look at your top two or three performers, can you describe a specific path upward for each of them that doesn’t require you to leave? If the path is vague, they’ve already mapped it, and it ends at the door.

  3. The handoff gap: when you’re in a meeting and you’re about to make a call, is there anyone in the room you’d trust to make it without you? Not someone you’re developing – someone who could step in tomorrow without a briefing. If the honest answer is no, you’re a single point of failure, and you’ve been paying the tax since the moment that became true.

You already know whether the tax is running. The two-week test told you. The ceiling signal told you. The handoff gap told you.

The harder question: which signal are you most tempted to explain away?

title: The Transition Tax
html:
Your organization paid approximately 22 hours this week to a cost that doesn’t appear on any balance sheet. That’s the newly promoted leader spending two hours a day navigating decisions they were never told they owned (10 hours), four direct reports each losing thirty minutes a day to unclear direction and recalibration (10 hours), and the original leader absorbing two hours of decisions that should never have reached their level. The promotion happened last month. The tax started the day you made it.

Nobody tracked those hours. Nobody will.

Here’s how it happened.

Maya spent six years becoming your best ops lead. She ran projects clean, kept her team intact during the hard quarters, and knew the difference between a process problem and a people problem. Last month you gave her a title, four direct reports, a new box on the org chart, and your genuine confidence that she was ready.

What you didn’t give her: a definition of what decisions she now owns and which ones still need your sign-off. A structured handoff of the relationships she inherited. A plan for the first ninety days that was about her development, not her team’s deliverables. Any scaffold at all.

So she’s doing what promoted leaders always do. She’s figuring it out.

Organizations grow people into leadership roles faster than they grow leadership capability.

Not because leaders are unwilling. Not because managers are failing. Because promotion is visible, fast, and cheap, and leadership infrastructure is invisible, slow, and expensive. So organizations do the visible thing. They hand someone a new title and call it an investment.

It isn’t. It’s a liability with a delayed payment schedule.

The research is specific about what that liability costs. According to Josh Bersin’s work on internal mobility, replacing a leader externally costs three to five times more than growing one from within. McKinsey’s data adds that organizations promoting internally are 2.2 times more likely to outperform peers, and their leaders reach full productivity 50% faster. The implication runs in both directions: internal development done well is a performance multiplier, and internal development done without infrastructure is the most expensive version of both outcomes at once. You promoted from within, which was right. You handed over a title without a handoff system, which is where the tax starts running.

The cost lands in three places simultaneously, which is part of why it’s so easy to miss.

The promoted person is operating without decision rights they can name, relationships they’ve had time to earn, or a framework for the ten situations they’ve never encountered before. They’re burning goodwill they don’t know they have by making calls that weren’t theirs to make, and deferring on calls they should own. They’re learning leadership by practicing it on the people they manage. That’s not professional development. It’s extraction.

The team under them is being managed by someone in the middle of figuring out what managing means. The cost is real and diffuse – slower decisions, unclear ownership, the particular exhaustion that comes from not knowing what your manager is trying to accomplish. High performers start looking for clarity, and some of them schedule the call with the recruiter who’s been in their inbox for three months.

The original leader – the founder, the VP above the new role – is now absorbing the gap between what the promoted person can do and what the role actually requires. You’re adding feedback loops that shouldn’t exist at your level, catching things that should have been caught earlier, making yourself available in ways that weren’t in the plan. The bottleneck you were trying to remove just moved one level down. And now it’s hiding.

This isn’t a management failure. It’s not a hiring mistake or a performance problem. It’s a design choice – one that most organizations make by default because they haven’t built an alternative. The alternative is expensive and invisible, and the default is cheap and fast, and most organizations are busy. So they choose the default.

The problem is that defaults compound.

Every underprepared leader produces more underprepared leaders. Every promotion without infrastructure teaches the next person what promotion looks like.

What actually promoting someone requires isn’t mentorship. It isn’t check-ins. It’s three specific things, and they all have to happen before day one in the new role. Together, they form the core of DELEGATE, the handoff framework at the center of CLUTCH.

Role clarity with decision rights. Not a job description – a map of what this person now owns, where the edges are, and what “escalate” means in practice. Decision rights that aren’t explicit get filled in by assumption, and assumption is where teams break.

An explicit relationship handoff. Who did this role interface with, what does each of those people need from this position, and what’s the current status of each relationship? This doesn’t happen automatically. It requires a conversation and a transfer of context.

A ninety-day capability plan. Not an onboarding checklist. A development arc: what does this person need to be able to do by day thirty, day sixty, day ninety that they can’t fully do today, and what’s the mechanism for building it?

Before you hand anyone a new title, three questions:

  1. Can this person name three decisions that will now be theirs to own that weren’t before, and three they’ll need to give up?

  2. Can you describe, specifically, what support they’ll receive in the first ninety days – and is that support structural or interpersonal? Lunch doesn’t count.

  3. If they struggled visibly in month two, what’s the plan that isn’t “have a conversation”?

These aren’t interview questions. They’re a conversation you have with yourself – or with your leadership team – before the title changes.

Think about the last promotion you made. Not a title change: a genuine transfer of leadership responsibility.

title: The Meeting Tax
html:
Your organization lost approximately 12 hours this week to a cost that doesn’t appear on any balance sheet. That’s five people, one shadow conversation per day, thirty minutes each, across a five-day week. It was processed in a parking lot, a Slack thread, and someone’s kitchen at dinner.

No one tracked those hours. No one will.

It’s 5:47 pm and Sarah is sitting in her car in the parking garage, phone out, typing the message she didn’t send from the conference room. Not because she forgot. Because the room didn’t feel like the place. Eleven minutes earlier, in the standup, she said “sounds good.”

She means neither word.

The Slack DM goes to the one colleague she trusts to read it without it becoming a thing. Her colleague will respond. They’ll reach a conclusion. It will inform what they both do tomorrow. None of it will appear in the meeting notes.

This pattern isn’t isolated. It’s a system.

The parking lot debrief, the Slack thread that opens eleven minutes after the standup, the dinner conversation that ends with a spouse knowing more about the organizational dysfunction than the leader does – these aren’t random. They’re the same channel, running in parallel, processing what the formal one wouldn’t.

This isn’t disloyalty. It’s architecture failure.

When formal channels don’t process what they need to, informal channels adapt. Every time, in every organization, without exception. This isn’t a character flaw in your team. It’s a design outcome. The shadow channel exists because the formal one left something unprocessed, and the organization found another way to carry it.

Keith Davis mapped this dynamic in his 1953 Harvard Business Review paper “Management Communication and the Grapevine” and found that shadow channels weren’t random gossip systems. They were highly structured, often more accurate than formal communications, and almost always filling a specific gap the formal system had created. The question organizational anthropologists keep asking isn’t how to eliminate shadow channels. It’s what gap they’re filling.

Dual-channel organizations pay twice for the same work.

The formal channel runs meetings, produces agendas, generates notes. The informal channel runs the actual decision-making, surfaces the real dissent, builds the alignment the formal channel couldn’t produce. Decisions made in the parking lot don’t appear in the meeting notes. Dissent processed in a Slack DM disappears when the thread does. The informal channel carries real organizational work without any of the accountability structures of the formal one – no record, no shared understanding, no way to know if what got decided actually held.

Three failure modes reliably produce shadow channels, and if you’re honest, you’ll recognize at least one of them in your last month of meetings.

The first is the meeting where dissent isn’t safe. The room reads the leader’s body language, calibrates to what’s wanted, and produces agreement. The parking lot produces the actual response. Amy Edmondson’s research on psychological safety documented this pattern precisely: teams in low-safety environments don’t stop having the real conversation – they relocate it. What looks like alignment in the room is often compliance, and compliance routes around the formal channel the moment the meeting ends. In CLUTCH’s 6C framework, this is what Command mode overstay produces: an authority gradient so steep that accurate dissent can’t surface where it would actually be useful.

The second is the agenda that never includes the real issue. Every organization has a topic that’s been on the informal agenda for months and never appeared on a formal one – the restructure nobody’s named, the performance issue everyone’s working around, the strategic question the leader hasn’t opened. When the formal channel consistently avoids what the organization most needs to process, the informal one picks it up by default.

The third is the leader who signals they’ve already decided. The question is asked. The room knows the answer is predetermined. The meeting becomes theater, and the shadow channel becomes the place where people process what it felt like to sit through it.

Each failure mode produces a different shadow channel. Together they tell you exactly what the formal system is failing to do.

Before your next all-hands, one question:

What would your team say in the parking lot after this meeting that they won’t say in the room?

If you can answer it, you already know where the formal channel is failing. If you can’t, that’s the more important answer.

Shadow channel audit – three signals:

  1. The signal that people agreed in the room but recalibrated in execution maps to the first failure mode: dissent isn’t safe, and compliance isn’t commitment.

  2. The signal that the same topic keeps surfacing informally but never formally maps to the second: the agenda is consistently avoiding what the organization most needs to process.

  3. The signal that your team stops asking questions once a direction is set maps to the third: the leader signaled the outcome before the room opened, and the meeting was theater.

If you recognize more than one, the formal channel has more than one gap.

You already know the topic. The one your team has been processing informally for months that has never appeared on a formal agenda.

title: The Clarity Tax
html:
Your organization lost approximately 12 hours this week to a cost that doesn’t appear on any balance sheet. That’s five people, one deferred decision per day, 30 minutes of delay each, every day this week. It shows up as a question nobody could answer without you.

Nobody tracked those hours. Nobody will.

The proposal has been sitting in a shared folder for three days.

It’s not complicated. The vendor needs a decision on scope before they can finalize the timeline. Two people on the team know enough to make the call. Either of them could have sent the email on Monday. Neither did, because they weren’t sure if they were supposed to, and asking felt like admitting they didn’t know something they should, and waiting felt safer than being wrong about their own authority.

It’s Thursday. The vendor follows up. The founder sees the thread, answers in four minutes, and moves on.

Nobody flags it as a problem. It wasn’t a crisis. It was just Tuesday, and Wednesday, and Thursday.

And it’s running in twelve other places you’re not watching.

The smartest person in the room is often the bottleneck.

Not because they’re bad at leading. Because their intelligence hasn’t been systemized. Every decision that routes through one brain – regardless of how capable that brain is – creates a single point of failure. The organization doesn’t slow down because the leader is wrong. It slows down because the leader is the only one who knows they’re allowed to be right.

The 12 hours is just what you can count. The Clarity Tax runs on everything the accounting system can’t see: the decision that got made wrong because the right person wasn’t authorized to make it, the initiative that never started because nobody was sure who could greenlight it, the vendor relationship that cooled while a folder sat untouched.

Ambiguity doesn’t feel like a problem from the inside. It feels like control. It taxes everyone underneath it.

The airline industry named this problem in 1978 and learned it the hard way.

United Airlines Flight 173 was approaching Portland with a landing gear indicator that wouldn’t confirm the gear was down. Straightforward troubleshooting, except the captain stayed in the problem for over an hour. The first officer knew the fuel state. The flight engineer knew the fuel state. Both of them said something – obliquely, carefully, in the language of people who understood that the authority structure in that cockpit made directness feel like insubordination. The captain processed their hints as background noise. The engines flamed out six miles from the runway. Ten people died.

The year before, two Boeing 747s had collided on a fog-shrouded runway in Tenerife, killing 583 people, still the deadliest accident in aviation history. The KLM captain – one of the most experienced pilots in the world – had begun his takeoff roll while a Pan Am 747 was still on the runway. His first officer had hesitations. He voiced them in the softest possible register. The captain didn’t stop. The authority gradient in that cockpit was so steep that a junior crew member’s uncertainty couldn’t overcome a senior captain’s momentum, even when the junior crew member was right and the captain was about to kill everyone on board.

NASA researchers H. Clayton Foushee and Robert Helmreich led the foundational work that followed. Analyzing the crash record, they found that more than 70% of aviation accidents involved not mechanical failure, not weather, but human error – and that the specific human errors clustered around three things: leadership failures, coordination failures, and decision-making failures. The aircraft were fine. The hierarchy was the hazard.

What followed was Crew Resource Management. The fix wasn’t to flatten the hierarchy. Captains still captained. The fix was to make authority explicit and obligation clear: every crew member wasn’t just permitted to raise a concern or name an error – they were required to. Speaking up stopped being an act of courage against the culture and became a structural requirement of the role. The first officer on Flight 173 had the information that would have saved ten lives. What he lacked wasn’t knowledge or nerve. He lacked a system that made it unambiguous that his job included saying it out loud, directly, regardless of how the captain might receive it.

The flight deck didn’t get flatter. It got clearer.

United Airlines implemented CRM training in 1981. The industry followed. The crash record changed.

Your organization has its own version of this dynamic, and it almost certainly isn’t in the cockpit. It’s in the proposal that sat in the shared folder for three days while two people waited to find out if they were the ones supposed to send it. The information existed. The authority to act on it didn’t – or wasn’t clear enough to act on without asking, and asking felt like admitting something, and admitting something felt like risk. So they waited. The vendor followed up. The founder answered in four minutes.

A system where one person makes all the calls isn’t a leadership structure. It’s a bottleneck with good intentions, and it produces the same outcome every time: the people closest to the problem have the information, and the system gives them no unambiguous path to act on it.

Decision rights don’t need to be complex. They need to be explicit.

Most leaders have never written down who is authorized to decide what – not because they’re withholding authority, but because it never occurred to them that the unwritten version wasn’t obvious to everyone else. It is not obvious. What feels like shared understanding from the top reads as ambiguity from the middle, and ambiguity defaults to waiting.

The evidence is specific on what clarity buys. Bain & Company’s research on decision rights found that organizations with explicit authority structures execute 25% faster than those with ambiguous ones. McKinsey’s 2019 research found that companies which clarify and delegate decision rights are twice as likely to report high financial performance. The infrastructure move is not a soft intervention. It is a speed and performance variable.

The infrastructure move itself is small and specific: map the decisions that recur in your organization, name who owns each one, and specify at what level they can act without asking. Not every decision – the ones that keep routing through you when they shouldn’t. That list is shorter than you think, and the act of writing it down is most of the work.

Three questions. Set a timer for 20 minutes:

  1. What are the five decisions that came to me this week that someone else could have made?

  2. For each one, does the person closest to it know they’re authorized to make it – and which mode they’re operating in at what level of latitude?

  3. What would need to be true for me to never see that decision again?

If you can’t finish in 20 minutes, that’s not a time management problem. That’s the answer.

The question nobody could answer without you this week wasn’t hard. It wasn’t even close. It was just sitting there, unassigned, in a folder nobody touched for three days.

Reply and tell me which decision it was. I read every response.

title: The Trust Tax
html:
Your organization lost approximately 18 hours this week to a cost that doesn’t appear on any balance sheet. That’s five people, one deferred decision per day, 45 minutes each, every day this week. It shows up as hesitation. Deferred action. The slightly longer pause before anyone tries anything new.

Nobody filed a report on it. Nobody will.

It’s Tuesday at 11pm and a founder is refreshing a shared document her team submitted four hours ago.

She’s not doing it because she thinks they’re incompetent. She’s doing it because the deliverable brief didn’t specify what done looks like, and there’s no review checkpoint until Friday, and the only way she knows how to get ahead of a miss is to stay close to the work. She’ll make three small edits. Send a message framed as a question. Go to bed later than she meant to.

Her team will notice in the morning. They’ll learn what they always learn: that the work flows back up eventually, so there’s limited point in treating it as fully yours.

Micromanagement isn’t a personality flaw.

It’s what happens when the infrastructure for safe delegation doesn’t exist, and the leader is the only one in the room being honest about that.

There’s a distinction worth naming here, because almost everything depends on it. Distrust of people is one thing. Distrust of infrastructure is another. The first is a character assessment. The second is an organizational diagnosis. Most micromanagement is the second one, consistently mislabeled as the first.

The leader who checks in three times before a deliverable is due isn’t necessarily convinced her team is incompetent. She may be operating in a system where outcome expectations were never defined, where decision rights were never clarified, where the only feedback loop available is her. Given that system, staying involved isn’t a flaw. It’s the rational response.

That doesn’t make it cheap.

The 18 hours is just what you can count. The Trust Tax runs on everything the accounting system can’t see: the idea nobody pitched, the risk nobody took, the decision that waited another day because the infrastructure for owning it doesn’t exist.

The team-side cost isn’t morale. It’s cognitive load – the constant low-grade weight of waiting for approval before acting, calibrating every decision against what the leader would want, learning over time that initiative is not just unrewarded but occasionally punished when it produces a result the leader would have done differently.

What follows is learned helplessness. Martin Seligman’s foundational research showed that individuals who repeatedly experience uncontrollable outcomes stop attempting to influence them, even when control later becomes available. Organizations produce the same pattern: a gradual, rational transfer of accountability upward. The team stops failing forward because they’ve learned the leader will absorb all failure anyway. Why own an outcome you’re not actually being trusted to control?

Physical therapists know this dynamic well. A patient who relies on a therapist to initiate every movement doesn’t just move less – they lose the capacity to initiate movement. The leader who stays involved to prevent failure gradually becomes the reason the team can’t function without them. More involvement, less ownership, more justification for involvement. From inside, it looks like a people problem. It’s a design problem.

You don’t fix this with trust exercises.

You fix it by building what makes delegation safe. Amy Edmondson’s research on psychological safety confirms the deeper cost: when people don’t know what they truly own, they hedge. They wait. They learn that initiative is risky and real authority is rare. Delegation ambiguity doesn’t just slow execution. It wastes the trust you’ve worked to build.

Minimum viable infrastructure for safe delegation has three components, and most organizations are missing at least two. Together, they form the front end of DELEGATE, the handoff framework at the center of CLUTCH.

The first is clear decision rights – not just an authority map, but a mode and a level. Who decides is only half the question. How they decide, and how much latitude they hold, is what most organizations never specify. Without answers to both halves, you haven’t given someone decision rights. You’ve given them ambiguity with a title attached.

The second is defined outcome expectations: not the process, the result. What does done look like? What would a good outcome tell us? Without a shared definition of success, the only way to know if the work is on track is to stay close to it.

The third is a feedback loop that isn’t the leader checking in. A status update system, a defined review point, a shared dashboard – anything that gives the leader visibility without requiring their constant presence. Without this, the choice is binary: stay involved, or go dark. Most leaders choose the former. You can’t blame them.

Before your next delegation attempt, three questions:

  1. Does this person know what they’re authorized to decide, and which mode they’re operating in at what level of latitude?

  2. Have I defined what a successful outcome looks like, specifically enough that we’d both recognize it?

  3. Is there a feedback mechanism in place that gives me visibility without requiring me to be the one asking?

If any answer is no, you haven’t delegated. You’ve assigned, and left the infrastructure gap open for micromanagement to fill.

The question worth sitting with: Are you micromanaging because you don’t trust your people, or because you haven’t built what they need to be trusted with?

Think about the last thing you delegated. Not assigned: delegated.

Reply and tell me what you gave them – the mode, the level, the line where their authority ended and yours began. Or whether you realize you never set it. I read every response.

title: Tax Season Is the Easy Part
html:
This is my first year filing as a business. Which means it’s my first year discovering just how many costs I’d been experiencing without tracking – until someone handed me a form and made me account for them.

That’s what April does. It forces a reckoning.

What it doesn’t do is send a bill for everything else.

Most organizations are paying taxes that will never appear on a return, never trigger an estimate, never generate a notice from anyone. They accumulate in the margin between what your people are capable of and what your systems are configured to let them do. They compound, quietly, until they show up as a retention problem, a missed quarter, or a decision that took three weeks longer than it should have.

The IRS wants to know what you spent. These taxes want to know what you lost.

And because nobody’s tracking them, most leaders have no idea how much they owe.

Starting on Monday, I’m going to name each one specifically.

The Trust Tax. Micromanagement isn’t a personality flaw – it’s what happens when the infrastructure for safe delegation doesn’t exist yet. The leader who can’t let go may be the only person in the room being honest about that.

The Clarity Tax. Five people deferring one decision per day is a number you can calculate. Most organizations never do. Ambiguous decision rights aren’t a culture problem. They’re a math problem.

The Meeting Tax. Your team has a meeting after the meeting. That’s the real meeting – and it’s running whether you’re in the room or not. When formal channels don’t process what they need to, informal ones adapt. That adaptation has a cost.

The Succession Tax – the one that’s already running, before anyone has left, before any crisis. Your best people can see the ceiling. They leave for organizations with somewhere to go.

The Transition Tax. Someone gets a new title, new direct reports, a new box on the org chart. Same support structure – which is to say, none. Organizations grow people into leadership roles faster than they grow leadership capability. The promotion is visible. The gap is not.

Each essay opens with a rough estimate of what that particular tax costs your organization this week. Not forensic accounting. Useful accounting. Enough to make the invisible feel real.

April ends. These don’t.

They keep running – in the hesitation before anyone tries something new, in the decisions that wait for you, in the people who left for somewhere with more headroom.

The IRS will always find a way to send the bill.

These costs won’t. That’s what makes them expensive.

Before the first essay: if someone handed you a bill for what your organization lost this week to costs that never appeared on any report, would you recognize the line items?

Subscribe now

title: They Educated It Out
html:
Everything this week argued for formation – the capacity built into how a person sees, not installed by a program. Plato showed us how organizations select against the people who did that work. Sophocles showed us what breaks when systems can’t develop their leaders or deliver truth to them. Homer showed us who pays. Yesterday: Marcus, the Stop Work Order, the interior architecture that no framework can reach.

The series made a case. But it left something unnamed – the capacity underneath all five of Monday’s lessons. Something that makes them possible.

Creativity.

Not as an artistic expression. As the capacity to generate the frame before you choose between options, to see what isn’t there yet, to make something that didn’t exist before your mind encountered the problem. This is what the humanities practice that the MBA cannot teach, structurally,.

The MBA teaches optimization. Decision frameworks. Financial modeling. The rigorous discipline of choosing well between options once they’re on the table. What it assumes – what it cannot examine by structural design – is the frame itself. Someone has to generate the options before you can optimize them. Someone has to see that the current frame is a choice before you can deploy the framework. The MBA begins at step two. It has no instrument for step one.

That prior act is what the humanities practice.

Every discipline in them is a sustained exercise in making something from incomplete materials. Literature produces meaning where none has been specified. Philosophy constructs arguments from first principles rather than received authority. History reads causation in complex systems and imagines the trajectories that didn’t happen. Drama inhabits a consciousness not your own and makes it real from the inside.

These aren’t complementary skills for the analytically trained. They are the prior capacity – and once you see that, Monday’s five lessons look different.

Narrative intelligence is not a communication skill. It’s the generative act of authoring coherence before it exists – the leader constructing a frame for why the change matters, not selecting the most accurate description of one. Moral imagination is not ethical training. It’s generating the consequence before it’s visible, seeing the cost the accounting system hasn’t named yet. Tolerance for ambiguity is the creative confidence that something can be built from the unresolved – that uncertainty is survivable because you trust your own capacity to make something from it. Deep listening and systems thinking are the same act at different scales: generating hypotheses from incomplete signals and constructing the invisible architecture of cause beneath the visible behavior.

Creativity isn’t the sixth capacity. It’s the engine underneath the other five. Without it, you can perform versions of them – assertive communication substitutes for narrative intelligence, rule-following substitutes for moral imagination – but the load-bearing kind requires generation. Remove it, and what remains are performances of leadership rather than the generative act itself.

Agamemnon had Odysseus. The best strategic mind in the Greek world, running the embassy with full institutional authority, carrying an offer of staggering material compensation. Ships. Cities. Kingdoms. His own daughter in marriage. The strategic case was airtight.

He could not generate. He had the full toolkit of optimization, and not one instrument for questioning the frame. The possibility that the currency itself was wrong – that what Achilles needed existed entirely outside the institution’s accounting system – was simply not available to him. He sent more ships. He sent more treasure. He escalated the same answer and called it problem-solving.

Not a failure of intelligence. A creativity failure – the specific kind the MBA produces: a leader who can optimize anything on the table and cannot conceive of what isn’t.

Agamemnon learned to optimize inside an institution. So did every leader you’ve ever promoted. The institution was school, and school was not designed to produce generators.

The most significant thing I watched schools do in twenty years in classrooms was not teach content badly. It was teach students, with remarkable consistency and efficiency, that there was a correct answer and their job was to find it. Every rubric. Every standardized assessment. Every lesson structured around a predetermined destination was the same instruction repeated: reproduce, don’t generate. The bell. The row. The coverage schedule that moved forward regardless of whether students had developed anything other than the ability to move with it.

By the time those students arrived in my classroom – or in leadership roles – the habit was installed. They were waiting for the frame. When the problem was genuinely open, the audience real, the answer not in the back of the book, the response was anxiety rather than curiosity. Not incapacity. Twelve years of reproduction practice, become reflex.

Sir Ken Robinson spent his career naming the mechanism: schools don’t merely fail to develop creativity – they actively educate it out. If you’ve never seen that famous TED talk, do yourself a favor: devote 20 minutes to watching this. You cannot build the habit of generating original thought in a system that consistently rewards reproducing the expected answer. The two practices are in direct competition, and school runs that competition for twelve years in one direction.

VC investor Ted Dintersmith drove to all fifty states in a single school year and found the diagnosis confirmed. He also found teachers who had refused the logic – not with resources, but with a different question. Not what should my students know but what do they need to be able to generate?

At McDonogh School in Owings Mills, Jennifer Smith (Read her work here) or founded the Middle School Academy as a structural answer to that question: an immersive term, separate from the regular curriculum, in which students take courses across the humanities, science, mathematics, and the arts – across grade levels, fifth graders alongside eighth graders – with no age-conferred expertise and no predetermined authority structure. When you can’t rely on age to determine who leads, you have to generate something else: shared frameworks, negotiated expertise, working relationships built from scratch under genuine uncertainty. That is the creative act at the organizational level. The Showcase at the end is where it becomes visible.

A standard assessment tests reproduction. The student demonstrates mastery of the material the teacher delivered, against a standard specified in advance, for an evaluator who already knows the answer. The student’s job is to prove they found it.

The Showcase has none of those features. The prompt was open. The work required generation – the student had to make something that didn’t exist before the Academy began. Originality can’t be pre-scored, so the standard isn’t fully specified. The audience is real – not an evaluator with an answer key but people genuinely encountering the work for the first time, forming their own responses, asking questions the student didn’t script. The frame – what the work is, why it matters, what it means – has to be authored by the presenter in real time, for an audience whose reactions can’t be predicted.

What gets revealed in that gap is whether the generative capacity is structurally available. You can coach eye contact and slide design. You cannot coach a student into having made something genuinely original if the formation that produces original thinking was never built. The student who spent twelve years in a reproduction system reaches for the nearest available frame – the internalized rubric, the presentation the audience probably wants – and when a question arrives that wasn’t scripted, the instinct is to locate the correct answer rather than think in public. Anxiety rather than curiosity. The reproduction habit, present. The student who has been through the humanities arrives already doing the thing: they have a claim – not the teacher’s claim, their claim – and when the frame gets challenged, the response is curiosity. That is what twelve years of rubrics cannot produce.

Twelve years of reproduction practice suppresses the generative reflex. The student who emerges from the factory-education model arrives at university already practiced in waiting for the frame – and the MBA meets them there, hands them the toolkit of optimization, and certifies them in it. Decision frameworks. Financial modeling. The rigorous discipline of choosing between options once they’re on the table. None of it wrong. All of it downstream of generation, and none of it asking the prior question.

By the time that person reaches a management role, the creative capacity has been depressed three times over – by school, by the business program, and by the organization’s own instinct to reward the person who arrives with the answer rather than the person who has the better question. Three institutions. One direction. No coordination required.

Tom Wujec has run the Marshmallow Challenge – build the tallest freestanding structure you can from spaghetti, tape, string, and a marshmallow on top, in eighteen minutes – with thousands of participants across industries. Kindergartners average twenty-six inches. CEOs average twenty-two. MBA graduates average ten. The gap between the CEOs and the MBAs is the telling number: both groups often have the same analytical training, but CEOs have spent years learning through iteration, recovering something the credential suppressed. The kindergartners haven’t been practiced out of the generative reflex yet – they prototype immediately, fail, adjust, and build again, the marshmallow on top from the start. MBA graduates spend the first fifteen minutes planning the optimal solution, build it once, and discover the marshmallow is heavier than the theory accounted for. It isn’t a difference in how their brains are wired. It’s a difference in what twenty years of formation practiced them to do.

Ajax is the organization’s failure – handed one frame for a decade, never asked to make another. The institution optimized him for a function and called it development.

Oedipus is the MBA’s failure – trained to resolve, to analyze, to move from problem to solution with maximum efficiency. Generation requires sitting inside the unresolved. The credential never required it.

Plato’s philosopher-king is school’s failure – the generative capacity was present at five, present at ten, quietly depressed by twelve, and by the time she reaches the promotion committee it reads as hesitation rather than depth. The organization selects the optimizer. It loses the generator.

Three institutions. Three failure modes. One root cause: the generative capacity was never built – or was systematically educated out – and replaced, at each stage, with a more refined version of the same instruction. Reproduce. Optimize. Execute. Never: generate.

The harder analytical point is not about MBA graduates specifically.

Hot take here: The educational system is not broken. It is working exactly as designed. The problem is that it was designed for an economy that peaked around 1890.

As the 19th century gave way to the 20th, public schools were redesigned around the logic of the factory floor. Students sat in rows, followed rigid schedules, progressed in batches, sorted by testing, and evaluated like quality-controlled products. School bells mimicked factory whistles. The goal was punctuality, compliance, and the efficient delivery of standardized content to large groups – because those were precisely the capacities the industrial economy required. The system produced them at scale. It still does. That is not a failure. It is a 130-year success at the wrong objective.

The MBA is not the cause of the problem. It is the logical conclusion of it – the final refinement of a pipeline that begins in kindergarten, runs through twelve years of reproduction practice, and arrives at a credential that certifies the optimizer. The business school took the raw material that the K-12 system produced and perfected it. A person trained from age five to find the correct answer, then trained from age twenty-two to choose efficiently between options, arrives in your organization precisely as the system intended: fluent, credentialed, and structurally unable to question the frame.

The marshmallow data makes this visible in eighteen minutes. But the mechanism runs for twenty-two years before anyone hands out the spaghetti.

What would a system designed for 2026 look like instead? Not a curriculum reform agenda – the design principles that distinguish the schools Dintersmith found from the ones he was expecting.

Replace coverage with depth. The factory model’s core assumption is that more content delivered equals more learning produced. It doesn’t – and in a world where AI can deliver any content on demand in seconds, the assumption doesn’t just fail, it inverts. What AI cannot do is generate the frame. The Showcase works because it demands one thing made well for a real audience rather than everything covered shallowly. The organizational equivalent: fewer initiatives pursued to actual completion, with genuine accountability for the generative quality of the work, not just its delivery on time.

Make the audience real. The single most powerful design change in every high-performing classroom Dintersmith found was this: the student’s work was seen by someone other than the teacher. A real client. A real community. A real panel. The stakes change when the audience is genuine. The organizational equivalent: ideas stress-tested by people who will be honest rather than people who are managed by the presenter.

Reward iteration, not the plan. The MBA graduates in the marshmallow challenge fail because their formation taught them to plan the optimal solution and execute it once. The kindergartners win because they were never trained out of prototyping. Organizations that hold postmortems only on failures – never on the planning process itself – are running the same logic. The design question: where in your system is iteration structurally rewarded rather than treated as evidence that the first plan was wrong?

Separate compliance metrics from formation metrics. The factory model measures what it can count: test scores, completion rates, grade-point averages. These measure reproduction reliably and formation not at all. The organizational equivalent is the performance review that measures execution against plan and calls it a leadership assessment. Formation metrics require observing what someone does when the frame isn’t provided, how they behave when they’re wrong in public, and whether the people around them generate more over time. They require the Showcase structure, not the rubric structure.

The diagnostic question for your next meeting: who in the room questions the frame before moving to solution? That’s the person who has the prior capacity – and who your organization may be selecting against without knowing it.

It’s worth noting who that person often is. The research on neurodivergent cognition – ADHD, autism, dyslexia – consistently shows elevated pattern recognition across unrelated domains, resistance to premature closure, and a tendency to question assumptions that neurotypical thinkers treat as given. These are not incidental features of atypical minds. They are, structurally, the generative capacities this essay has been arguing for. The factory model pathologized them – the student who questioned the frame instead of completing the assignment, who saw the problem differently than the rubric required, who couldn’t perform compliance on demand – and the organization inherited that pathology wholesale. The person most likely to question the frame before moving to solution is also the person most likely to have been identified as a problem somewhere between kindergarten and the MBA.

Most organizations are structured to suppress generation without knowing it. The meeting culture rewards the person who arrives with the answer. The performance review measures execution against plan. The problem that arrives pre-framed gets treated as given. Three mechanisms, one direction, running continuously – the same logic as the school, the same logic as the MBA, compressing the generative reflex one more time.

Interrupting that logic is not a culture initiative. It is an architecture decision – the same one Jennifer Smith made when she built a program whose entire structure refused the reproduction model. The same one the kindergartners execute instinctively before anyone trains it out of them.

The MBA teaches you what to do when the options are on the table.

The humanities teach you to question the table.

title: What Are You Practicing?
html:
This week I’ve been in Greece, in Rome, in the oldest texts the Western canon has to offer. Monday, I argued that the humanities produce formation, not skills – lessons built into the structure of how a person sees, not installed by a workshop or certified by a competency model. Tuesday, Plato showed us how organizations systematically select against the people who did that formation. Wednesday, Sophocles showed us three ways good leaders fail inside systems that couldn’t develop them, couldn’t deliver truth to them, couldn’t create the conditions to receive it. Thursday, Homer showed us what those failures cost – not the leaders at the top, but the people underneath them who had no part in creating the problem and no protection from its consequences.

All of it was outside. Systems. Structures. Organizational architecture.

Today I want to turn inward. Because there is one system none of those frameworks can build for you.

A year ago, I was sitting at my desk when a Stop Work Order came in at around 9 am.

I packed two Wegmans bags and a backpack of personal items – running shoes, a toothbrush, a Lego set of succulents – and took the MARC train home in the middle of the morning. I had been a leadership development specialist at USAID’s Bureau of Humanitarian Assistance. I had spent years building something I believed in – frameworks that let people work together more effectively under impossible pressure, systems that helped teams navigate conflict and deliver life-saving aid in rapidly changing crises. I had been preparing for an overseas deployment to Thailand. The work felt necessary and real and mine.

And then it was gone. Not slowly. All at once.

I remember sitting on that train not knowing what came next. That is the honest version – not that I immediately pivoted, not that the path forward was clear, not that the loss resolved itself into opportunity with any kind of speed. There was a period of not knowing. Of sitting inside the uncertainty without a framework for it. Of encountering, for the first time in a long time, a situation that my professional formation had no answer for. I had spent years helping other people navigate impossible pressure. Now the pressure was mine, and the frameworks were someone else’s problem.

I started reading the Stoics. Not for comfort. I was not looking for comfort. I was looking for a philosophy that was honest about the nature of uncontrollable events and rigorous – unsparing, actually – about what to do with them.

The real thing is considerably more demanding than its reputation suggests.

Here is what most people get wrong about Meditations.

They read it as a journal of self-improvement. Marcus Aurelius’s bullet journal. A Roman emperor who was very concerned with being more disciplined, more patient, more resilient. All true. All beside the point.

Meditations is a working document written by a man running an empire under conditions of continuous and compounding uncertainty. Plague. War. Political betrayal. Economic instability. Marcus spent most of his reign on campaign – not because he wanted to be a soldier but because the Danube frontier kept requiring his presence and the frontier didn’t care about his preferences. He wrote Meditations in military camps, in the margins of an impossible job, not as philosophy for posterity but as operational instruction to himself. Notes for how to function when the external environment is fundamentally uncontrollable and the only reliable system is your own response architecture.

That is not self-help. That is systems design for the interior life.

The distinction matters enormously for how you read him – and what you take from him into a leadership context.

The central architecture of Stoic philosophy – the thing Marcus returns to throughout Meditations in different forms, in different registers, with different degrees of exhaustion and conviction – is the dichotomy of control.

There are things within your control and things outside it.

The Stoics are not gentle about this distinction. What is outside your control is almost everything: the market, the behavior of other people, the decisions your board makes, the timing of a recession, whether the plague arrives in your province this winter or the next. What is within your control is almost nothing: your judgments, your intentions, your responses. The space between stimulus and response. That is the entire inventory.

When I first encountered this seriously – not as a quotation on a productivity website but as a working philosophy in the months after USAID – it was not reassuring. It was confrontational. It said: the situation you are in is not something you get to spend your interior resources on. The Stop Work Order, the dismantling of the work, the question of whether any of it would be preserved – those are outside your control. You do not get to carry them. You get to carry only what you choose to do next. It was a message I knew enough about myself that needed to hear in that moment.

That is a hard thing to hear when what you want to do is grieve the thing that was lost. The Stoics don’t say you can’t grieve. They say: grieve precisely, and then return to the question of what is actually yours to govern. Because the time you spend inside what you cannot control is time stolen from the only system you can actually build.

Most leadership development spends its energy on the things outside that inventory. How to influence others. How to manage up. How to build culture. How to design systems that produce the outcomes you want. All of it important. All of it operating in the territory Marcus spent his life clarifying as ultimately beyond your control.

He wasn’t arguing for passivity. He was arguing for precision. Stop spending interior resources on the things you cannot govern. Spend them entirely on the one thing you can.

That is not a meditation technique. That is operational infrastructure.

In the months after USAID, I started building GDC. I dusted off a manuscript I had written years earlier as a private gift to G – a promise made thirty years ago, finally kept – revised it, and published it as Balance, my first novel. I consolidated a decade of leadership frameworks into a “vehicle metaphor” – cyclinders (CREATE), gears (VOICES), navigation (6D) – and expanded that into a book: CLUTCH. And I kept tinkering with the long-running personal project that refuses to finish – a biography of the number Seven, which requires the kind of deep research that fiction mercifully does not. When you’re writing fiction, you can just make things up. Seven keeps demanding that I actually know things. That tinkering eventually became something more serious, and I started rereading every translation of the Iliad I could find – which became The Wrath of Archie Ellis, which became Thursday’s essay.

None of those things were available to me while I was spending interior resources on questions outside my control. The Stoics were not sympathetic about this. They would say: the months you spent asking whether the institution made the right decision were months that belonged to the work you haven’t built yet.

I think they were right. I also think it took longer than they would have approved of to get there.

Marcus writes: You have power over your mind, not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.

The translation flattens it slightly. What he actually means is more structural than inspirational: the architecture of your interior life is the only architecture you will ever fully own. Build it well. Maintain it deliberately. Don’t confuse it with the architecture of the external world, which you can influence but never control.

Here is where Marcus connects to everything this week has been about – and the connection is not a framework. It is a question.

Think about the Oedipus problem from Wednesday. The leader who is the last to know what everyone around them already knows. We spent time analyzing what the organization failed to build – the systems that make truth travel upward, the conditions that make dissent survivable. All of that analysis is real, and the infrastructure is worth building.

But Marcus would ask something prior to all of it: what happens inside the leader when the truth finally arrives?

Because the infrastructure can be perfect – the environment genuinely safe, the people genuinely willing – and the leader can still flinch. Can still make the person who delivered the difficult information pay a subtle cost that everyone in the room notices and no one names. Can still reach for the story that protects them over the story that’s true. Not because they are malicious. Because the interior architecture wasn’t built to receive what the external system finally delivered.

A leader with a developed interior architecture meets difficult information the same way Marcus met the Danube frontier: not with equanimity as a performance, but with equanimity as a practice. Not “I am fine with this” but “I have built the capacity to remain curious in the presence of things I would prefer not to be true – including things about myself.”

That capacity is not installed by a framework. It is built by practice. Daily, ordinary, unglamorous practice. In every small moment before the large ones arrive.

Which brings us to the question Marcus returns to constantly, in various forms, across all twelve books of Meditations: what are you practicing?

Not what are your values? Not what do you believe? What are you actually doing, day by day, in the ordinary moments before the pressure arrives?

A line attributed to the ancient Greek warrior-poet Archilochus has been passed through enough hands that no one checks the source anymore. Navy SEALs adopted it. David Goggins repeated it. James Clear adapted it for Atomic Habits – swapping "training" for "systems," which is actually the more useful frame. The Stoics understood the same thing two millennia ago: you do not rise to the occasion. You fall to the level of your preparation. Everyone who has touched this idea was talking about individuals. The response architecture available to you in the hardest moment is the one you have been building in every moment before it. The question for organizations is whether the system was designed to build that architecture — or just to assume it arrives fully formed.

You are always practicing something. The question is whether it’s what you intend.

Marcus kept writing in the military camps, not because the philosophy was incomplete. Because the practice required daily maintenance. Because the interior architecture, like any infrastructure, degrades without attention. Because even an emperor – perhaps especially an emperor – needed to return every morning to the same fundamental questions: what is within my control today, what is not, and where am I spending my interior resources?

I return to those questions. Not every day – I am not Marcus Aurelius, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. But often enough that they have become part of how I orient myself when the external environment is uncontrollable, which in my experience is most of the time.

He didn’t always succeed. He kept writing anyway.

He was working in one tradition. There are others…

I have a tattoo: Datta Dayadhvam Damyata.

Sanskrit, from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad – three instructions spoken by Prajapati to three orders of being, each hearing what they most need to hear. T.S. Eliot borrowed it for the closing of The Waste Land, which is where I first encountered it, though the words are several thousand years older than Eliot. I had it put on my skin because I wanted it somewhere I couldn’t put it down. Because the things worth practicing are the things worth making permanent. Because some arguments are too important to keep only in books.

Give. Sympathize. Practice control.

Three words. The whole argument in a different tradition and a different millennium. And – I’ll say it plainly – the whole argument this series has been making, compressed into a form old enough to predate every framework, every play, every poem I’ve cited this week.

Give – the outward orientation, the recognition that leadership is not accumulation but distribution. That kleos stolen is kleos lost. That the systems worth building are the ones that develop other people’s capacity, not protect your own position. The lesson narrative intelligence was pointing toward all along: the story you tell about your people is infrastructure.

Sympathize – the interior capacity to feel the situation accurately. To read what Achilles actually needs before the embassy fails. To hear what your team knows before the culture makes silence rational. To receive difficult truth with curiosity rather than contracting around it. Deep listening, moral imagination, tolerance for ambiguity – all of them are downstream of this one word.

Practice control – not control of the external environment, which Marcus spent twelve books clarifying is not yours to govern, but control of the response. The space between the stimulus and the action. The only inventory that is genuinely yours. The one system no framework can build for you.

This week, I was in Greece, in Rome, in the ancient world’s most enduring literature, looking for what the humanities give a leader that the MBA doesn’t. I found it in the same place across every tradition I visited: the insistence that the external architecture and the interior architecture are not separate problems. That you cannot build the systems without building the person operating them. That the formation is the foundation. That what you practice in the ordinary moments is what will be available to you in the extraordinary ones.

The Rolling Stone piece called these things skills. Five of them, neatly listed, teachable in the right program. This week I’ve been arguing something different – that they are not skills but lessons, not acquired but formed, not installed but lived. Formation doesn’t appear on a resume. It shows up in the moment when the information is incomplete, the stakes are real, and the response architecture is either there or it isn’t.

Give. Sympathize. Practice control.

Not skills. Scars.

Subscribe now

I want to know your three words – the principle, the phrase, the thing you’ve put somewhere you can’t put it down. Reply and tell me. I read every response.

And if you’re building both the external infrastructure and the interior architecture – that’s the work I do. Start with CLUTCH…

If you want to read CLUTCH before it launches, I’m releasing a limited number of Advance Reader Copies. You can request one below.

Interested in an Advanced Copy?

If you read this and recognized your organization in it – the missing authority map, the culture that never got built, the feedback loop that still runs through you – I’m worth a conversation. Thirty minutes. No pitch.
