title: The Oldest Management Failure on Record
html:
The Iliad opens with a single word.

Menis.

Wrath. Not anger, not frustration, not professional disagreement – wrath. The specific, total, civilization-altering fury of a person who gave everything an institution asked of them and watched the institution corrupt its own accounting system for a commander’s career advancement.

Homer chose this word first. Before the ships, before the battles, before the gods. Before Troy. The first word of the first poem in the Western literary canon is a management problem.

Yesterday I closed in Sophocles with a promise: the person who pays the cost of the Iliad’s leadership failure isn’t Agamemnon or Achilles. It’s Patroclus. Today I want to make good on that – and show something slightly different from what the tragedies showed us. Not what happens when the system fails the leader. What happens when the leader fails the system. And what it costs the people underneath when they do.

The Iliad is not a war story. It is the oldest management failure on record. And it has been waiting three thousand years for someone to read it that way.

I’ve spent the last several months rereading every translation I can find – Fagles, Wilson, the older Lattimore – because I’m working on a novel that retells the Iliad from the trenches of Ypres in 1917. The Wrath of Archie Ellis (Click here) puts Homer’s conflict into the mud of the Western Front, where Agamemnon is a British colonel operating inside a command structure that made dissent not just politically costly but literally insubordinate – and where Achilles is a soldier whose capacity everyone depends on and whose value the system has no language for expressing beyond the blunt instrument of rank. The colonel is looking for his general stars. The British officer class of 1917 ran almost entirely on this logic – careers built on the performance of men whose names appear nowhere in the dispatches. Homer understood it three thousand years earlier. He just had the honesty to show us what it costs.

What it costs is everything. And it starts with a prize.

Ten years. No victory. Two kinds of power that the organization has never learned to hold simultaneously.

Agamemnon is the commander – the highest title, the most ships, the political authority that holds the coalition together. Without him, there is no army. His authority is real, structural, and genuinely necessary.

Achilles is the best fighter – the most capable, the most feared, the person whose presence on the battlefield changes the outcome of every engagement he enters. The Trojans don’t fear the Greek army. They fear Achilles. Without him, the Greeks can fight. They simply cannot win.

These two things – Agamemnon’s authority and Achilles’ capacity – are not the same thing. And for ten years, the organization has been held together by the fiction that they are. That the person who holds the title is also the person whose judgment matters most. That command and competence live in the same body.

They don’t. And the Iliad is the story of what happens when that fiction finally breaks.

A good MBA program would call this a misalignment between authority and expertise. It would give you a framework for clarifying decision rights. It would suggest a RACI matrix.

Homer gives you something else. He gives you what that misalignment actually feels like from the inside – what it costs, in human terms, when the organization has no system for holding both kinds of power simultaneously. The case study tells you what went wrong. The poem makes you feel why it was inevitable.

The flashpoint is a prize. Briseis – a captive woman awarded to Achilles as the spoils of a raid. In the Greek honor economy, prizes aren’t property. They’re recognition made visible – the organization’s accounting system for value, the external signal that tells the community what a person is worth.

But there’s a deeper current running beneath the prize. The Greek word is kleos – the glory that outlasts you, the story people tell about you after you’re gone, the thing that makes you immortal in the culture’s memory. Kleos isn’t reputation. It’s narrative. It’s the account of who did what, why it mattered, and who deserves credit for it. And Achilles is generating it at a rate that threatens to eclipse everyone around him – including his commander.

In my book, Agamemnon is a colonel looking for his general stars. And Achilles is making that impossible.

Every Greek victory is becoming an Achilles story. Every battle won is another verse in a poem that has the wrong person at its center. Agamemnon cannot let this continue – not because he is irrational, but because the career logic of his position is entirely rational. He needs to be seen as the reason the Greeks are winning. Achilles is making that story impossible to tell.

So when the plague forces Agamemnon to return his own prize, he doesn’t absorb the recognition wound. He transfers it. He takes Briseis from Achilles – not because he wants her, but because the act of taking her says something in public about who outranks whom. It is a calculated career move dressed as a command prerogative.

He is stealing kleos and calling it authority.

This is the same failure mode that destroyed Ajax in Wednesday’s essay – the organization corrupting its own account of what a person is worth – but one register deeper. Ajax’s organization simply failed to speak. Agamemnon’s actively rewrites the record. The lesson from Monday holds in both cases: narrative intelligence isn’t just a leadership capacity. It’s an organizational obligation. When the institution controls the story of who did what, the integrity of that story is infrastructure. Corrupt it, and everything built on top of it becomes unstable.

You know this person. They’re the manager who presents the team’s work as their own in the executive meeting, who takes the win publicly, and ensures that the story of how it happened has their name at the center. Homer didn’t invent this character. He recognized him. He understood that kleos theft isn’t a moral failing in the first instance. It’s a career strategy. And he understood exactly what it costs when the person being stolen from figures out what’s happened.

In Wrath, my colonel is managing up by managing the narrative around his best officer. Decorated British generals built entire careers this way – taking credit for results, suppressing the dispatches that would tell the real story, ensuring that the kleos of the men underneath them fed upward into their own record rather than outward into the historical account. The Western Front didn’t invent this dynamic. It just made the cost of it visible in the most brutal possible terms.

Achilles understands exactly what has happened. His response is not irrational – within his framework, it is completely logical. If the organization can reclassify my value at will, the accounting system is corrupt. If the accounting system is corrupt, the relationship between my contribution and my reward is a fiction. And if that relationship is fiction, I have no reason to contribute.

He withdraws. Takes his Myrmidons back to the ships. Refuses to fight.

And the Greeks start losing.

Agamemnon sends an embassy. Three men: Odysseus the diplomat, Ajax the warrior (Yes, both of those guys, see yesterday’s post), and Phoenix the old mentor – the full institutional weight of the coalition behind them. They bring offers. Ships. Treasure. Cities. Kingdoms. Agamemnon’s own daughter in marriage. The material compensation is staggering. By any rational accounting, Achilles should return.

In Wrath, this scene happens in a dugout. The embassy arrives not with ships and treasure but with a promotion, a commendation, a letter from the general. The same offer, different currency. The same result.

He refuses everything.

His speech in response to Odysseus is one of the most analytically precise passages in ancient literature – and the dimension of it that most business readers miss is how far it goes beyond the immediate dispute. Achilles doesn’t just refuse the ships. He doesn’t dispute the value of the offers. He disputes the premise. Agamemnon is trying to compensate a recognition wound with resources – settling a debt denominated in honor with currency denominated in gold. It cannot work. Not because Achilles is irrational. Because the wound and the compensation are in different currencies entirely.

And then he goes further. He questions the entire value system that made kleos worth dying for in the first place.

He says: I have two fates available to me. Stay and fight and die young with eternal glory – kleos aphthiton, imperishable fame. Or go home, live long, and be forgotten. I chose the first fate. I gave everything the system asked of me. I fought. I bled. I built the kleos this army runs on. And the system took it anyway – took it for a commander’s career, reclassified it with a single public gesture, made it mean nothing. So what exactly was I fighting for?

That is not a negotiating position. That is an existential crisis produced by an organizational betrayal. Achilles built his entire identity around the value system of the institution. The institution corrupted that value system for a colonel’s promotion prospects. And now Achilles is sitting in his tent asking the question that every disengaged high performer eventually asks, quietly, before they leave: if the accounting was always this dishonest, did any of it mean anything?

The MBA program gives you retention frameworks for this moment. Compensation benchmarking. Engagement surveys. Career pathing conversations. All of them useful. None of them sufficient. Because none of them address what Achilles is actually asking – which is not “am I paid enough” but “does this institution see me accurately and is it willing to say so in public.”

You cannot answer that question with ships. The only thing that answers it is the leader who took the kleos standing up in public and giving it back – acknowledging that the accounting was wrong, that the value is real, that the institution is willing to pay the cost of correcting its own record.

Agamemnon never offers that. He offers everything except the one thing that would work.

Most leaders would rather send more ships.

The embassy fails. The formal channels are exhausted. The organization has done everything it officially knows how to do.

And it wasn’t enough.

What happens next is the dimension of the poem most business readers miss entirely – and it is the most important leadership lesson Homer has to offer.

The cost of the conflict at the top is not paid by Agamemnon. It is not paid by Achilles. It is paid by Patroclus.

Patroclus is Achilles’ closest friend – his companion since childhood, the person who knows him better than anyone in the army. As the Greek losses mount, as the Trojans push the Greeks back toward their ships, Patroclus goes to Achilles. Not with strategy. Not with argument. With grief. He tells Achilles that men are dying. That the army is breaking. That the conflict between two leaders has created a vacuum that is filling with bodies.

Achilles cannot return himself. His withdrawal is now a position – to reverse it publicly would be its own recognition wound, an admission that Agamemnon’s authority was legitimate after all. The impasse is total. So he does something that reveals both his love for Patroclus and the catastrophic depth of his organizational failure: he sends Patroclus into battle wearing his armor.

The proxy. The person who absorbs the consequences of a conflict he didn’t create and cannot resolve.

But notice what the armor is actually doing here. Patroclus is not just standing in for Achilles – he is being asked to perform a role, carry a function, represent a capacity that isn’t his. He looks like Achilles. The Trojans see Achilles’ shield, Achilles’ helmet, Achilles’ plume. They respond to the symbol rather than the substance. And Hector kills him precisely because the gap between the appearance and the reality is eventually visible – because you can put someone in the armor, hand them the symbols of the position, give them the title and the office and the reporting lines, but you cannot give them what the armor actually represents.

Think about what this looks like inside an organization. The senior engineer who quits and the company promotes the next person in line into the role – not because they’re ready, but because the role needs to be filled and the org chart needs to make sense. The head of sales who burns out and the VP who was doing fine as an individual contributor gets handed the team because someone has to. The founder who steps back and puts a COO in place without transferring the actual authority, the relationships, and the institutional knowledge that makes the role function. The promoted person is wearing the armor. They look like the role. They aren’t the role. And the organization, under pressure, discovers the gap.

The armor kills Patroclus. The underprepared promotion – the role without the real transfer of capacity and authority behind it – kills the person who accepts it. And the organization loses both: the performer who withdrew and the proxy who was sent in their place.

I think about Patroclus constantly while writing Wrath. He is everywhere in the First World War – every junior officer sent over the top by a command structure paralyzed by its own internal politics, wearing the symbols of an authority the system never actually transferred. Every middle manager caught in the crossfire of a conflict between the CEO and the head of sales, paying with their career or their health for a wound that lives two levels above them and that they had no power to resolve.

The cost of leadership conflict is almost never paid by the leaders. It is paid by the people underneath them who had no part in creating it and no protection from its consequences.

Homer made this the emotional center of the entire poem. He knew exactly what he was showing us.

Patroclus dies because three things failed simultaneously – and understanding the sequence matters as much as understanding the failures themselves.

It starts with emotional intelligence – what the CLUTCH framework (Click here) calls the clutch itself, the mechanism that enables a leader to read a situation accurately and respond to what’s actually there rather than what’s administratively convenient. Agamemnon cannot read what is actually in front of him. He looks at Achilles and sees a threat to his authority rather than a wound that needs repair. He sends Odysseus with ships and treasure because ships and treasure are what his framework tells him value looks like – and his framework has no instrument for measuring the distance between what someone needs and what the accounting system can provide. He authorizes the wrong currency not because he is malicious but because he genuinely cannot perceive the correct one.

A leader with developed emotional intelligence reads the situation before the embassy. They feel the gap between what they’re offering and what the situation requires. They recognize that Achilles’ withdrawal isn’t about the ships – that the speech in Book 9 isn’t a negotiating position, it’s a crisis of institutional faith, and the only response that works is the one that costs the leader personally. That’s not a strategic insight. It’s an emotional one. It requires the capacity to feel the situation accurately enough to respond to what’s real rather than what’s administratively available.

Agamemnon never develops this capacity - he must have been a STEM major, I jest. The EQ fails. And that perceptual failure lands in a system with two other structural failures already in place – each one making the EQ failure worse, each one removing another possible off-ramp before Patroclus puts on the armor.

The first is what you might call the integrity of the accounting system – the structural protection that ensures the relationship between contribution and recognition is honest and cannot be manipulated by those with the most power. An organization with that protection in place has a mechanism that says: you cannot publicly reclassify someone’s contribution for your own advancement. You cannot steal kleos and call it authority. Without it, the accounting system belongs to whoever holds the most power – which means it can always be weaponized by the person at the top. Agamemnon can steal kleos in the first place because there is no structural protection for the honesty of how value is assigned. The EQ failure would have had nothing to exploit if that protection were in place.

The second is the relational infrastructure – the trust architecture that makes it possible to survive a conflict like this, to have the hard conversation before it becomes a position, to repair the rupture before it calcifies into something irreversible. An organization with a healthy relational infrastructure has a repair mechanism built underneath the formal channels. There is a relationship between the two parties that predates and outlasts the conflict. There is a trusted third party with the standing to hold both people simultaneously. There is a structure for repair, not just escalation. The Greeks have none of this. When the embassy fails, there is nothing underneath it – no relationship between Agamemnon and Achilles that could survive the wound, no trusted third party with standing, no mechanism that creates the conditions for repair before the positions harden. Because the relational infrastructure isn’t there, the EQ failure compounds rather than corrects. The wound deepens. The impasse holds.

And Patroclus puts on the armor.

This is the complete causal chain. The EQ fails – Agamemnon cannot perceive what Achilles actually needs. The accounting system has no structural protection – he can steal kleos in the first place. The relational infrastructure has no repair mechanism – the wound calcifies into a position rather than being healed. Each failure enables the next. All three are operating simultaneously, each one closing another door before the final one shuts.

That is the architecture of the Iliad’s organizational collapse. Not any single failure. The sequence.

The MBA program gives you that diagnosis accurately. Misaligned incentives. Inadequate retention strategy. Failed conflict resolution. Poor succession planning. Every box is right. Every framework is applicable.

What the MBA program cannot give you is what Homer gives you – the weight of the sequence, the feel of each door closing, the specific grief of watching Patroclus put on armor that was never meant for him, and knowing exactly how this ends and being unable to stop it. That is not sentiment. That is information of a different order – information that gets inside you and changes how you see, that makes you recognize the sequence earlier, that makes you feel the moment when the accounting system is being corrupted before the withdrawal happens, when the relational infrastructure is thin before the conflict arrives, when the EQ is failing before the embassy is sent.

The case study tells you what went wrong. The poem makes you feel why it was inevitable. And feeling it accurately is the difference between a leader who diagnoses the recognition wound before the embassy and one who sends more ships.

This week I’ve been outside – in the systems, the structures, the organizational architecture that holds culture and protects how value is assigned and develops people beyond the function they’re currently filling. Every essay has been about what you build around the leaders in your organization.

Tomorrow I want to turn inward. Because there is one system, none of those frameworks can be built for you.

title: What Greek Tragedy Knew About Your Organization
html:
Monday, I argued that the humanities aren’t soft – that what they produce isn’t a set of skills but a set of lessons, a formation that gets built into a person rather than installed. Tuesday, I was in Plato, watching him diagnose the philosopher-king problem 2,400 years before we started calling it a succession crisis: the people most likely to pursue authority are the least likely to have done the formation that makes authority worth holding.

The ancient world has more to say. We’re not done.

Sophocles understood something about power that most organizations are still refusing to look at directly.

Here’s what most people get wrong about hubris.

We use it as a synonym for arrogance – the leader who got too big for their boots, who flew too close to the sun (ha!), who believed their own press. But that’s not what the Greeks meant. Hubris in tragedy isn’t a personality flaw. It’s a structural condition. It’s the point at which a leader’s greatest strength becomes the thing that destroys them – not despite their excellence, but because of it. And crucially: because no one around them could say so.

The Greeks didn’t build an art form around bad leaders. They built it around good leaders inside systems that couldn’t save them from themselves.

Ajax – The Organization That Never Said What You Were Worth

Ajax is the greatest warrior in the Greek army at Troy. Not the cleverest – that’s Odysseus – but the strongest, the most reliable, the one who holds the line when everyone else breaks, who carries Achilles’ body off the battlefield while the rest retreat. When Achilles dies, and his armor is awarded to Odysseus instead of Ajax, the Greek leadership makes what may have been the right strategic call. Odysseus was the better choice for what came next – the cunning, the diplomacy, the long game of getting everyone home.

They just never told Ajax what else he was worth.

Ajax doesn’t accept the decision and move on. He loses his mind. Kills a flock of sheep believing they’re his enemies. Dies by his own hand. The modern read is breakdown. The organizational read is different: Ajax was never given a framework for his value beyond the single metric he’d been recognized for. His entire identity was his performance on the battlefield. When the performance wasn’t enough – when judgment and cleverness were suddenly valued over strength and loyalty – he had no other story to tell about himself.

This is the lesson from Monday that the organization failed to build around him: narrative intelligence – not just the leader’s capacity to author coherence for others, but the organization’s responsibility to author a coherent account of what its people are actually worth. The armor decision may have been defensible. The failure was everything that didn’t happen around it – the conversation that never occurred, the acknowledgment that never came, the investment in Ajax as a whole person rather than a function. High performers who are passed over don’t just need better communication about the decision. They need a relationship with their own value that can survive it.

Ajax had no such relationship. Neither do most of the highest performers currently sitting in your organization, quietly doing the work, waiting for a decision that will tell them whether they matter.

This is the Teaching cylinder in CREATE (Click here to learn more) failing – the organization’s responsibility to develop people beyond their current function, not just deploy them in it. Sophocles knew exactly what he was showing us. The Greeks lost their greatest warrior not on the battlefield but in the aftermath of a promotion decision that was never properly held.

Ajax is a development failure. The organization knew what he was worth. It just never said so.

Oedipus Rex – The System That Couldn’t Deliver the Truth

Oedipus is not a bad leader. That’s the whole point. He solved the riddle no one else could crack. He saved Thebes. He is genuinely, demonstrably competent – and that competence is exactly what makes him catastrophic. Because when the truth starts surfacing, Tiresias the prophet already knows it. Jocasta his wife already knows it. The shepherd who was there at the beginning knows it. The entire system has the information.

It simply cannot get to the person at the center.

That is not an ancient Greek problem.

That is a Tuesday morning in your organization.

Tiresias tries. He tells Oedipus the truth directly, in the very first confrontation of the play. Oedipus dismisses him, accuses him of conspiracy, and sends him away. And after that, nobody tries again. Not because they don’t know. Everyone knows. Even the audience knows. Because in a single public exchange, Oedipus trained the entire court. Every person watching ran the same calculation and reached the same conclusion. The information stayed where it was. The leader remained in the dark. The gap between what the system knew and what the center could hear kept widening – quietly, rationally, invisibly – until it couldn’t.

This is the Culture cylinder of CREATE (Click here) misfiring. The environment produces anxiety rather than trust, silence rather than signal. It doesn’t announce itself. It accumulates one dismissed concern at a time, until the organization is full of people who know exactly what’s wrong and have learned, very rationally, to say nothing.

The leader experiences this as things being fine.

Right up until they aren’t.

Oedipus is a system failure. The truth existed. The system couldn’t deliver it.

Antigone – The Leader Who Got the Truth and Refused It

Creon is also not a bad leader. He’s a competent new executive trying to establish order after chaos, making what he genuinely believes is a defensible decision. Polynices was a traitor. Traitors don’t get burial rites. The rule must hold. Every step of his logic is locally reasonable.

And every step takes him further from a position he can safely reverse.

The scene that breaks me is Haemon. Creon’s own son – measured, loyal, not a radical – comes to his father and makes the case carefully. He doesn’t challenge the principle. He challenges the application. He tells Creon what the city is actually saying, what people are whispering, that the room is not with him on this one. He is doing everything right. He is the Challenger gear of VOICES (Click here) functioning exactly as it should – naming what isn’t being said, surfacing the uncomfortable data, giving the leader the information he needs before the cost of ignoring it becomes irreversible.

Creon sends him away.

Not because the argument is wrong. Because by that point, changing his mind has become, in his own accounting, more costly than being right. Every piece of contradictory evidence gets reframed as a challenge to defend against rather than information to integrate. Haemon tries. The chorus tries. Tiresias – the same prophet who tried with Oedipus – tries a third time. Creon hears all of it. He is not, like Oedipus, operating in an information vacuum. The truth reached him.

He simply wouldn’t receive it.

Antigone is what happens when the only person willing to challenge the leader is willing to die to do it.

That’s not courage. That’s a systems failure dressed as heroism.

Creon loses his son. His wife. His city’s faith. Every bit of it was reversible right up until it wasn’t. He had the information Oedipus never got – and it made no difference. Where Oedipus is a system failure, Creon is a character failure that becomes a system failure. The outcome is identical. The root is different. And the difference matters enormously for what you build.

Three plays. Three failure modes – and they escalate.

Ajax’s organization deployed its best people without developing them and lost them to a decision that was never properly held. Oedipus’s system couldn’t get the truth to the center, and collapsed under the weight of what it couldn’t say. Creon’s organization got the truth to the leader, and watched him refuse it, which is the most expensive failure of the three, because it means the system worked and the leader didn’t.

The Greeks understood that organizational collapse is almost never the result of bad intentions or insufficient effort. It’s the result of good leaders inside systems that couldn’t do three things: develop people beyond the role they were filling, deliver truth upward, and create leaders capable of receiving it when it arrived.

Those are not character problems. They are design problems.

The Teaching cylinder, the Culture cylinder, the Challenger gear – CREATE and VOICES are two of the three portions of the CLUTCH framework (Click here), is at its root, an attempt to build what Sophocles kept showing us was missing. Not better leaders in isolation. Better systems around the leaders that exist.

Sophocles staged these as tragedies because in his world, the system couldn’t be redesigned. The gods had already decided. The prophecy was already in motion.

You don’t have that excuse.

Tomorrow I go further back – to the poem that preceded the tragedies and in some ways contains all of them. The Iliad isn’t just three failure modes. It’s the complete causal chain, told at human cost. And the person who pays that cost isn’t Agamemnon or Achilles.

It’s Patroclus.

title: The Philosopher-King Problem
html:
Plato noticed something about power in 380 BC that most organizations are still pretending isn’t true.

In The Republic, he describes his ideal city – governed not by the ambitious, the elected, or the most recently promoted, but by philosopher-kings: people trained in long contemplation, deeply uncomfortable with authority, and actively reluctant to hold it. The best leaders, in Plato’s account, are the ones who have to be persuaded to lead. The worst are the ones who can’t wait to.

He wasn’t writing political theory. He was doing organizational diagnostics.

And he was pointing directly at the problem I named Monday: formation doesn’t announce itself. The people who did the hard work of it – the difficult texts, the uncomfortable seminars, the long discipline of being wrong in front of people who were paying attention – are not the people most likely to raise their hand. That’s the first failure. The second is that most organizations aren’t looking for them anyway.

The philosopher-king problem, in its modern form, is this: your promotion criteria select for visibility rather than capacity. For confidence, not judgment. For the desire to move up, not the ability to hold weight. And so the people who end up in leadership roles are disproportionately the people who wanted them, which, if Plato is right, is precisely the wrong filter.

Think about how leadership pipelines actually work. Someone performs well as an individual contributor. They raise their hand. They volunteer for the stretch assignment. They communicate ambition clearly and get promoted. None of those behaviors predict leadership capacity. They predict appetite for advancement, which is a different thing entirely.

The person who wanted the role is now in it. The person who would have been better in it never signaled that they wanted it – because the people most capable of holding authority quietly are often the least likely to pursue it loudly.

Plato called this the burden of return. The philosopher, having spent years developing judgment, has a responsibility to come back and lead. But the world of power is corrosive, and the people inside will resist being told that what they’re seeing isn’t the whole picture. So the philosopher stays where they’re comfortable. Someone else takes the role.

The ones who wanted to take it were never doing the contemplation.

This compounds in two specific ways.

The first is promotion by performance proxy. We promote people based on what they were good at, not what the new role requires. The best engineer becomes the engineering manager. The top salesperson becomes the VP of Sales. Individual excellence gets rewarded with leadership authority – and the skills that made someone exceptional as a contributor are almost never the skills that make someone effective when their job becomes making other people exceptional. The transition is rocky. We treat it as a people problem – coach them harder, give them feedback, send them to a workshop. Plato would call it a design problem. So would I. The role changed. The infrastructure around the person didn’t.

The second is confidence as competence. The candidate who speaks first, loudly, and with certainty tends to be read as leadership material – even when the certainty is manufactured and the speed is a coping mechanism for the anxiety of not knowing. Tolerance for ambiguity – one of the lessons I named Monday, and one of the most critical capacities for leaders operating in complex systems – reads as hesitation in most interview rooms. Careful thinking before speaking reads as lack of executive presence. We have built evaluation systems that systematically mistake the performance of confidence for the substance of judgment – and then promoted accordingly for decades.

Both problems share a root. The signals easiest to see in a candidate – assertiveness, visibility, stated ambition – are not the signals that matter most. But they’re the ones that survive a thirty-minute interview and a promotion committee discussion. The signals that matter most – how someone holds uncertainty, how they behave when they’re wrong, how much room they make for people who know more – are slow to reveal and hard to measure. So we don’t measure them. We measure what we can see. And we get more of it.

This is why the VOICES framework exists (Click here to learn more about VOICES) – not as a personality taxonomy, but as a diagnostic. If the only leadership presence your organization recognizes and rewards is the loud, certain, directive one, you’ve built a single-gear system. And single-gear systems stall the moment the terrain changes.

Do your promotion criteria measure leadership capacity, or leadership appetite?

Leadership cultures reproduce themselves. If the people who rise are the ones who perform with confidence and signal ambition, the next generation of leadership gets selected by those same people, using the same criteria, producing the same result. The philosopher-kings never get back in the room. The people who wanted the room keep running it.

Plato’s solution was radical: remove the choice entirely. Assign leadership to those most fit for it, whether they want it or not.

Draft the reluctant. Bench the eager.

You don’t have to go that far. But you do have to redesign what you’re looking for – and build the systems that make it visible. What does this person do when the situation has no precedent? How do they behave when they’re wrong in public? Do they make room for people who know more, or do they fill the space? What happens to the people around them over time – do they grow, or do they shrink?

These aren’t interview questions. They’re observation questions – and they require an organizational structure that creates the conditions to observe them. Most promotion processes don’t. They’re designed for efficiency, not accuracy. A thirty-minute interview and a calibration meeting will consistently select for the person who performs best under pressure, which is exactly the wrong test.

The CLUTCH (Click here) framework is, at its core, an answer to this problem. Not a training program for individual leaders, but an operating system that makes leadership capacity visible – through the decisions people make, the gears they shift between, the way authority moves through the organization over time. You can’t promote what you can’t see. Building the infrastructure that makes it visible is the work.

And the cost of not building it is paid in every leadership hire that looked right and landed wrong. In every brilliant individual contributor promoted into a role that needed a completely different person. In every organization that wonders why its leadership bench is thinner than it should be – not because the talent isn’t there, but because the system was never designed to find it.

Wednesday, I’m in Sophocles. Three plays. Three failure modes. All of them are still running in organizations near you right now.

Plato has been waiting 2,400 years for someone to take these questions seriously at the org-chart level.

The answers were never in The Republic. He just kept asking until the right people could no longer ignore the questions. Actually, it’s probably what got him killed. But that is another essay.

title: The Humanities Were Never Soft
html:
Five lessons. All of them are described as skills. None of them actually are skills.

Rolling Stone ran a piece this week making the case that business schools don’t teach what leadership actually requires. Narrative intelligence. Moral imagination. Tolerance for ambiguity. Deep listening. Systems thinking through human context. The list is right. The framing is the problem.

Here is that original piece.

Calling these things skills is how we keep mishandling them – treating them as optional, acquirable, subject to a two-day offsite and a Kirkpatrick Level 2 evaluation. A skill is something you acquire. Infrastructure is something you build into – something that holds weight even when you’re not consciously operating it.

These aren’t skills. They’re formation. And formation is different.

I have a sociology degree from LSE. I spent twenty years in classrooms and several more in leadership development within a federal humanitarian agency – rooms where people made decisions under pressure that most of us will never feel.

The capacities the Rolling Stone piece describes? I didn’t learn them in those rooms. I used them. They were already structural. Already load-bearing. The distinction matters because it changes what we think can be done about any of this.

What follows isn’t a counter-list. The RS piece had five items; I’m not replacing them with five better ones – and I’m not claiming the list is complete. These are lessons. Not exhaustive, not exclusive. Formation in the humanities tends to produce them, but the point isn’t the taxonomy. The point is that a lesson is different from a skill. A skill is something you acquire. A lesson is something that changes the structure of how you see. One gets installed. The other gets built in. And built-in is different.

Let’s walk through them – not to validate them, but to show what they actually do inside an organization.

Narrative intelligence is the capacity to understand that every decision is a story, and that stories land emotionally before they land logically. A leader with this capacity doesn’t just communicate clearly – they author coherence. They give people a frame for why the change matters and who they are inside it. Without it, culture runs cold. People execute without meaning. They comply without committing. Most communication training teaches delivery. Narrative intelligence is about what you’re actually building when you speak.

Moral imagination is the ability to see the ethical dimension of a decision early, before the compromise is made and the cost is accumulating. Culture crises don’t arrive overnight. They’re the compounded result of small exceptions, each of which seemed locally reasonable. A leader without moral imagination makes every one of those exceptions and calls it pragmatism. The humanities build this through the uncomfortable discipline of asking: who benefits, who’s invisible, what does this cost that we’re not counting. That’s not softness. That’s foresight with a longer horizon.

Tolerance for ambiguity is what lets a leader make a good decision when the information is incomplete, the map is wrong, and the terrain is changing. Most leaders who appear decisive are actually just intolerant of ambiguity. Confidence is a coping mechanism, not a capability. Literature rarely resolves cleanly. Neither does a scaling organization. The leaders who can hold uncertainty without collapsing into false clarity – or frozen inaction – are running a different internal architecture than the ones who can’t.

Deep listening is not active listening, which is a technique. It’s the interpretive muscle built by years of learning to notice what’s unsaid – tone, structure, silence, contradiction. The leader who hears fatigue before burnout, resentment before revolt, and innovation before it’s fully formed isn’t reading minds. They’ve developed the same attentional discipline a novelist uses to build a character. They know that what’s on the surface is never the whole story. Most organizations dramatically overvalue assertiveness. The ones that survive disruption tend to have someone in the room who can actually hear what’s happening.

Systems thinking through human context is the capacity to understand that culture determines behavior, behavior determines results, and that nothing in an organization is as isolated as it appears. The humanities teach this through history, philosophy, the long arc – they situate decisions in time and consequence. It’s the leadership stance most people never shift into, because it requires the uncomfortable admission that the system they built might be the problem.

Five lessons. None of them “teachable” in a twelve-week program. And none of them end of the list – just the five the RS piece named that are worth taking seriously.

Which creates an obvious problem.

Because by the time someone is in a management role, the formation has either happened or it hasn’t. You cannot install moral imagination in a workshop. You cannot build tolerance for ambiguity with a competency model. That formation takes years – difficult texts, uncomfortable seminars, the particular discipline of being wrong in front of people who are paying attention.

But formation and infrastructure are not the same thing. You can’t give someone twenty years of difficult texts at 35. What you can do is build systems that make those capacities possible – even in people who didn’t come up through the humanities. The formation happened, or it didn’t. The infrastructure is still yours to design: systems that reward moral imagination rather than punish it, decision frameworks that create space for ambiguity rather than demand premature resolution, cultures that make deep listening structurally safe.

That’s not retrofitting the person. That’s designing the conditions.

The Rolling Stone piece closes with a line worth keeping. “The future will belong to leaders who can calculate and contemplate.”

It’s right. But the way we’ll get there isn’t by adding contemplation to the curriculum. The organizations struggling most right now built their leadership infrastructure on a monoculture – one kind of knowing, one kind of formation, one framework for what rigor looks like.

The humanities produce a different kind of rigor. Slower, less legible, harder to certify. But it’s the rigor that holds when the situation has no precedent, the data is incomplete, and the human cost of a wrong decision is real and irreversible.

That’s not soft. That’s load-bearing.

I’m not arguing that every executive needs a literature degree or that philosophy seminars substitute for operational experience. I’m arguing that we’ve systematically excluded a certain kind of knowing from leadership formation – and that exclusion has a cost we’ve been paying in slow motion for twenty years. Trust deficits. Culture failures. Leaders who can optimize a system but cannot read it.

The humanities teach you to read.

Not text. Reality.

In a world moving faster than any playbook can track, the leader who can feel the moral temperature of a room – who can sense the fragile architecture of trust before it fractures – is doing something that can’t be automated and can’t be taught in a weekend.

What it can be is designed around.

Subscribe now

One of my favorite books is Plato’s Republic. Not because it’s comforting – it isn’t. But it keeps asking the question most organizations never ask long enough to answer: what does it actually mean for something to function well? There’s an entire essay in that. I’ll be back on Tuesday.

What’s the book that most changed how you lead? Reply and tell me.

And if you’re thinking about what this infrastructure actually looks like inside your organization – not the formation, but the systems that make these capacities possible – that’s the work I do.

title: The Room Was Running Without Me
subtitle: A lesson about lessons.
html:
The room was running without me.

I was near the door, watching a student lead a full-class debrief on a collaborative persuasive essay three of his peers had written on whether Andrew Jackson’s removal of the Cherokee Nation was justified. Not reading from it. Interrogating it. He was asking follow-up questions, pushing back on weak claims, redirecting the conversation when someone conflated government policy with inevitable history. The other students were tracking, responding, and building on each other’s arguments. I had said maybe four words in the last twenty minutes. The accountability structure I had spent weeks and months (this was probably April) building was doing exactly the work I would have otherwise done myself.

Seventh grade. American history. I didn’t have a name for it yet. I knew I had designed something.

Here is what nearly 20 years in that classroom actually taught me: the word “leadership” never appeared in my job description, and I was doing almost nothing else. Not teaching content. Designing accountability structures. Distributing authority before it was needed. Installing culture before installing curriculum. Every Socratic seminar protocol I handed to students, every peer revision structure built around evidence standards, every decision about which student ran which part of a simulation was an act of organizational design. I was simply not compensated as though it was.

The business world eventually noticed the gap. They named it leadership development, built conferences around it, wrote the books, and hired the consultants. What they built, almost without exception, was training. Skills programs. Workshops. The assumption underneath all of it is that leadership is something you learn – not something you design into a system. Schools had been doing the latter for over a century, in every building, every September. The knowledge didn’t transfer because the status didn’t travel with it. And so, business kept reinventing a broken answer to a problem that had already been solved elsewhere.

That gap is structural, and it has consequences. When a consultant tells a founder to “empower their team,” they are pointing at something middle school teachers have been building since September, in rooms full of twelve-year-olds, with no budget and constant real-time feedback from the most honest audience imaginable. Seventh graders DO NOT perform engagement out of politeness. You know immediately when the system isn’t working.

The three things that crossed directly from my classroom into the leadership work I now do with founders and executives aren’t insights I developed after I left teaching. They’re things I built on repeat, for years, in a building where no one thought to call it leadership. Here’s what organizations keep failing to do that every decent classroom does by default.

The first is decision rights distributed before they’re needed. In a well-designed classroom, students know which decisions belong to them before any situation tests it – who runs the Socratic seminar, who tracks the evidence standard, who calls the question when discussion drifts. By September, before any crisis forced the question, the authority map already existed. Founders almost always reverse this sequence. They clarify who owns what only after something goes wrong – precisely when clarity is hardest to establish, and the stakes are highest. The map gets drawn in the fire, which is the worst possible time to draw it.

The second is culture installed before content. I never taught the first unit – on colonization, on the Constitution, on the Trail of Tears – before the class knew how we worked. How we disagreed. What we did when someone cited a bad source. What it means to revise a claim under pressure. Leaders rush toward strategy before they have built the operating conditions that make strategy executable. The sequence is not a preference. It’s a prerequisite.

The third is feedback loops that run without the leader as gatekeeper. By October of any given year, my seventh graders were giving each other more precise, more actionable feedback on argument structure and evidence quality than most management teams exchange in a full quarter. Not because they were exceptional. Because I had built the criteria, the structure, and the practice into the room itself. The loop ran when I stepped back, because I designed it to run that way.

If your organization doesn’t have all three, you don’t have a team problem. You have a design problem.

Three questions worth sitting with:

  1. If you stepped out for two weeks tomorrow, which decisions would stall — and is that because your people lack judgment, or because you never mapped who owns what?

  2. Can your team name the three or four principles that govern how you make decisions together — or did you skip straight to strategy?

  3. When was the last time your team gave each other hard, useful feedback without you in the room?

That is what CLUTCH argues. Not that leaders need to work harder. The system needs to be designed to work when they step back. I built that case over 20 years in a classroom. I’ve spent the years since figuring out why I had to leave to be heard.

title: HAL 9000 Didn't Write My Novel. I Did.
html:
Go ahead. Open a new AI chat window. Type this prompt:

“Write me the next great American novel in the style of The Great Gatsby.”

I’ll wait.

What you’ll get back is competent and might tap-out at about 2000 words.

It’ll have the green light, a narrator with just enough wistfulness, sentences that gesture toward elegance. It will also be immediately, obviously, hollow. Because Fitzgerald wasn’t generating prose. He was processing the specific psychic wound of watching America confuse wealth with virtue, spectacle with meaning, and reinvention with redemption. That wound was his. The novel came from it.

And by the way, tell me the 2020s don’t mirror the Gilded Age. Unprecedented wealth concentration, technological disruption upending every industry at once, a new class of barons deciding the rules don’t quite apply to them, and an old guard furiously insisting that the new arrivals don’t deserve what they’ve built.

Someone is working on the next great American novel, and I can’t wait to read it.

In the meantime, Gatsby remains my favorite book.

I am a published author.

Boom.

I’m going to let that sit there for a second, because even typing it still feels a little surreal – and because somewhere, my old middle school English teachers are reading this and slowly dying inside. I still don’t know what a dangling participle is. I was a dyslexic kid who was not, by any traditional measure, destined to be a writer.

Last week, I published Balance – a love story about a CRISPR researcher named Ellie, and a promise I kept to my wife after thirty years to write her a romance novel “someday” – and now it is out in the world. Real pages. Real readers. I don’t think I understood what “someday” was costing her until the day I handed her a copy with her name in it. Thirty years is a long time to believe in someone who hasn’t quite believed in himself yet. Turns out having something to say mattered more than knowing the rules for saying it. She knew that before I did. Since then, my brain has hardly been able to contain my ideas. I have a leadership book coming out shortly, and in the pipeline, a retelling of the Iliad in the trenches of WW1, and my biography of the number Seven.

Thanks, hun, for giving me permission and the encouragement to do this. I’m a writer.

And lately I keep getting looped into what I’ll call the authorsphere – writers, publishing folks, people with strong opinions about craft and legitimacy, and who gets to call themselves a “writer.” There’s a freakout happening in those circles right now. Publishers pulling contracts, see “Shy Girl.” Accusations flying. And the forensic evidence being marshaled against suspected AI frauds?

The em dash.

Apparently, if your prose contains an em dash, HAL9000 wrote it. You are a fraud. You did not touch grass, live a life, or feel anything. You typed a prompt and laundered the output as literature.

I use em dashes constantly; for me, they are a break – I probably – should – use a comma, but this is how I think – therefore – also how I write. I also wrote my novel myself – every scene, every character, every plot decision, every late night wondering if any of this was any good. The em dash thing would be funny if it weren’t a stand-in for a much lazier argument: that using any AI tool, at any point, for any purpose, disqualifies the work.

That’s not a position about craft. It’s a position about gatekeeping. There’s a difference.

Here’s exactly what I used AI for.

LinkedIn intros. Instagram captions. When I finish a Substack piece of writing I’m proud of, I’ve already done the hard creative work – the thinking, the drafting, the revising. What I haven’t done is figure out how to game LinkedIn’s engagement algorithm or write a caption that stops the scroll on Instagram. I don’t know how to do that. I’m not sure I want to spend the time learning. Claude does know, so I ask: “Hey, create an optimized Instagram caption for this essay.” The creative thought is mine. The platform optimization is logistics. Nobody accuses a novelist of fraud for having a publicist.

Character revision – and this is the one that might horrify some people. Character revision. Early readers told me one character needed to show greater growth in confidence across the novel. They were right – I could feel it the moment they said it. What I couldn’t see was exactly where the gaps were, scene by scene, across 100,000 words I’d been living inside for years.

So I asked Claude to do what AI is genuinely good at: interpret data. I fed it the manuscript and asked it to track one specific character’s language across every scene – word choice, hedging versus assertion, the linguistic markers of confidence or its absence – and plot that arc linearly. What I got back wasn’t a rewrite suggestion. It was a graph.

The line zigzagged. Up, then down, then up again – confidence spiking and dipping in a pattern that felt accidental rather than earned. I wanted something different: a line that climbed slowly and distinctly, with the occasional setback that still read as forward motion. So I went back into the manuscript and started tinkering. The words were always mine. But treating those words as data – seeing where the character had been quietly dipping in scenes I thought were neutral – gave me a precision I couldn’t have found on my own. Each revision, I’d run it again. Watch the line respond. Adjust.

The tool showed me the data. I made the call.

The distinction I keep coming back to is this:

  • A shortcut replaces the creative process.

  • A tool serves it.

I had a story to tell. I believed it was worth telling. I sat down and told it, imperfect comma usage and all. When I needed help seeing something I couldn’t see on my own, I used tools that helped me see it. Then I made my own decisions.

That’s not so different from a filmmaker using editing software, or a musician using Pro Tools, or an architect using CAD. The software didn’t design the building. It made the designer’s vision executable.

The authorsphere’s anxiety is understandable.

The tools are new, the pace of change is disorienting, and yes, there are absolutely people using AI to generate hollow slop and calling it literature. That’s real, and it’s worth taking seriously. But the response has been to treat any use of AI as contamination – which means conflating the person who asked Claude to write their novel with the person who asked Claude to help them write a better one.

Those are not the same person.

Every knowledge worker is navigating some version of this right now. And the institutions meant to evaluate their work are quietly panicking. Not because the work is worse. Because they can’t tell anymore.

Think about what that actually means in practice. The admissions committee reading a personal essay that might be entirely the applicant’s voice or might be the applicant’s ideas routed through a tool that cleaned up the syntax and tightened the structure – and having no reliable way to know. The hiring manager reviewing a portfolio piece that reflects genuine expertise or reflects the ability to prompt-engineer a convincing simulation of it – and having no reliable way to know. The editor, the professor, the credentialing board, the peer reviewer – all of them holding work up to the light, looking for the watermark, and finding that watermarks don’t work the way they used to.

The panic isn’t aesthetic. It’s epistemological.

These institutions were not built to evaluate outputs in isolation. They were built to evaluate outputs as evidence of process – as proof that a particular kind of thinking happened, in a particular kind of person, over a particular kind of time. The résumé doesn’t just list what you did. It traces how you became someone who can do it. The dissertation isn’t just an argument – it’s a record of initiation. When the output can be produced without the process, the entire evaluation architecture starts to wobble. Not because the work is bad. Because the work is unreadable in the way these institutions were designed to read it.

That’s the real crisis. Not quality – legibility.

For generations, professional credentialing systems have been built around process as much as outcome. You prove you belong by demonstrating you did it the hard way. The bar exam. The dissertation. The portfolio. The byline history. These aren’t just measures of competence – they’re proof of initiation. You went through the thing. You earned the right to be evaluated by people who have also gone through it.

AI breaks that. Not because it makes the work worse, but because it decouples the outcome from the initiation ritual. And institutions that built their authority on administering the ritual don’t quite know what to do when the ritual becomes optional. So they call it fraud. They reach for the em dash as evidence. What they’re actually saying is: we don’t know how to evaluate you anymore, and that frightens us, and it’s easier to disqualify you than to admit we need new frameworks.

Meanwhile, the anxiety within the knowledge worker is entirely its own thing. The lawyer who used AI to draft the first pass of a brief and then spent three hours making it actually good. The teacher who generated a rubric outline and then rewrote every line of it to fit her kids. The consultant asked Claude to summarize 40 pages of research so he could spend his hours on insight rather than synthesis. The marketer who hasn’t written an unassisted first draft in two years and hasn’t told anyone.

The anxiety underneath it all is the same: If I use AI to do part of this, am I still the one doing it? Does the work still count? Do I still count?

We’re asking an identity question and calling it an ethics question. They’re not the same thing.

The ethics question is real and worth asking: Are you transparent about your process? Are you submitting AI output as your own thinking when it isn’t? Are you using the tool to avoid the hard work or to do harder work? Those matter. Answer them honestly, and you’ll know where you stand.

Hence, my mea culpa in this.

But the identity question – do I still count – that one’s a trap. Nobody asks whether a surgeon “really” performed the operation if she used robotic assistance. Nobody asks whether an architect “really” designed the building if he used CAD. The tool receded into the background because we had time to build consensus about what the human’s irreplaceable contribution actually was. The judgment. The training. The accountability. The call.

We haven’t built that consensus yet for knowledge work and AI. We’re in the uncomfortable middle, where the tools are here but the frameworks for thinking about them aren’t. So we’re improvising – some people pretending the tools don’t exist, some people pretending the tools are the work, and most people somewhere in the anxious middle, quietly using them and not quite saying so.

What I know from my own work – in coaching, in leadership consulting, in writing – is that the thing worth paying for was never the production of the output. It was the thinking behind it. The pattern recognition was built over years spent in rooms where hard decisions were made. The ability to ask the question that reframes the whole problem. The judgment about which of the ten possible paths is the right one for this person, this organization, this moment.

AI cannot do that. It can serve it. There’s a version of every knowledge worker’s job that gets better with these tools – more bandwidth for the irreplaceable parts, less time lost to the parts that were always just logistics.

The gatekeepers aren’t protecting quality.

They’re protecting legibility.

They know how to evaluate work made the old way. Work made with new tools, in new combinations, by people who don’t fit the traditional mold – that’s harder to categorize. And what can’t be categorized can’t be controlled. So it gets called fraudulent instead.

That’s the Gilded Age move, isn’t it? New money, new technologies, new methods of building something, and an old guard insisting the new arrivals don’t deserve what they’ve made because they made it differently. The anxiety was never really about standards. It was about who gets to set them.

That’s not a standard. That’s a tell.

I’m not a master craftsman of literary fiction. I know that. I was a dyslexic kid who couldn’t diagram a sentence, and I still can’t. But I had a story, and I told it, and I used every honest tool available to tell it better.

The em dash was mine.

The work was mine.

So here’s what I want to know:

Are you using AI as a tool, avoiding it entirely, or somewhere in the anxious middle – quietly using it and not quite saying so?

The comments are open. I promise not to check your em dashes.

⚠️ A note:

If you’ve read this on LinkedIn or Instagram and clicked through to my Substack, and made it to the end of this piece, thank you.

What you read there on LinkedIn and Instagram was roughly 50/50 AI-generated – a summary Claude helped me write to work within those platforms’ formats and algorithms. I can see the data. I know how many of you read the post versus how many click through to Substack. Some people only ever read the compressed version.

Proof:

I get it. We’re all busy. But in the attention economy, the summary has become the product – and what you read just now is the full version of the argument, not the summary. This essay is actually about that exact tradeoff. Which means, if you made it this far… thanks.

title: They Sent a Middle School Teacher to Save the World
subtitle: What happens when you optimize for the right kind of mind
html:
Let me tell you something about middle school teachers.

Before they teach a single concept, they have to be six different people. Developmental psychologist. Stand-up comedian. Curriculum designer improvising in real time because the lesson plan stopped working twelve minutes ago. Conflict mediator. Data analyst tracking thirty individual progress arcs. And – on any given Tuesday – an amateur nutritionist, and a de facto school counselor.

But the thing that doesn’t make it onto the resume or the performance review is this: the best middle school teachers are relentless, almost pathological assumption-challengers. They have to be. A twelve-year-old has no patience for “that’s just how it works.” She will ask why fourteen times in a row with genuine sincerity, and if you’ve been coasting on received wisdom and untested premises, she will find you out instantly.

Teaching middle school science, in particular, is a daily audit of everything you think you know. More than that, the best teachers learn to distrust the question they were handed and find the one underneath it. They hold multiple domains simultaneously. They make connections across disciplines because that’s how kids actually learn – not in silos, but in webs of association and meaning.

Andy Weir understood this. Project Hail Mary – novel first, now a film – builds its entire premise on it.

The selection decision

Ryland Grace is a snarky, brilliant, deeply human middle school science teacher. He wakes up alone on a spacecraft with no memory of how he got there, no mission briefing, and two dead crewmates beside him.

He is Earth’s only hope for survival.

The most interesting thing in the story isn’t the science, or the alien, or the extinction-level crisis. It’s the decision made by the people who put Grace on that ship. They didn’t choose a decorated specialist or a celebrated researcher. They chose the person whose thinking process was most likely to survive contact with the genuinely unknown.

Early in the mission, Grace realizes the crisis can’t be solved by the model everyone has been using. He doesn’t defend the model. He interrogates it – strips it back to first principles, identifies the assumption baked into the original question, and rebuilds from there. The solution lives underneath the premise that everyone else has accepted.

This is what a great science teacher does on a Tuesday afternoon when a kid’s question breaks the lesson plan. You don’t force the question back into the frame. You follow it somewhere new.

The Socratic Method + Scientific Method is leadership under pressure

Here’s the thing – those are all the same process: what do you already believe, why do you believe it, what would have to be true for that to be wrong, and now what?

Most organizations skip straight to “now what.” They inherit premises that stopped being accurate two funding rounds ago and build a strategy on top of them. The scaling crisis that looks like a people problem is actually a decision-rights problem. The communication breakdown that looks like a culture problem is actually a structural problem. Nobody sees it because nobody stopped to distrust the question they were handed.

Grace, alone in deep space with incomplete data, makes hypotheses instead of assumptions. He tests them. He updates. When the data contradicts his model, he doesn’t defend the model – he asks better questions. And then better questions than those.

When everything external was stripped away – the briefing, the crew, the mission context, his own memory – what remained was the cognitive architecture. A system for thinking built from years of classroom pressure, not a body of knowledge that depended on stable conditions to function.

Your leadership team will face unstable conditions. What remains when context disappears?

Rocky

At some point – I won’t spoil the how – Grace encounters Rocky, an alien engineer from a different star system, working alone on the same problem. No shared language. No shared biology. No shared frame of reference.

The assumption Grace never makes is that Rocky thinks like him. He approaches the relationship the way a great teacher approaches a new student – with genuine curiosity about how this particular mind works, what it already knows, and what shared vocabulary they can build from scratch. He asks questions. He listens to the answers. He revises his model of Rocky constantly, in real time, as new data arrives.

Most leadership teams walk out of meetings with different mental models of what was just decided, because no one stopped to ask the question underneath the question. Rocky and Grace don’t do that. Neither does a great seventh-grade science teacher.

That’s not chemistry. That’s infrastructure.

The Hail Mary selection committee optimized for cognitive architecture – specifically, the kind that forms when you’ve spent years being forced to question your own assumptions, synthesize across disciplines, and find the right question before reaching for an answer.

Most organizations promote expertise and depth of content – looking at you, high school teachers – sorry (not sorry). They build teams that are collectively brilliant on familiar ground but collectively helpless when the premise the plan was built on turns out to be wrong.

What’s left of your leaders when you strip everything else away?

Build the infrastructure.

Hire the assumption-challengers.

And pay your middle school teachers what they’re actually worth. The best thinkers in the business.

The Leadership Lab is a newsletter for founders, operators, and strategic partners who are tired of leadership advice that sounds good and does nothing.

title: Leadership Fitness Isn’t Neurology. It’s Design.
html:
Last week, the President of the United States told reporters that dyslexia should disqualify someone from the presidency. He said it four times in five days.

Embedded in those comments is an assumption worth examining carefully – not because of who said it, but because it doesn’t belong only to him. It lives inside organizations everywhere, quietly filtering out some of the most capable thinkers in the building.

The assumption: leadership fitness is a function of how your brain is wired.

That assumption isn’t just wrong. It’s the exact design flaw that keeps organizations stuck.

The Student the System Couldn’t See

I spent more than two decades teaching. For seventeen of those years, I worked at a K–12 school, which meant I didn’t just watch kids from September to June. I watched them over the years. I knew their families. I saw who they became.

That longitudinal view changes what you can see.

The student flagged for deficiency in fourth grade – I could watch him in eleventh. The kid the system had quietly written off as a struggling reader – I could see where she ended up. And what I saw, often enough that it stopped surprising me, was this: the students whose brains had been labeled as problems were, in many cases, the ones who went on to the most selective universities in the country. They were the best thinkers. The system just couldn’t see it.

I know this more personally than I’d like.

My own son is severely dyslexic. He was counselled out of the school where I taught – the same school where I showed up every day to help other people’s children learn. We found a specialized school. He received Orton-Gillingham instruction. It was, without exaggeration, life-changing. The difference between who he was before that intervention and who he became after it is the difference between a kid the system was losing and a kid who could finally show what he actually knew.

He is currently completing a five-year accelerated BS/MS program in mechanical engineering at one of the most selective engineering schools in the country. Dean’s List. Severely dyslexic.

But here’s what that path cost our family: my entire teacher’s salary – every dollar I earned at one school – went to pay tuition at another. That’s the math we lived. And I know we were the fortunate ones. Not every family can absorb that. Not every kid gets that intervention. Many don’t. They fall through the cracks, disengage, and carry something bitter about education and about their own intelligence for years longer than they should.

This essay is about what happens when those kids grow up – and what their brains are actually capable of when someone finally builds a system designed to find out.

One in Five Brains. Zero Intelligence Deficit.

Dyslexia is a processing difference. It is not an intelligence deficit.

The Yale Center for Dyslexia and Creativity is unequivocal: dyslexia is unrelated to overall intelligence. It affects roughly one in five people, which means it is almost certainly present in every leadership team, every boardroom, and every cabinet, whether anyone has named it or not.

What dyslexic cognition tends to produce isn’t a list of compensations. It’s a list of capacities. Big-picture synthesis. Pattern detection across domains. Narrative thinking – the ability to hold complexity as a story rather than a spreadsheet. Crisis navigation that doesn’t freeze in the face of ambiguity.

Researchers at Cambridge describe this as “explorer cognition” – the brain that thrives when the terrain is unfamiliar, and the old maps don’t work. The conditions that most demand leadership – volatility, uncertainty, crisis, disruption, the moment when the playbook stops working – are precisely the conditions where dyslexic cognition has a structural advantage.

Dyslexic thinkers aren’t scanning for the answer inside the known constraints. They’re looking for the frame that makes the constraints irrelevant.

That’s not a liability for leadership. That’s the job.

What the Research Actually Says

In 2018, EY partnered with Made By Dyslexia to map dyslexic thinking skills directly to workforce demand – in a report written entirely by dyslexic individuals at EY. The methodology is the message.

The six identified skill areas – Reasoning, Connecting, Exploring, Communicating, Imagining, and Visualising – map directly to the World Economic Forum’s most in-demand capabilities for the future of work. In 2022, LinkedIn added “Dyslexic Thinking” as an official skill on its platform. Nine hundred million professionals. The world’s largest career network.

EY’s conclusion was direct: a business where dyslexic strengths are understood and harnessed could become more innovative and better positioned for a rapidly changing world of work. Not more charitable. Not more accommodating. More competitive.

The President sees dyslexia as a disqualifier. LinkedIn sees it as a credential. One of them is reading the future correctly.

Fitness Isn’t Neurology. It’s Design.

The real question was never whether a leader has a learning difference.

The real question is whether the leader has built a system that extracts the best thinking from every kind of mind in the room – including their own.

Those are not the same question. And conflating them is where most organizations go quietly, expensively wrong.

The research locates fitness not in individual neurology but in the system the leader builds. A leader who builds a system that only works for one kind of brain hasn’t built a strong team. They’ve built a vulnerable one – and every problem that requires a different kind of thinking will eventually find the gap.

There’s an irony worth naming. The leaders most likely to build systems that work for every kind of thinker are often the ones who spent a lifetime surviving systems that weren’t built for them. They know what it costs to mask, adapt, and perform competence in someone else’s cognitive language. That instinct – the hard-won understanding that there are multiple ways to think, multiple routes to a right answer, multiple ways to demonstrate what you know – is exactly what leadership at scale requires.

My son is completing an accelerated graduate engineering degree because someone finally built a system designed to find what his brain could actually do. The system that couldn’t see him wasn’t measuring his potential. It was measuring its own limitations.

The same is true in every organization. The same is true in leadership.

The Double Work Nobody Talks About

Right now, in your building, on your team, inside your leadership structure, there are people doing double work. They are executing the job and simultaneously translating their best thinking into a format the system can recognize. They are performing competence in a cognitive language that isn’t native to them, while their actual strongest thinking goes untapped.

The cost isn’t the energy required to accommodate differences. The cost is what you never get – the pattern the conventional thinker didn’t see, the reframe that unlocked the stuck problem, the crisis navigation that didn’t freeze because the person leading it had spent their whole life finding new routes when the standard one was closed.

A leader who looks at dyslexia and sees disqualification has never had to think carefully about what thinking actually is – or what it costs an organization when you suppress the wrong kind.

The Double Work Diagnostic

Before you move on, sit with these four questions. They’re worth bringing to your leadership team:

1. Who on your team is translating? Who is doing double work – executing the job and converting their best thinking into a format the system can recognize? How would you know?

2. What problems keep returning unsolved? If a challenge has cycled through your team more than once without resolution, consider whether you’ve been applying one cognitive style to a problem that requires a different one.

3. Who have you called a poor communicator? Some of the people labeled “hard to follow” or “not concise” are thinking in a mode the system wasn’t designed to receive. Are they unclear – or are they untranslatable in your current structure?

4. Whose best thinking is the system actively suppressing? If your meeting formats, reporting structures, and decision processes were designed around one kind of mind, you already know the answer.

Leadership bottlenecks are design problems. What helps some helps all. A team that can only access one kind of intelligence isn’t a strong team – it’s a team waiting for the problem that exposes it.

If these questions are relevant, I’d like to discuss. The work I do with founders and leadership teams is built around exactly this: finding where your system leaves capacity on the table and redesigning it so that every kind of thinker can contribute at their best.

Subscribe now

If those questions hit a nerve, you’re not alone. Most of the organizations I work with – founders, leadership teams, schools, nonprofits, government agencies – arrive at the same place: they can see the problem clearly, but the system hasn’t caught up to what they know. The work is building the infrastructure that closes that gap.
