title: The Five Conversations Your Team Is Avoiding
html:
You already know something is off. You’ve known for a while. The question isn’t whether the conversations are happening. It’s why they’re not happening in the room where the decisions get made.

Most organizations have a short list of topics that circulate constantly in the spaces around formal meetings: in the parking lot after the all-hands, in the thread the team has without the founder, in the debrief on the way to the elevator. The same five or six subjects that never quite make the agenda. Not because people don’t care. Because the formal structure hasn’t made it safe, useful, or possible to raise them directly.

Here are the five conversations most teams are having everywhere except where it counts.

1. What we actually think about how decisions get made.

Most teams hold two theories simultaneously: how decisions are officially made, and how they actually get made. When those theories diverge significantly, and nobody names it, trust erodes quietly. People route around the official process because experience has taught them it doesn’t reflect reality. The conversation that needs to happen is an honest audit of who decides what, and whether the people doing the work have enough authority to do it well.

2. Where the real bottleneck is.

Somebody on your team knows exactly where work stops moving. They’ve watched the same project stall at the same point three times. They’ve identified the approval that never comes quickly, the calendar that is the single biggest constraint on company velocity. This is not gossip. It’s a structural observation – and the person holding it usually doesn’t feel safe delivering it upward without a frame that makes it land as data rather than a complaint.

3. Who is burning out, and why?

Burnout rarely arrives as a declaration. It arrives as a pattern: the contributor who used to volunteer and has stopped, the team that’s technically productive but has lost its energy. By the time someone leaves, there have usually been six months of signals that the organization didn’t know how to read. The conversation most teams aren’t having isn’t “is anyone struggling?” It’s “what is the system doing to people, and what are we willing to redesign?”

4. Whether the stated priorities match the actual ones.

Every organization has an official priority list and a revealed one, visible in where time, money, and attention actually go. When those lists don’t match, they produce a specific exhaustion: people working hard on things that don’t seem to matter, unsure whether to trust the roadmap or their own observation. The conversation that closes this gap requires a public, honest comparison of what was said versus what was done – without blame, but with enough candor to produce a correction.

5. What we’d do differently if we weren’t afraid of the answer.

There’s usually at least one significant decision that a meaningful portion of the team believes was wrong, or at least incomplete, but that never got revisited because raising it felt riskier than living with it. Organizations that can hold this conversation without it becoming a referendum on leadership are the ones that actually adapt.

None of these conversations is primarily about information. They’re about whether the formal system is safe and capable of holding what the informal system already carries. If the answer is not yet, the work isn’t to force the conversations. It’s to build the conditions that make them possible.

That usually starts with one honest exchange in one meeting where the quiet part gets said out loud – and nothing bad happens.

Three Questions to Bring Into Your Next Leadership Meeting

Not to sit privately. To use.

1. What’s the most important topic currently circulating in your organization’s informal channels that hasn’t made it into a formal conversation yet – and what does the system need to change before it can?

2. If the people closest to the work wrote an honest postmortem on the last major decision, what would it say about how that decision actually got made?

3. What would a team member have to believe about this organization to bring you genuinely critical feedback – and do those conditions currently exist?

Subscribe now

If those questions hit a nerve, you’re not alone. Most of the organizations I work with – founders, leadership teams, schools, nonprofits, government agencies – arrive at the same place: they can see the problem clearly, but the system hasn’t caught up to what they know. The work is building the infrastructure that closes that gap.

title: What Attila the Hun Knew That Your CEO Doesn’t
subtitle: I found the answer on my dad’s bookshelf.
html:
There’s a worn little hardback that lived on my father’s bookshelf for as long as I can remember. It wasn’t much to look at: eighty-six pages, a dramatic cover, a title that sounded like it belonged in a history class rather than a management seminar. Leadership Secrets of Attila the Hun by Wess Roberts, a former Army major turned insurance executive, whose slim volume would go on to become a New York Times bestseller translated into twenty-four languages.

I’m fairly certain it came home from the War College. My dad was career military, retired as an O-6 from the USAF, and this book had that unmistakable feel of something that got passed around among officers like contraband wisdom. Too fun to be doctrine. Too useful to ignore. I’ve since heard it referenced in military circles more times than I can count. Colonels and Command Sergeants Major will mention it with a knowing grin, the way people talk about a shared secret. It appeared in the Naval War College Review. Special operations veterans have called it a career-long companion. For a slim little book, it punched well above its weight class.

I picked it up as a teenager, probably out of curiosity more than ambition. I didn’t know yet that I’d spend the next few decades obsessing over how leaders are built, broken, and rebuilt. I just thought the idea of learning leadership from a fifth-century warlord was kind of wild.

It was. I remember the first time I read it distinctly. And it changed the trajectory of how I think about what leaders actually do.

What Attila Understood That Most Modern Leaders Don’t

Roberts did something clever. He took Attila, a man history remembers as “the Scourge of God,” and reframed him not as a barbarian but as a strategist. A unifier. A man who took a loose confederation of nomadic, multilingual, multiethnic tribes and forged them into the most dominant force the ancient world had seen.

The book is structured around what Roberts called “Attilaisms,” pithy, imagined speeches from Attila to his chieftains on topics like loyalty, decision-making, morale, discipline, negotiation, and the graceful handling of defeat. They read like the kind of wisdom you’d hear from a mentor who has no patience for pretense and no interest in impressing you. Just in making you better.

Here’s what stayed with me.

Pick Your Battles. No, Actually Pick Them.

One of the first lessons the book drills home is that great leaders are ruthlessly selective about where they spend their energy. Attila didn’t attack everything that moved. He was calculating, patient, and strategic about which conflicts to engage and which to let pass.

I think about this constantly in my coaching work. The leaders I see burning out fastest aren’t the ones facing the biggest challenges. They’re the ones who refuse to triage. Every email is urgent. Every disagreement is a hill to die on. Every initiative gets equal weight. Attila would have ridden right past half of it. Not because he was lazy, but because he understood that saying yes to everything is the same as saying yes to nothing.

Your Team Isn’t Watching Your PowerPoints

Roberts makes the point that Attila held himself to the same standards he expected of his warriors, and often to higher ones. His discipline wasn’t performative. It was the foundation of his credibility.

This is the principle I’ve come to call “modeling” in my own work, and it sits right at the heart of what makes or breaks a leader’s culture. You don’t get to talk about accountability while dodging your own feedback. You don’t get to preach vulnerability while armoring up in every meeting. Your people aren’t watching your PowerPoints. They’re watching your behavior. Attila knew that fifteen hundred years ago. We’re still learning it.

He Turned Captivity Into a Classroom

What fascinated me most, rereading Leadership Secrets of Attila the Hun as an adult, is that Roberts wasn’t describing one kind of leader. He was describing a leader who could move fluidly between roles. I think this was the seed for my VOICES framework – the idea that effective leaders don’t have one “gear.” They shift. Attila was a visionary who unified the tribes around a shared future, an operator who managed the logistics of campaigns spanning continents, a coach who developed chieftains and gave them real authority, and a sculptor who reshaped tribal structures to meet evolving threats. He spent part of his youth as a political hostage in a Roman court, and rather than wasting that time in resentment, he absorbed everything he could about how his adversaries thought, organized, and fought. He turned captivity into a classroom.

This is the quality I’ve come to think of as a leadership gearbox: the ability to shift between modes of presence without losing yourself in the process. The best leaders I’ve worked with, in schools, in government, in startups, share this quality. They’re insatiably curious. They treat every environment, even hostile ones, as a source of intelligence. And they know instinctively when the moment calls for vision, when it calls for precision, and when it calls for simply getting out of the way.

Attila understood tribal dynamics in ways that would make any modern org designer envious. He didn’t hoard talent at the center. He empowered his chieftains, gave them real authority, and held them accountable for results, not for process. He knew that a leader who needs to be the smartest person in every room has already lost. This one hit differently when I started coaching founders. So many early-stage leaders struggle with the transition from “I do everything” to “I build the team that does everything.” Attila made that transition with an entire civilization. The principle scales.

Morale Is Not a Perk. It’s Infrastructure.

Roberts dedicates serious attention to morale and discipline, not as soft skills, but as the structural underpinning of any effective organization. Attila treated the spirit of his warriors the way an engineer treats load-bearing walls. You don’t get to neglect it and then wonder why the building collapses.

I’ve seen this play out in every organization I’ve worked in. The schools where morale was treated as someone else’s problem were the schools losing their best teachers. The agencies where “resilience” was code for “just deal with it” were hemorrhaging institutional knowledge. Morale isn’t about pizza parties. It’s about whether people believe that their leader sees them, values them, and will fight for them.

Attila’s warriors followed him into impossible campaigns against the Roman Empire, not because they were afraid of him, but because they believed in what he was building. That’s morale as infrastructure. That’s the real secret.

The Chapter Nobody Writes

The chapter that surprised me most was the one on leaving well. Roberts writes about the importance of how a leader exits: stepping down, transitioning power, and handling defeat with dignity. It’s the leadership topic almost nobody talks about, and it might be the most important one.

I think about this chapter more than any other these days. When I left McDonogh School after seventeen years of teaching, I found myself reaching for Tennyson’s Ulysses to say what I couldn’t say in my own words – that the people I’d worked with were “souls that have toil’d, and wrought, and thought with me,” and that leaving them was one of the hardest things I’d done. But Tennyson also reminded me that “all experience is an arch wherethro’ gleams that untravelled world,” and that staying safe in a role you’ve outgrown is its own kind of failure.

The way you leave something tells the world everything about how you led while you were there. Do you burn bridges or build them on your way out? Do you hoard knowledge or transfer it? Do you make the transition about your ego or about the mission?

Attila, for all his ferocity, understood that a leader’s legacy isn’t written in the battles they win. It’s written in what survives after they’re gone. The act of releasing, of transitioning smoothly, might be the most underrated skill in all of leadership.

Eighty-Six Pages and Fifteen Hundred Years

The principles haven’t changed in fifteen hundred years. Be disciplined. Be curious. Be selective. Model the behavior you expect. Invest in your people. Handle defeat with grace. And when it’s time to go, go well.

My dad probably didn’t know that the little book on his shelf would become the first link in a chain that led me to a career built on helping people lead better. But that’s how these things work, isn’t it? The most important lessons don’t announce themselves. They just sit there on a bookshelf, waiting for someone to pick them up.

Thanks, Dad. And thanks, Attila.

Three Questions Attila Would Ask Your Organization

Before your next leadership meeting, sit with these:

  1. Where are you spending energy on battles that don’t matter, and what would it cost you to ride past them?

  2. If your team only watched your behavior and ignored every word you said, what would they learn about your actual values?

  3. If you left tomorrow, what would survive without you, and what would collapse?

If those questions hit a nerve, you’re not alone. Most of the organizations I work with – founders, leadership teams, schools, nonprofits, government agencies – arrive at the same place: the culture feels supportive, but performance has quietly stagnated. The work involves rebuilding the connection between safety and standards so your team gets both the trust and the challenge they actually need to grow.

I take on a handful of clients at a time because this work doesn’t happen in a single session. If that sounds like what you need, let’s talk. If not, the book and the essays aren’t going anywhere.

title: I Accidentally Wrote a Leadership Book. It’s a Romance Novel.
html:
This year, I wrote three books.

The first one – CLUTCH – is the one that makes sense. It’s the leadership book I’ve been building toward for years, drawn from every coaching engagement, every organizational redesign, every founder who called me because their company was growing faster than their ability to lead it. That one drops March 15 – the Ides of March. The original case study in what happens when a leader mistakes the system for himself.

The second is a biography of the number Seven. Prime, indivisible, resistant to simplification – a number that shows up across myths and maps and memory systems, not because the universe required it, but because we did. That one’s still in progress. It’s weird and wonderful, and I can’t stop working on it. This one is my personal passion project.

The third is a love-triangle romance novel.

I set out to write a love story – under a pen name, with a thin veil of deniability and, if I’m honest, embarrassment. The market for romance novels written by fifty-two-year-old men is, shall we say, unproven. I’ll out myself eventually. Probably when Dan Savage wants to interview me.

It started as a promise to my wife. She’d been saying for years that I should write fiction, and at some point, I ran out of excuses. It was my Misogi project for 2024. And I delivered a single, Kinkos-printed and bound version later that year. But she insisted it was good and that I should actually publish it. What I didn’t expect was the journey it would take me on. I read more fiction in the past year than in the previous ten combined. I read craft books and literary journals. I read Esther Perel and fell down rabbit holes in Slate and The Atlantic about how modern relationships actually work. So, when I was RIF’ed from USAID in February of last year, I suddenly had a lot of free time…

The book is about a couple who stop being careful with each other and start being honest instead. About what happens when love turns out to be bigger and stranger than the shape (a triangle in this case – cue New Order, IYKYK) you’d planned for it. I didn’t intend for me or my wife to be a template for any character. It’s not about us.

But there are moments.

There’s a man in the book who brings the woman he loves tea every morning – Earl Grey, no milk, two lumps of sugar. He does it without being asked. He does it even on the morning after she tells him something that changes everything between them.

That’s not us. But I bring my wife tea every morning. And when we upgraded from a queen bed to a king – more room than we’ve ever had – I still go looking for her in the middle of the night.

Just a little hidden easter egg for her.

OK, now it’s public. But not embarrassed by that. Love you, Gwen. 🍵❤️

Somewhere between the second draft and the fifth, I noticed a thread I hadn’t planned. The book is a love story – full stop. But woven through it is something quieter: women in science mentoring other women in science. It’s not the plot. It’s the thing that keeps showing up in the margins – in a lab late at night, in a hallway conversation that changes someone’s career trajectory, in the way one character grows because another one chose to invest in her instead of just moving on.

It’s subtle. But it ended up mattering to every character it touched. And when I read it back, I realized it was the only leadership philosophy I’ve ever believed in: the patient, invisible work of helping someone become more of who they already are.

Here’s the scene that stopped me.

A junior researcher is spiraling over data that doesn’t make sense, convinced she’s missed something obvious. And a senior scientist – instead of fixing the problem, which would have taken thirty seconds – pulls up a chair:

“What’s your instinct telling you?”

“That I’m missing something obvious. Something everyone else would catch immediately.”

“That’s frustration talking, not instinct.” She kept her voice gentle. “You’re right that the edit should be consistent. So if the cut is the same but the outcome varies, what else could be creating that variance?”

Jess’s eyes moved across the data. She sat up straighter. “Environmental stress. The conditions would change how the cell reads the edit, even if the edit itself is identical.”

“There it is.” Ellie smiled. “The code is only part of the story – context shapes what gets read and what stays silent.”

She spent the next hour beside Jess, not lecturing but questioning – letting Jess work through the implications herself. Which conditions should be standardized? How to document the variables. What it would take to make their results reproducible across labs, across patient populations, across the gap between a petri dish and a living human being.

“When I first started,” Ellie said eventually, “I made the exact same mistake. Spent two weeks convinced my experiment was broken before Dr. Harris asked me the same question I just asked you.”

“What question?”

“’What’s your instinct telling you?’” Ellie smiled. “I’d been so focused on finding the error that I stopped trusting my own thinking. The answer was there the whole time. I just needed someone to remind me I was capable of seeing it.”

“You should present this at the next team meeting. You caught it. You should be the one to flag it.”

Jess’s eyes widened. “Present it? But I nearly missed it entirely –”

“And then you didn’t. That’s science.”

“But you asked the right questions –”

“I asked questions you already knew the answers to. I just gave you permission to say them out loud. That’s what a good mentor does. But the work is yours. And the credit should be yours too.”

Jess swallowed. “Dr. Harris used to do that for you, didn’t he? Ask questions instead of giving answers?”

“How did you know that?”

“You mentioned him once. Early on.” Jess smiled, a little shy. “You said he was the first person who made you feel like a real scientist. Not a student pretending to be one.”

The memory landed with unexpected weight. Harris, with his rumpled blazers and his endless patience. The way he’d pushed her onto stages she wasn’t ready for, then stood in the back of the room, nodding, like he’d known all along she could do it.

“He was,” Ellie said. “And I’m trying to do for you what he did for me. Not because you need it – you’re already good. But because everyone deserves someone in their corner.”

“Say you’ll present. Say you’ll stand up in front of Singh and Kim and everyone else and tell them what you found.” Ellie held her gaze. “Say you’ll let them see what I see.”

A long pause. Then, slowly, Jess nodded. “Okay. I’ll do it.”

“Good.” Ellie squeezed her shoulder. “One more woman who learns to take up space.”

As she moved toward her own bench, she glanced back to see Jess staring at the data with new focus – shoulders looser now, a spark kindled behind her eyes.

This, Ellie, thought. This is why I chose this life. Not the boardrooms or the funding pitches. The light flickering on in someone else’s eyes. The moment when someone stopped doubting themselves long enough to see what they were capable of.

Afterward, a colleague watches this exchange and says, “That was well done. The Socratic approach. Most lead researchers would have fixed it for her and moved on.“

And then: “Building people up takes longer than doing the work yourself. Most senior scientists can’t be bothered. They’re too busy chasing the next publication, the next grant, the next rung.“

And then she says something I keep coming back to:

“I had a mentor like that once. Someone who asked questions instead of giving answers. It changed everything for me – not just how I did science, but how I saw myself doing it. How I understood what kind of leader I wanted to become.”

I wrote that scene thinking I was writing about science. I read it back and realized I was writing about every good manager I’ve ever had. The ones who made me feel like I’d figured something out on my own, only to realize years later that they’d been steering the whole time. The ones who understood that the point was never the problem – it was the person.

The light flickering on in someone else’s eyes. That’s the sentence that stopped me. Because that’s what the best leaders do. Not solve things. Not impress people with how fast they can fix it. They wait. They ask. They stand in the back of the room, nodding, like they knew all along you could do it.

Maybe that’s what all good love stories are – stories about the patient, invisible work of helping someone become more of who they already are. No pirates. No Scottish lords. Just the small, steady acts that hold people together.

The most romantic thing you can do for someone – in a marriage, in a team, in a life – is just keep showing up.

Right now, I’m in the part of writing that nobody romanticizes: the trimming. Cutting words. Killing sentences I love. That’s really hard. Running chapters past the women in my advance reader group and listening – really listening – when they tell me what rings true and what doesn’t. I’m chasing something in the prose that I don’t quite have yet. If you made me name it, I’d say Emily St. John Mandel – that quality where every sentence earns its place and nothing is there just because the writer liked the sound of it.

Between a leadership book launching next month, a novel that’s getting closer to the thing I want it to be, a biography of the number Seven that won’t leave me alone, and continuing to bring my wife her tea every morning, the next few weeks will be slower here while I finish what I started. I’m not going anywhere. I’m just doing the thing I keep telling other people to do: protecting the work that matters most, even when it means saying no to the work that’s merely visible.

I’ll be back soon. In the meantime, if you need me, I’ll be arguing with my editor about my dashes – seriously its the way I’ve always written. People don’t talk in semi-colons…

But before I go, think about the person who pulled up a chair for you.

Who asked instead of fixed. Who stood in the back of the room, nodding.

Now ask yourself: who are you not doing that for?

What are you going to do differently this week now?

title: Servant Leadership Is Making You Weak
html:
Servant leadership is the most popular idea in modern leadership, and no one is allowed to criticize it. It has the moral high ground. It sounds selfless. It flatters the leader’s self-image. And in many organizations, it’s producing leaders who can’t make hard calls – and calling that virtue.

Here’s the problem: somewhere between Robert Greenleaf’s original insight and today’s LinkedIn consensus, “servant leadership” stopped meaning “build conditions for others to succeed” and started meaning “put everyone else’s needs ahead of your own, always, no matter what.”

That second version isn’t leadership. It’s conflict avoidance with a halo.

I spent twenty years in classrooms before starting my consulting practice. And classrooms taught me something about service that most leadership books get wrong.

The best teachers I’ve ever worked with are deeply devoted to their students. They care enormously. They sacrifice time, energy, and comfort. But they are not servants to their students. Not even close.

A great teacher will look a talented student in the eye and say: “This isn’t your best work. I know what you’re capable of, and this isn’t it. Try again.” A great teacher will set a boundary that makes a student furious – because that boundary creates the conditions for growth. A great teacher will make an unpopular decision for the room, absorb the frustration, and not flinch – because the job isn’t to be liked. The job is to build something in people that they can’t yet build in themselves.

That’s not service in the way servant leadership gets practiced in most organizations. That’s architecture. It’s designing the conditions for growth, which sometimes means being the person who creates discomfort rather than removes it.

Here’s what I see when servant leadership goes wrong – and it does so almost every time.

The leader who won’t give hard feedback because “my job is to support my team.” So the underperformer never hears the truth. They continue to produce mediocre work, wondering why they’re not advancing, while the leader congratulates themselves on being empathetic. Meanwhile, the high performers on the team – the ones watching the low bar go unaddressed – quietly start updating their résumés.

The leader who won’t make a unilateral call because “I serve the team, I don’t dictate to them.” So every decision becomes a consensus exercise. Speed dies. The team spends three meetings debating an issue that requires direction and a deadline. The leader thinks they’re being inclusive. The team thinks nobody’s driving.

The leader who absorbs every problem that flows uphill because “that’s what servant leaders do.” They become the organizational shock absorber – protecting the team from discomfort, shielding them from hard realities, and taking on work that should be distributed. They burn out. And when they finally crash, the team they “served” has no idea how to function without them – because they were never asked to.

Three leaders. Three sincere commitments to serving their teams. Three teams that are disadvantaged by it.

The original insight behind servant leadership was genuinely powerful. Greenleaf’s question – “Do those served grow as persons? Do they, while being served, become healthier, wiser, freer, more autonomous?” – is one of the best diagnostic questions in all of leadership theory.

But notice what it actually asks. It doesn’t ask whether the leader is nice. It doesn’t ask whether the leader avoids friction. It asks whether the people being led are growing. Becoming more autonomous. Getting stronger.

By Greenleaf’s own standard, a leader who avoids hard conversations isn’t serving anyone. They’re protecting themselves from discomfort and calling it service.

Growth requires friction. Autonomy requires being challenged. Becoming stronger requires encountering resistance – not being shielded from it.

The best servant leaders in Greenleaf’s sense aren’t the gentlest people in the room. They’re the ones willing to be temporarily unpopular in the service of someone else’s long-term development. That’s a much harder kind of service than “How can I make your day easier?”

There’s a phrase I use with leaders I coach: serve the growth, not the comfort.

It changes every conversation it enters.

  • “Should I step in and fix this for them?” Serve the growth, not the comfort. Let them struggle. Be available, not rescuing.

  • “Should I soften this feedback?” Serve the growth, not the comfort. Say the true thing. Say it with warmth. But say it.

  • “Should I take this problem off their plate?” Serve the growth, not the comfort. The problem is the development opportunity. Taking it away isn’t service – it’s theft.

  • “Should I let the team decide this?” Maybe. But if you’re letting them decide because you’re afraid to lead, that’s not empowerment. That’s abdication dressed up as generosity.

The litmus test isn’t “Am I being helpful?” It’s “Are the people I lead becoming more capable, more autonomous, and more willing to do hard things – because of how I show up?”

If yes, you’re serving them.

If you’re just making things easier, smoother, and more pleasant, you might be serving yourself.

None of this means be harsh. None of this means that you should ignore your team’s needs. None of this means command-and-control is the answer.

It means the highest form of leadership service is building people who don’t need you. And building people who don’t need you requires being willing to do things that don’t feel like service in the moment: holding them accountable, creating productive friction, making unpopular calls, and caring enough about someone’s growth to tell them what no one else will.

That’s not the opposite of servant leadership. That’s what servant leadership was supposed to be before we sanded off every edge and turned it into a permission slip for niceness.

Free, always. Delivered to your inbox so you’re not waiting on an algorithm to decide what you see.

Subscribe now

Following along:

This is Essay 6 of 6. Here’s the full week:

You Only Have One Voice – why leaders default to a single mode. Your Best Move Is Killing Your Team – what happens when strengths go unchecked. You Didn’t Delegate. You Dumped. – The three questions most leaders skip: Who Decided How You Decide? – Why the decision process matters more than the decision. The Brain Your Org Chart Can’t See – the cognitive diversity your systems are designed to suppress. Servant Leadership Is Making You Weak – why the most popular idea in leadership is being practiced backward

These essays are drawn from ideas in a book I’m finishing called CLUTCH: How Leaders Build Systems That Run Without Them – and from twenty years of teaching, coaching, and systems consulting with organizations that were stuck and wanted to move.

I work with founders, leadership teams, schools, nonprofits, and government agencies – organizations where the culture feels supportive but performance has quietly stagnated. The work involves rebuilding the connection between safety and standards so your team gets both the trust and the challenge they actually need to grow.

I take on a handful of clients at a time because this work doesn’t happen in a single session. If that sounds like what you need, let’s talk. If not, the book and the essays aren’t going anywhere.

title: Before It Was a Framework, It Was a Fight
subtitle: How post-it notes in a federal crisis room and a grading rubric for middle schoolers led to the same uncomfortable truth about leadership
html:
I built the same tool twice. Well, maybe three times. Different lifetimes, different organizations, different stakes. I didn’t realize it until much later.

I built the same tool three times. Different lifetimes, different organizations, different stakes. I didn’t realize it until much later.

The first time, I was a teacher trying to solve a grading problem. The second time, I was a leadership coach trying to prevent a team from tearing itself apart. The third time, I was starting my own consulting practice and watching the exact same dysfunction play out in every client organization I walked into. All three times, the root cause was the same: people operating without a shared language for how decisions get made. And all three times, the fix was the same. Not more authority. Not better people. A common framework that made the invisible visible.

That framework eventually became the 6C Decision Compass, the navigation system at the heart of CLUTCH: How Leaders Build Systems That Run Without Them. But it didn’t start as a chapter in a book. It started with post-it notes and an argument about middle schoolers.

The 5C Rubric: Solving for Coherence

At McDonogh School, where I taught for 17 years, we launched the Middle School Academy – an immersive, experiential program that pulled students out of the regular curriculum for a concentrated period of exploration. Full credit to Jennifer Smith and Denise Wolf, two fifth-grade teachers who were the genesis of this idea over lunchtime conversations, who dared to imagine what if school were different. Think of Academy as a mid-semester term where middle schoolers could take a deep dive into courses spanning the humanities, science, mathematics, and the arts. Students from multiple grade levels worked side by side. Teachers designed courses from scratch. At the end, everyone presented their learning in a public showcase.

It was ambitious. It was also, predictably, controversial.

The objections were real and came from every direction. Eighth graders were working toward high school placements; any time in Academy was time away from “curriculum”. In a zero-sum curricular world, every hour given to an experimental program was an hour taken from something established. And here was the question that almost killed the whole thing: with 24 wildly different courses – from robotics to poetry to field ecology – how do you ensure a common level of rigor? What does excellence look like when one student is building a bridge, and another is writing a one-act play?

A small committee of teachers, myself included, was tasked with answering that question. The answer wasn’t standardized content. It couldn’t be. The whole point of Academy was diversity of experience. So instead, we built a universal rubric around five dimensions that transcended subject matter.

I called them the 5Cs: Collaboration, Critical Thinking, Communication, Commitment, and Character.

Each C had its own set of observable behaviors. Collaboration wasn’t just “works with others” – it meant compromising with peers, contributing meaningfully to the team, and listening with respect. Critical Thinking meant generating new ideas, making connections, and demonstrating effective problem-solving. Communication required active listening, relevant questioning, and clear articulation. Commitment was about initiative, self-direction, and time management. Character mapped to the school’s own Compass values: Respect, Kindness, Honesty, and Responsibility.

The measures were deliberately simple. Rarely. Sometimes. Often. Consistently. No percentages. No curves. Just an honest observation of whether a student was actually demonstrating the behavior. And importantly, no mastery. How do you master “communication”?

It worked. Not because the rubric was brilliant (if I may say so myself – they’re still using it even though I left years ago), but because it gave 24 different teachers, teaching 24 different things, a shared vocabulary for what mattered. A robotics teacher and a ceramics teacher could both look at a student and say, “She’s consistently strong in Critical Thinking but only sometimes demonstrates Commitment,” and mean the same thing. The rubric made evaluation transparent, and transparency made rigor possible across radical diversity.

I filed that lesson away. I didn’t know I’d need it again.

The Room Where It Happened

Years later, I was working at USAID’s Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance, embedded with TPQ – the Office of Technical Program Quality. If you’ve never heard of TPQ, that’s by design. These were the quiet specialists, the people the agency called when the question was too technical for generalists. Infant nutrition. Specialists in a particular kind of volcanic mudslide you only see in Indonesia. Water and sanitation in Afghan displacement camps. Every person in that office was a world authority in their field.

They were also collectively a decision-making disaster.

Not because they lacked intelligence. The opposite. When you fill a room with people who are each the foremost expert in their domain, you create a particular kind of dysfunction. Everyone has an opinion. Everyone’s opinion, within their lane, is probably correct. And everyone’s instinct – born from genuine expertise and genuine care – is to weigh in on everything, even decisions outside their specialization. The motivation is almost always good. These are people who entered public service because they believe in the work. A little ego, or realistically a lot, to be sure. But mostly it’s the compulsion of someone who knows what right looks like and can’t stand watching it go wrong.

The structural problem made everything worse. TPQ experts were frequently deployed to Disaster Assistance Response Teams (DARTs) and pulled from headquarters for weeks or months. Decisions were sometimes made without key people present. When those experts returned, the questions were immediate and sharp. How was that decision made? Who made it? Under what authority? By what criteria?

The teams had no framework for answering those questions. No shared language. No documented process.

The result was predictable. Trust eroded. Transparency became suspect. Psychological safety – the foundation of any high-performing team – began to crack. People didn’t feel informed. People didn’t feel included. People started questioning motives rather than processes, because when the process is invisible, the only thing left to question is intent.

And in this context, the stakes weren’t quarterly targets or product launches. Lives were involved. Real ones. The programming these teams advised on determined whether displaced populations received adequate nutrition, whether health responses reached the right communities, and whether emergency funds were kept away from terrorist organizations (Looking at you DOGE, with your claims of fraud, and waste - show me the indictments, please). Decision ambiguity wasn’t an organizational annoyance. It was a moral failure.

I was working with a particular team on TPQ where all of these tensions had converged. Leadership knew something was wrong. The team members knew something was wrong. Everyone wanted clarity, but nobody had a mechanism for creating it. So we built one.

Post-It Notes and Pattern Recognition

I designed what turned out to be a multi-day workshop. The first step was archaeological: go back through two years of decisions – every single one, big and small – and write each one on a post-it note. As simplified as possible. One decision per note. I wish I had a picture of that wall.

Then we stepped back.

This is the part that’s hard to teach in a book but easy to see in a room. When you put two years of decisions on a wall, patterns emerge. Not immediately. At first, it looks like chaos – a mosaic of yellow, green, and blue squares with no organizing principle. But if you’re patient, and you have someone in the room with a talent for pattern recognition and the 30,000-foot perspective to use it, the clusters start to form.

We moved post-it notes. We rearranged. We argued about where things belonged. And eventually, the decisions sorted themselves into four columns based on the nature of the decision: USG/Agency/BHA decisions (matters determined above the team’s authority), Operational Decisions (advising on existing or potential programming), Routine Execution (the daily work), and Crisis Response (emergencies requiring immediate action).

That first column was the most painful to populate. These were decisions where, regardless of your expertise, regardless of what you could see on the ground, the call had been made at a level so far above you that your input wasn’t just unwelcome – it was irrelevant. Gaza was a vivid example. The team, in fact, the whole agency, could see what was happening. They had people on the ground, in camps. They possessed the technical knowledge to respond effectively. But policy constraints, the Biden administration’s stance, and the guidance flowing down from leadership meant the full weight of their expertise could not be brought to bear. The Rohingya crisis carried the same anguish. The team knew what was right; yet people were dying. They knew what was feasible. But something was better than nothing, and nothing was what the decision architecture sometimes produced.

Naming those constraints didn’t make them less painful. But it made them legible. And legibility is the first step toward trust.

Seven Mechanisms

I went home after the first day and couldn’t stop thinking about the columns. Categories of decisions were useful, but categories alone don’t tell you how to decide. The team needed mechanisms, not just labels.

Not sure that I slept much that night, my mind full a-buzz, but I came back the next day with seven.

  • Consultation. The decision falls outside the team’s scope, but there may be latitude in the execution details. Apply other decision-making models. Document the results and rationale.

  • Command. The team lead decides, with or without input. Clear. Fast. Sometimes necessary.

  • Choice. Outcomes are determined by ranked-choice voting among present members with relevant subject-matter expertise. Results and rationale documented.

  • Cumulative. Outcomes are determined by majority vote.

  • Collaborative. Open discussion where multiple contributors share ideas and insights. The final decision emerges from collective input, though it may still be guided by a designated leader.

  • Consensus. A decision reaches consensus when at least 80% of the quorum supports it. The minority view is acknowledged and documented. The decision moves forward. This was crucial: consensus didn’t mean unanimity. It meant sufficient alignment to act without leaving the dissenting 20% feeling erased.

  • Core Expertise. Decisions are delegated to the team member whose narrow technical specialization makes them the most qualified person in the room – possibly the most qualified person in the world – to make that call.

Seven mechanisms. Each is suited to different conditions. The key insight wasn’t that any single mechanism was superior. It was that the team needed to name which one they were using before they used it.

The Grid

But mechanisms alone still weren’t enough. Seven ways to decide are useful. Knowing which way to use when is the actual problem.

The breakthrough came when we added a second axis. The Y axis captured the type of decision: national security and U.S. foreign policy, operational programming, routine execution, and crisis response. The X axis captured scope – who the decision affected: the whole agency, the team, a sub-team, or an empowered individual.

Then we mapped the seven mechanisms onto the intersections.

Some squares had only one option, and there was nothing to discuss. Where national security or agency-wide foreign policy met the broadest scope, the answer was Command. Full stop. In many of those cases, even the team leaders had been told what they were going to do. There was no room for interpretation, let alone debate.

But other squares opened up. Operational decisions affecting the whole team’s programming? Consensus was the only option. Which immediately surfaced a productive argument: What is consensus? Is it 80 percent agreement? 75 percent? Does the dissenting minority get their concerns documented? Does documentation actually matter if the decision moves forward anyway? Every team I worked with eventually developed its own definition, and that was fine. The point wasn’t uniformity across teams. The point was that within each team, the threshold was explicit, agreed upon in advance, and applied consistently.

The richest squares were the ones with multiple valid options. Routine operational matters affecting only a sub-team could be handled through Choice, Collaborative, or Consensus depending on time constraints, budget pressures, or other external factors. The grid didn’t prescribe a single answer. It prescribed a menu – a bounded set of legitimate mechanisms the team had already vetted and agreed to.

That was the whole point. Every decision, before it was made, got sorted into a square on the grid. And the options available in that square had been predetermined. The team didn’t have to relitigate the process every time a new decision showed up.

There is, I should note, a healthy irony in all of this. Establishing the criteria for each square required its own decision-making process – the very one we were building. How do you decide how to decide before you’ve decided how to decide? Every threshold we set, every mechanism we assigned to a square, was itself a decision that needed a mechanism. And the mechanism we were reaching for didn’t exist yet because we were still constructing it.

What made it work – and I say this without a touch of ego – is that the team trusted me and the process. As an external coach, I wasn’t a stakeholder in any of their technical debates. I didn’t have a lane to protect or a portfolio to defend. That meant I could serve as an independent arbiter when the conversation got stuck, when two equally valid perspectives created a logjam, when the consensus threshold for defining the consensus threshold threatened to become its own infinite loop. I could break ties without anyone feeling overruled, because I had no stake in the outcome beyond the system itself working.

That role – the trusted outsider who holds the process while the team holds the content – turned out to be essential. And it taught me something I later built into CLUTCH – sometimes the most important leadership move is making sure someone in the room has no agenda except clarity.

No need to convene the entire team for an emergency when subject-matter expertise was really the only voice needed. No need to agonize over whether the team lead had overstepped when the grid already specified that routine execution decisions at the sub-team level were hers to make.

Were there edge cases? Of course. Occasionally, a decision didn’t fit neatly into any square and required some wrangling. But the grid was loose enough to cover 99.9 percent of situations, and the rare exceptions actually reinforced the system: the team could point to the grid, acknowledge that this particular situation didn’t map cleanly, and have a brief, focused conversation about which square came closest. Even the exceptions used the shared language.

Buy-In Is the Whole Point

Here’s what made the grid work in practice, and what separates it from every decision-making framework that looks elegant on a slide deck and dies on contact with reality: buy-in.

Every person on the team had participated in building the grid. They had sorted the post-it notes. They had argued about which mechanism belonged in which square. They had debated the consensus threshold. They had agreed, before any specific decision was on the table, on the rules that would govern all future decisions.

That meant when a team member returned from a six-week DART deployment and asked, “How was that decision made while I was gone?” the answer wasn’t defensive. It was structural. A team leader could say: “It was routine execution at the sub-team level. I solicited input from the people in the room, but per the grid, this was ultimately my call.” And the returning expert could review the grid, confirm the process matched the agreed framework, and move on – not because they necessarily would have made the same decision, but because they trusted the process by which it was made.

That distinction matters enormously. Trust in outcomes is fragile; you only trust the decision if you agree with it. Trust in process is durable; you trust the decision because you trust the system that produced it, even when you might have chosen differently.

Anyone in the room knew in advance that while a team lead might ask for advice, certain decisions would ultimately be hers. Anyone returning from the field could read the meeting minutes, check the decision log, see which square the decision fell into, and verify that the documented mechanism matched the agreed-upon grid. The transparency wasn’t a retroactive justification. It was the architecture itself.

And eventually, it became shorthand. Once the whole team had bought into the system, nobody needed to narrate the logic or defend the process. You could just say: “Operational decision, affecting the whole team. We used Collaborative.” Nine words. Everyone knew what that meant: the boundaries, who had input, and how the call was made. No lengthy justification. No defensive posture. Just a coordinate on a map that everyone had helped draw.

As an artifact of that original work, I’ve included a copy of the framework above. I probably broke a security rule or two getting it out of the building; I emailed it to my personal account so I could think about it on the train during my commute, turn it over in my head at home, sketch refinements at the kitchen table. It wasn’t launch codes. It was a grid on a spreadsheet. But if anyone from the USAID security office is reading this, I’d like to think the statute of limitations has expired. And after what DOGE allegedly did with my personally identifiable information, I’d say we’re even.

And here’s the part that surprised me most: the grid didn’t reduce people’s sense of influence. It increased it. When decision rights are ambiguous, people either overreach – weighing in on everything, hoping something sticks – or withdraw, assuming their input doesn’t matter. The grid eliminated both failure modes. People knew exactly where their voice carried weight, which meant they invested that voice more fully in the squares where it mattered.

The Same Problem, Years Apart

I didn’t see the connection until much later. The 5C rubric and the 7C grid – and its eventual metamorphosis into the 6C Decision Compass – solved the same problem. A group of diverse specialists, each excellent in their own domain, needed a shared language to evaluate something that lacked an obvious common standard. For middle school teachers, the question was: What does rigor look like across 24 different courses? For TPQ experts: What does legitimate decision-making look like across dozens of technical domains? And for the business owners and team leaders I work with now, the question is quieter but no less urgent: How do I stop being the person every decision has to flow through before anything moves?

In all three cases, the answer was the same. You don’t standardize the content. You standardize the criteria. You give people a common vocabulary for the dimensions that matter, and then you trust them to apply it within their context.

The rubric didn’t tell the robotics teacher how to teach robotics. It told her what to look for when she watched her students work. The grid didn’t tell the nutrition expert how to advise on programming. It told the team how to make the decision about that programming – who should be involved and how much authority was being transferred.

Structure creates clarity. Clarity creates trust. Trust creates speed. That sequence held true in a middle school and in a federal agency responding to global humanitarian crises. The scale was different. The stakes were different. The sequence was the same.

From Government Tool to Leadership System

The grid worked. It worked so well that I started seeing the same dysfunction everywhere – not just in government but in startups, school leadership teams, nonprofit boards, and corporate departments. The symptoms were always the same: smart people, good intentions, eroding trust, and a leader slowly drowning under the weight of every decision routing back to them.

But the USAID grid was bespoke. One axis was calibrated for a federal agency neck-deep in technical expertise and geared for fast emergency response – two things that did not often go together well without friction. The decision types, the scope categories, and even the consensus thresholds were tuned for a very specific organizational context. You couldn’t hand that grid to a SaaS founder or a school principal and expect it to translate.

So the mechanisms stayed, though not all seven. “Cumulative” – majority vote – folded into Consensus; it was really just consensus with a lower threshold, not a distinct mode of thinking. “Consultation” became “Consultative,” a subtle but important shift from noun to adjective, emphasizing a mode of operating rather than a one-time event. And “Choice” evolved most dramatically: at USAID, it meant ranked-choice voting among present experts, a formal mechanism for a specific context. In the final framework, Choice became something broader and more powerful: full delegation, complete autonomy, the leader stepping back entirely. Same word. Different animal. Seven became six: Command, Consultative, Collaborative, Consensus, Core Expert, and Choice.

What needed replacing was the government’s unique axis. That answer came from Michael Hyatt’s work on delegation levels (shout out to Zachary Cochran), and it clicked immediately. Hyatt’s spectrum – from Level 1 (”Wait: do exactly as I say”) through Level 5 (”Own Completely: this is yours, start to finish”) – did something the USAID axis couldn’t: it described the degree of authority transfer in language that was universal. It didn’t matter whether you were running a humanitarian response team or a marketing department. The question “How much of this decision am I actually handing over?” applied everywhere.

When I overlaid the six decision modes with Hyatt’s five levels, the grid transformed. Instead of a government-specific diagnostic, it became a 6×5 matrix with 30 possible coordinates – each a precise description of how a decision will be made and how much ownership will be transferred. The principle was unchanged from that TPQ workshop: before any decision is made, name the coordinate. But now the coordinate system was portable.

“This is Consultative, Level 3. I want your recommendation, and I’ll make the final call.”

Twelve words that prevent twelve weeks of confusion. And twelve words that work whether you’re advising on infant nutrition programming in East Africa or launching a product feature in Austin.

The Lesson Underneath the Lesson

Frameworks don’t come from theory. They come from problems that won’t go away until someone builds a structure around them.

The 5Cs arose from a debate over whether experimental education could be rigorous. The 6Cs arose from a dispute over whether technical experts could trust each other’s judgment when some were 8,000 miles away during the decision. Both fights were really about the same thing: what happens when smart, caring people lack a shared way to evaluate what matters.

The answer, both times, was to make the criteria visible. Not to impose a single right answer, but to give people a common language for the dimensions that define quality – or in the case of decisions, legitimacy.

If you lead a team and you’ve ever felt the friction of people questioning decisions that seemed perfectly reasonable to you, the problem probably isn’t the decision. It’s the absence of a shared framework for understanding how that decision was made, by whom, and under what authority. Make that visible, and trust doesn’t just recover. It compounds.

That’s what the grid does. Not perfectly. Not in every situation. But consistently enough that a room full of the world’s foremost experts – people who had every reason to believe their individual judgment was sufficient – looked at a wall of post-it notes and agreed: we need this.

If they needed it, your team probably does too.

No call to action - no solicitations for you to subscribe or sign up for a “Chatt with Matt”. Just like my mind was a-buzzing on the way home after that first meeting, there was A LOT of interest in this grid, so I thought I would take some time to explain its evolution from a middle school tool to an instrument of government policy to what is in my book. If you’ve made it this far, one of my longest posts, congrats, and thanks. Hope you found it insightful to peek inside my process.

title: Gallup Stopped Measuring What Matters Most
html:
I use Gallup’s CliftonStrengths assessment with nearly every client I serve – founders, school leaders, and technical teams. I’ve built a significant part of my consulting practice on Gallup’s tools and philosophy.

But it’s not just the strengths work. I rely on Gallup’s data – and specifically its reputation for nonpartisan rigor – to make sense of the world beyond my practice. Just last week, I published an essay drawing on Gallup’s “Most Important Problem” research, the kind of long-running, methodologically consistent data that lets you cut through partisan noise and see what Americans actually care about.

I believe in the science. I point clients and readers to Gallup’s name as a mark of independence and credibility.

Which is exactly why I’m not going to be quiet about this.

On February 11, Gallup announced it will no longer publish presidential approval ratings or favorability ratings of political figures – ending an 88-year tradition that began during the Great Depression, when George Gallup first sent pollsters across the country to ask ordinary Americans what they thought of their president.

Their explanation? The ratings are now “widely produced, aggregated and interpreted” and “no longer represent an area where Gallup can make its most distinctive contribution.”

That’s not a strategy. That’s an exit.

The Measurement Company That Stopped Measuring

One of my personal mantras – one I bring into every coaching engagement and every leadership system I design – is simple: what gets measured gets done. Gallup taught me that. Their entire brand is built on the premise that what gets measured gets understood. They sell that idea to every organization that buys their engagement platform, every coach who gets certified in their methodology, every leader who sits down to debrief their Top 5.

And the thing that made Gallup Gallup – before the StrengthsFinder, before Q12, before the engagement surveys – was the radical, democratic act of asking Americans what they thought about power.

That was the original product. That was the mission.

Now they’ve decided it’s no longer where they “make their most distinctive contribution.” In 2026. During one of the most consequential political periods in modern American history. With independent institutions under pressure everywhere you look.

The timing doesn’t just raise questions. It answers them.

Who Actually Loses

Yes, other pollsters measure approval ratings. FiveThirtyEight aggregates them. The data will still exist in some form.

But the loss runs deeper than headlines.

Political science loses its longest continuous dataset. The American Presidency Project at UC Santa Barbara has called Gallup the only source that consistently asked the same approval question since the dawn of scientific opinion polling. Researchers studying presidential power, electoral behavior, and democratic accountability don’t just need a poll – they need the same poll, asked the same way, across decades. That continuity is irreplaceable. Every new pollster who picks up the question starts a new clock.

Methodological rigor loses its most visible champion. Gallup was one of the last major firms still conducting presidential approval polls using live telephone interviews – an expensive, rigorous methodology that most pollsters have abandoned for cheaper online surveys. When Gallup’s number disagreed with the aggregator’s, it meant something. That independent signal is gone.

And the American public loses something harder to name. When a major nonpartisan institution believes that tracking the public’s assessment of its leaders is worth doing – even when the results are inconvenient – that sends a signal about what a democracy owes itself. When that institution walks away, it sends a different signal entirely.

When institutions voluntarily retreat from accountability work, they don’t create a vacuum that gets filled. They create permission for the next institution to retreat, too.

You Don’t Get to Sell Courage and Practice Retreat

I sit across from leaders every week and tell them that self-awareness requires honest data. That you can’t build a healthy culture without rigorous measurement. That the hard numbers – even the uncomfortable ones – are the foundation on which everything else is built.

So when the company that built the temple of measurement quietly closes the door on the most publicly visible measurement it ever created – not because the methodology failed, but because the political environment got uncomfortable – I notice the gap between the sermon and the practice.

The Institutional Retreat Diagnostic

Gallup isn’t the only organization navigating this tension. If you lead one – or advise one – these are worth sitting with:

  1. What are we still measuring because it’s easy, and what have we stopped measuring because it’s uncomfortable?

  2. If we dropped our most publicly visible commitment tomorrow, would our explanation survive a single honest follow-up question?

  3. Are we evolving our mission – or editing it to avoid friction?

The Bottom Line

I’ll keep using CliftonStrengths – the science is sound, and it changes lives. But I’m not going to pretend this decision is just a business pivot.

Gallup made its name by believing that the voice of the people was worth measuring, especially when it was inconvenient for the powerful. Walking away from that work doesn’t reflect an “evolution.” It reflects a choice. And choices have consequences – for credibility, for public trust, and for every coach and consultant who points to Gallup’s name and says, “These are the people who believe in rigorous, independent measurement.”

I still believe in the measurement. I need Gallup to believe in it, too.

title: Whose Brain Is Missing from the Room Where It Happens?
html:
A leadership team I was working with at a government agency had been stuck on the same problem for three hours. These were people making decisions that affected field operations in crisis zones. Smart people. Aligned on values. Genuinely committed to getting it right. But every strategy session looped: the same questions, the same frameworks, the same impasse.

Then I noticed what was actually happening: everyone in the room processed information the same way.

Sequential. Verbal. Collaborative. They could all think on their feet, build on each other’s ideas in real time, and articulate their reasoning as they went. It looked like high-functioning teamwork. It felt like alignment. But they kept missing the same category of problem: the ones that required sitting with ambiguity, zooming out to system-level patterns, or asking a fundamentally different question than the one the data was answering.

They weren’t lacking intelligence. They were all intelligent in the same way.

Earlier this week, I wrote about delegation (aka, Just Handle It) and the three things most leaders fail to make explicit in the first thirty seconds of a handoff. That piece struck a nerve. Yesterday, I published the 6C Decision Matrix, a tool I developed to clarify not only what is decided but also how and by whom. That one struck a different nerve.

(A confession: I was tinkering with the layout yesterday morning and accidentally sent the essay out without the grid image attached. If you’re a subscriber, you received the essay without the grid in your email. Sorry!)

I went to bed last night with my head spinning about both essays and how the grid connects them. Because here’s what I’ve learned since building those frameworks: delegation clarity is necessary, but it’s not sufficient. Decision-mode clarity is necessary but not sufficient. You can nail every element of the handoff, choose exactly the right decision mode, and still fail if everyone involved in the decision processes information in the same way. The question isn’t only how you delegate or how you decide. It’s whose brain is in the room when it happens.

Most organizations treat cognitive diversity as a compliance issue. How do we accommodate this person? How do we help them succeed despite their diagnosis?

Both questions start from the same flawed premise: that there’s an optimal way to think, and the organization’s job is to smooth over the gaps when someone deviates from it.

But here’s what neuroscience keeps showing us: different brains don’t just process differently. They see differently. And that difference isn’t a deficit to manage. It’s a strategic capability most organizations systematically suppress.

The question isn’t “How do we accommodate this person?”

It’s “Which problems actually require this cognitive profile to solve?”

That reframe changes everything.

There’s a model from cognitive neuroscience, the explorer-versus-exploiter model, that maps perfectly to this.

Some brains are wired for exploration. They scan horizons, detect patterns across domains, navigate uncertainty, and get bored in stable systems. They start experimenting before the data says it’s safe. They connect ideas that no one else thought to put together.

Other brains are wired for exploitation. Precision. Consistency. Deep-system optimization. Quality control that doesn’t fatigue under repetition. They see the structural flaw hiding in plain sight, the edge case everyone else assumed wouldn’t matter.

Both are essential. Most organizations only design for one.

They hire for “culture fit,” which usually means “thinks as we think.” They build workflows that assume uniform processing: real-time brainstorming, open-plan offices, popcorn sharing in meetings. All are designed for individuals who think aloud and thrive in social environments. If your brain doesn’t work that way, the system doesn’t call you less capable. It quietly ensures your best thinking never reaches the room.

In a comment thread on the delegation essay, the issue of trust arose, and it’s worth pausing on because it reveals the same blind spot from a different angle.

I’ve served as a certified Speed of Trust facilitator, and the Covey framework does important work: it gives organizations a common language for why trust matters and how trust behaviors compound over time. I used it extensively at USAID. But here’s what I kept running into: the framework assumes trust looks the same everywhere. That building, maintaining, and honoring it follow a universal pattern. They don’t.

In some cultures, trust is built through direct confrontation. You earn credibility by challenging ideas openly, even forcefully. In others, trust requires protecting face. Publicly questioning a colleague’s reasoning doesn’t signal intellectual rigor. It signals disrespect. In some contexts, trust develops through personal relationships first and professional credibility second. In others, it’s the reverse. Erin Meyer maps this beautifully in The Culture Map, and anyone leading across borders or identities should read it.

At a global humanitarian organization with colleagues in Amman, Kyiv, Nairobi, and Washington, the Western, boardroom-centric trust model wasn’t wrong. It was incomplete. When we ran Speed of Trust workshops, the American and Northern European staff nodded along. Colleagues from East Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia were polite, but the framework didn’t land the same way because it wasn’t built for how they experienced trust. The behaviors Covey identifies as trust-building, things like “talk straight” and “confront reality,” can read very differently depending on the cultural operating system of the person hearing them.

This isn’t a flaw in those cultures. It’s glorious, actually. The range of ways humans build trust is one of the most sophisticated things about us. But you have to be aware of it, in much the same way you have to be aware of neurodiversity. Because when you design for one trust model and call it universal, you make the same mistake as when you design for one cognitive profile and call it normal. You end up measuring everyone against a standard that was only ever one way of being human. And people who don’t fit the template aren’t lacking in trustworthiness or intelligence. They operate from a different set of assumptions about how collaboration is supposed to work.

Trust frameworks tell you the relational conditions for sound decision-making. They don’t tell you whether you have the cognitive or cultural diversity to actually make them.

When I trace recurring organizational problems back to their root cause, the pattern is almost always the same: it’s not an execution failure. It’s a cognitive homogeneity problem.

Innovation keeps stalling? You probably need explorer brains, the ones who get bored with optimization and start seeing possibilities before the data proves it’s safe. If your roadmap feels incremental and no one is asking whether you’re solving the right problem, you don’t have a strategy issue. You have a thinking-style gap.

Quality keeps failing in the same category? You probably need exploiter brains, the ones who model structural integrity in real time and don’t miss the edge case. They’re not being pedantic. They’re seeing a resolution of detail that the rest of the team literally cannot access.

Strategic blind spots keep surprising you? You probably need pattern detectors, the people who will tell you what you don’t want to hear before it becomes what you can’t ignore. If your leadership team keeps getting ambushed by risks “no one saw coming,” it’s not that no one saw them. It’s that the people who saw them either weren’t in the room or weren’t heard when they spoke.

Execution keeps breaking at the handoffs? You probably need to pair systems thinkers with kinetic activators: one holds the whole architecture in mind, the other moves fast and adapts in real time. Separately, they struggle. Together, they’re the most effective execution team you’ve ever seen.

A startup I worked with decided to test this deliberately. They stopped hiring for culture fit and started treating cognitive composition as a strategic design decision, just as they’d always approached skill diversity and domain expertise. Within six months, the patterns shifted visibly. Innovation cycles are shortened. Quality failures dropped to a fraction of their previous rate. Strategic risks that had previously surfaced only in crises began getting flagged early. And attrition among their strongest performers, a persistent problem, fell dramatically.

Not because they got nicer. Because they got smarter about which brains they needed in which rooms.

The diagnosis is simple. Think about your last strategic planning session and ask four questions:

  • Who noticed a pattern nobody else saw?

  • Who asked the question that actually exposed the flaw in the group’s logic?

  • Who came back three days later with the synthesis everyone needed?

  • Who spotted the risk the optimists dismissed?

If you can name those people, you have cognitive diversity. If you can’t, or if those people have left, that’s your signal.

And if you’re the leader who just learned to delegate well, ask one more: Did I hand this off to someone who sees the problem the same way I do? Because a clean handoff to a cognitive twin isn’t delegation. It’s duplication.

The org chart shows who reports to whom. It doesn’t show whose brain you’re missing. And the problems you keep running into aren’t execution, strategy, or people problems.

They’re the sound of one kind of thinking trying to solve every kind of problem. And until you ask whose brain is missing from the room where it happens, the loop won’t break.
