title: Who Decided How You Decide?
html:
ChatGPT can synthesize 100 pages of market research in 30 seconds. It can draft a strategy memo, model three scenarios, and rank them by risk – before you’ve finished your coffee.

What it can’t do is walk into your Monday meeting and say: “This decision needs everyone’s input. But that one? I’m calling it, and here’s why. And that third one? It’s yours – I trust you to run with it.”

AI can process information faster than any leader alive. But the competitive advantage was never about processing information. It’s about knowing which type of decision you’re facing – and choosing the right approach before the conversation starts.

Most leaders never make that choice. They just decide the way they’ve always decided.

Every team has a default decision-making mode. Almost nobody chose it deliberately. It just emerged – from the founder’s personality, the company’s early crises, the habits that calcified before anyone noticed.

Some teams default to consensus. Every decision becomes a group conversation. It feels inclusive. It feels democratic. And it grinds to a halt on the decisions that needed someone to just call it. Meetings multiply. Timelines stretch. The pursuit of alignment becomes the enemy of momentum.

Some teams default to the leader making all decisions. It’s fast. It’s clear. And it creates a bottleneck that scales exactly as far as one person’s calendar allows. The team stops developing judgment because their judgment never gets tested. They wait. They defer. They learn that initiative is risky and real authority is rare.

Some teams default to collaboration – talking everything through, workshopping every choice, co-creating every plan. It builds camaraderie. It also burns hours on decisions that one person with the right expertise could have resolved in five minutes.

None of these modes is wrong. Every one of them is right – in the right context. The problem isn’t the mode. It’s using the same mode for everything.

Here’s what I’ve seen working with teams across government agencies, school districts, and startups: the most dangerous decision-making failure isn’t choosing wrong. It’s using the wrong process.

A consensus approach to an urgent call. A unilateral decision on something that needed buy-in. A collaborative workshop for a question that the subject-matter expert should have owned. The what of the decision might be fine. The how is what erodes trust.

Because every decision is also a message. It tells your team who matters, what’s expected, and whether they can act with clarity or need to wait for permission.

When a leader says “let’s discuss” but has already made up their mind, people learn not to trust the invitation. When a leader says “this is your call” but second-guesses every move, people learn that autonomy is theater. When a leader pulls rank on a technical question that the expert should own, the expert stops contributing – not out of spite, but out of logic.

The gap between what you say and how you actually decide is where trust quietly erodes.

There are really six modes available to you. Not one. Not two. Six – and each one answers a different question.

Command: Who must act, right now? “I’m making this call. Here’s my reasoning. Questions after, but the direction is set.” That’s not authoritarian. That’s clarity in a moment that requires it.

Consultative: Whose insight will sharpen my call? “I’m deciding this, but I want your perspective first. I’ll explain how your input shaped my thinking.” That’s genuine consultation – but only if you actually let the input land.

Collaborative: Where will co-creation build a better solution? “We’re building this together. I need everyone’s fingerprints on it because the implementation depends on shared ownership.” That’s not slow. That’s strategic.

Consensus: When is alignment more important than speed? “We need broad agreement before we move. Let’s work toward a direction everyone can support.” This is the right call when the decision won’t stick without genuine buy-in – and the wrong call for almost everything else.

Core Expert: Who’s best positioned to decide this? “You know this domain better than I do. This is your call. I’ll support whatever you decide.” That’s not abdication. That’s trust grounded in competence.

Choice: What should I fully release? “Here are the guardrails. Inside them, you own everything. I’ll check in on Thursday, but this is yours.” That’s not disengagement. That’s development.

Six modes. Six different messages. And your team hears every one of them – whether you name them or not. The difference is whether they hear clarity or have to decode it.

But naming the mode is only half the equation. Each mode also has a depth – a level of autonomy you’re actually granting inside it.

Saying “this is collaborative” doesn’t tell your team much if you haven’t decided whether that means “I invite your input but hold final approval” or “we co-create this, then you carry it forward, and I step back.” Both are collaborative. They’re not the same thing.

Michael Hyatt mapped five levels of delegation, from “do exactly what I say” to “own this completely.” Lay those levels across the six decision modes, and you get a grid – and that grid is where the real diagnostic lives. Every cell is a different combination of what kind of decision this is and how much authority you’re actually releasing.

Most leaders don’t default to a single mode. They default to one cell – and camp there for every decision, every person, every context. The grid makes that visible.

And that’s where the real damage happens – not from picking the wrong mode, but from saying one thing and doing another.

The 6C Decision Grid is one of the core frameworks in my forthcoming book CLUTCH: How Leaders Build Systems That Run Without Them. The book goes deeper: how to diagnose which cell you're stuck in, how to move deliberately across the grid as your team grows, and how to build decision architecture that doesn't depend on you being in every room. If this essay made you rethink how you make decisions, the book provides the full system.

But here’s where most leaders do real damage – not by picking the wrong mode, but by saying one thing and doing another.

“This is your call... but run everything by me first.” The words say autonomy. The behavior says control. People learn not to trust the words.

“Let’s build this together... then bring me what you’ve come up with and I’ll decide.” That’s not collaboration. That’s consultation dressed up as collaboration. People feel misled.

“I want your input on this.” But you’ve already decided, and everyone in the room can tell. Now “input” is theater – and next time you ask for it, no one will bother giving you their real thinking.

These mismatches don’t blow up in the moment. They erode trust silently. People stop listening to your words and start reading your behavior. They decode what you actually mean rather than what you say. And once a team learns to decode instead of trust, you’ve lost something that takes months to rebuild.

The AI parallel matters because it reveals what’s actually scarce. In a world drowning in information, the bottleneck isn’t analysis. It’s decision architecture – the ability to look at a situation and know not just what to decide, but how to decide it, who should be involved, and what kind of authority the moment requires.

That’s a human skill. And most leaders have never been taught it.

They’ve been taught to make good decisions. They’ve never been taught to design the decision process itself. So they default to one mode – the one that matches their personality – and wonder why some decisions land beautifully, and others generate confusion, resentment, or paralysis.

The fix isn’t a new framework on the wall. It’s a new habit: before the conversation starts, name the mode out loud.

“This is my call, and here’s why.” “I need your input before I decide.” “We’re deciding this together.” “We need alignment before we move.” “You’re the expert. This is yours.” “Here are the guardrails. You own the rest.”

Twelve words, in the right combination, that prevent twelve weeks of confusion. Try it once this week. Watch what happens in the room when people know – before anyone speaks – exactly what kind of conversation they’re in.

title: You Didn’t Delegate. You Dumped.
html:
Three words. Total confidence from the leader. Total confusion for everyone else.

They handed over the frame. They forgot the picture.

What does “it” look like when it’s done? What’s in bounds and what’s off limits? When should they check in – or should they not bother you at all? None of that was said. None of that was asked. The leader walked away feeling productive. The person left holding the work walked away guessing.

This is the most common delegation failure in organizations, and it has nothing to do with trust or control. It’s a clarity problem. The leader knows what they mean. They just didn’t say it.

Here’s what makes this invisible: from the leader’s perspective, the handoff felt generous. They gave someone ownership. They showed trust. They got out of the way.

But “getting out of the way” without setting the frame isn’t empowerment. It’s abandonment with accountability attached.

I learned this in classrooms long before I saw it in boardrooms. No teacher would hand a student a textbook and say, “learn chapter seven” without context, scaffolding, or success criteria. You’d never say “write an essay” without explaining what a good one looks like, what the boundaries are, and when it’s due. That’s not teaching. That’s hoping.

And yet leaders do this every day. They hand off a project with a vague ask and a tight deadline, then act surprised when the result doesn’t match the picture in their head – the picture they never shared.

Most delegation failures occur within the first 30 seconds. Not because the person receiving the work isn’t capable. Because three things were never made explicit:

What does done look like?

Not the task – the outcome. “Update the client” is a task. “The client knows X, Y, and Z, feels confident about the timeline, and has a single point of contact for questions” is a picture of done. One invites guesswork. The other invites execution.

Where are the boundaries?

Every handoff has invisible edges. Budget limits, stakeholder sensitivities, and decisions that require a check-in before action. When those boundaries aren’t named, capable people will cross them – not out of recklessness, but out of ignorance. And then trust takes a hit that was entirely preventable.

When do we check in?

Not “let me know if you need anything” – that puts the burden on the person with the least context. A real checkpoint sounds like: “Let’s sync on Thursday. Bring me where you are, what’s working, and where you’re stuck.” That’s not micromanaging. That’s making sure no one drives off a cliff in silence.

The teaching parallel matters because delegation is a teaching act, not a management act. Every time you hand something off, you’re either developing someone’s judgment or undermining it. You’re either building a driver or creating a passenger who’ll need you in the car next time, too.

The two-minute version: before your next handoff, answer three questions out loud – to the person, not just in your head.

  • What does done look like?

  • Where are the edges?

  • When do we sync?

That’s it. Three questions. Maybe ninety seconds of your time. The difference between a handoff that builds capability and one that just redistributes stress.

Delegation isn't handing someone a frame. It's making sure there's a picture inside it.

And the leaders who get this right don’t just free up their own calendars – they build teams that don’t need them in the room to make good decisions.

That’s not losing control. That’s the whole point.

title: Your Best Move Is Killing Your Team
subtitle: The Zidane Problem: When Your Greatest Strength Becomes Your Team's Biggest Cost
html:
Zinedine Zidane was the greatest player on the planet. The 2006 World Cup Final was his last match. He’d already scored a stunning Panenka penalty to put France ahead. He’d carried the entire tournament – goals against Spain, Portugal, Brazil. Ten minutes from the trophy.

Dear Reader, if you don’t know what a “Panenka” is, please Google it.

Then Materazzi said something about his sister. And the same fire that made Zidane unstoppable – the intensity, the pride, the refusal to be diminished – put his forehead into Materazzi’s chest on the biggest stage in sports.

Red card. France lost the shootout without him. Italy lifted the trophy.

The quality that made him extraordinary is the same one that destroyed the moment he’d spent his entire career building toward. Not a different Zidane. The same one. That’s what makes it tragic.

Nobody told him to stop being intense. Intensity was the whole point. The problem wasn’t the strength. It was the context. What once set him apart became the thing that took him out – and his team paid the price.

Leadership works the same way.

The thing that got you promoted – the decisiveness, the high standards, the open door, the ability to see the big picture – didn’t stop being valuable. But somewhere along the way, it shifted from an asset to a default. And defaults, left unchecked, create shadow effects that are invisible to the user.

Here’s what I mean.

The “high standards” leader who built her reputation on excellence. She’s the reason the work is sharp, the brand is trusted, and the team takes pride in output. However, over time, those standards have calcified into something more rigid. Feedback sessions feel like audits. People stop bringing unfinished ideas because the cost of imperfection is too high. The creative risk-taking that drove early wins has quietly disappeared–replaced by work that meets the bar but never exceeds it. Her strength didn’t change. Her team’s relationship to it did.

The “always available” leader who built his reputation on accessibility. He’s the first person people call. His door is never closed. He prides himself on being responsive, approachable, and present. But his availability has become a dependency. The team routes every decision through him – not because they can’t decide, but because they’ve learned that he’ll always be there to weigh in. His responsiveness trained them to defer to his judgment. He’s not developing leaders. He’s developing a line outside his office.

The “decisive” leader who built her reputation on speed. When others deliberated, she moved. When ambiguity paralyzed the room, she cut through it. But her speed has a cost she doesn’t see: no one else’s judgment is ever tested. The team has learned to wait – not out of laziness, but out of logic. Why invest in forming a position when she’ll have one in thirty seconds? Her decisiveness created clarity. It created passivity.

Three strengths. Three leaders who, from the inside, feel like they’re doing exactly what made them successful. Three teams that are quietly paying the price.

Every leadership strength has two expressions. There’s the version that elevates – where your standards sharpen the work, your availability builds trust, your decisiveness creates momentum. And there’s the version that distorts – where those same qualities, overused or applied without awareness, start producing the opposite of what you intended.

The critical insight: the two versions aren’t different behaviors. They’re the same behavior in different doses.

You don’t cross from one to the other by doing something new. You cross by doing what you’ve always done – just a little too long, a little too often, or in a context where it no longer fits.

And here’s what makes this hard to catch: from the inside, the distorted version feels identical to the elevated one. You’re still being decisive. You’re still holding high standards. You’re still available. The behavior hasn’t changed. But the impact has.

The gap between your intent and your team’s experience – that’s where the damage accumulates. Silently. Gradually. Until someone leaves, or stops trying, or tells you something in an exit interview that you wish you’d heard two years earlier.

This isn’t about becoming less of who you are. It’s about developing the awareness to notice when your signature strength has crossed a line you can’t see from where you’re standing.

The leaders who navigate this well don’t abandon their strengths. They develop a range around them. The high-standards leader learns when to celebrate progress, not just critique gaps. The available leader learns when not to answer the call – so someone else must. The decisive leader learns when to hold the silence long enough for another voice to fill it.

The strength stays. The rigidity goes.

Five strengths and their shadows. Find yours.

  1. Decisiveness on the balcony is speed, clarity, and momentum. In the basement, nobody else’s judgment ever develops – because yours is always faster.

  2. High Standards built your reputation. On the balcony, the work is sharp, the brand is trusted, and people take pride in output. In the basement, perfectionism has quietly killed every creative risk your team might have taken.

  3. Availability feels generous – and on the balcony, it is. Trust, responsiveness, and an open door. But in the basement, that open door has become a dependency. Your team can’t function without you in the room.

  4. Vision from the balcony provides people with meaning, direction, and strategic clarity. In the basement, it disconnects from execution. People are moved but confused – inspired with nowhere to go.

  5. Warmth creates safety, belonging, and loyalty. That’s the balcony. The basement version looks almost identical – except hard truths go unspoken, and conflict gets absorbed instead of resolved.

The balcony is what got you here. The basement might be what’s keeping your team from reaching its goals.

The question isn’t whether your strength has a shadow. It does. The question is whether you’ve noticed–or whether your team is bearing the cost of something you can’t see.

title: You Only Have One Voice (That’s the Problem)
html:
A guitarist who only plays power chords can fill a room. For about three songs. After that, everything starts to sound the same – loud, urgent, impressive in a narrow way. The audience doesn’t leave because the chords are bad. They leave because the range never changes.

Most leaders have the same problem. Not with volume. With voice.

Somewhere along the way – probably during the stretch that earned you the promotion, the reputation, the team – you developed a default mode. A way of showing up that worked so well it became automatic. Maybe you’re the person who brings structure to chaos. Maybe you’re the one who paints the vision and gets people fired up. Maybe you’re the steady hand who makes everyone feel safe.

That mode isn’t wrong. It’s your power chord. The problem is when it’s the only one you play.

I’ve spent twenty years watching this pattern up close. In classrooms, in boardrooms, in coaching sessions where a leader sits across from me, genuinely confused about why their team is stuck. The answer, almost always, is that the leader is bringing the same presence to every situation – and some situations need something entirely different.

The leader who’s brilliant at execution wonders why her team won’t take initiative. She’s so good at organizing the work that she’s taken ownership away from them. The leader who’s a natural encourager wonders why standards keep slipping. He’s so focused on making people feel safe that he’s never challenged them. The leader who inspires with vision wonders why nothing gets finished. She’s painted such a compelling picture of the future that no one’s managing the present.

Each of them is operating from a real strength. And each of them is stuck in a single gear.

Leadership isn’t one long stretch of smooth highway. The terrain changes. The weather changes. The load you’re carrying changes. And your team feels every shift – whether you adjust or not.

When the work is steady and the team is capable, what’s needed is space. Step back. Trust. Let them drive. But when deadlines compress and stakes rise, that same hands-off approach feels like an absence. Suddenly, the moment calls for structure, clarity, and decisiveness.

When morale dips and confidence wavers, people don’t need a project plan. They need to feel seen. But when good work plateaus and standards drift, warmth without honesty becomes a ceiling.

The leaders who navigate this well aren’t shapeshifters. They’re not performing. They’ve simply built a wider range – the ability to sense what the moment requires and respond with the right presence, not just their most comfortable one.

Think of it like a musician who’s mastered more than one key. They don’t abandon their signature sound. They expand it. The power chord is still there when the song calls for it. But so is the fingerpicking. So is the silence between notes.

The hard part isn’t learning new modes of presence. It’s recognizing that your default – the thing that got you here – might be the thing that’s limiting what comes next.

Not because it’s a weakness. Because it’s a strength you’ve overused.

The leader who’s all vision and no execution isn’t dreaming too big. She’s playing one chord. The leader who’s all structure and no warmth isn’t heartless. He’s playing one chord. The leader who makes everyone feel great but never pushes them isn’t soft. She’s playing one chord.

Range isn’t about being someone else. It’s about being more of yourself – in more situations, for more people, when it matters most.

A quick diagnostic. Six scenarios. Notice which ones feel natural and which ones make you flinch:

  1. Your team has lost sight of why the work matters. Do you re-cast the vision – or does that feel too abstract?

  2. A project is slipping. Do you bring structure and clarity – or does that feel like micromanaging?

  3. A strong performer is waiting for permission they don’t need. Do you step back – or does the silence make you nervous?

  4. Someone is stuck, repeating the same mistakes. Do you ask questions that help them see it – or do you just give the answer?

  5. Morale is low, and fear is creeping in. Do you name what you’re noticing – or do you push past it to the work?

  6. Good work has plateaued. Do you name the gap between where it is and where it could be – or do you let it slide?

The ones that made you uncomfortable? Those are your underdeveloped voices. Not weaknesses. Untapped range.

Your power chord got you here. Your range is what gets you – and your team – where you’re going next.

title: Your Boss Isn’t Difficult. They’re Dysregulated.
subtitle: Thoughts on a recent HBR piece: How to Manage an Insecure Leader
html:
I once worked with a leader whose door was always closed. Not metaphorically. Literally closed, every day, as a matter of practice.

Feedback of any kind – no matter how carefully delivered – is registered as a direct threat. Those who tried found themselves on the receiving end of a quiet, methodical vindictiveness. And yet this same leader would veer confidently into domains far outside her expertise, challenging specialists in their own lanes with a certainty she never displayed in the core responsibilities of leadership: communication, empathy, and team development.

That combination seems contradictory. It isn’t. The overreach is the insecurity. When a leader can’t tolerate “I don’t know enough about this to weigh in,” they’re usually the same person who can’t tolerate “That’s valid feedback, let me think about it.” Both require sitting with vulnerability – and for this leader, vulnerability wasn’t discomfort. It was dangerous.

The closed door wasn’t privacy. It was a perimeter. The vindictiveness wasn’t a strength. It was a warning system: “Do not come closer.” Don’t see what I don’t have.

Most leadership advice characterizes these individuals as “difficult” and advises you to manage around them. Set boundaries. Document everything. Update your resume. That advice isn’t wrong. But it misses the mechanism entirely.

Insecurity in leadership isn’t rare. It’s the norm. And it’s not a personality flaw. It’s a design problem.

The Patterns Under the Surface

New research from Jeffrey Yip and Dritjon Gruda, published in Harvard Business Review, provides a sharper lens on what’s actually happening: approximately 36% of adults exhibit an insecure attachment style. A 2024 Korn Ferry report found that 71% of U.S. CEOs experience symptoms of impostor syndrome. The leaders who appear most composed are often managing the most turbulent internal dynamics.

Yip and Gruda identify two insecure attachment patterns in leadership. Anxious leaders crave connection and reassurance; they draw teams close, then push people away when overwhelmed. You never know which version of the boss is entering the room. Avoidant leaders project control and resist vulnerability. Working with them feels like working around a wall.

But the leader I described is a third pattern the research doesn’t name cleanly: avoidant and overcompensating. This is the most disorienting version because the confidence looks real. The overreach into other people’s expertise reads as an assertion of authority. It takes time to recognize that the certainty in someone else’s lane is directly proportional to the fragility in their own.

What makes this pattern so destructive is that it attacks the very mechanism teams need to function: honest upward communication. When feedback is perceived as a threat, people stop offering it. When they stop offering it, the leader loses access to the information they need most. The system degrades from the inside – and the leader, sealed off behind a closed door, is often the last to know.

The System, Not the Person

The temptation is to label insecure leaders as the problem and move on. But here’s what twenty years in the classroom taught me: the most disruptive people in the room are usually the most dysregulated. And the response that feels most satisfying – confrontation, withdrawal, quiet resentment – almost never produces the outcome you want.

Yip and Gruda offer a useful sequence: Regulate, Relate, Reason. When someone’s nervous system is activated, logic doesn’t land. You must stabilize the system before you can connect, and connect before you can problem-solve. That ordering matters – and it applies to you as much as to them.

However, the deeper question isn’t how to manage a single dysregulated leader. The question is whether your organization has any infrastructure to detect this before it cascades. Most don’t. Most organizations promote people into leadership roles faster than they develop the emotional architecture to sustain them, then wonder why the system breaks under strain.

A leader with an insecure attachment style isn’t a broken person. They’re a predictable outcome of a system that rewards technical performance, ignores relational capacity, and treats leadership as a title rather than a design challenge.

The better question isn’t “How do I survive this person?” It’s “What does this environment need from me right now?” That reframe shifts you from a reactive to a diagnostic approach. From enduring to designing.

Two questions worth sitting with:

When your leader’s insecurity shows up, do you accommodate, withdraw, or confront – and is that pattern producing the results you want? I chose confront. I thought proving the gap would fix the system. It didn’t.

Are you regulating yourself before trying to regulate the relationship? I’ve been on the wrong side of this equation myself. You can’t steady someone else’s nervous system if yours is already hijacked.

The leaders who learn to read dysregulation with precision instead of frustration don’t just survive difficult bosses. They build the kind of relational infrastructure that makes entire teams more resilient.

That’s not managing up. That’s leading from wherever you sit.

title: Are You Redesigning — Or Just Coping Faster?
subtitle: Part 3 of 3: The Sculptor Series
html:
Here’s the trap: Sculptor thinking feels like Operator thinking if you’re not paying attention.

You can spend an hour “working on the business” and actually just be working in it. You can talk about systems while still managing around them. You can attend the strategy offsite, nod along to the consultant’s framework, agree that you need to “think more architecturally” – and then go right back to solving the same problems you were solving before.

The gap between Sculptor and Operator isn’t intellectual. Most leaders understand the difference. They’ve read the books. They know “working on the system” matters. They can explain it clearly.

The gap is behavioral. It’s the distance between knowing and doing. Between understanding that you should redesign the system and actually redesigning it. Between agreeing that you need to stop being the bottleneck and actually building the architecture that removes you from the center.

So how do you know which side of the gap you’re on?

Over the past two days, I’ve made the case for Sculptor – the leadership gear that removes rather than adds, that redesigns systems rather than optimizing within them. Today, I want to offer something practical: five questions that reveal where you actually are. Not where you think you are. Not where you’d like to be. Where you actually are.

These questions are uncomfortable. That’s the point.

Question One: What Problems From Six Months Ago Are You Still Solving Today?

Not variations. Not evolutions. The same fundamental problem.

Pull up your calendar from six months ago. Think about what consumed your attention. The conflicts. The bottlenecks. The quality issues. The coordination failures.

Now look at today. How many of those problems are still here? Not adjacent problems. Not new versions of old problems. The same underlying dysfunction is still generating symptoms that land on your desk.

The conflict between product and engineering that you mediate every other week – were you mediating it six months ago? The decisions that escalate to you because no one else is sure they have authority – were they escalating six months ago? The quality gaps that require your intervention – were they requiring your intervention six months ago?

If you’re honest, the answer is probably yes. For most leaders, it’s yes to more than they’d like to admit.

Operators solve problems. They get good at it. Efficient. Skilled. They can handle recurring issues faster than before, with less energy, and with better outcomes. That’s real progress, as far as it goes.

Sculptors ask a different question: Why does this problem keep recurring?

If you’re solving the same problems you were solving six months ago, you’re not sculpting. You’re coping. You’ve become efficient at managing dysfunction rather than eliminating it.

I don’t say this to criticize. Coping is a survival skill. When you’re overwhelmed – and most leaders are – managing recurring problems is often the only option that feels available. But coping has a ceiling. You can get faster at it, but you can’t escape it. The problem remains. And you remain attached to it.

What’s one recurring problem you could stop solving by redesigning the system that produces it?

Question Two: What Would Break If You Disappeared for Two Weeks?

Not what would be delayed. Not what would pile up. What would actually break?

The client relationship that only you can manage. The decision that only you can make. The conflict that only you can mediate. The context that lives in your head and nowhere else.

If you disappeared tomorrow – vacation, illness, sabbatical, whatever – what would genuinely fall apart?

This question isn’t about vacation planning. It’s a diagnostic for whether you’ve built a system or whether you are the system.

Amy Edmondson’s research on psychological safety illuminates why this matters. She found that teams perform best when people feel safe making decisions, surfacing problems, and taking initiative without waiting for permission. But that safety doesn’t happen by accident. It’s architectural. It comes from explicit clarity about who owns what, what decisions can be made locally, and what guardrails are in place to catch mistakes.

Most organizations have the opposite. Authority is implicit. Decision rights are unclear. People learn – through experience and by observing what happens when others act without permission – that the safe path is to escalate. To wait. To check with the leader before moving.

That’s not timidity. That’s rationality. The system trained them.

If you can’t disappear for two weeks without things breaking, you haven’t sculpted a system. You’ve become the load-bearing wall. And load-bearing walls can’t move.

What would need to be true for your team to function fully without you for two weeks?

Question Three: When Did You Last Kill Something?

Not deprioritized. Not paused. Not “put on the back burner until Q3.” Killed. Ended. Removed completely.

A meeting that no longer serves its purpose. A report no one reads, but everyone produces. A process that exists because it’s always existed, not because it’s still valuable. An initiative that sounded promising but never gained traction. A commitment you made that isn’t delivering what you thought it would.

When did you last end something like that? Actually end it, not just let it fade?

Sculptors carve. That means removal is a regular practice – not a crisis response, not an annual cleanup, but an ongoing discipline. They look at what exists and ask: Is this still earning its place?

Most leaders are far better at adding than removing. The incentives point that way. You can announce a new initiative. You can celebrate a new hire. You can point to a new process as evidence of progress. Removal is invisible. Nobody sends a company-wide email celebrating the meeting you eliminated or the project you shut down.

But addition without removal is accumulation. And accumulation creates drag.

The organization slows down not because the work got harder, but because there’s more friction. More meetings. More approvals. More coordination overhead. More legacy processes exist because no one ever stopped them, not because they’re still valuable.

If you haven’t killed something in the past month – really killed it, not just deprioritized it – you’re not sculpting. You’re accumulating. And accumulation is the enemy of transformation.

What’s one thing you’re tolerating that you could eliminate entirely?

Question Four: Can Your Team Describe How Decisions Get Made – Or Do They Just Know to Ask You?

This question reveals whether your organization has decision architecture or just decision defaults.

In many organizations, decision-making is implicit. There’s no map. There’s no clarity about who owns what, where input is required versus optional, what escalation looks like versus what local resolution looks like. Decisions happen – but they happen through habit, hierarchy, and guesswork.

When decision-making is implicit, it defaults upward. Always.

This is true regardless of what you’ve said. You can tell people to “take ownership” all day long. You can express frustration that decisions keep landing on your desk. You can genuinely want people to act with more autonomy.

But if decision rights aren’t explicit – if people don’t know, concretely, what they can decide without asking – they’ll escalate. Not because they’re incapable. Because escalation is safer than guessing wrong. The system has implicitly taught them that.

The test isn’t what you’ve told people. The test is whether they can articulate it.

Ask three people on your team: How do decisions get made around here? Not in theory. In practice. For a specific type of decision – a resource allocation, a client issue, a product trade-off – who decides? Where does input come from? What happens when there’s disagreement?

If they give you a clear, consistent answer – “I own X, you own Y, we collaborate on Z, here’s what escalation looks like” – you’ve done the Sculptor work. The architecture exists.

If they hesitate. If they give vague answers. If three people give three different answers. If they ultimately shrug and say, “I guess I ask you,” – the architecture doesn’t exist. You don’t have a decision system. You have a decision default. And the default is you.

What decisions that currently route to you could you explicitly delegate – with clear guardrails – this week?

Question Five: What Are You Tolerating That You’ve Stopped Seeing?

This is the hardest question because it asks you to notice what you’ve normalized.

Every organization has invisible tolerances. The friction everyone works around. The workaround became standard practice. The dysfunction frustrated new hires for three months until they got used to it. The thing that would shock an outsider but barely registers for you anymore because you’ve been swimming in it so long.

These tolerances accumulate. They become the water. And because they’re familiar, they stop feeling like choices. They feel like facts. That’s just how it is here.

But they’re not facts. They’re design choices – either ones you made explicitly, or ones that emerged by default and were never revisited. And as long as they stay invisible, they can’t be changed.

The Sculptor discipline is to keep seeing what others have stopped seeing. To maintain the beginner’s mind – the capacity to notice friction that everyone else has normalized.

There’s a simple way to access this: ask someone who hasn’t normalized it yet.

Ask someone new to your team: What seems harder here than it should be? Ask a trusted peer from outside: What stands out when you look at how we work? Ask yourself – honestly – What would I never design this way if I were starting from scratch?

The answers to those questions are where the angels are hiding. The organization that could exist – more adaptive, more capable, more ready for transformation – if you could just see what you’ve stopped seeing.

What friction have you normalized that a newcomer would find unacceptable?

The Compound Choice

Every week, you make a choice. Usually not consciously.

You can spend your time solving problems – or removing the systems that create them.

You can push harder on execution – or redesign what’s blocking it.

You can add more to your plate – or set something free.

Operators always choose the first path. It feels productive. It looks like leadership. The feedback loop is immediate: problem, solution, satisfaction.

But there’s a cost. The problems keep regenerating. The calendar stays packed. The exhaustion accumulates. And five years later, you’re still solving the same problems you were solving five years ago – just faster.

Sculptors choose the second path often enough that it compounds.

The fires stop starting. The decisions flow to the right level. The capacity appears. Excellence becomes structurally possible instead of heroically demanded. The organization learns to run without your constant intervention – not because you’ve abandoned it, but because you’ve built something that doesn’t need you at the center of everything.

That’s not working less. The best Sculptors I know work with great intensity. But they work on different things. Less time solving, more time redesigning. Less time managing symptoms, more time addressing root causes. Less time in the system, more time on the system.

That shift creates space. And space is what transformation requires.

Back to the Wave

This series started with a question: If 56% of companies are failing at AI transformation despite massive investment, and the 12% succeeding aren’t bigger or better-funded – just better-built – how do you actually build better?

The answer isn’t a framework, though frameworks help. The answer is a shift in orientation.

From adding to removing.

From solving to eliminating.

From Operator to Sculptor.

The organizations riding the wave aren’t the ones pushing hardest. They’re the ones that cleared the path. They saw what was blocking transformation – the implicit decision rights that created bottlenecks, the cultural signals that made experimentation unsafe, the accumulated processes that nobody had questioned in years – and they carved it away.

The angel was already in the marble. They just had to see it.

Where to Go From Here

The frameworks in this series – VOICES, CREATE, 6C – form the core of my forthcoming book, CLUTCH: How Leaders Build Systems That Run Without Them.

But the book won’t give you transformation. Only you can do that. The book gives you tools – lenses to see what you’ve stopped seeing, questions that reveal architectural gaps, frameworks to design systems that run without heroics.

The real work is yours.

Pick one recurring problem and ask what system produces it. Map decision rights and push authority to where context lives. Kill something that no longer earns its place. Build the capacity to disappear for two weeks without everything breaking.

One Sculptor move. Then another. Then another.

The wave won’t wait. But now you know what to carve.

Start here – pick one diagnostic this week:

  • What problem from six months ago are you still solving?

  • What would break if you disappeared for two weeks?

  • When did you last kill something?

  • Can your team describe how decisions get made?

  • What are you tolerating that you’ve stopped seeing?

Don’t fix anything yet. Just see clearly. Architecture starts with an accurate diagnosis.

title: What Changes When You Stop Adding
subtitle: Part 2 of 3: The Sculptor Series
html:
Yesterday, I introduced the Sculptor – the leadership gear that removes rather than adds, that redesigns systems rather than optimizing within them. The gear that looks at a recurring problem and asks, “How do I solve this?” but “Should this problem exist at all?”

Today, I want to explore what actually happens when leaders make that shift. Because the results are rarely what anyone expects.

The first thing that happens is nothing.

That’s the terrifying part. Sculptor’s work doesn’t produce immediate visible output. You’re not running a meeting. You’re not sending the email. You’re not putting out the fire. You’re sitting with a harder question: What’s causing this fire to keep starting – and can I redesign so it stops?

That silence feels like failure. Especially for leaders who’ve built careers on visible activity. Especially for founders who got where they are by outworking everyone else. Especially for anyone who’s been rewarded their entire professional life for solving problems quickly.

But the silence is where the real work begins.

The Removal Paradox

Here’s what I’ve observed working with founders and leadership teams over the past several years: the leaders who create the most capacity aren’t the ones who work the hardest. They’re the ones who eliminate the most.

This sounds like a productivity cliché until you observe it in practice. Because elimination isn’t about efficiency. It’s not about time management, priority matrices, or getting things done in fewer steps. It’s about architecture.

The question is not “How do I do this faster?” It’s “Should this exist at all?”

W. Edwards Deming saw this clearly. His insight – that 94% of problems are system problems – leads to an uncomfortable conclusion: most of what leaders spend their time on is managing the symptoms of systems they could redesign. The recurring conflicts. The bottleneck decisions. The quality gaps. The communication breakdowns. These aren’t random failures. They’re system outputs. The architecture is producing them.

Once you see that, you have a choice. You can improve your ability to manage the symptoms – more efficient, more skilled, more responsive. Or you can redesign the architecture.

The first path has a ceiling. The second path compounds.

Let me show you what I mean.

Pattern One: The Problem That Disappeared

A COO I worked with spent two hours every week – sometimes more – mediating the same conflict between her product and engineering teams. The details changed. The underlying pattern didn’t. Priorities weren’t aligned. Handoffs were messy. Both sides felt the other was blocking progress. Every week, she’d bring them into a room, facilitate a productive conversation, and leave believing that something had shifted.

Then the next week, the same conflict. Different surface issue, same fundamental tension.

Her Operator instinct – the instinct most of us have – said: Become a better facilitator. Improve communication. Implement a weekly sync to surface problems earlier. Get everyone aligned.

She tried all of it. The communication improved. The syncs got added. The alignment conversations happened. The conflict persisted.

When she finally asked the Sculptor question – Why does this conflict keep regenerating? – The answer was structural, not interpersonal.

Decision rights were ambiguous. Both teams thought they owned prioritization for the product roadmap. Both were correct, given how their roles had been defined. The conflict wasn’t a communication failure. It was an architectural failure. The system was designed to produce exactly this tension.

No amount of facilitation would fix that. She could mediate that meeting every week for the next decade, and the conflict would still regenerate. Because she wasn’t addressing the root. She was managing the symptom.

The Sculptor move was different. She spent one afternoon – not months, not quarters, one afternoon – mapping decision rights explicitly. Who owns what? Where input is required versus where it’s optional. What happens when there’s genuine disagreement?

The two-hour weekly mediation? Gone. Not because she got better at it. Because she removed the need for it entirely.

That’s the Sculptor result. The problem didn’t get solved. The problem disappeared.

Pattern Two: The Capacity That Appeared

A founder told me he had no time for strategic thinking. His calendar was wall-to-wall. One-on-ones stacked against team meetings, stacked against client escalations, stacked against operational reviews. When he looked at his week, there was no white space. He was drowning in meetings about meetings.

The Operator response would be time management. Batch similar meetings. Protect Friday afternoons. Wake up earlier. Find the margins.

He’d tried all of that. It wasn’t working. Whatever space he created got filled immediately. The system was producing meetings faster than he could eliminate them.

So we tried something different. For one week, he tracked not his meetings but his decisions. Every time someone came to him for input. Every time he approved something. Every time someone escalated because they weren’t sure what to do.

Then we sorted them: Which of these decisions actually required him? Not which ones he was good at making. Not which ones he had opinions about. Which ones genuinely couldn’t have been made by someone else with the right context and authority?

The answer: about 30%.

Thirty percent of his decisions actually needed his involvement. The other 70% reached him not because he was required, but because the system defaulted to higher levels. No one had explicitly defined decision rights. No one had clarified what “take ownership” actually meant. No one had built the guardrails that would let people decide confidently without escalating.

So they escalated. Not because they were incapable – they weren’t. Because escalation was safer than guessing wrong. The system had trained them.

He didn’t need better time management. He needed to redesign the decision architecture.

The Sculptor move wasn’t working more efficiently. It involved making decision rights explicit, defining guardrails clearly, and delegating authority to those with the context to make quick decisions.

Within a month, he’d reclaimed eight hours a week. Not by squeezing harder. By removing what shouldn’t have been there in the first place.

Pattern Three: The Excellence That Emerged

A director approached me, frustrated that her team’s work was good but never great. She’d raised the bar. Given more feedback. Pushed harder. Made her expectations clearer. Nothing changed. The work was competent and consistent, meeting requirements, but lacked spark.

Her Operator instinct said: push harder. More detailed feedback. Higher standards, communicated more forcefully. If the work isn’t excellent, demand excellence.

That’s what she’d been doing. It wasn’t working.

When she asked the Sculptor question – What’s making excellence hard? – the answer surprised her. It wasn’t motivation. It wasn’t capability. It was the process itself.

Her team was working on a three-week sprint cycle. By the time work reached her for final review, they’d already mentally moved on to the next sprint. Her feedback came too late. Not too late to be heard – too late to matter. They’d learned to settle for “good enough” and shift focus because the system didn’t allow iteration. Excellence requires refinement, and the process had no room for refinement.

She wasn’t seeing a motivation problem. She was seeing a systems problem.

The Sculptor move: feedback earlier in the cycle. Fewer approval gates. More iteration loops before the final review. She removed the structural barrier to excellence instead of demanding that people push through it.

The quality changed. Not because she raised her standards – she’d already done that. Because she removed what was preventing her standards from being met.

The Compound Effect

James Clear wrote that you don’t rise to the level of your goals – you fall to the level of your systems. I think about that line constantly when I work with leaders who are exhausted and stuck.

Operator effort is linear. You put in, you get out. Work harder, produce more. The math is straightforward – and limiting. There’s a ceiling: the hours in your day, the energy in your body, the attention you can sustain.

Sculptor’s effort compounds.

Every system you redesign is a problem you stop solving. That’s not a one-time savings. It’s recurring. The two-hour weekly mediation that disappeared? That’s 100 hours a year. The decisions that stopped routing upward? That’s not just time – it’s cognitive load, context-switching, the invisible tax of being the bottleneck for everything.

And the effects multiply. When you’re not mediating the same conflict every week, you have space to notice other patterns. When decisions flow to the right level, your team develops judgment faster because they’re actually exercising it. When excellence becomes structurally possible, people begin to pursue it without external pressure.

Liz Wiseman’s research found that Multipliers – leaders who amplify their team’s capability – get twice the output from the same people as Diminishers. Twice. Not 10% more. Double.

That’s not because Multipliers work twice as hard. It’s because they create systems in which capability can emerge, in which intelligence isn’t suppressed, and in which people can contribute what they’re capable of contributing.

Sculptor work is how you become a Multiplier. Not by adding your brilliance to every problem – that makes you a Diminisher, however well-intentioned. But by removing the structural barriers that prevent other people’s brilliance from showing up.

Why This Is Hard

Three forces work against Sculptor mode. They’re powerful, and they’re worth naming.

The first is visibility. No one congratulates you for the meeting you eliminated. The crisis that didn’t happen doesn’t make the quarterly report. The decision that flowed smoothly to the right person without your involvement – that just looks like nothing.

Organizations reward visible activity. Launches. Announcements. Initiatives. The executive who’s constantly in motion, solving problems, driving results, putting out fires – that person looks like a leader. The executive who quietly redesigned the system so the fires stopped starting – that person looks like they’re not doing much.

Sculptor work is invisible by nature. Its success is measured in absence: the problems that don’t recur, the decisions that don’t escalate, the conflicts that don’t regenerate. That’s hard to put in a performance review.

The second is ego. Sculptor work requires admitting that the system is the problem. And you probably built the system. Or you inherited it and chose not to change it. Either way, moving into Sculptor mode starts with an uncomfortable acknowledgment: this isn’t working, and I’m part of why.

Operator lets you be the hero. You swoop in, solve the problem, save the day. It feels good. It reinforces your value. It confirms why you’re in the room.

Sculptor requires a different posture. You’re not the hero – you’re the architect of a system that needed heroes and shouldn’t have. That’s a harder story to tell yourself.

The third is timing. Sculptor work is slow before it’s fast.

Operator produces visible results immediately. You leave the meeting feeling accomplished. You clear the inbox. You make the decision. The feedback loop is tight – action, result, satisfaction.

Sculptor produces results later. Sometimes much later. You redesign a decision process, and for a week, nothing changes while people adjust to the new model. You eliminate a meeting, and there’s a brief period of uncertainty before the new rhythm settles. You push authority downward, and the first few decisions are shakier than they would’ve been if you’d just made them yourself.

Organizations optimize for short-term visible progress. Sculptor work often looks, in the short term, like nothing is happening. The payoff comes later – but later isn’t what gets rewarded in most cultures.

These three forces – invisibility, ego, and timing – are why most leaders stay in Operator. It’s not that they don’t understand Sculptor intellectually. The books talk about “working on the business.” The consultants mention “systems thinking.” Everyone nods.

But when Monday morning comes, the incentives, the culture, and the psychology all push toward addition. Toward more. Toward Operator.

The Signal to Watch

Here’s what I’ve noticed across all three patterns – and dozens more I could share:

The leaders who successfully shift into Sculptor mode don’t start by asking What should I remove? That question is too abstract. It leads to paralysis or to cutting things that actually matter.

They start with a different question: What keeps regenerating?

The conflict recurs despite your best efforts to facilitate. The decisions that keep escalating despite your requests for ownership. The quality issues that persist despite your feedback. The fires keep reigniting, no matter how many times you put them out.

Recurring problems are system signatures. They’re the architecture making itself visible. When the same issue recurs, the system is telling you something: I’m designed to produce this. You can solve it as many times as you want – I’ll keep generating it.

Once you learn to read those signatures, you start seeing the design choices you didn’t know you’d made. The implicit decisions about authority. The unexamined assumptions about how information should flow. The inherited processes that once made sense no longer do.

What keeps regenerating? is the question that opens Sculptor mode. Not as an accusation. As an investigation. The goal isn’t blame. The goal is to see clearly.

Because you can’t remove what you haven’t seen.

What Comes Next

Tomorrow, in Part 3, I’ll share five diagnostic questions that reveal whether you’re actually sculpting or just operating faster – and how to close the gap between thinking about systems and actually changing them.

The wave won’t wait. But you don’t need more hours to ride it.

You might just need to see what you’ve been carrying – and set it down.

Pick one recurring problem – the one that keeps showing up no matter how well you handle it – and ask: What system is producing this?

Don’t solve it. Don’t optimize your response to it. Just trace it back. Find the architecture.

That’s where the carving starts.

title: The Angel in the Marble
subtitle: Part 1 of 3: The Sculptor Series
html:
Michelangelo reportedly said he saw the angel in the marble and carved until he set it free.

I’ve thought about that line for years – not as art history, but as a leadership philosophy. Because it captures something most leadership advice gets exactly backwards.

We’re trained to add. More communication. More check-ins. More initiatives. More dashboards. More off-sites. More urgency. The assumption underlying all of this is that transformation requires accumulation – that if we simply pile on enough effort, enough resources, enough pressure, something will finally shift.

But Michelangelo didn’t add the angel. He removed everything that wasn’t the angel. He didn’t build; he revealed. He looked at a block of stone and saw what was already possible, hidden beneath the excess. Then he carved.

That’s the leadership move almost no one teaches. And it’s the one that separates the organizations that transform from the ones that just thrash.

The Accumulation Trap

On Monday (2/2) and Tuesday (2/3) of this week, I wrote about the 56% of companies that have invested in AI and have nothing to show for it. The data came from PwC’s 29th Global CEO Survey – 4,454 executives watching the wave build, most of them drowning in it.

The vanguard 12% weren’t working harder. They had built systems that enabled transformation.

But here’s the question that the essay didn’t answer: How do you build better when you’re already maxed out?

I ask this because the leaders I work with aren’t lazy. They’re exhausted. Their calendars look like Tetris games played by someone losing badly. Their to-do lists reproduce overnight. Every meeting spawns two more. They’re operating at capacity – running flat out just to stay in place – and then someone tells them they also need to lead a transformation.

The instinct, when you hear that, is to find more capacity. Wake up earlier. Stay later. Protect Sunday afternoons for “strategic thinking.” Squeeze an offsite into the already-groaning Q2 schedule. Add a transformation initiative to the already crowded priority list.

That instinct is wrong. Not because effort doesn’t matter – it does. But because you can’t add your way out of a system problem. Most transformation failures are systemic problems.

W. Edwards Deming – the statistician who helped rebuild Japanese manufacturing after World War II – spent decades studying why organizations succeed and fail. His conclusion was stark: 94% of performance problems are system problems, not people problems. When something isn’t working, the issue is almost never effort or talent. It’s the invisible architecture that shapes how effort gets applied and how talent gets used.

Think about what that means. Ninety-four percent.

When adoption stalls, we blame the workforce. When quality slips, we blame the team. When transformation fails, we often attribute the failure to resistance to change. However, Deming’s research suggests that one should look elsewhere. Look at the system. Consider the incentives, information flows, decision rights, and feedback loops. Look at the architecture.

The leaders are still stuck in the 56% – they’re trying to add transformation to a system designed to resist it. They’re pushing harder on the accelerator while the parking brake is still engaged.

The 12% did something different. They released the brake first. They started removing.

The Gear Most Leaders Skip

In my work with founders and leadership teams, I use a framework called VOICES – six leadership stances for different terrain. If you read last week’s Wave series, you’ve seen this before. If not, here’s the short version.

Think of VOICES as gears in a vehicle – each one designed for different conditions:

  • Visionaries set direction and paint the horizon. Where are we going?

  • Operator drives execution with discipline. How do we get there?

  • Independent empowers ownership by stepping back. Who owns this?

  • Coach develops capability through feedback and reflection. How do I help you grow?

  • Encourager fuels belief and resilience through hard stretches. What do you need to keep going?

  • Sculptor reshapes the systems themselves. What’s blocking us – and can I remove it?

Most leaders default to two gears regardless of what the moment requires: Visionary and Operator.

It makes sense. These are the gears that got rewarded. Visionary is what “leadership” looks like in the popular imagination – the inspiring speech, the strategic clarity, the compelling vision of the future. Operator is what organizations measure – the execution, the results, the getting-it-done. Both are visible. Both are heroic. Both put the leader at the center of the story.

The other four gears require a harder material. Independent means stepping back when you want to step in. Coach means investing in someone’s development when it would be faster to just do it yourself. Encourager means tending to morale and belief when you’d rather focus on results. And Sculptor means admitting the system you built – or inherited and didn’t change – might be the problem.

So leaders skip them. Not consciously. They just reach for what’s familiar, what’s rewarded, what’s worked before. Visionary when they need to inspire. Operator when they need to deliver. Back and forth between two gears while four others rust.

For founders, especially technical founders, first-time founders, anyone who built something from scratch – Operator dominates. It’s the gear that got them here. They outworked competitors. They pushed through obstacles. They made things happen through sheer force of will and relentless execution. Operator isn’t just a gear for them; it’s an identity.

But Operator has a ceiling.

You can push harder within a system only until you hit the system’s limits. And when the system itself is the problem – when the architecture is what’s blocking transformation, not the effort – no amount of Operator energy will break through. You’ll just burn hotter while going nowhere.

That’s where Sculptor comes in.

Sculptor doesn’t optimize within the system. Sculptor redesigns the system. It asks a fundamentally different question: not How do I get this done? but What’s making this harder than it needs to be – and can I remove that instead?

This is the gear most leaders skip. Not because they don’t value it. Not because they haven’t heard that “working on the business” matters as much as “working in the business.” They skip it because no one taught them how to use it.

Leadership development programs focus on doing more: communicating more clearly, delegating more effectively, coaching more frequently, and inspiring more consistently. The assumption is always addition.

Nobody teaches you to look at a recurring problem and ask: What if this problem shouldn’t exist at all?

Nobody teaches you to remove.

The Accidental Diminisher

Liz Wiseman’s research on Multipliers offers a window into why Sculptor matters – and why skipping it costs more than most leaders realize.

Wiseman studied leaders across industries, trying to answer a simple question: Why do some leaders double the intelligence and capability of their teams while others – often without meaning to – cut it in half?

The answer wasn’t charisma. It wasn’t an experience. It wasn’t even raw intelligence. It was behavior.

Multipliers create space for others to think, take risks, and grow. They ask questions instead of providing answers. They challenge people to stretch beyond what they thought possible. They create an environment in which intelligence can emerge and capability can compound.

Diminishers – often the smartest, most capable, most well-intentioned people in the room – do the opposite. They rescue too quickly. They solve problems before others have a chance to struggle. They dominate the airtime. Their brilliance casts a shadow.

What struck me most in Wiseman’s work was her concept of the “accidental diminisher.” These aren’t bad leaders. They’re often exceptional performers who got promoted precisely because of their ability to deliver results. They work hard. They care deeply. They’re trying to help.

But their help is the problem.

When you rescue too quickly, people stop trying. When you solve problems before others can engage, you train the organization to wait for you. When your speed leaves no space for others to figure things out, you become the bottleneck – not because you’re controlling, but because the system has learned to depend on you.

The accidental diminisher is a leader stuck in Operator. They’re working hard, producing results, solving problems – and slowly training their organization to need them for everything. The system contracts around them. Decisions route upward. Initiative atrophies. When transformation requires distributed intelligence, risk-taking, and adaptation, the system can’t deliver it.

Sculptor breaks that pattern.

Not by working less. By working differently. By asking: What would need to change so this problem stops regenerating? What am I holding that someone else could own? What system am I compensating for that I could redesign instead?

Why Sculptor Is the Transformation Gear

Go back to that 56%.

They didn’t fail because they chose the wrong AI tools. Most of them chose fine tools – capable, well-designed, appropriate to their use cases. They failed because they installed new technology into old systems. Systems designed for a different era. Systems are optimized for different problems. Systems built on assumptions that no longer hold.

Then they wondered why adoption stalled.

Here’s what I’ve watched happen, over and over: A company invests in AI. The pilot works beautifully – small team, clear use case, motivated early adopters. Leadership celebrates. The rollout begins. And then... nothing. Adoption plateaus at 15%. The tool exists. People aren’t using it.

The Operator response is predictable: more training, more communication, more pressure. Town halls explaining the strategy. Dashboards tracking adoption metrics. Nudges, reminders, and “change management initiatives” are designed to encourage individuals to adopt the new behavior. Charisma sells the idea to the workforce.

None of it works. Because the technology was implemented in a system that made using it more difficult than not using it. The workflows don’t accommodate it. The incentives don’t reward it. The cultural signals say the safe play is the smart play, and using the new tool visibly – experimenting with it, potentially failing with it – doesn’t feel safe.

Until that changes, nothing changes.

The Sculptor question is not “How do we get people to adopt this?”

It’s What’s making adoption hard – and can we remove that?

That’s a fundamentally different orientation. Operator adds pressure. Sculptor removes friction. Operator demands different behavior within the same system. Sculptor redesigns the system until the desired behavior becomes the path of least resistance.

The vanguard didn’t give better speeches about transformation. They redesigned structures, incentives, and processes until adoption became easier than resistance. They carved away what was blocking the change they wanted to see.

The Removal Discipline

Here’s what makes Sculptor uncomfortable: it often appears to involve doing less.

Kill the meeting that no longer serves its purpose. Eliminate the approval gate that adds delay without adding value. Stop requiring the report no one reads. End the initiative that looked good in the planning deck but never gained traction. Decline the project that would be desirable but isn’t essential.

This is deeply uncomfortable for leaders who’ve been rewarded their entire careers for addition. Launching things. Announcing things. Building things. The leadership narrative is one of accumulation – more revenue, more headcount, more products, more initiatives. Nobody hands out awards for the meeting you eliminated or the project you killed.

But removal creates capacity. And capacity is what transformation requires.

Think about your own calendar. How much of it is spent managing problems that shouldn’t exist? Mediating conflicts that stem from unclear decision rights. Chasing updates that a better system would surface automatically. When answering questions, people could answer them themselves if they had the appropriate context. Sitting in meetings that exist because they’ve always existed, not because they’re still valuable.

Every recurring problem you manage is a system design failure. Every decision that routes to you unnecessarily is an architectural gap. Every workaround your team has normalized is a signal that something needs to be redesigned, not optimized.

Amy Edmondson’s research on psychological safety illuminates why this matters. She found that the highest-performing teams aren’t the ones that make fewer mistakes – they’re the ones that surface mistakes earlier, learn from them faster, and adapt more quickly. But that only happens when the system makes it safe to speak up. When the architecture rewards candor instead of punishing it.

Most organizations have the opposite architecture. They’ve built systems that teach people to hedge, to hide problems, to wait for permission, to avoid visible failure. And then leaders wonder why transformation stalls.

The Sculptor sees those systems. Instead of working harder to overcome them, asks: What would need to change so that the desired behavior becomes the natural behavior?

The First Sculptor Question

Most leaders, when they encounter a problem, ask: How do I solve this?

Sculptors ask something different: Should this problem exist at all?

That’s not a productivity hack. It’s not a time-management technique. It’s a fundamental reorientation in how you see your role.

Because many of the problems leaders spend their days solving are artifacts of systems they inherited or created – systems that made sense once but don’t anymore, or never made sense but nobody questioned them.

The meeting that exists because it’s always existed. The approval process was designed for a risk profile that the company outgrew years ago. The reporting cadence aligned with the previous CEO’s communication preferences. The coordination overhead exists only because the two teams lack shared visibility into each other’s work.

These aren’t problems to solve. They’re problems to eliminate. And the only way to eliminate them is to see them clearly – not as fixed constraints, but as design choices. Choices that can be unmade.

What am I managing that shouldn’t require management?

That’s the first Sculptor question. Sit with it. If you’re honest, you’ll find more answers than you want. Problems you’ve normalized. Friction you’ve accepted. Workarounds you’ve stopped noticing because you’ve been doing them so long.

The angel is hidden in there. The organization that could exist – more adaptive, more capable, more ready for transformation – if you could just clear away what’s obscuring it.

What Comes Next

This is Part 1 of a three-part series.

Tomorrow, in Part 2, I’ll explore what actually happens when leaders shift into Sculptor mode – the counterintuitive results, the patterns I’ve observed, and why the changes are rarely what anyone expects.

Thursday, in Part 3, I’ll share five diagnostic questions that reveal whether you’re actually sculpting or just operating faster – the gap between thinking you’re working on the system and actually changing it.

The frameworks in this series – VOICES, CREATE, 6C – form the core of my forthcoming book, CLUTCH: How Leaders Build Systems That Run Without Them. But the principle underneath them is simpler than any framework:

Stop adding. Start removing.

The angel is already in the marble.

Free, always. Delivered to your inbox so you're not waiting on an algorithm to decide what you see.

Subscribe now

Before you go, one question to sit with:

What’s one problem you’ve solved at least three times in the past month? Not a variation. The same underlying issue is resurfacing.

That’s your system talking. That’s the marble showing you where the angel might be.

Don’t fix it yet. Just notice it. We’ll get to the fixing.

If you’re already feeling the bottleneck:

I work with founders, leadership teams, schools, non-profits, and government agencies – organizations where the systems haven’t kept pace with the mission. The work is architectural: figuring out what to remove, not just what to add.

If you’re tired of solving the same problems and ready to start carving, let’s talk. I take on a limited number of clients at a time because this work goes in-depth. If the timing doesn’t work, the book and the essays aren’t going anywhere.
