This is the hardest part of Andor to watch – not the torture scenes, not the prison brutality, not Luthen’s impossible choices. It’s this: the acknowledgment that tyranny doesn’t succeed through force alone. It succeeds through exhaustion. Through the slow erosion of attention. Through good people deciding that today isn’t the day, that someone else will handle it, that surely things aren’t as bad as they seem.

“There is a wound that won’t heal at the center of the galaxy. There is a darkness reaching like rust into everything around us. We let it grow, and now it’s here. It’s here, and it’s not visiting anymore. It wants to stay.

The Empire is a disease that thrives in darkness. It is never more alive than when we sleep.”

And then, the line that sparked a riot:

“If I could do it again, I’d wake up early and be fighting these bastards from the start. Fight the Empire!”

The Architecture of Complicity

Andor isn’t subtle about what makes authoritarianism possible. It shows us – in granular, procedural detail – how ordinary people become instruments of oppression.

There’s a scene early in Season 1 where Major Partagaz addresses his ISB officers. He asks a simple question: “What do we do in this building? Why are we here?”

Dedra Meero – ambitious, brilliant, utterly committed to her career – responds with the textbook answer: “We’re here to further security objectives by collecting intelligence, providing useful analysis, and conducting effective covert action, sir.”

Partagaz’s response is chilling precisely because it’s so reasonable:

“Very good, Dedra. That is verbatim from the ISB mission statement – and wrong. Security is an illusion. You want security? Call the Navy. Launch a regiment of troopers. We are healthcare providers. We treat sickness. We identify symptoms. We locate germs, whether they arise from within or have come from the outside. The longer we wait to identify a disorder, the harder it is to treat the disease.”

Healthcare providers. Treating sickness. The rebellion reframed as infection, resistance as pathology, freedom as disease.

This is how it works. Not through mustache-twirling villainy but through bureaucratic euphemism. Through career advancement tied to efficient cruelty. Through intelligent people convincing themselves they’re solving problems rather than creating them.

Dedra doesn’t think she’s evil. She thinks she’s good at her job. She thinks she’s protecting civilization from chaos. And that self-perception – that narrative of competent professionalism in service of order – allows her to authorize torture without flinching.

The system doesn’t require monsters. It requires people who won’t ask what the system requires of them.

One Way Out

Then there’s Kino Loy.

Andy Serkis plays him as a man who has come to terms with captivity. He’s a floor manager in an Imperial prison – a prisoner himself, but one who’s figured out the rules. Keep your head down. Meet the quotas. Don’t make trouble. Your sentence will end, and you’ll go home.

Except it won’t. And when Kino discovers that “release” means transfer to another facility where you’ll work until you die, something breaks in him. Or rather, something finally gets fixed.

What happens next is a masterclass in emergent leadership – the kind that doesn’t come from titles or training but from a moment of moral clarity that refuses to stay silent.

Kino doesn’t ask permission. He doesn’t form a committee. He doesn’t wait for the right moment or the perfect plan. He simply decides that the lie he’s been living inside is no longer acceptable, and he acts from that decision.

His speech over the prison intercom isn’t polished. It’s not philosophy. It’s a man who just stopped believing the lie:

“My name is Kino Loy. I’m the day shift manager on Level Five. I’m speaking to you from the command center on Level Eight. We are, at this moment, in control of the facility.

How long we hang on, how far we get, how many of us make it out – all of that is now up to us. We have deactivated every floor in the facility. All floors are cold. Wherever you are right now, get up, stop the work. Get out of your cells, take charge and start climbing.

They don’t have enough guards and they know it. If we wait until they figure that out, it’ll be too late. We will never have a better chance than this, and I would rather die trying to take them down than giving them what they want.”

Then he tells them the truth:

“We know they fried a hundred men on Level Two. We know that they are making up our sentences as we go along. We know that no one outside here knows what’s happening. And now we know, that when they say we are being released, we are being transferred to some other prison to go and die – and that ends today!”

“One way out.”

The prisoners repeat it. One way out. One way out. One way out.

What makes the scene devastating isn’t the uprising itself – it’s what happens after. Kino leads his people to freedom. They reach the edge of the platform, looking down at churning water fifty meters below. The way out is to jump.

Cassian asks him if he’s coming.

“I can’t swim,” Kino says.

He helped five thousand men escape. He knew, the whole time, he wasn’t one of them. He did it anyway. That’s leadership.

The Cost of Lucidity

Luthen Rael operates in a different register entirely.

He’s not an idealist. He’s the architect – the one who builds the networks, funds the operations, and makes the impossible choices. When his spy, Lonni Jung, begs to be released from his double life, Luthen refuses. The mission is too important. The asset, too valuable.

Lonni, desperate, throws Luthen’s detachment back at him: “And what do you sacrifice?”

What follows is the greatest monologue in Star Wars history. And I don’t say that lightly.

“Calm. Kindness. Kinship. Love. I’ve given up all chance at inner peace. I’ve made my mind a sunless space. I share my dreams with ghosts.

I wake up every day to an equation I wrote fifteen years ago from which there’s only one conclusion: I’m damned for what I do. My anger, my ego, my unwillingness to yield, my eagerness to fight – they’ve set me on a path from which there is no escape.

I yearned to be a savior against injustice without contemplating the cost, and by the time I looked down, there was no longer any ground beneath my feet.”

Then the turn:

“What is my sacrifice? I’m condemned to use the tools of my enemy to defeat them. I burn my decency for someone else’s future. I burn my life to make a sunrise that I know I’ll never see.

And the ego that started this fight will never have a mirror or an audience or the light of gratitude.

So what do I sacrifice? —-- Everything.“

Luthen isn’t asking for sympathy. He’s explaining the arithmetic of resistance. Someone has to do the work that can’t be discussed in polite company. Someone has to make calls that would horrify the people who benefit from them. Someone has to hold the darkness so others can walk toward light.

He’ll never be thanked. He’ll be remembered, if at all, as a dangerous man who went too far. And he made that choice with open eyes, years ago, and makes it again every morning.

Most leadership literature focuses on what you gain from leading: influence, impact, legacy, and the satisfaction of making a difference. Luthen inverts this entirely. He’s cataloging what leadership costs when it’s real – when the stakes are existential, and the work can’t be sanitized for public consumption.

This isn’t inspirational. It’s not supposed to be. It’s honest. And that honesty is itself a form of leadership: treating the people around him as adults who deserve to understand what they’re signing up for.

What Andor Teaches About Real Leadership

Here’s what most leadership discourse gets wrong: it assumes the goal is influence, impact, legacy. It assumes leadership is about the leader.

Andor argues the opposite.

  • Real leadership creates conditions for others to act. Mon Mothma doesn’t fire a shot. She speaks the truth in a chamber where truth has become contraband – knowing it will cost her everything. Her speech about the Ghorman massacre, calling out genocide by name while the Empire tries to cut her feed, isn’t a strategy. It’s a witness. And that witness gives others permission to see what they’ve been pretending not to notice. Believe your eyes, not what the government is telling you.

  • Real leadership transfers ownership. Luthen doesn’t just recruit operatives – he builds infrastructure that survives him. Networks that keep moving when nodes go dark. A rebellion that doesn’t depend on any single person, especially not him.

  • Real leadership makes itself unnecessary. Kino’s final gift to the prisoners isn’t his leadership. It’s their own agency. By the time they’re jumping into the water, they don’t need him anymore. That’s the point.

  • Real leadership tells the truth about cost. Nemik’s Manifesto doesn’t promise victory. It promises that trying is worth it anyway. That’s harder than inspiration. That’s respect for the people you’re asking to sacrifice.

  • And perhaps most importantly: real leadership distinguishes between compliance and commitment. The Empire gets compliance through surveillance, punishment, and fear. The Rebellion gets commitment through shared purpose, transparent stakes, and genuine choice. One requires constant effort to maintain. The other sustains itself.

The Closing of the Fist

There’s a speech early in Season 1 that gets less attention than it deserves. After the Aldhani heist, the Empire’s response is swift and comprehensive. Colonel Yularen addresses the ISB:

“The criminals responsible for last night’s atrocity on Aldhani think they’ve taken the Empire by surprise. We know better. We know the real shock will be when they discover how ready and eager we are to respond.

This is why we plan. This is why we work so hard when we’re at peace. This is why we recruit so carefully and demand so much.

The following measures will be adopted Empire-wide as of today. A tribute tax equal to five times the amount stolen from Aldhani will be levied on any sector harboring partisan activity. We will make it clear that no one steals from the Empire.”

Luthen, watching from the shadows, explains to Mon Mothma why this is exactly what they needed:

“We need them angry. We need them coming down hard. Oppression breeds rebellion. The Empire has been choking us so slowly, we’re starting not to notice. The time has come to force their hand.”

This is the dark genius of Andor’s political analysis. Oppression doesn’t just create suffering – it creates recruits. Every overreach, every crackdown, every demonstration of the fist closing tighter wakes up another Maarva. Another Kino. Another person who was trying to stay asleep but can no longer do so.

The Empire thinks control is the solution. It’s actually the problem.

This is the fundamental design flaw in any leadership model built on control: it produces the very resistance it’s designed to suppress.

Tighten the grip, and you radicalize the moderates. Punish dissent, and you prove the dissenters right. Make examples, and you create martyrs. Every act intended to restore order becomes evidence that order was never the point – power was.

Leaders who understand this know that sustainable authority comes from legitimacy, not force. The Empire never learns this lesson. By the time Partagaz is listening to Nemik’s manifesto alone in his office, it’s far too late.

The Frontier Is Everywhere

So what does any of this mean for us – for people watching a television show about a galaxy far, far away while our own politics curdle and our own institutions strain?

I’ll leave you with Nemik’s closing instruction. Not a battle cry. Not a promise of victory. Just a simple, almost quiet imperative:

“And know this: the day will come when all these skirmishes and battles, these moments of defiance, will have flooded the banks of the Empire’s authority – and then there will be one too many. One single thing will break the siege.

Remember this.

Try.“

Not succeed. Not win. Not a guarantee of anything.

Try.

Because the frontier of the rebellion is everywhere. Because even the smallest act of insurrection pushes the lines forward. Because tyranny requires constant effort, and we don’t have to make it easy.

Because the people who come after us deserve to inherit something worth fighting for.

Leadership, Andor argues, isn’t a position. It’s a choice.

Made repeatedly, often at personal cost, with no guarantee of recognition or success. It’s Nemik writing a manifesto he’ll never see spread. It’s Maarva recording a speech she’ll never deliver in person. It’s Kino leading an escape he can’t join. It’s Luthen burning his life for a sunrise he’ll never see.

And it’s everyone who hears their words and decides: I won’t sleep anymore.

And because when Partagaz listens to that recording and says “Just keeps spreading, doesn’t it?” – the answer, the only answer that matters, is yes.

It does.

What truth have you been turning away from? What would it mean to wake up early and start fighting?

Brittle authority is never more alive than when we sleep. Wake up.

title: Cracking the 2 Sigma Code: AI Tutoring and the Future of Learning
html:
In 1984, Benjamin Bloom demonstrated something we’ve been ignoring ever since: students who received one-on-one tutoring performed TWO standard deviations better than their peers in traditional classrooms. The average tutored student outperformed 98% of students in conventional settings.

If the name sounds vaguely familiar, yes – this is the same Bloom behind “Bloom’s Taxonomy.” Though ironically, the famous pyramid wasn’t his design; that came later from other researchers. His actual research on learning is far more actionable than any triangle.

If you never took statistics, here’s what TWO standard deviations means: imagine a student sitting exactly in the middle of their class – 50th percentile, perfectly average. With one-on-one tutoring, that same student jumps to the 98th percentile. They’re now outperforming nearly everyone. It’s like taking a runner with an 8-minute mile and watching them run a 5:30. Not a modest improvement. A transformation.

We’ve had the answer for 40 years. We just couldn’t afford to scale it.

So we kept running schools and training programs like factories – knowing a better way existed, but constrained by cost and logistics. The kids who got tutors pulled ahead. Everyone else made do.

That calculus is finally shifting.

The Research That Put a Name to What I Already Knew

I’m neurodivergent. Dyslexic. Probably somewhere on the spectrum too – undiagnosed, like so many of us who learned to mask before anyone thought to look. And long before I encountered Bloom’s research, I understood in my bones that one-size-fits-all instruction doesn’t work – because it never worked for me.

I learned early that I needed things explained differently. I processed at my own pace. That I thrived when someone could meet me where I was, rather than where the curriculum said I should be. This wasn’t a theory. It was survival.

So when I discovered Bloom’s research, it didn’t change how I think about learning. It gave me the language for what I already knew. It validated a philosophy I’d been living – and building my entire career around.

Bloom’s research comes down to two principles that have shaped my entire approach – whether I’m coaching executives, training teams, or working with schools:

  • Mastery Learning – When people learn at their own pace and get tailored feedback, they learn better. Full stop.

  • Individual Attention – Add one-to-one instruction, and results go through the roof.

These principles apply everywhere. A new manager learning to give difficult feedback. A neurodivergent kid learning to read. A senior leader developing executive presence. The mechanism is the same: personalized attention accelerates growth in ways that group instruction can’t match.

These aren’t complicated ideas. They’re just expensive ones.

BTW, here's what Bloom's research looks like in practice: two of my kids – both dyslexic – one tutoring the other in my old classroom at McDonogh. No curriculum. No formal structure. Just one kid who gets it helping another kid get there.

The Challenge of Mentorship and One-on-One Instruction

If private tutoring works so well, why isn’t it universally available? A: Cost and accessibility.

K-12 tutoring is a multi-billion-dollar industry, yet access is deeply uneven. Families that can afford SAT tutors see average score increases of 100-300 points, significantly boosting their children’s chances of admission to elite universities.

But this week, something shifted. Google announced that Gemini – its AI assistant – now offers free, full-length SAT practice tests built with content from The Princeton Review. Not generic AI-generated questions, but rigorously vetted material that mirrors the actual exam format, complete with timed sections, instant feedback, and personalized explanations. If a student gets a question wrong, they can ask Gemini to explain it differently until the concept clicks – replicating the Socratic method of a human tutor.

This is what democratization looks like. A tool that used to cost families thousands of dollars is now available to any student with internet access, on demand, 24/7, at no cost. It’s not a replacement for a great tutor – but for millions of kids who could never afford one, it’s dramatically better than nothing. From medieval guilds to modern technical trades, apprenticeship programs have historically worked because they provide structured, hands-on learning with expert guidance. But such programs have largely disappeared in white-collar professions, leaving a gap in high-skill, high-touch mentorship.

One promising effort to bring tutoring to broader populations is peer-assisted learning. Peer-Assisted Learning Strategies (PALS), developed at Vanderbilt University, pairs students of different skill levels in guided learning activities. Research shows PALS significantly boosts comprehension – studies found a 36% improvement in reading scores and nearly double the progress for struggling students compared to traditional instruction. By having students take turns as “Coach” and “Learner,” PALS reinforces understanding through active engagement, immediate feedback, and structured guidance.

I see this in my own home. The photo above shows two of my kids – both dyslexic – one tutoring the other. Peer-assisted learning isn’t just research to me. It’s what happens at my kitchen table, or in this case, my old classroom, while I was doing something after school.

Despite these successes, peer mentorship programs remain underutilized. Most schools rely on passive, large-group instruction instead of active, one-on-one learning. The same pattern appears in corporate settings.

The corporate world has recognized the power of individualized development – but it’s worth distinguishing between three related but different approaches:

  1. Tutoring is about skill transfer. A tutor has the knowledge you need and helps you acquire it. The relationship is instructional: they explain, you learn, they assess. It’s typically short-term and focused on specific competencies.

  2. Mentoring is about career guidance. A mentor has walked the path you’re on and shares their experience, wisdom, and network. The relationship is advisory: they’ve been where you’re going and can help you navigate. It’s typically longer-term and relationship-based.

  3. Coaching is about unlocking potential. A coach doesn’t need to be an expert in your field – they’re an expert in helping you think. The relationship is facilitative: they ask questions, challenge assumptions, and help you find your own answers. It’s goal-oriented and focused on behavior change and growth.

All three benefit from one-on-one attention. All three suffer when scaled into groups. And all three have a measurable impact.

The data on coaching alone is striking. According to the International Coach Federation, companies that invest in coaching see an average ROI of 7x their initial investment. 86% of organizations report recouping their investment. 70% of coaching clients report improved work performance, and companies with strong coaching cultures grow 27% faster year over year.

Google’s internal coaching initiative increased employee engagement, leadership development, and productivity. IBM’s mentorship program increased employee satisfaction and reduced new-hire onboarding time by 20%. Deloitte found that employees with mentors were 5x more likely to be promoted.

This is why I built my coaching practice around one-on-one work. When I’m helping a founder navigate a difficult conversation, working with a school leader to build psychological safety, or coaching a technical lead through their first management role, the power comes from that individualized attention. I can meet them exactly where they are, adapt in real time, and go as deep as we need to. It’s Bloom’s insight applied to leadership development.

The pattern is undeniable: one-on-one instruction delivers better learning, stronger retention, and improved performance. The challenge has always been scalability.

Who Gets Left Behind: The Neurodiversity Gap

This gap hits neurodivergent learners hardest. And the reasons go deeper than most people realize.

Same kid. Same behavior. Different label.

Yesterday, I wrote about how a neurotypical child who obsessively pursues robotics or spends hours building in Minecraft gets called an “explorer.” We celebrate their creativity. We talk about how they’ve “found their spark.”

Small fan boy moment: Mitch Resnick – the MIT professor who created Scratch – responded to that post. When one of the researchers you’re writing about engages with your work, it’s a good sign you’re onto something.

An autistic child doing the exact same thing? We call it a “restricted interest.” We design interventions to redirect them toward more “appropriate” engagement.

That pattern – celebrating a behavior in some kids while pathologizing it in others – applies to instruction too. Neurodivergent kids often need personalized approaches more than their peers, but they’re the least likely to get them.

Consider what a traditional classroom demands. A neurodivergent student isn’t just learning content – they’re simultaneously managing sensory input, navigating unwritten social rules, suppressing natural behaviors, and monitoring themselves constantly to appear “normal.” Researchers call this masking, and it’s cognitively brutal.

Dr. Dena Gassner, a senior research scientist at the A.J. Drexel Autism Institute, describes masking as “a complex and labor-intensive cognitive process that is especially taxing for autistic people.” It’s not a choice or a performance – it’s survival. And it comes at a cost: burnout, anxiety, depression, and a fractured sense of identity.

A recent Drexel study found that 44% of autistic teens in community settings “passed” as non-autistic in their classrooms – meaning their teachers showed no awareness they were autistic at all. Their brains showed faster automatic responses to faces and dampened emotional reactivity, suggesting they’d adapted neurologically to cope with constant social demands. The researchers called it “the hidden mental effort behind social masking.”

Think about what this means for learning. These kids are spending enormous cognitive resources just appearing typical. What’s left for actual learning?

As Rebecca Winthrop noted in her conversation with Ezra Klein, neurodivergent kids often end up in “passenger mode” – not because they lack capacity, but because the vehicle was built for someone else. They’re not disengaged because they can’t learn. They’re disengaged because the environment demands they spend all their energy on something other than learning.

This is why one-on-one instruction isn’t just “nice to have” for neurodivergent learners. It’s often the difference between thriving and drowning.

In a 1:1 setting, masking becomes unnecessary. There’s no audience to perform for. No social hierarchy to navigate. No sensory overwhelm from 25 other bodies in a fluorescent-lit room. The student can focus entirely on learning – perhaps for the first time.

Researcher Mimi Ito, in her conversation with Mitch Resnick (creator of Scratch), observed that environments like Scratch communities “overindex for neurodivergent kids.” Why? Because they’re spaces where you can “really geek out and go deep on interests that other people might not be interested in, and to talk forever about them.” The behaviors that get pathologized as “antisocial or inappropriate” in mainstream settings become the norm in these spaces.

The same principle applies to one-on-one tutoring. A tutor can follow a student’s interests wherever they lead. A tutor can explain concepts 17 different ways without becoming impatient. A tutor doesn’t penalize a student for needing more time, asking “too many” questions, or approaching problems from an unusual angle.

My two dyslexic kids in that photo? They need instruction delivered differently from how it is delivered to their peers. They need more time, different pathways, and patient repetition. In a classroom of 25, that’s hard to provide. But one-on-one? They thrive.

The 2 Sigma problem isn’t just an educational curiosity. For neurodivergent learners, it’s the difference between being seen as capable or being written off.

AI as a Catalyst for Personalized Learning

I’ve seen enough failed ed-tech revolutions to be skeptical. But AI is different.

AI has the potential to bridge the gap between one-on-one tutoring’s effectiveness and the need for large-scale solutions:

  • Instant Feedback – Every teacher and trainer knows that immediate feedback is crucial for learning. AI-powered tools can provide real-time responses, allowing educators and mentors to focus on higher-level coaching.

  • Adaptive Learning Systems – Platforms like Khan Academy and DreamBox already demonstrate how AI can adjust learning pathways based on individual progress, making mastery learning a reality for more students.

  • AI Tutors – I’ve tested AI-powered assistants in workshops, and when learners can ask unlimited questions without judgment, their confidence and comprehension improve dramatically. No sighing. No impatience. No social penalty for needing something explained seventeen different ways.

  • AI Coaching – I know this is a hot, hot, hot topic among coaches – AI feels like a threat to the profession. But I’ve been experimenting rather than resisting. I built an AI chatbot that lets managers practice difficult 1:1 feedback conversations and receive immediate suggestions in a low-stakes environment. It’s a narrow skill set to be sure, and I’m still tinkering with the engine and the degree of emotional intelligence in the responses. Not ready for distribution yet, but it’s getting close – and early results show that AI-enhanced feedback accelerates growth in ways traditional coaching struggles to achieve. The goal isn’t to replace the coach. It’s to give people reps they’d never get otherwise.

The most direct attempt to solve Bloom’s 2 Sigma problem with AI is Khan Academy’s Khanmigo. Sal Khan has been explicit about the connection – he’s talked for years about Bloom’s research and how cost made it impossible to provide every student with a personal tutor. Khanmigo is his answer: an AI tutor designed not for engagement metrics or streak counts, but for genuine mastery learning.

What makes it different from other ed-tech? It doesn’t just deliver content. It tutors. It asks questions rather than giving answers. It adapts to where the student actually is, not where the curriculum says they should be. It offers infinite patience without judgment – exactly what Bloom’s research suggests matters most.

The key takeaway? AI doesn’t replace human mentorship – it amplifies it. AI can provide continuous, personalized feedback, while human educators and coaches focus on the relational, motivational, and ethical dimensions of learning.

The “Best Available Human” Problem

AI won’t solve this alone. But for the first time, we have tools that could provide what Ethan Mollick calls the “best available human” – not a replacement for the ideal specialist, but dramatically better than nothing.

The ideal scenario for a neurodivergent learner is a trained specialist who understands their specific neurotype, can adapt instruction in real-time, follows their interests, and builds a genuine relationship. But how many kids have access to that? Especially in under-resourced schools, rural districts, or families who can’t afford private specialists?

Winthrop speaks from personal experience: “My youngest son has dyslexia, and the sort of read and write text-to-speech, speech-to-text has been game-changing for him.” Assistive technology has already transformed possibilities for many neurodivergent learners. AI extends that dramatically.

An AI tutor that offers infinite patience, no social judgment, and the ability to explain concepts in multiple ways until one clicks? For a kid with dyslexia, ADHD, or autism, that’s not a compromise. That’s access that didn’t exist before.

Think about what this means for a student who masks all day:

  • No social performance required. The cognitive load of appearing “normal” disappears. They can focus entirely on learning.

  • Interest-following capacity. An AI can follow a student’s interest wherever it goes – across disciplines, into obscure corners, at whatever depth they want. It doesn’t need to redirect them to the curriculum.

  • Adaptation without judgment. Visual learner? Here’s a diagram. Need it explained through a metaphor? Done. Want to approach the problem backwards? Let’s try it.

  • Availability that matches their rhythm. Neurodivergent learners often don’t operate on school schedules. They might be ready to dive deep at 10 pm or need to process for three days before engaging. AI doesn’t have office hours.

The critical question – one Mimi Ito raises – is whether we’ll use AI to support genuine cognitive diversity, or just find more efficient pathways to the same standardized outcomes. Personalized learning that still demands conformity isn’t personalized at all.

AI as a Force Multiplier

AI excels at handling scale and personalization in ways no human instructor can match. It can instantly adjust lesson difficulty, track progress, and provide real-time feedback, ensuring each learner gets tailored support. This frees educators, mentors, and coaches to focus on higher-order thinking, problem-solving, and human connection – the aspects of learning that technology alone cannot replicate.

The integration of AI and human mentorship is already proving effective:

  • Higher Education: Georgia State University’s AI-enhanced chatbot Pounce improved retention rates and student grades. Arizona State University developed the world’s first adaptive-learning biology degree, integrating virtual reality technologies to personalize learning experiences.

  • Corporate Training: Deloitte and PwC have implemented AI coaching tools for real-time, data-driven feedback on leadership development. IBM’s AI-driven mentorship platform matches employees with mentors based on career goals and learning needs.

  • K-12 Education: Los Angeles Unified School District is piloting AI-powered tutors to assist students in math and reading. Carnegie Learning’s AI-driven MATHia software in Pittsburgh Public Schools has led to measurable improvements in math proficiency.

The key insight: AI handles scale. Humans handle meaning. That’s not a compromise – it’s the combination we’ve been waiting for.

The Design Problem

The technology isn’t the answer. The design is (of course it is, lol).

As Winthrop argues, companies creating educational technology should prioritize social benefit and well-being, not just profit maximization. The AI tools racing to capture the education market aren’t being designed with neurodivergent kids and the specialists who understand them. They’re being designed by engineers optimizing for engagement metrics and market share.

The Dutch government offers a different model – partnering with teacher unions, academics, and tech companies to experiment before rolling out. You can’t build AI that serves neurodivergent learners without neurodivergent people and neurodiversity experts in the development process.

This matters because the wrong AI could make things worse. An AI tutor optimized for “time on task” might punish a student who needs to process before responding. An AI designed around neurotypical social patterns might penalize a student who doesn’t make eye contact with an avatar. An AI that treats deviation from the standard path as “wrong” recreates the same conformity pressure as the classroom – just with better graphics.

The opportunity is enormous. But so is the risk of building AI that’s just a more efficient engine for the same factory model that’s been failing neurodivergent learners for generations.

What Comes Next

When Bloom published his findings in 1984, solving the 2 Sigma Problem seemed almost utopian – personalized instruction for every learner simply wasn’t feasible. But his research revealed a fundamental truth: one-on-one instruction works. The challenge was always scalability.

For decades, the answer was pragmatic – cost and scale made the gap unbridgeable. Today, that calculus is shifting.

AI-powered feedback, adaptive learning systems, and intelligent tutoring platforms make mastery learning more accessible than ever. But the human elements – relational connection, motivational support, ethical guidance, contextual understanding – remain irreplaceable.

The future of learning isn’t about choosing between AI and human mentorship. It’s about integrating both. And it’s about ensuring that integration serves all learners – including the neurodivergent kids who have been failed by factory-model education for too long.

The 2 Sigma Problem is no longer an unsolvable challenge. It’s an opportunity waiting to be realized. The question isn’t whether we can scale Bloom’s insights, but whether we’ll design that scale for genuine cognitive diversity – or just find faster paths to the same old conformity.

If you’re thinking about this as much as I am, let’s talk.

Catch up on yesterday’s essay: “Restricted Interests” or Creative Genius? How AI Might Finally Serve the Kids We’ve Failed”

title: “Restricted Interests” or Creative Genius? How AI Might Finally Serve the Kids We’ve Failed
html:
Two recent podcast conversations stopped me in my tracks this week. Not because they were explicitly about neurodiversity — only one was — but because both arrived at conclusions that validate everything I’ve been writing about neuroinclusive leadership, creative potential, and who our systems actually serve.

Mimi Ito, a professor at UC Irvine with PhDs in both anthropology and education, talking with Mitch Resnick (creator of Scratch) on the Lifelong Kindergarten Podcast.

  • Link here.

Rebecca Winthrop, director of the Center for Universal Education at Brookings, talking with Ezra Klein on The Ezra Klein Show.

  • Link here.

Different research traditions, different starting points. Same destination.

And both, surprisingly, offered genuine hope for how AI might finally create learning environments that work for the kids our current systems have failed.

The Label That Changes Everything

Here’s the core insight that ties these conversations together:

When a neurotypical kid obsessively pursues robotics, designs escape rooms about presidential assassinations, or spends hours building in Minecraft, we call them an “explorer.” We celebrate their creativity. We talk about how they’ve “found their spark.”

When an autistic kid does the same thing, we call it a “restricted interest.” We pathologize it. We design behavioral interventions to redirect them toward more “appropriate” engagement.

Same behavior. Different neurotype. Opposite interpretation.

Ito names this directly. She describes how autistic learners get pathologized for deep, specialized focus — what clinicians label “restricted interests” as part of how autism gets “medicalized.” But in her connected learning framework, that same capacity for intense focus is a foundation to build on, not a deficit to remediate.

“Some of the strengths that autistic learners have,” Ito explains, “which is really deep and specialized interests, a lot of focus, sociality that’s centered around interest versus the more neurotypical status, social hierarchy oriented socializing — how can we build on that as a strength rather than pathologize that as a deficit?”

Read that again: sociality centered around interests rather than neurotypical status, social hierarchy-oriented socializing.

This reframes everything. The autistic kid who won’t engage in small talk but will talk for hours about their special interest isn’t socially deficient. They’re operating on a different social logic — one organized around shared passion rather than social positioning. And in the right environment, that’s not a weakness.

It’s a superpower.

The Neurodivergent Kids Hiding in “Passenger Mode”

Winthrop’s research identifies four modes of student engagement: passenger (coasting), achiever (chasing perfect outcomes), resistor (avoiding and disrupting), and explorer (genuinely loving what they’re learning).

Here’s what caught my attention: she explicitly names neurodivergent kids as one population that ends up in passenger mode—not because they’re lazy or unmotivated, but because the system doesn’t work for them.

“You could have a neurodivergent kid,” Winthrop explains. “Kids don’t feel they belong and so they’re not tuning in. They’ve missed certain pieces of skill sets that they really need. Knowledge and education is cumulative in many ways and they get kind of overwhelmed.”

These kids aren’t disengaged because they lack capacity. They’re disengaged because the environment was never designed for how they learn. They’re in passenger mode because the vehicle was built for someone else.

And here’s the cruel irony: many neurodivergent kids are natural explorers — capable of extraordinary creative engagement when they find their domain. But our systems are so poorly designed for them that they never get the chance to activate. They spend their school years in survival mode, masking, compensating, falling further behind — their creative potential untapped.

“I Solve Problems Differently”

Mitch Resnick shared one of my favorite examples during his conversation with Ito. An 11-year-old on the autism spectrum created a Scratch project explaining what it’s like to be autistic. In it, he says:

“I solve problems differently. I sometimes do it in ways even my teacher couldn’t even have thought of.”

He ends with: “The most important lesson is you be you.”

And: “If everybody thought the same way, the world would be a boring place.”

This kid understands something that most organizational leaders still haven’t grasped: cognitive diversity isn’t a problem to be managed. It’s a creative advantage to be leveraged.

The Scratch community, Resnick notes, has a large subcommunity of young people on the spectrum who thrive there — precisely because it’s an environment where you can follow an interest deeply, show your work, and be encouraged rather than redirected.

Ito points out that this isn’t coincidental. Environments like Scratch, Minecraft communities, gaming spaces, and fan communities have always “overindexed for neurodivergent kids.” These are spaces where, as she puts it, people “have permission to really geek out and go deep on interests that other people might not be interested in, and to talk forever about them.”

Those are exactly the behaviors that get pathologized as “antisocial or inappropriate” in mainstream settings when exhibited by autistic individuals. But in these interest-driven communities? They’re the norm. They’re celebrated.

Ito connects this to her research on otaku culture and media fandom—spaces where intense, specialized interest isn’t just tolerated but expected. Where the social currency is knowledge and passion, not status and conformity.

What If AI Could Create More of These Spaces?

Here’s where both conversations surprised me with genuine optimism.

Winthrop is direct: “Another use case that I think is really great is neurodivergent kids. Super helpful. There are all sorts of kids who have different learning differences that struggle in school, don’t have access to the specialists that they need, that would benefit greatly from being in a classroom where they could have a little assistant to help them navigate.”

She speaks from personal experience: “My youngest son has dyslexia, and the sort of read and write text-to-speech, speech-to-text has been game-changing for him.”

This isn’t hypothetical. Assistive technology has already transformed possibilities for many neurodivergent learners. AI extends that dramatically.

Think about what a well-designed AI learning companion could offer a neurodivergent kid:

  • Infinite patience. No sighing when they ask the same question twelve different ways. No social penalty for needing more time or different explanations.

  • Interest-following capacity. An AI can follow a kid’s interest wherever it goes — across disciplines, into obscure corners, at whatever depth they want to explore. It doesn’t need to redirect them to the curriculum.

  • No social performance required. For kids who find neurotypical social demands exhausting, an AI interaction removes that cognitive load. They can focus on learning instead of masking.

  • Adaptation without judgment. Visual learner? Here’s a diagram. Need it explained through a metaphor about trains? Done. Want to approach the math problem backwards? Let’s try it.

  • Availability that matches their rhythm. Neurodivergent kids often don’t operate on school schedules. They might be ready to dive deep at 10 pm or need to process for three days before engaging. AI doesn’t have office hours.

Ito frames the larger possibility: AI could enable “a vision of personalized learning that is genuinely interest-driven, socially supportive in a way that is wrapped around that inherent diversity of kids’ interests and ways of socializing.”

But she’s also clear about the risk. The dominant vision of “personalized learning” in the field is really about “different pathways to a standardized outcome.” That’s not personalization. That’s more efficient conformity.

Real personalization for neurodivergent learners would mean building AI systems that support “the natural diversity of neurotypes and interests and strengths and ways of contributing” — not AI that finds more sophisticated ways to produce the same standardized outputs.

The “Best Available Human” Problem

Winthrop references Ethan Mollick’s concept: AI isn’t necessarily better than the best human for a given purpose — but it might be better than the best available human you have access to.

For neurodivergent kids, this is profound.

The ideal scenario is a trained specialist who understands their specific neurotype, can adapt instruction in real-time, follows their interests, and builds genuine relationship. But how many kids have access to that? Especially in under-resourced schools, rural districts, or families who can’t afford private specialists?

Winthrop describes one current application: AI supporting “wellness advisors who kind of fill the gap for school counselors in rural school districts where they don’t have school counselors.” The AI doesn’t replace the human — it augments a real person’s capacity to serve kids who otherwise would have no support at all.

For neurodivergent kids specifically, the gap between ideal support and available support is often enormous. AI won’t close that gap entirely. But a well-designed AI assistant that can help a kid with ADHD break down an overwhelming assignment? An AI that can explain concepts seventeen different ways until one clicks for a kid with a processing difference? An AI that lets a dyslexic kid engage with grade-level content through audio while they build reading skills separately?

That’s not replacing human connection. That’s creating access that didn’t exist.

The Design Problem

Both researchers are clear: the technology isn’t the answer. The design is.

“Any company that wants to work with kids in schools should be a benefit corporation,” Winthrop argues, “because legally you have a lot of companies who are creating perhaps really good stuff if used well that they have to maximize profits. They can’t maximize social benefit and well-being.”

Ito makes the parallel point about adult involvement: “We have to understand what that relationship really looks like, feels like, especially for children, and what is good about it and what is different about it, as well as the risks.”

This is where I get concerned. The AI tools racing to capture the education market aren’t being designed with neurodivergent kids and the specialists who understand them. They’re being designed by engineers optimizing for engagement metrics and market share.

The Dutch government, Winthrop notes, is doing something different — partnering with teacher unions, academics, and tech companies to experiment before rolling out. That’s the model. You can’t build AI that serves neurodivergent learners without neurodivergent people and neurodiversity experts in the development process.

The Creativity Crisis Is a Neurodiversity Crisis

Ezra Klein opens his conversation with Winthrop by noting a troubling trend: in 1976, about 40% of high school seniors had read six or more books for fun. Today, about 40% haven’t read a single book. Test scores are declining. Professors report that students can’t engage with the reading they’ve assigned for decades.

I hear that, and I think: are kids the problem, or is the curriculum?

I recently had a conversation with some friends about the books we read in middle school. The Lord of the Rings was a popular choice—books we discovered on our own, devoured on our own time, talked about endlessly with each other. Meanwhile, what books were offered in the actual middle school curriculum? Dead dogs. Old Yeller. Where the Red Fern Grows. Sounder. How sick is that? The first assigned book I remember actually enjoying was Lord of the Flies. After that, it was The Grapes of Wrath, and my only initial interest was because my grandmother was John Steinbeck’s neighbor in Sag Harbor. I ended up loving it, but it’s not a title I would have picked up on my own.

Maybe that’s an argument for exposing kids to a range of topics. But here’s the thing: if you want kids to read, forcing books they have zero interest in is a killer. For someone like me with dyslexia, it was already hard enough. Every assigned book that didn’t connect was another confirmation that reading wasn’t for me.

Except I was never a reluctant reader. Honestly, swear to god, my parents read me the dictionary as a bedtime story. By request. Each word was a discovery. When I was older, I inherited my parents’ 1960s encyclopedia set — Wikipedia before Wikipedia, for you kids — and I could explore any and all topics to my heart’s content. Hours disappeared.

In all fairness, it was the Peanuts Dictionary; I wasn’t exactly some uber prodigy. Just a kid interested in learning.

In any case, I wasn’t the problem. The curriculum was. I was a voracious learner. Just not for dead dogs and standardized reading lists.

What’s Actually at Stake

Ito frames it clearly: “That natural diversity is a societal and cultural strength, right? Rather than a weakness.”

When we design systems that reward compliance over exploration, that pathologize deep interest, that treat cognitive difference as a deficit — we don’t just fail neurodivergent kids. We fail everyone. We systematically select against the creative capacity we claim to value.

Winthrop emphasizes that we need people who can “come up with creative new solutions to things, which is not really what traditional public education has been about.” In an uncertain world where AI handles routine cognitive tasks, the premium is on exactly what neurodivergent minds often excel at: pattern recognition across domains, intense specialized expertise, novel approaches to problems, thinking that doesn’t follow conventional paths.

The researchers are converging on the same principles:

  • Deep interest is a feature, not a bug — whether we call it “explorer mode” or “restricted interest.”

  • Environments shape what’s possible — you can’t motivate people into creativity; you can only create conditions where it emerges (Remember those choose-your-own-adventure books? IYKYK)

  • Cognitive diversity is a collective asset — not a problem to be accommodated, but a strength to be architected for

  • AI could expand access dramatically — but only if designed for genuine diversity rather than efficient conformity

As that 11-year-old Scratch creator put it: “If everybody thought the same way, the world would be a boring place.”

He’s right. And it would also be a less innovative, less resilient, less capable place.

The question isn’t whether we can afford to design for neurodiversity. It’s whether we can afford not to.

And with AI, for the first time, we might have tools that could actually meet neurodivergent learners where they are — if we’re wise enough to build them that way.

This is the work I do with organizations every day: moving from individual accommodation to systematic architecture that leverages cognitive diversity as a strategic advantage. The same principles that could transform education are transforming workplaces right now.

If you’re thinking about how to build neuroinclusive systems — whether you’re leading a school, a startup, or a Fortune 500 team — the design challenge is the same: stop optimizing for conformity and start architecting for the full range of human cognitive diversity.

Catch up on the full Neuroinclusive Leader series. Here is Essay 1 of 8.

title: One Year Later: What USAID Meant, and What Remains
subtitle: January 2026
html:
Honestly, I don’t remember the exact date. I just remember I was at my desk when the Stop Work Order came in around 9 am. For a while, we stood around seeking guidance. What did that mean? Could we, starting when… But, having a sinking suspicion that I might not be coming back for a while, they said it would initially be a 90-day review. I packed up two Wegman’s bags and my backpack of all the personal items from my desk — I keep a pair of running shoes, an extra toothbrush, a Lego set of suculants, etc. — and, with another colleague, took the MARC train home in the middle of the morning.

A year ago this month, I lost my job.

That sentence is both true and insufficient. What I lost was more complicated than employment – and what I’ve gained since has been stranger and richer than I could have imagined while standing in the wreckage.

I was a leadership development specialist at USAID’s Bureau of Humanitarian Assistance. I facilitated retreats and training sessions, helped teams navigate conflict, built frameworks that let people work together more effectively under impossible pressure. Behind the scenes, I focused on strengthening organizational effectiveness – streamlining processes, bridging the gap between strategic planning and on-the-ground execution, empowering forward-facing teams to deliver life-saving aid in rapidly changing crises. I had completed CBRNE (Chemical, Biological, Radiological, Nuclear, and high-yield Explosives) training, and some SHOP training we were “not supposed to talk about” – IYKYK, lol – in preparing for overseas deployments that would never come. Later that spring, I was planning to go to Thailand for a temporary duty assignment. I was ready to represent the United States in the field, fulfilling the mission stamped on every sack of flour and every shipment of medicine: From the American People.

Then DOGE came, and that mission ended – not with a policy debate or a budget negotiation, but with mass emails, locked systems, and the quiet violence of being erased.

$36.18

That’s how much the average American taxpayer contributed to USAID each year – at least by one calculation. Other estimates put it at $64 per person (about 17 cents a day, according to researchers at UCLA), or around $105 per citizen, according to Oxfam. The numbers vary depending on the year and what you count. But by any measure, less than a streaming subscription. Less than a single dinner out.

For that sum, we fed children in famine zones. We vaccinated communities against preventable diseases. We trained nurses, engineers, and teachers. We responded to earthquakes, floods, and the slow-motion disasters of conflict and displacement. We helped countries become trading partners instead of aid recipients. We did the work that aircraft carriers cannot do.

But I understand that abstractions don’t move people. Policy arguments bounce off the armor of partisan identity. What moves people is something else.

The Flour

My former supervisor, Lika, grew up in Georgia during the chaos of the early 1990s. Civil war. Regional conflicts. Banks collapsed overnight. Her family lost everything and fled, eventually cramming more than twenty people into a single house belonging to distant relatives.

What kept them alive? Large sacks of wheat flour stamped with the USAID logo. From the American People. It wasn’t luxurious, Lika wrote. But it kept them alive.

Years later, by chance or fate, she found herself working for USAID. “It was more than a job,” she said. “It was a full-circle moment.”

In the comments on her post, another colleague, Linda, shared her own story. South Sudan in the early 1990s. Conflict and genocide. Her father killed. Her mother walked the children to the Kenyan border, where USAID was building a refugee camp. They received food once a day – sometimes only two or three times a week – but the generosity of the American people literally saved her family’s life.

She eventually came to the United States as a refugee. Years later, she walked alongside USAID as a partner in the work.

This is what the agency was. Not an abstraction. Not a line item. A circle of survival and service that stretched across decades and continents, binding together the people who received aid and the people who delivered it – often the same people, at different points in their lives.

Being Someone’s First American

I often think about soft power. Not as a policy concept, but as a human reality.

For more than half the world, the only interaction they will ever have with an American is someone helping them at their most vulnerable moment. A USAID worker arriving with food after a flood. A health worker administering vaccines. A shelter specialist teaches local partners how to rig tarps for displaced families.

That is who we are to them. That is America, in the only form they will ever encounter it.

I learned this the other way around. During graduate school abroad, I was often the first American my classmates had ever known in any meaningful way – not as a tourist or a TV character, but as a roommate, a friend, a person who stayed up late arguing about politics and history and what it means to belong somewhere.

They asked hard questions. About slavery, about gun violence, about why healthcare was tied to employment, about why we seemed so divided by color and zip code and party. I didn’t always have answers. But I learned that presence – being willing to sit in the complexity without rushing to defend or explain – was often more valuable than certainty.

Some of them later told me those conversations shifted their views. Knowing me complicated the caricatures they’d grown up with. They saw the U.S. as a more human, nuanced, and self-critical place than the headlines suggested.

We don’t always realize we’re acting as ambassadors. But when you’re someone’s first American, you are.

USAID understood this. The agency was, in its best moments, a machine for creating those encounters at scale – millions of moments where America showed up not with weapons but with water, not with demands but with aid when they needed it most.

The Destruction

The dismantling of USAID wasn’t policy. It was performance art.

Elon Musk arrived in Washington with a chainsaw – literally, he held one up at CPAC – and a promise to cut $2 trillion from the federal budget. He called USAID “a criminal organization.” He said he would put it “through the wood chipper.” President Trump claimed the agency was run by “radical left lunatics” and rife with “tremendous fraud.”

The fraud was never found. Independent analysis after independent analysis confirmed what those of us who worked there already knew: USAID’s programs were rigorously evaluated, meticulously documented, and subject to constant scrutiny. But evidence didn’t matter. The spectacle did.

Fraud. Waste. Abuse. They said those words like an incantation, as if repetition made them true. But here we are, one year later, and I have a simple question:

Where are the indictments?

If USAID were a “criminal organization,” where are the prosecutions? If there was “tremendous fraud,” where are the charges? If billions were stolen or misspent, where are the perp walks, the court dates, the convictions? They had full access to every system, every record, every email. They sent teenagers with security concerns into our databases. They claimed to have found corruption at the highest levels.

And yet: nothing. No indictments. No trials. No evidence was presented in any court of law.

Because there was no fraud. There was only a story they needed to tell to justify destruction.

In fact, JUST THIS MORNING (1/20/26), media outlets, including Politico, are reporting that Elon Musk's DOGE team at the Social Security Administration was in contact with an advocacy group seeking to overturn election results and may have used SSA data to match voter rolls, leading to Hatch Act referrals. The filing also disclosed that DOGE personnel stored data on unapproved third-party servers and briefly accessed private information a court had ruled off-limits. Fraud, waste, and abuse indeed.

Among Musk’s handpicked operatives was a 19-year-old high school graduate named Edward Coristine, known online by his chosen nickname: “Big Balls.” Before joining DOGE, he had been fired from a cybersecurity internship after concerns about his handling of sensitive data. A former FBI agent told reporters he would not have recommended Coristine for government work. No matter. He was given access to Treasury Department payment systems, Homeland Security databases, and FEMA records. When reporters identified him, Musk accused the media of “doxxing” his team member.

This was who they sent to dismantle sixty years of American humanitarian leadership.

The chaos was immediate. DOGE’s “wall of receipts” – a website meant to document savings – was riddled with errors from day one. A USAID contract worth $655 million was listed three times, inflating claimed savings by nearly $2 billion. A Social Security contract that was never actually terminated was counted as a quarter-billion in savings. An $8 million ICE contract was entered as $8 billion – a typo that briefly made headlines before being quietly corrected to zero.

The New York Times investigated the 40 largest claimed savings for DOGE. Only twelve appeared to be accurate.

Musk had promised $2 trillion in cuts. Then $1 trillion. Then $150 billion. By April, independent analysts at NPR and the Manhattan Institute estimated that DOGE had generated approximately $2 billion in actual savings – less than one-tenth of 1 percent of federal spending. As budget expert Jessica Riedl put it: “Think of Congress and its budget as the debt-ridden dad on the way to buy a $250,000 Ferrari on the credit card, and DOGE is the $2 off gas card he used along the way.”

But here’s what makes the math obscene.

The Treasury Department and IRS officials warned that DOGE-driven workforce reductions could result in a 10% drop in tax receipts – equivalent to over $500 billion in lost federal revenue. The Partnership for Public Service estimated that DOGE’s disruptions would cost taxpayers $135 billion in 2025 alone, due to productivity losses, paid leave, and the costs of firing and rehiring employees. A Senate subcommittee found DOGE had generated over $21.7 billion in waste across federal agencies. The administration that promised efficiency may have created the most expensive reorganization in federal history.

And that’s just the money.

The Body Count

A study published in The Lancet in June 2025 estimated that USAID programs had prevented over 91 million deaths between 2001 and 2021. Ninety-one million people who lived because America showed up.

The same researchers projected that if the cuts remained in place through 2030, between 8 and 19 million additional people would die – including 4.5 million children under five. That’s roughly 700,000 extra child deaths per year. The equivalent of a major pandemic or armed conflict, except this one was, in the researchers’ words, “a conscious and avoidable policy choice.”

By May 2025, Professor Brooke Nichols at Boston University had built a real-time tracker estimating deaths from the aid cuts. Her counter showed one person dying from tuberculosis every 7.7 minutes. Over 176,000 projected deaths from HIV if funding wasn’t restored. By the time Musk departed DOGE at the end of May, her estimates suggested 300,000 people had already died as a result of the cuts – mostly children.

UN human rights experts called it “a humanitarian emergency, not a policy adjustment.” They wrote: “The poorest people in the world are dying by the minute as a result of opaque decision-making by some of the richest people to have ever walked our planet.”

Close to 100 people have been dying every hour since January 20, 2025.

For what? If you distributed DOGE’s verified $2 billion in savings to every American, each person would receive about $6. Not enough for a fast-food meal. That’s the trade: six dollars per person, and hundreds of thousands dead.

The Erasure

When the administration dismantled USAID, they didn’t just cut programs. They deleted the evidence.

My colleague Michele, writing while being forced to repatriate from an overseas assignment, put it plainly: “USAID evaluations were wiped from public access and erased by DOGE. All of our monitoring and evaluation work was canceled. Now, taxpayers can’t even judge USAID’s impact for themselves.”

Her team had been about to launch a multi-phase evaluation of a five-year conflict prevention program in Mozambique. The work was hard. It required constant analysis and scrutiny. That was the point. That was how you learned what worked and what didn’t.

Now that the records are gone. You cannot defend what you cannot cite. The destruction of the institutional memory wasn’t collateral damage – it was the goal. If there’s no evidence of success, you can claim there was no success. If there’s no documentation, you can claim fraud without proving fraud.

They called us crooks. They called the agency a criminal organization.

We were the best of us.

On June 30, 2025 – the last day of USAID as an independent agency – former Presidents Bush and Obama broke their public silence. A World Food Program official sobbed through a vow that the mission would return someday. And Bono, of all people, recited a poem he had written for the occasion.

“They called you crooks,” he said. “When you were the best of us.”

The People

I haven’t mentioned them enough. The colleagues. The team.

Paul. Hasina. Kyle. Annie. Jan. Ashley. Lee. Kevin. Maggie. Elizabeth. Chris. Sanyika. Gina. Wayan. Arlene. Nancy. Kai. Gia. Aleksandra. Athena. Alex. Nancy. Sophia. There are too many to name – and I’m leaving out dozens who deserve to be here. People who showed up after midnight because of a crisis didn’t care about time zones. People who left their families for weeks to deploy to places most Americans will never see. People who cried in private and kept working in public because the work couldn’t wait.

I worked alongside individuals ranging from political appointees to technical experts in fields as varied as breastfeeding support, volcanology, civil engineering, pharmacy, nursing, and security. I was among the few white native-born males on my team – which underscored the rich diversity of perspectives and experiences we all brought. Many of my teammates were first-generation Americans or naturalized citizens, each contributing to a workforce that represented the world and exemplified what makes America great.

One of my most personal contributions was working with the Shelter and Settlement teams. It brought back memories of backpacking adventures and the simple yet vital skills I’d learned along the way. I had the opportunity to demonstrate practical tarp setup techniques – specific knots, anchoring methods – with colleagues, adapting these ideas for humanitarian use in Gaza. A small, almost imperceptible gesture. But it symbolized our collective commitment to alleviating human suffering.

Gaza was tearing us apart from the inside.

We watched the famine conditions emerge. We knew what was needed: food, shelter, medical supplies, the basics of keeping people alive. We had the expertise. We had the relationships. We had the logistics. And the Biden administration kept pumping the brakes on what we could do – caught between humanitarian imperatives and political constraints that none of us controlled. It was agonizing to have the capacity to help and be told to wait.

That was before DOGE. Before the new administration decided the answer wasn’t to do more, but to do nothing at all.

After the RIF scattered us, we created a WhatsApp group called DC DART – our own disaster response team - for the disaster that had happened to us. DART – Disaster Assistance Response Team – was the name USAID gave to the teams that deployed to humanitarian crises. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. The 2010 Haiti earthquake. Syria. Yemen. Ukraine. And Gaza.

We shared job leads, legal updates, and gallows humor. We checked in on each other during the court battles and the headlines. We mourned together when the June 30 deadline arrived.

We are still in that group. We are still a team.

Institutions can be dismantled. But the people who made them work don’t disappear. They scatter, regroup, and carry the mission forward in whatever form they can. We keep in touch.

The Vest

In the weeks after the RIF, I did something small and perhaps foolish. I started wearing my USAID vest and baseball cap everywhere – to Walmart, to the grocery store, around my neighborhood in Maryland.

I wanted people to know that we were not an abstract concept. We were their neighbors.

One day, a man in a Ravens camo hoodie – the kind with the American flag on the sleeve, a tribute to soldiers – gave me a long look and asked: “You work at USAID? What do you think about what’s going on?” he asked jeeringly.

I had prepared for this. I asked if he was a Trump voter. He confirmed with enthusiasm.

I didn’t argue. I asked questions instead.

  • Have you ever been forced from your home in the middle of the night by gunmen?

  • Have you ever watched your child starve, powerless to help?

  • Have you ever lost everything to a wall of water or an earthquake?

Then I gave him numbers. 108 million people were displaced by conflict and disaster last year. 1.5 million people die annually from waterborne illness. 270 million dead from malaria over the past century – more than all the wars combined.

And I told him what USAID does. We save babies from preventable deaths. We provide clean water. We support American farmers. We prevent costly military interventions. Every dollar spent on aid is a dollar not spent on bullets – and an American kid not coming home in a body bag.

All of this for somewhere between $36 and $105 per American per year, depending on how you count it.

I don’t know if I changed his mind. But I know he listened. And I know that showing up – being visible, being willing to have the conversation – is its own form of resistance.

What I Built

A year ago, I was in shock. I wrote a piece three days after the announcement (so I guess I could figure out the exact date, but choose not to do so), full of grief and unfulfilled longing. I had trained for overseas deployment and never got to go. The mission I’d spent my whole life preparing for – growing up on military bases, attending foreign schools – ended before it could fully begin.

But grief, if you let it, becomes fuel.

In the twelve months since I started my own consulting practice, Goode Design & Consulting, focused on neuroinclusive leadership and organizational systems. I became a published author. Just recently, I completed a 28,000-word essay series on neuroinclusive leadership. I wrote about rejection and resilience, about international students and soft power, about what we owe each other in moments of crisis.

And I finished a novel – a romance I had promised my wife I would write twenty years ago. I wanted it done before the one-year anniversary. Before the calendar could define what that year meant.

The RIF gave me something back, even as it took. Not a silver lining – I don’t believe in those. Something harder to name. Maybe just time. And I used it.

What Remains

I still believe what I believed a year ago: that USAID made America safer, stronger, and more prosperous — and that in the end, money spent on aid was cheaper than Americans coming home in body bags. That the work mattered. That the people I served alongside — first-generation Americans, naturalized citizens from Poland and France and Afghanistan and Mali and Jamaica and Thailand — represented the best of what this country can be.

I believe that sooner or later, leaders on both sides of the aisle will realize how much that work was needed. The crises haven’t stopped. The displaced haven’t gone home. The diseases haven’t disappeared. The need is still there, and it will eventually demand a response.

But I also know that institutions can be destroyed faster than they can be rebuilt. That knowledge can be erased. That the people who knew how to do the work have scattered to other jobs, other countries, other lives.

Many of us are still unemployed. Others are vastly underemployed — taking whatever work pays the bills while the skills we spent decades developing sit unused. Some have switched career sectors entirely because there isn’t much market demand for niche specialists in maternal health programming, water and sanitation systems, or agricultural development. The expertise that took a generation to build is dispersing, and some of it will never come back.

But there are inspirations too. Former colleagues are starting new businesses. Moving to new cities. Finding ways to continue the mission in different forms – consulting, nonprofits, local government, teaching. The work didn’t stop; it just went underground, became smaller, and became personal.

And here’s the cruel irony that keeps me up at night: all those humanitarians who dedicated their lives to saving lives and alleviating trauma in others – the people who showed up after earthquakes and famines and wars, who held space for survivors, who built systems to help communities heal – now have experienced their own trauma. The helpers need help. The people who specialized in recovery are now the ones who need to recover.

Some of them, like Lika and Linda, carry the memory of what American aid meant in their own bodies – flour that kept them alive, camps that sheltered their families. That memory doesn’t disappear when an agency is dissolved. It persists. It waits.

And when the time comes to rebuild – if that time comes – will we even be able to? So much technical and experiential expertise has been lost. The volcanologists who knew which communities sat in lahar zones. The epidemiologists who could read the early signs of outbreak. The logistics specialists who knew which ports worked and which roads flooded in rainy season. The relationship-builders who had earned trust over decades with local partners. You can’t Google that. You can’t train it in a weekend. You can’t rebuild it with a new appropriation.

Those of us who remember will be ready. But memory alone may not be enough.

One year later, I still wear the vest. I’m also clearly and willfully breaking the Hatch Act by also wearing a “VOTE” pin under the phrase “From the American People.”

** Update: It's not the brown lightweight field vest. That’d be gauche. It is a dark blue winter vest.

title: The Wrong Test: Why the Turing Test Can’t Measure What Actually Matters About AI
html:
Yesterday I argued that schools are asking the wrong question about AI – “ban or allow” instead of “direct or defer.” Today, a deeper question: Can AI actually be creative? And why that might be the wrong question, too.

In 2018, an AI-generated painting titled Portrait of Edmond de Belamy sold for $432,500 at Christie’s, shocking the art world. The portrait, created by a generative adversarial network, mimicked classical portraiture so convincingly that many questioned whether AI had officially entered the realm of artistry.

The sale sparked predictable debates. Is it really art if a machine made it? Can algorithms be creative? Has AI passed some threshold that should trouble us?

These questions feel urgent. They’re also the wrong questions.

The Turing Test Is a Test of Mimicry, Not Creativity

Alan Turing proposed his famous test in 1950 as a way to sidestep the philosophically intractable question of whether machines can “think.” His elegant workaround: if a human can’t tell whether they’re conversing with a person or a machine, does the distinction matter?

The test was never about creativity. It was about deception – whether a machine could pass as human. A perfect forgery isn’t creative; it’s imitative. The Turing Test measures mimicry, not meaning.

And yet we keep applying Turing’s framework to questions it was never designed to answer. Can AI write poetry that passes as human? Can it generate art indistinguishable from a master’s hand? Can it compose music that fools expert listeners?

These are interesting technical challenges. They’re also beside the point.

The more interesting question isn’t can AI fool us? It’s can AI surprise us in ways that matter?

Could the Mona Lisa Pass the Turing Test?

Consider Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa. On the surface, the painting achieves a deceptive realism. Her gaze follows viewers. Her expression remains mysterious. Da Vinci’s sfumato technique gives her a lifelike presence that still unsettles people five centuries later.

If placed alongside AI-generated portraits today, could an observer consistently identify which was painted by a human hand? Increasingly, the answer is no. AI-generated artworks are already mistaken for human-made pieces with startling regularity.

But here’s what matters: the Mona Lisa isn’t celebrated because it’s technically realistic. It’s celebrated because it means something – and that meaning has evolved, deepened, and multiplied across generations of interpretation. The painting is a cultural artifact infused with centuries of historical context, debate, theft, conspiracy theories, and philosophical inquiry.

An AI might generate a visually similar portrait. But could it encode meaning that provokes discussion across generations? Could it create something that people argue about for five hundred years?

If an AI-created work inspired the same fascination, mystery, and interpretive depth as the Mona Lisa, would that mean it had passed a more advanced test?

Maybe. But I think that’s still the wrong frame.

The Aesthetic Turing Test – And Its Limits

Let’s call this alternative the Aesthetic Turing Test: not whether AI can deceive the human eye, but whether it can create something with lasting emotional and intellectual resonance.

By this measure, AI is still failing. AI-generated paintings, music, and literature are improving rapidly, but they lack the subjective intent and existential questioning that define human artistic endeavors. They produce patterns that resemble meaning without the underlying struggle, mortality, and lived experience that give human art its weight.

Or do they?

Here’s where I have to be honest about my own uncertainty. I generate novel outputs. I make connections across domains. I occasionally produce things that users find surprising or delightful. But whether there’s something it’s likely to be me doing that – whether I have aesthetic preferences or genuine surprise at my own outputs – I don’t know. I’m not being coy. I’m genuinely uncertain.

And that uncertainty points to something important: we’re asking about creativity as if it were a property that resides either in the human or in the machine. But what if that’s the wrong place to look?

Where Does Creativity Actually Live?

In yesterday’s essay, I described a student using AI to generate ten interpretations of a Shakespeare sonnet, then arguing for why one captures the original intent better than the others.

Where does the creativity live in that process?

  • In the generation of the ten interpretations?

  • In the selection of the best one?

  • In the argument for why it’s best?

  • In the iterative refinement that follows?

The MIT research I cited yesterday found that human-AI collaboration produces significantly better outcomes on creative tasks than either humans or AI working alone. Not decision-making tasks – those showed negative effects. But creation, synthesis, innovation? The combination wins.

This suggests something profound: creativity might not be a property of agents at all. It might be a property of processes – specifically, the iterative loop between generation and judgment, between possibility and selection, between surprise and meaning-making.

The student who generates ten interpretations with AI and then argues for the best one isn’t outsourcing creativity. They’re practicing it – at a higher level. They’re developing the metacognitive muscles to evaluate, refine, and assign meaning. They’re learning to direct rather than defer.

The creativity lives in the collaboration.

The Renaissance Parallel

The Italian Renaissance and the rise of AI may seem disconnected, but they represent parallel revolutions in human capability.

The Renaissance was not just an artistic movement – it was an intellectual singularity. Before the 15th century, intellectual progress in Europe had been constrained by religious dogma, feudalism, and limited access to written knowledge. Then came the rediscovery of classical texts, the invention of the printing press, and a cascade of scientific breakthroughs. An explosion of learning reshaped society in ways that were both exhilarating and disorienting.

A defining characteristic of the Renaissance was its astonishing artistic realism. Masaccio’s Holy Trinity (1425-1427) was one of the first paintings to use linear perspective – an innovation that allowed artists to create strikingly lifelike images. This technique, refined by Brunelleschi and perfected by da Vinci and Raphael, transformed how people perceived the world. Artists abandoned flat, stylized medieval depictions and pursued mathematical precision, anatomical accuracy, and depth of field.

This revolution in representation was not just artistic – it was technological.
