The ability to create depth, shadow, and movement on a two-dimensional surface signaled a fundamental shift in human perception. And it was deeply unsettling to those who lived through it. The boundaries of knowledge and human potential expanded so rapidly that people struggled to make sense of their place in an evolving world.

Sound familiar?

The printing press didn’t eliminate writers. It democratized literature and created entirely new forms of expression – the novel, the newspaper, the pamphlet, the scientific journal. The artists who thrived weren’t those who resisted the new techniques. They were those who mastered them and pushed further.

Beyond the Turing Test: The Next Creative Threshold

The Turing Test was a starting point, not a destination. If AI can already deceive us in conversation and visual art, the real test may be whether it can create meaning – not just patterns that resemble meaning, but something that compels us to reinterpret our existence.

I’m skeptical that AI alone can do this. Meaning requires a meaning-maker and a meaning-receiver. It requires context, history, mortality, and stakes. A painting means something different when you know the artist died the year after completing it. A poem hits differently when you learn it was written in a refugee camp.

But AI in collaboration with humans? That’s different.

The most successful applications of AI won’t prioritize replacement. They’ll prioritize what I’d call human-AI co-creativity: AI handling technical generation while humans focus on higher-level decision-making, emotional nuance, and assigning meaning.

AI can assist with early drafts, suggest unexpected combinations, and iterate faster than any human could alone. This frees artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers to focus on what humans do best: selection, judgment, interpretation, and the existential weight of being a mortal creature trying to make sense of existence.

The Neuroinclusive Dimension

There’s another angle here that connects to yesterday’s argument about education.

For many neurodiverse thinkers, the generation phase of creative work is the bottleneck. Executive function challenges make it hard to get started. Processing differences create friction between the idea and its expression. The blank page becomes an enemy.

AI changes this equation dramatically.

If creativity lives in the loop – in the iteration between generation and judgment – then AI can remove the barrier that has historically prevented many brilliant minds from demonstrating their creative capacity. The student with ADHD who struggles to produce a first draft can now generate multiple starting points and focus their energy on the higher-order work of selection and refinement.

This isn’t cheating. It’s an architectural inclusion. It’s recognizing that the bottleneck was never the lack of creative capacity – it was the mismatch between how we’ve traditionally structured creative tasks and how diverse minds actually work.

The Question We Should Be Asking

The question isn’t: Can AI be creative? That frames creativity as a binary property that an agent either has or lacks.

The question isn’t: Can AI pass the Turing Test? That reduces creativity to mimicry.

The question isn’t even: Can AI pass an Aesthetic Turing Test? That still locates creativity in the output rather than the process.

The question is: Can human-AI collaboration produce creative outcomes that neither could achieve alone – and can we learn to do this well?

The P&G-Wharton study I referred to yesterday suggests yes. The MIT meta-analysis suggests yes, specifically for creative tasks. The Renaissance suggests that new tools don’t end human creativity – they amplify it, democratize it, and push it into territory previously unimaginable.

The Singularity will not replace human creativity. It will reshape it.

The real question is whether we’re ready to teach the next generation how to collaborate with AI in ways that prioritize human judgment, meaning-making, and ethical application. Whether we’re ready to build systems that amplify human potential rather than replace it.

AI will not eat the artist’s lunch – if we design it well, it will set the table for an entirely new creative feast.

The skills this requires – prompt engineering, bias recognition, source verification, creative collaboration, ethical reasoning – are teachable. They’re assessable. And they should be at the center of every curriculum that claims to prepare students for the world they’re actually entering.

title: The Wrong Question: Why “Ban vs. Allow” Misses the Point About AI in Schools
html:
As promised, this isn’t really a new essay, but a revisitation and revision of a post I made on LinkedIn in August. The bones of the original post are there, but with some more edits — and probably some hot takes for other educators.

====

K-12 education isn’t just standing at a crossroads – it’s standing at one while asking for directions to the wrong destination.

The prevailing debate about AI in schools – should we ban it or allow it? – misses the question that actually matters: What kind of collaborator do we want our students to become?

Not whether they’ll use AI. They will. The question is whether they’ll learn to direct it or defer to it. Whether they’ll develop the metacognitive muscles to evaluate, refine, and override machine output – or whether they’ll become passive consumers of algorithmic suggestions.

This isn’t a distant workforce concern. It’s already here. And the clock is ticking.

The Evidence Is In – And It’s Decisive

When people talk about AI in schools, the examples often sound abstract: what if students use it to cheat on essays? But in the workplace, AI is already proving itself as a full-fledged teammate. One of the clearest demonstrations came from a landmark study at Procter & Gamble, in partnership with Wharton Business School.

P&G didn’t test AI in a lab. They asked employees to do what they already do in one of the world’s most competitive industries: develop new product ideas to solve real business challenges. These weren’t hypothetical exercises – they were authentic, high-stakes problems with the same constraints and market realities that drive billion-dollar brands.

The results were striking:

  • AI matched human teams in quality. Individuals using AI scored 0.37 standard deviations higher than solo workers without AI – putting them on par with full human teams.

  • AI made work faster. Individuals with AI finished tasks about 16% faster.

  • AI unlocked breakthrough ideas. Teams using AI were three times more likely to generate solutions ranked in the top 10% for quality.

  • AI improved collaboration and morale. By helping dissolve professional silos, AI led both R&D and commercial experts to produce more balanced, cross-functional solutions. Participants reported feeling more excited, energized, and less anxious.

But here’s where we need nuance. A recent paper from MIT’s Center for Collective Intelligence found that, on average, AI-human combinations do not outperform the best human-only or AI-only systems. Before you dismiss the P&G findings, though, read the fine print: the MIT researchers found that creative tasks showed significant positive effects for human-AI collaboration, while decision-making tasks often showed negative effects.

  • Read more about that MIT study here.

  • Here is the P&G study.

Product ideation – exactly what P&G tested – is a creative task. The MIT research doesn’t undercut the P&G findings; it clarifies them. Human-AI collaboration wins where it matters most for 21st-century work: creation, innovation, synthesis. The iterative loop possible with generative AI makes it better suited for human collaboration than earlier AI systems designed primarily to complete specific tasks.

If AI can deliver these results in one of the world’s most competitive corporate environments, the question for education becomes urgent: why wouldn’t we equip students with the skills to use it the same way?

But this raises a deeper question – one I’ll explore tomorrow: Can AI actually be creative?

Sure, AI can analyze datasets, optimize processes, and generate summaries. But creativity? The skeptic’s objection is fair: isn’t AI just recombining patterns from its training data? Can a system without subjective experience produce genuine novelty – or only sophisticated mimicry?

Here’s my preview of where that argument lands: the Turing test is the wrong test. Turing asked whether a machine could pass as human – a test of mimicry, not creativity. The more interesting question isn’t “can AI fool us?” but “can AI surprise us in ways that matter?” And perhaps most importantly: does creativity live in either the human or the AI, or does it emerge in the iterative loop between them?

The student who uses AI to generate ten interpretations of a Shakespeare sonnet, then argues for why one captures the original intent – where does the creativity live? In the generation? The selection? The argument? The refinement?

More on that tomorrow in my next post... For now, the practical point stands: whatever we decide about machine creativity, we know that human-AI collaboration produces outcomes neither achieves alone. That’s the skill worth teaching.

The Hidden Stakes: Neuroinclusion

Here’s an angle the mainstream debate almost entirely ignores: AI may be the most powerful neuroinclusive technology education has ever seen.

Traditional classrooms are built on an industrial-age model: standardized pacing, uniform instruction, and identical expectations. For neurodiverse learners – students with ADHD, dyslexia, autism, processing differences – this model has always been a poor architectural fit. We’ve responded with accommodations: extra time, separate testing rooms, and modified assignments. But accommodations are retrofits. They’re band-aids on a system that wasn’t designed for cognitive diversity in the first place.

AI changes the architectural possibilities entirely.

AI’s strength lies in pattern recognition and personalization at scale. It can adapt content and delivery in real time based on how a student is interacting with a lesson. For neurodiverse learners who may need more repetition, multi-sensory engagement, or pacing adjustments, this adaptability is transformational.

Consider the specifics:

  • A student with ADHD may benefit from shorter, interactive modules that reward progress quickly, while a learner with dyslexia might receive visual and audio cues alongside text to reinforce comprehension.

  • AI-powered tools can break complex tasks into manageable steps for students with executive function challenges, addressing the task paralysis that derails so many capable minds.

  • Real-time dashboards can show educators which students are struggling, where they’re excelling, and how their engagement levels fluctuate – enabling intervention before frustration sets in.

Early evidence suggests that AI tools can provide real-time, personalized support while reducing educators’ administrative burdens. Adaptive learning platforms adjust complexity, pacing, and modality to meet individual needs. For students who become overwhelmed by long assignments, AI can break work into shorter sets, celebrate progress, and provide instant feedback – building confidence alongside competence.

This reframes the entire debate. Schools that ban AI aren’t just leaving students unprepared for the workforce – they’re removing scaffolding that neurodiverse learners desperately need. They’re choosing accommodation over architecture. They’re treating AI as a cheating risk when it could be the most equalizing force in education since the Americans with Disabilities Act.

The neuroinclusive argument isn’t separate from the workforce argument. It’s the same argument, sharpened. We’re not just asking: will students be ready for AI-enabled work? We’re asking: will all students have access to the tools that let them demonstrate what they actually know?

The Policy Landscape Has Shifted

When I first wrote about this topic last summer, the policy environment was fragmented and cautious. That’s changed dramatically.

As of early 2025, 33 states and their departments of education now have official guidance or policy on the use of AI in schools. In April 2025, President Trump signed an executive order to create new educational and workforce development opportunities for America’s youth centered on AI literacy. The Department of Education followed with formal guidance affirming that AI use is allowable under existing federal education programs, provided it aligns with statutory requirements.

The National Science Foundation has issued funding opportunities specifically for K-12 AI education, prioritizing three themes: teacher professional development, curricula and instructional materials, and technology tools that bring AI into classrooms. States like Colorado have published K-12 AI Skills Progression Guides aligned with computer science standards. Utah launched an AI steering committee and hosts educator summits with stipends for lesson-plan development.

Yet even as policy catches up, the vision often lags. Ed-tech leaders see state policies still focused on tool management rather than a coherent vision for the workforce of the future. As one nonprofit leader put it: “The workforce isn’t at the center of the conversation yet, because truly nobody can describe the jobs of the future. And so it’s very hard to have a policy conversation about how we rethink the way we teach career pathways.”

He’s right – and wrong. We can’t predict specific jobs. But we can identify the skills that will matter: the ability to collaborate with AI as a partner, to direct rather than defer, to evaluate output rather than accept it. Those skills are teachable now.

The Equity Question We’re Not Asking

There’s a dimension to this debate that makes me uncomfortable – and should make you uncomfortable too.

If AI-enhanced learning is only available to students in well-funded districts, we risk widening educational inequalities rather than closing them. Independent schools pioneering AI integration may inadvertently increase the gap with under-resourced public schools. Students whose families can afford AI tutoring tools at home gain advantages that compound over time.

This isn’t hypothetical. The digital divide has already shown us how technology adoption without equity planning creates new forms of stratification. AI could be different – it could be the great equalizer, providing every student access to personalized instruction previously available only through expensive private tutoring. Or it could become the newest vector for inequality.

The school where I used to work prided itself on a curriculum philosophy they called #LifeReady. But so far, it’s still struggling with whether – let alone how – to embrace AI. My bottom line: you can’t be “life ready” while leaving neurodiverse students without adaptive tools, under-resourced schools without access to AI-enhanced learning, and all students without practice collaborating with the technology that will define their working lives.

Policymakers must prioritize making AI-driven learning tools accessible to all. Otherwise, the #LifeReady promise becomes #LifeReadyForSome.

From Tool to Teammate: What This Actually Looks Like

About fifteen years ago, I presented a bold proposal: we needed a computer science curriculum for Middle School. I envisioned it as a framework for teaching problem-solving, iteration, and design thinking – all the 21st-century skills students needed.

Fast forward to just before COVID. I went to our provost with a very different recommendation: we should sunset the Middle School CS program.

Why? Two reasons. First, if the real goal was problem-solving and iteration, those skills could be embedded across the curriculum, not siloed in a single course. Second – and more importantly – I had become convinced that coding itself was no longer the existential skill everyone assumed. AI was already on the horizon.

Some colleagues thought I was reckless. But look at the job market now:

  • CS graduate unemployment has risen to 7.8% in 2024–2025, more than double the rate from a decade ago.

  • Traditional software development postings are down nearly 17% year-over-year, as companies shift toward AI-enabled platforms that require fewer coders for the same output.

  • Demand for AI/ML-related roles has surged by 39%, especially in areas like data interpretation, AI integration, and human–machine collaboration.

  • 41% of CS graduates are underemployed, working in jobs that don’t require their degree.

This doesn’t mean computer science is obsolete. But it means that coding alone is no longer the existential skill. The new existential skill is the ability to work with AI as a collaborator: to prompt it, refine its ideas, and channel its strengths into creative, high-quality outcomes.

The P&G study underscores this point. The winning teams didn’t succeed because of their coding ability. AI doesn’t care where you put the semicolon. They succeeded because of their capacity to partner with AI as a teammate.

What AI Literacy Actually Requires

If AI is going to be a teammate, students must become fluent in AI literacy – the ability to understand what it can do, where it fails, and how to use it responsibly. That includes:

Prompt Engineering – crafting precise, detailed prompts to generate high-quality results. This is a form of metacognition: thinking carefully about what you want, what you know, and how to communicate both.

Bias Recognition – spotting and mitigating algorithmic or cultural biases in outputs. Students need to understand that AI systems reflect the data they were trained on, with all its historical inequities.

Source Verification – validating facts and tracing claims back to reliable origins. AI confidently produces plausible-sounding nonsense. Students must develop the epistemic humility and research skills to check.

Creative Collaboration – blending machine-generated ideas with original human thinking to produce stronger outcomes. This is not about using AI to replace thinking; it’s about using AI to extend it.

Ethical Reasoning – wrestling with questions of academic integrity, intellectual property, and the societal implications of human–machine work.

This is not an “extra.” It’s the new baseline for academic and workplace readiness. Just as digital literacy became essential in the internet era, AI literacy must become a core competency for every graduate.

A Day in the Life: 2035

Picture this:

A student starts their morning using AI to simulate the spread of a hypothetical virus across different countries, then collaborates with classmates to propose public health interventions.

In English, they use AI to generate multiple interpretations of a Shakespeare sonnet, then debate which one best captures the original intent.

In art, they co-create a short animated film with AI-generated storyboards, then refine character designs by hand.

A neurodiverse student uses AI-powered note-taking tools that summarize lectures in real time, generate practice quizzes, and provide multi-modal review options that match their learning preferences.

Throughout the day, all students log their AI interactions, noting which outputs they trusted, which they rejected, and why. Teachers use these logs to assess critical thinking, creativity, and ethical reasoning – not just the end product.

By graduation, they aren’t just AI users – they’re AI collaborators, equipped to enter a workforce where the best teammate might not be human.

The Real Choice

The next generation won’t be divided into those who “know the content” and those who don’t. It will be divided into those who can partner effectively with AI – and those who can’t.

If we want students to thrive, we must:

  1. Reevaluate curriculum to focus on skills that AI amplifies rather than replaces.

  2. Redesign assessments to measure higher-order thinking, creativity, and ethical judgment.

  3. Provide professional development so teachers can confidently integrate AI – not as an add-on, but as a partner.

  4. Ensure equitable access so AI-enhanced learning doesn’t become another vector for inequality.

  5. Build for neuroinclusion so that AI’s adaptive capabilities serve every learner, not just the neurotypical majority.

  6. Model responsible AI use at every level of the school system.

Banning AI might feel protective in the short term. But in the long term, it risks producing graduates who are underprepared for reality – and it denies neurodiverse students tools that could finally let them show what they’re capable of.

The choice isn’t between protecting students from AI or abandoning them to it. The choice is between teaching them to direct AI or leaving them to defer to it.

One path leads to obsolescence. The other leads to opportunity.

Matt Goode is a “retired” educator with 20 years experience in the classroom. He specializes in neuroinclusive leadership development. He works with founders, school leaders, and technical teams on organizational systems and psychological safety. His Neuroinclusive Leader essay series is available on Substack.

title: Building the Neuroinclusive Organization – From Systems to Culture
subtitle: Essay 8: Neurodiversity Series
html:
About six months into working with a fast-growth startup, I watched the CEO do something I’d never seen before.

He pulled up a spreadsheet during a leadership offsite – not a revenue model or a hiring plan, but a cognitive diversity map.

It showed each team’s composition: how many explorer brains vs. exploiter brains, how many verbal processors vs. written processors, how many people thrived in ambiguity vs. those who needed structure to perform.

“We used to hire for ‘culture fit,’” he said. “Then we realized we were just hiring people who thought like us. And we kept hitting the same blind spots.”

So they redesigned.

Not by lowering standards. Not by “accommodating” neurodivergent employees as an afterthought.

By treating cognitive diversity as a strategic composition principle – the same way they thought about skill diversity, experience diversity, and domain expertise.

They stopped asking, “Can this person succeed in our system?”

They started asking, “What problems require this cognitive profile to solve effectively?”

Here’s what changed in six months:

Innovation cycle time: 8 weeks → 5 weeks (explorer brains now owned early-stage R&D without being forced into execution modes that killed their momentum)

Quality escapes: 12 per quarter → 2 per quarter (exploiter brains now owned quality gates without being pressured to “move faster”)

Strategic blind spots caught: Previously 0 caught before crisis → Now 7 identified and mitigated early (pattern-detectors finally had pathways to surface risks without being labeled “negative”)

Attrition of top performers: 40% annually → 8% annually (neurodivergent talent stopped burning out from camouflage requirements)

The results weren’t subtle.

Not because they got nicer.

Because they got smarter about how different brains complement each other.

That’s when I realized: the future of work isn’t accommodations.

It’s performance-centric talent design where cognitive diversity is an explicit strategy – not a compliance box to check.

And building that requires redesigning three levels: hiring, team composition, and leadership development.

We’ve explored how organizations are built around neurological fiction. We’ve matched cognitive profiles to organizational problems. We’ve tuned CREATE, navigated friction with 6C, and learned to shift gears with VOICES. We’ve designed neuroinclusive workflows. Now we arrive at the synthesis question: How do you build an entire organization – from hiring to leadership – around these principles? Not as a pilot program or a diversity initiative, but as the operating system itself?

Level 1: Neuroinclusive Hiring

Let’s start at the beginning – because if your hiring process filters out cognitive difference before it ever contributes, nothing downstream will fix it.

The Current Broken System

Job descriptions full of neurotypical proxies:

  • “Excellent communication skills.” Translation: you process verbally in real-time and perform charisma on demand.

  • “Team player.” Translation: you socialize the way we socialize and enjoy the collaboration formats we’ve normalized.

  • “Culture fit.” Translation: you think, talk, and process information the same way we do.

None of these measure competence. They measure cognitive conformity.

Interviews that assess social performance over actual work:

  • “Tell me about a time when you demonstrated leadership.”

  • “How would you handle conflict with a difficult teammate?”

  • “Where do you see yourself in five years?”

These questions don’t surface problem-solving ability. They surface storytelling fluency under social pressure – a skill that has nothing to do with whether someone can architect systems, write clean code, or design elegant solutions.

For neurodivergent candidates – especially autistic professionals who struggle with real-time social performance – these interviews are cognitive minefields.

They’re being assessed on their ability to perform neurotypicality, not their ability to do the job.

The Neuroinclusive Redesign

Job descriptions specify cognitive requirements, not credentialing proxies:

Before: “Excellent communication skills”

After: “Ability to document technical decisions clearly in writing and provide context for choices made”

That’s specific. That’s measurable. And it doesn’t assume one processing style.

Someone who writes exceptional documentation but struggles with small talk? They meet the requirement.

Someone who’s charismatic in meetings but can’t document their thinking? They don’t.

You’ve just screened for actual job competence instead of neurotypical performance.

Before/After: Senior Engineer Role

Before job description:

  • Excellent communication skills

  • Strong team player

  • Must thrive in fast-paced environment

  • Culture fit essential

Result: 3 great autistic candidates self-select out. You never see their résumés.

After job description:

  • Documents technical decisions with clear rationale (written)

  • Collaborates through code reviews, design docs, and async discussion

  • Delivers projects on time with measurable quality standards

  • Cognitive requirement: Pattern recognition, systems thinking, detail orientation

Result: Those same 3 candidates apply. One becomes your best systems architect.

Interviews assess actual work, not social performance:

Work samples over behavioral questions. “Here’s a problem. Show me how you’d solve it.”

Asynchronous challenges over real-time pressure tests. “Here’s a case study. Take 48 hours. Send us your analysis.”

Multiple interview formats. Some candidates interview best live. Some interview best in writing. Some need to show you the work, not tell you about it. Offer all three.

Skill demonstrations over “Tell me about a time when...” Stop asking people to perform past competence through narrative. Let them demonstrate current competence through work.

Before/After: Interview Process

Before: 4 rounds of behavioral interviews. “Tell me about a time you demonstrated leadership under pressure.”

Result: Autistic candidate freezes. Can’t access examples in real-time. Appears “not ready for senior role.” You pass.

After: Round 1: Async case study (48 hours). Round 2: Work sample review. Round 3: Technical depth discussion with pre-shared questions. Round 4: Team fit conversation focused on work style preferences.

Result: Same candidate submits brilliant case study analysis. Demonstrates exceptional systems thinking. Gets hired. Becomes top performer within 6 months.

Framework connection:

Culture: Make hiring norms explicit and documented. If “culture fit” is part of your process, define it in behavioral terms. What does it actually mean? And make sure it’s measuring contribution, not cognitive conformity.

Relationships: Clarify “who decides” in the hiring process. Is this a consensus decision? A hiring manager call? A Core Expertise decision from the team lead? Ambiguity creates anxiety – especially for neurodivergent candidates trying to navigate an already-stressful process.

Ethics: Protect cognitive diversity as a value, not a legal checkbox. Stop treating neurodivergent hiring as compliance. Start treating it as competitive advantage.

Level 2: Neuroinclusive Team Design

Hiring is just the beginning.

If you hire one neurodivergent person into a neurotypical system and don’t redesign the collaboration norms, you haven’t built inclusion.

You’ve just set someone up to burn out.

The Current Broken System

Teams built for “culture fit” homogeneity:

Everyone processes the same way. Everyone communicates the same way. Everyone works the same hours, thrives in the same meeting formats, and regulates in the same environments.

It feels efficient – until you realize you’re solving the same problems the same way and missing everything outside your cognitive frame.

Collaboration modes assume neurotypical processing:

Real-time brainstorms. Open-plan offices. Stand-up meetings. Popcorn sharing. All designed for brains that think out loud, process quickly, and thrive in social environments.

If your brain doesn’t work that way, you’re not “less collaborative.” You’re just being asked to collaborate in a format that suppresses your capacity.

Conflict treated as personality clash, not cognitive friction:

When the ADHD product manager and the autistic engineer disagree, it’s not a personality problem. It’s a speed vs. precision collision that needs a navigation protocol, not a performance improvement plan.

The Neuroinclusive Redesign

Cognitive diversity as a composition principle:

Deliberately mix explorer and exploiter brains.

Map team cognitive profiles the same way you’d map CliftonStrengths or technical skills.

Ask: Do we have pattern-detectors? Do we have systems-thinkers? Do we have big-picture strategists? Do we have kinetic innovators?

If everyone on the team thinks the same way, you don’t have diversity. You have an echo chamber with different résumés.

Before/After: Product Team Composition

Before: 5 verbal processors, all neurotypical, all hired for “culture fit”

Result: Fast execution on known problems. Zero breakthrough innovation. Blind to structural risks. One major quality failure costs $400K.

After: 2 explorer brains (ADHD, dyslexic), 2 exploiter brains (autistic, detail-oriented), 1 bridge brain (can translate between modes)

Result: Explorer brains identify 3 new market opportunities. Exploiter brains catch 5 structural flaws before shipping. Quality failure rate drops to near-zero. Revenue from new opportunities: $2.1M in 12 months.

Role clarity mapped to cognitive strengths:

Stop forcing cognitive mismatch.

Put autistic professionals in systems architecture, quality control, pattern detection – roles where precision compounds and structural integrity matters.

Put dyslexic thinkers in strategy, crisis navigation, client storytelling – roles where big-picture synthesis and narrative thinking drive value.

Put ADHD brains in innovation, rapid prototyping, novelty detection – roles where momentum is the resource and experimentation is the mode.

Then let them collaborate across their differences instead of fighting their wiring.

Collaboration protocols that don’t assume uniform processing:

Async options for all “collaborative” work. Stop treating real-time as the default. Make it the exception.

Multiple ways to contribute: written, verbal, visual. All count.

Explicit norms about response time, meeting purpose, decision authority. Don’t make people reverse-engineer the invisible rules.

Framework connection:

6C: Use the Decision Compass to navigate cognitive friction.

When precision brain and speed brain collide → Consultative mode (speed brain decides timing, precision brain provides quality gates).

When verbal processor and written processor collide → Choice mode (set the outcome, let people choose their path).

When expert and generalist collide → Core Expertise mode (domain authority decides).

You’re not eliminating friction. You’re designing protocols that turn friction into complementarity.

VOICES: Team design requires Sculptor gear. You’re not coaching individuals to adapt. You’re architecting the container that holds cognitive diversity.

Level 3: Neuroinclusive Leadership Development

Here’s where most organizations stall.

They hire neurodivergent talent. They redesign some workflows. They create Slack channels for async communication.

But they never train leaders to actually lead neurodivergent teams.

And without that, the whole system reverts to neurotypical defaults the moment pressure hits.

What’s missing isn’t good intentions. It’s leadership capacity.

CREATE Model Integration

Teach leaders to tune each CREATE cylinder for cognitive diversity.

  • Culture: Make invisible norms visible. Document “how we do things here.” Eliminate the decoding tax.

  • Relationships: Eliminate ambiguous decision rights. Use RACI. Make “who owns what” structurally explicit.

  • Execution: Offer process flexibility. Focus on outcomes, not conformity. Let people choose their workflow.

  • Agility: Build transition buffers. Give advance notice. Stop treating “moving fast” as synonymous with “pivoting without warning.”

  • Teaching: Adapt feedback to processing style. Ask people how they learn best – then honor it.

  • Ethics: Protect cognitive difference. Measure impact, not optics. Challenge “culture fit” as promotion criteria.

When leaders can tune each cylinder for cognitive diversity, you’re not accommodating neurodivergence.

You’re activating it as organizational capacity.

VOICES Development

Train leaders to recognize which gear neurodivergent employees need.

Build Sculptor capacity as the primary neuroinclusive gear. Before you Coach an individual, check if the system needs redesign.

Practice gear-shifting based on cognitive load, not just task type.

High cognitive load (transitions, crises, ambiguity) → Shift to Operator (clarity) or Sculptor (redesign the stressor).

Low cognitive load (steady state, routine work) → Shift to Coach (growth) or Encourager (recognition).

Before/After: Leadership Response to Performance Issue

Before: “Your autistic engineer seems disengaged in sprint planning. Coach her on speaking up more.”

Result: Engineer spends cognitive budget performing engagement. Code quality drops. She starts job searching.

After: Leader recognizes system problem, shifts to Sculptor gear. Adds async sprint planning option. Engineer contributes brilliant written analysis that redesigns entire sprint approach. Engagement problem disappears.

CliftonStrengths Integration

For leaders who already use strengths-based frameworks, there’s a natural integration point.

CliftonStrengths – when used carefully – can proxy for cognitive operating systems without requiring disclosure or diagnosis. This is especially valuable because it:

  • Gives people agency over how they describe their thinking

  • Removes the clinical/deficit framing

  • Provides language many organizations already use

  • Lets people opt in to cognitive diversity conversations on their own terms

Here’s how strengths themes often map to neurodivergent cognitive styles:

Autistic-style processing often shows up as:

  • High Analytical: Pattern recognition, systematic thinking, data-driven decisions

  • High Deliberative: Risk assessment, careful consideration, quality control

  • High Consistency: Fairness through systems, rule clarity, structural integrity

  • High Discipline: Process excellence, routine mastery, predictable execution

What this means for leadership: These individuals thrive in Core Expertise and Command decision modes. Give them clear systems, explicit expectations, and roles where precision compounds. Don’t force them to “be more spontaneous” or “go with the flow” – that’s fighting their cognitive operating system.

ADHD-style processing often shows up as:

  • High Ideation: Novel connections, creative problem-solving, generative thinking

  • High Activator: Momentum-driven, urgency as resource, kinetic ideation

  • High Adaptability: Pivots easily, thrives in flux, responds to immediate demands

  • High Maximizer: Optimization through iteration, excellence through experimentation

What this means for leadership: These individuals thrive in Choice decision modes. Set the outcome, provide guardrails, then get out of their way. They need autonomy to activate hyperfocus. Rigid process-heavy work will disengage them – not because they’re “not committed,” but because their brain needs movement to think.

Dyslexic-style processing often shows up as:

  • High Strategic: Big-picture synthesis, pattern detection across domains, seeing 10 steps ahead

  • High Futuristic: Vision-casting, possibility thinking, narrative strategy

  • High Connectedness: Systems thinking, relational mapping, holistic understanding

  • High Context: Meaning-making through story, historical pattern recognition

What this means for leadership: These individuals thrive in Consultative and Collaborative modes where they can talk through strategy. Their brilliance emerges through verbal synthesis, not written analysis. Don’t ask them to “document everything first” – let them think out loud, then capture the insights.

Anxiety-driven processing (often co-occurring with neurodivergence) shows up as:

  • High Deliberative: Risk modeling, scenario planning, anticipating failure modes

  • High Responsibility: Accountability, follow-through, completing what’s started

  • High Restorative: Problem detection, fixing what’s broken, preventing recurrence

  • High Consistency: Fairness, equity, protecting against harm

What this means for leadership: These individuals thrive in Consultative mode where their risk assessment is explicitly gathered as input rather than dismissed as “negativity.” Their threat modeling prevents disasters – if you create space for it.

How to use this in practice:

  1. Review your team’s CliftonStrengths reports through a cognitive diversity lens. Look for patterns. Do you have too many Analytical + Deliberative profiles and zero Ideation + Activator? You might be over-indexed on exploitation and under-indexed on exploration.

  2. Use strengths language to design roles and collaboration. Instead of saying “Sarah is autistic, so she needs structure,” you can say “Sarah is high Analytical + Deliberative, so she owns quality architecture while Mark’s high Ideation + Activator means he scouts new opportunities.” Same outcome, more agency for Sarah.

  3. Map decision friction to strengths collisions. When high Activator (momentum-driven) collides with high Deliberative (risk-aware), that’s not personality conflict – that’s speed vs. precision. Use 6C Consultative: Activator decides timing, Deliberative provides quality gates.

  4. Don’t weaponize strengths to avoid neurodiversity conversations. The integration point isn’t “we don’t need to talk about neurodivergence because we have strengths.” It’s “strengths gives us a shared language to design around cognitive difference without requiring disclosure.”

Important caveat: Not all high Analytical people are autistic. Not all high Activator people have ADHD. Strengths are descriptive, not diagnostic. Use them as design inputs for how people think, not as labels for who they are. The goal is to create systems where everyone can work in their cognitive sweet spot – whether or not they ever name neurodivergence explicitly.

Neuroinclusive Leadership as Core Competency

Here’s the shift that has to happen:

Neuroinclusive leadership isn’t a specialization.

It’s the baseline competency for leading in complexity.

Because cognitive diversity isn’t just about fairness. It’s about adaptive capacity.

Homogeneous teams execute efficiently within known parameters. But they can’t see disruption coming from outside their frame. They optimize – but they don’t innovate.

Cognitively diverse teams are messier. They have more friction. They require better systems.

But they see more. They solve different kinds of problems. They adapt faster when the terrain shifts.

And the organizations that figure this out first won’t just access untapped talent.

They’ll build systems that hold their shape without dependency on heroic leadership.

The Deepest Truth

Here’s what I’ve come to understand after years of coaching leaders through this work:

Your CREATE, VOICES, and 6C frameworks were already neuroinclusive.

You didn’t build them for personality dependence. You built them for system design.

They work for neurodivergent teams because they eliminate the two things neurodivergent professionals struggle with most: ambiguity and heroic leadership.

CREATE makes culture explicit, relationships clear, execution flexible, agility structured, teaching adaptive, and ethics protective.

VOICES gives leaders multiple gears so they’re not forcing every brain through the same leadership stance.

6C makes decision authority visible so people don’t have to decode invisible hierarchies through social cues.

When all three frameworks integrate, something powerful happens:

You’re not accommodating cognitive difference.

You’re designing intelligent infrastructure that lets every brain contribute without camouflage.

Framework Connection: Full Integration

CREATE Engine

When all six cylinders fire for cognitive diversity, neurodivergence stops being a “thing to manage” and becomes organizational capacity.

  • Culture creates belonging without requiring masking.

  • Relationships eliminate social navigation through structural clarity.

  • Execution measures outcomes, not optics.

  • Agility builds transition buffers instead of rewarding instant adaptation.

  • Teaching tailors feedback to processing style.

  • Ethics protects the right to work differently.

VOICES Gearbox

Sculptor becomes your primary neuroinclusive gear – because systemic barriers require systemic redesign, not individual coaching.

But you need all six gears to lead neurodivergent teams through complexity:

  • Visionary with milestones (big picture + structure).

  • Operator with autonomy (process options, not mandates).

  • Inclusive with multiple input channels (async + sync).

  • Coach tailored to processing style (written, verbal, narrative).

  • Encourager celebrating outcomes (not performance of normalcy).

  • Sculptor redesigning systems (not forcing adaptation).

6C Compass

Eliminates the decision ambiguity that creates anxiety and masking.

Different cognitive styles thrive in different decision modes – so offer the full range.

  • Autistic brains → Core Expertise and Command (clarity reduces anxiety).

  • ADHD brains → Choice (autonomy activates hyperfocus).

  • Dyslexic brains → Consultative (talk it through before deciding).

  • Anxiety-driven brains → Collaborative with structure (inclusion without chaos).

Three Diagnostic Questions

Before we move to implementation, three questions to surface where your leadership capacity needs development:

1. If your top performer processes information differently than you do, would you recognize their excellence – or coach them to “improve their presence”?

This reveals whether you’re measuring impact or measuring cognitive conformity. If the answer makes you uncomfortable, you’re probably optimizing for the latter.

2. When you lose neurodivergent talent, do you blame the person – or audit the system?

If your exit interview says “not a culture fit” or “struggled with collaboration,” ask: Did they struggle, or did our collaboration design filter them out? The first is a people problem. The second is a system problem.

3. Can you name which CREATE cylinder is misfiring for neurodivergent employees on your team right now?

If you can’t, you’re not yet thinking systemically. And if you’re not thinking systemically, you’re still trying to coach individuals into broken systems – which means you’re still stuck in two gears.

The Neuroinclusive Systems Audit

You’ve now seen the full architecture – hiring, team design, leadership development, and how CREATE, VOICES, and 6C integrate. Here’s how you diagnose where your organization stands.

Run this audit not as a compliance exercise but as a strategic assessment of where cognitive capacity is being unlocked versus suppressed.

Hiring

  • [ ] Do job descriptions specify cognitive requirements or neurotypical proxies?

  • [ ] Do interviews assess work or social performance?

  • [ ] Is “culture fit” actually “brain type fit”?

Team Design

  • [ ] Is cognitive diversity a composition principle?

  • [ ] Are collaboration modes flexible or mandatory?

  • [ ] Is role clarity explicit enough to eliminate social navigation?

Workflow

  • [ ] Can people contribute asynchronously?

  • [ ] Are sensory needs honored without stigma?

  • [ ] Do we measure outcomes or “presence”?

Leadership

  • [ ] Can leaders name which CREATE cylinder is misfiring for neurodivergent employees?

  • [ ] Do leaders use all six VOICES gears or default to 1-2?

  • [ ] Do leaders make 6C decision modes explicit?

Culture

  • [ ] Can neurodivergent employees succeed without masking?

  • [ ] Are invisible norms made visible?

  • [ ] Is cognitive difference protected as a right, not accommodated as a burden?

The 90-Day Neuroinclusive Transformation Roadmap

If you’re ready to move from awareness to architecture, here’s the path:

Month 1: Audit + Awareness

Run the Neuroinclusive Systems Audit.

Identify which CREATE cylinders misfire for neurodivergent employees.

Map current decision friction using the 6C framework.

Month 2: Design + Pilot

Redesign one high-friction system (meetings, feedback, or hiring).

Train leaders on VOICES gear-shifting for cognitive diversity.

Pilot neuroinclusive workflow on one team.

Month 3: Scale + Embed

Document what worked. Iterate what didn’t.

Embed neuroinclusive practices into the CREATE operating system.

Build neuroinclusive leadership capacity into ongoing development.

What success looks like:

  • Month 1: You can name which systems create cognitive friction and for whom

  • Month 2: One team reports reduced masking and increased contribution quality

  • Month 3: Leaders can shift gears based on cognitive load, not just their comfort zone

This isn’t a one-time initiative.

It’s a systems redesign that compounds over time.

There’s no such thing as a neutral organization.

Just systems designed for some brains and not others.

The question isn’t whether you can build neuroinclusive infrastructure.

It’s whether you’re willing to admit that the systems you’ve normalized as “best practices” might just be cognitive preferences that got mistaken for universal standards.

And once you see that, you can’t unsee it.

You can redesign.

You can build systems that unlock capacity instead of suppressing it.

You can create organizations where cognitive difference isn’t tolerated – it’s leveraged.

Because the teams that figure this out won’t just be more inclusive.

They’ll be more resilient, more adaptive, and more capable of solving the problems that cognitively homogeneous teams keep missing.

This is the work. Not because it’s morally correct – though it is. Not because it’s legally required – though in some contexts it will be. But because the future belongs to organizations that can hold cognitive complexity without flattening it.

And you now have the frameworks to build that organization.

The question is whether you’ll use them.

Neuroinclusive Organization Self-Assessment

Rate your agreement with each statement on a scale of 1-5: (1 = Strongly Disagree, 5 = Strongly Agree)

1. Our hiring process screens for actual job competence rather than neurotypical performance (communication style, culture fit, interview charisma).

  • 1 = Performance-focused / 2 = Mostly performance / 3 = Mixed / 4 = Mostly competence / 5 = Competence-focused

2. We deliberately design team composition for cognitive diversity (explorer/exploiter, verbal/written, structure/ambiguity) as a strategic principle.

  • 1 = Homogeneous / 2 = Mostly homogeneous / 3 = Some diversity / 4 = Deliberate mixing / 5 = Strategic composition

3. Leaders can tune all six CREATE cylinders for cognitive diversity and recognize which cylinder is misfiring for neurodivergent team members.

  • 1 = Cannot tune / 2 = Limited tuning / 3 = Some tuning / 4 = Regular tuning / 5 = Systematic tuning

4. Leaders regularly shift between all six VOICES gears based on cognitive needs, not just their comfort zone (especially Sculptor for system redesign).

  • 1 = Stuck in 1-2 / 2 = Use 2-3 / 3 = Use 3-4 / 4 = Use 4-5 / 5 = Use all 6 fluidly

5. We use the 6C Decision Compass to navigate cognitive friction (speed vs. precision, verbal vs. written) rather than labeling it as “personality conflict.”

  • 1 = Never / 2 = Rarely / 3 = Sometimes / 4 = Usually / 5 = Always

Scoring Guide:

20-25 points: You’re building neuroinclusive infrastructure systematically. Consider: How can you scale these practices across the organization? What would it take to make this your default operating system?

15-19 points: You’re implementing neuroinclusive practices but likely have gaps. Consider: Which level (hiring, team design, leadership development) needs the most work?

10-14 points: You’re aware of neuroinclusive principles but still relying on accommodation vs. architecture. Consider: Run the Neuroinclusive Systems Audit above – which area has the most checkboxes unchecked?

5-9 points: Your organization is likely optimized for one brain type. Consider: Start with the 90-day roadmap – Month 1 is audit and awareness.

Next Steps Based on Your Score:

If you scored 15+:

  • Document your neuroinclusive practices systematically

  • Train other leaders in your organization on CREATE + VOICES + 6C integration

  • Measure: Can you quantify the ROI of reduced masking and increased contribution?

If you scored 10-14:

  • Pick one level to redesign: hiring, team composition, or leadership development

  • Use the 90-day roadmap: Audit → Design → Pilot → Scale

  • Start with highest-friction area (usually meetings or hiring)

If you scored below 10:

  • Begin with leadership training: Can your leaders name the six CREATE cylinders and six VOICES gears?

  • Redesign one job description: Remove neurotypical proxies, add cognitive requirements

  • Add async option to one recurring meeting and measure contribution quality change

Regardless of score: The frameworks you need – CREATE, VOICES, 6C – are already designed for cognitive diversity. They eliminate ambiguity, protect multiple processing styles, and make leadership scalable. The question isn’t whether to adopt new frameworks. It’s whether to use the ones you have for their highest purpose: building organizations where every brain can contribute without camouflage.

The business case is clear.

Organizations that get neuroinclusive leadership right reduce attrition, catch blind spots earlier, and build systems that don’t depend on heroic leadership.

I’ve spent 20 years coaching leaders through this work—from independent schools to USAID to tech startups. I have the complete diagnostic tools, the frameworks, and the implementation roadmaps. But let’s start simple.

title: Designing Work for Different Brains — The Neuroinclusive Workflow
subtitle: Essay 7: Neurodiversity Series
html:
I was sitting in a conference room watching a senior product designer – brilliant, award-winning, the kind of talent companies fight over – get performance-managed out of an organization.

Not for poor work. Her designs were exceptional.

Not for missing deadlines. She shipped early, consistently.

The issue, according to her manager, was “engagement.”

She didn’t speak up enough in meetings. She worked with headphones on most of the day. She declined optional social events. She preferred Slack over Zoom. She asked for written agendas before discussions and often sent her thoughts via email afterward instead of contributing in real time.

“She’s just not collaborative,” the manager said.

I asked to see her work.

It was some of the best design thinking I’d seen in years – thoughtful, user-centered, systematically rigorous. Her async contributions in shared docs were thorough, insightful, often the thing that unstuck the team when they’d been circling the same problem for days.

But none of that mattered.

Because the performance that counted wasn’t the work.

It was the performance of engagement in formats the organization had decided were “professional.”

Real-time presence. Vocal participation. Visible enthusiasm. The aesthetics of collaboration.

She could do exceptional work quietly – or she could perform collaboration loudly.

The system had decided only one of those was leadership material.

Here’s what actually happened next: I asked the CEO to run an experiment. Keep her performance metrics (quality, timeliness, impact) exactly the same. But stop measuring “engagement” in meetings. Instead, count her async contributions in shared docs as collaboration.

Three months later, she’d contributed to four major product decisions that wouldn’t have happened without her input. But in the old system, none of that would have counted – because it didn’t happen in real time, in front of people, with visible enthusiasm.

That’s when I asked the question that shifted the conversation:

“What if the system is the problem – not the person?”

Because here’s the thing about “reasonable accommodations”:

The phrase itself presumes the system is fine and the person needs adjustment.

But what if the system was never neutral to begin with?

What if the workflows, the meeting structures, the performance norms we’ve institutionalized as “best practices” are just cognitive preferences that got mistaken for universal standards?

We’ve mapped how organizations are built around a neurological fiction. We’ve explored how different cognitive profiles solve different problems. We’ve tuned the CREATE engine, navigated decision friction with 6C, and learned to shift leadership gears with VOICES. Now we arrive at the design question that makes all of it operational: How do we actually structure work so different brains can contribute without camouflage?

From Accommodation to Architecture

The dominant frame for neurodiversity at work is accommodation.

Someone discloses. HR approves adjustments. The person gets noise-canceling headphones, a quieter desk, permission to skip some meetings.

It’s well-intentioned.

But it’s still operating from a deficit model.

The message – implicit but unmistakable – is: The system is correct. You need help fitting into it.

And every “accommodation” reinforces that framing.

But here’s what happens when you shift from accommodation to universal design:

You stop asking, “How do we help this person succeed despite their brain?”

You start asking, “How do we design work so all brains can contribute without camouflage?”

Because universal design principles – borrowed from architecture, adapted to knowledge work – don’t create special exceptions.

They create better defaults.

Curb cuts were designed for wheelchairs. But they help parents with strollers, travelers with luggage, delivery workers with carts. They make the system work better for everyone, not just the people who needed them most.

The same logic applies to neuroinclusive workflows.

Async-first communication doesn’t just help autistic employees who need processing time. It helps parents managing school pickup, global teams across time zones, anyone who thinks more clearly in writing than in real-time speech.

Explicit decision rights don’t just reduce anxiety for neurodivergent professionals. They eliminate ambiguity for everyone – especially new hires, remote workers, and anyone navigating a complex org structure.

Outcome-focused performance doesn’t just protect ADHD employees who work in bursts. It raises the bar for everyone by making results – not optics – the measure that matters.

This isn’t about making work easier.

It’s about making work accessible to more kinds of intelligence.

And when you do that, you don’t just include more people.

You unlock capacity you didn’t know you were missing.

The Five Neuroinclusive Workflow Design Principles

Let’s make this concrete.

These aren’t accommodations. They’re architecture.

1. Asynchronous-First Communication

Why it matters:

Real-time communication favors brains that process verbally, quickly, and socially. But some of the best thinking happens slowly, in writing, alone.

For autistic and anxious processors especially, async communication isn’t a workaround – it’s how they access their full cognitive capacity. The pressure to respond in real time splits attention between what to say and how to say it without misreading social cues. Remove that pressure, and suddenly the depth is available.

But this benefits everyone.

Async communication creates a written record. It respects different time zones. It lets people contribute during their peak cognitive hours instead of during the scheduled meeting slot.

It turns “being responsive” into “producing thoughtful input” – which is what actually moves work forward.

Before/After:

Before: Daily standups require everyone to report verbally. The pattern-detector who needs time to synthesize stays silent. The fast-talker dominates. Decisions get made without the deepest thinking.

After: Standup prompts posted in Slack 24 hours ahead. People contribute live OR async within 24 hours. Both count equally. The pattern-detector contributes a written analysis that shifts the entire sprint direction – something that never would have surfaced in the 15-minute live meeting.

How to build it:

Default to written updates. Use Slack threads, shared docs, recorded video walkthroughs.

Make synchronous meetings the exception, not the rule. Reserve real-time for decisions that genuinely require live debate – not for information that could’ve been a memo.

Create norms: “We respond within 24 hours, not 24 minutes.” “Meetings have agendas sent 48 hours in advance.” “You can contribute live or async – both count.”

Framework connection:

This is Execution cylinder work. You’re redesigning how work flows – and shifting from measuring real-time performance to measuring outcomes.

2. Multiple Input Channels

Why it matters:

Different brains process differently.

Some think by talking. Some think by writing. Some think spatially and need to draw it. Some think kinetically and need to move while they process.

If your collaboration design only recognizes one mode – usually verbal, real-time discussion – you’ve just filtered out every brain that works differently.

And you don’t even know what you’re missing, because those ideas never made it into the room.

Before/After:

Before: Strategy session = whiteboard brainstorm. Verbal processors dominate. Written processors stay quiet or force themselves to “participate” in a format that suppresses their thinking. Best ideas never surface.

After: Strategy session = three pathways: (1) Live discussion for verbal processors, (2) Shared doc for written processors, (3) Visual board for spatial thinkers. Synthesis happens after all three contribute. The written processor’s risk analysis prevents a $2M mistake. The spatial thinker’s diagram becomes the new product architecture.

How to build it:

Offer pre-reads before meetings so people can process the content before the discussion.

Provide written summaries after so people who couldn’t track the conversation in real time can still integrate the outcome.

Use visual dashboards so people who think spatially can see the system at a glance.

Let people choose their mode: contribute live, contribute in writing, contribute via recorded video. All three are valid.

Framework connection:

This is Inclusive gear in action. You’re not just inviting everyone to participate – you’re designing systems where all voices can contribute in their native mode.

3. Explicit Clarity Rituals

Why it matters:

Ambiguity is cognitively expensive – especially for autistic professionals who struggle with implicit social cues and anxiety-driven brains who spiral in uncertainty.

“We’ll figure it out as we go” feels empowering to some. To others, it feels like being asked to navigate without a map.

And every moment spent reverse-engineering “who decides this?” is a moment not spent doing the work.

Before/After:

Before: “We all own this project.” Translation: no one knows who decides what. The autistic engineer spends hours trying to figure out if she’s allowed to make technical decisions. She’s paralyzed by ambiguity. The project stalls.

After: RACI for every project. Decision log after every major decision. The engineer sees “Technical architecture = Core Expertise (Engineering Lead)” and moves forward confidently. Project ships two weeks early because no one’s spending cognitive budget on social decoding.

How to build it:

Decision logs. After every major decision, document: What was decided? Who decided? Why? What’s next?

Visible priorities. Not just OKRs in a slide deck – live dashboards that show what’s in flight, what’s blocked, what’s next.

Documented “who owns what.” Use RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) for every project. Eliminate “we all own it” ambiguity.

Framework connection:

This makes decision authority visible without forcing people to ask. It eliminates the social decoding tax and lets people focus on contributing their expertise instead of navigating invisible hierarchies. This is 6C in practice – making decision modes explicit so people know where they stand.

4. Sensory Flexibility

Why it matters:

Open offices are productivity theater.

They look collaborative. But for many neurodivergent brains – especially autistic and ADHD professionals – they’re sensory assault.

Fluorescent lights. Ambient noise. Visual chaos. Unpredictable interruptions. The constant hum of other people’s conversations.

For neurotypical employees, these might be minor irritations. For neurodivergent employees, they’re constant cognitive drains. Every moment spent managing sensory input is a moment not spent thinking.

And the compounding effect over eight hours? Exhaustion that looks like disengagement but is actually just overload.

Before/After:

Before: Open office. Mandatory in-person attendance. The autistic analyst produces decent work but seems “disengaged” by 2pm. Manager assumes motivation problem.

After: Quiet zones with booking system. Remote work option 2 days/week. Headphone norms (”headphones = focus mode, not antisocial”). Same analyst now produces exceptional work consistently because she’s not burning cognitive budget on sensory management. Promotion follows.

How to build it:

Quiet zones with booking systems. Let people work in silence when they need to focus.

Movement options. Standing desks. Walking meetings. Permission to pace while on calls.

Headphone norms. Normalize “headphones on = focus mode, not antisocial behavior.”

Lighting control. Dimmable lights. Windows. Let people adjust their sensory environment.

Framework connection:

This is Culture cylinder work. Because belonging doesn’t mean “can you socialize here?” It means “can you regulate here?”

Can your nervous system settle enough to do your best work – or is the environment itself a barrier?

5. Outcome-Focused Performance

Why it matters:

Process conformity punishes cognitive difference.

If your performance reviews measure “executive presence,” “visibility,” “enthusiasm,” or “collaboration style,” you’re not measuring work quality.

You’re measuring how well someone performs neurotypicality.

And every time you penalize someone for working differently – even when their outcomes are exceptional – you’re teaching them that camouflage is more valuable than contribution.

Before/After:

Before: Performance review: “Strong technical skills, but needs to work on visibility and speaking up in meetings.” Translation: your work is excellent but you don’t perform engagement the way we recognize it. No promotion.

After: Performance review redesigned: “Impact: Led three critical system redesigns that improved reliability 40%. Quality: Zero production incidents in 18 months. Collaboration: Provides thorough async analysis that catches edge cases others miss.” Result: Promotion based on actual contribution, not performance of charisma.

How to build it:

Judge deliverables, not optics.

Does the work meet the standard? Did they move the project forward? Did they solve the problem?

If yes, stop docking them for “not looking engaged enough in the standup.”

Separate impact from style. Leadership has many faces. Execution has many modes. Stop requiring just one.

Framework connection:

This is Ethics cylinder work. You’re protecting the right to work differently – not as a favor, but as a design principle.

The Explorer vs. Exploiter Model Applied to Role Design

These five principles redesign how work flows. But there’s a deeper design question: how do we match people to roles based on their cognitive operating system? That’s where the explorer/exploiter model becomes essential.

Here’s where cognitive neuroscience meets org design.

There’s a model in evolutionary psychology – explorer vs. exploiter – that maps beautifully onto neurodivergent cognitive styles.

Some brains are wired for exploration:

Scanning horizons. Detecting patterns across domains. Navigating uncertainty. Thriving in novelty. Seeing possibilities others miss.

These are often dyslexic and ADHD brains – the ones who get bored in stable systems, who start experimenting before the data says it’s safe, who connect ideas no one else thought to put together.

Other brains are wired for exploitation:

Precision. Consistency. Deep-system optimization. Quality control that doesn’t fatigue. Turning ambiguity into clarity through rigorous process.

These are often autistic and detail-oriented brains – the ones who see structural flaws, who build systems that scale, who make sure the innovation doesn’t break when it hits production.

Both are essential.

Explorers find new territory. Exploiters make it livable.

But here’s where most organizations fail:

They force explorers to exploit – putting ADHD brains in repetitive, process-heavy roles and wondering why they disengage.

And they force exploiters to explore – putting autistic brains in ambiguous, rapidly-shifting contexts and wondering why they struggle.

The turn:

Stop forcing cognitive mismatch.

Design roles that match cognitive operating systems.

Put explorer brains in R&D, strategy, business development – domains where novelty is the resource and pattern-detection across uncertainty is the skill.

Put exploiter brains in systems architecture, quality assurance, operations – domains where precision compounds and structural integrity matters more than speed.

Then let them collaborate across their differences instead of fighting against their wiring.

Concrete example:

Product team redesign: Explorer brain (ADHD product manager) owns vision and market scanning. Exploiter brain (autistic engineer) owns architecture and quality gates. They use 6C Consultative mode: PM decides timing, but must gather engineer’s input on technical feasibility. Result: Fast innovation that doesn’t break production. Both brains working at full capacity.

Framework Integration: CREATE, VOICES, 6C

Let’s connect this back to the full system.

CREATE Execution:

This cylinder misfires when execution systems assume uniform processing.

When you default to real-time synchronous communication, you’ve just designed execution for one kind of brain.

Neuroinclusive execution redesigns the workflow itself – async-first, multiple input channels, outcome-focused performance.

VOICES Sculptor:

Workflow design is Sculptor work.

You’re not coaching individuals to adapt to the system. You’re reshaping the system so adaptation isn’t required.

This is the gear most leaders skip – because it requires admitting that “the way we’ve always done it” might not be universal best practice. It might just be familiar.

6C Choice:

Neuroinclusive workflows operate in Choice mode by default.

Set the outcome. Define the guardrails. Then let people choose their path.

Some will work 9-5. Some will work in bursts. Some will process live. Some will process async.

All deliver the same quality – just through different cognitive routes.

The Neuroinclusive Workflow Checklist

Here’s how you know if your workflows are designed for cognitive diversity – or quietly demanding cognitive conformity.

Ask yourself these 12 questions. Be honest. The goal isn’t perfection – it’s awareness of where the friction lives.

Culture & Norms:

  1. Do we require real-time presence or real-time results? → Are people judged for being online during work hours, or for delivering outcomes?

  2. Can people contribute asynchronously and still be considered “engaged”? → Or is engagement only recognized when it’s visible and vocal?

  3. Do we judge “culture fit” or “contribution fit”? → Are we screening for cognitive conformity, or for impact?

  4. Are collaboration modes flexible or mandatory? → Can people choose how they collaborate, or is there one “right” way?

Clarity & Structure:

  1. Are decision rights explicit or inferred from social cues? → Can people see who decides what, or do they have to reverse-engineer it?

  2. Do we offer processing time before requiring responses? → Or do we expect instant contribution in every meeting?

Performance & Measurement:

  1. Do we measure “face time” or “output quality”? → Are people rewarded for being visible, or for doing excellent work?

  2. Are feedback formats flexible or standardized? → Can people receive coaching in writing, or is it always delivered live in 1:1s?

  3. Do we design roles for cognitive profiles or generic “skills”? → Are we matching brains to problems, or forcing square pegs into round holes?

Autonomy & Flexibility:

  1. Can people regulate sensory input without social penalty? → Can they wear headphones, work remotely, adjust lighting – or is that seen as “not being a team player”?

  2. Do we protect focus time or reward constant availability? → Is “deep work” valued, or is responsiveness the primary performance signal?

  3. Can people work in their peak cognitive hours? → Or do we require everyone to be “on” 9-5 regardless of when their brain works best?

Three Diagnostic Questions

Before we close, three questions to surface where your workflows might be demanding cognitive conformity:

1. When someone delivers exceptional work but doesn’t “look engaged,” what do you do?

If your first instinct is to coach them on presence, visibility, or communication style – rather than celebrating the quality of their output – you’re optimizing for optics over outcomes. That’s not performance management. That’s camouflage enforcement.

2. How many of your “collaboration rituals” are actually just real-time verbal processing requirements?

Walk through your weekly meeting rhythms. How many could function asynchronously? How many genuinely require everyone in the room at the same time? If the answer is “most of them,” you’re not designing for collaboration. You’re designing for one cognitive style and calling it teamwork.

3. When was the last time you redesigned a workflow instead of coaching someone to adapt to it?

If three people struggle with the same system, that’s not three people problems. That’s one system problem. Sculptor first – redesign the workflow. Then Coach for individual growth within better-designed systems.

There’s no such thing as a neutral workflow.

Just design choices that unlock some brains and constrain others.

The question isn’t whether your systems work.

It’s who they work for.

And when you shift from accommodation to architecture – from helping individuals adapt to broken systems to redesigning systems that don’t require adaptation – you don’t just create inclusion.

You create intelligent infrastructure.

Systems that let every brain contribute without camouflage.

Workflows that measure outcomes, not optics.

Organizations where cognitive difference isn’t tolerated – it’s leveraged.

Because the teams that figure this out won’t just be more humane.

They’ll be more capable. More adaptive. More innovative. More able to solve problems that cognitively homogeneous teams keep missing.

And the organizations that learn to design work for different brains won’t just retain more talent.

They’ll unlock the cognitive capacity they’ve been systematically filtering out – and discover that neuroinclusive design wasn’t accommodation at all.

It was competitive advantage they couldn’t see because they’d mistaken their own cognitive preferences for universal truth.

Next in this series: In Essay 8, we’ll bring it all together – building the neuroinclusive organization from hiring through team design to leadership development. You’ll see how to make cognitive diversity a strategic composition principle, not a compliance checkbox.

Workflow Design Self-Assessment

Rate your agreement with each statement on a scale of 1-5: (1 = Strongly Disagree, 5 = Strongly Agree)

1. People can contribute meaningfully to decisions and projects without attending real-time meetings – async contributions count equally.

  • 1 = Must be live / 2 = Mostly live / 3 = Some async accepted / 4 = Async valued / 5 = Async equals live

2. We explicitly document decision rights (who decides what) rather than expecting people to infer authority through social cues.

  • 1 = All inferred / 2 = Mostly inferred / 3 = Some documented / 4 = Mostly documented / 5 = Fully explicit

3. Performance reviews measure outcomes and impact rather than “presence,” “visibility,” or communication style.

  • 1 = Style-focused / 2 = Mostly style / 3 = Mixed / 4 = Mostly outcomes / 5 = Outcomes only

4. People can regulate their sensory environment (headphones, quiet spaces, lighting, remote work) without being seen as “not a team player.”

  • 1 = Not acceptable / 2 = Discouraged / 3 = Tolerated / 4 = Supported / 5 = Normalized

5. We design roles and workflows to match cognitive operating systems (explorer vs. exploiter, verbal vs. written, etc.) rather than forcing uniform processes.

  • 1 = One way only / 2 = Minimal flexibility / 3 = Some matching / 4 = Regular matching / 5 = Systematic design

Scoring Guide:

20-25 points: Your workflows likely support cognitive diversity well. Consider: Which specific design choices create this flexibility? Can you document and share these practices?

15-19 points: Some workflows are inclusive but friction points remain. Consider: Which of the five principles (async-first, multiple input channels, explicit clarity, sensory flexibility, outcome-focus) is weakest in your organization?

10-14 points: Your workflows may be demanding significant cognitive conformity. Consider: Use the 12-question checklist above – which questions revealed the biggest gaps?

5-9 points: Workflows are likely optimized for one cognitive style. Consider: Your best performers may be succeeding despite your systems, not because of them.

Next Steps Based on Your Score:

If you scored 15+:

  • Document what makes your workflows neuroinclusive

  • Identify which teams or functions still have rigid structures

  • Share your workflow design practices with other leaders

If you scored 10-14:

  • Pick one of the five principles to implement first (async-first is often highest ROI)

  • Redesign one high-frequency ritual (daily standup, weekly planning, performance reviews)

  • Measure: Does contribution quality improve when you add flexibility?

If you scored below 10:

  • Start with outcome-focused performance: Remove one “style” criterion from next review cycle

  • Add async option to one recurring meeting: “Contribute live or via doc within 24 hours – both count”

  • Create one explicit decision log: Document who decided what and why for your next major decision

Regardless of score: Read Essay 8 to learn how to build neuroinclusive principles into hiring, team composition, and leadership development – because workflow design is just one piece of building organizations that leverage cognitive diversity as competitive advantage.

The business case is clear.

Organizations that get neuroinclusive leadership right reduce attrition, catch blind spots earlier, and build systems that don’t depend on heroic leadership.
