title: Shifting Leadership Stance for Different Brains
subtitle: Essay 6: Neurodiversity Series
html:
A few months ago, I was coaching a founder who couldn’t figure out why his team kept stalling.

He was brilliant – genuinely visionary. He could paint the future in a way that made investors lean forward and early employees say yes before they’d even seen a pitch deck. His energy was infectious. His conviction was magnetic.

But three months into building the product, his engineering lead – autistic, meticulous, exceptional at systems thinking – had quietly started looking for other jobs.

“I don’t understand,” the founder said. “I’ve been so clear about where we’re going. I’ve told them the vision a dozen times. Why aren’t they moving?”

I asked him to walk me through a recent team meeting.

He opened with the big picture. The problem they were solving. The market opportunity. The world they were building toward. Twenty minutes of storytelling. Pure Visionary gear.

Then he said, “So… make it happen. You all know what to do.”

But they didn’t.

Because vision without structure isn’t inspiration for some brains.

It’s cognitive overwhelm.

His engineering lead needed milestones, dependencies, decision rights, and quality gates. She needed to see the system beneath the vision – how the pieces connected, who owned what, where the handoffs happened.

But the founder had one gear: Visionary.

And when that didn’t work, he shifted to his second gear: Operator – checking in daily, asking for updates, trying to drive execution through proximity.

But he never shifted into the gear she actually needed: Sculptor.

The one where you stop trying to inspire or manage people into performance and start redesigning the systems that make performance possible.

That’s when I introduced him to VOICES – not as a leadership philosophy, but as a gearbox.

Because the problem wasn’t that he was a bad leader.

It’s that he was stuck in two gears – regardless of what the moment, or the brain he was leading, actually needed.

You’ve seen this pattern before in this series – leaders stuck in two gears, unable to shift when the moment or the person requires something different. Now let’s unpack what all six gears actually do, and when neurodivergent teams need each one.

The Over-Reliance Problem

We’ve established that most leaders get stuck in Visionary + Operator mode. But what does it actually look like to shift through all six gears? And more importantly – which gears do different brains need most?

Because leadership isn’t about finding the right gear and staying there.

It’s about shifting – reading what the person and the moment need, and toggling between stances in real time.

And when you’re leading neurodivergent teams, that shifting becomes even more essential.

Because different brains don’t just need different communication styles.

They need different leadership gears – and at different times.

What feels like clarity to one brain feels like ambiguity to another.

What feels like autonomy to one brain feels like abandonment to another.

What feels like collaboration to one brain feels like cognitive overload to another.

If you stay in one gear, you’ll connect with the brains wired like yours – and lose everyone else.

VOICES Applied to Neurodivergent Leadership

Let’s walk through the gearbox – not as theory, but as diagnostic.

Because each gear unlocks capacity for some brains and creates friction for others.

Visionary: Big Picture Activation

When it works:

Dyslexic thinkers thrive here. Big picture, pattern detection across domains, strategic narrative. They see where things are going before the data proves it. They connect ideas that seem unrelated. They synthesize complexity into clarity.

For these brains, Visionary leadership isn’t just inspiring – it’s cognitively activating. It gives them the altitude they need to see the whole system at once.

When it breaks:

Autistic professionals can feel untethered without concrete steps. Vision without structure creates anxiety, not momentum. “Where are we going?” is interesting. “How do we get there?” is essential.

ADHD brains lose focus without tangible next actions. Big picture is great – for about 90 seconds. Then the question becomes: “Okay, but what do I do right now?” If the answer is “just keep the vision in mind,” you’ve lost them.

Neuroinclusive shift:

Pair vision with visible milestones. Give the “why” and the “what by when.” Paint the future and map the first three steps. Connect the big picture to the small actions that make it real.

You’re not abandoning vision. You’re making it actionable for brains that need structure to move.

Operator: Systematic Execution

When it works:

Autistic professionals often excel here. Clear systems. Repeatable processes. Quality control that doesn’t fatigue. Execution with precision.

For these brains, Operator mode feels like cognitive relief. The ambiguity is gone. The rules are clear. The path is visible. They can focus on doing the work exceptionally well instead of decoding what “good” even means.

When it breaks:

ADHD brains stagnate in rigid structures. “Follow this exact process in this exact order” is the fastest way to kill momentum. They need room to iterate, to pivot, to discover the path by walking it.

Dyslexic thinkers feel micromanaged. Operator mode can read as “I don’t trust you to find your own way” – which for brains wired for exploration feels like being put in a box.

Neuroinclusive shift:

Offer process options, not process mandates. “Here are three ways to get to the outcome. Pick the one that works for your brain.” “The deliverable is X. The path is yours to design.” “We need to hit these milestones. How you structure your days is up to you.”

You’re not abandoning accountability. You’re calibrating autonomy to cognitive style.

Inclusive: Multiple Entry Points

When it works:

Inclusive mode creates safety for neurodivergent voices to surface without masking. It says, “Your perspective matters. Your way of thinking adds value. You don’t have to perform normalcy to belong here.”

For many neurodivergent professionals, this is the gear that finally lets them breathe.

When it breaks:

If “inclusion” means “everyone processes verbally in real-time,” you’ve excluded half your neurodivergent team.

If “inclusive” looks like open brainstorms, popcorn sharing, and spontaneous collaboration, you’ve just designed a system that only includes one kind of brain.

Inclusive isn’t about creating one big conversation where everyone participates the same way.

It’s about creating multiple pathways so different brains can contribute in the ways they actually work.

Neuroinclusive shift:

Multiple input channels. Async written contributions for brains that think before they speak. Verbal processing for brains that discover their ideas by talking. Visual mapping for brains that think spatially.

Real inclusion isn’t one-size-fits-all participation.

It’s designing systems where every brain has a viable entry point.

Coach: Tailored Development

When it works:

Coach mode, when done well, is transformational.

Tailored feedback in the person’s processing style:

  • Written feedback for autistic brains who need to re-read and integrate without social performance pressure.

  • Verbal walkthroughs for ADHD brains who process kinetically and need to talk it through.

  • Narrative framing for dyslexic brains who think in stories and need context to make meaning.

When you adapt your coaching to their processing mode, feedback actually lands. It integrates. It shifts behavior.

When it breaks:

Generic feedback. Neurotypical-normed “presence” coaching. Performance reviews that penalize people for not making eye contact, not “showing enthusiasm,” not “being more visible.”

This isn’t coaching. It’s camouflage enforcement.

You’re teaching people to perform neurotypicality – not to grow in their actual work.

Neuroinclusive shift:

Ask, “How do you receive feedback best?” – and honor it.

Then deliver feedback on outcomes and specific contributions, not on their performance of engagement.

You’re not lowering standards. You’re raising uptake by meeting people where their brains actually learn.

Encourager: Outcome Recognition

When it works:

Encourager mode recognizes effort and progress – not just neurotypical markers of “engagement.”

It sees the quiet focus. The deep thinking. The meticulous follow-through. The pattern someone noticed that no one else saw.

For neurodivergent employees who’ve spent their careers being told they’re “not collaborative enough” or “need to work on presence,” hearing “your work is exceptional” – without the implicit “but” – can be transformational.

When it breaks:

Praising the wrong things.

“Great eye contact in that meeting!” “I love how enthusiastic you sounded on that call!” “You really brought the energy today!”

If the person spent cognitive budget performing those things instead of doing their actual work, you’ve just reinforced masking.

Neuroinclusive shift:

Celebrate outcomes and specific contributions, not performance of normalcy.

“The way you caught that edge case saved us a week of rework.” “Your analysis shifted how I’m thinking about the whole problem.” “You saw a pattern no one else noticed – that’s the kind of thinking we need more of.”

You’re not ignoring social skills. You’re prioritizing impact over optics.

Sculptor: Systems Redesign

When it works:

This is the neuroinclusive gear.

Sculptor is where you stop trying to coach individuals into broken systems and start redesigning the systems themselves.

You’re not asking, “How do I help this person succeed in our current meeting structure?”

You’re asking, “What if our meeting structure is the problem?”

You’re not asking, “How do I coach this person to be more visible?”

You’re asking, “What if visibility is a neurotypical performance metric that has nothing to do with leadership impact?”

Sculptor mode is where you shift from accommodating difference to designing for it.

It’s the gear where you say:

“Our stand-ups are forcing real-time verbal processing. Let’s redesign them with async options.”

“Our performance reviews penalize people for not performing charisma. Let’s rewrite the criteria to measure impact.”

“Our office layout is sensory chaos for half the team. Let’s create quiet zones and flexible work options.”

When it breaks:

When leaders skip Sculptor entirely and try to solve systemic barriers through Coaching or Encouragement.

“I know the open office is hard for you – have you tried noise-canceling headphones?” “I know you struggle in brainstorms – maybe practice speaking up more?” “I know you feel excluded – keep bringing your whole self, it’ll get easier.”

This isn’t leadership. It’s individualizing a systems problem.

You’re putting the burden of adaptation on the person instead of redesigning the conditions that create the friction.

Neuroinclusive shift:

Make Sculptor your default for systemic barriers.

Before you coach an individual struggle, ask: Is this a person problem or a system problem?

If the system is broken, Coach won’t fix it. Only Sculptor will.

Gear-Switching Scenarios

Let’s show VOICES in action across common situations:

Sprint planning with ADHD product manager:

  • Start: Visionary (here’s where we’re going, here’s why it matters)

  • Middle: Sculptor (here’s the flexible structure that lets you innovate within guardrails)

  • End: Operator (here are the non-negotiable deliverables and dates)

Performance feedback with autistic analyst:

  • Start: Coach (I want to understand your experience first)

  • Middle: Inclusive (here’s what I’m observing – what am I missing?)

  • End: Operator (here’s what needs to change, and here’s exactly how to measure it)

Team pivot with mixed cognitive styles:

  • Announce: Command (we’re changing direction, here’s why)

  • Process: Sculptor (build 48-hour transition buffer, offer async processing time)

  • Engage: Consultative (I need your input on implementation after you’ve had time to think)

Different cognitive styles require different gear sequences – and most leaders never learn to shift.

The Turn: From Coaching Individuals to Sculpting Systems

Here’s what most neurodiversity training gets wrong:

It tries to teach leaders to be better Coaches or more Inclusive.

But the real work is Sculptor.

Because you can coach someone on “executive presence” all day long – but if your definition of executive presence is neurotypical communication performance, you haven’t helped them grow. You’ve just taught them to mask more convincingly.

You can create “inclusive” spaces where everyone’s voice is welcome – but if the only recognized mode of contribution is real-time verbal processing, you haven’t included everyone. You’ve just included the people whose brains happen to work that way already.

The shift happens when you stop asking, “How do I help neurodivergent employees succeed in my systems?”

And start asking, “What systems design would let all brains contribute without camouflage?”

That’s Sculptor work.

And it’s the gear most leaders never shift into – because it requires admitting that the systems you’ve built, the norms you’ve normalized, the “best practices” you’ve institutionalized might not be neutral.

They might just be familiar.

Integrating the Frameworks

We’ve tuned the CREATE engine for cognitive diversity. We’ve built the 6C navigation system for decision friction. Now let’s see how the VOICES gearbox integrates with both.

VOICES + CREATE: Which Gears Activate Which Cylinders

Let’s connect this back to CREATE – because each VOICES gear activates different parts of the leadership engine.

Sculptor shapes Culture and Execution. When you redesign norms and workflows, you’re not just being nice – you’re recalibrating how the whole system operates.

Inclusive protects Relationships and Ethics. When you create multiple pathways for contribution, you’re building trust and protecting the right to work differently.

Coach drives Teaching and Agility. When you tailor feedback and normalize iteration, you’re making growth sustainable – not just for high performers, but for all cognitive styles.

Visionary anchors Culture and Agility. When you pair vision with structural clarity, you create both meaning and momentum.

Operator powers Execution and Relationships. When you offer process options (not mandates), you create accountability and autonomy.

Encourager reinforces Culture and Teaching. When you celebrate outcomes (not optics), you signal what actually matters – and people learn what to optimize for.

The gears don’t operate in isolation. They work together – when you know which gear the moment needs.

VOICES + 6C: Matching Gears to Decision Modes

Different VOICES gears naturally pair with different 6C Decision Compass modes.

Visionary often uses Consultative – “Here’s where we’re going, I need your input on how we get there.”

Operator uses Command or Core Expertise – “Here’s the process” or “You own this domain, execute accordingly.”

Inclusive uses Collaborative or Consensus – “We’re building this together, everyone’s input shapes the outcome.”

Sculptor uses Choice – “Here’s the outcome and the guardrails. You decide how to get there.”

Coach uses Consultative – “I’m here to help you grow, but the learning is yours to own.”

Encourager doesn’t decide – it reinforces. It recognizes progress and contribution wherever it shows up.

The integration point: when you know which gear you’re in, you know which decision mode fits.

And when the whole team can name both, you’ve built a system where leadership doesn’t depend on one person holding all the context.

The VOICES Gear Shift Guide for Neurodivergent Teams

Let’s make this immediately usable.

Which gear each cognitive style needs most:

  • Autistic brains: Operator (clear systems) + Sculptor (redesign ambiguity out)

  • ADHD brains: Visionary (big picture + urgency) + Coach (tailored, kinetic feedback)

  • Dyslexic brains: Visionary (strategic narrative) + Inclusive (multiple input modes)

  • Anxiety-driven brains: Operator (predictability) + Encourager (progress recognition)

Which gear creates friction for which brain type:

  • Autistic: Visionary without milestones creates untethered anxiety

  • ADHD: Operator without autonomy kills momentum

  • Dyslexic: Operator without context feels micromanaged

  • Anxiety-driven: Inclusive without structure creates decision paralysis

When to shift gears based on cognitive load, not just task type:

  • High cognitive load (transitions, crises, ambiguity) → Shift to Operator (clarity) or Sculptor (redesign the stressor)

  • Low cognitive load (steady state, routine work) → Shift to Coach (growth) or Encourager (recognition)

The “Sculptor First” principle:

Before you Coach an individual struggle, check if the system needs redesign.

If three people are struggling with the same thing, it’s not three people problems. It’s one system problem.

Sculptor first. Then Coach for individual growth within redesigned systems.

Self-Diagnostic: Which Gears Are You Stuck In?

Look at your calendar from the last two weeks:

  • How many meetings started with vision but had no concrete next steps? (Visionary overuse)

  • How many times did you specify exact processes rather than outcomes? (Operator overuse)

  • When did you last redesign a system rather than coach an individual? (Sculptor underuse)

Ask your team: “What do you need from me that I’m not giving you?” Their answer will tell you which gear you’re avoiding.

Pattern recognition: If you keep coaching the same struggle across multiple people, that’s your signal to shift to Sculptor.

Three Diagnostic Questions

Before we close, three questions to surface which gears you’re overusing – and which you’re avoiding:

1. When was the last time you shifted out of Visionary or Operator mode – and what gear did you shift into?

If you can’t remember, you’re stuck in two gears. That’s not bad leadership – it’s predictable leadership. And predictable leadership can’t read the room well enough to meet different brains where they work.

2. Which gear makes you most uncomfortable – and is that the gear your team needs most right now?

Leaders avoid gears that don’t feel natural. But if your team is struggling and you’re only using your comfortable gears, you’re not leading adaptively. You’re leading rigidly and hoping people adjust. Ask your team: “What do you need from me that I’m not giving you?” Their answer will tell you which gear you’re avoiding.

3. Are you trying to Coach someone through a problem that requires Sculptor work?

If you keep coaching the same struggle across multiple people, stop coaching. Start redesigning. Individual adaptation can’t fix systemic barriers. Sculptor first, then Coach for growth within better-designed systems.

There’s no such thing as one leadership style that works for everyone.

Just leaders who know how to shift gears – and leaders who don’t.

The question isn’t which gear you prefer.

It’s whether you can read what the person in front of you needs right now – and toggle accordingly.

Because neuroinclusive leadership isn’t about being all things to all people.

It’s about having enough gears that you can meet different brains where they actually work.

And when you do, you don’t just get better morale.

You get better outcomes – because you’ve unlocked cognitive capacity that rigid, one-gear leadership leaves on the table.

Next in this series: In Essay 7, we’ll design neuroinclusive workflows from the ground up – moving from accommodation to architecture. You’ll see the five workflow design principles that make work accessible to all cognitive styles, and learn why “reasonable accommodations” actually reinforce the problem they’re trying to solve.

VOICES Gear Flexibility Self-Assessment

Rate your agreement with each statement on a scale of 1-5: (1 = Strongly Disagree, 5 = Strongly Agree)

1. I can clearly identify which VOICES gear I’m using in real-time and shift gears based on what the person or situation needs.

  • 1 = Stuck in 1-2 gears / 2 = Limited shifting / 3 = Some flexibility / 4 = Good flexibility / 5 = Fluid gear-shifting

2. When I see individual struggles repeated across multiple people, my first response is to redesign the system (Sculptor) rather than coach individuals.

  • 1 = Always coach / 2 = Usually coach / 3 = Mixed / 4 = Usually redesign / 5 = Always redesign first

3. I adapt my feedback delivery (Coach gear) to match how each person processes information, not just my preferred style.

  • 1 = One format / 2 = Minimal adaptation / 3 = Some adaptation / 4 = Regular adaptation / 5 = Fully personalized

4. I can recognize when vision (Visionary) creates anxiety rather than clarity for certain brain types, and pair it with structure.

  • 1 = Rarely recognize / 2 = Sometimes / 3 = Often / 4 = Usually / 5 = Always

5. When I recognize outcomes (Encourager), I celebrate impact and specific contributions rather than performance of engagement.

  • 1 = Celebrate performance / 2 = Mostly performance / 3 = Mixed / 4 = Mostly impact / 5 = Impact-focused

6. I use all six VOICES gears regularly, not just my comfortable 1-2 gears.

  • 1 = Use 1-2 only / 2 = Use 2-3 / 3 = Use 3-4 / 4 = Use 4-5 / 5 = Use all 6

Scoring Guide:

25-30 points: You’re likely shifting gears fluidly. Consider: Can you teach this flexibility to other leaders? What makes gear-shifting natural for you?

18-24 points: You’re expanding beyond 1-2 gears but still have underused gears. Consider: Which gear scored lowest? That’s likely the gear your team needs most from you right now.

12-17 points: You’re probably stuck in Visionary + Operator mode. Consider: Try Sculptor next time you see a repeated individual struggle – redesign the system, not the person.

6-11 points: Limited gear flexibility is likely creating friction. Consider: Ask your team “What do you need from me that I’m not giving you?” – their answer reveals which gears you’re avoiding.

Next Steps Based on Your Score:

If you scored 20+:

  • Document which gear sequences work for which situations

  • Mentor other leaders on gear flexibility

  • Identify: which gear do you still underuse?

If you scored 12-19:

  • Identify your lowest-scoring gear

  • Use it deliberately in your next three leadership interactions

  • Notice: what changes in team response?

If you scored below 12:

  • Start with Sculptor: identify one systemic barrier and redesign it

  • Before your next 1:1: ask “How do you receive feedback best?” and honor it (Coach)

  • When you recognize good work: name the specific contribution, not the person’s “energy” (Encourager)

Regardless of score: Read Essay 7 to learn how to design workflows that work for all brains from the ground up – because even with gear flexibility, you need systems architecture that doesn’t require constant leadership intervention.

The business case is clear.

Organizations that get neuroinclusive leadership right reduce attrition, catch blind spots earlier, and build systems that don’t depend on heroic leadership.

title: When Cognitive Styles Collide
subtitle: Essay 5: Neurodiversity Series
html:
I was in the room when it happened.

A product team, mid-sprint planning. Two brilliant people – both essential to the work – locked in what looked like a personality conflict but was actually something deeper.

The product manager was pacing. “We need to ship this feature now. The market window is closing. We can iterate later.”

The lead engineer hadn’t moved. “We can’t ship it now. There are three edge cases we haven’t tested. If we push this live and it breaks, we’ll spend the next month in crisis mode instead of building the next thing.”

The PM: “You’re overthinking it. We don’t need perfection, we need momentum.”

The engineer: “I’m not overthinking. I’m thinking. There’s a difference.”

The room went quiet.

The manager – well-meaning, conflict-averse – tried to smooth it over. “Let’s all just be flexible here. Meet in the middle.”

But here’s what no one said out loud:

Flexibility isn’t neutral.

For the PM, “being flexible” meant slowing down – which for someone whose brain works through momentum often means losing the thread that makes focus possible in the first place.

For the engineer, “being flexible” meant compromising on quality thresholds – which for someone whose brain notices structural patterns feels like being asked to ignore flaws they can literally see in the system.

Neither was wrong.

They weren’t even in conflict about the goal. They both wanted the product to succeed.

They were in conflict about how different brains process risk, urgency, and quality – and no one had given them a language to navigate it.

That’s when I introduced the 6C Decision Compass.

Not as a conflict resolution tool.

As a friction navigation protocol.

Because what looked like a personality clash was actually decision friction in disguise.

The 6C Decision Compass: A Brief Primer

Before we map the collision patterns, let me explain what the 6C Decision Compass is and why it matters for neuroinclusive teams.

The 6C Decision Compass is a decision-making framework that maps six modes of authority and input:

  • Command – I decide

  • Consultative – I decide, but gather input

  • Collaborative – We decide together

  • Consensus – We agree broadly

  • Core Expertise – The expert decides

  • Choice – I set guardrails; you decide

Most leaders use one or two modes by default and call it “leadership style.” They’re Command leaders or Collaborative leaders, and they apply that mode regardless of context.

But neuroinclusive leadership requires toggling – matching decision modes to cognitive profiles, contexts, and the type of decision being made. Because the friction you’re seeing isn’t about personality. It’s about mismatched decision modes colliding with incompatible brain types.

If CREATE is the engine with six cylinders that need to fire in sequence, and VOICES is the manual gearbox that lets you shift between leadership modes, then 6C is the navigation system that tells you which gear to use for which terrain. It makes decision authority explicit so people aren’t constantly decoding invisible power structures.

When you can say “This is a Core Expertise call, you own it” or “This is Consultative, I’m deciding but I need your input first,” you eliminate the cognitive tax of figuring out who has permission to decide what. People can focus on the decision itself, not on navigating social uncertainty.

And for neurodivergent professionals especially, that clarity is the difference between contributing expertise and spending energy managing ambiguity.

Now let’s look at where friction happens most – and how the Compass helps you navigate it.

The Friction No One Wants to Name

Here’s the conversation most inclusion training won’t have:

Neurodivergent strengths don’t just complement neurotypical approaches.

Sometimes they collide.

And most leaders, when they see this friction, default to one of two responses:

“Everyone just be flexible.”

Or: “Let’s agree to disagree and move forward.”

Both sound reasonable. Both ignore the neurology.

Because flexibility is neurologically expensive for some brains and nearly effortless for others. Asking someone to “just be flexible” with structural ambiguity when their brain specializes in pattern recognition is like asking someone to run a marathon while doing mental math. Possible? Maybe. Efficient? Not even close.

Asking someone to “slow down and think it through” when momentum is the only thing keeping focus intact is like asking someone to paddle upstream while the current is pulling them forward. You can do it – but you’re fighting your own cognitive wiring to make it happen.

This isn’t about personality. It’s about how different brains process uncertainty, time pressure, and structural integrity.

And if you want neuroinclusive teams to actually work – not just coexist politely – you need systems that expect friction and build navigation protocols.

That’s where the 6C Decision Compass stops being a decision-making tool and starts being a cognitive translation system.

The Three Cognitive Collisions That Stall Teams

Let’s name the patterns. Because once you see them, you’ll recognize them everywhere.

Collision 1: Speed vs. Precision

One brain says: “We need to move NOW while the momentum is here.”

Another brain says: “We need to check these three variables first or we’ll have to redo it.”

This isn’t about one person being impulsive and the other being cautious. It’s about different cognitive relationships with time and risk.

For some brains, momentum is the resource. Interest creates focus. Delay kills both. The urgency isn’t manufactured – it’s the cognitive condition under which hyperfocus becomes possible. “Move now” isn’t recklessness. It’s the brain saying, “I can see the whole solution right now, and if we wait, I’ll lose the thread.”

For other brains, structural integrity is the priority. Precision isn’t perfectionism – it’s pattern recognition applied to risk. “Check these variables first” isn’t stalling. It’s the brain saying, “I can see three points of failure everyone else is missing, and if we ignore them, we’ll pay for it later.”

Or as that engineer put it in the meeting: “I’m not overthinking. I’m thinking. There’s a difference.”

Both are right. Both are seeing something real.

And if your decision-making system doesn’t have a protocol for navigating this, you get one of two outcomes:

Either the fast brain bulldozes the precise brain (and you ship something broken),

Or the precise brain blocks the fast brain (and you miss the window entirely).

6C Solution:

Mode: Consultative

Structure: The momentum-driven brain decides timing (they own momentum as a resource), but must gather the precision-oriented brain’s input on quality gates before executing.

Alternative: Core Expertise – whoever has domain authority on this specific decision owns it. If it’s a “move fast or lose the market” call, that’s strategy expertise. If it’s a “will this break the system?” call, that’s technical expertise.

The key is making decision authority explicit – so friction doesn’t become personal.

Collision 2: Verbal Processing vs. Written Processing

One brain says: “Let’s talk this through in real-time.”

Another brain says: “I need to think and write before I speak.”

This one shows up in every meeting, every brainstorm, every “quick sync.”

For some brains, thinking is talking. They process out loud. Ideas form through conversation. The back-and-forth isn’t just collaboration – it’s how their brain works. Silence feels like stalling.

For other brains, talking interrupts thinking. They need internal processing time before external articulation. Speaking in real-time doesn’t unlock their best ideas – it forces them to choose between appearing engaged and actually thinking.

And when your meeting culture defaults to “let’s riff on this,” you’ve just designed a system that captures fast-talker ideas and filters out deep-thinker ideas.

Not because the deep thinkers don’t have ideas. Because the format doesn’t give those ideas time to form.

6C Solution:

Mode: Choice

Structure: Set the outcome (we need everyone’s input on this decision), but let people choose their processing path. Some people contribute live. Some people contribute in writing afterward. Both count.

Alternative: Collaborative with asynchronous input – post a written brief 24 hours before the meeting. Let people process and contribute in a shared doc. Then use the live meeting to synthesize, debate, and decide – not to generate ideas from scratch.

The shift is subtle but critical: you’re not asking people to “be flexible about how they communicate.” You’re designing multiple pathways to the same outcome.

Collision 3: Structured Process vs. Emergent Discovery

One brain says: “We need a checklist and timeline.”

Another brain says: “I don’t know what I’m doing until I start doing it.”

This is the planner vs. explorer tension – and it plays out in every project kickoff, every execution plan, every “how are we going to do this?” conversation.

For structured brains, process creates safety. A checklist isn’t micromanagement – it’s cognitive scaffolding. It reduces decision fatigue. It makes the invisible visible. When the steps are clear, the brain can focus on execution, not navigation.

For emergent brains, rigid process feels like cognitive constraint. They don’t know the best path until they start moving. The process reveals itself through iteration. Forcing them to map everything up front doesn’t create clarity – it creates paralysis.

Both approaches are valid. Both solve real problems. And both need to coexist if you want teams that can both execute reliably and innovate adaptively.

6C Solution:

Mode: Consultative on milestones + Choice on daily execution

Structure: The structured brain gets predictability (”we need X by Y date”), the explorer brain gets autonomy (”you decide how you get there”).

Alternative: Separate what from how – the structured brain defines the deliverable and the quality standard, the emergent brain chooses the workflow.

This isn’t compromise. It’s complementarity by design.

You’re not asking people to meet in the middle. You’re building systems where different cognitive styles each get what they need to perform.

Mapping Decision Modes to Cognitive Styles

Here’s where the 6C Compass becomes strategically powerful – different cognitive styles thrive in different decision modes.

Autistic professionals often thrive in Core Expertise and Command environments – where the rules are clear, the logic is transparent, and the decision path is structurally sound. Ambiguity doesn’t feel like freedom; it feels like cognitive noise.

ADHD brains often excel when given Choice – autonomy over how, when, and in what order they tackle work. The structure isn’t the timeline; it’s the outcome. That autonomy activates hyperfocus.

Dyslexic thinkers often need Consultative or Collaborative modes – the chance to talk through strategy, synthesize inputs, and build the idea verbally before committing to a path. Their brilliance shows up in real-time synthesis, not pre-formed written proposals.

Anxiety-driven cognition performs best in Consultative mode – where their threat modeling and scenario planning are explicitly gathered as input rather than treated as pessimism. They need to know their risk assessment will inform the decision.

Most leaders default to 1-2 modes for everything. Neuroinclusive leaders use all six – and know which cognitive profiles need which modes to perform their best.

What Breaks When You Don’t Use 6C

Let’s name the anti-patterns – because seeing what breaks helps you understand what the Compass actually fixes.

Here’s what happens without explicit decision modes:

  • Meetings run 2x longer because no one knows who’s deciding

  • Neurodivergent professionals assume they need permission for everything (unclear when Core Expertise applies)

  • Decisions get re-litigated because authority was never clear (was it Command or Collaborative?)

  • Innovation slows because people won’t move without explicit authorization

  • The fastest talker wins, not the best thinker

  • Pattern-detectors stop speaking up because their input arrives “too late”

  • Structure-oriented brains get labeled “inflexible” when they’re actually preventing disasters

This isn’t a neurodiversity problem. It’s a leadership clarity problem that neurodivergent professionals expose.

Quick audit: In your last five decisions:

  • Could your team name which mode you were using?

  • Did you explicitly say “This is Command, I’m deciding” or “This is Collaborative, we’re deciding together”?

  • Were people clear on when their input was shaping the decision vs. informing it?

If you answered no to these, you’re creating decision anxiety – and your neurodivergent team members are bearing the highest cost.

Why the 6C Compass Unlocks Neuroinclusive Leadership

Here’s what makes the 6C Decision Compass essential for mixed-brain teams:

It does three things that most decision-making systems don’t.

1. It Eliminates the Cognitive Decoding Tax

For many neurodivergent professionals, ambiguity around “Am I allowed to decide this?” creates constant low-grade anxiety. Every decision becomes a social decoding exercise: Do I have permission? Will I be seen as overstepping? Should I wait for approval?

When you name the decision mode – “This is Core Expertise, you own it” or “This is Consultative, I’m deciding but I need your input first” – you eliminate that cognitive tax.

People can focus on the decision itself, not on navigating invisible authority structures.

2. It Designs for Cognitive Complementarity

Different brains thrive in different modes.

Pattern-recognition brains often excel in Core Expertise and Command – where the logic is clear, the rules are explicit, and the decision path is structurally sound.

Momentum-driven brains often thrive in Choice – where autonomy activates hyperfocus and movement creates clarity.

Big-picture thinking brains often need Consultative – where they can talk through strategy, synthesize inputs, and build the idea verbally before committing to a path.

When you treat “good decision-making” as one mode applied uniformly, you’re designing for cognitive conformity.

When you use the 6C Compass, you’re designing for cognitive complementarity.

3. It Scales Neuroinclusive Systems

When anyone on the team can name the decision mode, you’re no longer the bottleneck.

“This feels like a Collaborative decision – we all need to weigh in.”

“Actually, I think this is Core Expertise – whoever knows the client best should call it.”

“Can we make this a Choice decision? Set the outcome, let people choose the path?”

When the system holds the decision logic, not just the leader, you’ve built infrastructure that scales.

And scaling neuroinclusive leadership means moving from “the leader navigates every friction point” to “the team has a protocol for navigating friction without you.”

6C + VOICES: Matching Decision Modes to Leadership Gears

Here’s where the integration gets powerful.

Different VOICES gears naturally pair with different 6C decision modes.

When you’re in Coach mode, you’re usually using Consultative or Collaborative – gathering input, co-creating solutions, building ownership through inclusion.

When you’re in Sculptor mode, you’re often setting Choice with clear guardrails – defining the outcome and constraints, then letting people find their own path within that structure.

When you’re in Operator mode, you might need Command for execution speed – clear directive, tight timeline, minimal deliberation.

When you’re in Encourager mode, Consensus might be appropriate – building broad agreement and collective momentum.

The mistake most leaders make is staying in one gear and forcing one decision mode regardless of context.

But neuroinclusive leadership requires toggling – shifting between gears and decision modes based on what the situation and the cognitive profiles in the room actually need.

That’s not indecisiveness. That’s adaptive precision.

6C + CREATE Relationships: When “Who Decides” Is Never Ambiguous

Let’s connect this back to CREATE – because the Relationships cylinder fires cleanly when decision authority is structurally explicit.

When “who decides” is ambiguous, relationships become navigation tools instead of collaboration tools. People spend energy figuring out informal power dynamics instead of contributing their expertise.

But when you use the 6C Compass to make decision modes explicit, the Relationships cylinder can do what it’s designed to do: build trust, clarity, and collaborative capacity.

“Is this my call?” is no longer a question people have to reverse-engineer through social cues.

It’s answered by the system.

And that clarity – that cognitive relief – is what lets neurodivergent professionals focus on their actual work instead of decoding invisible protocols.

The 6C Translation Guide for Neurodivergent Teams

Here’s how to name decision modes in ways that reduce anxiety and activate clarity:

Command: “I’m deciding this, here’s why, here’s the timeline.” → Reduces ambiguity. Provides structure. Works well when urgency is high and deliberation time is low.

Consultative: “I’m deciding, but I need your input first. Here’s the question I’m working through.” → Honors expertise without creating decision paralysis. Good for brains that think out loud.

Collaborative: “We’re deciding together. Everyone’s input shapes the outcome.” → Use with async options (written pre-work, post-meeting input) to include introverted and slow-processing brains.

Consensus: “We need broad agreement before moving forward. Let’s work toward alignment everyone can support.” → Useful when buy-in matters as much as the decision itself. Requires extra processing time for neurodivergent team members.

Core Expertise: “You own this decision because you have the domain knowledge. I trust your judgment.” → Reduces anxiety about overstepping. Activates competence-based confidence.

Choice: “Here’s the outcome and the constraints. You decide how to get there.” → Activates autonomy-driven focus. Reduces micromanagement friction. Honors different pathways to results.

There’s no such thing as frictionless collaboration. Just teams that have protocols for navigating friction – and teams that don’t.

The question isn’t whether cognitive styles will collide. It’s whether you’ve built systems that turn collision into complementarity.

Because when you do, you don’t get compromise.

You get the precision and the momentum.

The structure and the emergence.

The deep thinking and the fast execution.

You get teams that can hold multiple cognitive truths at once – and make better decisions because of it.

That’s not compromise. That’s the competitive advantage everyone’s looking for but most organizations are systematically filtering out.

Next in this series: In Essay 6, you’ll learn how to shift between all six VOICES leadership gears – and discover why most leaders get stuck in just two. I’ll show you which gears neurodivergent professionals need most, and how Sculptor mode becomes your primary neuroinclusive gear for systems redesign.

Decision Friction Self-Assessment

Rate your agreement with each statement on a scale of 1-5: (1 = Strongly Disagree, 5 = Strongly Agree)

1. When I make decisions, I explicitly name which mode I’m using (Core Expertise, Command, Consultative, etc.) so the team knows how authority is structured.

  • 1 = Never / 2 = Rarely / 3 = Sometimes / 4 = Usually / 5 = Always

2. My team has clear protocols for when to use real-time discussion vs. asynchronous input for decision-making.

  • 1 = No protocols / 2 = Vague protocols / 3 = Some protocols / 4 = Clear protocols / 5 = Well-established protocols

3. When cognitive friction emerges (speed vs. precision, verbal vs. written, structure vs. emergence), we have systems to navigate it rather than just asking people to “be flexible.”

  • 1 = No systems / 2 = Minimal systems / 3 = Some systems / 4 = Good systems / 5 = Robust systems

4. I can identify which decision modes different team members thrive in based on their cognitive profiles.

  • 1 = Cannot identify / 2 = Vague sense / 3 = Some clarity / 4 = Clear identification / 5 = Systematically mapped

5. People on my team can focus on contributing expertise rather than spending energy decoding who has permission to decide what.

  • 1 = High decoding tax / 2 = Significant tax / 3 = Moderate tax / 4 = Low tax / 5 = Minimal tax

Scoring Guide:

20-25 points: Your decision-making likely supports cognitive diversity well. Consider: Can you document your 6C decision protocols? Which specific practices prevent decision friction?

15-19 points: You’re creating some clarity but decision friction likely still emerges. Consider: Which collision pattern (speed vs. precision, verbal vs. written, structure vs. emergence) shows up most often in your team?

10-14 points: Decision ambiguity may be creating cognitive overhead. Consider: Try naming the decision mode explicitly in your next three decisions. Notice what changes in clarity and contribution quality.

5-9 points: Decision friction is likely a major source of cognitive tax. Consider: Your team is probably spending significant energy on “Who gets to decide?” rather than “What’s the best decision?”

Next Steps Based on Your Score:

If you scored 15+:

  • Document your decision-making protocols

  • Train your team to name decision modes themselves

  • Identify which modes you underutilize (most leaders overuse 1-2 modes)

If you scored 10-14:

  • Pick your next important decision: Name the mode before the discussion starts

  • Map your last 3 cognitive collisions to the patterns above – which one repeats?

  • Design one 6C protocol for your most common friction pattern

If you scored below 10:

  • Start simple: In your next team meeting, say “This is Consultative – I’m deciding but I need your input”

  • Notice: Does naming the mode reduce the “who’s deciding?” anxiety?

  • Identify one chronic decision friction point and map it to a 6C solution above

Regardless of score: Read Essay 6 to learn how the VOICES gearbox helps you shift between leadership stances based on what different brains need. Because even with clear decision modes, you’ll need to shift how you show up for different cognitive profiles.

The business case is clear.

Organizations that get neuroinclusive leadership right reduce attrition, catch blind spots earlier, and build systems that don’t depend on heroic leadership.

I’ve spent 20 years coaching leaders through this work—from independent schools to USAID to tech startups. I have the complete diagnostic tools, the frameworks, and the implementation roadmaps. But let’s start simple.

Book a free call. Let’s figure out where you are.

We’ll diagnose what’s happening in your systems, identify where friction is costing you capacity, and map whether this work makes sense for you right now. No pitch. No obligation.

title: Mistuned? Why High-Performing Teams Still Lose Their Best People
subtitle: Essay 4: Neurodiversity Series
html:
A few years ago, I was working with a leadership team trying to understand why their best people kept leaving after 18 months.

Exit interviews were polite. “Pursuing other opportunities.” “Better fit elsewhere.” The usual scripts.

But when I dug deeper – when I asked the question behind the question – a pattern emerged.

It wasn’t the workload. It wasn’t compensation. It wasn’t even the mission.

It was the constant cognitive dissonance of working in a system where nothing was ever quite explained.

“How do we make decisions here?” “It depends.”

“Who has final say when there’s disagreement?” “We all kind of figure it out together.”

“What does success look like in this role?” “You’ll know it when you see it.”

For neurotypical employees, this ambiguity felt like trust. Like autonomy. Like a collaborative, non-hierarchical culture.

For neurodivergent employees, it felt like a daily cognitive tax they couldn’t afford to keep paying.

One person put it this way: “I can do my job. I’m good at my job. But I’m spending half my energy trying to reverse-engineer the invisible rules of how things work here. And I’m exhausted.”

They didn’t need empathy training. They needed architectural clarity.

That’s when I realized: most leaders think building neuroinclusive organizations requires a whole new framework – new policies, new training programs, new HR initiatives.

They don’t.

They need to understand how the framework they’re already using works differently for different brains.

CREATE – Culture, Relationships, Execution, Agility, Teaching, Ethics – isn’t neurotypical by default. It’s a systems model. And systems can be tuned. The question isn’t whether CREATE works for neurodivergent teams. It’s whether you’ve tuned each cylinder to unlock cognitive capacity instead of demanding cognitive conformity.

Because here’s the thing about engines: you can have all six cylinders firing – Culture, Relationships, Execution, Agility, Teaching, Ethics – and still have half your team running on fumes. Not because the cylinders don’t work. But because they’re calibrated for one kind of brain, and you never realized it was a choice.

The CREATE Engine: A Brief Primer

Before we tune each cylinder for cognitive diversity, let me explain what CREATE is and why the engine metaphor matters.

CREATE is a diagnostic framework I developed for understanding how organizations actually function – not how they say they function in vision statements, but how the daily architecture of work either enables or constrains human potential. It stands for Culture, Relationships, Execution, Agility, Teaching, and Ethics – six interconnected systems that determine whether your organization can perform under pressure or breaks down when it matters most.

I think of CREATE as a six-cylinder engine. Each cylinder does distinct work, but they’re not independent. They fire in sequence, and they depend on each other. Culture sets the norms that shape Relationships. Relationships determine who has authority in Execution. Execution reveals whether you have the Agility to adapt when plans hit reality. Agility requires Teaching – the capacity to learn and adjust. And Ethics governs whether all of this serves people or just extracts from them.

When all six cylinders are firing in sync, the engine hums. Decisions get made with clarity. Teams adapt without chaos. People grow without burning out.

But here’s what most leaders miss: you can have all six cylinders technically functioning and still have half your team running on fumes. Not because the cylinders don’t work, but because they’re calibrated for one kind of brain. And if you’ve never questioned that calibration – if you’ve assumed your systems are neutral when they’re actually optimized for neurotypical processing – you’re not just leaving performance on the table. You’re systematically burning out the cognitive profiles you need most.

What follows is a guide to tuning each cylinder for cognitive diversity. Not as an accommodation strategy, but as operational intelligence. Because when you design systems that work for different brains, you don’t just help neurodivergent employees. You build a more resilient, more adaptive, more capable engine for everyone.

So let’s tune the engine. Starting with the cylinder where everything either begins – or quietly dies.

Culture: From Vibe to Visibility

Let’s start with Culture – because this is where neuroinclusive design either takes root or dies quietly.

For neurotypical employees, culture often feels intuitive. It’s “the vibe.” It’s “how we do things around here,” absorbed through osmosis, through watching, through pattern-matching social cues and adjusting accordingly. For many neurodivergent employees – especially autistic professionals – that same “vibe” feels like paralyzing ambiguity.

Culture audit: Can someone succeed in your organization if they:

  • Never attend happy hour?

  • Don’t make small talk before meetings?

  • Ask for written agendas instead of “just rolling with it”?

  • Wear headphones to manage sensory input?

If you answered “probably not” to any of these, your culture isn’t inclusive – it’s neurotypical-exclusive.

“Be collaborative” – but what does that actually mean? Respond to every Slack message within the hour? Attend every optional meeting? Volunteer ideas in real-time even when you need processing time? “Take initiative” – but how much? And in which domains? And do I ask first, or will that look like I lack confidence? “We value authenticity” – but which parts of authenticity? The parts that look like extroversion? Or actual authenticity, which for some people is quiet, task-focused, and energized by depth rather than breadth?

When culture is implicit, neurotypical employees navigate through social fluency. Neurodivergent employees navigate through constant cognitive modeling – reverse-engineering the unwritten rules while simultaneously trying to do their actual jobs. That’s not culture. That’s a decoding tax.

The cost shows up everywhere. They spend more energy managing social uncertainty than solving problems. They second-guess every interaction. They rehearse before speaking. They burn out not from the work, but from the invisible labor of figuring out how to work here. And because the exhaustion doesn’t announce itself as “I’m trying to decode your implicit norms,” it gets misread as disengagement, low initiative, or poor culture fit.

What neuroinclusive Culture looks like: You make the invisible visible. You document “how we do things here” – not as bureaucracy, but as clarity. You create explicit communication norms: “We respond to Slack within 24 hours, not 24 minutes.” You define what collaboration actually means in your context: “Collaboration here means co-creating solutions in shared docs, not performing enthusiasm in meetings.” You specify decision rights: “On project X, you own the decision. On project Y, you provide input but Leader Z decides.”

This isn’t micromanagement. It’s cognitive relief. Because when the rules are explicit, people can stop spending energy guessing and start spending it contributing. If “culture fit” is part of your hiring process, define it in behavioral terms, not vibes. If “executive presence” is part of your promotion criteria, specify what you actually mean – and make sure it’s measuring leadership impact, not neurotypical communication style.

Culture done right doesn’t just prevent burnout. It transforms who gets to show up as their full selves without constant translation.

Relationships: From Social Fluency to Structural Clarity

The Relationships cylinder is where role clarity becomes neuroinclusive design, and where most organizations accidentally create cognitive landmines.

Here’s what happens in most organizations: relationships are managed through social navigation. You figure out who really makes decisions by watching meeting dynamics. You learn whose opinion matters by noticing who gets deferred to. You decode power structures through subtext, through who interrupts whom, through who gets invited to which conversations. For neurotypical employees, this is just how work works. For neurodivergent employees – especially those who struggle with social cue interpretation or find office politics cognitively expensive – it’s a persistent drain on executive function.

Every ambiguous “we all own this” project becomes a minefield of invisible expectations. Every “let’s collaborate” initiative becomes a guessing game about who’s actually responsible for what. Every org change becomes an exercise in re-mapping informal power structures no one will explicitly explain. The cognitive budget spent decoding these dynamics is budget not spent on expertise, insight, or innovation.

They avoid asking for help because they can’t figure out who to ask. They miss opportunities because they didn’t realize certain conversations were the real decision-making forums. They’re told they need to “build relationships” but can’t decode which relationships matter or how to build them in ways that feel authentic rather than performative.

What neuroinclusive Relationships look like: You eliminate the social decoding tax by making authority and accountability structurally explicit.

Here’s what explicit decision rights look like:

  • “You own this decision. Consult me, but it’s yours.”

  • “I’m deciding this. Your input shapes the decision, but I’m accountable.”

  • “We’re deciding together. We don’t move until we agree.”

When “who owns what” is clear, autistic professionals especially can focus on competence instead of politics. When decision rights are documented, ADHD brains don’t have to track informal power dynamics – they can direct their questions to the right person and move forward.

Use RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) for everything. Not because you’re bureaucratic, but because clarity is kind. Eliminate “we all own it” ambiguity – that phrase is neurotypical code for “figure it out through social cues.” Protect expertise-based authority. Let people lead from their strengths without having to perform dominance to be heard.

When Relationships are tuned correctly, trust doesn’t come from reading the room. It comes from knowing exactly where you stand and who you can count on. That’s not just neuroinclusive design – that’s how high-functioning teams operate regardless of neurotype.

Execution: From Process Conformity to Outcome Diversity

The Execution cylinder is where cognitive diversity either compounds productivity or creates friction, and where most leaders accidentally filter out their best work by optimizing for process uniformity.

Most execution systems are designed around a single assumption: everyone processes information the same way. But they don’t. Some brains need written instructions before they can start. Others need to talk it through first. Some need hard deadlines to activate focus. Others need autonomy and will deliver early if you just get out of the way. Some need structure and predictability. Others need novelty and will disengage if the process feels repetitive.

When you design execution systems that assume uniform processing, you’re not creating efficiency. You’re creating a cognitive filter that only lets one kind of brain work at full capacity.

ADHD brains stall in rigid, sequential workflows that don’t allow for iterative problem-solving. Autistic brains struggle when instructions are vague or change mid-process without explanation. Dyslexic brains lose access to their strategic brilliance when forced to document everything in writing before they’ve had a chance to talk it through.

You get compliance. But you don’t get their best work. And because the process looks efficient on paper – everyone following the same workflow, everyone hitting the same checkpoints – you don’t see what you’re losing. You just notice that certain people seem “less engaged” or “struggle with follow-through,” never questioning whether the workflow itself is the problem.

What neuroinclusive Execution looks like: You design multiple pathways to the same outcome. You focus on deliverables, not process conformity. You let people choose their workflow as long as the output meets the standard. You offer both written and verbal briefing options. You separate “what needs to happen” from “how you make it happen.”

Process flexibility in practice:

  • Outcome-defined work: “Deliver X by Friday, work when/how you process best”

  • Multiple input channels: Written, verbal, visual – take your pick

  • Async default: Real-time only when synchronous is actually necessary

One leader told me: “I thought this would create confusion. Instead, everyone got clearer on what actually mattered.”

This doesn’t mean chaos. It means calibrated autonomy – enough structure to create alignment, enough flexibility to let different brains do what they do best. Stop measuring process. Start measuring outcomes. If someone delivers excellent work but never speaks in the standup, that’s not a problem – that’s a brain working the way it works. If someone needs noise-canceling headphones and flexible hours to produce their best thinking, that’s not an accommodation. That’s operational intelligence.

Execution done right doesn’t just reduce friction. It unlocks capacity you didn’t know you had.

Agility: From Pivoting to Preparing

The Agility cylinder is where most neuroinclusive design efforts fail – because leaders confuse speed with adaptability and end up rewarding one kind of brain while destabilizing another.

Here’s the thing about pivots: for neurotypical employees, they can feel energizing. A change of direction. A new challenge. Momentum. For many neurodivergent employees – especially autistic and ADHD professionals – sudden pivots aren’t agility. They’re dysregulation. Because transitions are neurologically expensive. Shifting contexts burns executive function. Changing plans mid-process isn’t just inconvenient – it’s cognitively destabilizing.

And when you treat “moving fast” as synonymous with “being agile,” you’re actually creating a system that rewards one kind of brain and punishes another. You announce a pivot in Monday’s all-hands and expect everyone to adjust by Tuesday. While neurotypical team members are already brainstorming the new direction, neurodivergent team members are still processing what just happened – not because they’re slow, but because their brains need time to reorient the entire system they’d built around the previous plan. By the time they’ve caught up, they’re labeled “resistant to change.”

I once watched a product team pivot from feature A to feature B in a Monday standup. By Wednesday, the engineering lead – autistic, brilliant systems thinker – was being called “slow to adapt” because he hadn’t contributed to the new direction yet. But he wasn’t being slow. He was doing what his brain required: reorienting his entire mental model before he could assess the implications. When he finally spoke on Friday, his input revealed three structural problems the team had missed in their rush to “move fast.” But by then, the damage to his reputation was done.

The real cost isn’t the pivot itself. It’s the cognitive whiplash of being expected to adapt, ideate, and contribute simultaneously. And because the neurodivergent employees who struggle with this often don’t say anything – they’ve learned that naming this difficulty gets read as inflexibility – you lose their insight entirely. They check out. They stop offering ideas. They become the “reliable executors” who never push back, and you mistake their silence for alignment.

What neuroinclusive Agility looks like: You build transition buffers. You give advance notice when possible – even 48 hours makes a difference. You explain why the change is happening, not just what’s changing. You offer asynchronous processing time – a shared doc where people can think through implications before the live discussion. You separate “we’re changing direction” from “we need your input on how” so people aren’t expected to ideate and integrate simultaneously.

Real agility isn’t speed. It’s adaptive capacity. And adaptive capacity requires time to metabolize change – not just react to it. Build transition protocols. When plans change, don’t just announce – prepare. Give people time to process before you expect contribution. Normalize “I need a day to think about this” as strategic, not resistant.

Agility done right doesn’t slow you down. It ensures everyone’s moving in the same direction instead of half your team sprinting forward while the other half is still reorienting.

Teaching: From Uniform Feedback to Personalized Development

The Teaching cylinder is where leaders either unlock growth or accidentally reinforce masking, and where most feedback systems optimize for performance theater rather than actual development.

Here’s the problem with most feedback systems: they’re designed for one kind of processing. Real-time. Verbal. Delivered in 1:1s where the expectation is that you’ll respond, process, and adjust on the spot. For neurotypical employees, this often works. They can think and talk simultaneously. They can metabolize feedback in the moment and articulate next steps.

For many neurodivergent employees, this same format is cognitively expensive. Some brains need time to process feedback separately from the social dynamics of receiving it. Some need it in writing so they can re-read and integrate without the pressure of real-time response. Some need concrete examples, not abstract principles, because their brains don’t generalize the same way.

When you design feedback systems that assume one processing style, you’re not developing people. You’re teaching them to perform development in the format you recognize. They leave 1:1s nodding and smiling – because they’ve learned that’s the expected response – but they haven’t actually integrated the feedback. Or worse, they integrate it too literally, applying a specific correction in one context to every context, because you didn’t explicitly map the boundary conditions.

And because you’re measuring receptiveness to feedback rather than application of feedback, you miss the gap entirely. You think they’re developing. They’re actually just getting better at looking like they’re developing.

What neuroinclusive Teaching looks like: You adapt your feedback delivery to their processing mode – not the other way around. You offer written feedback options because some brains process text better than speech. You separate “what happened” from “what it means” because some brains need the data before the interpretation. You use concrete examples, not abstract principles, because generalizing from abstraction is harder for some cognitive profiles. You give processing time between feedback delivery and action planning.

This isn’t lowering standards. This is increasing feedback uptake by meeting people where their brains actually work. Ask people how they receive feedback best – then honor it. Create multiple formats: live 1:1s, written summaries, recorded video walkthroughs. Let people choose the one that lets them actually learn, not just perform receptiveness.

Teaching done right doesn’t just improve individual performance. It creates a culture where growth is real, not performed.

Ethics: From Inclusion Theater to Protection of Difference

The Ethics cylinder is where neuroinclusive leadership becomes a moral architecture, not just a strategy, and where organizations reveal whether they actually mean what they say about valuing diversity.

Because here’s what most leaders miss: neuroinclusive ethics isn’t about being nice. It’s about protecting the right to work differently – even when it looks like “low engagement” to neurotypical observers. Even when it doesn’t photograph well for the company culture deck. Even when it challenges your assumptions about what “good leadership” looks like.

This is where the rubber meets the road. Organizations say they value diversity – then penalize people for not showing up the way they expect. They say outcomes matter – then dock someone’s performance review for “not being visible enough.” They say they want innovation – then filter out the cognitive profiles most likely to see what they’re missing because they don’t “fit the culture.”

The Ethics cylinder asks: are we building systems that serve people, or demanding that people serve our systems? Are we measuring impact, or measuring conformity? Are we protecting the right to cognitive difference, or are we just performing inclusion while quietly rewarding sameness?

What neuroinclusive Ethics look like: You measure outcomes, not “face time.” You protect asynchronous work as a legitimate mode of contribution. You challenge “culture fit” as a hiring criterion because “fit” is often neurotype conformity in disguise. You redesign “executive presence” criteria to assess leadership impact, not communication style.

Make it explicit: “We protect the right to work differently.” Not as a policy add-on, but as a design principle that shapes how every other cylinder operates. Then audit your systems against it. Every time you see “professionalism,” “presence,” “collaboration,” ask: are we measuring impact, or are we measuring conformity?

This is the Ethics cylinder doing what it’s designed to do: ensuring that the system serves people, not the other way around. And when you get this right, something shifts. Neurodivergent employees stop spending energy on camouflage and start spending it on contribution. Neurotypical employees benefit too, because clarity, autonomy, and outcome-focus aren’t accommodations – they’re good design for everyone.

Ethics done right doesn’t just protect difference. It transforms what excellence looks like.

Six Diagnostic Questions

Before we close, six questions to surface where your CREATE engine might be demanding cognitive conformity without realizing it:

1. Culture – Does “fitting in” actually mean “thinking like us”?

Look at your last three exits. Did the people who left process information differently than the people who stayed? If your culture feels intuitive to some and exhausting to others, you’re not building trust through ambiguity – you’re creating a decoding tax that only some brains can afford to pay.

2. Relationships – How much cognitive energy are people spending just figuring out who to ask?

When someone needs help, can they look it up – or do they have to decode informal hierarchies through social cues? If “building relationships” is treated as a core competency but you’ve never documented who owns what, you’re demanding political fluency as a prerequisite for contribution.

3. Execution – Are you rewarding outcomes, or rewarding the performance of a specific work style?

Look at your last performance review cycle. Did anyone get feedback about “how” they work that had nothing to do with the quality of what they delivered? If “doesn’t speak up in standups” or “works odd hours” shows up as a concern, you’re measuring process conformity, not impact.

4. Agility – When was the last time you called someone “resistant to change” who just needed time to process it?

Think about your last major pivot. Who adapted fastest? Who went quiet? If the people who went quiet were also your deepest thinkers, you didn’t have a resistance problem – you had a dysregulation problem. Real agility includes everyone, not just the brains that pivot in real-time.

5. Teaching – Are people actually integrating your feedback, or just performing receptiveness?

Look at your feedback loops. Do people nod, smile, and then not change? That’s not a motivation problem – that’s a format problem. If you’re only offering one mode of feedback delivery, you’re teaching people to perform growth in the style you recognize, not actually grow.

6. Ethics – How many of your “high performers” are running on fumes?

When was the last time someone burned out after getting a good performance review? If the answer is “recently,” you have a camouflage problem. They were meeting your standards – but the cost of meeting those standards became unsustainable. And you didn’t see it because you were measuring output, not energy.

There’s no such thing as a neutral system. Just design choices that unlock some brains and constrain others.

The question isn’t whether CREATE works for neurodivergent teams. It’s whether you’ve tuned it to let different brains do what they do best – without demanding they pretend to be someone else first.

Because the organizations that figure this out won’t just be more inclusive. They’ll be more resilient, more innovative, and more capable of solving the problems that cognitively homogeneous teams keep missing.

And the leaders who learn to tune their systems for cognitive diversity won’t just retain more talent. They’ll unlock capacity they never knew existed – in the people who were already there, just waiting for the architecture to catch up to their potential.

Next in this series: In Essay 5, you’ll learn how to navigate the inevitable friction when different cognitive styles collide. I’ll show you how the 6C Decision Compass helps you turn cognitive friction from conflict into complementarity – and why most “personality clashes” are actually decision-making mismatches in disguise.

CREATE Cylinder Health Check

Rate your agreement with each statement on a scale of 1-5: (1 = Strongly Disagree, 5 = Strongly Agree)

1. CULTURE: The “rules of how we work here” are explicitly documented rather than absorbed through social observation.

  • 1 = Completely implicit / 2 = Mostly implicit / 3 = Partially explicit / 4 = Mostly explicit / 5 = Fully documented

2. RELATIONSHIPS: Decision authority and role ownership are structurally clear, not decoded through social fluency.

  • 1 = Very ambiguous / 2 = Mostly ambiguous / 3 = Somewhat clear / 4 = Mostly clear / 5 = Completely explicit

3. EXECUTION: People can deliver excellent work using different processes, as long as outcomes meet standards.

  • 1 = One way only / 2 = Limited flexibility / 3 = Some flexibility / 4 = High flexibility / 5 = Outcome-focused design

4. AGILITY: When we pivot or change direction, we build in transition time before expecting contribution.

  • 1 = Never / 2 = Rarely / 3 = Sometimes / 4 = Usually / 5 = Always

5. TEACHING: We adapt feedback delivery to match how people process information, not just our preferred style.

  • 1 = One format only / 2 = Minimal adaptation / 3 = Some adaptation / 4 = Regular adaptation / 5 = Fully personalized

6. ETHICS: We explicitly protect the right to work differently, even when it challenges our norms.

  • 1 = Not protected / 2 = Minimally / 3 = Somewhat / 4 = Significantly / 5 = Core design principle

Scoring Guide:

25-30 points: Your CREATE engine is likely well-tuned for cognitive diversity. Consider: Which specific practices create this environment? How can you document and share them?

18-24 points: Some cylinders are tuned well, others may be creating friction. Consider: Which cylinder scored lowest? That’s your highest-leverage intervention point.

12-17 points: Multiple cylinders are likely demanding conformity. Consider: Start with Culture and Relationships – these two shape everything else.

6-11 points: Your engine may be calibrated exclusively for neurotypical processing. Consider: This isn’t permanent – it’s just current state. Pick one cylinder to retune as a pilot.

Next Steps Based on Your Score:

If you scored 20+:

  • Document what’s working in your top-scoring cylinders

  • Identify which practices could apply to lower-scoring cylinders

  • Share your approach with other leaders – this is rare

If you scored 12-19:

  • Identify your lowest-scoring cylinder

  • Use the relevant section above to design one specific intervention

  • Measure before/after: What changes in engagement, output, or retention?

If you scored below 12:

  • Start with Culture: Document three implicit norms explicitly

  • Then tackle Relationships: Create RACI for your three most ambiguous projects

  • These two changes will cascade through other cylinders

Regardless of score: Read Essay 5 to learn how to use the 6C Decision Compass when different cognitive styles create friction. Because even with a well-tuned CREATE engine, different brains will see problems differently – and that friction is valuable if you know how to navigate it.

The business case is clear.

Organizations that get neuroinclusive leadership right reduce attrition, catch blind spots earlier, and build systems that don’t depend on heroic leadership.
