title: Cognitive Camouflage: The Hidden Tax on Your Best Performers
subtitle: Essay 3: Neurodiversity Series
html:
I was three months into coaching a VP of Engineering when she finally told me the truth.

We’d been working on leadership presence, stakeholder management, all the surface-level stuff her CEO flagged in her last review. She was technically brilliant – everyone agreed on that. But she “wasn’t showing up like a leader.” She “needed to be more visible.” She “could work on executive presence.”

In our fourth session, I asked a different question.

“What does a typical day cost you – energetically?”

Long pause.

Then she said something I’ll never forget:

“By 2pm, I’m done. Not because the work is hard. Because pretending isn’t.”

She wasn’t talking about imposter syndrome. She was talking about something far more expensive.

She was talking about the cognitive budget she spent every single day just to appear neurotypical.

Making eye contact in meetings even though it fractured her ability to listen. Smiling and nodding during small talk she found meaningless. Suppressing the hand movements that helped her think. Forcing herself to speak up in real-time even though her best ideas came hours later, alone, in writing. Performing enthusiasm in the exact register her manager expected, even when the thing being celebrated felt obvious or irrelevant.

“I’m good at my job,” she said quietly. “But I’m exhausted by the performance around my job.”

Before you read further, look at your attrition data differently. Pull the names of people who left in the last two years. Now ask: How many were described as “brilliant but struggled with executive presence”? How many were “great thinkers but didn’t play the political game well”? How many got positive performance reviews right before they quit? Those phrases? They’re masking fatigue disguised as performance problems.

I recognized what she was describing immediately – because I’d been watching my daughter do the same thing for years.

My daughter is autistic. Every day after school, she comes home and collapses. Not because the academics are hard – she’s brilliant. But because she’s spent seven hours monitoring her facial expressions, suppressing her stims, translating her thoughts into the communication style her teachers expect, and performing a version of herself that doesn’t trigger confusion or concern in the adults around her.

She calls it “keeping the mask on.” And by the time she gets home, she’s spent.

The psychologist who evaluated her explained that masking – the cognitive labor of appearing neurotypical when your brain processes the world fundamentally differently – isn’t just exhausting. It’s expensive. It taxes executive function, drains working memory, and leaves less capacity for everything else: learning, connecting, creating, thinking.

Sitting across from this VP, I realized: her performance review wasn’t measuring her leadership capacity.

It was measuring how well she could camouflage.

The Tax You’re Not Tracking

Here’s what most leaders don’t understand about neurodivergent employees:

Your highest performers aren’t just doing their jobs.

They’re doing their jobs while spending 30-40% of their cognitive capacity pretending to process information the way you do.

That’s not a metaphor. That’s math.

Here’s the business case you’re missing: If a neurodivergent professional spends 30% of their cognitive load on masking, and they’re working 50 hours a week, you’re paying for 50 hours but getting 35 hours of contribution. Multiply that by salary ($120K = $36K in lost capacity annually), by tenure, by the number of neurodivergent people in your organization. Now calculate the cost of replacing them when they burn out at 18 months. The “accommodation” wasn’t the expense – the masking tax was.

Every meeting where they have to track social cues instead of content.

Every performance review where “presence” matters more than outcomes.

Every open office where they’re managing sensory overload while trying to solve complex problems.

Every “quick sync” that derails three hours of deep work because your culture valorizes responsiveness over thought.

This isn’t discomfort.

It’s expensive.

And you’re paying for full cognitive capacity while getting a fraction – because the rest is being spent on camouflage.

Researchers call it “masking” – the sustained effort required to hide neurodivergent traits and perform neurotypical behavior. And the data is unambiguous: masking doesn’t just create fatigue. It creates a predictable burnout curve that shows up in every metric you claim to care about.

Decreased creativity. Slower problem-solving. Higher error rates. Increased sick days. And eventually – usually right around the 18-month mark – attrition.

Not because they couldn’t do the work.

Because the camouflage requirement became unsustainable.

What Camouflage Actually Looks Like

Let’s be specific about what we’re asking people to hide.

Appearing “engaged” in meetings designed for neurotypical communication.

For many autistic professionals, eye contact isn’t just uncomfortable – it’s cognitively expensive. It splits attention between tracking facial expressions and processing content. So they develop workarounds: looking at foreheads, nodding at precise intervals, mirroring body language. All of it burns executive function that could be solving the actual problem being discussed.

Hiding stims and self-regulation behaviors.

The hand movements, the fidgeting, the rocking, the need to pace while thinking – these aren’t distractions. They’re how certain brains regulate attention and process complexity. But because they don’t look “professional,” people learn to suppress them. And every minute spent suppressing a stim is a minute not spent thinking clearly.

Translating thoughts into expected formats.

Some brains think in systems, in spatial models, in non-linear webs of association. But if your culture demands linear, verbally-articulated, real-time responses, those brains have to do translation work before they can contribute. It’s like being forced to solve a calculus problem but only being allowed to show your work in prose. Possible? Sure. Efficient? Not even close.

Performing enthusiasm in ways that feel unnatural.

Not everyone signals excitement the same way. For some, enthusiasm is visible – vocal inflection, visible energy, spontaneous celebration. For others, it’s quiet – deep focus, meticulous follow-through, sustained intellectual engagement. But if your culture only reads the former as “engaged,” the latter learns to perform it. And performance is exhausting.

Real-time processing when you need reflection time.

There are brains that think best in motion – rapid-fire, associative, iterative. And there are brains that think best in stillness – deep, integrative, pattern-recognizing. If your meeting culture valorizes the first and pathologizes the second, you’re not measuring intelligence. You’re measuring processing speed. And you’re losing the insights that only emerge when given space to form.

None of this is optional for the person doing it.

It’s the price of entry.

And the cost accumulates – not just daily, but hourly – until the system breaks.

The Camouflage-Forcing Systems You’ve Normalized

Here’s the part that makes this so insidious:

The systems creating the camouflage requirement don’t feel like exclusion.

They feel like “professional standards.”

They feel like “best practices.”

They feel like “how work gets done here.”

But let’s name them for what they are – because until you see them as design choices rather than neutral defaults, you can’t redesign them.

Stand-up meetings that punish processing time.

The daily standup. The weekly all-hands. The “quick sync” that’s never actually quick. These rituals are built for brains that process verbally, in real-time, in front of others. But for anyone who needs time to integrate before articulating, or who thinks more clearly in writing, or who finds social performance cognitively expensive – these meetings aren’t “collaborative.” They’re camouflage requirements. You’re not getting their best thinking. You’re getting their best performance of thinking.

Open offices that assault sensory systems.

The fluorescent lights. The ambient noise. The lack of visual boundaries. The unpredictable interruptions. For neurotypical employees, these might be minor annoyances. For neurodivergent employees – especially autistic and ADHD professionals – they’re constant cognitive drains. Every moment spent managing sensory input is a moment not spent solving problems. And the compounding effect over eight hours? Exhaustion that looks like disengagement but is actually just overload.

“Culture fit” that means “communicates like the founder.”

This one shows up in hiring, in promotions, in performance reviews. “Not sure they’re a culture fit.” Translation: they don’t communicate the same way we do. They don’t socialize the same way. They don’t perform enthusiasm in the register we recognize. But culture fit isn’t neutral. It’s neurotype fit. And every time you screen for it, you’re filtering out cognitive difference before it ever gets a chance to contribute.

Real-time brainstorms that favor fast talkers over deep thinkers.

The whiteboard session. The “let’s riff on this” meeting. The “all ideas welcome” environment that actually means “all ideas that can be articulated in the next 90 seconds while making eye contact and not appearing too attached to them.” These formats don’t surface the best ideas. They surface the ideas that require the least translation time. And the pattern-recognizing, systems-thinking, deeply-integrative ideas? They don’t make it into the room. Not because they don’t exist – but because the format filtered them out.

Performance reviews that measure “presence” over outcomes.

“Could be more visible in meetings.” “Needs to work on executive presence.” “Should take more opportunities to build relationships across the org.”

None of these are about work quality. They’re about performance of engagement. And for neurodivergent employees, that’s the signal – the moment they realize that no matter how well they execute, they’ll always be penalized for not camouflaging effectively enough.

Every single one of these systems is a choice.

And every single one can be redesigned.

When Culture Under Pressure Reveals Who’s Safe

Let’s map this to CREATE – because this isn’t just an HR issue. It’s a systems design issue.

When I work with leaders on the masking tax, I trace it back through the CREATE framework. Culture enforced the neurotypical norm. Relationships stayed ambiguous because explicit communication felt “too rigid.” Execution didn’t flex for different cognitive styles. This isn’t six separate problems – it’s one systems failure expressing itself in six places.

The Culture cylinder is where this shows up most clearly – and most invisibly.

In my book Clutch, I use the NASA Challenger disaster as a case study. Engineers knew the O-rings would fail in cold weather. They said so. Explicitly. Repeatedly. But the organizational culture under pressure prioritized schedule over safety, perception over truth. And the people with the critical information learned – through a thousand small signals – that their input wasn’t welcome.

For neurodivergent employees, the dynamic is structural, not situational.

They don’t need a crisis to learn that their way of processing isn’t valued. They learn it in every meeting where “speaking up” is the only recognized form of contribution. In every performance review that penalizes depth for not looking like speed. In every “culture fit” assessment that treats neurotypical communication as the standard and everything else as deviation.

Culture under pressure reveals who feels safe telling the truth.

And for neurodivergent professionals, the pressure isn’t occasional.

It’s constant.

Because the camouflage requirement is the pressure.

This is why the Relationships cylinder matters so much in neuroinclusive design. Role clarity doesn’t just reduce ambiguity – it protects neurodivergent employees from having to navigate unwritten social rules.

When “who owns what” is explicit, autistic professionals especially can focus on the work instead of decoding the invisible protocols around how to ask for help, when to speak up, how much small talk is required before getting to the point.

Ambiguity isn’t just uncomfortable for some brains. It’s cognitively expensive. And every moment spent trying to reverse-engineer social expectations is a moment not spent doing the thing you hired them to do.

But here’s where most leaders stall out:

They Vision. They Operate. They move fast, they execute hard, they drive outcomes.

But they never shift into VOICES Sculptor gear – the mode where you actually redesign the systems creating the camouflage requirement.

Because that would require slowing down long enough to ask:

“What if the way we’ve always done things isn’t neutral – it’s just familiar?”

The Camouflage Audit: Five Rituals That Force Masking

Let’s make this actionable.

Here are five workplace rituals that – when examined closely – reveal themselves as camouflage requirements. And for each, a redesign option that doesn’t lower standards but expands capacity.

1. All-hands meetings with “popcorn sharing”

What it forces: Real-time verbal processing. Social performance. Spontaneous articulation with no prep time.

What it costs: Anyone who thinks before they speak, processes in writing, or finds public performance cognitively expensive either stays silent (and gets dinged for “not engaging”) or performs (and burns cognitive budget they needed for actual work).

Redesign option: Rotate between live discussion and async input. Post discussion prompts 24 hours in advance. Create a shared doc where people can contribute written responses. In the live meeting, synthesize themes and go deeper on a few – but stop treating “talked in the meeting” as the only valid form of participation.

2. Open-plan offices with “collaboration zones”

What it forces: Constant sensory management. Visual and auditory vigilance. The performance of “being collaborative” even when you need to focus.

What it costs: Sensory overload compounds hourly. For ADHD brains, every interruption resets focus. For autistic brains, unpredictable stimuli create constant low-grade stress. Productivity craters. Error rates climb. By midday, people are managing environment, not solving problems.

Redesign option: Create quiet zones with booking systems. Normalize headphones as “focus mode,” not antisocial behavior. Let people work from home on deep-work days without it counting against them in “collaboration” assessments. Stop treating physical presence as a proxy for engagement.

3. Mandatory video-on Zoom culture

What it forces: Performance of presence. Eye contact simulation (which for many means staring at a camera instead of actually listening). Managing how you look while trying to think.

What it costs: Split attention. Some people process better when they can look away, move, doodle, pace. Forcing video-on turns a cognitive tool (audio-only focus) into a performance requirement.

Redesign option: Default to video-optional. If someone’s contribution quality doesn’t depend on seeing their face, stop requiring it. Save video-on for moments where visual cues actually matter – client pitches, sensitive conversations – and make it the exception, not the default.

4. “Bring your whole self to work” messaging that actually means “perform extroversion”

What it forces: A specific style of authenticity – the kind that’s visible, verbal, emotionally expressive, and socially fluent.

What it costs: People whose “whole self” is quiet, task-focused, and energized by depth rather than breadth learn quickly that the invitation isn’t actually for them. It’s for the version of themselves that looks like the people who already fit.

Redesign option: Reframe authenticity as “do your best work in the way that works for you” – not “perform a specific kind of personality.” Measure outcomes, not performance of engagement. Let people bring their whole capacity, however it shows up.

5. Annual reviews that assess “executive presence” or “cultural ambassador” qualities

What it forces: Conformity to a communication style that’s been institutionalized as “leadership.”

What it costs: Brilliant strategists, systems thinkers, and execution engines get passed over for promotion – not because they can’t lead, but because they don’t look like leaders when “looking like a leader” means neurotypical communication norms.

Redesign option: Separate impact from style. Assess: Are they moving the work forward? Do people trust them? Are they solving problems others can’t? If yes, stop penalizing them for not performing charisma. Leadership has many faces. Stop requiring just one.

Three Diagnostic Questions

Before we close, three questions to surface where your systems might be forcing camouflage without realizing it:

1. Where does “professionalism” actually mean “neurotypical communication style”?

Look at your performance review language. Your hiring rubrics. Your promotion criteria. Every time you see “presence,” “polish,” “gravitas,” “cultural fit” – ask: are we measuring impact, or are we measuring how well someone mirrors the communication style we’re used to?

2. How many of your collaboration rituals actually require real-time, synchronous, verbal contribution to be effective?

Most meetings don’t. But we default to them because they feel collaborative. Meanwhile, the best ideas are getting filtered out before they’re ever voiced – not because people don’t have them, but because the format doesn’t allow time to form them.

3. When was the last time someone burned out after getting a good performance review?

If the answer is “recently,” you probably have a camouflage problem. They were meeting your standards – but the cost of meeting those standards became unsustainable. And you didn’t see it because you were measuring output, not energy.

There’s no such thing as a neutral workplace norm.

Just design choices that include some brains and exclude others.

The question isn’t whether neurodivergent employees can perform in your systems.

It’s whether your systems are designed to extract performance – or unlock capacity.

Because the cost of camouflage isn’t just human.

It’s economic.

You’re paying for talent you’re not fully accessing.

You’re burning out people you can’t afford to lose.

And you’re missing insights you’ll never even know existed – because the people who saw them learned long ago that their way of seeing doesn’t count.

Next in this series: In Essay 4, you’ll see how the CREATE framework you already use can be tuned for cognitive diversity – not as a “neurodiversity initiative” but as operational intelligence. I’ll show you how each cylinder (Culture, Relationships, Execution, Agility, Teaching, Ethics) either unlocks or constrains neurodivergent capacity, and why your existing framework already contains the architecture for neuroinclusive design.

Masking Tax Self-Assessment

Rate your agreement with each statement on a scale of 1-5: (1 = Strongly Disagree, 5 = Strongly Agree)

1. Our workplace norms and expectations are explicitly documented rather than absorbed through social osmosis.

  • 1 = Not documented / 2 = Minimally documented / 3 = Partially documented / 4 = Well documented / 5 = Fully explicit

2. People on my team can succeed without masking neurodivergent traits (stimming, needing processing time, preferring written communication, managing sensory needs).

  • 1 = Cannot succeed / 2 = Very difficult / 3 = Possible but costly / 4 = Generally supported / 5 = Fully supported

3. Our performance reviews measure outcomes and impact rather than “presence,” “visibility,” or communication style.

  • 1 = Style-focused / 2 = Mostly style / 3 = Mixed / 4 = Mostly outcomes / 5 = Outcomes-focused

4. I can identify specific systems in our organization that require neurodivergent employees to spend cognitive energy on camouflage rather than contribution.

  • 1 = Cannot identify / 2 = Vague sense / 3 = Some clarity / 4 = Clear identification / 5 = Systematically mapped

5. When high performers leave after positive reviews, we investigate whether masking fatigue contributed to their departure.

  • 1 = Never / 2 = Rarely / 3 = Sometimes / 4 = Usually / 5 = Always

Scoring Guide:

20-25 points: Your systems likely minimize masking requirements. Consider: Can you document what makes your environment less camouflage-intensive? What practices could other leaders learn from?

15-19 points: You’re reducing some camouflage requirements but likely have blind spots. Consider: Which of the five rituals in the Camouflage Audit apply to your organization? What would it take to redesign one?

10-14 points: Your systems may be forcing significant masking without your awareness. Consider: Look at your last three exits of high performers. Were any described as “brilliant but...” or received coaching on “presence” before leaving?

5-9 points: Masking requirements are likely creating hidden costs throughout your organization. Consider: Calculate the cognitive load tax: if 30% of capacity is spent on camouflage, and average salary is $100K, you’re paying $30K per person annually for performance theater instead of contribution.

Next Steps Based on Your Score:

If you scored 15+:

  • Audit one system for camouflage requirements using the five rituals framework

  • Document what your team does well (explicit norms, flexible formats, outcome-focused assessment)

  • Share practices with other leaders – this is rare and valuable

If you scored 10-14:

  • Pull performance review language from the last year: count how many times you see “presence,” “visibility,” “polish,” “gravitas”

  • For each instance, ask: “Was this about impact or about communication style?”

  • Redesign one high-frequency ritual (daily standup, brainstorm format, review process)

If you scored below 10:

  • Review your attrition data: Who left in the last 18 months who was described as “brilliant but didn’t fit” or “struggled with executive presence”?

  • Calculate the replacement cost of one departure. That’s your baseline for what masking requirements are costing you.

  • Choose ONE camouflage-forcing system to redesign (start with meetings – highest frequency, clearest intervention)

Regardless of score: Read Essay 4 to see how the CREATE framework – the system you’re already using – can be tuned for cognitive diversity. Because you don’t need a new framework. You need to see how your existing one works differently for different brains.

The business case is clear.

Organizations that get neuroinclusive leadership right reduce attrition, catch blind spots earlier, and build systems that don’t depend on heroic leadership.

I’ve spent 20 years coaching leaders through this work—from independent schools to USAID to tech startups. I have the complete diagnostic tools, the frameworks, and the implementation roadmaps. But let’s start simple.

title: The Infographic of Broken Dreams: A Brief Rant on Leadership Slop
html:
They say a picture is worth a thousand words – but not if it already has a thousand words on it.

Scrolling through LinkedIn and Instagram has become an exercise in watching people try to cram an entire MBA curriculum into a single image. The algorithm demands sacrifice, and brother, are we sacrificing – mostly our eyesight and our will to live.

You know the ones. “47 LEADERSHIP HACKS THAT WILL TRANSFORM YOUR TEAM 🚀💡🔥” crammed into a single graphic with a gradient background that screams “I just discovered Canva.” Seven different fonts fighting for dominance. Bullet points nested inside bullet points. A sidebar. Three callout boxes. An icon library that looks like emoji vomit. And somehow, impossibly, a QR code.

All on one image.

It’s the all-you-can-eat buffet approach to wisdom: quantity over quality, volume over value, and if we can fit enough words onto a single JPEG maybe nobody will notice we’re just repackaging “be nice and work hard.”

A Brief History of Crimes Against Clarity

Remember the Afghan War PowerPoint slide? That glorious spaghetti diagram that looked like what happens when you ask AI to visualize a migraine? General Stanley McChrystal took one look at it and said, “When we understand that slide, we’ll have won the war.”

At least that monstrosity was meant to be part of a presentation – context provided separately by an actual human explaining things. These Instagram infographics? They’re trying to be the entire war strategy, the briefing, the appendices, and the executive summary all in one 1080x1080 pixel square.

It’s like they looked at that Afghan slide and thought, “You know what this needs? More information and less space.”

Edward Tufte is Weeping Somewhere

Edward Tufte literally wrote the book on visual communication. Multiple books, actually. The Visual Display of Quantitative Information is sitting on design shelves gathering dust while LinkedIn gurus create what Tufte would call “chartjunk” – but somehow worse, because at least chartjunk was usually trying to display actual data.

These infographics aren’t chartjunk. They’re everything-junk.

Tufte’s principles are devastatingly simple:

  • Maximize data-ink ratio: Every element should convey information

  • Avoid chartjunk: Decoration that interferes with understanding

  • Show the data: Let the information speak for itself

  • Encourage comparison: Make relationships visible

The leadership infographic industrial complex looked at these principles and said, “What if we did the exact opposite of all of that?”

Maximum decoration. Minimum actual information. Data buried under seven layers of gradients and drop shadows. And the only comparison you can make is “this one has slightly fewer emoji than the last one.”

Tufte would call it “contempt for the audience.” I call it a hostage situation, with your eyeballs as the hostages.

Richard Mayer Would Also Like a Word

And then there’s Richard Mayer, who spent his career studying how people actually learn from multimedia. He came up with 12 principles. These one-page monstrosities violate all of them simultaneously:

  • Coherence Principle: Cut the extraneous crap (violated by: cramming in 63 numbered tips)

  • Signaling Principle: Highlight what actually matters (violated by: making everything the same size in different colors)

  • Redundancy Principle: Don’t overload people with the same information in multiple formats (violated by: icons + text + more text + decorative text)

  • Spatial/Temporal Contiguity: Put related information together (violated by: putting everything everywhere because there’s nowhere else to put it)

But do the “50 Ways to Be a Better Boss” infographic makers care? They do not. They’re out here treating white space like it’s a moral failing, speedrunning cognitive overload like it’s an Olympic sport.

Between Tufte and Mayer, we have decades of research on visual communication. And yet here we are, in the hellscape of “23 TRAITS OF EXCEPTIONAL LEADERS” where every principle is honored in the breach.

What Years of Teaching Taught Me

I used to teach kids how to create presentations. Not because I had mad graphic design skills – I don’t – but because years in a classroom taught me some basic rules about communication.

The fundamental truth: If you’re trying to teach something, clarity beats comprehensiveness every single time.

A good visual should have:

  • One main idea

  • Enough breathing room that your eye knows where to land

  • A reason to exist beyond “the algorithm likes images”

If your infographic needs footnotes, you’ve already lost.

If someone needs to zoom in to read it, you’ve already lost.

If it takes longer to parse your graphic than it would to just read a paragraph, what are we even doing here?

The Context Problem (Or: Why Workshop Handouts ≠ Instagram Posts)

Here’s where this gets tricky. I’ve facilitated plenty of workshops where participants asked for a one-pager or some sort of documentation as a take-away. This is a good request. People want to remember what they learned. They want something to reference later. They want to share it with their teams.

In that context – with you standing there explaining things, the workshop’s shared experience still warm, and the ability to ask questions – a dense one-pager actually works. It’s a memory aid, not a teaching tool. It’s anchored to the conversation you just had.

But then someone takes that workshop handout, screenshots it, strips away all the context, and posts it to LinkedIn with “POWERFUL INSIGHTS 💡” and suddenly it’s doing a job it was never designed to do.

The difference:

  • Workshop handout: “Remember when we discussed X? Here’s the framework we built together.”

  • Instagram infographic: “Here is X with no setup, no examples, no nuance, and you have 2.5 seconds to absorb it while scrolling past a dog video.”

One is a souvenir. The other is trying to be the entire vacation.

And look, I get the impulse. You spent three hours facilitating a great session. You want to share that value with people who couldn’t attend. Noble goal! But the solution isn’t to cram the entire workshop onto a single image and call it “accessible.”

Some actual best practices for sharing frameworks digitally:

  1. Pick one piece: Share the most compelling insight, not the entire model. One wedge of the pie, not the whole bakery.

  2. Lead with context: A short paragraph explaining why this matters before showing what it is. Revolutionary, I know.

  3. Assume zero prior knowledge: Your workshop participants had three hours with you. Instagram has 2.5 seconds. Act accordingly.

  4. Make peace with multiple posts: If your framework has six parts, that’s six pieces of content. Not six sections crammed onto one graphic.

  5. Link to the real thing: Use the post to drive people to a PDF, a blog post, a video – somewhere they can actually learn instead of just squinting.

  6. Test the phone view: If you can’t read it clearly on your phone without zooming, no one else can either. That’s not engagement, that’s an eye exam.

The hard truth? Most frameworks worth teaching can’t be taught in a single image. And trying to force it just creates visual noise that helps no one.

The Greatest Irony

These “thought leaders” posting “40 ESSENTIAL COMMUNICATION SKILLS 📊✨” on infographics so dense they require a magnifying glass and a prayer are the same people charging $5,000 to teach you executive presence.

It’s like getting fitness advice from someone who gets winded opening a jar of pickles.

Or minimalism tips from a hoarder.

Or – and hear me out – leadership clarity from someone whose visual communication strategy is “JUST PUT ALL OF IT IN THERE.”

If your leadership framework requires 73 numbered points on a single image, you don’t have wisdom. You have a hoarding problem with bullet points and a fundamental misunderstanding of what an infographic is supposed to do.

A Modest Proposal

Here’s a wild idea: maybe hire an actual graphic designer?

I know, I know. Revolutionary. But there are literally thousands of talented designers on Fiverr, Upwork, and 99designs who would love to take your 47-point manifesto and turn it into something that doesn’t make people’s eyes bleed. For like, $50-$200.

That’s it. That’s the cost of not assaulting your audience’s visual cortex.

Less than your monthly LinkedIn Premium subscription. Less than that leadership book you bought and didn’t read. Less than one fancy coffee per day for a week.

But no. Instead, we get template #47 from Canva with every text box filled in because we paid for the whole canvas, we’re gonna use the whole canvas.

What This Could Be Instead

Here’s the thing: infographics can actually be great. A single compelling stat. A simple comparison. A visual metaphor that makes a concept click. Think Ben Franklin’s Join or Die. Or Charles Joseph Minard’s famous flow map of Napoleon’s Russia campaign.

But that requires choosing. Editing. Having the confidence to say, “This one thing matters most.” Minard’s point: This is what happens when you invade Russia in the winter.

Instead, we get everything bagels masquerading as insight – all the toppings, none of the bread, and you’re supposed to eat it off a screen while scrolling past forty other everything bagels that look exactly the same.

So what would a good one look like?

[Imagine generous white space here]
[One compelling image or data point]

Be clear.
Be kind.
Get out of the way.

Three lines. Not 73.

Epilogue: Look, I get it. The algorithm rewards this stuff. People are trying to build audiences and demonstrate expertise and fit into the 1080x1080 or 4:5 attention economy.

But maybe – maybe – we could collectively agree that if your “quick visual guide” requires people to screenshot and zoom in on their phone to read your 8-point font, it’s not actually a visual guide. It’s a PDF that got lost and ended up on Instagram.

Just a thought. From someone with no graphic design skills whatsoever, but enough years in a classroom to know the difference between teaching and cramming.

And someone who’s been asked for plenty of one-pagers after workshops – which is great! Just know that what works in a room with context doesn’t necessarily work floating naked on the internet.

Choose wisely.

title: Matching Brains to Organizational Problems
subtitle: Essay 2: Neurodiversity Series
html:
A few years ago, I was observing a leadership team struggle through a decision.

Smart people. Aligned on values. Genuinely committed to getting it right. But the conversation kept looping – same questions, same frameworks, same impasse.

Then I noticed something: everyone in the room processed information the same way.

Sequential. Verbal. Collaborative. They could all think on their feet, build on each other’s ideas in real time, and articulate their reasoning as they went.

It looked like high-functioning teamwork.

But they kept missing the same kind of problem – the ones that required zooming out, sitting with ambiguity, or asking a fundamentally different question than the ones the data was answering.

They weren’t lacking intelligence. They were lacking cognitive diversity.

They’d all been hired, promoted, and rewarded for thinking in a particular way. And now that sameness – the thing that made them feel like a cohesive team – was creating a strategic blindspot they couldn’t see from inside their own thinking patterns.

Quick diagnostic: Think about your last strategic planning session. Who noticed the patterns no one else saw? Who asked the “dumb question” that actually exposed the flaw in your logic? Who came back three days later with the synthesis everyone needed? Those are your neurodivergent thinkers – whether they’re diagnosed or not. And if you can’t name anyone who fits that description, that’s your signal.

Because the problem wasn’t that these leaders weren’t smart enough.

It’s that they were all smart in the same way.

The Question No One’s Asking

Most leaders treat neurodiversity as a compliance issue.

They ask: “How do we accommodate this person?”

Or, if they’re more progressive: “How do we help this person succeed despite their diagnosis?”

Both questions start from the same flawed premise – that neurodivergence is a deviation from an optimal cognitive norm, and the organization’s job is to smooth over the gaps so the person can still perform.

But here’s what that framing misses:

Different brains don’t just process differently. They see differently. And that difference isn’t a bug to fix – it’s a strategic capacity most organizations are leaving entirely untapped.

The question isn’t “How do we accommodate this person?”

It’s “Which organizational problems actually require this cognitive profile to solve effectively?”

Because once you stop thinking of neurodiversity as diagnosis categories to accommodate and start thinking of it as a cognitive toolkit, everything changes.

You stop designing for conformity.

You start designing for complementarity.

The Cognitive Profiles Your Strategy Is Missing

Let’s be specific.

When I work with organizations stuck on the same recurring problems – innovation stalls, quality failures, strategic blind spots, execution gaps – I don’t start by looking at competencies or credentials.

I start by looking at cognitive profiles.

Because certain kinds of problems don’t yield to certain kinds of thinking. And if your team is cognitively homogeneous, you’ll keep solving the same problems while the others compound quietly in the background.

Here’s what I mean – and what these cognitive styles actually unlock:

Autistic cognition – Pattern recognition at scale. Systems thinking. Logical consistency. Quality control that doesn’t fatigue under repetition. The ability to hold a mental model of an entire system and notice when one variable is out of alignment.

When an autistic analyst says “This doesn’t match the pattern,” they’re seeing variance that neurotypical brains average out into noise. When they say “This feels structurally wrong,” they’re detecting inconsistency at a resolution most teams can’t access. This isn’t nitpicking – it’s the brain that sees the structural flaw everyone else has been working around.

Dyslexic cognition – Big-picture strategy. Narrative thinking. The ability to synthesize across domains and see connections others miss. Crisis navigation that doesn’t freeze under ambiguity.

When a dyslexic strategist says “This feels off,” they’re detecting structural misalignment three moves down the road. While others optimize within known constraints, dyslexic thinkers are scanning for the paradigm shift, the reframe, the entirely different way of solving the problem. In evolutionary terms, this is “explorer” cognition – the brain that thrives when the terrain is unfamiliar and the old maps don’t work.

ADHD cognition – Novelty detection. Rapid pattern-switching. The ability to hyperfocus when interest aligns with task. Kinetic ideation – thinking that happens through movement, through trying, through iterating in real time rather than planning in advance.

When an ADHD innovator says “What if we tried this completely different approach?” they’re offering a solution that wasn’t constrained by how things have always been done. This is the brain that catches the early signal everyone else filters out as noise. The one that gets bored with stable systems and starts experimenting before the data says it’s time.

Anxiety-driven cognition – Threat modeling. Scenario planning. Risk mitigation that doesn’t require a crisis to activate. The brain that’s already asking “what if this fails?” while everyone else is celebrating the launch. This isn’t pessimism – it’s predictive vigilance. And in high-stakes environments, it’s the cognitive profile that prevents catastrophic blindspots.

Now here’s the part most leaders miss:

None of these profiles are better than the others.

They’re complementary.

And when you treat them as such – when you stop trying to force every brain into the same workflow and start matching cognitive profiles to organizational problems – you don’t just get better accommodations.

You get better solutions.

The Business Case You’re Not Seeing

This isn’t academic theory. The ROI is measurable.

JPMorgan Chase’s Autism at Work program reports a 50% increase in productivity among teams with autistic professionals in technology roles. Microsoft’s neurodiversity hiring initiative shows 30% improvement in quality assurance outcomes. SAP reports that teams with neurodivergent members are 30% more productive than those without.

The gains aren’t coming from “accommodation costs” being offset. They’re coming from accessing pattern recognition, systems thinking, and quality control that neurotypical teams simply can’t match.

The question isn’t whether you can afford to hire neurodivergent professionals.

It’s whether you can afford to keep solving problems with only one cognitive toolkit.

From Accommodation to Architecture

Let’s map this to CREATE – because this isn’t just about hiring. It’s about system design.

When I trace innovation failures or quality breakdowns back through the framework, the issue almost never lives in individual performance. It lives in Execution – specifically, in the assumption that execution systems should be designed for linear, sequential processing.

Most organizations build their workflows like assembly lines: clear steps, predictable handoffs, uniform expectations for how work gets done. And for certain kinds of problems – the ones where the path is known and the variables are controlled – that works beautifully.

But innovation bottlenecks, strategic blind spots, and quality failures don’t respond to linear thinking.

They require non-linear cognition.

They need the brain that sees the whole system at once.

The brain that notices the pattern everyone else missed.

The brain that asks “but what if we’re solving the wrong problem?”

And if your execution systems are designed exclusively for neurotypical processing, you’re not just making life harder for neurodivergent employees.

You’re systematically excluding the cognitive tools you need to solve your hardest problems.

This is where cognitive complementarity becomes a design principle, not a diversity initiative.

You don’t redesign execution to be “nicer.”

You redesign it because certain organizational problems literally cannot be solved by cognitively homogeneous teams.

Decision-Making Through a Neurodivergent Lens

Let’s get even more specific – because this plays out in how decisions get made.

The 6C Decision Compass maps six decision-making modes: Command, Consultative, Collaborative, Consensus, Core Expertise, Choice. Most leaders assume these modes are context-dependent – you choose the right one based on urgency, complexity, or stakeholder buy-in.

But here’s what I’ve observed working with neurodivergent professionals:

Cognitive profile doesn’t just influence how someone works. It influences which decision-making mode they need to perform at their best.

Autistic professionals often thrive in Core Expertise and Command environments – where the rules are clear, the logic is transparent, and the decision path is structurally sound. Ambiguity doesn’t feel like freedom; it feels like cognitive noise. Give them clarity, and they’ll execute with a precision most teams can’t match. But force them into a Collaborative decision process where the social dynamics are as important as the logic? You’ve just introduced a cognitive tax that has nothing to do with their ability to solve the problem.

ADHD brains often excel when given Choice – autonomy over how, when, and in what order they tackle work. The structure isn’t the timeline; it’s the outcome. Tell them what needs to happen and why it matters, then let them find their own path. That autonomy activates hyperfocus. But lock them into rigid, sequential workflows with no room for improvisation? You’ve turned their greatest strength – adaptive, kinetic problem-solving – into a liability.

Dyslexic thinkers often need Consultative mode – the chance to talk through their thinking out loud, to build the idea in real time through conversation rather than pre-formed written briefs. Their brilliance doesn’t show up in the first draft of the memo. It shows up in the way they synthesize across inputs, connect disparate ideas, and reframe the entire question mid-discussion. But if your culture requires “come to the meeting prepared with a written proposal,” you’ve just filtered out the cognitive profile most likely to see the strategic opportunity everyone else missed.

Anxiety-driven cognition performs best when decisions include explicit risk assessment – when scenario planning and threat modeling aren’t treated as pessimism but as essential inputs. These are the people who will save you from overconfidence bias. But only if you create decision structures where “what could go wrong?” is a valued question, not a mood-killer.

This isn’t about accommodating preferences.

It’s about designing decision structures that unlock cognitive capacity instead of suppressing it.

The Organizational Bottleneck Matrix

Here’s where this gets practical.

Stop thinking about neurodiversity as a talent pipeline issue. Start thinking about it as a problem-solving architecture issue.

Different organizational bottlenecks require different cognitive profiles. And when you map them explicitly, hiring becomes strategic – not because you’re “checking a diversity box,” but because you’re matching brains to problems.

Innovation stalls → You need explorer brains. Dyslexic and ADHD cognition excel here. These are the thinkers who get bored with optimization and start experimenting before the data proves it’s safe. They don’t wait for permission to see differently – they literally can’t help it. If your product roadmap feels stale, if your strategy feels incremental, if everyone’s solving the same problem slightly better instead of asking if it’s the right problem – you don’t have an innovation problem. You have a cognitive homogeneity problem.

Quality failures → You need exploiter brains. Autistic cognition, detail-oriented processing, the kind of thinking that doesn’t fatigue under repetition and doesn’t miss the edge case everyone else assumes won’t matter. These are the people who see the system-level inconsistency that’s been hiding in plain sight. They’re not being pedantic – they’re modeling structural integrity in real time. If your quality control keeps missing the same category of error, it’s because you don’t have enough brains wired to notice inconsistency at that resolution.

Strategic blind spots → You need pattern detectors. Autistic and anxiety-driven cognition both excel here – one sees structural patterns, the other sees threat patterns. These are the people who will tell you what you don’t want to hear before it becomes what you can’t ignore. If your leadership team keeps getting surprised by risks “no one saw coming,” it’s not that no one saw them. It’s that the people who saw them either weren’t in the room or weren’t listened to when they spoke.

Execution gaps → You need systems thinkers + kinetic activators. Pair autistic cognition (who can hold the whole system in mind and see where dependencies break) with ADHD cognition (who can move fast, iterate in real time, and adapt when the plan hits reality). Separately, they might struggle – one needs structure, one needs autonomy. Together, they’re the execution engine most organizations are trying to build with homogeneous teams and wondering why it keeps stalling.

This isn’t theory.

This is the pattern I see again and again when teams finally start solving the problems that had been chronic for years.

They didn’t get smarter.

They got cognitively diverse.

The Turn: From Deficit to Design

Here’s the shift that has to happen – and it starts with language.

Stop saying “accommodation.”

Start saying “optimization.”

Because when you design a meeting structure that allows for written pre-reads and post-meeting async input, you’re not accommodating ADHD or autistic employees.

You’re optimizing for insight capture.

When you create decision protocols that separate thinking time from speaking time, you’re not accommodating introverts or slow processors.

You’re reducing groupthink and increasing decision quality.

When you build workflows that allow for hyperfocus blocks and non-linear task sequencing, you’re not accommodating neurodivergent work styles.

You’re unlocking the conditions under which certain kinds of problems actually get solved.

The cognitive profiles you’re calling “accommodations” are actually the missing tools in your problem-solving toolkit.

And the systems you’re designing to “help people succeed despite their differences” are systematically preventing those differences from doing what they do best: solving the problems neurotypical cognition keeps missing.

Three Diagnostic Questions

Before we close, three questions to surface where your organization might be leaving cognitive capacity on the table:

1. What problems keep recurring despite hiring “smart people”?

If you keep hitting the same walls – innovation stalls, quality failures, strategic blind spots – the issue isn’t intelligence. It’s cognitive homogeneity. You’re hiring people who think the same way, which means they’ll see the same solutions and miss the same problems.

2. Where are you designing workflows around one cognitive style and calling it “best practice”?

Linear, sequential, verbally-driven, real-time collaboration isn’t a neutral default. It’s a cognitive preference that’s been institutionalized. And every time you call it “best practice,” you’re filtering out the cognitive profiles that could solve the problems you can’t.

3. When was the last time someone saw a problem no one else noticed – and how did your system respond?

If the answer is “we told them it wasn’t a priority” or “we asked them to focus on their assigned work,” you’ve just trained pattern-detectors to stop detecting. And the next time they see something critical, they won’t say anything. Not because they stopped seeing it – but because your system taught them their way of seeing doesn’t count.

There’s no such thing as an average brain.

Just cognitive profiles your strategy hasn’t learned to leverage yet.

The question isn’t whether neurodivergent employees can succeed in your systems.

It’s whether your systems are designed to solve the problems only they can see.

Because the cost of cognitive conformity isn’t just human.

It’s strategic.

And the organizations that learn to match brains to problems won’t just be more inclusive.

They’ll be more resilient, more adaptive, and more capable of solving the challenges neurotypical cognition keeps missing.

Next in this series: In Essay 3, I’ll show you the hidden tax your best performers are paying – the cognitive camouflage requirement that’s draining 30-40% of their capacity before they even start their actual work. You’ll learn to recognize masking fatigue before it becomes attrition, and understand why your “executive presence” feedback might be measuring camouflage skill rather than leadership capacity.

Cognitive Diversity Self-Assessment

Rate your agreement with each statement on a scale of 1-5: (1 = Strongly Disagree, 5 = Strongly Agree)

1. I can clearly identify which recurring organizational problems might require different cognitive styles to solve.

  • 1 = Cannot identify / 2 = Rarely identify / 3 = Sometimes identify / 4 = Usually identify / 5 = Clearly identify

2. Our team composition intentionally includes people who think and process information in fundamentally different ways.

  • 1 = Not at all / 2 = Slightly / 3 = Somewhat / 4 = Significantly / 5 = Deliberately and systematically

3. When someone identifies a problem others missed, our system treats their perspective as valuable insight rather than tangential concern.

  • 1 = Rarely valued / 2 = Sometimes valued / 3 = Usually valued / 4 = Consistently valued / 5 = Actively sought

4. Our workflows and decision-making processes work well for people who think non-linearly, need processing time, or work best asynchronously.

  • 1 = Don’t work at all / 2 = Work poorly / 3 = Work adequately / 4 = Work well / 5 = Designed for this

5. I understand which specific cognitive profiles (pattern detection, systems thinking, strategic synthesis, etc.) would help solve our current organizational bottlenecks.

  • 1 = No understanding / 2 = Slight understanding / 3 = Moderate understanding / 4 = Strong understanding / 5 = Clear and specific understanding

Scoring Guide:

20-25 points: You’re likely leveraging cognitive diversity as strategic architecture. Consider: How can you document and scale your approach? What specific outcomes can you attribute to cognitive complementarity?

15-19 points: You recognize the value of different thinking styles but may not be systematically designing for them. Consider: Which organizational problems keep recurring? What cognitive profile might solve them? How could you intentionally design for that profile?

10-14 points: Your systems may be designed for cognitive conformity even if your intentions are inclusive. Consider: When was the last time someone who thinks very differently from you solved a problem your team had been stuck on? If you can’t remember, that’s your signal.

5-9 points: You’re likely selecting for cognitive sameness and experiencing the strategic costs. Consider: Look at your recurring problems – innovation stalls, quality failures, strategic blind spots. These aren’t execution problems. They’re cognitive homogeneity problems.

Next Steps Based on Your Score:

If you scored 15+:

  • Map your current team’s cognitive profiles (even informally – who spots patterns? who sees big picture? who catches risks?)

  • Identify which organizational bottlenecks align with which cognitive strengths

  • Design one pilot project that deliberately pairs complementary cognitive styles

If you scored 10-14:

  • Audit your last three recurring problems: What cognitive profile might have caught them earlier?

  • Interview one person on your team who thinks very differently from you: “What do you see that others miss?”

  • Choose one workflow to redesign: Can it work for both linear and non-linear thinkers?

If you scored below 10:

  • List your three biggest organizational bottlenecks (innovation, quality, strategy, execution)

  • For each, ask: “What if this isn’t an execution problem but a cognitive toolkit problem?”

  • Read the Organizational Bottleneck Matrix section again – which cognitive profiles are you missing?

Regardless of score: Read Essay 3 to learn how the “masking tax” is bleeding your best performers – and how to recognize cognitive camouflage before it becomes burnout and attrition. Because before you can leverage cognitive diversity, you need to stop asking people to hide it.

The business case is clear.

Organizations that get neuroinclusive leadership right reduce attrition, catch blind spots earlier, and build systems that don’t depend on heroic leadership.

I’ve spent 20 years coaching leaders through this work—from independent schools to USAID to tech startups. I have the complete diagnostic tools, the frameworks, and the implementation roadmaps. But let’s start simple.

Book a free call. Let’s figure out where you are.

We’ll diagnose what’s happening in your systems, identify where friction is costing you capacity, and map whether this work makes sense for you right now. No pitch. No obligation.

title: The Average Brain Myth Is Bleeding Your Best Talent
subtitle: Essay 1: Neurodiversity Series
html:
For years, I sat in leadership meetings – literally in the pews, as it were – and wouldn’t say a word for an hour. My colleagues would debate, riff, build on each other’s ideas in real time. I’d nod. I’d listen. I’d stay quiet.

And then I’d go for my afternoon run.

That’s when it would hit – the flood of ideas, the connections I’d been tracking, the feedback I should have offered, the questions that mattered most. My brain needed movement and solitude to do its work. I’ve come to understand about myself that I am a slow processor and a deep thinker. The insights don’t arrive on command. They arrive when the pressure lifts.

But here’s what leaders saw: a lack of engagement. A lack of interest. Maybe even a lack of leadership potential.

The structure and pace of the meetings didn’t allow for thinking time. Often held during lunch, there was relentless pressure to get stuff done – though ironically, decisions often didn’t get made either. We’d talk in circles, rush to conclusions, then revisit the same issues two weeks later because no one had actually thought about them.

I wasn’t disengaged. I was designed differently.

My silence wasn’t absence. It was discipline. I was doing the cognitive work others skipped – the slow, careful pattern recognition that happens when you resist the pressure to speak before you’re ready.

But the system had already decided what “engagement” looked like. And it looked nothing like me.

You probably have your own version of this story. Maybe you’ve watched someone go quiet in meetings and wondered if they cared. Maybe you’ve written them off as “not leadership material” because they don’t think out loud. Or maybe you are the person who goes quiet – and you’ve learned to read your own silence as a professional liability rather than a different way of processing complexity.

That’s when I realized: we’ve built entire organizations around a neurological fiction.

What Happened When I Redesigned the Room

When I started facilitating meetings at the organizational level, I brought this understanding with me.

I began building in pauses – actual thinking time before asking participants to respond. Not vague “let’s take a moment” pauses. Structured silence: “We’re going quiet for three minutes. Get out a notepad if you need to. Walk to the window if that helps. When we come back, we’ll hear from people who rarely speak first.”

Something remarkable happened.

The pauses didn’t just help the slow processors like me. They helped everyone. The “muggles” – the quick thinkers who normally dominated the airspace – became better listeners. Instead of their brains racing ahead to their next comment, they actually heard what others were saying.

The quality of the dialogue shifted. Decisions became sharper. Follow-through improved.

Neurodiversity-friendly design wasn’t just accommodation. It was better practice, period.

But it got me thinking: if a simple structural shift could unlock that much collective intelligence, what else were we missing? It wasn’t the people who needed fixing. It was the norms and structure of the meetings – the system itself – that was the issue.

We’ve designed leadership cultures that reward speed over depth, mistake verbal processing for critical thinking, and privilege extroverted cognition while wondering why our decisions lack nuance. We call it “collaboration” when it’s often just performance. We promote people who think out loud and overlook people who think deeply.

And then we’re surprised when our leadership pipelines are narrow, our decisions are shallow, and our best thinkers burn out trying to conform to a rhythm that was never built for them.

I wasn’t the problem. The system was.

The question isn’t “How do we get quieter people to speak up?” The question is: “How do we build systems that unlock the intelligence already in the room – including the intelligence that doesn’t perform on cue?”

Because if we keep building leadership cultures that reward only one way of thinking, we’re not developing leaders. We’re selecting for sameness and calling it strength.

The Myth We Keep Building For

The “average employee” is a myth – an imaginary person who thinks in predictable patterns, communicates on cue, and thrives in standardized environments. Someone who loves back-to-back meetings, makes crisp eye contact, answers quickly in real time, and never needs a minute to process before responding.

They don’t exist. Yet our systems are still designed for them.

Hiring rubrics. Feedback models. Performance metrics. Meeting structures. Leadership assessments. Almost all of them assume a uniform way of processing information, managing attention, and demonstrating competence. And when someone doesn’t conform – when they need thinking time before speaking, or write more clearly than they talk, or can’t track a conversation while maintaining eye contact – we don’t redesign the system.

We ask the human to adapt.

To perform. To mask.

This isn’t just a moral failure. It’s a strategic one.

Because neurodiversity – ADHD, autism, dyslexia, and the broader spectrum of cognitive variance – isn’t a deficit to accommodate. It’s a design advantage we’re systematically suppressing.

The Innovation We’re Leaving on the Table

McKinsey’s research shows that companies in the top quartile for ethnic and cultural diversity outperform their peers by 36% in profitability. That’s not a rounding error – for a $100M company, that’s $36M in performance difference. But here’s what most organizations miss: that advantage doesn’t come from demographic representation alone. It comes from cognitive friction – from different brains seeing different patterns in the same data.

Teams with neurodivergent members consistently outperform homogeneous ones in pattern recognition, systems thinking, and nonlinear problem-solving. Not because neurodivergence is a superpower. Because cognitive variance creates the conditions for breakthrough thinking.

But here’s the paradox we’re living in:

We say we want creativity – but we reward conformity.

We say we value difference – but we demand cognitive disguise.

We claim we’re building inclusive cultures – but we’re still measuring contribution through a neurotypical lens.

And the cost isn’t the energy required to “accommodate” neurodivergent professionals.

The cost is the chronic cognitive load required for them to pretend to think like everyone else.

It’s the double work of not only doing your job – but doing it as if your brain processes information the same way as the person who designed the job description. It’s the executive function tax of translating your natural workflow into someone else’s preferred communication style. It’s the attention residue left over after every meeting where you spent more energy managing how you’re perceived than actually contributing what you know.

If you’ve ever watched a brilliant mind burn out in your organization, this is likely why. The system demanded they spend more energy managing perception than contributing insight. Eventually, that math stops working.

Why Leaders Can’t See It: The Two-Gear Trap

When I coach leaders through this blindspot, I almost always find the same pattern.

They operate in only two gears – Visionary and Operator.

They cast vision. They drive outcomes. They move fast. They’re deeply committed to performance, to results, to momentum. And that commitment is genuine.

But neurodivergent professionals don’t just need speed and direction.

They need Coach and Inclusive gears – leaders who pause, ask, listen, and co-design. Who create space for processing. Who understand that silence isn’t always hesitation; sometimes it’s integration.

Here’s the part that makes this so difficult: these leaders think they’re being supportive. They genuinely care about their people. They’ve read the inclusion training materials. They’ve nodded through the bias workshops.

But they’ve never learned to listen beyond their own brain type.

So when someone goes quiet in a meeting, they read it as disengagement – not as evidence that the meeting design itself excludes a certain kind of thinking.

They don’t ask: “How do you process best?”

They ask: “Why aren’t you speaking up?”

The framing reveals everything.

Because what we’re witnessing isn’t a people problem. It’s a systems problem dressed up as a performance issue.

And that’s where the heroic leadership myth does its most insidious work. Because instead of adapting systems to fit different brains, we reward the leaders who can force-fit people into existing structures. We promote the manager who “handles difficult personalities” – never questioning whether the system itself is what made those personalities seem difficult in the first place.

That’s not inclusion.

That’s endurance theater.

And it’s bleeding organizations dry of the very cognitive diversity they claim to need.

Culture, But for Whom?

Let’s connect this to the CREATE framework – because when I trace burnout and attrition back through the system, it almost always starts in the same place: Culture.

Not the culture you describe in your values deck.

The culture you design through your norms.

Because culture, at its core, is just the accumulated set of behaviors your system rewards and punishes. And when culture is built for the “average brain,” neurodivergent employees experience it as a constant cognitive guessing game.

What looks like “good culture” to some – spontaneous collaboration, open-plan offices, real-time brainstorming, speak-up-to-show-engagement norms – can feel like cognitive landmines to others.

Norms like “respond quickly to signal alignment” or “make eye contact to show you’re listening” aren’t neutral. They’re calibrated for neurotypical processing. And they don’t just exclude thoughtful voices – they actively teach those voices to stay silent.

Because if the cost of contributing is performing a neurotype you don’t have, most people will eventually stop paying it.

They’ll stop speaking up in meetings.

They’ll stop offering the pattern they noticed that no one else saw.

They’ll stop pointing out the systemic flaw everyone’s been working around.

Not because they don’t care.

Because the system has taught them that their way of caring doesn’t count.

This is what I mean when I say the CREATE model starts with Culture. You can’t build trust (Relationships), execute effectively (Execution), or adapt intelligently (Agility) if your foundational norms are systematically filtering out cognitive difference.

And here’s the part that makes this so urgent:

Once that filtering becomes normalized, it becomes invisible.

You stop seeing it as exclusion. You see it as “culture fit.”

You stop recognizing it as a design flaw. You see it as a “communication issue.”

And the brilliance you’re losing? It doesn’t announce itself on the way out. It just quietly stops showing up.

What Neuroinclusive Design Actually Looks Like

So what does repair look like?

Let’s map it through CREATE – my framework for organizational systems design. CREATE stands for Culture, Relationships, Execution, Agility, Teaching, and Ethics – the six domains that determine whether your systems unlock or constrain human potential. For neurodivergent professionals, the repair work starts with Culture but touches every domain.

Here’s what that looks like in practice:

Culture – Stop designing for the average brain. Start by asking: when you hire for “culture fit,” are you actually screening for “brain type fit”? Because if your norms reward one way of processing information, you’re not building culture – you’re building conformity. Neuroinclusive culture doesn’t mean one more slide in the inclusion deck. It means interrogating what your systems are actually rewarding. It means recognizing that “speak up to show engagement” isn’t a neutral expectation – it’s a cognitive tax on anyone who thinks before they talk.

Relationships – Build trust through cognitive flexibility, not cognitive conformity. In 1:1s, ask “How do you process best?” – not “Why didn’t you contribute in the meeting?” Create pathways for contribution that don’t all require real-time verbal performance. Separate thinking time from speaking time. Let people contribute asynchronously. We don’t call adjustable desks an “accommodation” for tall people. We call them good design. The same principle applies here.

Execution – Redesign decision-making protocols. Not everyone thinks out loud. Not everyone needs a whiteboard session to see the system. Create multiple entry points for input: written briefs before meetings, post-meeting reflection windows, and decision documents that allow for async feedback. The goal isn’t to slow down – it’s to stop leaving insight on the table because you’re only listening in one cognitive register.

This isn’t about lowering standards.

It’s about raising the ceiling by removing artificial cognitive barriers.

Because here’s what most leaders miss: when you design for cognitive diversity, you don’t just help neurodivergent employees. You help everyone. Clarity helps everyone. Multiple modes of contribution help everyone. Separating thinking from performing helps everyone.

You’re not accommodating differences.

You’re designing better systems.

The Economic Case No One’s Making

Let’s be direct about the numbers – because this isn’t just a moral argument.

73% of neurodivergent professionals report masking at work daily. That’s not a soft stat. That’s a cognitive load tax that shows up in every performance metric you’re already tracking – if you know how to read them.

Neurodivergent employees leave jobs at twice the rate of their neurotypical peers. Not because they can’t do the work. Because the sustained effort of pretending burns them out faster than the work itself.

Innovation cycle times slow when teams lack cognitive diversity – because everyone’s seeing the same problems through the same lens, which means you’re solving for speed but missing the solutions that require a different way of seeing.

If you’ve watched someone brilliant flame out in your organization – someone whose departure genuinely surprised you because “they were doing so well” – this is probably why.

The performance metrics looked fine.

But the energetic math didn’t.

And by the time you saw the exhaustion, they’d already been running on fumes for months.

Three Diagnostic Questions

Before we close, three questions worth sitting with – not as rhetorical provocations, but as genuine leadership diagnostics:

1. When you hire for “culture fit,” are you actually hiring for “brain type fit”?

Look at your last five hires. What communication style do they share? What processing speed? What mode of presence? If they all think the same way, you haven’t built diversity – you’ve built an echo chamber with different résumés.

2. How much cognitive energy are your best people spending pretending to be someone else – and what could they create if they didn’t have to?

This is the invisible tax. The one that doesn’t show up in your productivity dashboards but shows up in your retention data, your innovation pipeline, and the ideas that never get voiced because the effort of translation felt too high.

3. If your systems only work for one kind of brain, how many kinds of problems can you actually solve?

Cognitive homogeneity creates strategic fragility. You can execute efficiently within known parameters – but you can’t see the disruption coming from outside your frame. That’s not a diversity problem. It’s a risk-management problem.

There’s no average brain.

Just average systems – and leaders brave enough to redesign them.

The question isn’t whether your best people can adapt.

It’s whether your systems are designed to deserve them.

Because the cost of cognitive conformity isn’t just human.

It’s strategic.

And the organizations that figure this out first won’t just be more inclusive.

They’ll be more resilient, more innovative, and more capable of solving the problems no one else can see yet.

Next in this series: In Essay 2, I’ll show you the cognitive toolkit you’re not using – the specific pattern recognition, systems thinking, and nonlinear problem-solving capabilities that neurodivergent professionals bring. You’ll learn why these aren’t “accommodations to make” but advantages to unlock, and how to identify these capabilities in your current team. This isn’t about hiring differently (yet). It’s about seeing differently.

Meeting Design Self-Assessment

Rate your agreement with each statement on a scale of 1-5: (1 = Strongly Disagree, 5 = Strongly Agree)

1. Our meetings include structured thinking time before asking people to contribute.

  • 1 = Never / 2 = Rarely / 3 = Sometimes / 4 = Usually / 5 = Always

2. People on my team can contribute meaningfully without speaking in real-time during meetings.

  • 1 = Not possible / 2 = Rarely / 3 = Sometimes / 4 = Usually / 5 = Always

3. When someone is quiet in a meeting, I assume they’re processing thoughtfully rather than disengaged.

  • 1 = Never / 2 = Rarely / 3 = Sometimes / 4 = Usually / 5 = Always

4. Our meeting culture values depth of contribution over speed of response.

  • 1 = Speed strongly valued / 2 = Speed valued / 3 = Both equally / 4 = Depth valued / 5 = Depth strongly valued

5. I can clearly see how our current meeting design might exclude certain ways of thinking.

  • 1 = Not at all / 2 = Slightly / 3 = Somewhat / 4 = Clearly / 5 = Very clearly

Scoring Guide:

20-25 points: Your meeting design likely supports cognitive diversity well. Consider: What specific practices create this environment? How can you document and scale them?

15-19 points: You’re creating some space for different processing styles, but there’s room for more intentional design. Consider: Which meetings could benefit most from structured thinking pauses? Who on your team processes best in writing?

10-14 points: Your meetings may be inadvertently excluding thoughtful contributors. Consider: What would happen if you built 3-5 minutes of silence into your next strategic discussion? Who might contribute differently if given that space?

5-9 points: Your meeting culture is likely rewarding speed over depth and verbal processing over careful thinking. Consider: When was the last time your “quietest” team member offered an insight that changed your thinking? If you can’t remember, that’s your signal.

Next Steps Based on Your Score:

If you scored 15+:

  • Document what’s working in your meeting design

  • Identify which practices could be shared with other leaders

  • Consider: Are there other systems (hiring, feedback, decision-making) where similar principles could apply?

If you scored 10-14:

  • Choose one recurring meeting to redesign with structured thinking time

  • Ask three people on your team: “How do you process best?” and “What would help you contribute more effectively?”

  • Experiment with providing meeting materials 24 hours in advance

If you scored below 10:

  • Start with your next important meeting: Build in one 3-minute thinking pause before asking for input

  • After the meeting, notice: Who contributed that doesn’t usually speak first? What quality of thinking emerged?

  • Ask yourself: “Am I measuring engagement by participation performance, or by quality of contribution?”

Regardless of score: Read Essay 2 to learn how to identify the cognitive diversity that’s already in your team – and how to create the conditions for those different ways of thinking to strengthen your decisions, not slow them down.

The business case is clear.

Organizations that get neuroinclusive leadership right reduce attrition, catch blind spots earlier, and build systems that don’t depend on heroic leadership.

I’ve spent 20 years coaching leaders through this work—from independent schools to USAID to tech startups. I have the complete diagnostic tools, the frameworks, and the implementation roadmaps. But let’s start simple.

Book a free call. Let’s figure out where you are.

We’ll diagnose what’s happening in your systems, identify where friction is costing you capacity, and map whether this work makes sense for you right now. No pitch. No obligation.
