title: Questions for Leaders and Teams in 2026
subtitle: A Followup from Yesterday's Piece
html:
Yesterday, I reflected on an article I read over the weekend in the HBR. If you haven’t read my post from Monday (1/5,) go back and take a look at it now.

The piece explored the architecture around leaders — the cultural scaffolding, the incentives, the systemic drift — the second half turns the lens inward again. Not to return to the old paradigm of “fix the leader,” but to acknowledge something both humbling and empowering:

Even when systems shape us, we still make choices inside those systems.

And the quality of those choices can either reinforce the drift… or interrupt it.

As I sat with the HBR article (and, honestly, with my own patterns), I found myself returning to a quieter truth beneath all the structural analysis: there are questions only leaders can answer for themselves. No strategy, no workshop, no reorganized operating model can substitute for a leader’s willingness to pause and ask, What is actually running me right now? or What version of myself am I reinforcing without realizing it?

And the same is true for teams.

Teams, like individuals, develop a typical self — shaped by habits, shortcuts, fears, and unspoken agreements. And they also have a maximal self — a version of the group that emerges in flashes: the meeting that actually moved something forward. In this project, the collaboration felt frictionless, the moment when honesty felt easier than politeness.

Part II is about returning to those truths.

It offers a set of questions for leaders to examine their own patterns, unlearn what no longer serves them, and reclaim authorship over their impact. And then it widens the frame again — inviting teams to have the kinds of conversations that shift collective identity, not just individual behavior.

If Part I made the case that leadership development must evolve as a system,
Part II is the reminder that systems change through people — one honest reflection, one reset ritual, one small commitment at a time.

Let’s begin with leaders, and then move to teams.

FOUR QUESTIONS EVERY LEADER SHOULD ASK

The article begins with a truth that lands like a mirror held at eye level: “No one operates at maximal performance all the time.”

We are invited to examine the gap between our grounded, centered maximal selves and our reactive, adaptive typical selves – shaped by what the article calls “habitual behaviors, default adaptations, and everyday patterns of interaction.” Closing that gap requires honesty, ritual, and a willingness to examine not just personality but context.

Here are the four questions that matter most.

1. What adaptations run my leadership when I’m under stress?

The article names the unconscious strategies many leaders use to stay safe: “pleasing,” “over-performing,” “self-editing.” None of these adaptations is inherently wrong. They are simply the stories you once needed to survive, though survival strategies have a half-life.

The article offers a weekly reflection: “List three moments when you felt most yourself and three when you felt hijacked.” This exercise is less about cataloging incidents and more about reclaiming authorship. Patterns emerge. Motives come into focus. Choice becomes possible again.

2. Is the system rewarding my best self – or punishing it?

One of the most important insights in the article is this: “Organizations don’t just hire leaders to change them; they hire them to preserve their sense of continuity.”

This is not cynical. It is accurate. It means your maximal self may not be the version of you the system actually rewards. Some cultures punish dissent while preaching innovation. Some elevate harmony over honesty. Some expect psychological safety for teams while offering little of it to leaders.

So ask: “What version of me gets rewarded here – and am I willing to keep reinforcing that version?”

This is not a judgment. It is clarity. And clarity, more than anything else, is what liberates.

3. Where am I performing leadership instead of practicing it?

The article warns that as leaders advance, “the risk of exposure increases,” creating an incentive to cling to expertise, polish, and control – performing leadership rather than practicing it. But maximal performance is not born of certainty. It’s born of curiosity.

The article recommends a practice I love: “Establish an ‘ignorance goal’ – a topic where you intentionally practice not knowing.” It is remarkable how much integrity and clarity surface when leaders stop performing competence long enough actually to explore.

4. What is one thing I need to unlearn this quarter?

The authors write: “Real change requires unlearning.”

Every leader has habits that once served them well – being the fixer, the diligent one, the calm one, the expert – but now constrain the range of who they can become. The quarterly ritual: identify three once-useful habits that now limit impact, then choose one to mute – not eliminate, just lower the volume.

Identity is not a static artifact. It is a living system.

The Final Question Beneath All the Questions

The article offers a quiet, almost whispered truth: “Your best self is a version of you waiting for conditions that support it.”

So the real question becomes: “What system conditions would allow me to show up as my best self more consistently – and who do I need to enlist to help create them?”

Because leadership is not simply personal work. It is ecosystem work. Cultural work. Architectural work. When leaders’ inner work meets an outer system capable of holding it, something remarkable happens: their best selves cease to be aspirational and become operational.

FOUR CONVERSATIONS EVERY TEAM SHOULD HAVE

The article reminds us that “no one operates at maximal performance all the time,” and teams, just like individuals, develop what the authors call “habitual behaviors, default adaptations, and everyday patterns of interaction.” Teams drift. Teams compensate. Teams self-protect in ways that minimize collective intelligence.

If we want leaders to show up as their best selves, we must equip teams to do the same. Here are four conversations that elevate a team’s typical self closer to its maximal one.

1. When are we at our best?

The article invites leaders to recall moments when they felt aligned with their true selves. Teams should engage in the same reflective practice. The point is not nostalgia; it is pattern recognition. When a team names the moments when it felt most like itself – aligned, energized, grounded – it begins to discern the conditions under which those moments arise.

Your best moments are not accidents. They are a blueprint.

2. What patterns pull us away from our best selves?

People slip into “pleasing, over-performing, and self-editing.” Teams slip into their collective equivalents: conflict avoidance, silence mistaken for alignment, protecting turf instead of purpose, local optimization at the expense of shared success, workarounds instead of real conversations, polite meetings followed by private frustration.

The article offers a piercing truth: “Habitual behaviors masquerade as identity.” Teams must stop confusing who they are with what they repeat. This is the moment where a team reclaims authorship.

3. Where does our system work against us – and what’s in our power to change?

HBR reminds us that identity drifts when “structures, incentives, and cultural expectations” contradict aspirations. Teams experience this constantly through fuzzy priorities, unclear decision rights, misaligned metrics, inconsistent direction, and emotional labor that remains unnamed.

When a team feels perpetually “off,” the cause is rarely the team itself. It is the system around the team. Naming this is not blame. It is agency. Teams cannot fix everything – but they can influence far more than they realize.

4. What commitments will help us close the gap this quarter?

The article lands on a truth that holds equally for teams: “Sustaining your best self is a discipline of awareness, intention, and continual reinvention.”

Teams do not transform through inspiration. They transform through rhythm – quarterly commitments, micro-experiments, tension-naming habits, clarity resets, learning rituals. Small commitments compound. Quiet, consistent practices become cultural gravity. And as teams shift, leaders shift alongside them.

Are you ready for 2026?

A leader’s best self is never only an individual achievement. It is a relational phenomenon – reflected, reinforced, or restricted by the people around them. When teams practice clarity, candor, reflection, and reinvention, they expand the space in which leaders can be grounded, courageous, and human. They become part of the architecture that sustains leadership, rather than conditions leaders must work around.

In 2026, the teams that learn to operationalize their best selves will do more than function well. They will become cultural stabilizers – the groups that hold shape when complexity hits, that absorb tension without losing coherence, that elevate leaders instead of overwhelming them.

Teams like that don’t happen accidentally. They are built – through reflection, through alignment, through ritual, and through a shared commitment to becoming the kind of system that makes everyone better.

title: The Leadership Development Reckoning of 2026
subtitle: Why L&D Needs a System, Not a Syllabus
html:
Inspired by the HBR article “Leaders, Bring Your Best Self into the New Year” (Carucci & Chamorro-Premuzic, January 2026)

I took a deliberate pause from writing at the end of last year. Not a burnout collapse or a dramatic retreat, but a conscious step back – the kind where you realize the best parts of your life have been waiting patiently for you to stop multitasking long enough to notice them. I spent more time with people I love, cooked slowly, lingered in conversations that didn’t orbit work, and created little pockets of stillness where I could hear myself think again.

And of course, because I can’t help it, I read. A lot.

One of the pieces that stayed with me was a deceptively gentle but quietly radical article in Harvard Business Review. If it’s behind a paywall, apologies – most places allow a handful of free reads. But the opening line alone is worth the click:

“No one operates at maximal performance all the time.”

A simple sentence, but an utterly profound truth – and in many ways, the starting point of a larger reckoning.

The authors describe a divide between our maximal self – the best version of who we are when everything aligns – and our typical self, the one shaped by pressure, politics, exhaustion, and the invisible scaffolding that holds our organizations together. They note that leaders who manage to narrow this gap “consistently deliver better results and build healthier teams.”

I believe this deeply. And yet, as I read, a parallel truth kept rising like a tide: leaders aren’t struggling because they don’t know who their best selves are. They’re struggling because the systems they inhabit rarely make space for that version to exist.

We tend to talk about leadership as if it is an act of personal virtue, a psychological tightening of the core. But identity is contextual. Courage is contextual. Even values are contextual. And organizations – with their cultural antibodies, competing incentives, and unspoken rules – shape leaders far more than leaders shape their organizations.

Carucci and Chamorro-Premuzic name this drift with painful accuracy, describing “a kind of existential burnout: achieving outcomes that please others but fail to nourish their own sense of purpose,” alongside the “habitual behaviors, default adaptations, and everyday patterns of interaction” that pull people away from their intentions.

Most leaders know this feeling intimately: the subtle erosion of authenticity in the name of survival.

But what struck me is that these “default adaptations” aren’t solely psychological. They’re architectural. When you zoom out, they are predictable responses to systems that reward conformity over courage, political navigation over principled dissent, performance over learning, and heroic individualism over shared clarity.

So, in the spirit of building on the HBR article rather than merely echoing it, here are the five shifts leadership development must make in 2026 – if we want leaders’ maximal selves to be accessible not only in rare, brilliant moments but in the rhythm of their daily work.

1. Strategy: Leadership Development Must Become the Interpreter of the Business

The article offers a line that is both elegant and provocative: “Leadership development is not a journey of self-discovery but of self-reinvention.”

Reinvention is essential – but reinvention cannot happen divorced from the work.

For years, leadership development has functioned almost like a parallel curriculum, orbiting just outside the gravitational pull of real business needs. Companies move toward AI transformation, operating model redesign, customer experience overhaul – and L&D rolls out workshops on “effective communication” and “strategic mindset.” Good topics, just not strategic ones.

Leaders do not need abstract concepts. They need discernment – the capacity to connect what they are learning to the actual business decisions, pressures, and tradeoffs they face. If AI is reshaping the workflow, leaders don’t need an AI 101 primer. They need to learn where human judgment still leads, where AI accelerates, and where AI should be prevented from interfering. They need the ability to slow down the rush toward efficiency long enough to ask: What is the actual problem we’re solving? And where does technology serve – versus distort – good leadership?

Leadership development should not be a syllabus. It should be the interpretive arm of the strategy.

2. Architecture: Culture Lives Between Meetings, Not Within Workshops

The authors write that leaders slip unconsciously into “pleasing, over-performing, and self-editing,” while “mistaking old survival strategies for their true identity.” They also name leaders’ fears – “being wrong,” “losing control,” “disappointing others” – as well as the behavioral fallout: “staying silent,” “avoiding conflict,” “over-editing themselves with senior stakeholders.”

These are not personality flaws. They are predictable outcomes of the systems we place leaders in. One of the sharpest lines in the article is this: “Political skill – the art of fitting in – is rewarded far more consistently than transformative courage.” And the follow-on warning: “Cultural antibodies attack deviation.”

Exactly.

Leaders do not underperform because they are fragile, resistant, or misaligned. They underperform because many organizations run on an operating system built for a different era – one that disproportionately rewards safety, sameness, and social calculation. If we want leaders to be courageous, we must redesign the conditions that currently punish courage. If we want leaders to create psychological safety, we must first extend it to them. If we want leaders to think systemically, we must stop burying them in tactical overload.

Leadership cannot thrive inside an architecture that contradicts it.

3. Design: Co-Creation Is the Only Way to Bridge Best Self and Daily Self

The article recommends a deceptively simple reflection practice: “Identify three moments when you felt most yourself and three when you felt off-track.”

It is elegant and helpful, but it surfaces a larger idea: leaders rarely feel “off-track” in isolation. They feel off-track because they are navigating incoherent systems. Most leaders are managing a complexity debt few development programs ever acknowledge: competing priorities, unclear decision rights, cross-team friction, emotional labor, strategic ambiguity, and a steady drip of not knowing what will matter most next week.

This is why co-creation in leadership development is not a nice-to-have – it’s essential infrastructure. We must stop designing leadership programs for leaders and start designing programs with them. Not after the fact. Not once a year in an advisory council. But in quarterly cycles of shared sensemaking, prototyping, feedback, and reinvention.

The article encourages leaders to “revisit your aspirational identity every 90 days.” Organizations should mirror that rhythm. Every quarter, leaders should be in conversation about the realities reshaping their work – and the supports required to meet them with integrity.

Co-creation is not a facilitation technique; it is cultural oxygen.

4. Delivery: Stop Delivering Content. Start Delivering Relevance.

The article makes an important distinction between learning mode and performance mode, noting that as leaders rise, “the risk of exposure increases,” making it harder to ask naïve questions or to learn publicly. So leaders retreat into performance mode – the safe, polished, self-edited version of themselves.

But here’s the more profound truth the article gestures toward: leaders stay in performance mode not only because of fear, but because of bandwidth. Most leaders today live in a near-constant state of cognitive triage: decision firefighting, context switching, emotional caregiving, strategic uncertainty, cross-functional conflict. Performance mode becomes the only way to stay upright.

Learning becomes sustainable only when it is directly connected to the tensions leaders are already carrying, embedded in real workflows instead of abstract programming, paced to reduce cognitive load rather than add to it, and modeled by senior leaders who are willing to practice what the article calls “publicly modeling vulnerability, such as admitting when they’ve changed their mind.”

When executives do this inside development environments, something shifts. The air gets lighter. Leaders breathe again. Learning becomes communal rather than performative.

5. Measurement: We Don’t Need Precision – We Need Insight

The article warns that “identity-hardening is one of the biggest barriers to change,” and it recommends that leaders engage in rituals of unlearning – naming habits that were once strengths but now create limitations.

Organizations need this same unlearning. We must release ourselves from the idea that measurement requires perfect precision or punishing dashboards, and replace it with measures that illuminate rather than surveil. Measures that help leaders see their impact, understand their patterns, and develop agency over their own growth.

The article closes with a line that I find both grounding and expansive: “Sustaining your best self is not a matter of willpower. It’s a discipline of awareness, intention, and continual reinvention.”

Leadership development should adopt this same ethos – a discipline, a rhythm, a commitment to noticing, adjusting, and evolving in partnership with leaders, not in parallel to them.

Where Leadership Development Must Go in 2026

Leaders don’t need more pressure to be their best selves. They need systems that prevent them from being drawn away from their best selves.

The real obstacles are not personal deficiencies. They are systemic ones: chronic overload, cultural antibodies, fuzzy expectations, political incentives, and misaligned architecture. If leadership development wants to matter in 2026, it must focus on psychological safety for leaders – not just their teams – rewarding intelligent risk-taking, reducing avoidable friction, institutionalizing co-creation, supporting identity shifts, and using measurement as insight, not judgment.

The HBR article is a call to inner alignment. This is a call to system alignment.

A leader’s best self is not a personal triumph. It is a structural possibility. When organizations build the right conditions, leaders’ best selves stop being aspirational moments and become the operating norm.

title: If I Were President: The First 100 Days
subtitle: MALAA - Make America Less Annoying Again
html:
During the 2020 presidential election, I was teaching middle school. Like many teachers, I wanted my students to understand the political process without turning the classroom into a cable-news reenactment. So instead of debating candidates, we studied how platforms are built – what they include, what they signal, and what they reveal about values.

One of their projects was simple: research a few issues, create a party platform, and deliver a stump speech.

Yes, an actual stump. I brought one into the classroom.

The assignment was loosely inspired by NPR’s This I Believe series – not because I wanted polished policy proposals, but because I wanted clarity. What do you believe? What frustrates you? What would you fix first if you had the power?

What surprised me wasn’t the politics. It was the patterns.

Across wildly different viewpoints, the same complaints kept surfacing: systems that wasted time, rules that made no sense, processes that felt intentionally confusing. The kids weren’t arguing left versus right. They were arguing why things were so needlessly hard.

This piece is a grown-up version of that assignment.

It’s not satire, exactly. And it’s not a serious campaign platform, either. It’s a thought experiment built around a simple premise: before we ask people to trust institutions with the hardest problems, maybe we should prove we can fix the small, obvious ones.

What follows is my imaginary first hundred days as president – focused not on ideology, but on friction. On the little design failures that quietly drain time, money, and patience from everyday life.

Consider it a stump speech for common sense.

====

My fellow Americans, we’re more divided than ever. But you know what unites us? We ALL hate changing our clocks twice a year. We ALL lose the TV remote in the couch. We ALL wonder why avocados are either rocks or mush with no in-between.

Here’s my platform: Fix the stuff that makes everyone’s life unnecessarily complicated.

No red states. No blue states. Just people who want their grocery store to have milk in the same place every time.

This isn’t about ideology. It’s about eliminating stupid friction so Americans can focus on what actually matters. Three problems everyone hates. Three solutions everyone understands. Zero committees harmed.

Executive Order #1:

End Daylight Saving Time

Arizona and Hawaii were right all along.

Executive Order #2:

Move the Super Bowl to Saturday

If the host city is on the West Coast, the kickoff is 1:00 pm local time. The biggest party of the year shouldn’t require a sick day.

Executive Order #3:

Halloween Is Always the Last Friday in October

Consistent. Safe. Parents can enjoy it. Kids get maximum candy. Costume parties don’t collide with school nights. Done.

“If government can’t fix the obvious stuff that makes daily life harder than it needs to be, it has no business tackling the complicated stuff.”

Week 1: Democracy, Just A Little Less Sucky

So let me be explicit. In the opening phase of this administration, I am not issuing executive orders or fast-tracking legislation on:

  • Campaign finance reform

  • Open or closed primaries

  • Ranked-choice voting

  • Electoral college reform

  • Constitutional amendments of any kind

Not because they’re off the table forever – but because they don’t belong in the opening move. I have very serious thoughts about all of those issues and how to reform and remake our great Republic. But, this isn’t that kind of post. Those issues require: Broad public deliberation, Legislative buy-in, clear sequencing, and, most importantly, trust that the process itself isn’t rigged.

Double the Size of the House of Representatives: Sidestepping the potential for more gerrymandering shithousery, and the Constitutional considerations of an Executive messing with Article 1, just play along for this first one. 435 representatives for 335 million people means each rep has 770,000 constituents. That’s too many. Double it to 870 reps. Smaller districts = better representation = government closer to the people. Fight me on that.

Automatic Voter Registration: You turn 18, you’re registered. Opt-out if you want. Democracy should be opt-out, not opt-in.

Week 2: My Body is Not Your Profit Center

End Pharmaceutical Ads on TV: You don’t need a commercial telling you to “ask your doctor about” a drug you can’t pronounce for a condition you never heard of. If you need medicine, your doctor will tell you. Every other developed country figured this out, except, strangely, New Zealand.

Taxpayer Dividend on Drugs: If a pharmaceutical drug was developed using any federally funded research, it must be sold to U.S. citizens at cost + 10%. You shouldn’t pay for the “innovation” twice – once in taxes and again at the pharmacy. If a company refuses, the patent becomes public property immediately.

If Doctors Charge for Missed Appointments, Patients Can Charge for Delays: Your doctor charges $100 if you’re a no-show? Fine. But if your appointment starts more than 15 minutes late, your fee drops by $10 for each 10-minute delay. Waiting room time is YOUR time too.

Medical Necessity Means Medical Necessity: Insurance may challenge fraud. Insurance may require second opinions. Insurance may not override clinical judgment with a spreadsheet or AI. Doctors practice medicine. Insurance companies process claims. Those roles should not be interchangeable.

Plain-English Medical Bills: One page. Total cost. What insurance paid. What you owe. No more decoding 14-page statements written in medical billing hieroglyphics.

Week 3: If You’re the Product - You Get Paid

Opt-In Data Sales Only: Companies cannot sell or share customer data unless you explicitly opt in. No pre-checked boxes. No “by using this site…” nonsense. Your data belongs to you.

The Data Dividend: If a company sells your anonymized data to a third party, you are entitled to a “Data Royalty.” A percentage of that sale must be credited back to your account or sent to a national digital trust fund in your name. If you are the product, you should get paid.

Week 4: I Customer, You Service

Subscription Cancellation Fairness: If you can sign up in two clicks, you can cancel in two clicks. No phone calls. No retention specialists. No “tell us why you’re leaving.” If a company can take your money instantly, it must let you stop just as easily.

Junk Mail Is Illegal: Mail delivered to “Current Resident,” “Occupant,” or any name that is not yours is prohibited. If someone wants to reach you, they should know who you are.

Stop Asking Me About My Car’s Warranty: Robocalls referencing expired vehicle warranties, or that I am prequalified for a loan, or urgent legal matters exist to scare and deceive. Any call in this genre will be blocked at the carrier level and subject to a per-attempt fine. If a message is legitimate, it can be sent in writing.

Press Zero for a Human: At any point in an automated phone call, pressing “0” must connect you to a live human being. No endless menus. No voice recognition games. No looping into oblivion. If a company is large enough to use an automated phone system, it is large enough to provide a person who can help. Pressing zero means I need a person. And the answer should always be yes.

Week 5: Technology Works For You Now

Video Calls Work Like Text Messages: Zoom, Teams, FaceTime, Google Meet – full interoperability required. Just like you can text between an iPhone and an Android, you should be able to video call across platforms. The technology exists. Make it happen.

One Charger to Rule Them All: USB-C for everything. iPhone, Android, laptops, tablets, and electric toothbrushes. Companies have 18 months to comply or pay a “proprietary connector tax.” Ditto: a subset for lawn and power tools, etc., and yet another for EVs. Plugs are standardized on one end; why not on both?

Social Media Chronological Feed Mandate: Every platform must offer a “show me everything chronologically” option. No algorithm required. Just posts from people I follow, in order. Let ME decide what I want to see. Gosh, remember Tweetdeck, iykyk.

TV Remote “Find Me” Button: Every TV sold in America must have a “find my remote” Bluetooth button that makes the remote beep. This solves a problem in 100 million households instantly.

Internet Forms – Stop Asking for State AND Zip Code: Your zip code contains your state. Databases exist. If I enter 21042, the system knows I’m in Maryland. Stop making me type both.

The “Low Battery” Warning Standard: Smoke detectors and smart devices are prohibited from chirping “Low Battery” between the hours of 10:00 PM and 8:00 AM. They must wait until a civilized hour to demand a 9-volt battery change.

Week 6: Make Flying Suck Less

The Middle Seat Gets Both Armrests: It’s not left or right politics – it’s basic human decency. You’re squished between two strangers at 30,000 feet. You get the armrests.

TSA PreCheck: $10, Lasts Forever: Security theater shouldn’t be a profit center. Background check costs $10. You pay once. You’re good forever unless you commit a crime. Simple.

Plane Tarmac Rule Enhancement: If the plane sits on the tarmac for 30+ minutes, everyone gets free WiFi for the entire flight. Airlines will suddenly figure out how to manage delays better.

Week 7: Stop Making Driving Harder

Gas Pump Simplification Act: Insert card. Pump gas. Done. No zip code. No car wash offer. No receipt question. No rewards program pitch. No solicitation for X charity – you’re a multibillion-dollar petro conglomerate, YOU round up and donate.

Zipper Merge is Mandatory: Taught in every driver’s ed course. Signs on every highway. Merge at the merge point, not at the very end. Traffic flow improves. Road rage decreases. This is infrastructure policy and will be a significant focus of the Department of Transportation.

Construction Zone Transparency: Every construction zone must display what’s happening and when it ends. Areas with cones and without workers lose “construction zone penalties” after two hours.

The “Actual Safety” Speed Camera Law: Speed cameras can only be placed in high-accident zones or school zones – never at the bottom of a hill or behind a hidden sign. 100% of the fine must go toward local road repairs or the nearby school, not the general city fund or a private camera company.

Week 8: Grocery Shopping, But A Little Less Annoying

Standardized Grocery Store Layouts: I don’t care what the actual layout is, but every grocery store in the country must follow the same basic template. You should be able to walk into any grocery store in America and know where the milk is. This saves millions of collective hours annually.

Bananas, Melons, and Avocados Sorted by Ripeness: Stores must sort this genre of produce into three bins: “Today,” “2-3 Days,” “4-5 Days.” Science and supply chain coordination make this possible.

Self-Checkout is 5% Cheaper: You’re doing the work. You get the discount. Also, those weight sensors are abolished – just scan and go.

Week 9: Let’s Live Like Neighbors Again

Government-Funded “Library of Things”: Every county has a Library of Things where you can check out a power drill, a ladder, a pressure washer, and a carpet cleaner for free. Nobody needs to own a tool they use once a year. Saves Americans billions. Reduces waste. Builds community.

No Gas-Powered Leaf Blowers: Gas leaf blowers are loud, polluting, and unnecessary. Get a rake. Use an electric blower if you must. Or be happy with a composting lawn. Leaves are not trash – they’re mulch. Your neighbors, your kids, and your lungs will all be better off.

Week 10: School Is Hard Enough As Is

School Start Times for Teens - 9 am or Later: The science is clear. Teenagers’ brains aren’t awake at 7 am. Later start times improve grades and mental health and reduce car accidents. This is a no-brainer.

No Homework Unless It’s Reading or Practicing an Instrument: Elementary school kids don’t need worksheets. They need to play, read, and sleep. If homework doesn’t involve reading books or music practice, it doesn’t go home.

School Communications Come in One Weekly Digest: Each school sends one predictable, once-a-week communication with everything parents need to know: events, deadlines, forms, schedule changes. Emergencies are the only exception.

Week 11: Suck It HR

All Job Posts Must Include Salary and Benefits: Upfront. In the posting. No more “competitive salary” or “depends on experience.” Salary range required. Health insurance details required. PTO policy required.

Job Descriptions Written by the Actual Manager: Not HR. Not a recruiter. The person who will manage the role writes the description. If they can’t articulate what they need, the position doesn’t exist.

Interview Process Fairness Rules: More than 3 rounds? Candidates get paid $100/hour for each additional round. “Fast-paced environment” must be defined in plain English. If I upload a resume, auto-fill the application – don’t make me type my work history twice.

Week 12: Shower Time

Shampoo Bottles That Don’t All Look the Same: For the 100% of Americans over 50 who wear readers, shampoo, conditioner, and body wash bottles must have different shapes or raised text you can read by touch. Taking a shower shouldn’t require perfect vision.

Standardized Shower Temperature Controls: Every shower has a “favorite temperature” button. My car is coded to adjust the seats and mirrors to my fob, rather than my wife’s settings. Set it once, press it every time. No more scalding or freezing while you find the sweet spot.

THE CAMPAIGN SLOGAN

“Let’s fix the annoying stuff first. Then we’ll tackle the hard problems.”

title: Are you leading the business or holding it together?
subtitle: Resolution #10: Stop Being the Hero – Start Building the System
html:
“2026 will reward leaders who build systems, not saviors.”

There’s a moment inside nearly every growing business that arrives quietly, wrapped in praise:

“I don’t know how you do it.”

At first, it feels flattering. Affirming. Like evidence that your dedication matters.

But one founder told me:

“I started hearing that phrase three times a week. Then I realized – they weren’t admiring me. They were depending on me.

And dependence dressed as admiration is still dependence.”

This is Resolution #10 – the capstone in my series on building a business that holds its shape. [Start from the beginning: Audit Your Leadership System – Not Your Org Chart]

That’s the Heroic Trap.

And it is one of the most seductive – and destructive – forces inside a scaling business.

Because here’s the truth: Heroic leadership looks responsible. But it builds fragility, not strength.

The Founder Who Couldn’t Leave

Last year, a founder asked me a question, half-joking:

“What would happen if I disappeared for two weeks?”

I asked him back: “What do you think would happen?”

He paused. Then started listing:

Deals slowing down, decisions backing up, team members waiting for clarification, clients are escalating for reassurance, projects are drifting, the emotional tone of the team is quietly dipping

And then he said:

“So... I guess I can’t leave.”

Exactly.

This is what I call The Two-Week Stress Test – the fastest way to reveal how much weight your business is still placing on you.

If your absence shakes the system, your presence has been masking the cracks.

The Two-Week Stress Test (The Diagnostic)

If you stepped away for two weeks with no laptop, no Slack, no check-ins – what would happen?

Would decisions get made? Would projects move forward? Would the team know what to prioritize? Would clients get served? Would the culture hold?

If the answer to any of these is “no” or “probably not,” you’ve found where your system is still leaning on you.

That founder ran the diagnostic in his head.

Then he realized: “I’m not leading this business. I’m holding it together.”

What Heroic Leadership Actually Looks Like

When I diagnose these systems with founders, I find five patterns:

1. Decisions routed through one person

I asked a leadership team: “Who can approve this budget?” Four people looked at the founder.

Not because they couldn’t decide – but because they’d never been taught how.

2. Work held together by emotional intuition

One team member told me: “We wait to see if he seems stressed before we escalate.”

Your “sense” of urgency becomes the team’s operating manual.

3. Invisible knowledge silos

“I don’t know how he knows when a client is about to churn. He just... knows.”

The expertise is in your head – never translated into process.

4. Unstable operating rhythms

The rituals change depending on your energy, bandwidth, or proximity.

5. Shadow leadership roles

People wait for you to “bless” the work, even when you don’t want to be the bottleneck.

This isn’t incompetence. It’s system architecture by accident.

The organization grows. Your involvement grows with it. And slowly, without noticing, you become the glue holding everything in place.

Not because you want to – but because no one else knows where the glue actually goes.

That’s not heroism. That’s fragility with good intentions.

The Hidden Cost of Staying Heroic

I watched this play out with a founder who prided herself on “never letting anything drop.”

Then she got pneumonia. Four days in bed.

When she came back, two deals had stalled (because no one knew the terms), a project had gone sideways (because the team was afraid to make the call without her), and three people had spent the week in analysis paralysis.

Nothing catastrophic. Just... drift.

That’s what fragility looks like – not collapse, but the slow erosion of momentum the moment the hero steps away.

And here’s what heroic leadership costs you personally:

You can’t take real time off. You can’t think strategically because you’re drowning in tactical. You resent the team for “needing” you – even though you trained them to. You lie awake at 2am thinking about things that should’ve been someone else’s job.

That’s not dedication. That’s unsustainable.

The Shift: From Hero to Architect

That founder who couldn’t leave?

He spent six months rebuilding his system using the frameworks from this series.

Here’s what he did:

He audited where the system wobbled without him (Resolution #1)

He clarified what “good” actually meant so the team could self-correct (Resolution #2)

He mapped who decides what using the 6C Decision Framework (Resolution #3)

He built a leadership bench before he needed it (Resolution #4)

He eliminated bottlenecks by mapping the 32-step processes hiding in people’s heads (Resolution #5)

He strengthened psychological safety so people could flag problems early (Resolution #6)

He installed operating rhythms that ran without him (Resolution #7)

He clarified who owns what so there was no more “shared responsibility” confusion (Resolution #8)

He deployed people’s strengths strategically so they stopped compensating (Resolution #9)

All of it leading to one outcome: A business that runs on structure, not strain.

The Transformation

Six months later, I asked him the same question:

“What would happen if you disappeared for two weeks?”

He smiled.

“I actually did. Took my family to Iceland. No laptop...

When I got back, three things had shipped, two client issues had been resolved, and the team had made a strategic pivot I would’ve endorsed.

Not because I wasn’t important – but because the system finally was.”

What Changed (The Real “After” Picture)

Here’s what that founder told me about his daily experience:

What stopped:

  • Answering 47 Slack messages on Saturday to keep Monday running smoothly

  • Being the switchboard for every cross-functional question

  • Rewriting decks at midnight because no one knew what “good” looked like

  • Feeling guilty every time he wasn’t immediately available

What started:

  • Team making strategic calls without needing his blessing

  • Problems getting flagged early instead of escalated in crisis

  • Monday mornings focused on strategy instead of triage

  • Breathing room to think about the next 12 months instead of the next 12 hours

He said:

“The business became lighter.

Not because the workload changed – but because the leadership load finally rested on the system, not the individual.”

Here’s the Difference

Heroic system: Founder answers 47 Slack messages on Saturday to keep Monday running smoothly.

Systems-based: Monday priority reset (Resolution #7) surfaces blockers. Decision framework (Resolution #3) clarifies who owns the call. Role clarity (Resolution #8) means no one’s waiting for the founder’s approval.

Same business. Different architecture.

Want to measure your system’s dependence on you? I’ve built a 2-minute Founder Freedom Index that reveals where the fragility lives and what your next moves should be. Reply “send it” and I’ll share it.

The Psychology: Heroic Cultures Run on Adrenaline. Systems Cultures Run on Structure.

A heroic culture depends on:

  • Adrenaline

  • Intuition

  • Constant vigilance

  • Your personal stamina

  • Emotional temperature management

A systems culture depends on:

  • Clear structure

  • Predictable rhythms

  • Shared understanding

  • Distributed capability

  • Psychological safety

Adrenaline has a shelf life. Structure doesn’t.

How the Nine Resolutions Build This System

Here’s how everything connects:

Resolutions 1-2 audit the system and define success – so you know what “good” looks like without you in the room.

Resolutions 3-5 fix decision friction, build the bench, and eliminate bottlenecks – so work moves without you being the switchboard.

Resolutions 6-8 strengthen safety, build rhythms, and clarify roles – so the culture holds under pressure and people know their lanes.

Resolution 9 deploys strengths strategically – so people work in their natural gear instead of compensating.

All of it leads here: A business that runs on structure, not strain.

The Roadmap: Your Four Steps From Hero to Architect

Step 1: Run the Two-Week Stress Test Identify where you’re still the glue

Step 2: Document one heroic pattern per week Turn your intuition into process (If people ask “What would Matt do?”, write down what Matt would do and why)

Step 3: Delegate one “only I can do this” task per month Build capability in others (Most “only I can do this” tasks are really “only I’ve done this so far”)

Step 4: Install one operating rhythm that removes you from daily decisions (Monday priority resets mean people stop asking “What should I work on?”)

This isn’t about working less. It’s about working on the system instead of in it.

Your Identity Shift for 2026

This resolution isn’t about becoming less “hands-on.”

It’s about becoming someone who stops being the safety net – and starts building the system that holds the work.

It’s the difference between walking into the office thinking “What fires do I need to put out today?” versus “Is the system creating the conditions for people to succeed?”

Same day. Different operating system.

That identity creates structure. Structure creates sustainability. Sustainability creates freedom.

Because once you see yourself as an architect of systems instead of a hero in the trenches, everything downstream becomes cleaner, lighter, and more scalable.

Your team stops depending on your heroics. Your business stops requiring your constant presence. Your life stops revolving around being indispensable.

And your organization finally becomes something that can outlast you – and outgrow you.

Not because you don’t care. But because you care enough to stop being the single point of failure.

The Question That Changes Everything

So here’s what I want you to ask yourself:

Are you building a business, or are you building a monument to your own indispensability?

Because monuments don’t scale. Systems do.

And when someone says “I don’t know how you do it,” don’t hear it as a compliment. Hear it as a diagnostic.

Because if your business only works because of your heroics, you haven’t built a business – you’ve built a dependency.

Take 30 seconds: What’s one thing you’re doing right now that only works because of your personal involvement? Drop it in the comments – I read every one.

Your 2026 Resolution (That Will Actually Stick)

Say it out loud: “I will stop being the safety net – and start building the system that holds the work.”

This resolution sticks because identity drives behavior. Not goals. Not intentions. Identity.

Once you see yourself as a systems architect, your decisions start aligning with that reality automatically.

Because real leadership isn’t about holding everything together. It’s about designing a system that holds itself.

And it’s about building a team that can sustain the work whether you are in the room or across the ocean.

🔧 Free Tool: The Founder Freedom Index

I’ve built a 2-minute Founder Freedom Index that measures how much your business depends on you personally versus your systems.

It reveals:

  • Where the fragility lives

  • Where the system is underbuilt

  • Where the heroics are hiding

  • What your next moves should be to shift from hero to architect

Want it? Reply “send it.”

Want help building your 2026 system architecture – using all 10 resolutions as your roadmap?

Reply “system.”

I open a few clarity sessions each month.

The Beginning, Not the End

This isn’t the end of the series – it’s the beginning of the work.

You now have ten resolutions that, together, form a complete system for building a business that holds its shape:

  1. Audit your leadership system

  2. Name your priorities clearly

  3. Eliminate decision friction

  4. Build your leadership bench

  5. Map and eliminate bottlenecks

  6. Strengthen psychological safety

  7. Install operating rhythms

  8. Clarify role ownership

  9. Deploy strengths strategically

  10. Build systems, not heroics

Each resolution is a thread. Together, they weave the architecture.

The question isn’t whether you’ll face pressure in 2026. You will.

The question is: Will your system hold when you do?

Because a business that can hold its shape for two weeks… can hold its shape for thirty years.

The Pause Before 2026

And here’s the part I want to model — not just teach.

I’m signing off for a few weeks.

Not because the work slows down.
Not because the pressure disappears.
And not because the world gives leaders a clean runway in December.

I’m stepping back because I refuse to build a business that collapses the moment I take a breath.

I’m doing what I ask every founder to do:

Let the system hold.

Let the architecture do its job.

Let the people in your life — not the people in your inbox — be the ones who get your attention for a moment.

Over the next few weeks, I’ll be:

  • Traveling with my kids

  • Logging real miles on real trails

  • Touching sunlight and not Slack

  • Letting my nervous system reset

  • Filling the tank for the year I plan to storm into, not tiptoe into

This is the work behind the work.
Optionality.
Headspace.
Perspective.
The same things I’ve spent this entire series urging you to build.

Because 2026 won’t reward leaders who grind themselves flat. It will reward leaders who have the capacity — the mental, emotional, and operational runway — to lead at altitude.

I’m practicing what I preach so I can come back sharper, clearer, and ready to build with you in the new year.

So while I’m offline, ask yourself the question that closes this entire series:

Could your system hold if you stepped away for a few weeks?

If the answer is no — good. You now have the roadmap to change it.

See you in 2026.

Let’s build systems that hold their shape — and leaders who can breathe again.

title: Are you asking people to be someone they're not?
subtitle: Resolution #9: Stop Asking People to Be Someone They’re Not
html:
“You hired people for their strengths – then asked them to work against type.”

A few months ago, during a CliftonStrengths workshop, a team member said something that hit the room like truth dropped from a height:

“I think I’ve been evaluated for traits I don’t actually have.”

The room went silent.

She didn’t say it with frustration. She said it with relief – like she finally understood the friction she’d been carrying for years.

Her manager looked at her: “What do you mean?”

“I’m Strategic and Ideation,” she said. “But my performance reviews focus on whether I’m consistent with follow-through. That’s not where I’m wired to shine.”

The manager paused.

“Oh. I’ve been evaluating you against my strengths, not yours.”

This is Resolution #9 in my series on building a business that holds its shape. [Previous: Role Ambiguity Creates Friendly Fire – Not Collaboration]

Exactly.

This is the quiet cost inside so many organizations: People lose energy not because the work is hard, but because the work isn’t aligned with how they naturally think, feel, and operate.

Competence Is Not the Same as Energy

Here’s what most leaders miss:

Someone can be good at something and still be drained by it.

That’s not a strength. That’s compensation.

Strengths aren’t about what you CAN do. They’re about what you do with natural efficiency and energy.

When teams work with their strengths:

  • Decisions happen faster

  • Collaboration becomes smoother

  • Problems get solved at higher altitude

  • Stress becomes manageable

When teams work against their strengths:

  • Resistance increases

  • Burnout accelerates

  • Every task feels heavier than it should

Friction isn’t always a workflow problem. Sometimes it’s a talent alignment problem.

The High-Talent Team Running in Sand

Last year, I ran a strengths workshop for a team that was stacked with raw talent:

Strategic thinkers. Activators. Relators. Analysts. Communicators. Organizers.

If you looked at their profiles, you’d assume they were unstoppable.

But in practice, they felt stuck. Tired. Out of sync.

When we mapped their strengths to their actual responsibilities, it became obvious why:

Their Strategic people were stuck in reactive work – doing what they were “good at” but what drained them.

Their Relators were buried in spreadsheets – legacy responsibilities no one had revisited.

Their Executors were waiting on collaboration-heavy tasks – because the founder’s style was consultative, and everyone mirrored it.

Their big-picture thinkers had nowhere to aim the vision.

Their detail-oriented people were playing cleanup at the end of projects instead of being involved upfront where their precision actually mattered.

The founder looked at the board and said:

“I hired them right. I deployed them wrong.”

That’s the moment everything shifted.

The Redesign

We spent the afternoon redesigning responsibilities around their natural wiring.

The Strategic thinkers moved to quarterly planning instead of daily operations. The Relators shifted to client relationships instead of spreadsheets. The Executors got clear ownership of time-sensitive deliverables – no more waiting on endless input loops. The big-picture thinkers took ownership of long-range strategy sessions. The detail-oriented people moved upstream to project design, not just cleanup.

Same people. Same business. Different deployment.

Six weeks later, the founder told me:

“We didn’t add headcount. We didn’t work faster. We just stopped fighting people’s wiring.”

What Strategic Deployment Actually Looks Like

Here’s a concrete example:

Take someone with high Strategic.

Bad deployment:

  • Daily task management

  • Routine operations

  • Reactive problem-solving

Good deployment:

  • Quarterly planning

  • Scenario modeling

  • Identifying patterns across projects

Take someone with high Relator.

Bad deployment:

  • Data analysis

  • Process documentation

  • Solo execution work

Good deployment:

  • Client relationship management

  • Team cohesion building

  • Cross-functional coordination

Same person. Radically different energy output.

The Hidden Cost of Working Against Type

Working against type doesn’t just slow execution – it quietly erodes confidence.

People start to think they’re not good at their jobs when really, they’re just not wired for the jobs they’ve been given.

That’s not a performance problem. That’s a deployment problem.

And it’s expensive:

Energy drain – People compensating using strengths no one names or recognizes

Invisible labor – Good performers working twice as hard to produce half the results

Quiet attrition – Your best people leave because they never got to work in their genius zones

Where Strengths Misalignment Hides

1. “Good at it” ≠ Strength Competence without energy is compensation, not contribution.

2. Legacy responsibilities People still doing things they’ve outgrown or never enjoyed.

3. The founder’s preferences Teams unintentionally mirror the founder’s style – even when it doesn’t fit them.

4. The wrong success metrics Evaluating big-picture thinkers on detail perfection. Or relationship-builders on rapid solo execution.

Once you see it, you can fix it.

Want to map your team’s strengths to their roles? I’ve built a Strengths Deployment Guide that identifies misalignment and helps you redesign responsibilities around natural wiring. Reply “send it” and I’ll share it.

The Diagnostic

Here’s the test to identify misalignment on your team:

Ask each team member:

  • “What part of your job energizes you?”

  • “What part drains you?”

  • “If you could redesign your role, what would you shift?”

If more than 30% of someone’s role is in the “drains me” column, you have a deployment problem.

Not a performance problem. A deployment problem.

The “After” Picture

Three months after their strengths overhaul, that team sent me an email:

“Our Strategic leads stopped feeling like they were drowning in tactical requests. Our Relators stopped dreading spreadsheet reviews. Our Executors stopped waiting for endless input loops.

We didn’t work faster. The work just stopped fighting us.”

That’s the difference.

Strengths-aligned teams:

  • Collaborate faster

  • Make cleaner decisions

  • Stay in their genius zones

  • Communicate more naturally

  • Produce more with stress

  • Bounce back from setbacks faster

They don’t burn out at the same rate. They don’t conflict at the same frequency. They don’t question themselves as often.

They’re built for altitude.

This Is Where Role Clarity Becomes Powerful

This is where your role clarity from Resolution #8 becomes powerful:

You’ve defined who owns what. Now you need to ensure the “who” is naturally suited for the “what.”

Role clarity + strengths alignment = execution without friction.

Your Identity Shift for 2026

This resolution isn’t about becoming a better “manager of people.”

It’s about becoming someone who stops asking people to compensate – and starts putting them where they naturally excel.

It’s the difference between walking into a performance review thinking “Why isn’t this person meeting expectations?” versus “Are we asking this person to work against type?”

Same underperformance. Different operating system.

That identity creates structure. Structure creates alignment. Alignment creates energy.

Because once you see yourself as someone who deploys talent strategically, everything downstream becomes cleaner, lighter, and more sustainable.

Your team stops compensating. Your culture stops burning people out on misaligned work. Your organization stops losing good people to bad deployment.

And your best performers finally get to work in their genius zones.

The Question That Changes Everything

Here’s what I want you to ask yourself:

How much of your team’s “underperformance” is actually just misalignment?

Because if you’re evaluating people against strengths they don’t have, you’re not measuring performance – you’re measuring compensation.

And compensation always has a shelf life.

Take 30 seconds: Who on your team might be compensating rather than contributing from their strengths? Drop it in the comments – I read every one.

Your 2026 Resolution

title: Who actually owns this?
subtitle: Resolution #8: Role Ambiguity Creates Friendly Fire – Not Collaboration
html:
“If two people own it, no one owns it.”

A few months ago, in the middle of a retreat, I asked a leadership team a deceptively simple question:

“Who owns onboarding?”

Half the room raised their hands.

I looked around. “Okay... so who’s accountable when onboarding fails?”

The hands slowly went down.

Then one person said quietly: “I guess... all of us? None of us?”

Exactly.

This is Resolution #8 in my series on building a business that holds its shape. [Previous: Stop Setting Goals – Start Building Rhythms]

That’s the thing about role ambiguity: It doesn’t look like chaos. It looks like over-helping.

What Over-Helping Actually Looks Like

Role ambiguity looks like:

Three people are reviewing the same document because no one knows whose approval actually matters.

Someone is redoing work their teammate already finished because they didn’t know it was done.

A designer starting a deck, then discovering someone else had already begun one.

A PM is scheduling a client call, only to learn another PM already has it.

Good intentions create duplication. Collaboration creates confusion. Teamwork creates friction.

Nobody is being territorial. They’re just operating in different versions of “my job.”

The Friendly Fire Problem

Last spring, I worked with a team that was intensely collaborative, smart, and genuinely kind.

They liked each other. They communicated constantly. And they were accidentally creating conflict every week.

Why?

Because their roles overlapped like a Venn diagram drawn by a toddler.

Two people were leading client communication. Three people were leading program strategy. Nobody owned data. Everybody owned the “urgent” work. And the founder owned... all of it.

Nothing was broken. Everything was blurry.

The symptoms were subtle but corrosive:

People started apologizing constantly – for stepping on toes they didn’t know existed.

Handoffs got dropped because both people thought the other person had it.

Decisions stalled because no one knew whose call it was.

The founder told me: “We aren’t fighting. We’re accidentally stepping on each other.”

Exactly.

It wasn’t interpersonal friction. It was system friction.

The Mapping Session

We spent two hours mapping who owned what.

Not job descriptions – those are wish lists.

We mapped:

  • Who decides

  • Who executes

  • Who supplies input

  • Who gets informed

  • What “done” means

  • What “good” means

  • Where handoffs occur

By the end:

One person owned client communication (with input from the other). One person owned the program strategy (with the other two as consultants). One person finally owned data. And the founder stepped out of “all of it” and into “specific things.”

Here’s what that looked like in practice:

BEFORE: “Marketing and Product own the launch together.”

AFTER: “Product owns the launch timeline and deliverables (accountable). Marketing executes the campaign (responsible). Sales is informed of launch dates. The founder approves the budget.”

One sentence became four lines. But those four lines eliminated weeks of ambiguity.

What Changed

Three weeks later, the friendly fire stopped.

Not because people liked each other more – but because they finally knew whose call it was.

The founder sent me a note:

“We had our first project where no one apologized for ‘stepping on toes.’ Because there were no toes to step on – everyone knew their lane.”

Six months later, he told me:

“The work didn’t get easier. It just finally got simpler.”

Because clarity is the opposite of chaos. And simplicity is the opposite of overwhelm.

The Most Common Sentence I Hear in Teams

During facilitation sessions, there’s one line I hear more than any other:

“I thought that was my job.”

Sometimes said with pride. Sometimes with exhaustion. Sometimes with resignation. Sometimes with fear of stepping over a line.

Here’s the truth:

Teams rarely struggle because people don’t care. They struggle because people don’t know.

They don’t know:

  • Who owns the outcome

  • Who holds the pen

  • Who is consulted

  • Who gets informed

  • What “finished” looks like

  • What “good” looks like

People will work hard in ambiguity. They just won’t work efficiently.

And they’ll work emotionally.

Where Role Ambiguity Hides

Here’s where to look for role ambiguity in your own team:

1. Anything labeled “shared responsibility” Shared = blurred = bottlenecked

2. Any handoff between two people Every pass is an opportunity for misunderstanding

3. Any project where the founder is “involved” If you’re always involved, no one knows who truly leads

4. Legacy expectations Old roles never fully retired, new roles never fully defined

If you find these patterns, you’ve found your friction points.

🔧 Want to map your role architecture? I’ve built a Role Clarity Grid that defines ownership, decision rights, input pathways, and quality expectations. Reply “send it” and I’ll share it.

Clarity Is Kindness

Here’s what most founders miss:

Clarity is kindness.

When you don’t define roles clearly, you’re not empowering people – you’re burdening them with constant uncertainty about whether they’re doing the right thing.

One of the biggest cognitive stressors inside teams is uncertainty – not big uncertainty, but everyday “Is this my lane?” uncertainty.

When people know their lane, they relax. When they relax, they contribute. When they contribute, the team performs.

This is why role clarity and psychological safety are inseparable (Resolution #6).

Clarity reduces conflict before it begins. Ambiguity creates conflict no one can name.

This Is Where Decision Clarity Becomes Operational

This is where your decision clarity from Resolution #3 becomes operational:

You’ve defined who decides. Now you need to define who owns the outcome of that decision – and who supports it.

Decision frameworks tell you the process. Role clarity tells you the people.

Both are required.

The “After” Picture

Teams with clear roles experience:

  • Fewer escalations to the founder

  • Fewer misunderstandings

  • Faster decisions

  • Less defensiveness

  • Cleaner accountability

  • Stronger collaboration

  • Reduced emotional labor

  • A calmer work culture

Not because the work got easier. But because when expectations are explicit, execution becomes automatic. When they’re implicit, execution becomes emotional.

Your Identity Shift for 2026

This resolution isn’t about becoming a more “organized” leader.

It’s about becoming someone who eliminates role ambiguity – because unclear expectations create invisible conflict.

It’s the difference between walking into a project kickoff thinking “Everyone should just collaborate” versus “Who owns what by when?”

Same project. Different operating system.

That identity creates structure. Structure creates clarity. Clarity creates peace.

Because once you see yourself as someone who defines expectations explicitly, everything downstream becomes cleaner, lighter, and less emotional.

Your team stops apologizing for stepping on toes. Your meetings stop circling around who’s responsible. Your culture stops running on anxiety about boundaries.

And your organization stops treating role confusion as a personality conflict.

The Question That Changes Everything

Here’s what I want you to ask yourself:

How much of your team’s conflict is actually interpersonal – and how much is just structural ambiguity wearing a human face?

Because most “people problems” are really “clarity problems.” And clarity problems have clarity solutions.

Take 30 seconds: What’s one area where you have “shared responsibility” that’s actually creating confusion? Drop it in the comments – I read every one.

Your 2026 Resolution

Say it out loud: “I will eliminate role ambiguity – because unclear expectations create invisible conflict.”

This resolution sticks because identity drives behavior. Not goals. Not intentions. Identity.

Once you see yourself as someone who creates explicit clarity around roles, your decisions automatically align with that reality.

This isn’t about defining more work. It’s about defining the work less emotionally.

It’s about giving everyone the psychological safety of knowing:

  • Where they stand

  • What is expected

  • What success looks like

  • Where support is needed

  • Where autonomy is earned

Clarity is kindness. Clarity is alignment. Clarity is performance.

  • Decision rights (Who has final say?)

  • Input pathways (Who must be consulted?)

  • Quality expectations (What does “good” look like?)

  • Definition of done (What does “finished” mean?)

title: Does your week run on rhythm or chaos?
subtitle: Resolution #7: Stop Setting Goals – Start Building Rhythms
html:
“You don’t rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.” – James Clear

A founder told me recently, “We set clear goals every quarter. We just... don’t hit them.”

I asked: “What happens between the goal-setting and the deadline?”

Long pause.

“We... work on stuff?”

Exactly the problem.

So I asked him a different question: “What are your operating rhythms?”

He blinked. Paused.

“We meet when we need to.”

This is Resolution #7 in my series on building a business that holds its shape. [Previous: High Standards Need High Safety – or They Break People]

That’s the leadership equivalent of saying you’ll “work out when you feel like it.”

There is no performance without a pattern. No consistency without cadence. No alignment without ritual.

Because here’s the truth: every scaling company eventually learns that its team doesn’t follow its goals. Your team follows your rhythms.

The Team That Thought They Communicated Well

Last year, I worked with a team that genuinely believed they were excellent communicators.

Everyone was responsive. Everyone felt informed. Everyone “checked in” frequently.

Except for the week before I arrived, they’d had three different conversations about the same client issue – in Teams, in email, and in a hallway.

No one realized they were solving the same problem until the client asked why they’d gotten conflicting answers.

So I asked them basic questions:

How do decisions flow through the team? When do priorities reset? How do cross-functional updates happen? What’s your weekly rhythm?

I got seven different answers.

They didn’t have a communication system. They had communication hope. And hope is not an operating rhythm.

What Life Without Rhythms Actually Feels Like

Without rhythms, every week feels like you’re starting from scratch.

Every Monday is a negotiation. Every meeting is a surprise. Every deadline sneaks up on you. Every question routes back to the founder.

It’s not chaos – it’s just exhausting.

The founder carries what the system should hold. And carrying isn’t scaling.

The Intervention: Three Simple Rhythms

We built three rhythms for that team:

  1. Monday at 9 am: Priority Reset Not a status update. A forcing function. “Here are the three outcomes we’re driving this week. What’s blocking you?”

  2. Wednesday at 2 pm: Cross-Team Sync Not a meeting to share feelings. A coordination ritual. “What decisions do you need from another team to keep moving?”

  3. Friday at 4 pm: Weekly Retro Not a debrief. A feedback loop. “What worked? What didn’t? What do we adjust next week?”

That’s it. Three hours a week.

What Changed

Three weeks later, the founder sent me a message:

“We had our first week where no one interrupted me with a ‘quick question’ that could’ve waited for stand-up.”

Translation: The rhythm was finally doing the work he used to do.

Six months later, he told me:

“I used to spend Monday mornings telling people what to work on. Now I spend them asking what they’re learning.”

Same workload. Same team. Different system.

The rhythm was holding what he used to carry.

Why Rhythms Work When Goals Don’t

Goals are abstractions. Rhythms are behaviors.

Goals say: “We want better accountability.” Rhythms say: “Every Thursday at 2pm, we review commitments.”

Goals motivate. Rhythms deliver.

This is why your resolution isn’t about designing goals for 2026. It’s about designing the loops that make those goals unavoidable.

The Psychology: Rituals Remove Decision Fatigue

Humans are notoriously inconsistent when relying on willpower. But we’re extremely consistent when following rituals.

Rituals remove:

  • Decision fatigue

  • Ambiguity

  • Daily negotiation

  • Emotional bandwidth drain

They create:

  • Predictability

  • Accountability

  • Cohesion

  • Stability

Predictable loops create predictable output.

This is why high-performing teams feel calm even under pressure. Their rituals do the heavy lifting.

Want to design your operating rhythms? I’ve built an Operating Rhythm Builder that helps you structure priority resets, feedback loops, and coordination rituals. Reply “send it” and I’ll share it.

The Four Questions Every Rhythm Should Answer

Here’s the test:

Ask four people on your team these questions separately:

1. What are we doing? (Weekly priorities) 2. How are we doing it? (Workflows + handoffs) 3. How is it going? (Progress check) 4. What needs to adjust? (Course correction)

If you get four different answers, you don’t have operating rhythms. You have operating improvisation.

Three Types of Rhythms You Need

1. Forcing Functions (Prevent drift) Monday priority reset that aligns the team before work scatters

2. Feedback Loops (Capture learning) Friday retro that documents what worked and what didn’t

3. Coordination Rituals (Prevent siloing) Wednesday sync that surfaces cross-team dependencies early

Most teams have too many meetings and too few rhythms.

The difference? Meetings are reactive. Rhythms are structural.

“Without Me” Is the Real Test

Your 2026 resolution isn’t: “I will build operating rhythms.”

It’s: “I will build operating rhythms that run without me.”

Because if your system only works when you’re personally enforcing it, you don’t have a system – you have supervision.

Systems should:

  • Run without being pushed

  • Alert you when something is off

  • Maintain their shape during stress

  • Support the team when you’re not in the room

That’s what real scaling feels like. A shift from force to flow.

Where This All Connects

This is where everything from the previous six resolutions comes together:

You’ve audited your system (Resolution #1).

You’ve defined success (Resolution #2).

You’ve clarified decisions (Resolution #3).

You’ve built the bench (Resolution #4).

You’ve mapped bottlenecks (Resolution #5).

You’ve strengthened safety (Resolution #6).

Now you need the rhythms that make all of it sustainable.

Without rhythms, every insight becomes a one-time intervention. With rhythms, every insight becomes a permanent upgrade.

The “After” Picture

When operating rhythms click into place, leaders notice:

  • Fewer surprises

  • Fewer dropped balls

  • Fewer urgent clarifications

  • Shorter meetings

  • Clearer ownership

  • A calmer emotional tone

  • More strategic headspace

Not because people changed. Not because workloads decreased. But because the system began holding what the leader used to carry.

Rhythms create organizational oxygen – the space between the urgent and the important.

You can breathe. Your team can breathe. The work becomes sustainable.

Your Identity Shift for 2026

This resolution isn’t about becoming a more “organized” leader.

It’s about becoming someone who builds rhythms that hold the work – so you don’t have to.

It’s the difference between walking into Monday thinking “What fires need putting out?” versus “What’s on the priority reset this morning?”

Same Monday. Different operating system.

That identity creates structure. Structure creates rhythm. Rhythm creates sustainability.

Because once you see yourself as someone who designs rhythms instead of managing urgency, everything downstream becomes cleaner, lighter, and more predictable.

Your team stops negotiating priorities every morning. Your calendar stops filling with “quick syncs.” Your nervous system stops treating every week like improvisation.

And your business stops depending on your constant intervention.

The Question That Changes Everything

Here’s what I want you to ask yourself:

Are you building a business that runs on your constant intervention, or one that runs on reliable rhythms?

Because intervention is heroic. Rhythms are scalable.

Take 30 seconds: What’s one weekly rhythm you could add that would eliminate a recurring problem? Drop it in the comments – I read every one.

Your 2026 Resolution

Say it out loud: “I will build rhythms that hold the work – so I don’t have to.”

This resolution sticks because identity drives behavior. Not goals. Not intentions. Identity.

Once you see yourself as someone who builds rhythms, your decisions start aligning with that reality automatically.

Not in March. Not after launch. Not once the dust settles. Now.

Because the rhythm you build today is the performance you experience tomorrow.

  • Weekly cadence (priority resets)

  • 1:1 structure (feedback loops)

  • Project stand-ups (forcing functions)

  • Cross-team syncs (coordination rituals)

  • Retro cycles (learning capture)

  • Quarterly planning (strategic reviews)
