title: Can your team say the hard thing?
subtitle: Resolution #6: High Standards Need High Safety – or They Break People
html:
“High expectations don’t break teams. Lack of safety does.”

This fall, I worked with a team that looked perfect on paper.

Brilliant people. Clear mission. Solid budget. Leadership that genuinely cared.

But they had one quiet pattern: They avoided saying the hard thing.

No one wanted to embarrass a teammate. No one wanted to be the difficult one. No one wanted to risk conflict.

As a result: Decisions dragged. Rework increased. Frustration grew underground.

And the founder couldn’t figure out why such talented people were executing so slowly.

This is Resolution #6 in my series on building a business that holds its shape. [Previous: Your Bottleneck Isn’t Incompetence – It’s Invisible Heroics]

When I asked them privately what was happening, one person said something that stopped me cold:

“We don’t talk about problems until they’re big enough to be safe to name.”

That sentence is the exact opposite of psychological safety. And yet – it’s incredibly common.

The Experiment That Changed Everything

So we ran an experiment.

In their next team meeting, I prompted the team lead to ask: “I want everyone to name one small thing that’s been bugging them – something too minor to bring up before.”

Silence.

Then someone said: “The project timeline in the deck doesn’t match what engineering thinks is realistic.”

Then: “I’ve been unclear on who owns the customer feedback loop.”

Then: “I think we’re solving the wrong problem for this client.”

Fourteen minutes. Seven small problems. All of them fixable – if they’d been named two weeks earlier.

The founder looked around the room and said: “Why didn’t anyone say this before?”

Another silence.

Then someone said quietly: “We didn’t think it was safe to.”

The Team That Fell Apart

During the first year of the pandemic, I watched one of the most talented teams I’d ever worked with quietly unravel.

Not because they lacked skill. Not because the workload was unreasonable. Not because people were unwilling to stretch.

They fell apart because they had no psychological safety left in the tank.

Fear replaced candor. Caution replaced initiative. Silence replaced disagreement.

People stopped asking questions because questions felt dangerous.

By the end of that year, three people had quit – not for better offers, but because they couldn’t sustain the emotional cost of working in a low-safety, high-pressure environment.

The founder was devastated.

“I thought I was pushing them to excellence,” he said. “I was just pushing them away.”

That year changed how I think about leadership.

It taught me this: The moment of crisis is the wrong time to start building safety. You build it early, deliberately, and long before you need it.

What High-Performing Teams Actually Know

Here’s what I see constantly:

Founders who hire brilliant people, set ambitious goals, and then wonder why execution feels fragile.

The answer? They built high challenge without high safety.

They assumed talent would compensate. It doesn’t.

Google’s Project Aristotle studied 180 teams and found that psychological safety was the single strongest predictor of team effectiveness – more than talent, more than resources, more than structure.

Amy Edmondson’s research shows the same pattern:

High challenge + high safety = the learning zone High challenge + low safety = anxiety zone Low challenge + low safety = apathy zone Low challenge + high safety = comfort zone

Teams don’t need less challenge. They need more safety to handle the challenge that already exists.

High talent without safety is a car without traction – the engine spins harder, but the vehicle doesn’t move.

What Safety Actually Looks Like

Psychological safety is not about comfort. It’s about capacity.

It’s not:

  • Endless affirmation

  • Softening every message

  • Avoiding accountability

  • Protecting feelings at the cost of clarity

It’s:

  • Speaking the truth without punitive consequences

  • Asking questions without fear of judgment

  • Naming problems early

  • Disagreeing respectfully

  • Giving and receiving feedback cleanly

  • Owning mistakes without shame

  • Leaders modeling vulnerability, not perfection

Safety is built in micro-moments, not grand speeches.

Like when a PM raises her hand in a leadership meeting and says: “I think we’re about to make a mistake.”

And the founder says: “Tell me more” – not defensively, just curiously.

That’s 30 seconds. But it signals to the entire room: Dissent is valued, not punished.

Three Daily Practices That Build Safety

1. Start every 1:1 with: “What’s one thing I should know that you haven’t told me yet?”

This signals you’re looking for the unsaid, not just the status update.

2. Publicly thank someone who disagreed with you in a meeting

“Sarah pushed back on my timeline estimate, and she was right. Thank you for saying it.”

3. Admit when you changed your mind based on feedback

“I was going to do X, but after hearing from the team, we’re doing Y instead.”

These aren’t dramatic gestures. They’re deliberate signals that truth-telling is expected, not exceptional.

Want to build safety systematically? I’ve built a Safety Micro-Moments Checklist with daily leadership behaviors that signal “dissent is valued.” Reply “send it” and I’ll share it.

The Team That Rebuilt

Three months after we rebuilt safety on that team, the founder told me something had shifted.

“People started flagging problems in Teams before they became fires. Engineering pushed back on unrealistic timelines – and the product thanked them for it. Someone admitted they’d made a costly error and, instead of hiding it, asked for help fixing it.”

The work didn’t get easier. But the climate changed.

And in a high-challenge environment, climate is everything.

The Psychology: Teams Retain What They Feel

Here’s what matters:

Teams retain what they feel, not what they’re told.

If a team feels safe when you give feedback, the feedback lands. If they don’t, even the clearest message gets filtered through fear.

Your job isn’t to manage the work. It’s to manage the climate in which the work becomes possible.

This is why strengthening psychological safety early works: It preloads the climate your team will need when the stress inevitably hits.

Your Identity Shift for 2026

This resolution isn’t about becoming a “nicer” leader.

It’s about becoming someone who builds climate as deliberately as you build strategy.

It’s the difference between walking into a tense meeting thinking “We need to push harder” versus “What’s making it unsafe to speak up?”

Same tension. Different operating system.

That identity creates structure. Structure creates climate. Climate creates capacity.

Because once you see yourself as someone who manages climate, not just output, everything downstream becomes cleaner, lighter, and more sustainable.

Your team stops hiding problems until they’re fires. Your meetings stop feeling performative. Your culture stops burning through good people.

And your organization stops mistaking silence for alignment.

The Question That Changes Everything

Here’s what I want you to ask yourself:

Are you building a high-challenge team, or a high-challenge, high-safety team?

Because one creates performance. The other creates attrition.

Take 30 seconds: When was the last time someone on your team disagreed with you openly? If you can’t remember, that’s your answer. Drop it in the comments – I read every one.

Your 2026 Resolution

Say it out loud: “I will build psychological safety as a daily discipline – not a crisis response.”

This resolution sticks because identity drives behavior. Not goals. Not intentions. Identity.

Once you see yourself as someone who builds climate deliberately, your decisions start aligning with that reality automatically.

Not after the burnout. Not after the conflict. Not after the silence. Before.

Because safety isn’t a reaction. It’s a discipline. And discipline is what separates teams that scale cleanly from teams that splinter under pressure.

This checklist helps you build safety through simple, daily leadership behaviors:

  • Micro-acknowledgments that signal “I see you”

  • Curiosity prompts that replace judgment

  • Non-punitive feedback phrases

  • Early-problem surfacing routines

  • Safety rituals for meetings and 1:1s

Want it? Reply “send it.”

title: Who's compensating for your broken systems?
subtitle: Resolution #5: Your Bottleneck Isn’t Incompetence – It’s Invisible Heroics
html:
“Heroics look like help. But they function like bottlenecks.”

This summer, I stood at a whiteboard with a leadership team, mapping their client onboarding process.

On paper, it was seven steps. Clean. Linear. Professional.

Then I asked them to map the real process – not the one in the slide deck.

Who actually touches it? Who checks it? Who corrects it? Where does it stall? Where do people wait? Who becomes the “go-to” when something falls through the cracks?

By the time we finished, the board had 32 steps, five loops, and three unnamed responsibilities that had been silently absorbed by people who didn’t technically own them.

32 steps, yup.

This is Resolution #5 in my series on building a business that holds its shape. [Previous: Stop Absorbing the Shock – Start Building the Bench]

One team member stared at the board and laughed – that uncomfortable laugh when you realize you’ve been working twice as hard as necessary.

“I had no idea I was doing all that.”

Another said: “I didn’t know anyone else was doing any of this.”

The room went quiet.

Because suddenly they could see it: the invisible architecture that had been quietly exhausting them.

And the founder said what I hear in almost every workshop:

“We built a process without realizing how much of it still lives in people’s heads.”

The Hero Who Became the Bottleneck

A few weeks before that workshop, I’d been on a call with another founder.

He told me, almost apologetically: “The team comes to me because I fix things fast.”

He wasn’t bragging. He was exhausted.

So I asked him a simple question: “Is that speed solving the problem, or hiding it?”

He went quiet.

Then: “Oh. I think I’m the bottleneck.”

And he was – but not because he was slow. Because everyone relied on his speed.

He had become the system’s accidental hero – the person everyone routed work through because it was easier than fixing the friction underneath.

Two weeks later, he called me back.

“I stopped answering quick questions on Slack. Forced people to figure it out or bring it to the weekly meeting.”

“And?”

“Three of them figured it out. One brought it to the meeting and we documented the answer. Nobody’s asked me since.”

That’s the hidden truth in most scaling companies: Heroics look like help. But they function like bottlenecks.

Bottlenecks Aren’t People – They’re Patterns

When a company hits complexity, bottlenecks hide inside:

Invisible Handoffs

Sales thinks ops owns the kickoff call. Ops thinks sales does. The client waits three days.

Undefined Ownership

Everyone assumes someone else is tracking the contract details. Nobody is.

Well-Intended “I’ll Just Do It Myself” Moments

The founder answers a question in 30 seconds instead of documenting it. Now that answer lives only in his head.

These aren’t character flaws. These are system blind spots.

And here’s the problem: Nobody can fix what nobody can name.

What Happened After They Could See It

Three weeks after that whiteboard session, the founder texted me a screenshot.

It was a client onboarding that had just completed – in 4 days instead of 11.

“What changed?” I asked.

“We assigned the three orphaned tasks. Gave someone actual ownership of the kickoff call. They just... did it.”

Same people. Same capability. Different system.

That’s the effect of making the invisible visible:

  • Fewer escalations

  • Cleaner ownership

  • Smoother handoffs

  • Less rework

  • More trust in the system

And the founder? Back to strategic altitude.

Not because he worked less – but because he stopped doing the wrong things.

The Hidden Tax of Bottlenecks

Before they mapped it, the team thought the problem was that people were working too slowly.

Turns out, people were working heroically – just inside a system designed to waste their effort.

One of the managers told me later:

“I thought I was bad at my job because I was always behind. Turns out I was doing three people’s jobs – I just didn’t know which parts were actually mine.”

That’s the hidden tax of bottlenecks:

Not just slow work. Not just wasted time. But good people quietly burning out while compensating for bad design.

Want to uncover your hidden bottlenecks? I’ve built a Bottleneck Analyzer that reveals hidden handoffs, overloaded roles, and accidental heroics masking system failures. Reply “send it” and I’ll share it.

The Bottleneck-to-Flywheel Shift

In my forthcoming book Clutch Leadership, I call this the Bottleneck-to-Flywheel shift:

Moving from an organization that depends on heroic compensation to an organization that runs on intentional rhythm.

A bottleneck is simply a place where the system still leans too heavily on one person’s knowledge, context, memory, or speed.

A flywheel is when the work moves cleanly – even when that person isn’t there.

The difference? Visibility.

When you illuminate a friction point:

  • Shame drops

  • Clarity rises

  • Collaboration increases

  • The system becomes self-correcting

Humans improve what they can see. Systems fail where the patterns are invisible.

Your Identity Shift for 2026

This resolution isn’t about becoming a better “problem solver.”

It’s about becoming someone who makes friction visible so the system can solve itself.

It’s the difference between walking into a meeting thinking “I need to fix this” versus “Where is the system breaking down?”

Same problem. Different operating system.

That identity creates structure. Structure creates clarity. Clarity creates rhythm.

Because once you see yourself as someone who illuminates system failures instead of compensating for them, everything downstream becomes cleaner, lighter, and more sustainable.

Your team stops needing you to rescue them. Your processes stop depending on heroics. Your organization stops running on invisible labor.

And you stop burning out trying to be everywhere at once.

The Question That Changes Everything

Here’s what I want you to ask yourself:

How many of your “rock stars” are actually just covering for system failures you haven’t mapped yet?

Because heroics feel productive in the moment. But over time, they’re just expensive workarounds for problems you could’ve fixed.

This is where your system audit from Resolution #1 becomes surgical: You’re not just seeing that there’s drag – you’re identifying exactly where it lives.

Take 30 seconds: What’s one task you keep doing yourself because “it’s just faster”? Drop it in the comments – I read every one.

Your 2026 Resolution

Say it out loud: “I will stop compensating with heroics and start designing systems that hold without me.”

This resolution sticks because identity drives behavior. Not goals. Not intentions. Identity.

Once you see yourself as someone who illuminates friction rather than compensating for it, your decisions automatically align with that reality.

Not when the workload spikes. Not when the fires pop. Not when the system cracks. Early. On purpose. With visibility.

  • Tasks stuck in knowledge silos

  • Accidental heroics masking system failures

It takes under 10 minutes.

title: Who's ready to lead when the fire hits?
subtitle: Resolution #4: Stop Absorbing the Shock – Start Building the Bench
html:
“If the system only works when you absorb the shock, it’s not scaling – it’s straining.”

Two months ago, on a coaching call, a founder told me something I’ve heard more times than I can count:

“I know I need to build my leadership bench – but right now isn’t a good time,”

I asked him when a good time might be.

He laughed. Paused. Then said quietly:

“Probably after the next fire.”

Which is – of course – exactly when it’s too late.

This is Resolution #4 in my series on building a business that holds its shape. [Previous: Speed Isn’t About Work Ethic. It’s About Decision Clarity.]

Because by the time the fire hits, the bench you needed is the bench you didn’t build. And the shock you’re absorbing is the shock the system wasn’t designed to handle.

The Business That Ran on One Person’s Exhaustion

That founder’s company was already burning – he couldn’t see the smoke yet.

Three months earlier, I’d met one of his managers in a BootCamp cohort. Talented. Respected. High-capacity. Precisely the kind of person who should have been part of his leadership bench.

I asked her a simple question: “What decisions are fully yours?”

She looked confused.

“I’m not actually sure. I think I’m… assisting leadership more than being leadership.”

She was performing the role without the recognition. Absorbing pressure without the authority. Carrying responsibility she didn’t technically own. Waiting to be told she was ready – while quietly proving it every day.

And her founder? He wasn’t failing her intentionally.

He was doing something far more common – waiting for leaders to emerge instead of preparing them to lead.

Six months later, she left.

Not for more money. Not for a fancy title. Not for a better office.

She left for a company where someone saw her as a leader before she had to earn it through struggle.

Where the bench wasn’t accidental. Where leadership wasn’t a reward. Where the system made space for her to grow before the fire demanded it.

The Silent Warning Sign

Here’s the line I hear constantly from founders:

“My team is great – they just need more time.”

No.

Great teams don’t need more time. They need more people capable of carrying the load.

Because when every escalation loops back to you… When every crisis waits for your context… When every final decision needs your blessing…

You haven’t scaled leadership. You’ve scaled dependency.

And dependency always snaps under pressure.

Not because your team is weak. But because the system has quietly trained them to rely on the one person whose bandwidth will always run out first: you.

Building vs. Triaging

There’s a difference between building leaders and triaging crises.

Building looks like: Coaching someone through a decision they could’ve made alone.

Triaging looks like: Making the decision yourself because there’s no time to explain it.

One creates capacity. The other drains yours.

Most founders tell themselves they’re building when they’re actually just surviving.

You don’t build the bench:

  • When someone is already overwhelmed

  • When the team is already stretched thin

  • When you’re already drowning

  • When the stakes are already high

By then, you’re not building. You’re compensating.

The companies that scale smoothly? They pre-load leadership capacity long before the crisis demands it. They build altitude into the system early – so when the pressure hits, the structure holds.

The Bench Depth Test

Here’s the diagnostic I use with founders:

If you stepped away for two weeks, who would handle:

  • Client escalations

  • Team performance issues

  • Conflicting priorities

  • Stalled projects

  • Role disputes

  • Cross-functional coordination

  • High-stakes decisions

If you can’t name at least two people who could carry these essentials, your bench isn’t ready.

That doesn’t mean you’ve failed. It means you’re building the business on a single beam.

And single beams crack under stress.

If you can name them? You’ve built redundancy where it matters most – not in processes, not in playbooks, but in leadership capacity.

You’ve built a system that can absorb pressure without pulling you back into the center every time something shakes.

Want to map your leadership bench? I use a Leadership Bench Depth Audit with every founder I coach. It reveals who’s genuinely ready now, who could be ready with targeted coaching, and where your bench is thin. Reply “send it” and I’ll share it.

What It Looks Like When the Bench Actually Works

Last quarter, a founder I work with took a two-week vacation – his first real time off in three years.

When he got back, I asked him how many fires he had to put out.

“None,” he said. Then after a pause: “Actually… I think they forgot I was gone.”

That’s not abandonment. That’s the bench working.

Decisions got made without hesitation because leaders knew exactly what they owned. Stress is distributed rather than bottlenecked because the system no longer relies on one person’s stamina. And for the first time in years, he got something back that money can’t buy:

Headspace.

Not because he was working less – but because he was no longer the only person strong enough to hold the weight.

This is what scaling actually feels like. Not bigger. Lighter.

Your Identity Shift for 2026

This resolution isn’t about becoming a better “delegator.”

It’s about becoming someone who builds leaders before the fire demands them.

It’s the difference between walking into a meeting thinking “I need to handle this” versus “Who on my team could handle this with the right coaching?”

Same situation. Different operating system.

That identity creates structure. Structure creates capacity. Capacity creates headspace.

Because once you see yourself as someone who pre-loads leadership capacity, everything downstream becomes cleaner, lighter, and more sustainable.

Your team stops waiting for your blessing. Your calendar stops filling with decisions that shouldn’t need you. Your nervous system stops treating every week like crisis management.

And your business stops depending on your durability.

The Question That Changes Everything

So here’s what I want you to ask yourself:

Is your business actually scaling – or are you the one absorbing the shock?

Because shock absorption has a shelf life. Your stamina does. Your calendar does. Your nervous system definitely does.

Leadership capacity doesn’t. It compounds. It distributes weight. It creates stability that doesn’t hinge on your presence, your energy, or your heroics.

If the system only works when you cushion every impact, that’s not resilience – it’s deferred fragility.

Scaling starts the moment your business stops depending on your durability and starts depending on its own.

Take 30 seconds: Who on your team could step into a leadership role tomorrow if you gave them the authority and coaching? Drop it in the comments – I read every one.

Your 2026 Resolution

Say it out loud: “I will build leaders before I need them – because if I wait until the fire is already burning, I’m not building. I’m surviving.”

This resolution sticks because identity drives behavior. Not goals. Not intentions. Identity.

Once you see yourself as someone who pre-loads leadership capacity, your decisions start aligning with that reality automatically.

This isn’t idealism. It’s operational sanity.

Your business will never grow faster than your people.

If your team isn’t actively preparing for the next version of the company, you will always be the one compensating for the gap. Always the shock absorber. Always the contingency plan. Always the person holding more weight than the system was designed to require.

Future capacity isn’t something you discover in a crisis. It’s something you build quietly, deliberately, before the pressure hits.

  • Who could be ready with targeted coaching

  • Where your bench is thin or overextended

  • Where the system is still leaning on heroics

  • Where the quiet, overlooked leaders are hiding in plain sight

It’s simple. Fast. Brutally clarifying.

title: Why are decisions taking so long?
subtitle: Resolution #3: Speed Isn’t About Work Ethic. It’s About Decision Clarity.
html:
“Speed is rarely about work ethic. It’s almost always about decision clarity.”

Two months ago, at a leadership retreat, I watched a team spend 22 minutes debating a decision that should’ve taken two.

Everyone spoke. Everyone nodded. Everyone re-explained their position. Everyone kept glancing at the founder.

They weren’t confused. They weren’t cautious. They weren’t lacking context.

They were stuck because no one knew who was supposed to decide.

This is Resolution #3 in my series on building a business that holds its shape. [Previous: If Your Team Can’t Name Your Priorities, You Don’t Have Any]

That wasn’t indecision. That was decision friction – and it’s one of the highest hidden costs inside scaling companies.

People assume slow execution is a motivation problem. It’s not.

It’s a cognitive load problem.

Because when people have to calculate mentally:

  • Who actually owns this

  • How this kind of decision should be made

  • Whose input is required

  • Who needs to be informed

  • And when it’s “safe” to act

…they hesitate.

Not because they’re incapable. But because the system is ambiguous.

Ambiguity creates drag. Drag kills speed. And speed is a systems problem long before it’s a people problem.

What Decision Friction Actually Feels Like

Two patterns show up in almost every company:

The Silent Delay

A PM keeps a decision in her inbox for three days.

Not because she’s avoiding it – but because she genuinely doesn’t know if it’s her call, her VP’s call, or the founder’s call.

So she waits. Not from fear – from ambiguity.

The “Just to Be Safe” Escalation

A senior leader forwards everything upward because no one ever defined what autonomy actually means at their level.

“Safe” becomes code for: “I’m unclear.”

These aren’t performance issues. They’re system issues masquerading as people issues.

And until the system gets clearer, no amount of coaching, feedback, or motivation will fix the drag.

The Retreat Moment That Changed a Company

During a retreat last year, I asked a leadership team to sort their recent decisions into categories.

We dumped dozens of sticky notes onto the table – hiring, budgets, product choices, pricing, client escalations.

Then I asked: “Which of these were yours to decide – and which should not have been?”

Silence.

Then one leader finally said, “I didn’t know we were supposed to decide some of these.”

Another added: “I didn’t know we were allowed to decide these.”

The founder went quiet, staring at the table covered in color-coded confusion.

After a long moment, he exhaled:

“I thought I was empowering them. Turns out I was just… hoping they’d figure it out.”

We rebuilt their entire decision system that afternoon.

By the next quarter, they weren’t guessing anymore. They were moving.

Enter the 6C Decision Framework (Your Team’s New Operating System)

Here’s the backbone of decision clarity – your 6C Model:

1. Command A leader decides unilaterally. Use when speed matters more than input: “We’re launching Friday.”

Command isn’t domineering. It’s decisive – when time is the constraint.

2. Consultative A decider seeks input, then chooses. Use when you need perspective, not permission.

This is the sweet spot for most strategic calls.

3. Collaborative A small group co-creates the decision. Best for interdependent work across functions.

Collaboration here is structured, not a free-for-all.

4. Consensus The team collectively agrees. Rare. Expensive. Intentional.

Reserve it for values-level or identity-level choices – the things you need everyone to own, not just follow.

5. Core Expertise The decision belongs to the expert, not the most senior person. “If it’s legal, legal decides. If it’s design, design decides.”

This distributes judgment where it actually lives.

6. Choice Low-stakes decisions anyone can make autonomously. No approvals. No bottlenecks. No waiting.

Choice decisions keep the system moving without clogging leadership bandwidth.

The 6Cs aren’t bureaucracy. They’re cognitive unburdening. They remove the guesswork that slows companies down.

When people know how a decision should be made and who owns the call, their hesitation disappears – and speed returns.

Want to map your decisions to the 6Cs? I use a Decision Quick Card with every leadership team I coach. It clarifies who decides, how the decision gets made, and what can move autonomously. Reply “send it,” and I’ll share it.

Why This Isn’t Bureaucracy – It’s Cognitive Unburdening

People don’t need more authority to move fast. They need more certainty.

When every decision is placed inside one of the 6Cs, the ambiguity tax disappears.

People stop wondering if they can decide and start executing how they already know how to decide.

Execution gets cleaner. Escalations drop. Speed becomes predictable.

Because once the system removes the guesswork, the team stops hesitating and starts moving.

The “After” Picture – Three Months Later

This is what the founder told me a quarter later:

  • Meetings were 30–40% shorter

  • Escalations dropped dramatically

  • Decisions got made at the right level

  • The team moved faster without added pressure

  • He stopped being the bottleneck

And here’s the part that mattered most:

Nothing else had changed. Not the people. Not the strategy. Not the goals.

Just this: The team finally knew how decisions were made.

Once the system carried the clarity, they no longer needed to look to the founder for permission, interpretation, or direction.

Speed didn’t come from working harder. It came from removing the guesswork.

Your Identity Shift for 2026

This resolution isn’t about becoming a more “decisive” leader.

It’s about becoming someone who removes the guesswork so your team can move without hesitation.

It’s the difference between walking into a Monday meeting asking, “Why is this taking so long?” versus “Which decisions are still unclear?”

Same problem. Different operating system.

That identity creates structure. Structure creates clarity. Clarity creates speed.

Because once you see yourself as the leader who eliminates decision friction, everything downstream becomes cleaner, lighter, and faster.

Your team stops hesitating. Your meetings stop circling. Your decisions stop boomeranging.

And execution stops depending on you being in the room.

The Two-Minute Decision Audit

Ask yourself:

“How many decisions come back to me not because they should – but because the process is unclear?”

If the answer is anything above “a few,” your people aren’t slow. Your system is.

Because decisions don’t boomerang upward due to incompetence. They boomerang because the architecture hasn’t told people who owns what, how calls get made, or when autonomy actually applies.

Fix the system, and the boomerangs stop. Fix the clarity, and the speed returns.

Take 30 seconds: What’s the one decision that keeps coming back to you that shouldn’t? Drop it in the comments – I read every one.

Your 2026 Resolution

Say it out loud: “I will eliminate decision friction.”

This resolution sticks because identity drives behavior. Not goals. Not intentions. Identity.

Once you see yourself as someone who removes guesswork, your decisions automatically align with that reality.

No extra hours. No extra meetings. No heroic effort.

Just deliberate clarity – the kind that speeds up every corner of your business because people finally know how to decide, when to decide, and who decides what.

This isn’t about working harder. It’s about designing a system that moves faster because ambiguity isn’t dragging it down.

🔧 Free Tool: The 6C Decision Quick Card

I use this with every leadership team I coach.

It clarifies – in under 2 minutes:

  • Who decides

  • How the decision gets made

  • Who provides input

  • Who must be informed

  • What can move autonomously – without circling back to you

If you want it, reply “send it.”

title: Can your team name your top three priorities?
subtitle: Resolution #2: If Your Team Can't Name Your Priorities, You Don't Have Any
html:
Last week, I asked a CEO to name his top three priorities for 2026.

He paused. Gestured vaguely. Then said:

“Growth, excellence, and… being more strategic?”

I wrote them down. Then I asked his leadership team the exact same question.

I got nine different answers.

Nine.

This is Resolution #2 in my series on building a business that holds its shape. [Previous: Audit Your Leadership System – Not Your Org Chart]

And these weren’t junior folks. These were his closest advisors – smart, seasoned, aligned, loyal. People he trusted with the company’s direction.

I turned the sheet toward him. He stared at it for a long moment, then exhaled:

“I think I’ve been managing vibes, not priorities.”

He said it with a wry smile – half embarrassed, half relieved.

But here’s what I told him:

That’s not a failure. That’s a breakthrough.

Because clarity isn’t lost through incompetence. It’s lost through assumption. And once you see the fuzziness, you can finally fix it.

Where the Confusion Actually Lives

Most founders assume unclear priorities show up as chaos or disorganization.

They don’t.

They show up like this:

A VP standing in a hallway, debating whether to approve a $12K software purchase.

She has the authority. She has the budget. She has the context.

But she hesitates.

Not because she’s unsure of the decision. Because she’s unsure of the definition.

She doesn’t actually know what “strategic” means this quarter.

Is it revenue? Platform stability? New market expansion? Retention? Runway? Margin?

So she does what smart, responsible leaders do when the stakes are ambiguous:

She escalates it. Just to be safe. Just to avoid misalignment. Just to protect the business.

Multiply that hesitation across a forty-person company, and it’s no mystery why execution slows to a crawl.

Fuzzy owner priorities don’t create chaos. They create bottlenecks.

And bottlenecks create drag. And drag creates burnout. And burnout eventually turns into resentment.

Not because people lack commitment. But because the system is producing mixed signals – and everyone is just trying not to make the wrong call.

This Is Where System Clarity Actually Comes From

In my workshops, this pattern shows up in 80% of organizations:

  • Three different strategy decks… each with slightly different goals

  • A 2023 PowerPoint still quietly steering decisions

  • A spreadsheet someone built that accidentally became the operating plan

  • A Slack thread that somehow became “the thing we’re all doing now”

Your team isn’t confused because they’re careless. Your team is confused because the system is inconsistent.

Mixed signals create mixed execution. Mixed execution creates hesitation. Hesitation creates drag.

It’s not personal. It’s architectural.

Owner clarity → team clarity → organizational velocity. It’s a straight line.

When the system sends one signal, the team moves as one. When it sends five, everyone slows down trying not to break anything.

Why This Resolution Works (Psychology Perspective)

Behavioral researchers call this implementation intentions:

Not “we’ll be more focused,” but “If it’s Q2, then our top three priorities are X, Y, Z.”

It’s the difference between: A motivational slogan and a decision-making filter.

Teams don’t need inspiration. They need pre-decisions.

The more cues you establish – when X happens, we do Y – the faster your organization moves.

Because humans don’t follow concepts. Humans follow clarity.

Your Identity Shift for 2026

This resolution isn’t about becoming a more “organized” leader.

It’s about becoming someone who can name the work so clearly that the team could execute without you in the room.

It’s the difference between walking into a leadership meeting asking “Are we making progress?” versus “Which of our three priorities moved this week?”

Same meeting. Different operating system.

That identity creates structure. Structure creates clarity. Clarity creates speed.

Because once you see yourself as the leader who names the work, not the leader who rescues the work, everything downstream becomes cleaner, lighter, and faster.

Your team stops guessing. Your meetings stop drifting. Your priorities stop competing.

And execution stops depending on proximity.

The Alignment Test (And Its Teeth)

If you want to know how aligned your company actually is, try this:

Ask five people to write down your top five priorities for 2026. No discussion. No prompting. No hints.

I ran this exercise with a founder last month.

Five leaders. Five lists.

Priority #1 ranged from:

  • “Scale revenue”

  • “Improve retention”

  • “Launch the new platform”

Same company. Same context. Same leadership team.

Three completely different definitions of “what matters most.”

When he saw the mismatched answers, he went quiet for a moment and said:

“How did I let this happen?”

He didn’t. He simply assumed alignment without ever testing for it.

Most leaders do.

Because alignment feels obvious – until you ask people to write it down.

Want to test your own alignment? I use a Success Metrics Alignment Worksheet with every leadership team I coach. It forces the kind of clarity most companies think they have – but don’t. Reply “send it” and I’ll share it.

Stop Managing Vibes – Start Naming the Work

You cannot “focus” your way into a good year. You can only name your way into one.

And that starts with answering the question most founders avoid:

“What does a good year actually look like?”

Not thematically. Not philosophically. Not aspirationally.

Operationally. Measurably. Repeatably.

So when someone tells me: “This year, we’re going to be more focused.”

I don’t nod politely anymore.

I ask: “Focused on what, exactly?”

And then I wait.

Because if you can’t answer that question crisply – your team doesn’t stand a chance.

Clarity isn’t a vibe. It’s a standard. And until the standard is visible, your organization will always move slower than it should.

Take 30 seconds: What’s the one priority your team would name if you asked them right now? (And is it the one you’d want them to name?) Drop it in the comments – I read every one.

Your 2026 Resolution

Say it out loud: “I will name the work so clearly that my team could execute without me in the room.”

This resolution sticks because identity drives behavior. Not goals. Not intentions. Identity.

Once you see yourself as the leader who names the work, your decisions start aligning with that reality automatically.

You stop managing by vibe and hoping for the best. You start creating clarity that scales – the priorities, the definitions, the measurables, the boundaries.

Because when you shift identity, the work shifts with you.

🔧 Free Tool: Success Metrics Alignment Worksheet

I use a Success Metrics Alignment Worksheet with every leadership team I coach. It forces the kind of clarity most companies think they have – but don’t.

It sharpens:

  • The true top 3–5 priorities (not 12)

  • What “good” actually means for each one

  • What measurable progress will look like

  • What gets deliberately deprioritized

If you want it, reply “send it.”

If you’d rather walk through this together, reply “clarity.” I open a few short sessions each month, and this is one of the most valuable conversations I have with founders.

title: Everything I Know About Coaching, I Learned from Ted Lasso
subtitle: Why a fictional football coach reveals the shift teachers – and advisors – need most
html:
A quick note before we begin…

I’m currently supporting the faculty at an independent school as they integrate CliftonStrengths into their advisory program. They’re rolling it out thoughtfully – year by year – and right now, only the freshmen have taken the assessment and know their strengths.

Which means my training isn’t about memorizing 34 strengths or understanding domains. It’s about helping teachers make a fundamental distinction between two very different skill sets: teaching and coaching.

Because even without strengths language, teachers need to understand how coaching works – and more importantly, how it’s different from what they already do brilliantly in the classroom.

Today I was putting the finishing touches on my slide deck, and found myself typing two words: “Stay curious.”

The moment I hit enter, something clicked. That phrase – so simple, so central to coaching – opened a creative floodgate. I realized I’d seen that exact principle embodied perfectly in a show I’d resisted watching for years.

That’s what this essay is really about.

I’ve spent twenty years as a teacher, advisor, and middle school dean – followed by years designing leadership systems at USAID and coaching teams through complex human dynamics. With that background, you’d think I would have learned everything I know about effective coaching from formal trainings, PD sessions, or credentialing programs.

But the clearest, most accurate example of great coaching I’ve ever seen didn’t come from a workshop or a textbook. It came from a fictional, mustachioed football coach who didn’t even know the offside rule.

Before you roll your eyes – hear me out.

Because here’s the part I don’t usually admit: I almost never watched Ted Lasso at all.

The character debuted years ago in an NBC commercial where Ted becomes the new coach of Tottenham Hotspur – a detail that, as a lifelong Arsenal fan, was enough to shut it all down immediately. Spurs? Absolutely not. Interest terminated on sight.

I take my football seriously. Football is life.

So I skipped the show entirely. I didn’t watch a single episode while it aired. Only after the entire series had concluded – and after enough people insisted, “Matt, you of all people need to see this” – did I finally give in and binge it.

And to my surprise, beneath the biscuits, the mustache, and the Premier League loyalties I’d rather not discuss, I found something else entirely:

The most accurate, human, psychologically grounded depiction of authentic coaching I’ve ever seen on television.

Because there’s a moment that plays out inside every school: a student hovers in your doorway before asking a question; another blurts out an answer a beat too quickly; another “forgets” an assignment with a look that signals something deeper than laziness. Young people rarely narrate their inner lives directly. Their truth shows up first in behavior – brief, flickering signals adults must learn to read with care.

Teachers respond the way they were trained: They interpret. They analyze. They jump to meaning.

Teaching is about clarity.
Coaching is about curiosity.

In a classroom, interpretation is essential. It helps teachers hold patterns over time and guide learning with intention.

But in coaching – and in advisory – that same instinct becomes the very thing that shuts down a student’s voice before it ever has the chance to emerge.

Teaching is interpreting behavior.
Coaching is inviting meaning.

And this is where Ted Lasso, of all people, becomes such an unexpected teacher. Not because he uses coaching vocabulary – but because he embodies the posture, presence, and restraint that authentic coaching requires.

And the show gives us example after example.

But First: A Critical Distinction (and a Lesson in First Impressions)

Let’s be clear about something: Ted Lasso is a terrible football coach.

He doesn’t know the game. He can’t diagram plays. He doesn’t understand offsides rule. When his team needs tactical expertise, he turns to Nate, Beard, and Roy – people who actually know football.

And when I first saw him in that NBC commercial, he seemed like a clown. A joke. Comic relief about American ignorance of the beautiful game.

But here’s the thing about first impressions: they’re often wrong.

Ted looked like a clown because he didn’t have football expertise. But that’s precisely what made him brilliant at something else entirely.

Because Ted is a brilliant people coach.

  • Athletic coaching is about expertise: knowing the game better than your players, teaching technique, designing strategy, and making tactical decisions.

  • People coaching is about believing in their capacity, asking questions that unlock their own wisdom, creating conditions for growth, and holding space for self-discovery.

Athletic coaches need to know more than their players.
People coaches need to believe their clients are creative, resourceful, and whole.

Ted knows nothing about football. But he knows people. And that’s why the show works – it demonstrates what happens when someone chooses presence, curiosity, and belief over expertise and interpretation.

This is also a lesson in avoiding snap judgments – which is exactly what coaching requires.

When a student shows up at your door acting like they don’t care, or asks fifteen questions about an assignment, or rushes through their work, your first impression might be: They’re being difficult. Again.

But coaching requires you to pause at that behavior long enough to ask: What if I’m wrong? What if there’s another story here?

Ted looked like he didn’t belong. That first impression was accurate – he didn’t belong as a football tactician. But he absolutely belonged as a people coach.

The same is true for your students. Their behavior might look like one thing. The meaning behind it might be something entirely different.

This is the exact shift teachers need to make in advisory work.

  • In the classroom, you’re the athletic coach: you know the content, you design the learning, you guide the strategy.

  • In advisory, you’re the people coach: you trust students to discover their own answers, you ask rather than tell, you believe rather than fix.

Here are seven lessons from Ted that show what that looks like – and how they map to the Behavior → Meaning → Action framework students are craving:

1. Establishes and Maintains Agreements (Season 1, Episode 1 - “Pilot”)

The Scene: Ted’s first team meeting. The players are skeptical, the press is mocking him, and everyone expects him to perform confidently. Instead, he says, “I’m gonna fail. Probably fail a lot.”

The Lesson: Most leaders walk into new situations trying to prove they belong. Teachers do this too – especially early in the year when you’re establishing authority and credibility.

Ted does the opposite – he establishes authentic agreements about what he WILL bring (curiosity, belief, support) and what he needs from them (patience, honesty, effort). No false expertise. No hidden agendas. No pretending he knows the offside rule.

He’s admitting upfront: I’m not here because I know football better than you. I’m here because I believe in people.

Ted calls it “being straight with folks.”

The Connection to Your Framework: Ted isn’t interpreting their skepticism as a sign of disrespect or resistance. He’s creating the conditions where honest meaning can emerge later. He’s saying: I won’t jump to conclusions about your behavior. Let’s start with what’s real.

The Insight: Co-creating the relationship from day one creates safety. Pretending creates suspicion. In advisory, especially, students can smell inauthenticity instantly. You don’t need to pretend you have all the answers about their lives. You need to be clear about what you’re actually offering: invitation before interpretation.

2. Cultivates Trust and Safety (Season 1, Episode 4 - “For the Children”)

The Scene: Richmond has just been humiliated on the field. The locker room is silent, defeated. And Ted walks in and hangs the “BELIEVE” sign – not after a win, not after progress, but after they’ve gotten demolished.

The Lesson: Here’s what most teachers miss in advisory: trust isn’t built through competence or perfect advice. It’s built through unconditional positive regard, even when students are struggling.

The team thinks he’s delusional. But what Ted’s actually doing is creating a container of belief that exists independent of results. That’s psychological safety – the conviction that your value isn’t contingent on your performance.

An athletic coach might hang that sign after a win – as a reward, as validation.
Ted hangs it after a loss – as a foundation, as faith.

This is the advisory equivalent of saying: “I see how hard today was. I believe in you anyway.”

The Connection to Your Framework: Ted sees the behavior (the loss, the defeat). He doesn’t interpret it as a lack of effort or character. He doesn’t rush to fix it. He holds space for them to find their own meaning in the struggle – and he believes they will.

This is what it looks like to stay at the door long enough for students to step into the room.

The Insight: Trust comes from believing in students before they give you evidence that they deserve it. Not after. That’s what creates the foundation every coaching relationship – and every advisory relationship – needs. Results follow trust, not the other way around.

3. Maintains Presence (Season 2, Episode 8 - “Man City”)

The Scene: Ted freezes during the match. His vision narrows. He can’t breathe. He has to leave the sideline – the one place a coach is supposed to stay.

The Lesson: Here’s the dirty secret of coaching – and teaching – when YOUR stuff interferes, you can’t serve the student. This is the competency most teachers violate while pretending they’re fine.

Ted’s panic attack is the moment he realizes he needs help. And critically, he gets it. He doesn’t push through. He doesn’t “lean in.” He tells Dr. Sharon, “Something’s really wrong with me,” and he does the work to fix it.

Most teachers? They keep showing up broken and call it “being dedicated.” They confuse authenticity with bleeding on students who didn’t cut you.

The Connection to Your Framework: You can’t help students access meaning when your own unprocessed meaning is flooding the room. Ted recognizes his basement behavior (anxiety, disconnection, panic) and does the work to understand what it means – so he can show up from his balcony again.

The Insight: Teaching requires stability. Coaching requires presence. And presence requires self-awareness. Knowing when your internal state is no longer safe for someone else’s growth – and stepping back – is sometimes the most responsible act.

Coaching doesn’t require honesty. It requires a safe space where it is possible.

4. Listens Actively (Season 1, Episode 2 - “Biscuits”)

The Scene: Ted asks Nate – the invisible kit man everyone ignores – “What do you think we should do about our set pieces?” Then he waits. He leans in. He nods. He takes Nate’s answer seriously when it finally comes.

The Lesson: This scene is perfect because it shows Ted doing what athletic coaches almost never do: admitting he doesn’t know and genuinely asking someone else.

An athletic coach would design the set pieces themselves – that’s their job. Ted asks Nate – and then actually listens.

Active listening isn’t just hearing words. It’s believing the quietest person in the room has something valuable to say.

This is coaching presence: Ted doesn’t rescue Nate. He doesn’t fill the silence. He doesn’t soften the question. He stays at the door – at the behavior – long enough for Nate to step into the room.

And when Nate does, it changes everything. That one question changes Nate’s trajectory from the margins of the club to the strategic heart of it.

The Connection to Your Framework: Ted notices the behavior (Nate watches everything, knows the game deeply). He doesn’t interpret it (”Nate’s shy” or “Nate lacks confidence”). He invites Nate to make meaning of what he’s been observing. And Nate chooses the action – the strategic insight that helps the team.

Behavior → Meaning → Action.

This is what happens in advisory when adults stop supplying meaning and start inviting it.

The Insight: Most teachers ask questions but don’t wait for answers. They’re just reloading their own interpretation while students talk. Ted waits. He receives. He believes the student has something worth saying. That’s the difference between listening and performing listening.

5. Evokes Awareness (Season 2, Episode 1 - “Goodbye Earl”)

The Scene: Roy Kent’s retirement party. He’s adrift – no longer a player, not sure who he is anymore. Ted asks, “What do you want to do next?”

The Lesson: Ted doesn’t give Roy advice. He doesn’t fix his problem. He doesn’t say, “You should coach!” or “Have you thought about commentary?” He asks the question that makes Roy think differently about his future – a future Roy hasn’t really considered because he’s been too busy being angry about his past.

An athletic coach would tell Roy what to do – they’d have a plan, a strategy, a next step. Ted asks Roy to discover his own answer.

That’s coaching – evoking awareness in the client, not downloading your wisdom onto them.

This is the critical distinction for teachers moving into advisory work:

Teaching (athletic coaching): Here’s what I think this means.
Coaching (people coaching): What does this mean to you?

Roy eventually discovers the answer on his own – and that’s why it sticks.

The Connection to Your Framework:

“This is where agency lives. This is where coaching starts. Access meaning through inquiry – not interpretation.”

Ted sees Roy’s behavior (anger, drift, disconnection). He doesn’t interpret it or fix it. He asks Roy to make sense of it himself. And that meaning leads to Roy’s own action.

The Insight: The best coaches – and advisors – aren’t the most intelligent people in the room. They’re the ones who ask questions that make students feel like the smartest person in the room. One creates dependency. The other creates agency.

6. Facilitates Growth (Season 1, Episode 10 - “The Hope That Kills You”)

The Scene: After Richmond chokes on penalty kicks, Ted designs practice around the thing they failed at. The team practices penalties. Over and over. Missing. Trying again. Missing. Trying again.

The Lesson: Here, Ted actually does function like an athletic coach – he designs the practice, sets up the conditions, and creates the structure.

But notice what he doesn’t do: he doesn’t rescue them. He doesn’t take the kicks for them. He doesn’t soften the difficulty.

Growth doesn’t happen in comfortable spaces. It happens in the repetitive, frustrating, unglamorous work of trying the thing you failed at until you don’t fail anymore.

Ted creates conditions where they can learn from failure. He holds the space. He watches them struggle. He lets them build the muscle memory of resilience.

This is advisory in its purest form: creating conditions where students confront difficult emotions safely, without being saved from discomfort.

The Connection to Your Framework:

“Coaching ends with a future-oriented choice. Tiny. Doable. Chosen by the student.”

Ted doesn’t tell them how to fix their penalty kicks. He creates the conditions for them to practice the action over and over until they develop their own mastery. The action is theirs.

The Insight: Facilitating growth means designing experiences that stretch students, not shielding them from discomfort. If you’re protecting students from hard things, you’re not developing them – you’re infantilizing them. Love doesn’t mean easy. It means believing they can handle hard.

7. Empowers Through Curiosity (Season 1, Episode 8 - “The Diamond Dogs”)

The Scene: The dart game at the pub. Rupert is mocking Ted, the crowd is laughing, and before Ted throws the winning dart, he tells them all: “Be curious, not judgmental.”

The Lesson: This might be the whole game. This is the line that separates athletic coaching from people coaching.

Athletic coaches make judgments – they have to. This player is better than that one. This strategy works; that one doesn’t. That’s their job.

But people coaching isn’t about having answers – it’s about asking better questions. When you approach every interaction with genuine curiosity instead of judgment, you unlock what the student already knows. You create space for them to discover their own wisdom rather than adopt yours.

That’s the coaching standard in seven words. It’s also a coaching doctrine for teachers in advisory.

Judgment collapses possibility.
Curiosity keeps it open.

It’s the same instruction I give faculty when we work on neutral observation:

Interpretation (athletic coaching): “You seem disengaged.”
Curiosity (people coaching): “I noticed you stayed quiet. What was happening for you?”

The difference is everything.

The Connection to Your Framework: Curiosity allows you to stay with the behavior without jumping to interpretation. It’s what invites the student to make meaning. It’s what creates the conditions for them to choose their own action.

Be curious.

Invitation before interpretation.

Choice before correction.

The Insight: Curiosity is a discipline, not a personality trait. It’s a choice you make in the moment when your brain wants to judge, fix, or solve. Ted chooses curiosity. Every time. Even when judgment would be easier, faster, or more satisfying. That’s what makes him a people coach instead of just a nice guy with opinions.

Why These Scenes Matter for Teachers

Schools already have the architecture for coaching: advisory groups, small communities, and a relational culture.

But what many lack is the skill set Ted models so consistently – and it’s not about football expertise. It’s about:

  • Noticing behavior without jumping to interpretation

  • Inviting meaning instead of supplying it

  • Holding space for students to choose their own action

  • Staying curious instead of certain

  • Believing students are creative, resourceful, and whole

This is why faculty wrestle with coaching work: Interpretation is how teachers survive the classroom. It is a professional reflex, a point of pride. It’s what makes you a great athletic coach in your subject area.

But advisory work requires a different muscle: staying with the behavior long enough for the student to offer the meaning.

Ted Lasso succeeds as a leader because he never confuses interpretation with understanding. He knows that meaning belongs to the person living it – not the person observing it. He knows he doesn’t have football expertise – so he gets out of the way and lets the people with expertise (Nate, Beard, Roy) do that work, while he focuses on what he does know: people.

And that is the lesson teachers are perfectly positioned to embrace.

Students are craving adults to help them make sense of themselves.

In the classroom, you’re the athletic coach: you know the content, you design the learning, you guide the strategy.

In advisory, you’re the people coach: you trust students to discover their own answers, you ask rather than tell, you believe rather than fix.

Teaching guides learning.
Coaching guides self-awareness.
Advisory lives at their intersection.

When teachers learn to pause at the behavior – to notice without assuming, to ask without steering, to hold the moment without rushing – students step into the room with more clarity and confidence.

They stop performing the identity adults assign them.
They begin discovering their own.

title: Could your business survive two weeks without you?
subtitle: Resolution #1: Audit Your Leadership System — Not Your Org Chart
html:
“If you stepped away for two weeks—no laptop, no Slack—would your business hold its shape… or would the seams start showing?”

If you read my last essay, you know why this question matters. If you didn’t, you can still feel it in your stomach.

Because this isn’t really about a vacation. It’s about exposure.

It reveals something an org chart never will: Whether your business runs on systems— or on you.

And here’s the pattern that shows up every time I coach a founder through this moment:

Their business isn’t wobbling because the people are wrong. It’s wobbling because the architecture underneath the work is still implicit, invisible, or living entirely in the leader’s head.

Which is why every January, I watch owners sit down to “plan the new year” and end up rearranging names on an org chart—dragging boxes around like furniture, hoping a better layout will create a better system.

It never does.

Because structure isn’t the source of clarity. Systems are.

People don’t need a new arrangement. They need a shared operating logic. Clear decision pathways. Clean handoffs. Visible priorities. Standards that don’t evaporate when you’re not in the room.

Most leaders don’t have a structure problem. They have a system problem.

And until you name that honestly, the business will keep leaning on your presence instead of its own design.

This series is about changing that— not through heroics, but through architecture.

Because a business that can hold its shape for two weeks… can hold its shape for thirty years.

The Identity Shift That Actually Changes Behavior

This resolution works because it shifts identity, not tasks.

You’re not becoming someone who “audits systems.” You’re becoming someone who sees systems first, people second— someone who instinctively looks for patterns, handoffs, decision paths, and clarity before rearranging names on a chart.

And that shift—quiet, subtle, almost invisible— changes everything.

It’s the difference between walking into a Monday meeting asking “Who dropped this?” versus “Where did the handoff fail?”

Same problem. Different operating system.

Because once you start seeing the system, the org chart stops being the hero. It becomes a supporting actor. The structure, not the source.

And every decision you make in 2026 begins to flow from that higher altitude: less reaction, more design. Less rearranging, more architecting. Less “Who do I put here?” and more “What does the system need to carry?”

Where “People Problems” Are Really System Problems

When a business wobbles, it’s never random. It’s because the architecture underneath is misfiring.

Let me show you what that actually looks like.

Slow Execution

It’s rarely a capability problem.

Your team has no idea which decisions they own… and which ones still require your sign-off.

So they wait. Or they escalate “just to be safe.” Or they make the cautious choice—the one that protects them, not the timeline.

Not a talent issue. A Clarity failure.

When people don’t know the boundary, they protect themselves. When they do know the boundary, they move.

Constant Rework

Classic handoff failure.

Person A assumes Person B knows X. Person B assumes Person A already handled Y. And the work slips straight through the space between them.

Not a performance issue. An Execution breakdown— a system gap masquerading as a personnel problem.

When expectations live in people’s heads, the work wobbles. When expectations live in the system, the work flows.

Teams “Not on the Same Page”

This one’s everywhere.

I worked with a founder who kept saying, “My team just isn’t executing.” Turns out they were executing—just on different definitions of “urgent.”

He thought urgent meant client-facing. His ops lead thought urgent meant payroll-adjacent.

Both were right. Neither knew the other’s rulebook.

That’s Culture misfiring. Invisible assumptions aren’t harmless— they’re one of the most expensive forms of systemic friction.

The CREATE Model: Your System-Level Diagnostic

Before we go any further, here’s the lens that makes all of this work:

The six cylinders of organizational health — what I call the CREATE model — become your diagnostic tool. Not a framework you memorize. A pattern your eyes start seeing everywhere.

C — Culture Are expectations visible, consistent, and lived?

R — Relationships Does trust move fast enough for work to move fast?

E — Execution Are decisions clean, handoffs crisp, and processes carrying their own weight?

A — Agility Does the organization shift smoothly, or only when you shove?

T — Teaching Are leaders developing leaders, or quietly absorbing the load themselves?

E — Ethical Decision-Making Are choices aligned with values, even under pressure?

When one of these cylinders misfires, the pattern becomes unmistakable.

🔧 Want to see where your cylinders are misfiring? I’ve built a 3-minute diagnostic that shows you exactly where your business is still leaning on heroics instead of structure. Reply “send it” and I’ll share it.

What Changes When You Adopt This Identity

When you adopt the identity of a leader who diagnoses systems first, everything changes.

You stop reacting to symptoms. You stop personalizing every hiccup. You stop blaming individuals for problems the architecture created.

Instead:

  • You start seeing patterns — the repeating loops hiding beneath the noise.

  • You eliminate friction at the root — not by working harder, but by redesigning the path.

  • You create more stability with less effort — because clarity scales better than vigilance.

  • You reduce the company’s dependence on you — not by stepping back, but by building forward.

This isn’t more work. It’s different work. The kind of work that actually scales — because it turns leadership from heroics into design.

Your 2026 Resolution

Say it out loud: “I will see my business as a system — not an org chart.”

This resolution sticks because identity drives behavior. Not goals. Not intentions. Identity.

Once you see yourself as a systems-builder, your decisions start aligning with that reality automatically.

You stop dragging people around the board, hoping configuration will solve clarity. You start strengthening the architecture beneath them— the decisions, the handoffs, the rhythms, the guardrails.

Because when you shift identity, the work shifts with you.

Your First Step: The Two-Week Test

Ask yourself:

“What would wobble if I disappeared for two weeks?” “What would hold?” “Where would the seams start to show?”

Those answers aren’t hypothetical. They’re diagnostic.

They reveal—quickly, honestly, and without ego—where your system is strong, where it’s stretched, and where the work is still being held up by memory, instinct, or proximity instead of design.

And once you see those wobble points clearly, the path forward becomes unmistakable:

Not rearrange the roles. Not rework the org chart. But repair the system underneath the roles.

Take 30 seconds: What’s the one thing that would absolutely require you if you disappeared tomorrow? Drop it in the comments—I read every one.

That’s the work of 2026. And it’s the work that turns a two-week absence from a stress test… into proof your architecture is finally doing the heavy lifting.

🔧 Free Tool: The Founder Absence Stress Test

I’ve built a 3-minute diagnostic that shows you exactly where your business is still leaning on heroics instead of structure—where you’re compensating, where the system is thin, and where judgment is still living in your head instead of the architecture.

If you want it, reply “send it.”

If you’d rather talk through what this looks like inside your business, I open a limited number of short clarity sessions each month. Reply “clarity” and I’ll reserve one for you.

title: Freedom by Design: Building Systems That Stand Without You
subtitle: Essay 5 of 5
series: Systems that run without you series
html:
Could You Leave for a Two-Week Vacation?

There’s a question I often ask founders and senior leaders, and it usually lands with a mix of honesty, longing, and discomfort:

“If you stepped away for two full weeks – no laptop, no Slack, no check-ins – could you trust the business not just to hold steady, but to keep moving forward?”

The reactions are remarkably consistent. Some leaders laugh softly, trying to make light of what feels weighty. Others draw in a sharp breath, already imagining what might wobble or stall. Many simply pause – a long, thoughtful silence that reveals far more than their words could.

That moment has very little to do with a hypothetical vacation. It’s about what the question exposes.

For most leaders, the anxiety isn’t that something might go wrong while they’re away. It’s the realization that too much depends on their ongoing presence for things to go right at all. And if the idea of stepping back introduces tension rather than ease, it’s not an indictment of your capability or commitment – it’s a signal that the system surrounding you isn’t fully built yet.

This pattern is common. Many companies scale faster than their internal architecture matures. Leaders compensate by becoming the connective tissue – the person who holds the context, the logic, the decision pathways, the quality bar. Their presence fills the structural gaps, allowing the business to function through proximity rather than design. It works for a while. Until the business outgrows the human buffer holding it together.

Optionality – the ability to step back without the organization losing its rhythm – isn’t about making yourself unnecessary. It’s about building a company where your presence enhances the work rather than stabilizes it. A company where momentum doesn’t depend on your vigilance, where clarity doesn’t evaporate when you’re not in the room, and where the operating system continues to hum even when you’re out of sight.

This kind of optionality isn’t indulgent. It’s intentional. And, with the right architecture, it’s entirely achievable.

Optionality Is the Highest Form of Leadership

I don’t define a strong company by how well it performs when the leader is in the room. Almost any organization can appear functional under those conditions. A founder’s presence naturally compensates for everything the system can’t yet hold. Their clarity fills the gaps. Their instincts smooth the rough edges. Their vigilance keeps all the invisible seams from splitting open.

But leadership isn’t measured by what happens when you’re present. Leadership is measured by what continues to happen when you’re not.

This is what I mean by optionality—the ability to step back without the work collapsing inward, the confidence that standards will hold without monitoring, that judgment won’t erode in your absence, and that momentum won’t slow simply because you aren’t the one pushing it forward. Optionality is quiet proof that the system—not the leader—is carrying most of the load.

And it’s important to name something leaders often misunderstand: optionality is not abandonment. It is not the absence of leadership. It’s the presence of architecture.

When systems are thoughtfully designed, they don’t diminish the leader—they elevate everyone. They give teams the structure and stability they need to exercise judgment without hesitation, to move with steadiness rather than caution, and to take responsibility without waiting for permission or proximity. In these environments, a leader’s presence becomes additive instead of essential. Their contribution becomes intentional rather than reactive.

A company with real optionality doesn’t need its leader every minute. But it deeply benefits from their presence when they choose to step in. That is the distinction high-capacity leaders are actually seeking—not irrelevance, but freedom. Not detachment, but the ability to show up from a place of clarity and strategic intent instead of necessity or vigilance.

And that freedom isn’t a reward of success.

It’s a result of design.

The False Safety of Constant Involvement

Continuous involvement almost always feels like leadership. It feels like care – a sign that you’re present, invested, and willing to shoulder the weight with your team. In the early stage of a company, that instinct is often what keeps the business alive. Your proximity fills gaps the system can’t yet hold. Your presence reassures people that nothing essential will slip. And your ability to react quickly gives the organization a sense of momentum it couldn’t generate on its own.

But involvement and effectiveness are not the same thing, and over time the distinction becomes expensive.

When your team grows accustomed to your proximity as their primary source of clarity, something subtle begins to shift in the culture. People learn to wait rather than decide. They hesitate where they should act. They seek reassurance instead of exercising judgment – not because they lack ability, but because the system has quietly trained them to believe your presence is the safest path. In that environment, even the most capable employees become tentative. Initiative thins out. Ownership becomes conditional rather than embodied. Progress starts to depend more on your availability than on the team’s design.

And slowly, almost without anyone noticing, your calendar becomes the operating system of the company. Meetings rearrange themselves around your schedule. Decisions land only when you weigh in. Ambiguity dissolves only when you are in the room to interpret it. Without meaning to, you become the gravitational center of the organization – the place teams orbit when they need clarity, alignment, or momentum.

This is the trap high-capacity leaders fall into not because they lack discipline, but because their instincts have been shaped by earlier seasons of the business. What once looked like commitment now functions as constraint. What once provided stability now limits the organization’s ability to stand on its own. And what once signaled strength now signals that the architecture around you has stopped evolving while the complexity of the work has continued to grow.

The real work of scale begins when leaders recognize this shift for what it is – not a personal failing, but a structural invitation. A call to build a system where clarity doesn’t depend on proximity, where ownership doesn’t require oversight, and where your presence becomes a choice grounded in contribution rather than a necessity grounded in survival.

What Breaks When You Leave Reveals the System You Have

When I run executive offsites or conduct system architecture audits, there’s one exercise I come back to every time because it reveals more truth, more quickly, than any spreadsheet or dashboard ever could. I ask leaders to imagine stepping away tomorrow – completely, cleanly – and identify what would wobble. Not collapse. Not ignite. Just wobble.

The responses are always illuminating.

  • A founder will quietly acknowledge, “This client relationship still lives entirely in my head.”

  • A product leader will realize, “This decision keeps landing on my desk because no one feels fully authorized to own it.”

  • A project owner will notice, “This initiative doesn’t have anyone who sees it end-to-end.”

  • And almost every leadership team uncovers some version of, “People escalate too quickly because they’re not sure where the guardrails actually are.”

Each answer becomes a window into the real architecture of the company – the parts of the system that are sturdy, the parts that are thin, and the parts that aren’t actually systems at all but memories, habits, or good intentions you’ve been holding in your head.

What wobbles in your absence is the part of the organization still dependent on tacit knowledge rather than explicit design. It’s the work held in muscle memory instead of structure. It’s the judgment that hasn’t been distributed because it’s never been articulated. And it’s the clearest diagnostic signal you can gather as a leader: not what people can’t do, but what the system hasn’t yet taught them how to do on their own.

And here’s the insight that catches many leaders by surprise: the problem is almost never the people.

It’s the design.

The wobble reveals where expectations are implicit rather than visible, where ownership hasn’t been anchored, where decision rights haven’t been codified, and where momentum still depends on your presence instead of the system’s stability. Once you see that clearly – once you see the architecture rather than the symptoms – the work becomes less about effort and more about intention. It becomes a design problem, not a personal one. And design problems are solvable.

You Don’t Become Optional by Stepping Back. You Become Optional by Designing Forward.

Optionality isn’t created by stepping back; it’s created by clarity. Leaders don’t become less essential by removing themselves from the work. They become less essential by building the infrastructure that reliably carries what they’ve been holding. When the architecture is strong, your presence becomes a contribution rather than a requirement – a source of refinement, not rescue.

Here’s what that architecture looks like in practice:

1. Clarify Decision Rights
Most organizational stress begins with blurred boundaries. People rarely hesitate because they lack intelligence or initiative – they hesitate because they’re unsure who decides, how decisions should get made, or what “done” is supposed to look like. When those elements are explicit, decision-making becomes cleaner, faster, and far less dependent on proximity to the leader. Decision clarity creates decision confidence, and confidence is what allows judgment to scale.

2. Embed Guardrails, Not Gates
Guardrails preserve standards without forcing every choice to route back through you. They answer the quiet questions that slow teams down: What guides good judgment when you’re not here? What are the principles behind the decisions you tend to make instinctively? When those principles are visible, people don’t need permission to move forward – they already know how to think. Guardrails don’t slow teams down; they keep them aligned while they move quickly.

3. Build Cadence Before Capacity
 Many leaders try to hire their way out of complexity, only to discover that more people simply amplify whatever rhythm already exists. Scale isn’t held by headcount – it’s held by cadence. Weekly resets that anchor priorities. Predictable reviews that lower anxiety. Clean handoffs that prevent drift. Rituals that stabilize the pace of the organization. Without cadence, capacity just adds noise. When rhythm comes first, velocity becomes sustainable.

4. Audit the Bottlenecks
 Every decision, approval, or clarification that still routes through you is a piece of data. It reveals where authority hasn’t yet been embedded in the system and where clarity is still living in your head instead of the architecture. Label those moments without judgment. Then ask: Is this load essential, or is it inherited? Architects redesign inherited load. Operators simply carry it.

Freedom Isn’t a Feeling. It’s a System.

Most leaders carry a quiet dream of spaciousness – the kind of time that allows them to think more deeply, build more intentionally, and lead from a higher altitude instead of reacting from the ground level. But that freedom doesn’t suddenly appear when you finally “catch up” or when the fires die down for a week or two. It doesn’t arrive as a reward for endurance. It arrives when the system is designed to make room for it.

Freedom is not the result of working harder.
Freedom is the result of architecture.

It emerges the moment clarity stops living in your head and becomes visible to everyone else. When roles are structured so that authority and accountability sit in the same place. When trust isn’t something you reinforce through constant involvement but something your operating rhythm distributes on its own – through predictable cadences, explicit standards, and shared understanding. Freedom appears when the organization can breathe without you holding its ribs in place.

Being able to step away for two weeks with genuine confidence isn’t indulgent. It’s diagnostic. It tells you more about the health of your system than any dashboard or performance review ever could.

If the company holds – and even advances – while you’re gone, that’s data. It means the architecture is sound. It means judgment has been scaled. It means the culture doesn’t rely on proximity for stability. And it means your leadership has evolved from heroic intervention to durable design.
