You see it in leadership meetings that revolve around outcomes but ultimately make decisions based on energy, mood, or whoever speaks last – a dynamic HBR describes as “decision volatility,” where clarity collapses under the weight of unstructured conversation. And you see it in founders who champion empowerment publicly but privately believe that the safest, fastest path is still to take the work back and do it themselves.

Stress can certainly create motion. But motion is not momentum.

If you want real speed – the kind that feels stable, consistent, and rooted rather than frantic – you need something far more deliberate. Not more dashboards. Not more headcount. Not another surge of heroic effort. What scaling organizations actually need is scaffolding: the rhythms, guardrails, and shared architecture that make clarity predictable instead of occasional.

This scaffolding becomes the invisible lattice that holds decision-making, accountability, and trust in place. McKinsey’s research on high-performing operating models shows that companies with explicit decision pathways and reliable cadences make faster, higher-quality decisions than those relying on constant escalation or improvisation. And Amy Edmondson’s work adds another layer: psychological safety isn’t created by proximity to a leader – it’s created by shared expectations and consistent structures.

That’s the real advantage of architecture. It doesn’t just tell people what to do – it teaches them how to lead through complexity without relying on your proximity to make the system function.

The Shift From Effort to Architecture

Most founders I work with don’t actually crave control. What they crave is confidence – the quiet assurance that if they step away, the company won’t lose its footing. They want to trust that decisions made in their absence will reflect the same values and standards they would have chosen, and that excellence won’t rise and fall based on their proximity. What they long for isn’t oversight – it’s a system they can rely on.

They want a company that becomes stronger when they step back, not one that wobbles. A team that leads with judgment instead of waiting for permission. A structure that distributes clarity rather than concentrating fragility in one or two people. And organizations like that don’t materialize through heroic effort or goodwill. They emerge through design.

Designing for scale isn’t about adding bureaucracy or formalizing everything to death. It’s about creating the conditions in which people can move with confidence – where expectations are visible rather than implied, where decision rights are explicit rather than assumed, and where feedback is grounded in shared standards rather than personal preference. HBR has written extensively on this: clarity, not charisma, is what sustains performance in growing organizations.

It means shaping roles where authority and accountability sit in the same place. It means codifying the decision principles you instinctively use so others can apply them without hesitation. It means building meeting rhythms that stabilize the team instead of spinning it. And it means replacing heroic responsiveness with operating structures that are predictable, humane, and durable – the kind McKinsey identifies as the hallmark of high-performance operating models.

Because the truth is simple: the most scalable system is not the one that automates the most work. It’s the one that amplifies human judgment without requiring heroic effort to function.

That is the work I do with my clients – founders, directors, and operators who move quickly, think deeply, and can feel the strain underneath even when the metrics look strong. Sometimes a single 60-minute session surfaces six months of hidden friction. Sometimes, a redesigned rhythm can change the entire emotional climate of a team.

So if you’re feeling that heaviness, don’t mistake it for a personal limitation. The ceiling you’re hitting isn’t about you – it’s structural. And once you can see the architecture clearly, you can begin to design your way past it.

If You Feel the Ceiling, You’re Not Broken – You’re Ready

If everything still routes through you, it isn’t a sign you’re falling short. It’s a signal that the company has outgrown the operating system that worked in the early days. What feels like personal pressure is almost always structural pressure – the weight of a system asking one person to carry what was never meant to rest on a single set of shoulders.

This isn’t about effort. It’s about architecture.

You don’t need more urgency.
You don’t need longer hours.
You don’t need to push harder or tighten your grip.

What you need is better design – the kind of design that turns clarity into capacity and transforms your presence from a requirement into a multiplier. This is exactly what research from McKinsey and Harvard Business Review keeps finding: organizations don’t scale because leaders work more. They scale because leaders redesign the system underneath the work.

And if you want to see what that looks like inside your own organization – the decisions that bottleneck, the rhythms that create drag, the handoffs that quietly leak trust, the roles that depend too heavily on your judgment – I built something to make those patterns visible.

👉 Chatt with Matt – a 30-minute clarity audit for scaling teams.

It’s not another meeting. It’s a diagnostic – a way to surface the architecture you already feel but haven’t yet named.

Because scaling doesn’t have to feel heavier as you grow. And you don’t have to keep carrying what the system can be designed to hold instead.

title: Why Growing Companies Feel Heavier at High Speeds
subtitle: A Relativity Lesson for Leaders
html:
Introduction to the Series: The Architecture of Scale

There’s a counter-intuitive truth at the heart of physics that every founder learns eventually — not in a lab, but in their calendar.

In Einstein’s world, the faster an object moves, the heavier it becomes.
Velocity increases mass.
Speed creates weight.

In scaling companies, the same phenomenon plays out every day.

What begins as light, fast, exhilarating momentum slowly becomes something denser — decisions take longer, clarity gets harder to maintain, and the organization starts to feel strangely heavy even as the numbers look good. Leaders often misread this heaviness as a personal failing:
If I were better at delegating…
If the team were more aligned…
If I just pushed a little harder…

But the weight isn’t a sign that you’re doing something wrong.
It’s a sign that you’re moving fast enough for the physics of scale to show up.

Just like in relativity, speed exposes architecture.

In the early stage, your clarity and proximity act like a gravitational field — keeping everything aligned simply because you’re close. But as speed increases, that early operating model hits its limit. The system becomes heavier than the structure designed to carry it.

And the instinctive moves leaders make in response — stepping in, reorganizing, accelerating harder — often increase the weight instead of redistributing it.

This series is about that weight.

It’s about the moment every scaling leader feels but rarely names:
Why does everything still come through me?
Why does speed feel slower now?
Why does the team need more clarity the more we grow?

Over the next five essays, I’m going to break down the real architecture of scale — the operating systems, decision pathways, rhythms, and design choices that determine whether a company becomes lighter as it grows…or collapses under its own speed.

Here’s where we’ll go:

1️⃣ The Hidden Breakpoint in Scaling Teams
Why the early operating system eventually collapses — and how to spot the invisible ceiling before you hit it.

2️⃣ The Heroic Trap
How stepping in feels responsible but slowly centralizes fragility and creates learned dependence.

3️⃣ The Architecture Beneath the Org Chart
Why reorgs fail — and why behavior changes only when architecture changes.

4️⃣ The Hidden Drag of Fast Teams
Why speed without structure becomes chaos — and how high-performing teams actually accelerate.

5️⃣ Freedom by Design
How to build a company that moves forward when you step back — optionality without irrelevance.

Each essay is practical, rooted in research (HBR, McKinsey, MIT Sloan, Edmondson), and focused on one core idea:

Scale isn’t a function of effort.
It’s a function of architecture.

If your company has reached the point where speed feels heavy, where decisions are clustering around you, or where the team is growing faster than the system built to support it, this series will help you see the underlying structures clearly — and give you the language and tools to rebuild them with intention.

Because in leadership, just like in physics, speed doesn’t have to create weight.
Not if the architecture is designed to hold it.

Let’s get into it.

title: The Leadership Crisis Inside Cybersecurity – and What the C-Suite Must Do Now
html:
Over the past week, I had several conversations with my sister and just watched as she managed her team. She manages one of the largest cybersecurity teams in her company. She was trained as a mathematician before moving into cyber – someone wired for patterns, structure, and clarity – and she brings that same analytical rigor to her leadership. She’s exceptional in every way that matters – respected by her people, trusted by executives, and responsible for work that rarely slows down long enough to take a full breath. Her days stretch across escalation calls, cross-functional negotiations, shifting priorities, and a constant awareness that even small decisions carry real-world consequences.

Yet what stood out wasn’t the threat landscape, the tooling, or the complexity of her environment. It was something quieter, more human, and far more structural than any single incident or vulnerability.

Cybersecurity has a leadership pipeline problem.

Not a talent shortage.
Not a lack of technical capability.
A leadership pipeline problem.

And as my sister described her world, the symptoms came into focus – mid-level leaders carrying workloads that would normally be distributed across entire teams. High performers are edging toward burnout, not because they lack skill, but because the systems around them haven’t evolved quickly enough to bear the weight of their responsibilities. Decision rights are buried under layers of implied “accountability.” Promotion paths that reward technical mastery but not leadership readiness. Teams are doing mission-critical work without strategic access. And people are asked to lead other human beings without ever being taught how.

This is the invisible fragility inside an industry tasked with preventing visible disasters.

As my sister talked through her day-to-day reality – sometimes with clarity, sometimes with frustration – you could hear the tension that forms when capable leaders are placed in systems that no longer match the speed or complexity of their environment. She’s in meetings all day, moving from one escalation to the next, navigating demands from engineering, compliance, product, and the executive suite – each with its own urgency, each assuming someone else has already provided the context. She’s doing exceptional work within a system that hasn’t been updated to reflect the dramatic expansion of the role.

And the deeper truth becomes unavoidable: this isn’t a cybersecurity issue. It’s an executive design issue.

The structure is outdated.
The incentives are misaligned.
The expectations exceed the resources.
And the system is producing outcomes it was never built to sustain.

So what can COOs, CIOs, and CEOs actually do?

A great deal – if they’re willing to redesign the environment their leaders are asked to operate within. Not after the next re-org. Not when things “calm down.” Now.

Below is what they must address.

1. Stop Forcing Technical Excellence and People Leadership Into the Same Pipeline

As my sister described how her own managers grow inside the organization, a familiar pattern emerged: the best individual contributors are often pushed – or quietly funneled – into management. It sounds efficient on paper. It’s rarely efficient in practice.

The abilities that make someone exceptional in threat modeling, architecture, or incident response are not the abilities required to lead people. Technical mastery draws on precision, depth, and independent focus. People leadership requires influence, conflict navigation, prioritization, emotional steadiness, and the ability to shape culture and communication under stress.

These are different muscles. And more importantly, distinct identities.

Yet many organizations still treat them as though they belong to a single ladder. That’s how accidental managers are made – brilliant technical minds who never wanted to lead humans but accepted the role because the organization offered only one way to advance.

My sister sees this play out constantly. Some of her strongest architects quietly admit they never wanted direct reports. Others love mentoring people but have no desire to deepen their technical specialization. The system doesn’t distinguish these aspirations, so leaders inherit responsibilities that clash with who they are.

The solution is structural: two equal-status career paths.

Technical Mastery.
People Leadership.

Both valued. Both compensated. Both visible.

When companies build dual ladders, something powerful happens. Attrition falls because people can finally grow in ways aligned with their strengths. Technical experts stay in roles where they can make their greatest impact, rather than being diverted into work that drains them. And leadership roles become intentional rather than accidental.

The teams my sister leads offer clear proof. The groups that consistently thrive are the ones led by people who chose leadership because they genuinely want to develop and steward others – not because they had no other way to move forward.

Dual pathways aren’t perks. They’re the scaffolding that stabilizes the entire organization.

2. Close the Accountability–Authority Gap

Another theme my sister brought up – almost in passing, but with unmistakable weight – is how often her managers are held responsible for outcomes they cannot fully influence.

They’re accountable for policies written elsewhere.
They’re responsible for the tools selected, even though they weren’t consulted.
They inherit risks introduced by systems they don’t own.
They respond to incidents triggered by teams far outside their span of control.

This mismatch creates a kind of quiet instability – leaders who care deeply but feel perpetually exposed, never sure whether they’re succeeding or simply absorbing the consequences of decisions made above or around them.

The organizational impact is predictable. Decision-making slows because the ground beneath people feels uncertain. Risk aversion grows, and cross-functional collaboration frays. Turnover increases among the very leaders whose continuity matters most.

My sister’s stories make this clear. She describes managers who must defend timelines they didn’t commit to, enforce standards they weren’t consulted on, and clean up downstream consequences of upstream decisions. Not because anyone intends harm – but because the system hasn’t recalibrated.

Executives can fix this by realigning authority to match responsibility:

  • Clarify who truly owns what.

  • Give leaders actual influence over the systems they’re accountable for.

  • Eliminate “shadow accountability” – where someone is responsible in practice but not in structure.

A RACI chart won’t fix culture on its own, but it stops the erosion of trust that occurs when people absorb consequences without control. When responsibility and authority are back in alignment, leaders regain stability, clarity, and the ability to lead with steadiness rather than defensiveness.

3. Simplify the System: Tooling, Workload, and Expectations

My sister also talked about the sheer fragmentation surrounding cybersecurity work. The problem isn’t that teams lack capacity – it’s that the environment around them makes sustained focus almost impossible.

Tool sprawl.
Audit cycles are stacked so tightly that teams can’t incorporate what they’ve learned.
Shifting priorities without aligned resourcing.
Context switching that pulverizes attention.
Incident cycles that arrive in waves without time for a true reset.

None of this reflects the team’s capability. It’s a reflection of design.

Her days often include jumping between five different platforms before lunch, juggling alerts that range from trivial to urgent, and trying to safeguard deep work time that evaporates under relentless context switching. The fragmentation itself becomes the enemy.

Organizations must stop designing for peak load and start designing for sustainable load. That means:

  • consolidating tools

  • aligning workflows

  • tightening alerts to reduce noise

  • removing the cognitive tax of constant minor issues

  • creating staffing and time buffers for surge periods

When the environment is coherent, teams move from survival to strategy. Burnout recedes not because people toughen up, but because the architecture finally supports the work.

Burnout isn’t a personal failure. It’s an architectural failure. And architecture is the responsibility of the executive suite.

4. Redefine What Success Actually Means for Cyber Leaders

One of the most poignant themes from my conversation with my sister is this: cyber leaders don’t burn out because the work is too difficult. They burn out because the work is invisible.

Success is defined by the absence of disaster.
If nothing happens, people assume everything is fine.
If something goes wrong, people assume cybersecurity failed.

This logic rewards firefighting and ignores prevention – the work that actually protects organizations long before the crisis.

My sister talked about the pride her team feels when they quietly eliminate a category of risk or refactor an architecture to remove an entire class of vulnerabilities. But those wins rarely become visible outside the team. Prevention disappears into silence.

Executives can change this by measuring what truly reflects value:

  • time to patch

  • architecture hardening

  • measurable risk reduction

  • cross-functional alignment

  • leadership’s impact on team stability

These aren’t soft metrics. They are leading indicators of resilience. And when executives elevate them, something essential happens: the work becomes visible. People feel seen. The meaning returns.

Shift what you measure, and you shift what people feel. Shift what people feel, and the organization’s capacity changes.

5. Where I Come In

Everything my sister described is the same terrain I encounter inside organizations across industries: the unseen structures that quietly shape performance, the leadership systems that determine whether people thrive or slowly erode, and the design choices that either stabilize an organization or quietly drain it.

Cybersecurity will never stand still. Threats will evolve. Regulations will shift. Attack surfaces will grow.

But the human system surrounding cybersecurity doesn’t have to remain chaotic or brittle. It can be redesigned – intentionally, coherently, sustainably.

And when it is, the entire organization steadies.
The pressure redistributes.
The talent stays.
The work becomes strategic instead of frantic.

This is where the executive calculus becomes impossible to ignore: rebuilding leadership capacity internally isn’t just healthier – it’s fiscally responsible.

The research is unequivocal:

  • Externally hired leaders fail at nearly twice the rate of internally developed leaders (Harvard Business Review; Corporate Leadership Council).

  • External leaders require 18–24 months to reach the contextual fluency that internal successors already possess.

  • The actual cost of an external leadership hire is 1.5–3x salary once you factor in search fees, onboarding drag, cultural mismatch, and the productivity dip that accompanies every transition.

  • By contrast, companies that promote from within see 20–30% higher retention, faster ramp times, and significantly stronger long-term performance.

Put simply:
It is always more expensive to hire a leader than to build one. And far more dangerous to assume a stressed leadership pipeline will self-correct through recruitment.

Leaders like my sister don’t burn out because the work is too hard – they burn out because the structure around the work is too thin. Strengthen that structure, and you don’t just retain leaders; you unlock their full value.

That is the opportunity in front of the executive suite: Build the system around the people who protect your organization – not the other way around. When you do, performance rises, turnover falls, resilience compounds – and leaders like my sister don’t just carry the system.

They shape it.

title: Closing the Loop on Psychological Safety: What the Research Makes Clear
subtitle: Essay 5 of 5
html:
Closing the Loop on Psychological Safety: What the Research Makes Clear

Over the past week, I published a series of essays on psychological safety – a topic I didn’t come to academically, but experientially. Like many people, I learned the hard way during the pandemic. Not because I had psychological safety, but because I didn’t. COVID coincided with dramatic leadership turnover where I worked, and the combination of crisis plus toxic leadership created a kind of pressure cooker. It pushed me out of an organization I cared about, and it shoved me straight into the work of understanding why some teams bend under strain while others quietly break.

That’s when I first dove into the research – Amy Edmondson’s decades of scholarship on learning teams, speaking-up cultures, and high-stakes coordination. I devoured The Fearless Organization and found myself mapping her concepts onto everything I was seeing on the ground. I’d already been familiar with Google’s Project Aristotle before COVID – I used it in building teams and even in a novel advisory project I called “Squads” – but the pandemic cast that work in a new light. Suddenly, this wasn’t theory; it was survival.

So when Edmondson, along with Michaela Kerrissey and Hassina Bahadurzada, published a major new study in May 2024, I read it immediately. And last week, after writing a whole series reflecting on psychological safety in practice, I decided to return to the source material – to the data itself – and distill what this study actually shows about how psychological safety behaves under real-world stress.

What the study reveals isn’t just supportive of psychological safety. It’s defining. It reframes performance, burnout, resilience, and the true operational cost of fear.

1. Psychological Safety Doesn’t Reduce Burnout by Making Work Easier – It Reduces Burnout by Making Work Shared

Burnout is too often misdiagnosed as a simple equation of volume: too much work, not enough hours. But the data reframes it entirely. Burnout isn’t primarily about workload – it’s about containment. People burn out when they are forced to hold everything themselves: the questions they can’t ask, the mistakes they can’t admit, the concerns they can’t raise. It’s the secrecy, not the strain, that exhausts them.

In teams with higher psychological safety, that pressure doesn’t stay locked inside one person’s mind or one person’s shift. It’s shared. It’s spoken aloud. It becomes a collective challenge instead of a private crisis. The burden moves from “mine alone” to “ours to solve.”

And the shift isn’t symbolic – it’s measurable. A single standard-deviation increase in psychological safety led to a 0.72-point decrease in burnout. In this kind of research, that’s enormous. Most leadership or culture interventions nudge burnout by 0.10 to 0.20 points. A change of 0.72 is four to seven times larger – the kind of movement you normally only see when something fundamental in the system changes. And it happened during a crisis, when conditions were deteriorating, not improving.

Burnout didn’t decline because the workload lightened. It declined because the silence did.

2. Psychological Safety Doesn’t Just Help People Stay Engaged – It Changes Whether They Want to Stay at All

What keeps people in an organization is rarely a ping-pong table or a wellness seminar. People stay when they trust that telling the truth won’t cost them – when they can raise a concern without being punished, ask for help without looking weak, or flag a risk without being branded difficult. Psychological safety strengthens that trust more than any perk or program ever could.

And again, the effect isn’t subtle. The researchers found that higher psychological safety produced a 0.63-point increase in willingness to stay – a shift that, in survey research, is enormous. Most retention drivers move the needle by a tenth of a point, maybe two. A jump of 0.63 is the kind of movement you’d normally expect from a major policy change or a significant compensation overhaul. But here, it emerged from one thing: people feeling safe enough to speak up.

And remember: this wasn’t measured in calm conditions. People were exhausted, understaffed, and carrying the emotional weight of a global crisis. Yet psychological safety still pulled retention upward.

Psychological safety isn’t a morale booster.
It’s a retention mechanism.
Fear makes people leave.
Safety makes them stay.

3. Psychological Safety Doesn’t Just Work in the Moment – It Accumulates Like Institutional Memory

This may be the most important finding in the entire study – and the one most leaders overlook. Psychological safety measured in 2019 predicted lower burnout and higher retention in 2021. In other words, the teams that weathered the crisis best were the ones that had already built the habit of speaking up before the crisis ever began.

Psychological safety isn’t a switch you flip when things get hard. It’s a foundation you lay when things are still manageable.

Teams that had practiced open communication – the everyday moments of asking for help, pointing out problems early, challenging assumptions respectfully – carried something into the crisis that others did not: an emotional reserve. They had evidence from their own past that telling the truth was safe. They remembered that the last time they raised a concern, the sky didn’t fall. They had muscle memory for collaboration.

So when uncertainty spiked and conditions deteriorated, their instinct wasn’t silence or self-protection. It was coordination. It was information-sharing. It was, “Let’s talk about what we’re seeing.”

That’s the compounding nature of psychological safety.
It isn’t built in the moment you need it.
It’s built in all the moments before.

Psychological safety is a long game – and the returns accumulate.

4. Psychological Safety Protects the People Who Face the Highest Interpersonal Risk

One of the study’s most humane findings is how unevenly the benefits of psychological safety are distributed – and how powerfully it protects the people who have historically had the least protection. The buffering effect was strongest among physicians, women, and people of color – groups who often operate with narrower margins for error, greater scrutiny, and fewer truly safe avenues to express uncertainty.

When psychological safety is low, these groups bear the highest interpersonal cost. The risks are greater, the penalties sharper, the silence heavier. But when psychological safety is high, they experience the greatest lift – more freedom to ask questions, more room to admit doubt, more access to help without fear of judgment.

Psychological safety levels the playing field. It makes the work equally navigable for everyone, not just those with positional or cultural advantage.

In that sense, psychological safety isn’t just a performance mechanism. It functions as a justice mechanism – redistributing safety, voice, and protection in ways that teams rarely achieve on their own.

5. Psychological Safety Can Partially Offset Material Shortages – But Not When Deprivation Is Extreme

The researchers describe psychological safety as a “social resource” – something that grows in importance precisely when material resources decline. This draws from the conservation-of-resources model, which suggests that when staffing is thin, equipment is unreliable, or time is scarce, the human system relies more heavily on whatever resources remain. And one of the most powerful is how freely people can speak.

Psychological safety doesn’t make shortages disappear. It can’t conjure new staff or fix broken equipment. But it does make the system more adaptive. When people feel safe to tell the truth, they coordinate faster, raise issues earlier, catch errors before they cascade, and recalibrate expectations together. It turns scarcity into a shared problem rather than a hidden crisis.

The study is clear that psychological safety isn’t a miracle cure. In conditions that are truly catastrophic – completely bottomed out – even the strongest social resources can’t fully counteract the damage. But in the vast majority of stressful, constrained environments, psychological safety meaningfully moderates the harm. It keeps teams functional when conditions are fraying.

Which is why reducing psychological safety efforts during difficult times is such a costly mistake. It’s like cutting your emergency brakes because gas is expensive.

6. Psychological Safety Increases Adaptive Capacity, Not Comfort

A comforting team is not the same as a capable one. One of the quiet misconceptions about psychological safety is that it makes work softer or easier. The study makes the opposite clear: psychological safety isn’t about comfort – it’s about honesty. In high-uncertainty environments, decisions are made with incomplete information, ambiguous signals, and shifting conditions. The only way to navigate that complexity is if people feel safe enough to voice doubts early, before small issues become expensive ones.

Teams with high psychological safety weren’t “happier teams” in the superficial sense. They were sharper teams. They noticed anomalies sooner. They said the uncomfortable thing before it metastasized. They had the courage to stop the train when everyone else felt pressured to keep it moving. Their advantage wasn’t mood – it was information flow.

And information flow is what drives adaptability.
Psychological safety didn’t cushion the work.
It clarified it.

It created the conditions for teams to see clearly and respond quickly – the core ingredients of true capability.

7. Psychological Safety Reduces Errors by Changing How Quickly Truth Arrives

Most teams don’t fail because someone made a mistake. They fail because someone hid one. The study reaffirms one of Edmondson’s core insights: in high-psychological-safety environments, error rates don’t increase – error reporting does. And that reporting is what allows teams to learn, adjust, and prevent small slips from turning into catastrophic failures.

Low psychological safety doesn’t get rid of problems. It gets rid of visibility.

And invisible problems are the most expensive kind. They compound quietly. They spread unchecked. They show up late, when the cost of correction is highest and the options are fewest.

Psychological safety doesn’t protect teams from mistakes. It protects them from escalation through silence.

8. Psychological Safety Enables Leaders to Lead Honestly, Not Perfectly

One of the most powerful lines in the study is also one of the simplest: leaders must be “open about not knowing.” That isn’t weakness. It’s the foundation of real-time problem-solving. When leaders perform certainty, everyone else performs silence. People hide their questions, suppress their concerns, and mask the very information leaders most need to hear.

But when leaders model humility – when they say, “I’m not sure,” or “Let’s figure this out together” – the entire system relaxes into truth-telling. Information surfaces earlier. Issues are named while they are still small. Doubt becomes data instead of a private burden.

This shift creates more than psychological safety. It creates what I often call coordination safety – the ability for a team to distribute cognitive load without shame or fear. It allows people to think together, name reality quickly, and solve problems collectively instead of alone.

Humility isn’t soft. It’s catalytic.

9. Psychological Safety Reduces Organizational Costs in Every Direction

When you pull the study’s findings together, the economic picture comes sharply into focus. Psychological safety doesn’t just shape how people feel – it reshapes how the entire system performs.

When burnout goes down, errors and absenteeism drop with it.
When turnover decreases, hiring and training costs fall.
When information flows freely, rework declines and agility rises.
When trust increases, issues escalate sooner and decisions get made faster.

These aren’t soft benefits. They’re operational gains.

Which is why the real message of this research is so important: psychological safety is not empathy work – it’s efficiency work. It improves the economics of how teams function. It’s the opposite of indulgent. It’s pragmatic, measurable, and financially significant.

Fear is expensive.
Silence is expensive.
Burnout is expensive.
Replacing talent is very expensive.

Psychological safety is one of the rare interventions that reduces all of those costs at the same time – not by adding perks or programs, but by removing the friction of fear and restoring the speed of truth.

title: Tool in Focus: Mapping Your Rituals to the Stretch Zone
subtitle: Essay 4.5 of 5
html:
Why real psychological safety isn’t soft – and how to build the rituals that create disciplined, courageous teams.

There’s a persistent myth in modern leadership that psychological safety means being “nice” – lowering standards, softening edges, avoiding conflict, and creating a high-support, low-challenge environment where everyone feels good but very little actually moves. But that picture isn’t psychological safety at all. It’s overaccommodation dressed up as care.

Real psychological safety isn’t the absence of tension; it’s the presence of constructive tension – the kind that aligns people around shared standards rather than protecting egos. It’s the environment where candor becomes possible because it serves something larger than comfort: the mission, the customer, the craft, the standard.

And in environments where safety is real, people can:

  • Name misalignment early – before it calcifies into rework or resentment.

  • Challenge without blame – because dissent is contribution, not insubordination.

  • Offer upward feedback – because silence is more dangerous than honesty.

  • Own errors without shame – turning mistakes into information, not identity.

This is the zone where trust and rigor coexist, and performance compounds. And research is clear: teams that operate in this dual condition consistently outperform peers on speed, innovation, and resilience.

Only one quadrant – High Safety × High Accountability – creates what I call The Stretch Zone: the environment where people are courageous and disciplined, candid and committed, experimental and execution-focused. It’s the adult version of the Zone of Proximal Development (see Essay 4) – the place where challenge doesn’t overwhelm, and comfort doesn’t stagnate, where people grow because the conditions make growth possible.

The other three zones produce predictable failure modes:

  • Low safety + high accountability → Anxiety & quiet compliance

  • High safety + low accountability → Comfort & slow drift

  • Low safety + low accountability → Apathy & disengagement

Which means the question for leaders is not:

“How do I make people comfortable?”
But rather: “How do I build conditions where people can stretch and stay grounded?”

Mapping Your Rituals to the Stretch Zone

A practical way to locate your rituals on the Safety × Accountability grid and redesign them for the Stretch Zone.

Leadership isn’t expressed through a list of values; it lives in the rituals a team returns to day after day. Stand-ups, reviews, retros, 1:1s, planning cycles – these are the moments where culture becomes real or quietly collapses into performance. This tool is designed to help you look at those rituals with intention and redesign them so they consistently reinforce the environment you want to build.

STEP 1 – List Your Recurring Touchpoints

Capture the meetings, rhythms, and moments where people learn:

  • daily stand-ups

  • weekly team meetings

  • project reviews

  • Retrospectives

  • 1:1s

  • leadership team syncs

  • Post-mortems

  • quarterly reviews

  • onboarding checkpoints

These are not logistical spaces – they are psychological signals. As Edmondson notes, safety is shaped less by grand gestures and more by repeated micro-interactions.

McKinsey’s research echoes the same truth:

“The highest-leverage improvements come from redesigning the rituals you already have – not adding new ones.”

STEP 2 – Score Each Ritual on Two 1–5 Scales

Safety (1 – 5)

1 = filtered, guarded, political
3 = open but inconsistent
5 = candid, upward voice present, truth travels early

Accountability (1 – 5)

1 = vague expectations, drifting focus
3 = moderate clarity but uneven challenge
5 = crisp standards, direct feedback, outcome ownership

Have multiple people score independently; the gaps are data.

STEP 3 – Plot Each Ritual on the Grid

Use the scoring logic:

  • Safety 1–2 → Low Safety

  • Safety 4–5 → High Safety

  • Accountability 1–2 → Low Accountability 

  • Accountability 4–5 → High Accountability

Place each ritual:

  • Apathy Zone (Low Safety × Low Accountability)

  • Comfort Zone (High Safety × Low Accountability)

  • Anxiety Zone (Low Safety × High Accountability)

  • Stretch Zone (High Safety × High Accountability)

STEP 4 – Identify the High-Leverage Ritual to Redesign

Choose the ritual that is:
✓ mission-critical
✓ high-frequency
✓ currently in Comfort or Anxiety

This is your highest ROI culture lever.

STEP 5 – Diagnose the Placement with Reflection

If it’s in the APATHY ZONE:

  • Where is safety missing? Where is clarity missing?

  • What expectations have become assumed instead of explicit?

If it’s in the COMFORT ZONE:

  • Where are we avoiding productive tension?

  • Where is accountability under-specified?

  • Where am I softening truth in the name of care?

If it’s in the ANXIETY ZONE:

  • Where does intensity exceed grounding?

  • Where is dissent unsafe?

  • Where do I need to buffer standards with relational trust signals?

If it’s in the LEARNING ZONE:

  • What behaviors make this productive?

  • How do we replicate this rhythm elsewhere?

  • What is the next 5% improvement?

This is how you turn ritual diagnostics into culture shifts.

STEP 6 – Redesign One Ritual This Month

Not five.
Not all of them.
One.

Choose a redesign action:

  • Add structured feedback prompts

  • Rotate meeting leadership (voice equity)

  • Introduce smart-failure post-mortems

  • Make expectations explicit at the beginning of each meeting

  • Normalize “permission to challenge” moments

These aren’t tactical tweaks – they’re structural signals:

  • Structured prompts flatten status.

  • Rotated leadership distributes power.

  • Smart failure reduces shame.

  • Explicit expectations anchor accountability.

Together, they move the ritual toward the Stretch Zone.

Where Do I Signal Care – But Avoid Challenge?

Leaders often soften their edges because they care. They want to shield people from discomfort, disappointment, or overwhelm. But research from Robert Kegan and McKinsey is unmistakably consistent: growth requires friction – not punitive pressure, but purposeful challenge. When leaders protect their teams from stretch, it can feel compassionate in the moment, yet it quietly limits potential and reinforces dependence.

The opposite dynamic shows up just as often. Standards are high, but the relational grounding is low. Expectations are clear, but the emotional buffer is thin. High expectations are healthy; unbuffered intensity is not. As Harvard Business Review has shown, psychological safety is the strongest moderator of how feedback lands—the same message can be experienced as motivating or demoralizing depending on the climate in which it’s delivered.

Leading in the Stretch Zone means holding two truths at the same time: people rise when challenged and open when safe. It asks leaders to combine clarity with curiosity, direction with humility, and feedback with compassion. When these elements come together, teams become resilient rather than reactive, innovative rather than cautious, and capable of learning in real time rather than bracing against it.

The Stretch Zone is not a soft place. It is a structured, human, disciplined environment where:

  • truth travels early

  • standards are visible

  • support is consistent

  • mistakes lead to learning

  • voice flows upward, not just downward

  • and accountability becomes shared stewardship, not surveillance

To borrow from James Clear in Atomic Habits: Organizations don’t rise to their level of ambition. They rise to the conditions leaders create for them.

title: Psychological Safety × Accountability
subtitle: Essay 4 of 5
html:
Why the best leaders don’t balance trust and standards – they integrate them.

There’s a question leaders whisper far more often than they’ll admit aloud:

“I want people to feel safe… but I’m afraid we’ll lose our edge.”

I hear this everywhere – in federal agencies navigating political volatility, in founder circles wrestling with scale, in boardrooms where the stakes are high and time is short. Most recently, I heard it from a VP in a fast-growth tech company who looked worn down by what he believed was an impossible tradeoff: protect people or push them; build trust or demand excellence; create comfort or cultivate discipline.

That tension isn’t a failure of leadership – it’s a misunderstanding of how people learn and grow.

And this is where my entry into the field diverges from most voices writing about leadership. Before I ever coached executives or redesigned systems, I spent decades as a teacher. And anyone who has taught – truly taught – knows something most leaders never learn:

People grow at the intersection of safety and challenge.
Not safety alone. Not challenge alone.
The stretch lives in the middle.

In education, we call this the Zone of Proximal Development – the space in which a learner can do more with guidance and support than they can do on their own. Too much comfort, and learners stall. Too much pressure, and they shut down. But in the right conditions – the right blend of trust, clarity, and rigor – something remarkable happens: they surprise themselves.

That same developmental principle applies to adults. I call the organizational version the “Stretch Zone.”

It is the adult expression of the ZPD: a high-trust, high-clarity environment where expectations are unmistakable, where speaking up is not a gamble but a norm, and where learning happens publicly rather than in private silos. It’s the climate in which people take genuine ownership, not because they fear consequences, but because they’re invested in the mission and confident in the system around them.

And here is the central insight:

Psychological safety and accountability are not opposites.
They are co-requirements of adult learning and high performance.

Edmondson’s research at Harvard, Google’s Project Aristotle, and work from MIT Sloan, Stanford, and the Academy of Management Journal all point toward the same conclusion: trust doesn’t dilute standards – it enables them. Safety is what turns accountability from surveillance into stewardship.

Where one of these elements is missing, organizations slip into two predictable patterns:

  • Comfort without momentum – high safety, low clarity. People feel good, but nothing moves.

  • Compliance without engagement – high standards, low safety. Work gets done, but thinking shuts down.

But when both are high?

That’s the Stretch Zone – the environment where people rise into challenge rather than shrink away from it.

It’s where pressure becomes productive instead of corrosive.
Where candor becomes contribution instead of critique.
Where mistakes become information instead of indictment.

And although I now see this daily in organizations, the truth of it was etched into me long before I ever coached a senior leader.

What I learned about human psychology teaching middle schoolers

When a middle-schooler doesn’t feel safe, they don’t risk being wrong.
They don’t admit confusion.
They don’t raise their hand even when the answer sits fully formed in their mind.
They fold inward. They self-protect. They retreat into quiet because quiet feels safer than exposure.

And when a student feels pressure without support, they don’t accelerate – they disconnect. Their minds leave the room long before their bodies do. They stare past the page. They shrink themselves because smallness feels survivable. Anyone who has stood at the front of a classroom knows this look: the look of a learner who is present in name only, navigating the material with caution instead of curiosity.

But alter the conditions – establish clear expectations, create room to try, normalize mistakes that aren’t tied to shame – and something far more powerful emerges. Students begin to lean toward difficulty rather than away from it. They ask the second, harder question. They try approaches they’ve never attempted. They recover faster after missteps because the environment teaches them that a misstep is not a verdict, but an invitation. They start taking intellectual risks that would feel impossible in a climate of threat.

What many leaders overlook is that this dynamic does not disappear with age.
It simply acquires a professional vocabulary.

Adults aren’t different creatures. They’re children with more experience, more language, and more elaborate defenses. The psychology hasn’t changed – only the stakes have.

A student who won’t risk being wrong becomes an employee who won’t name the risk. A child who hides confusion becomes a manager who hides emerging problems until they harden. A teenager who braces for criticism behaves exactly like a director who edits themselves into strategic silence because candor feels dangerous.

The instincts are identical – self-protection over exposure.

And when leaders treat psychological safety and accountability as interchangeable levers, they inadvertently activate these same instincts. They generate friction where they intend to generate growth.

Because you cannot demand excellence from an environment that punishes vulnerability. And you cannot cultivate excellence in an environment that avoids standards and structure.

The Stretch Zone is not a managerial preference; it is a developmental necessity. It is the only space where human beings – regardless of age, title, or talent – reliably move from potential to actual performance.

Safety as the engine of true accountability

Modern leadership still clings to a dangerous myth: that accountability is what happens when pressure rises.

It isn’t.

Pressure alone produces anxiety, distortion, and political behavior – not ownership.

When people feel threatened, they don’t step forward into responsibility; they drift sideways into self-protection. Instead of offering their full perspective, they begin to calculate what is safest to say, trimming nuance and editing themselves before anyone else has the chance. Their updates become technically accurate but strategically hollow, scrubbed clean of the early intuitions and subtle warning signs that leaders most need to hear. They participate, but only in the safer, narrower ways that shield them from scrutiny. And from the outside, this can look deceptively like discipline. Leaders often misread the polished reports, the procedural compliance, and the quiet agreement around the table as signs of alignment and professionalism, when in reality the organization is tightening in all the ways that make learning impossible. People are no longer solving problems; they’re reading the room.

Threat doesn’t produce accountability. It produces distance – emotional, cognitive, and relational.

Real accountability emerges from a fundamentally different place: a belief that the work truly matters and that the environment is sturdy enough to hold the truth. When people trust both the standard and the system upholding it, they stop performing safety and begin practicing stewardship. They don’t hide inconvenient information or soften their assessments; they offer their best thinking because they know it will be met with curiosity rather than punishment. In these teams, difficult conversations are not deferred to hallway whispers or late-night messages. They happen in the room, at the precise moment when candor can still shape the direction of the work.

In environments like this, dissent does not require permission. It is simply part of how the team makes sense of complexity together. And mistakes are not treated as moments of exposure but as data – signals the system needs to adapt, improve, and stay honest.

As this climate establishes itself, candor ceases to be an act of bravery and becomes an act of alignment. People don’t share because they’ve mustered courage; they share because the culture has normalized truth as a form of respect.

Once psychological safety is consistent and expectations are unambiguous, people move differently. They stretch toward difficult problems instead of tiptoeing around them. They take bigger creative risks because curiosity outweighs self-preservation. They ask more incisive questions because the goal is clarity rather than survival. They surface risk earlier, when it is still small enough to be changed, instead of waiting until it has hardened into crisis. And importantly, they learn publicly – not because they enjoy vulnerability, but because they understand that transparency accelerates the work.

None of this is softness. It is the most sustainable form of rigor: rigor built on trust rather than fear, rigor that strengthens rather than strains, rigor that treats people as the system’s intelligence instead of its liability. When safety and standards rise together, accountability shifts from compliance – something enforced – to commitment, something shared by people who know the work matters and trust the environment enough to contribute fully.

Leadership is pedagogy in practice

The longer I work with organizations, the clearer it becomes: Leadership is applied pedagogy, and organizational design is applied learning theory.

Everything leaders do – consciously or not – shapes the learning environment their people inhabit. The smallest interactions, the tone of a meeting, the way ambiguity is handled, even the pauses before a leader responds – all of it signals something about what is safe, what is valued, and what is allowed. And the patterns I watched play out in classrooms for years show up with astonishing fidelity in adult systems. The contexts change. The stakes rise. The vocabulary gets more sophisticated. But the underlying psychology – how humans respond to safety, clarity, challenge, and relational trust – remains remarkably consistent.

This is why psychological safety can never be reduced to an HR initiative or a cultural “nice-to-have.” It is not a mood or a perk or an interpersonal preference. It is the foundational condition that allows people to think boldly, name issues early, and test ideas without worrying that visibility will cost them standing, credibility, or belonging. Without that condition, even the best strategies stall because people spend more cognitive energy on self-protection than on problem-solving.

No strategy – however elegant – compensates for an environment where people are bracing. No headcount plan substitutes for a culture where people are filtering. No OKR framework rescues a team that is performing certainty instead of practicing truth.

What leaders are truly doing, whether they articulate it or not, is architecting the learning environment their team will have to think inside of. They are determining whether learning accelerates or collapses. Whether information flows or bottlenecks. Whether dissent strengthens the work or disappears into private channels. Every system tells the truth about how it was designed.

In organizational life, the conditions that create a healthy adult learning environment are remarkably consistent, and they mirror what strong educators have always known:

  • Trust that steadies people enough to try – the kind of relational grounding that reassures people that visibility is not a liability. When trust is present, people stop managing impressions and start contributing insight.

  • Clarity that removes guesswork and creates direction. Ambiguity forces people into protective behaviors; clarity liberates their cognitive bandwidth for actual work. It transforms scattered effort into focused effort.

  • Standards that challenge without shaming – expectations that inspire stretch rather than fear. High standards without humiliation generate the kind of productive tension that fuels growth and excellence.

  • Voice that ensures truth travels early instead of late. When voice is structurally supported rather than merely permitted, teams surface risks while they are still reversible rather than after they have calcified.

  • Support that transforms mistakes into shared insight instead of private burden. Robust support structures signal that missteps are not career-defining events but part of an adaptive learning process.

Individually, each of these conditions matters. But together – when they reinforce one another – they create an environment where stretch becomes natural instead of rare. People begin to lean into difficulty rather than avoid it. They ask harder questions, notice earlier inflection points, and collaborate with a level of sincerity that feels radically different from the posturing and politeness that dominate more brittle cultures.

And when these conditions take hold, performance changes in ways leaders often don’t anticipate. The team becomes less guarded and more generative. Meetings shift from choreography to contribution. Energy that once went toward managing fear is suddenly available for solving actual problems. Insight compounds because people are no longer navigating interpersonal danger; they’re navigating the work.

Strategy can set direction.
Resources can expand capacity.
But only conditions unlock capability.

Organizations don’t rise to the level of their ambition; they rise to the level of the environment leaders create for them.

The real leadership question

At this point in the series, we’ve traced the early signals of silence, explored why safety accelerates speed, and examined the invisible tax fear imposes on systems. With this essay, we add the fourth truth: rigor and trust must rise together or they collapse together.

The question at the heart of this, the one that sits beneath every essay so far, is this:

Where have you leaned too far into comfort or too far into control –
and what might become possible if you stopped choosing between them?

Most cultures don’t need reinvention. They need a subtle but intentional redesign of the conditions that govern how people speak, challenge, question, and learn.

What you are ultimately building is the organizational equivalent of every great classroom:

  • clear enough that people know what excellence looks like;

  • courageous enough that they can name the truth;

  • structured enough that participation is required;

  • human enough that the stretch feels supported rather than scrutinized.

The Stretch Zone is exactly that: not a place where people are pushed harder, but a place where they are supported better. Where standards aren’t softened but scaffolding is strengthened. Where accountability shifts from surveillance to shared stewardship.

And in a landscape where organizations are often either brittle from pressure or sluggish from over-accommodation, the ability to cultivate this environment may be the sharpest competitive advantage a modern leader can create.

When safety and rigor rise together, performance becomes sustainable, learning becomes continuous, and momentum becomes collective.

Five Questions to Gauge the Stretch Zone

(Adapted from Edmondson’s work and practical systems coaching)

Use a 1–5 scale:

  1. Team members hold each other accountable respectfully.

  2. It’s clear what is expected of me in my role.

  3. Feedback is welcomed and acted upon – across all levels.

  4. Leaders model learning from mistakes and encourage reflection.

  5. People are encouraged to take ownership – not just tasks, but outcomes.

I’ve also included a simple Google Form – built on Edmondson’s five questions – that you can copy and use to track this dimension of psychological safety with your team. Click here for a copy of that form.

These aren’t abstract cultural ideals – they are behavioral signatures of high-learning, high-rigor systems. Research from Harvard, MIT Sloan, and HBR consistently shows that teams scoring high on these items adapt faster, innovate more consistently, and navigate complexity with far less friction.

They also reveal whether accountability flows only downward or truly circulates throughout the system – an essential marker of upward psychological safety, the single strongest predictor of whether teams challenge assumptions early.

What emerges from this reflection is not just cultural data – it’s a performance map:

Where energy flows.
Where ownership thrives.
Where fear or ambiguity slows everything down. –

The practical question is simple:

Which of these five items, if improved even slightly, would create the biggest shift in how your team works, learns, and leads?

What happens when we separate safety from standards

Across sectors – tech, education, humanitarian response – I see two patterns whenever organizations separate psychological safety from accountability:

Culture as Cushion
Leaders overcorrect for safety by avoiding directness. Expectations blur; performance drifts; frustration grows. Harvard Business Review calls this pseudo-harmony – the appearance of cohesion covering the absence of candor.

Accountability as Weapon
Standards are high, but dissent is punished. People comply without engaging. Problems surface late. Leaders get filtered data. Risk-taking evaporates. Accuracy becomes more dangerous than silence.

The Stretch Zone is the alternative – disciplined, human, sustainable. A space where feedback signals respect rather than risk.

And here is what leaders often forget:

AI will never build this for you.

AI can measure output, summarize feedback, and detect patterns in language.
But it cannot feel the temperature of a room.
It cannot read the emotional voltage beneath silence.
It cannot sense the hesitation before someone speaks the hard truth.
It cannot replace the human work of building trust.

That work begins in presence.
It grows through practice.
And it scales through design.

title: Tool in Focus: The Safety Tax Calculator
subtitle: Essay 3.5 of 5
html:
How to put rough numbers on what fear is costing your team

In the last essay, The Safety Tax, we named something most teams feel but rarely quantify.

We looked at how fear shows up in everyday behaviors – hesitation to ask for help, avoidance of conflict, delayed escalation – and how those micro-moments become macro-costs: rework, slower decision-making, missed innovation, and the quiet disengagement of smart people who stop offering their best thinking.

We walked through a short diagnostic, adapted from Amy Edmondson’s research, with questions like:

  • It is difficult to ask other members of this team for help.

  • When someone makes a mistake, it is often held against them.

  • Concerns are often escalated too late.

Those reverse-coded items don’t just describe a culture; they diagnose it. When they score high, you’re not just managing projects – you’re managing the unintended consequences of fear.

So if Essay 3 was about seeing the tax, this one is about measuring it.

Not with forensic precision, but with enough clarity that you can finally look your leadership system in the eye and say:

“This is what fear is costing us. And we don’t have to keep paying it.”

That’s where The Safety Tax Calculator comes in.

The Safety Tax Calculator

A practical tool for quantifying silence, hesitation, and psychological risk.

The brilliance of this tool is its simplicity. It’s not built for perfect fidelity. It’s built to:

Make the invisible visible – to convert cultural drag into something you can see, interrogate, and decide against.

If you completed the earlier diagnostic or used the Google Form, this tool is the next step. It takes what your team feels and turns it into something you can roughly estimate, not just vaguely sense.

Here’s how it works.

1. Choose the Behavior

Your leading indicator of fear

Start with one observable behavior that matters in your context. For example:

  • Speaking up when something feels off

  • Sharing dissent or counterpoints

  • Escalating risks early

  • Admitting uncertainty or asking for help

These are the first places fear shows up – weeks or months before it appears as a missed deadline, a blown rollout, or a quiet resignation.

In the last essay, we noted that hesitation before speaking up = delayed insight, and that avoidance of conflict = compounded misalignment. Here, we zoom in on one of those behaviors and treat it like a measurable variable.

Why this matters:

Research from MIT’s Human Dynamics Lab shows that high-performing teams share information early, freely, and frequently. Teams with slower, filtered communication consistently underperform – even when they have more expertise on paper.

Leaders often mistake quietness for personality:

“She’s just introverted.”
“He’s conflict-averse.”

But these behaviors are not quirks. They’re system signals.

2. Estimate the Latency

The delay between knowing and naming

This is the heart of the calculator.

Ask:

  • How long does someone wait before raising the issue?

    • Hours?

    • Days?

    • Two weeks

  • Do people wait for the “right” meeting because they don’t want to “bother” anyone?

  • Do concerns show up only when they can’t be avoided?

Amy Edmondson’s work – and subsequent studies in Administrative Science Quarterly – describe this as interpersonal risk latency: the invisible delay between noticing an issue and feeling safe enough to name it.

Even a two-day delay in a complex system creates measurable downstream drag.

A coaching question to ground this:

  • If your team had perfect psychological safety, how fast would you hear about problems?

  • How far is today from that ideal?

That gap is part of your safety tax.

In Essay 3, we talked about how “Concerns are often escalated too late” is a red flag. Here, we turn that red flag into a rough number.

3. Assign the Cost of Delay

Where culture becomes quantifiable

Now we translate latency into drag.

Ask three questions:

a. What rework does this delay create?

Does a three-day silence:

  • Turn a minor bug into a week of cleanup?

  • Turn a small concern into a complete project reset?

  • Force a team to redo work that could’ve been corrected in an afternoon?

Even rough estimates work:

  • “We lost about 6 hours last time this happened.”

  • “We spent an extra sprint fixing something we could have prevented.”

  • “It pushed our decision cycle back a week.”

b. What opportunity cost did we miss?

This category is rarely tracked – and almost always the largest.

Did the delay:

  • Close a partnership window?

  • Erode a client’s confidence?

  • Give a faster competitor the opening they needed?

This is the part of the tax that almost never shows up on internal dashboards, but leaders feel it in their gut.

c. What emotional labor did it create?

This is the portion leaders consistently underestimate.

Fear creates:

  • Quiet resentment

  • Burnout through anticipation (“I know this will blow up later, but I don’t feel safe to say it yet.”)

  • Lower creativity

  • Second-guessing

  • Avoidance patterns

McKinsey refers to this cumulative effect as organizational drag – the friction that slows execution, fatigues talent, and erodes decision quality.

In Essay 3, we named this in plain language:

  • Over-prepping for routine meetings

  • Postponed decisions

  • Conflict is avoided instead of being addressed

Here, the calculator helps you see those not just as “annoyances” but as quantifiable drag.

Fear is expensive. Drag multiplies.

4. Calculate the Quarterly Burn Rate

Your “fear budget” line item

This is not a finance exercise for your controller. It’s a shift in perspective for your leadership.

Choose:

  • Behavior: e.g., “Escalating risk”

  • Average latency: e.g., 10 days

  • Estimated cost of each delay: e.g., 8 hours of rework + opportunity loss

  • Frequency per quarter: e.g., 4 instances

Run a rough calculation. No spreadsheet perfection required.

Leaders are often stunned when they realize:

  • A single 10-day hesitation, repeated across a 12-person team, can easily exceed the cost of:

    • A training program

    • A consultant

    • An annual offsite

    • A dedicated project manager

In the last essay, we said:

“Because once you can see the tax, you can finally begin to reduce it.”

This is what “seeing it” can look like: not as a vague sense of “things feel slow,” but as an estimated cost you can no longer dismiss.

Fear is often the most expensive – and least budgeted – line item in your organization.

5. Reframe the Numbers

The goal isn’t accuracy – it’s awakening

Let’s be clear:

You are not building a perfect financial model.
You are building awareness.

The calculation shifts fear from:

  • Soft issue → Operational variable

  • Cultural squishiness → Performance bandwidth

  • Interpersonal discomfort → Strategic drag

As soon as leaders see fear as a budget line, they start designing against it:

  • Clear meeting norms (Who speaks when? How do we surface dissent?)

  • Faster decision cycles (Where are decisions stuck? Why?)

  • Explicit dissent pathways (How can people disagree safely?)

  • Sharper role clarity (Who owns which decisions?)

  • Defined escalation protocols (What’s the “early warning” channel?)

  • Psychological safety rituals (Regular “red flag” rounds, after-action reviews, learning debriefs)

This is how safety stops being abstract and becomes architecture.

6. The Coaching Moment

Where the tool becomes a transformation

This is the pivot point.

Ask yourself – or your leadership team:

If fear had a cost center in your organization, what would its budget be?

Then:

What becomes possible if you reduce that spend by just 10%?

This moves the conversation from: guilt → awareness → ownership → redesign.

Because the truth is:

  • The meetings that run longer than they should

  • The ideas that arrive after the window closes

  • The people who play it safe even when you say you want candor

Those aren’t just “communication issues.” They’re cost overruns in disguise.

A Neurodiversity-Forward Note

Not all latency equals fear

One crucial nuance as you start using this tool: Not every delay is fear-based.

For neurodiverse team members and slower processors, hesitation may reflect:

  • genuine processing time

  • sensory overload

  • preference for written communication

  • unclear or chaotic meeting structure

This is why meeting design is an inclusion practice, not a bureaucratic one.

  • Clear agendas

  • Predictable turn-taking

  • Visual thinking tools

  • Asynchronous input channels

These don’t just make things “tidier.” They lower interpersonal risk – and they help you distinguish between:

  • Fear-based latency and

  • Cognitive-processing latency

Both are valid. Only one is a cultural tax.

When you treat all latency as fear, you misdiagnose.
When you ignore fear-based latency, you underdiagnose.
The work is learning to tell the difference.

Coaching Reflection: Where Am I Taxing My Team?

Let’s bring this back to you as a leader.

1. What’s the cost of what’s not being said on my team right now?
Silence isn’t the absence of information; it’s the presence of risk. Studies in Organization Science show that unspoken concerns are some of the strongest predictors of downstream failure – not because people don’t know what to do, but because they don’t feel safe enough to say what they see.

2. Where might my tone, pace, or presence be making it harder to speak up early?
The Yale Center for Emotional Intelligence notes that leaders communicate safety or threat within milliseconds through nonverbal cues alone. Your facial expression, your interruptions, your speed of response – they’re all part of the system.

3. Am I removing blockers – or am I unintentionally being one?
McKinsey’s research on organizational health is clear: leaders often create constraints unintentionally, by being too quick with opinions, too slow with curiosity, or too selective about whose input they solicit. –

4. If my team could safely name the one thing I’m not seeing, what truth might finally become visible?
And how would our system shift if that truth could be said without fear?

In Essay 3, we said:

“Because when reverse-coded items score high, they don’t just describe the culture – they diagnose it.”

The Safety Tax Calculator is what you use next: to estimate what that diagnosis is costing you – and to begin designing something better.

Because psychological safety isn’t the work you do after the work.

It’s the work that makes all other work possible.

title: 3. The Safety Tax
subtitle: Essay 3 of 5
html:
What fear costs your team – and why the quietest people may be your most expensive

Several years ago, I worked with a team of subject matter experts. On paper, they looked like the kind of group that should have been sprinting. But they weren’t. They were stuck – constantly missing deadlines, continually reworking deliverables, and constantly surprised by issues they felt they “should have caught earlier.”

At first glance, it looked like a resourcing problem. They said what many teams say: “We just don’t have enough people to move faster.” But as we listened more closely, a different storyline emerged – one that research from Harvard, MIT Sloan, and Stanford has documented for years.

It wasn’t capacity.
It wasn’t competence.
It wasn’t commitment.

It was fear – subtle, quiet, and everywhere.

No one wanted to raise red flags until it was too late.
Feedback, when given at all, tended to float around the edges of the real issue.

Meetings were polite but shallow – what psychologists call “surface acting,” where people perform collaboration without engaging emotionally or intellectually.

Retrospectives felt like rituals, not learning environments.

This wasn’t dysfunction in the dramatic sense. It was something far more common and far more costly: a climate where people didn’t feel safe enough to tell the truth early. And when fear enters a system, it behaves like a tax.

We eventually named what was happening: the safety tax – the hidden cost of a culture where people hold back. And like most taxes, it doesn’t take one big bite. It accumulates quietly, quarter after quarter, in rework, in delayed concerns, in cautious decisions, in creativity dampened before it could even be offered.

You feel it in:

  • Rework that could’ve been avoided if someone had spoken up sooner.

  • Silence that masks early risk signals until the cost is higher.

  • Missed innovation, because the boldest ideas are often the most vulnerable to offer.

  • Decision latency, the delay between when someone sees a problem and when they feel safe enough to name it, is one of the strongest predictors of project slippage.

The quietest people on that team weren’t disengaged; they were calculating risk. And those calculations – invisible to leadership – were the most expensive part of the system.

As Edmondson has written repeatedly, “fear is the enemy of forward motion.” But McKinsey’s organizational research adds dimension: fear also erodes decision quality. When people filter their insights for safety rather than accuracy, leaders make decisions with incomplete data – and the cost multiplies downstream.

So the question isn’t: “Why won’t my people speak up?”

The real question is: “What have we designed – intentionally or unintentionally – that makes speaking up feel costly?”

Because once you can see the tax, you can finally begin to reduce it.

The most expensive thing on your team may be the thing no one is saying

Psychological safety isn’t just about how people feel. It’s about how much it costs to do the most basic, everyday acts of collaboration – asking for help, naming a mistake, questioning an assumption, offering a dissenting view. These behaviors form the backbone of learning organizations, and yet they’re the first to erode when fear creeps in.

Research across industries – from Edmondson’s early hospital studies to later work at Google, MIT, and INSEAD – shows a clear pattern: when these behaviors become risky, people don’t stop doing the work. They simply stop doing the learning that makes the work resilient. They adapt, yes – but not upward. They adapt around the system. And that detour? That’s the tax.

Let’s name it:

Hesitation before speaking up = Delayed insight

A Stanford study on “voice suppression” found that even a few seconds of hesitation can change the course of a meeting – the moment passes, the idea withers, and the team moves forward with incomplete data.

Avoiding difficult feedback = Compounded conflict

Unaddressed tension doesn’t fade; it calcifies. What could’ve been a five-minute correction becomes a five-week misalignment.

Withholding concerns = Rework and reputational risk

This is the pattern McKinsey documents in “decision bottleneck” cultures: the risk isn’t the mistake – it’s the delay in naming it.

Over-prepping for routine meetings = Burnout by bureaucracy

Organizational psychologists call this “defensive preparation.” It inflates emotional labor, increases cognitive load, and leads to the very burnout leaders often misdiagnose as “underperformance.”

Postponed decisions = Slower cycle times, unclear ownership

The research is clear: fear lengthens decision cycles more reliably than complexity does. These aren’t soft costs. They show up in project slippage, team churn, scope creep, and strategic confusion. They show up in the quiet resignation of smart people who stop offering their best thinking because it no longer feels worth the interpersonal risk.

And here’s the most important part: The longer these behaviors go unnamed, the faster they normalize. Silence becomes strategy. Over-preparation becomes expectation. Caution becomes culture.

Ask yourself:

Where in your system do these costs already exist – and what might your team accomplish if they didn’t have to pay this tax every day?

Measuring the tax: A trust diagnostic

Start with five questions, drawn from and adapted from Edmondson’s research, to help you locate fear-based behavior. Use a 1–5 scale (1 = Strongly Disagree, 5 = Strongly Agree):

  1. It is difficult to ask other members of this team for help.

  2. When someone makes a mistake, it is often held against them.

  3. In this team, people are sometimes rejected for being different.

  4. Conflict is avoided, even when it needs to be addressed.

  5. Concerns are often escalated too late.

I’ve also included a simple Google Form – built on Edmondson’s five questions – that you can copy and use to track this dimension of psychological safety with your team. Click here for a copy of that form.

These questions may look simple, but their predictive power is anything but. Reverse-coded items like these are some of the strongest markers of psychological unsafety identified in Edmondson’s original work and later replicated in studies across aviation, healthcare, tech, and finance. When people struggle to ask for help, fear judgment for mistakes, or hide differences, it signals a workplace where emotional risk feels too high – and where collaboration becomes laborious rather than liberating.

If these resonate – especially the reverse-coded items – you are not simply managing a team. You’re managing the unintended consequences of fear.

And fear leaves fingerprints everywhere.

Research from the Academy of Management Journal shows that when employees believe mistakes will be penalized, they shift from learning behavior to self-protective behavior. Teams become more compliant, less candid. Conflict gets displaced rather than resolved. Problems are managed privately until they become too big to hide, which is why late escalation is one of the most evident signs that safety is eroding beneath the surface.

This is not a sign that your people lack courage. It’s a sign that your conditions are shaping their behavior in ways that inhibit truth, trust, and forward motion.

Ask yourself:

  • What are these questions revealing about the emotional math your team members are doing before they speak?

  • And how might your system be unintentionally teaching them that silence is safer than contribution?

Because when reverse-coded items score high, they don’t just describe the culture – they diagnose it.

What the research tells us – and what leaders forget

In Edmondson’s landmark study on clinical teams, she discovered something profoundly counterintuitive: the teams with the highest error rates weren’t worse – they were safer. Nurses and physicians on those teams felt secure enough to report problems, surface near misses, and document mistakes transparently. Their error rates reflected reality, not competence. As Edmondson noted, “the better the climate, the more people speak up.”

In contrast, teams with low reported error rates weren’t more effective – they were simply quieter. They hid mistakes, worked around them, or tried to fix issues privately rather than risk the interpersonal exposure of reporting them. What leaders often misinterpret as “clean performance” is, in practice, what organizational psychologists call “error silence.” The literature is clear: low error reporting is often a sign of high interpersonal risk, not high capability.

What’s striking is how consistently this pattern appears across sectors. Aviation safety studies show that near-miss reporting is highest on flight crews with strong psychological safety climates. Manufacturing research documents that teams with open reporting catch defects earlier and reduce downstream failures. Education and healthcare studies reveal that faculty and clinicians who feel psychologically safe share concerns earlier – leading to earlier interventions and measurably better outcomes. And yes, the same findings have been reproduced in tech and finance: the most innovative teams are often those most willing to surface small failures quickly.

The absence of reported problems does not indicate health. It often indicates fear.

And when fear becomes cultural – when it shapes the micro-behaviors, the unspoken rules, the informal channels people use to avoid exposure – the tax becomes exponential.
