title: 4. Learning to Learn in the Machine Age
subtitle: Essay 4 of 7
series: EQ in the Age of AI series
html:
Adaptability Is the New Intelligence

The half-life of knowledge keeps shrinking. What we mastered five years ago may already be obsolete.

In this era of automation, the advantage no longer belongs to the most informed – but to the most adaptable. That capacity to absorb, unlearn, and relearn is what leadership coach Erika Andersen calls learning agility – the meta-skill behind every other skill, the quiet engine of human relevance.

But agility isn’t merely intellectual. It’s existential.

It’s the art of staying alive to change – curious enough to explore, humble enough to revise, vulnerable enough to be seen learning again. It is the discipline of remaining a student even when you are expected to teach.

Artificial intelligence can master content. It can summarize, synthesize, and scale information far beyond human capacity. What it cannot do is wrestle with uncertainty, reframe belief, or find meaning in the space between knowing and not knowing. That’s the province of emotional intelligence – the awareness that transforms knowledge into wisdom and motion into understanding.

This has profound implications for how we design learning itself. Most corporate L&D programs, and most schools, still cling to a “canon” of knowledge – knowledge-that – as though mastery were a static state. But the future belongs to those who cultivate knowledge-how – the capacity to think, question, adapt, and connect ideas across shifting contexts.

Curricula may change, but the deeper challenge remains: we are still training people for certainty in an age that rewards awareness. We have optimized for recall when the real work is reflection. We have rewarded compliance when the future demands curiosity.

From my Educational Philosophy, something that I started at Hopkins nearly 25 years ago, but has remained largely unchanged since then.

For me, learning has never been about subjects. It has always been about life.
I aspire to know, even if through a glass darkly.
I do not lead an unexamined life.
I am the dialectic. I am a student.

And perhaps that’s the only durable learning model left – to stay unfinished on purpose.

Because in the machine age, the question isn’t how much we know. It’s whether we still have the courage to keep learning. And the quiet secret of agility is emotional intelligence: curiosity, humility, vulnerability, and the resilience to begin again.

Washington’s Hidden Superpower: Learning in Public

George Washington was not the most brilliant strategist of his age, but he was, undeniably, the most learnable. Over the course of two decades, he evolved from a rigid young officer chasing glory into a statesman capable of shaping a republic. That arc – from ambition to wisdom – remains one of the clearest portraits of learning agility in history.

We’ve seen the same pattern echoed in later leaders. Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. once said of Franklin D. Roosevelt, “A second-class intellect, but a first-class temperament.” What he meant as faint praise turned out to be the essence of Roosevelt’s genius. In moments of crisis, it wasn’t intellect that steadied the nation – it was emotional resilience. The fireside calm, the confident uncertainty, the steady voice that turned collective fear into forward motion. In a world saturated with information, it’s still emotional intelligence that moves people.

Leadership doesn’t live in the mind alone; it lives in the nervous system. It’s not about how smart you are but how grounded you can remain when everything else begins to unravel. Washington understood that long before anyone could name it. When he resigned his commission at the end of the Revolution, he did so with a single, unadorned line: “Having now finished the work assigned me, I retire from the great theatre of action.”

That restraint – the willingness to let go when he could have held on – is what learning agility looks like in motion. It is the quiet pivot from command to consciousness, from controlling outcomes to designing systems that endure beyond the individual. Hamilton captured it best when he reflected, “If I say goodbye, the nation learns to move on. It outlives me when I’m gone.”

What Washington modeled in that moment is what modern leaders still struggle to master: the ability to trust the culture they’ve built more than the control they once held. Real leadership is not the accumulation of authority; it’s the distribution of stability. It’s knowing when to ease off the clutch, to create enough space for others to accelerate.

That kind of wisdom can’t be automated. It can only be learned – slowly, through humility, awareness, and the steady rhythm of emotional self-regulation that keeps a leader from mistaking movement for progress.

Four Human Catalysts of Learning Agility

Leadership coach Erika Andersen describes learning agility as being “learnable” – the ability to keep growing even as conditions shift around you. She identifies four elements that make this possible: Aspiration, Self-Awareness, Curiosity, and Vulnerability. Each one fuels the emotional resilience required to navigate change without losing direction.

Washington modeled all four, centuries before the language existed. His evolution wasn’t just political; it was psychological. It showed what emotional intelligence looks like when lived out over time – a kind of adaptive consciousness that turns ambition into stewardship.

Aspiration was his anchor. Every action pointed to a cause larger than himself – liberty, unity, the fragile idea of democracy. In EQ terms, this was Self-Actualization in motion: purpose translated into perseverance. Washington’s vision expanded his resilience. He endured winter after winter not through willpower alone, but through meaning. For modern leaders, the lesson is clear: when your vision outlasts your comfort zone, endurance becomes a form of hope.

Coaching Insight:
Keep a vision that outlasts your comfort zone. Purpose expands resilience – it converts pressure into progress.

Reflection Point:
What vision in your work still feels bigger than your current capacity – and how might that stretch sustain you?

Self-Awareness defined his leadership style. He was unthreatened by brilliance, surrounding himself with minds as forceful as Hamilton and Jefferson. That required Self-Regard balanced with Reality Testing – a grounded sense of self strong enough to invite dissent. The best leaders still do this: they build teams that expose their blind spots rather than protect their egos. Awareness, when practiced with humility, becomes a design tool for better systems.

Coaching Insight:
Build teams that expose your blind spots rather than reinforce them. Awareness, practiced with humility, becomes a design tool for better systems.

Reflection Point:
Who in your circle tells you the truth you least want to hear – and when was the last time you thanked them for it?

Curiosity kept him evolving. Washington studied agriculture, European tactics, and governance until the end of his life – not out of vanity, but from genuine fascination. This was Flexibility paired with Problem Solving, a restless engagement with the world that turned information into insight. In the modern organization, curiosity functions the same way: it’s the renewable energy that keeps learning loops alive. Every domain, even the non-obvious ones, becomes usable data for how you lead.

Coaching Insight:
Treat every domain as usable data for how you lead – even the non-obvious ones. Curiosity keeps the system adaptive.

Reflection Point:
Where in your current role have you stopped asking questions – and what might reopen that line of inquiry?

And finally, Vulnerability – the quiet trait most often mistaken for weakness. His “spectacles moment” at Newburgh remains one of the purest demonstrations of emotional intelligence in leadership history. When Washington acknowledged his failing eyesight before his officers, he revealed humanity without losing authority. That’s Emotional Expression integrated with deep Empathy. It was a small act of truth-telling that dissolved rebellion more effectively than any command. The modern corollary is simple: let people see the human behind the leader. Presence is what earns trust when power cannot.

Coaching Insight:
Let people see the human behind the leader. It doesn’t diminish authority – it deepens it. When trust has form, collaboration has flow.

Reflection Point:
Where does trust in your organization exist only as intention – and what small act of honesty could give it structure?

Together, these four elements form the emotional circuitry of learning agility – the bridge between head and heart, between knowing and becoming.

In the language of CREATE, they ignite Agility, the piston that connects Culture, Execution, and Ethics. When aspiration fuels awareness, when curiosity coexists with vulnerability, leadership stops being a posture and becomes a practice – a dynamic equilibrium between confidence and humility, control and learning.

Washington mastered that balance not through brilliance, but through presence.
And presence, as ever, is what keeps leadership human in the age of automation.

From “Expert” to “Experimenter”

AI will soon handle expertise more efficiently than we ever could.
What remains irreplaceable is the experimenter’s mindset – the willingness to hold uncertainty without paralysis, to move forward without needing the map to be perfect.

George Washington practiced this on a national scale. The Constitution itself was an experiment; his presidency, a prototype. Every decision he made helped design the office he occupied.

In a letter to James Madison just before taking office, he wrote,

“It is my wish and intention to conform to the public desire and expectation, with respect to the style proper for the Chief Magistrate to live in; it might be well to know (as far as the nature of the case will admit) what these are before he enters upon it.”

That phrasing – “before he enters upon it” – reveals the experiment in real time. Washington understood that he wasn’t simply inheriting a role; he was inventing one. He approached the unknown not with certainty but with design thinking – observing, testing, iterating. Where Jefferson wrote ideas and Adams argued principles, Washington modeled precedent. He didn’t just think through democracy; he embodied it.

That kind of emotional foresight – the capacity to sense how leadership will feel to others before history confirms it – is what makes Washington more relevant in the age of AI than many who followed. He made decisions not because he knew they’d work, but because he trusted that iteration would. His leadership was a series of hypotheses tested in public view – refined not by ego, but by feedback.

Modern leadership requires the same humility. The systems we build, the cultures we shape, the technologies we unleash – all of them are experiments in human alignment. Expertise alone can’t navigate that terrain. Only emotional intelligence can hold the tension between confidence and curiosity long enough to learn.

Coaching Insight:
Replace perfectionism with iterative integrity – act, learn, adjust. In a world of accelerating feedback loops, reflection speed is more valuable than reaction speed.

Reflection Point:
Where in your leadership are you waiting to be certain – when what’s needed is the courage to begin?

Emotional Intelligence as the Engine of Adaptation

Learning agility isn’t cognitive alone – it’s emotional endurance.

The data tell the same story: according to EQ-i 2.0, high performers navigating rapid change consistently score strongest in Optimism, Stress Tolerance, and Flexibility. Those aren’t moods; they’re muscles – trained through self-awareness, purpose, and deliberate practice.

George Washington built those muscles long before psychology had the language for them. His rituals were simple but profound: daily letters, moments of prayer, solitary walks. These weren’t distractions from leadership – they were leadership. Each routine created a boundary between stimulus and response, giving emotion a place to settle before decision.

He practiced what we might now call emotional hygiene – metabolizing stress before passing it on. In doing so, he turned chaos into calm direction. His stillness wasn’t passivity; it was preparation. He understood that composure was contagious.

Modern leaders face the same demand. In a world of constant acceleration, our nervous systems become the true governors of strategy. Emotional endurance is what allows intellect to function under pressure – the stabilizing current beneath adaptation itself.

From History to Habit: The CREATE Application

In the end, agility isn’t just an individual trait – it’s a cultural rhythm. Every domain of CREATE contains a hidden invitation to learn: a way to translate emotional intelligence into momentum.

When practiced together, they form a learning flywheel – a system that refuels itself through reflection, humility, and shared growth.

  • Culture → Aspiration
    Revisit the why before you redesign the how. Meaning renews motion.

  • Relationships → Vulnerability
    Let people see the learner, not just the leader. Credibility grows through honesty, not perfection.

  • Execution → Curiosity
    Institutionalize retrospectives – fail, learn, document. Progress is iteration made visible.

  • Agility → Self-Awareness
    Pause quarterly to map your growth edges. Speed without reflection is drift.

  • Teaching → Modeling
    Share your learning process, not just your results. Transparency multiplies wisdom.

  • Ethical Decision-Making → Humility
    Admit uncertainty; invite collective intelligence. Integrity is a shared act of discernment.

Each domain strengthens the others – creating a living loop where emotional intelligence sustains velocity without losing humanity.

That’s the true engine of adaptive leadership: not perpetual motion, but perpetual learning.

The Human Advantage

AI will master calculation.

That’s inevitable – and, in many ways, desirable. My wife is an accountant; she jokes she may be the last generation to do that work by hand. She’s probably right. Crunching numbers and issuing reports are things machines will always do faster, cheaper, and with fewer errors.

But transformation – the work of becoming – remains human terrain. Only people can metabolize fear into curiosity, pressure into courage, and data into meaning. Only we can bridge the gap between information and insight, between what is known and what is understood.

That’s the real distinction of leadership in the age of AI: not the ability to process inputs, but the willingness to be transformed by them.

George Washington understood this long before algorithms. His evolution from ambitious officer to tempered statesman reminds us that progress isn’t the betrayal of principle – it’s fidelity to purpose over time.

He didn’t fear change; he embodied it with grace. And that’s the invitation before us now.

As machines learn to think, we must remember how to learn – and lead – with heart.

A Gentle Invitation

If you’d like to build your own learning agility roadmap – integrating CliftonStrengths, EQ-i 2.0, and the CREATE Leadership Framework into a single system for growth – let’s design it together.

title: 3. The Five Facets of EQ AI Can’t Replicate
subtitle: Essay 3 of 7
series: EQ in the Age of AI series
html:
The Paradox of Progress

Artificial intelligence can now imitate empathy, mimic tone, and even predict behavior. What it still cannot do is feel consequence – the subtle awareness of how decisions land on others.

That awareness is the foundation of emotional intelligence. EQ isn’t the opposite of intelligence; it’s what keeps intelligence human. It’s the feedback system that converts insight into impact.

When I coach leaders through the CREATE Framework, I see the same five capacities emerge again and again – each one a distinctly human skill no algorithm can master. These aren’t just competencies; they’re conscience in motion.

And as strange as it sounds, the best case study I’ve found doesn’t come from Silicon Valley.

It comes from the 18th century

1. Self-Awareness – The Lens of Legacy

When Washington addressed his officers at Newburgh, the war was nearly won, but morale was collapsing. Facing the men who had followed him through years of uncertainty, he paused, reached for his spectacles, and said quietly:

“Gentlemen, you will permit me to put on my spectacles, for I have grown not only gray, but almost blind in the service of my country.”

In that simple gesture, he disarmed the room. The rebellion dissolved – not through command, but through connection.

That moment revealed the emotional truth behind leadership: I am human too.

It was an act of self-awareness – the first pillar of emotional intelligence, and the first cylinder of the CREATE engine: Culture and Clarity. Washington understood not only his message but his symbolism. He knew that how he showed up mattered as much as what he said. His vulnerability transformed authority into trust.

Coaching Insight:
Today’s leaders may wield digital rather than military power, but the principle remains the same: presence shapes perception.

In an era of Slack messages and executive dashboards, tone still travels faster than policy.

Reflection Prompt:
What does your team read between your lines – in your pauses, your phrasing, your silence?

2. Self-Regulation – Calm as Competence

Washington’s genius wasn’t in fiery rhetoric; it was in restraint. At moments when rage or pride could have ruled, he paused.

When his officers tested his patience, or when Congress stalled his plans, he held his tongue – not out of passivity, but principle. That pause was his power.

The EQ-i 2.0 calls this Impulse Control – the ability to choose your response rather than react to circumstance. It’s the emotional governor that prevents the engine from over-revving.

In the CREATE framework, it sits between Execution and Ethical Decision-Making – the hinge where discipline meets integrity.

In the VOICES model, it’s what lets leaders downshift from “Operator” to “Coach,” listening before speaking, guiding before judging.

Coaching Insight:
In AI-accelerated organizations, tempo is the new temptation. The constant hum of notifications, dashboards, and deadlines can make speed feel like progress. But self-regulation is the discipline of slowing the decision just long enough for wisdom to catch up with urgency.

That’s what turns reaction into response and urgency into intentionality.

It’s not slowness – it’s steadiness. The quiet leadership skill that keeps judgment clear even as the world accelerates.

Reflection Point:
What decisions in your world would benefit from one extra beat of reflection?
Where might a pause create more power than a push?

3. Motivation – Purpose Over Power

CliftonStrengths would describe Washington’s drive as a blend of Responsibility and Focus – a commitment to principle over personal ambition.

He twice relinquished ultimate power: once after victory, and again after the presidency. Each time, he modeled a truth that remains rare even now – that leadership’s highest act isn’t taking control, but letting go of it.

That’s intrinsic motivation in motion: action guided by meaning, not metrics. It’s what happens when clarity of purpose outpaces the pursuit of performance.

Coaching Insight:
In a metrics-obsessed age, remember that purpose fuels performance longer than pressure. Motivation anchored in values outlasts any quarterly target or machine-learning cycle.

It’s what separates momentum from mastery – the difference between being driven and being directed.

Reflection Point:
Where does your ambition serve your principles – and where might it still compete with them?

If you paused the pursuit for a moment, what meaning would you want your movement to serve?

4. Empathy – Connection as Command

Washington’s empathy was pragmatic. He read morale like weather – sensing the storm before the rebellion. Newburgh was one such moment, but it wasn’t the only one. During brutal winters, he walked the camps, listened to grievances, and saw not statistics, but suffering.

Empathy, for him, wasn’t softness. It was systems-awareness – an understanding that emotion is data, and often the most predictive data we have. He grasped what modern organizations still forget: people broadcast early warnings long before systems do.

In today’s terms, empathy is the leader’s early-detection system – the ability to sense pressure before it becomes resistance, and to translate that insight into action before it becomes attrition.

Coaching Insight:
Empathy scales through design. Leaders can institutionalize it through listening rounds, psychological safety surveys, mentorship networks, and open channels for dissent – the same human infrastructure Washington built through presence and personal example.

In the CREATE model, this is Relationships & Connection: trust as strategy, humanity as architecture.

Reflection Point:
How do you listen to your organization?

Are you hearing emotion as noise – or treating it as data that reveals where alignment, trust, or energy are leaking from the system?

5. Social Skill – The Architecture of Trust

Washington united fractious colonies and skeptical officers into a functioning whole. That wasn’t charisma; it was relational engineering – the deliberate design of trust loops and feedback systems that allowed diverse people to act as one.

He built alignment through rhythm: councils, correspondence, personal visits, and the visible discipline of fairness. These weren’t symbolic gestures. They were structural reinforcements of trust.

In emotional intelligence, this is Social Skill – the ability to turn empathy into execution.

In CREATE terms, it’s Relationships translating into Execution. Connection becomes coordination. Understanding becomes momentum.

Coaching Insight:
Modern leaders must build the same architecture – meeting rhythms, cross-team rituals, and transparent communication channels that convert emotion into alignment. When trust has form, collaboration has flow.

Reflection Point:
Where does trust in your organization exist only as intention?

What systems, rhythms, or rituals could give it structure – so that empathy doesn’t just inspire, but scales?

The Human Equation

Across these moments – the spectacles at Newburgh, the pause before anger, the surrender of power, the walks through winter camps – a pattern emerges. What made Washington extraordinary wasn’t access to better information; it was the quality of his attention.

Artificial intelligence can process faster, predict further, and mirror tone with uncanny precision. But what it cannot do is care – to feel the weight of consequence, the nuance of timing, the invisible shift in trust that precedes change.

Those are the human signals that powered Washington’s leadership – and they remain the core circuitry of emotional intelligence today.

Self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, and social skill are more than competencies; they’re coordinates of consciousness. Together, they form the EQ engine that keeps intelligence human. They are the mechanisms that translate insight into integrity – what turns capability into character.

AI can analyze data; it cannot discern meaning.
It can simulate empathy; it cannot sustain trust.
It can optimize performance; it cannot choose principle over profit.

The leaders who thrive in the age of AI will not be those who outsource emotion to efficiency, but those who integrate both – who know when to trust the algorithm, and when to listen to the silence beneath it.

That’s what the machine can’t learn: awareness in motion.

From Historical Hero to Modern Mirror

EQ isn’t new.

It’s just newly urgent.

Washington’s leadership reminds us that emotional intelligence has always been the silent multiplier behind great systems – the quiet circuitry that keeps power humane.

AI may out-compute us, but it can’t yet care.
It can mimic empathy, but it can’t mean it.

And caring – intelligently, intentionally, consistently – remains the decisive advantage.

Because leadership has never been about processing more information, it’s about sensing what matters, responding with humanity, and keeping the system aligned with its purpose.

If emotional intelligence is the steady rhythm of leadership, learning is its motion. Caring may be the decisive advantage, but curiosity is the force that keeps it alive.

Every generation faces disruption; ours happens to be automated.
The question isn’t whether machines will learn faster – they already do.
The question is whether we will stay learnable.

In the machine age, adaptability isn’t technical – it’s emotional.
To keep learning is to keep listening, recalibrating, and remaining open to feedback.
That’s what keeps the human engine responsive – not just efficient, but evolving.

A Gentle Invitation

If this resonated and you want a tailored map – your strengths, your system, your shifts – let’s design it.

👉 Schedule a Clarity Chatt with Matt

title: 2. The New Leadership Divide: Why EQ Outpaces IQ in an Automated World
subtitle: Essay 2 of 7
series: EQ in the Age of AI series
html:
When Machines Outsmart, Humans Must Out-Feel

Automation has already out-analyzed us.
Algorithms out-predict, out-calculate, and out-optimize.

But they still can’t care.

That’s the paradox of the AI age: intelligence alone no longer differentiates leaders – emotional intelligence does. Soon, everyone will have access to the same digital horsepower. Anyone can feed a spreadsheet to an LLM and ask it to surface market opportunities.

The best leaders don’t try to compete with machines; they complement them. They understand that while artificial intelligence processes data, only human intelligence processes meaning.

I see this shift every day. The most effective leaders aren’t the ones with perfect résumés or the highest test scores. They’re the ones who can sit calmly in ambiguity, hear the emotion behind silence, and rebuild trust when uncertainty spikes.

There’s a line I love:

“Knowledge is knowing that a tomato is a fruit.
Wisdom is knowing not to put it in a fruit salad.”

It stays with me – not because it’s clever, but because it captures the essential divide between information and discernment.

In an age where AI can deliver answers instantly, knowledge has become abundant. What’s scarce is the ability to pause, sense, and apply that knowledge with context – to know what fits, what doesn’t, and what timing demands restraint.

That’s the real leadership challenge now: not knowing more, but knowing when and how to use what you know.

EQ is the listening instrument for that timing – the felt awareness that tells you when the system is under strain, when to shift gears, when to ease the clutch, and when to let the engine breathe.

Because the future doesn’t belong to those who know everything, it belongs to those who can feel when it’s time to act – and when it’s time to wait.

Two Operating Systems in One Mind

Neuroscience tells us that leaders operate with two primary neural networks: the Analytic Network (AN) and the Empathic Network (EN).

The Analytic Network excels at logic, planning, and pattern recognition – the precision tools of modern management. The Empathic Network, by contrast, governs connection: empathy, trust, intuition, and moral reasoning – the heartbeat of leadership.

Here’s the catch: when one is active, the other naturally powers down. You can’t analyze and empathize at full volume. It’s like trying to press the gas and the brake at the same time.

That’s why the best leaders don’t pick a side. They learn to toggle between networks – to shift from analysis to empathy and back again without losing traction.

That toggling is the modern leadership superpower. It’s not about thinking less. It’s about feeling smarter – knowing when logic needs to yield to listening, and when emotion needs the clarity of structure.

AI already dominates the Analytic Network – the realm of data integrity, computation, and pattern matching.

But the Empathic Network remains distinctly, beautifully human. It’s the only one capable of sensing tone, timing, and trust – that subtle moment between push and pause, when a decision turns from transactional to transformational.

That’s why emotional intelligence is no longer “soft.”

It’s the strategic infrastructure that determines whether the hard systems we build can actually function – the wiring that keeps intelligence connected to intention.

In the language of systems, EQ is the clutch – the mechanism that lets leaders shift between analysis and empathy without grinding the gears. It’s what keeps the engine (CREATE) humming and the gears (VOICES) responsive. Without it, even the most powerful system stalls.

When leaders develop emotional intelligence, they’re not learning how to feel more – they’re learning how to listen better. They begin to sense when the system needs torque, traction, or simply space to breathe.

That’s how modern leadership moves – not through constant acceleration, but through conscious calibration.

This ability to shift between networks – from head to heart, from analysis to empathy – is what keeps a leader adaptive in motion. Because leadership isn’t a static equation; it’s a living system that requires continual tuning.

Each decision, each interaction, becomes a micro-moment of rebalancing – an invitation to notice which network is driving and which needs to re-engage.

That awareness is where agility begins. EQ doesn’t just soften intelligence – it stabilizes it under stress.

And that’s the essence of learning agility – the leadership engine that keeps everything else moving forward, even when the terrain keeps changing.

The Leadership Engine: Learning Agility

The ability to learn faster than your environment changes is now the only sustainable advantage left – and that’s where emotional intelligence fuels the system. In a world moving at algorithmic speed, leaders can’t rely on static expertise; they need dynamic awareness.

Self-awareness keeps you grounded. Curiosity keeps you adaptive. Vulnerability keeps you real. Together, they create the human circuitry behind agility – the emotional wiring that turns uncertainty into forward motion.

Leaders with high EQ don’t cling to certainty; they cultivate capacity – the range and resilience to navigate what’s next. They understand that growth isn’t a straight line; it’s a rhythm. It accelerates and eases, speeds and steadies, responding to the terrain ahead. Like an engine, agility isn’t measured by how fast you can go, but by how well you can adjust.

Leadership coach and author Erika Andersen, founder of Proteus International, calls this quality being learnable. She describes it as the blend of aspiration, curiosity, and self-awareness that allows people to adapt again and again. Automation can replicate knowledge, but it can’t replicate learning. Because learning isn’t just the transfer of information – it’s the transformation of awareness. It’s what happens when reflection meets action, when self-observation becomes self-correction, and when clarity is earned through motion rather than memorization.

True learning is an act of humility. It asks leaders to pause long enough to notice what the system is telling them – to sense where friction builds, where alignment slips, and where trust needs repair. It’s less about collecting insight and more about translating it into wiser action.

That’s what emotional intelligence makes possible. It’s the clutch that connects reflection to adaptation – the feel that tells you when to shift, when to hold, and when to let the engine breathe. In the CREATE model, it’s the balance between Culture and Agility, between stability and evolution. It’s the same rhythm Washington mastered: turning ambition into wisdom, movement into meaning.

Learning agility, then, isn’t speed. It’s sensitivity – the ability to stay attuned to change without losing coherence, to move fast and stay human at the same time.

From Metrics to Meaning

Traditional performance dashboards track output – tasks completed, deadlines met, goals achieved. But EQ-mature leaders track something deeper: outcomes that actually sustain performance over time.

They ask different questions.

  • Psychological safety: Are people speaking the truth?

  • Relational trust: Are we moving together?

  • Emotional alignment: Do our values still drive decisions?

These are not soft metrics. They are leading indicators of system health – the human equivalents of oil pressure, temperature, and torque. Ignore them, and the system eventually overheats.

In my coaching practice, I rely on two primary psychometric tools to read those signals: CliftonStrengths and EQ-i 2.0. Both measure how people lead and perform, but they illuminate different layers of the system.

CliftonStrengths identifies your natural patterns of thought, feeling, and behavior – the talents that power your best work when refined into strengths. It’s a snapshot of how you’re wired to operate.

EQ-i 2.0, by contrast, measures your emotional intelligence – the skills that determine how effectively you perceive, express, and manage emotion in yourself and others. It’s less about what you do and more about how you connect while doing it.

Viewed separately, each offers insight. Viewed together, they form a blueprint.
Strengths reveal the architecture of your engine; EQ shows how smoothly it runs. One explains how power is generated; the other reveals how that power is transferred to people.

That’s why I often stack both assessments. Together, they shift leadership from personality to practice – from what drives you internally to how your drive affects those around you.

To model some vulnerability, I’ll share my own data. My profile blends Strategic, Learner, and Relator strengths with high scores in Self-Actualization and Stress Tolerance. That combination explains why I’m drawn to complex systems – and to the people inside them. But, like many leaders, I’ve learned that curiosity and drive can easily outrun emotional expression. EQ is what brings that calibration, ensuring that speed doesn’t outpace connection.

In that sense, emotional intelligence isn’t just another dashboard light – it’s the instrument panel itself, the part of the system that tells you not only how fast you’re moving, but how your movement affects those around you.

Metrics can prove the value of EQ, but they can’t teach it.

Emotional intelligence spreads the way trust does – not through policy, but through proximity. People don’t learn EQ from dashboards; they learn it from leaders who embody it.

That’s why the next evolution of leadership isn’t about training more analysts – it’s about coaching more humans. Because culture doesn’t change when you tell people to act differently.

It changes when they experience someone listening differently.

The Human ROI

Organizations that invest in emotional intelligence don’t just end up with “nicer” teams. They get measurable, repeatable returns.

According to Gallup’s 2024 State of the Global Workplace, teams led by emotionally intelligent managers report up to 23% higher engagement, 27% higher profitability, and 40% lower turnover. When leaders intentionally build trust and psychological safety, employees are more likely to speak truth, share ideas, and challenge assumptions – the very conditions that fuel innovation.

Research from Harvard Business Review and Korn Ferry echoes this pattern: high-EQ leaders make better decisions under stress, adapt faster to disruption, and are twice as likely to retain top talent through periods of volatility. The data tells a clear story – EQ doesn’t replace performance metrics; it strengthens them.

Emotionally intelligent cultures show faster adaptation to change, clearer decision-making, and stronger accountability – not because people are nicer, but because they feel known, heard, and trusted. When fear subsides, contribution rises.

That’s the conversion point: EQ turns connection into performance.

It’s what transforms human capital into collective intelligence – the shared awareness that allows systems, teams, and strategies to move as one coherent whole.

A Gentle Call to Leaders

If you’re wondering where to begin, start small.

Before the next big decision, pause – and ask yourself: What emotion is driving me right now?

That single act of awareness is what separates reaction from leadership. It’s the clutch moment – the quiet shift from motion to meaning.

Because in the end, the leaders who thrive in the age of AI won’t be the ones who think the fastest. They’ll be the ones who feel the clearest – those who can listen inwardly, calibrate wisely, and move forward with presence.

title: 1. Why This Series Exists: EQ in the Age of AI
subtitle: Essay 1 of 7
series: EQ in the Age of AI series
html:
It Started With a Paradox

I spend my days helping leaders design systems that make human work work better.

As a solopreneur, I rely on AI the way some rely on teams – as a silent, tireless partner that helps me move faster, think clearer, and ship awork that would otherwise stay stuck in notebooks. It isn’t just a tool. It’s a multiplier.

But AI isn’t just part of how I build. It’s part of how I think.

Before consulting, I spent years in and around education – designing systems, coaching leaders, and trying to bridge the gap between theory and practice. Though I’ve moved beyond that sector professionally, I haven’t moved on from it intellectually. I still think often about learning – how we grow, how we teach, and what education looks like in a world where machines can now teach themselves.

Much of my writing lives at that intersection: between AI and emotional intelligence, systems and soul, the future of work and the future of learning. It’s where my curiosity loops back, again and again.

Because no matter how fast the tools get, the deeper questions remain:
What kind of humans are we designing for? And how do we make sure they’re not left behind?

Lately, I’ve noticed something strange. The more we automate, the more people ache for the parts of leadership that can’t be automated – clarity, empathy, meaning.

Every dashboard, every KPI, every leadership algorithm kept leading me back to one realization: we’ve become better at managing systems than we have at managing ourselves.

And that’s where this series began – with the quiet recognition that the next competitive advantage isn’t artificial intelligence.

It’s applied emotional intelligence.

Yes, AI will transform. It will disrupt. In some cases, it will even destroy systems, roles, and entire ways of working. But that’s only half the story.

Because just as much as AI will dismantle, it will also create – new tools, new workflows, new forms of value we haven’t yet imagined. It’s both demolition and design. Not a clean upgrade, but a messy re-architecture of how we think, lead, and build.

The leaders I work with aren’t just asking, “How do we keep up?”
They’re asking, “What do we want to build in the rubble?”

That’s the real opportunity – not just to brace for the future, but to shape it. Intentionally. Ethically. With enough emotional intelligence to remember what all this technology is ultimately for: better human outcomes.

A few weeks ago, a senior executive asked me, “How do I lead when I’m surrounded by people – and machines – that can think faster than I can?”

That question landed hard. Because under it was another: What’s left for us when the thinking is outsourced?

We’re entering an era that won’t just test our intellect. It will test our humanity.

And that’s why I’m writing this series – to help leaders navigate that threshold with both rigor and soul. To remember that while IQ might be the engine’s horsepower, EQ is the skill of learning to drive stick – the awareness in motion that tells you when to ease off the clutch, when to shift, and when to let the engine breathe simply.

Why Washington

As I worked through the early drafts of this series, I kept coming back to one unlikely case study: George Washington.

As a decidedly apolitical figure, he occupies a rare place in American memory – known well enough that most people can sketch the broad contours of his life, yet distant enough to remain almost mythic. He’s less a politician than a symbol: of restraint, integrity, and a kind of leadership shaped more by character than charisma.

That’s part of what makes him such a useful mirror in the age of AI. In a world defined by velocity and noise, he reminds us that stillness is also a form of strength – that clarity and presence still matter more than cleverness or volume. Leadership isn’t always about being the loudest voice; sometimes it’s about being the quietest listener.

He lived long before algorithms or machine learning. Yet, his leadership reads like a modern manual on emotional intelligence – grounded in self-awareness, impulse control, empathy, ethical foresight, and a steady commitment to mentoring others into leadership. –

Washington was both systemic and soulful – a founder who didn’t rely on personality to move people but on design that outlasted him. He modeled what I often describe as a balanced engine: six cylinders of culture, trust, execution, adaptability, teaching, and ethics working in unison beneath the surface – CREATE before its time.

And when he did act, he shifted gears with discernment. He knew when to advance, when to hold, and when to yield – a living example of VOICES long before the framework had a name.

He didn’t build an empire; he built a culture. And that distinction is as relevant to AI-era organizations as it was to a fledgling democracy.

Because the challenge hasn’t changed – only the speed.

Why Emotional Intelligence Now

We’re living through the fastest redefinition of work in human history. AI, automation, and analytics are rewriting what competence even means.

Yet no matter how advanced the tools become, people still need to feel seen, safe, and significant. That doesn’t change with technology – it becomes more urgent because of it.

Emotional intelligence isn’t a counterweight to AI. It’s the interface that makes intelligence usable, sustainable, and humane. Without it, intelligence becomes extraction – data without discernment, output without empathy. With it, intelligence becomes design – systems that listen, adapt, and serve.

Because AI may amplify horsepower, but only EQ teaches us how to drive it.

It’s the awareness in motion – the quiet listening that tells us when to shift, when to slow, and when to let the engine breathe.

Why Me

I’ve spent two decades at the intersection of education, leadership, and system design – from classrooms to federal agencies to executive boardrooms.

I’m not a futurist; I’m a facilitator. My work lives in the space between data and dignity – helping people see that culture isn’t an outcome. It’s architecture.

And like any good structure, it must be designed to adapt – to shifting weight, new tools, and faster systems.

This series is my way of mapping that architecture for an age when the boundaries between human and machine are blurring. It’s both an argument and a field guide – and, more than anything, an act of hope.

Because emotional intelligence isn’t disappearing. It’s evolving – becoming the adaptive framework that keeps human leadership steady as everything else accelerates.

EQ is what helps the structure breathe. It’s what keeps the cylinders aligned and the gears responsive, reminding us that even in an age of automation, the system still runs best when it listens.

Why This Series

Each essay in this series is a different lens on the same truth: the leaders who will thrive in the next decade will be those who can think deeply, feel clearly, and act ethically – all at once.

What began as scattered notes – half reflections, half experiments – eventually crystallized into seven essays.

Each one explores a different gear in the system, a different way emotional intelligence translates from awareness into action.

  1. The New Leadership Divide – balancing head and heart in the age of automation.

  2. The Five Facets of EQ AI Can’t Replicate – translating empathy into execution.

  3. Learning to Learn in the Machine Age – emotional intelligence as adaptive muscle.

  4. Coaching the Human Back into Leadership – mentorship as system design.

  5. The Ethical Compass in an Algorithmic World – slowing down when speed tempts us to forget.

  6. Emotional Intelligence as Strategy – EQ as infrastructure, not inspiration.

  7. The EQ Flywheel – how awareness becomes alignment, action, and renewal.

Together, these essays form a map – not for managing machines, but for designing the humanness that makes systems work.

Because culture isn’t code.

It’s chemistry.

And when leaders tune into that frequency – the quiet hum between intellect and intuition – they build something AI still can’t: cultures that feel alive.

A Gentle Invitation

If this series resonates, it’s probably because you already feel the same tension I do – that quiet pull between speed and soul, data and discernment, information and wisdom.

You’ve likely sensed it in your own work – the hum beneath the dashboards, the ache for meaning that no metric quite measures.

I don’t claim to have all, or even any, of the answers.

This series is simply my attempt to map the questions – to get them out of my head and into the marketplace of ideas, where they can be challenged, reshaped, and refined.

I hope you’ll join that dialogue. Comment, repost, disagree, expand – that’s how intelligence evolves. After all, who doesn’t love a good Hegelian dialectic?

Because the point isn’t to resist technology. It’s to reclaim humanity – not as nostalgia, but as strategy.

To remember that leadership, like driving, is still a felt art: you listen for the engine, sense the timing, and shift with care.

Let’s build that future – intentionally, emotionally, and together.

title: Thoughts on: What's Holding Your Back from Being A Great Leader - from HBR
html:
One Clear Idea

This week’s idea came from the cover of Harvard Business Review.
It featured executive coach Muriel Wilkins – and the headline stopped me cold:
“What’s Holding You Back from Being a Great Leader?”

I listened to her IdeaCast interview on a walk – and ordered her book that night.

Her point landed fast:
It’s not your skills that hold you back.
It’s the beliefs you’re still carrying that once helped you – but don’t anymore.

Listen to the HBR podcast here.

“I need it done now.”
“I can’t make a mistake.”
“If I can do it, so can they.”

These aren’t bad beliefs.
In fact, they likely helped you rise.
But they’ll quietly stall you – and your team – if you never reexamine them.

A client once told me:

“It’s not the hours that drain me – it’s showing up every day in a role I haven’t rethought in years. I’m stuck.”

She wasn’t the problem.
Her beliefs were.
Outdated. Unquestioned. Misaligned with the scale of her leadership.

So we shifted focus:
Not what she was doing – but why she was doing it.

That’s where change actually starts.

This Week’s Coaching Prompt

“What belief might have helped me succeed in the past – but is quietly holding me back now?”

Try this reflection:

  • What part of my leadership feels harder than it should?

  • What assumptions do I hold about how I “have” to lead?

Where am I creating urgency – or perfectionism – without meaning to?

This isn’t therapy.
It’s pattern-breaking.

One Practice to Try: Run a Belief Audit

Take 15 minutes this weekend. Reflect or journal:

  • What’s a recurring challenge I face with my team?

  • What’s the belief behind my usual response?

  • Is that belief still true – or just familiar?

Then reframe:
“I can’t make a mistake” → “I can make progress, even if it’s imperfect.”
“I need it done now” → “I’ll prioritize what matters – not just what’s fast.”
“If I can do it, so can they” → “I’ll meet people where they are.”

This isn’t a full rewrite of your identity.
It’s just a software update for your leadership OS.

Why This Matters Right Now

Hidden blockers don’t shout.
They whisper.
And that whisper shapes your tone, your pace, your culture.

You can’t delegate what you don’t examine.
And you can’t scale leadership on beliefs that aren’t built to scale.

The question isn’t: “Am I doing it right?”
It’s: “Am I leading from beliefs that match the leader I want to become?”

Your Move: Choose One Belief to Reframe This Week

Here’s how:

  1. Name it: What belief might be subtly driving your default?

  2. Unpack it: Where did it come from? When did it help?

  3. Reframe it: What’s a version that fits the leader you are becoming?

BTW, please read what I wrote about this reframing process, and how it begins with naming it, here.

Then watch what shifts – not just in you, but around you.

Please share this with someone who’s outgrown an old belief but hasn’t said it out loud yet.

They don’t need a whole reinvention.
Just a more useful story.

title: Upskilling as a Leadership Act
html:
When the middle thins, everyone must learn to lead.

In my last essay, I wrote about the hollowing of the middle – the quiet collapse of the connective layer that once turned vision into action and culture into continuity. It was never just a story about structure. It was a story about what happens when we optimize for speed and inadvertently erode the spaces where meaning is made.

This essay is part two: the rebuild.

Because as organizations have flattened and technology has scaled, something deeply human has been lost in translation. AI can now synthesize vast amounts of information, forecast patterns, and even write the memos we used to labor over. But what it can’t do is teach. It can’t model self-awareness, build trust, or turn uncertainty into shared understanding.

What’s gone missing isn’t middle management as a layer of control – it’s middle management as a layer of learning. The relational infrastructure that once helped people grow, that turned mistakes into lessons and friction into alignment, has quietly disappeared.

The future doesn’t need more managers to enforce efficiency.

It needs more teachers – leaders who cultivate capability, not dependency. Leaders who can slow the conversation just long enough for others to think, make meaning, and reconnect the dots between purpose and performance.

Because leadership, at its best, isn’t about directing work.

It’s about developing wisdom – in people, in systems, and in the shared culture that outlasts any single role.

The New Mandate

According to the World Economic Forum’s 2025 Future of Jobs Report, 63% of employers cite skill gaps as the top barrier to transformation, and 85% plan to prioritize upskilling in the next five years. On its face, that sounds like a rational response to a rapidly changing world – invest in training, close the gap, move on.

But that statistic hides a deeper truth: learning is no longer an HR function; it’s a leadership function.

Upskilling isn’t just about transferring knowledge – it’s about transforming capability. It’s not a compliance exercise; it’s a cultural one. The organizations that will thrive in this next era aren’t the ones with the most courses or the most significant training budgets. They’re the ones where learning has become leadership’s daily practice.

We don’t need more programs.

We need more leaders who model curiosity, who create the psychological safety for others to ask hard questions, and who treat reflection not as a luxury, but as a discipline.

In these organizations, learning is baked into the culture. Coaching replaces control. Questions carry as much value as answers. Leadership and learning are no longer separate acts – they are the same motion, the same mindset, the same muscle.

The Managers Were the Mentors

When we flattened organizations, we didn’t just remove oversight – we removed the people who taught.

Middle managers were never simply conduits for information or compliance. They were the translators of culture – the ones who gave direction and emotional meaning. They carried the informal feedback loops, the hallway conversations, and the micro-coaching moments that made learning continuous and personal. Their leadership was lived, not announced – the quiet cadence of support, correction, and belief that helped others grow into their potential.

As Gloria St. Martin-Lowry writes in A Guide for New Middle Managers, these leaders “anchor motivation through clarity, feedback, and coaching.” They ensure that every employee understands not just what to do, but why it matters.

Now, in many organizations, that layer has disappeared – and with it, the scaffolding of human growth. People are being promoted faster but developed more slowly. Titles are advancing; wisdom is not.

Again, see my recent posts about EQ in the Age of AI. AI is crushing the domain of knowledge, but only humans can have wisdom. See my analogy about tomatos being a fruit…

It’s a quiet irony of the modern era: in flattening the org chart for efficiency, we created a new kind of bottleneck – a learning bottleneck. We gained speed, but lost the teachers who knew how to turn momentum into mastery.

Upskilling as Emotional Infrastructure

The Gallup Global Leadership Report (2024) reframes leadership not as a hierarchy of authority, but as the ability to meet four fundamental needs of followers: Trust, Compassion, Stability, and Hope. It’s a simple framework, but one with profound implications.

And it’s not theory. Gallup’s data show that employees who believe their manager cares about their development are nearly five times more likely to be engaged – a finding that reinforces what most of us already know intuitively: people don’t grow because they’re managed; they grow because they’re mentored.

When done well, upskilling becomes the modern mechanism for meeting these four needs:

  • Trust – When leaders share what they’re learning, they model integrity and transparency. Growth becomes a shared journey, not a silent expectation.

  • Compassion – When leaders coach instead of critique, they make growth feel safe. They replace judgment with curiosity.

  • Stability – When learning is embedded into the rhythm of work, it anchors teams amid change. Reflection becomes the pulse that steadies the system.

  • Hope – When organizations invest in development, they communicate belief in people’s potential – a subtle but powerful act of faith.

This is what technology can’t replicate. AI can process data, optimize tasks, and scale knowledge – but it can’t communicate belief. It can’t look someone in the eye and say, I see more in you than you see in yourself – and I’ll help you get there.

In that sense, upskilling isn’t just a strategy for capability. It’s a practice of care. It’s the modern vehicle for trust – and the bridge between efficiency and belonging.

From Training to Teaching

Most organizations have training programs.
Few have teaching cultures.

At first glance, the distinction seems semantic – a matter of labels. But dig deeper, and it reveals a structural blind spot.

Training is transactional: What do you need to know to perform?
Teaching is transformational: What do we need to understand to progress?

Training fills knowledge gaps. Teaching builds adaptive capacity.
Training reinforces the process. Teaching redefines possibility.
Training ensures compliance. Teaching ignites creativity.

That distinction marks the line between efficiency and evolution – between organizations that survive disruption and those that lead through it.

When viewed through the lens of organizational systems, training is a programmatic input; teaching is a cultural output. Training happens within HR. Teaching happens everywhere leaders show up with curiosity and humility. It’s not a course or a competency – it’s a way of operating.

In Goode Designs’ CREATE Leadership Framework, Teaching is the central gear that drives modern performance. It’s how the system converts clarity into capability, strategy into skill, and culture into continuity. Each of the six cylinders fires more efficiently when leaders teach through it:

  • Culture – Define what’s worth learning. Teaching keeps the “why” visible and connected to every decision.

  • Relationships – Make learning social and safe. People don’t learn from authority; they learn from trust.

  • Execution – Turn workflow into learnflow. Every deliverable becomes a feedback loop, every project a prototype.

  • Agility – Treat experimentation as data, not failure. Teaching reframes mistakes as insights.

  • Teaching – Multiply leadership by passing experience forward. This is how influence scales without hierarchy.
    Ethical Decision-Making – Lead with humility, not certainty. The best teachers model integrity by staying open to being taught.

The organizations that thrive in the next decade will not be the ones that simply train better; they’ll be the ones that teach by design. They’ll turn reflection into infrastructure – embedding curiosity, feedback, and shared sense-making into how work gets done.

Teaching, at this level, is not a soft skill. It’s a strategic capability. It is how leaders make culture visible and strategy sustainable. It’s how they turn human connection into a competitive advantage.

Because in an era when AI can replicate information but not insight, teaching remains the last mile of leadership – the human layer where clarity becomes commitment and learning becomes belonging.

Rebuilding the Middle as a Mesh

The future of leadership isn’t a pyramid – it’s a mesh.

We don’t need to rebuild the middle layer; we need to reimagine it as a living network of mentors, coaches, and learners who share what they know in real time. Hierarchies distribute authority. Networks distribute wisdom. In a complex, fast-moving environment, the value of leadership lies not in its position on the chart, but in its proximity to learning.

This new architecture of leadership doesn’t eliminate structure; it changes what structure is for. It shifts the question from Who reports to whom? to Who learns from whom? The organizations that will thrive aren’t those with the flattest lines, but the richest connections – where knowledge flows laterally, trust compounds, and insight travels faster than approval chains.

That might look like:

  • Rotational “learning stewards” who facilitate post-project reflections and capture lessons before momentum fades.

  • Cross-team mentorship circles that pair institutional memory with emerging energy.

  • AI-powered learning hubs that curate and surface wisdom from across the organization – ensuring expertise is shared before it’s lost.

  • Internal office hours where peers teach peers, because the best answers are often one desk – or one Slack thread – away.

In The Middle Manager as Innovator (MIT Sloan Management Review, 2023), Ingvild De Paoli, Silvia Profili, and Alessia Sammarra found that leaders who actively coach others are 2.4× more likely to drive both innovation and retention. Their finding reframes teaching not as a detour from productivity, but as its source.

Teaching doesn’t take time from work.
Teaching is the work.

It is the connective act that transforms experience into intelligence – the quiet, compounding habit that keeps organizations not just efficient, but alive.

Leadership as a Learning System

Flattened organizations often fall into two powerful illusions:

  • That communication equals connection.

  • That efficiency equals effectiveness.

Both are seductive – and both are false.

Because human systems don’t scale on communication alone, they scale on comprehension. Information is abundant. Meaning is scarce. And in every team, someone has to turn noise into narrative – to connect the dots between what’s happening and why it matters.

That someone used to be the middle manager – the quiet interpreter who turned directives into dialogue and helped teams translate pressure into progress. But as that layer has disappeared, the need hasn’t. It has simply shifted.

Now, that work belongs to everyone.

The next generation of organizations will not succeed by communicating faster, but by understanding deeper. They will scale through sensemaking – through leaders and teams who can pause long enough to align, reflect, and learn.

That’s where upskilling reclaims its truest purpose. It doesn’t just transfer skills; it restores culture as a living system of learning. It reintroduces the connective tissue between humans and purpose – the very muscle memory that keeps organizations from fragmenting under the weight of their own efficiency.

Upskilling, at its best, is not an HR initiative. It’s a cultural intervention – a way of rebuilding what flattening stripped away: meaning, mentorship, and momentum.

The Leadership Flywheel

When leadership becomes teaching, something profound happens.

Leaders model learning.
Teams mirror it.
Systems adapt to it.
Trust compounds.

That’s the flywheel of a learning culture – a self-reinforcing loop where growth no longer depends on mandate, but on momentum. It’s how organizations begin to grow faster than the rate of change, because they’ve shifted from reacting to the future to rehearsing for it.

Teaching transforms leadership from a position of authority into a practice of generosity – the daily act of turning experience into shared intelligence. When every leader becomes a teacher, every challenge becomes a classroom. Every mistake becomes curriculum. Every conversation becomes culture.

That’s the quiet revolution unfolding in the best organizations today:

Not a return to hierarchy, but the rise of humanity – where leading and learning have finally become the same act.

In the end, sustainable leadership isn’t about titles or tenure – it’s about transmission. The organizations that will endure aren’t those that communicate the most, but those that teach best – where knowledge flows freely, trust compounds naturally, and growth becomes a collective reflex.

Because when leadership becomes teaching, learning stops being an activity and becomes a way of life.

Reflection Prompt

“Who are the quiet teachers in your organization – and what might change if you recognized them as your most valuable leaders?”

title: Candy, Crises, and the Cost of Compassion
html:
Americans will spend $3.9 billion on Halloween candy this week.

That’s nearly half of what the U.S. government spent in an entire year – through USAID’s Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance – to deliver food, water, shelter, and medical care to people who’d lost everything to war, famine, and disaster.

Think about that ratio for a moment. One night of candy. Six months of global lifesaving work.

This morning, I read a piece on NPR that quoted my former boss, Sarah Charles, discussing what U.S. assistance to Jamaica might have looked like after Hurricane Melissa – a Category 5 storm that devastated the Caribbean.

Click here, for that story...

She described what BHA used to do before it was dismantled: pre-positioning relief supplies in Miami and Haiti weeks before hurricane season. Coordinating with local governments so aid could flow as soon as airports reopened. Embedding water and sanitation specialists ahead of landfall to prevent cholera outbreaks in the chaos that follows.

This wasn’t “charity theater.” It was precision disaster response, built on decades of hard lessons and dozens of other crises. Teams who knew that the difference between 100 deaths and 10,000 often came down to having the right supplies in the right place 48 hours before anyone else thought to move.

That machinery operated on roughly $8.4 billion annually during the Biden Administration – less than 1% of the federal budget.

It’s largely gone now. The expertise is scattered. The systems were dismantled. The institutional knowledge – the kind you can’t rebuild with an executive order – is gone, forever.

Consider this:

Have you ever lost everything to a wall of water? Most of us haven’t. Most of us never will.

But last year, 108 million people were displaced by conflict or natural disasters —not over decades, but in 2024. That’s more than the combined populations of California, Texas, and Florida, suddenly homeless.

When walls of water swallowed coastlines after the Indian Ocean tsunami, or when monsoon floods engulfed Bangladesh, USAID helped in the immediate aftermath, delivering food and clean water. But the agency stuck around, engineers helped restore clean water systems, rebuilt bridges and shelters, and supported farmers with flood-resistant seeds and livelihood grants.

The goal wasn’t charity. It was stability. Rebuilding dignity one well, one pump, one field at a time.

Forty-five million children suffer from acute malnutrition – the kind where their bodies start consuming themselves, where a simple respiratory infection becomes a death sentence because there’s nothing left to fight with.

That’s not hyperbole; it’s the latest estimate from the UNICEF/WHO/World Bank Joint Malnutrition Report (2024), based on 2022 data – the most recent global count.

In 2023–2024, those spoonfuls became measurable lives saved. In Yemen, USAID’s Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance provided over $40 million in funding and supplies – including ready-to-use therapeutic food and fortified milk – to treat more than 140,000 children suffering from severe acute malnutrition, saving an estimated 17,000 lives. In South Sudan, where floodwaters and conflict cut off entire regions, USAID’s partners reached over 2 million children, admitting 338,000 for lifesaving treatment – an estimated 42,000 of them survived because that help arrived in time. And in Somalia,

BHA-supported clinics continued to deliver high-energy food pastes and train mothers to recognize the earliest signs of wasting – likely saving another 10,000 to 15,000 children.

It wasn’t glamorous, and it rarely made headlines.

But line by line, crisis by crisis, USAID turned American values into survival. It saved lives, just not necessarily American lives, except when it did:

For nearly two decades, America’s top defense leaders have said the same quiet truth: diplomacy and development are national security. Former Trump Secretary of Defense Jim Mattis warned Congress, “If you don’t fund the State Department and USAID fully, then I need to buy more ammunition.” Robert Gates, SecDef under *BOTH* George W. Bush and Barack Obama, put it more bluntly: “Development is a lot cheaper than sending soldiers.”

Each of them understood what USAID has always represented – a frontline defense against instability, extremism, and the kind of desperation that draws troops into conflict zones. But what’s often missed is that USAID doesn’t just save lives over there – it saves lives here.

USAID’s Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance was built to fight these crises at scale.

When earthquakes flattened cities, BHA deployed search-and-rescue teams and emergency medical units within hours. When droughts pushed families to the brink of starvation, they delivered high-nutrition food that could save a child’s life in weeks. When disease outbreaks threatened to spiral into epidemics, they funded rapid-response teams to contain the spread before CNN arrived.

They helped families find shelter when everything they owned was buried under rubble. They saved babies from preventable deaths – not with experimental treatments, but with oral rehydration salts that cost pennies. They delivered clean water to refugee camps, stopping cholera before it could kill thousands. They vaccinated children against measles in war zones.

The work wasn’t glamorous. It rarely made headlines. But it was the difference between a crisis and a catastrophe.

And it costs each American about $117 per year, roughly what many of us spend on Netflix, Spotify, and a couple of lattes each month.

As we hand out candy tonight, I’m holding both truths:

  • We can mobilize $3.9 billion overnight for sugar and costumes. We once mobilized $8.4 billion annually to keep the most vulnerable people on Earth alive.

  • We can move mountains when we want to. We can build supply chains that deliver candy corn to every zip code in America. We can coordinate logistics that would make military planners weep with envy – all for a holiday that exists because we decided it should.

Both reveal what we value. Both show what we’re capable of when we decide something matters.

One is sweet. The other is sacred.

Only one reveals our character.

The question now isn’t whether we can afford compassion. We’re spending half the annual humanitarian budget on a single night of candy. The money exists. The logistics capability exists. The expertise existed until we decided to dismantle it.

The question is: which story do we want the world to tell about us?

Both futures are possible.

We’re choosing one right now.

title: It’s Not a Quiz. It’s a Mirror.
html:
I Built a Tiny System That Thinks Like a Leader

A few weeks ago, I was sitting on the floor of my office – surrounded by graph paper, flowcharts, and index cards.

I wasn’t mapping a client’s org.
I was mapping mine.

Not just the work I do – but the invisible systems underneath it.
Where momentum flows.
Where friction builds.
Where I’m still the glue.

And where I needed to design better.

That session turned into a question:

“What if leadership tools weren’t just reflective – but adaptive?”

What Looks Like a Quiz, Thinks Like a System

That question became a project.
That project became a form.
But not just a form.

Here’s what’s actually under the hood:

  • 500+ lines of code

  • 115+ if/then conditionals

  • 1 form that adapts in real time

  • Custom paths based on how you lead

  • Personalized reports, written in plain language

  • Embedded coaching prompts, written by hand

  • And a fully styled UI, down to the last pixel of margin

It might look like a 90-second leadership tool.

But it’s really a systems diagnostic – for leaders who are still too central to their own system.

Why I Built It This Way

This might look like an online quiz…

But I didn’t build it to tell you who you are.
No Hogwarts house.
No “Congrats, you’re a Hufflepuff with mild burnout!”

Because you don’t need a label.
You need a mirror – one that shows where your leadership system is quietly working against you.

What I built instead is a diagnostic.

One that adapts to how you think.
One that reflects how your team is experiencing your system.
One that doesn’t flatter – but clarifies.

I wanted a tool that showed you where your structure is silently failing you.

  • When decisions continuously loop back to you

  • When momentum stalls, unless you nudge it

  • When you can’t unplug without the inbox whispering

That’s not a capacity problem.
That’s a design problem.

And good design doesn’t mean more dashboards.
It means the right questions – in the right order – that reflect your system back to you.

Try the Leadership System Diagnostic (LSD)

Yep, I called it LSD.
Because it shifts your perspective.

OK, funny enough, this acronym was totally unplanned.

Unlike some of my other more purposeful wordsmithing to get something like “CREATE” or “VOICES” – two of my actual leadership frameworks – this one was a total accident.

For most of the development, I just called it “the quiz.”But once I saw the pattern – LSD – I figured, well… it’s short, hopefully sticky, and shifts how you see things.

(Full disclosure, Mom, because she reads this – I’ve never actually done LSD…)

So LSD —— I went with it.

👉 Take it here

What you’ll get:

🧭 - Your current leadership posture
🚧 - Where friction is really coming from
🌱 - What kind of help would actually shift momentum
⏩ - What “worth it” looks like six months from now

It’s short. It’s sharp.

When I was designing it, I kept seeing a Plinko game – no two paths are ever the same. And for each answer, the quiz adapts – because your system isn’t generic.

This Week’s Coaching Prompt

Where in your system is progress still contingent on your presence — and what shift in structure or trust could change that?

Try asking:

  • What stalls when I step away?

  • What loop still depends on me to run?

  • Where is my team mirroring my uncertainty?

Your Move

✅ Take the diagnostic (Sorry, I just couldn’t call it a trip)
✅ Forward it to your co-founder or team lead
✅ Use one question in your next 1:1

If a 90-second form can spot the cracks in your system…
Just imagine what a 90-day redesign could do.

If you’re interested, schedule a 30-minute clarity call with me afterwards to debrief your results.

title: You Took a Week Off - But Still Checked Email Every Night
html:
A Personal Reflection

I’m looking ahead at my calendar – and in a couple of weeks, I’m headed to Palm Springs for a break with friends. It’s been on the calendar since before the RIF. I love the desert, and am so looking forward to some night photography in Joshua Tree.

And honestly, it got me thinking.

When we take family vacations, my wife almost always brings her work laptop with her.
Not because she wants to – but because there are things in her role that only she can do.

It’s not about distrust. It’s about structure.
There’s no real backup. No system to hold things up when she’s out.

And it becomes a quiet handbrake on her actually getting away.
The laptop sits in the corner like a little pressure valve – just in case.

That same pattern shows up for so many leaders I coach:
The PTO that’s never truly “off.”
The inbox is tethered to identity.
The break that still includes “just checking real quick…”

That’s not leadership.
That’s load-bearing you.

One Clear Idea

Taking time off is a leadership test – and most leaders are quietly failing it.
Not because they didn’t plan.

But because they didn’t build a system that can breathe without them.

A founder recently told me:

“I was supposed to unplug. But I still checked email at midnight – just to make sure nothing burned down.”

Sound familiar?

What’s breaking isn’t your calendar.
It’s your safety net.

The problem isn’t taking time off.
It’s about tethering yourself to the inbox just to feel safe.

That’s not rest.
That’s a system dependent on you.

And it means agility is missing – not from your product, but from your people.
Because if you can’t step away, your company can’t step up.

This Week’s Coaching Prompt

What needs to change so your absence doesn’t equal anxiety?

Start with one of these:

  • Who assumes the lead when you’re gone – and do they know it?

  • What’s a decision-making gap that keeps you glued to your inbox?

  • Where have you delegated tasks, but not trust?

The CREATE Lens: Agility

This is about resilience – not just individual, but organizational.
Agile companies aren’t just fast. They’re anti-fragile.
And that starts with a leadership system that survives your silence.

If your company’s adaptability hinges on your availability,
then the next sprint might run straight through your vacation.

A Tool to Try: The “Week Off Without Panic” Protocol

Take 15 quiet minutes to map this:

  • Roles – Who owns what while you’re out? Are they empowered to act?

  • Decisions – What’s the threshold for someone needing your input?

  • Emergencies – What counts as one? Who decides that?

  • Comms Norms – What’s the default? Silence? Updates? Daily check-ins?

Then ask a trusted team member:
Would this actually hold if I stepped away tomorrow?

Why This Matters Right Now

Your absence is inevitable – either by design or by disaster.

The founder who never truly leaves never truly leads.
You’re still the glue. But your business needs a guide.

If rest requires constant inbox checks,
your company isn’t agile. It’s fragile.

Your Move: Test a Resilient Week-Off Plan

Run a mini-simulation:

  • What would break?

  • Who would stall?

  • Where do you need to give away more trust?

Don’t wait for a health scare or burnout to force the handoff.
Build it now – so you can leave and exhale.

Please forward this to someone who’s still checking email on vacation –
not because they don’t trust their team,
but because the system makes them feel like they can’t step away.

You don’t have to do more.
You have to build what lets you step back –
so your leadership still speaks, even when you’re silent.

title: Building My Own AI Growth System: DALE and the Unexpected Consultant
html:
When I left USAID after the RIF, I didn’t just lose a job – I lost the structure that organized my work and life.

For twenty years as a teacher (heck, I had to use the “facilities” on someone else’s schedule), I’d lived inside other people’s systems. Meetings, bells, deadlines, accountability — they gave shape to my days. Suddenly, I had to build all that from scratch – for myself.

And that loss of structure didn’t just affect my calendar; it seeped into everything – my health, my energy, even my workouts. I stopped taking the focused 60-minute “lunch break” I’d always used for exercise. The cortisol, the stress, the uncertainty all added up. Regrettably, I think I’m the heaviest I’ve ever been.

And because I’m a systems thinker, my response to chaos is always the same: design clarity.

So I did what I’ve always done when I hit a wall – I started mapping.

I sketched what my business needed to function: how leads come in, how relationships progress, and how I wanted every touchpoint to feel human, not transactional. I had the architecture in my head long before I had a tool to match it.

That was the moment DALE began — not as code, but as a coping mechanism.

Meet DALE – My AI Growth Agent

DALE is a fully integrated AI agent that lives inside Google Sheets.

When I get a new LinkedIn follower, Substack subscriber, quiz participant, or have a meaningful conversation, DALE takes over:

  • Reads: the contact details I’ve added – name, role, company, and a short bio, or note from our exchange

  • Classifies: the lead using my proprietary persona map

  • Generates: bullet points for a first-contact or follow-up message

  • Schedules: the next step is to directly post an event to my Google Calendar

And just to be clear: following me on LinkedIn doesn’t drop you into some mechanical selling machine. DALE isn’t a black hole. It’s more like a relational compass.

If you follow, subscribe, or comment – awesome. Chances are, we already know each other, and you’re not exactly my ICP (unless you are, in which case… reach out, lol).

The Unexpected Consultant

My business is, by design, high-touch and relational. That’s the Relator in me – one of my top CliftonStrengths. Relators are driven by genuine connection. We’d rather go deep than wide; we build trust through authenticity, shared effort, and follow-through. It’s not networking for its own sake – it’s about earning the right to collaborate. I genuinely enjoy the people side of the work.

So I built systems for myself so I could spend more time connecting with humans, not marketing or selling.

And now that I’m working for myself, I want to actually enjoy it – not grind endlessly or replace one kind of burnout with another. I want a business that lets me do what I love – coaching, designing clarity, building leaders – while also making space for life. The same principles I teach about sustainable systems apply to me too: structure creates freedom.

From Strengths to Systems
