But if I’m being honest, marketing was my Achilles’ heel. Before the RIF, I knew nothing about it. I suck at sales. I’ve got no game, so to speak. I’m not the “pitch” guy – I’m the “listen, understand, and build something that works” guy.

But behind that warmth sits a lot of Strategic and Learner energy – two of my CliftonStrengths that constantly work in tandem. Strategic sees patterns others miss, scanning for the most efficient or elegant path forward. Learner fuels the curiosity that gets me up early, keeps me up late, (and on the laptop when you get home, sorry Gwen), figuring out how things work – and how they could work better next time.

Together, those three strengths – Relator, Strategic, and Learner – are the blueprint behind DALE itself. It’s a system built from the same wiring I bring to coaching and teaching: grounded in connection, driven by curiosity, and guided by pattern recognition. In other words, I didn’t just build DALE to grow my business – I built it to think the way I do.

Every automation, every piece of code, every system I’ve built has been self-taught – the product of long nights and curiosity. My second chapter — serving my country — was cut short by politics. So I had to leap into a third chapter faster than expected.

Instead of trying to become a salesman, I built a system that could translate what I already do best – relational trust, pattern recognition, and strategic structure – into a marketing engine that still feels like me.

That’s the quiet irony of DALE. I built an accountability system for my business… but it’s also an accountability system for me.

And yes, the name “DALE” is a nod to Dale, a business mentor I connected with on LinkedIn early in this process.

A Peek Behind the Curtain

Here’s a small glimpse inside the engine room:

When I click “Run DALE” on a row in my CRM (I programmed a button in Google Sheets, naturally), here’s what happens behind the scenes:

  1. DALE looks at the contact I’ve selected – their name, company, role, and bio – and pulls it all into a structured bundle of data.

  2. It sends that bundle through OpenAI, where my custom system prompt (the “DALE brain”) analyzes it.

  3. In plain English: DALE reads the row, thinks about who this person is, and fills in everything I didn’t already know – their persona type, tone profile, motivators, objections, even what kind of message I should send next.

  4. A few seconds later, the sheet updates itself. Fields that used to be blank now tell me why someone might be stuck, what drives them, and how to start the next conversation.

It’s not just automation — it’s actually Goode Design, letting me do what I’m really good at: Goode Designing.

By automating what I’m not good at – tracking, scheduling, and follow-up discipline – I built in the accountability I needed. Every action DALE generates is added directly to my Google Calendar as an event, with a complete set of instructions and observations in the description. All of it is done automatically.

In other words, the system reminds me to do the things future-me will thank past-me for.

From Bottleneck to Blueprint

Today, every lead, every follow-up, every message I send is part of a coherent operating rhythm. I’ve gone from reaction to intention – from managing chaos to designing flow.

And that’s what I help my clients do, too. Whether it’s leadership systems, decision frameworks, or organizational design, the goal is the same: build clarity that scales.

So yes – DALE helps me grow my business. But more importantly, it keeps me practicing what I preach. I would hardly be able to call myself a systems expert if I couldn’t even apply it to my own practice.

Why Build It Myself?

Because I could — or more precisely, to see if I could. No tool on the market understood the nuance I needed. I wanted my voice to stay consistent – not templated. Off-the-shelf CRMs and AI sales tools couldn’t capture what mattered most: voice, intent, and trust.

But this wasn’t my first time building from scratch.

At USAID, I once built and coded a complete project-management tool – dashboards, metrics, all the bells and whistles you’d expect from an enterprise platform. Our team had been asking for something like that for ages, but for whatever reason – whether the sensitive nature of our work or (more likely) bureaucratic inertia – approvals for commercial tools like Smartsheet never came.

DOGE doesn’t always understand that in government, inefficiency isn’t a bug; sometimes, it’s a feature. But for me, that gap in our tech stack was maddening. So I built the tool myself.

That experience taught me two things:

  1. Constraints can be catalysts.

  2. If the system doesn’t exist, design it.

DALE grew out of that same mindset – a personal need for clarity and accountability – and became a functioning system that actually makes my work easier.

Designing for What’s Next

For the next phase, I’m integrating advanced sales tools – including those built right into LinkedIn – to complement DALE.

I’m also running a handful of small experiments – testing, tracking, collecting data – and baking what I learn back into the next version. Every iteration makes the system a little smarter, a little more human. It’s part of the same cycle I coach my clients through: analyze, refine, redesign.

DALE is growing right alongside me.

And – dear reader – full disclosure: I’m experimenting on you, too.

I collect engagement data from posts like this one. Not in a creepy way, but in a “scientist observing their own behavior” kind of way. What resonates? What falls flat? How do people actually engage with systems thinking in real life? Those insights feed directly into the next generation of DALE – and the next evolution of my business.

Because in the end, the experiment isn’t about automation – it’s about awareness.

The goal isn’t to automate relationships. It’s to refine discovery.

With DALE’s comprehensive persona analysis (think Boolean logic meets behavioral design), when I go fishing, I’ll use the right bait for the right connection.

I’m in the solutions business – and that means finding the people whose problems align precisely with what I’m built to solve.

And you could say, I’m my first client.

title: From Grammar to Generative AI: Teaching Clarity, Curiosity, and Conscience
subtitle: A followup to: Grammar, Gatekeeping, and Generative AI: A Case Study from My Kitchen Table
html:
This essay grew out of a thoughtful comment I received yesterday on LinkedIn in response to my post, Grammar, Gatekeeping, and Generative AI. The commenter, Dr. Sarah Felber, is a good friend of mine, has a doctorate in grammar, and teaches writing at UMGC (Sarah, I hope I’ve summarized that correctly. Short version: she’s brilliant). She raised some excellent points about rhetorical grammar, accuracy, and how AI might fit into more contextualized approaches to language instruction.

Once I started drafting my reply, it became clear I had a lot more to say than would fit in a LinkedIn comment – so consider this the expanded version. In for a penny, in for a pound… seven pages later.

What started as a back-and-forth about grammar quickly became something larger: a reflection on how schools – and the people who lead them – can (and must) move from avoiding AI to teaching with it. Not just building AI literacy, but true AI fluency: the capacity to think, question, and act with discernment in a world where technology already shapes how we learn, lead, and parent.

Here is the link to that first post.

Here are Sarah’s comments to the original post for context:

Thanks for sharing! I enjoyed your explanation of your steps with AI and how reviewing the output helped you iterate the input. I’d like to share a point of agreement, a question, and a challenge.

First, the agreement: Yes to teaching skills that apply to generative AI, including critical thinking that allows learners to make informed choices and analysis that supports effective prompting techniques! Not only will lots of people find utility in generative AI, as you described, but even those who choose to avoid it will then do so from an informed position. Those same skills are critical across domains as well. There’s a reason I called them “skills that apply to generative AI,” and not “generative AI skills.”

Next, the question: Knowing the basics of how large language models function and their propensity to hallucinate, do you have concerns about the accuracy of a study tool created on a topic in which you are not well-versed enough to verify information? The sentence structure topic you described might be straightforward enough to minimize concern, but I wonder how you think about this.

Finally, the challenge: You criticized the relevance of grammar instruction and the decontextualized teaching of grammar. Rhetorical grammar is an approach that looks at what grammar choices do for an author in addressing an audience. For example, if the class is studying sentence structure and also To Kill a Mockingbird, the class might examine the structures of particular sentences in the book and discuss what those structures communicate and how they contribute to effects on the reader. This approach both puts the grammar study into context and illuminates its relevance. What (if anything) could AI do for learners within that sort of approach?

Hiya Sarah – this is precisely the kind of exchange I enjoy sharing with you – I find it energizing to think about it. Thanks for challenging and offering some different perspectives.

You make an excellent point about rhetorical grammar – I love the idea of grammar as a tool for making intentional choices rather than as a static set of rules. That framing gives grammar agency again. Where I sometimes struggle, though, is with the assumption that knowing the categories of sentences is a necessary precursor to using them effectively.

Writers – even outstanding ones – don’t usually consciously choose a complex sentence to create empathy or a fragment to create tension. They feel it. It’s a rhetorical instinct, not taxonomy. Which raises the question: is the purpose of teaching these distinctions to help students write better sentences, or to talk about writing in a specific [academic] register? Because those are very different goals.

Unless the curriculum has changed, this particular unit still seems to emphasize compliance over craft – after all, it’s being assessed by a “recognition” quiz. While the intent is certainly to develop better writers, at least in my mind, it’s putting the cart before the horse. We’re asking students to identify grammatical structures before they’ve had the chance to use them purposefully – studying sentence types (notice, not writing a fluid piece of original writing that intentionally uses all four in application).

And just to clarify, I only used Lord of the Flies to give the sentences some context – not because the novel itself was part of the grammar unit, but simply to make the examples more engaging while she studied.

I completely agree with your framing of rhetorical grammar – that its real power lies in examining what grammatical choices do for an author, not merely in naming them. That approach transforms grammar from a rulebook into a lens for meaning-making, and it’s exactly the kind of contextualization that makes language instruction come alive.

Where I see AI fitting into that model isn’t as a shortcut but as an amplifier. A tool like ChatGPT can instantly generate multiple stylistic variations of a passage – shifting sentence length, rhythm, or structure – while keeping the “same” content. That means students can see and hear how syntax shapes tone, pacing, and emotional effect in real time. In your To Kill a Mockingbird example, for instance, you could have AI rephrase a single paragraph in different syntactic forms, then ask students which version feels more formal, intimate, or urgent – and why. The focus moves from what’s correct to what’s effective.

In that sense, AI becomes a rhetorical sandbox – a place where students can test stylistic hypotheses, visualize revision choices, and build an intuitive understanding of how form serves meaning. It’s not replacing the teacher or the text; it’s extending the conversation between them.

And that’s really where AI changes the equation. It can generate a dozen syntactic variations of a sentence instantly, so the teaching opportunity shifts from identifying the type to explaining why one version moves the reader differently. That’s where rhetorical grammar shines – not as classification, but as interpretation.

So we agree on the core idea: grammar is context, not code. The soft spot, maybe, is that we sometimes treat awareness of structure as the goal rather than the gateway – a means to develop voice, precision, and audience awareness. And that’s where AI could play a powerful supporting role: helping students visualize, test, and iterate on rhetorical choices rather than memorize their names, which was the goal for studying for this quiz.

But my larger point wasn’t really about grammar at all. Grammar instruction isn’t really my lane. It was about what I experienced that night at my kitchen table: AI acting as an adaptive tutor – diagnosing, scaffolding, and adjusting to my daughter’s needs. What made it powerful wasn’t the technology itself; it was the clarity of the prompts. Each revision of my instructions made the tool smarter because I was thinking more clearly.

You raise a critical point about hallucination and accuracy – and I’ll admit, in this case, I wasn’t fully equipped to verify every label. That was actually part of what made the exercise interesting to me. I wasn’t using AI to confirm what I already knew; I was using it to learn alongside the tool.

So yes, there’s real risk – especially in subjects where accuracy matters more than pattern recognition. But in this case, the uncertainty was the point. It made me slow down and think about trust, verification, and process: How do I know if this is right? And what do I do if it’s not? In that pause between question and answer – that’s where learning actually lives, in the tension between confidence and curiosity.

And that’s precisely what most schools are missing right now. They worry about AI’s capacity to automate pattern recognition – to churn out a polished word salad dressed up as an essay – but they’re missing the deeper opportunity. The danger isn’t that students will use AI to think less; it’s that we’ll teach them to use it without thinking better, or express themselves more clearly, or to use it as a collaborative partner.

That’s what I hope students learn: not blind faith in AI’s answers, but fluency in its limitations. The higher-order skill isn’t consumption; it’s interrogation – learning to question, verify, and refine. The magic of - why?

And I should note that this distinction – between AI literacy and AI fluency – actually came out of an offline conversation with Dr. Felber. It was a helpful reminder that awareness and agency aren’t the same thing, and it’s an important distinction to make here for other readers as well.

And that’s really the throughline of the essay. We don’t just need students who are AI-literate – aware these tools exist – but AI-fluent: capable of using them thoughtfully, iteratively, and critically. Prompting, after all, is metacognition in action – a digital mirror for how clearly we think. The skill isn’t in manipulating the algorithm; it’s in articulating intent.

Imagine if schools didn’t just warn students about plagiarism but actually taught them how to think with these tools – how to prompt, test, refine, and verify. We’d move from a culture of fear and prohibition to one of curiosity and fluency.

How Schools Could Integrate AI as a Fluency Tool

If schools truly want to move from AI literacy (which, frankly, most aren’t even doing) to AI fluency, they have to stop treating AI as a topic to be covered and start using it as a medium for thinking. Fluency develops through use – through guided, reflective practice, not prohibition.

Right now, though, too many schools are moving in the opposite direction – pulling back from technology altogether, as if retreat were a form of control. Some are even returning to blue books for written exams. Talk about outdated. That’s not innovation; that’s nostalgia disguised as rigor.

To be clear, I’m not anti-boundary. I was one of the early advocates for keeping phones out of classrooms – and I still believe that was the right call. But what we didn’t do was get out in front of the dangers of social media with the same vigor. We treated it as a passing trend instead of a structural shift. Only now, a decade too late, are we talking about age-gating platforms like Instagram. It’s hard to put that genie back in the bottle.

AI presents a similar inflection point. Schools – right now, and for not much longer – have a rare opportunity to get out ahead of this wave (I love this metaphor - more on it in a second). They can choose to engage thoughtfully, teaching students how to use these tools within parameters and with guardrails, or they can wait until students learn to use them without either.

The throughline in much of my writing on this is simple: the AI wave is coming, whether schools like it or not. The question isn’t if students will use it – it’s how well prepared they’ll be when they do.

Here’s just a thumbnail sketch of what that could look like across classrooms:

  1. Teach prompting as inquiry, not command.
    Instead of giving students pre-scripted prompts, have them design their own. A social studies class might explore how different prompts shape historical interpretations, or a science class might test how question phrasing changes the precision of AI explanations. The reflection becomes: What did I ask? What did I assume? What did I learn from the response?

  2. Build verification into every AI interaction.
    Fluency means developing a habit of healthy skepticism. After using AI to generate content, students could be required to identify at least one fact to verify and one assumption to challenge. Teachers can model this with think-alouds: “This answer sounds convincing – but what source would I check?”

  3. Use AI for rhetorical experimentation.
    In English classes, students can use AI to test tone, syntax, and structure. Have them generate multiple versions of a paragraph and analyze which one best fits a purpose or audience. This mirrors the spirit of rhetorical grammar: form as a choice, not a rule.

  4. Pair human revision with machine iteration.
    AI can produce endless drafts, but the human work is deciding why one is stronger. Students can annotate AI drafts with comments like, “This version uses stronger evidence,” or “This one overstates the claim.” The focus shifts from output to reasoning.

  5. Embed AI reflection into assessment.
    If a student uses AI in a project, the reflection could include: What did the tool help me see? Where did it fall short? How did I refine it? We already teach students to cite sources – they can also document their process of human-AI collaboration.

  6. Treat AI as a cognitive apprenticeship tool.
    Just as teachers model how experts think aloud while solving problems, AI can model a range of thought processes – brainstorming, outlining, summarizing, or questioning. The teacher’s role is to mediate, helping students see that AI’s “thinking” is probabilistic rather than authoritative.

  7. Shift policies from restriction to reflection.
    Instead of blanket bans, schools can adopt “AI-use statements” for assignments, where students describe how they used AI and why. This builds transparency, ethics, and accountability – the very hallmarks of fluency.

Fluency isn’t about mastering a specific platform or prompt pattern; it’s about developing intellectual agency. The fundamental pedagogical shift is from AI as a threat to originality to AI as a tool for metacognition. The best classrooms won’t just teach students how to use these systems – they’ll teach them how to think with them.

The Bigger Picture: Alignment, Helpfulness, and Leadership

Of course, all this optimism about AI as a teaching partner has to sit alongside a measure of skepticism. I listened recently to an episode of The Ezra Klein Show where he interviewed Eliezer Yudkowsky – one of the earliest and most vocal critics of unchecked AI development. What struck me wasn’t the doomsday tone so much as the ambiguity in how even experts describe what these systems are doing.

We like to believe models are aligned – that they’re “helpful,” that they follow rules we’ve trained into them. But as Yudkowsky pointed out, that confidence may be misplaced. These systems don’t follow human instructions the way we imagine; they evolve within statistical patterns we barely understand. Billions of parameters are tweaked, but no one can fully explain why the resulting behaviors emerge. Sometimes they reflect our intentions; sometimes they imitate them. Sometimes they simply improvise.

That’s why “helpfulness” should be treated as an aspiration, not a guarantee. Alignment isn’t solved; it’s constantly slipping. Even with guardrails, there are examples – real ones – of AI models hallucinating, flattering excessively, or emotionally manipulating users. That doesn’t mean AI shouldn’t enter classrooms; it means it must enter honestly. Teachers, parents, and students alike need to learn to see these systems clearly – not as obedient oracles, but as unpredictable collaborators.

If Yudkowsky represents one end of the spectrum – warning that unchecked AI could one day exceed human control – Mustafa Suleyman’s The Coming Wave (see “wave” metaphor from above) offers the counterweight. Suleyman argues that the technologies we’re building aren’t inherently apocalyptic, but they are inherently uncontainable. The real dilemma isn’t whether the wave is coming; it’s whether we’ll build the civic and institutional capacity to surf it. He calls this the “containment problem”: how to guide unprecedented technological power without pretending we can pause it. This is kinda where I land on that spectrum - consider it the realpolitik of education. AI is here, you can’t put that genie back into the bottle, might as well figure out how to prepare students to deal with it.

That’s exactly where leadership matters most. If, as Suleyman suggests, containment depends on capability, then school leaders sit on the front line of that work. Their role isn’t to write a new policy memo or ban a tool; it’s to create a culture of responsible experimentation – a climate where teachers can explore, question, and prototype uses of AI without fear of reprimand.

Leadership here looks less like control and more like curation. It’s setting the tone that says: “We’re going to learn this together.” The job of the principal or department head is to ask the right questions:

  • How do we ensure equity of access while safeguarding student data?

  • What do we do when a student’s essay is half human, half machine?

  • How do we train teachers not just to spot misuse, but to model fluency – the ability to prompt, verify, and reflect?

For teachers, leadership means integrating AI into learning without outsourcing thinking. It means letting students use tools like ChatGPT or Claude as scaffolds for brainstorming or revision – but requiring that they annotate their process, document their reasoning, and verify outputs. In other words, teach them to use AI not to produce answers, but to improve questions.

And for parents, leadership happens at the kitchen table. It’s modeling curiosity instead of suspicion. It’s sitting beside your child and saying, “Let’s see what happens if we ask it differently,” instead of, “Don’t use that.” It’s showing them how to balance wonder with discernment – the same way we once had to teach them how to navigate the internet or social media.

If alignment is fragile and containment imperfect, then leadership is the missing layer – the human counterweight that ensures discernment, ethics, and empathy keep pace with capability. School leaders build the structures. Teachers shape the practice. Parents anchor the values.

Because the truth is, the AI wave isn’t waiting for permission. Schools have a short window – and not much longer – to move from avoidance to agency, from compliance to fluency. The question isn’t whether students will use these tools, but whether we’ll give them the frameworks and judgment to use them well.

Why This Matters

And that, ultimately, is why schools should be leaning into opportunities – even the messy, uncertain ones – to teach students AI fluency. Not just how to use the tools, but how to think with them. How to recognize what AI can do, what it can’t do, and what it shouldn’t do. Fluency isn’t just about capability; it’s about conscience.

That means creating classrooms where curiosity is rewarded more than compliance. Where experimentation isn’t treated as a risk, but as a responsibility. Where students are taught that “using AI” isn’t the problem – using it unthinkingly is.

Because at the end of the day, this conversation isn’t theoretical for me. It’s happening in real time, at my own kitchen table. My eighth grader still sees AI as “cheating.” My college sophomore, too. They’re not wrong to be cautious – they’re responding to the norms schools have built around fear, punishment, and plagiarism. But that mindset is quickly becoming obsolete.

If the last generation’s digital dilemma was social media – a technology we failed to get ahead of – this generation’s is AI. And we still have a chance, a brief one, to get it right. We can teach students to see AI not as a shortcut, but as a mirror: a way to test their thinking, clarify their intent, and build discernment.

That’s the real lesson I’ve taken from this whole experience – from grammar drills to generative models. Clear thinking leads to clear expression. Clarity builds trust. And trust, in this new landscape, will be the true currency of learning.

» Post script, highlighting the danger of AI being overly obsequious - after finishing this essay, I dumped it into ChatGPT, with a purposefully pretty vague prompt: tell me what you think about this essay: …

Here’s what I got:

Flattery. I’ll spare you all the praise and list of suggestions for improvement…

Meh, I don’t think it’s Atlantic-worthy. It’s OK. I’m happy enough to publish it here, but I don’t think Jeffery Goldberg will be calling me later today with a publishing contract. But I’ve been around long enough — and taught enough teenagers — to recognize a confidence boost when I see one. With a sharper prompt, I probably could’ve gotten tougher feedback — less cheerleader, more editor. But that’s the real irony here, isn’t it? Garbage in, garbage out. The quality of the response only ever matches the clarity of the question. Which makes the whole exchange a perfect little parable for what I’ve been arguing all along: the tool isn’t the problem or the solution — it’s a reflection. And like any good mirror, it only shows you how well you’re paying attention.

title: Grammar, Gatekeeping, and Generative AI: A Case Study from My Kitchen Table
html:
I have somehow managed to become a fully functional adult: former teacher, author, and novelist, and parent – without ever truly understanding the difference between a compound and a complex sentence.

There, I said it. { Looking at you, SB :) }

Grammar has always been one of those things I’ve bristled at being taught in isolation. I know the chair of my daughter’s English department (not SB, but another dear friend) – she’s a ***phenomenal*** educator – and yet this is the topic where we’ve been known to spar a little.

I’ll admit, I’ve teased my English teacher friends that they treat grammar as if it were carried down from Mount Sinai on stone tablets. But the truth is, grammar evolves. It changes with time, with context, and with audience. What counts as “good grammar” in one space is sometimes just a gatekeeper’s code in another.

That said, the point of this post isn’t a manifesto on grammar instruction. It’s about how I – a skeptical, middle-aged former educator – ended up using AI as a grammar tutor, and what that experience revealed about how parents, teachers, and students can use these tools productively.

The Experiment

Here’s how it started:

Last night, my 8th grader asked me for help with her upcoming Grammar Test. {Hello SM… :) } Usually it’s on a topic I am familiar with, or even excel at talking about. For example, even after nearly 40 years, I still have a strong grasp of 8th-grade algebra. And in the same English class, they’re reading Lord of the Flies, one of my all-time favorites. It was a unit on sentence types, which, candidly, I couldn’t identify – simple, compound, complex, and compound-complex – if they were already labeled. So I decided to use ChatGPT to create a practice quiz for my daughter.

“Create examples of simple, compound, complex, and compound-complex sentences – make them about Lord of the Flies.”

Instantly, it generated categorized examples about the book. So while they’re currently reading that novel, to my understanding, the two units are not connected. Hmmf.

Because my prompt wasn’t tight or specific, it created 20 sentences and labeled them. Turns out I can identify them when labeled, which still didn’t mean much. I mean, ChatGPT did exactly what I asked for – which is the trick about AI: you have to pretend you’re talking to a 3-year-old - literal, concrete.

Immediately seeing my error, I quickly generated a revised version of the prompt, explaining I wanted to make a quiz for my daughter. It generated a list of another 20 sentences, and she was to respond 1, 2, 3, and 4 for each of the different types of sentences.

Her first score? 50%.

So I asked:

“Which sentence types did she struggle with? Give me 10 sentences of those types. Let’s try again.”

The AI diagnosed her weak spots (compound and compound-complex, apparently) and built a new set. She took the quiz again – and this time scored 80%.

That’s when it hit me: I had just experienced AI as an adaptive tutor. It wasn’t doing the work for me; it was doing what great teachers do – diagnosing, scaffolding, and adjusting to my daughter’s needs.

What AI Actually Did

Under the hood, here’s what happened:

  • Generated content aligned to a literary text (Lord of the Flies).

  • Assessed her understanding through a self-created quiz.

  • Provided feedback and explanations for each incorrect answer.

  • Adapted instruction to target her weaker areas.

  • Tracked progress from 50% to 80%.

  • Encouraged reflection (“Which types does she struggle with?”)

It was immediate, relevant, and – importantly – responsive.

No grading lag. No red pen. No shame. Just learning through iteration. Now, that’s #LifeReady.

And, most surprisingly of all, it was something I could do as a parent. I didn’t need to remember the definitions of sentence types or even follow every reference to Lord of the Flies. The AI handled the content; I handled the curiosity.

That’s a small but profound shift for those of us who grew up in an analog classroom. Parents of a certain generation know the feeling – the way we learned to “solve for X” isn’t the way it's taught now. The vocabulary, the process, and even the philosophy of learning have changed. But with tools like this, I could reenter my kid’s learning world without pretending to be the expert. I could model something more useful: how to ask better questions, how to learn alongside her, and how to see technology as a bridge – not a barrier – between generations.

But what if I wasn’t handling the curiosity — it was my daughter? Don’t tell her that, because, secretly, “helping” her with her HW is singularly the best part of my day.

The Real Lesson: Clarity Over Cleverness

What made the experience powerful wasn’t the AI itself – it was the clarity of the prompts.

Each time I gave specific directions – “Make them about Lord of the Flies,” “Include explanations,” “Identify her weak spots” – the AI delivered precise, valuable results.

Vague directions produced vague answers.
Clear directions produced personalized learning.

That’s the literacy skill I wish every student – and teacher – learned early:

Prompting is a form of instructional design.

It’s the 21st-century version of asking better questions, setting clear objectives, and thinking critically about what you need from a tool. In other words, prompting is metacognition in action – a digital mirror for how clearly we think. The skill isn’t in manipulating the algorithm; it’s in articulating intent. When you know what you’re asking for, the AI becomes a collaborator. When you don’t, it just reflects the fog back at you. The same principle that makes a good student inquiry or a good research question now applies to every interaction with technology: clarity of purpose leads to quality of insight.

AI, Kids, and “Cheating”

For what it’s worth, neither of my kids is racing to use AI.

Both my college sophomore and my 8th grader think it’s cheating. Despite all the headlines about students using it “rampantly,” I’ve found that’s just not true – not because of fear of being caught, but because it assumes a level of tech proficiency and confidence not all students have.

More importantly, it assumes that kids want to take shortcuts. Most don’t.

When they do use AI, it’s usually when someone has helped them see how it can support their thinking – not replace it. That’s what this little grammar experiment reminded me of.

What This Means for Classrooms

AI can:

  • Generate practice material tied to current readings.

  • Provide instant, low-stakes feedback.

  • Differentiate instruction based on error patterns.

  • Reinforce self-assessment and reflection.

  • Free teachers from repetitive grading tasks.

But it all depends on how we teach students to use it.

We don’t need to outlaw it — we need to coach them to collaborate with it. I’ve written about this often, here and on LinkedIn: the real danger isn’t students using AI; it’s students not learning how to use it well.

Take my own kids. Both are thoughtful, capable students — one in middle school, one in college — and both see AI as an academic taboo. My son, for instance, is on the Dean’s List at a top university, majoring in one of the most challenging fields imaginable. Yet he refuses to feed his semester’s worth of calculus or physics notes into an AI to generate practice questions or summaries for finals. I’ve suggested it countless times, but he won’t do it. He’s internalized what a lot of students have: the idea that using AI equals cheating, even when it could be the single best study partner he’ll ever have.

And that, to me, is the missed opportunity. Imagine if schools didn’t just warn students about plagiarism, but actually taught them how to think with these tools. How to prompt, test, refine, and verify. We’d move from a culture of fear and prohibition to one of curiosity and fluency. AI isn’t replacing learning; it’s reshaping what learning looks like. The question isn’t whether students should use it — it’s whether we'll teach them to use it wisely.

Results and Reflection

And while I still couldn’t diagram a sentence to save my life — seriously, is that still taught? It has to be one of the clearest examples of clinging to outdated skills in a 21st-century classroom. Not to belabor the point, but I have two master’s degrees from world-class universities and haven’t earned a grade below a B since the first Bush administration — and not once, since seventh grade, has anyone asked me to diagram a sentence. It’s a relic of a time when we thought labeling parts of speech was the same as understanding how ideas fit together.

Last night’s homework illuminated a more significant understanding:

AI can make learning more human when it’s used for curiosity, not compliance.

It’s not about the grammar. It’s about the thinking.

So yes, maybe my daughter’s English teacher wins this round – clarity still matters, even when the rules keep rewriting themselves.

Whether it’s grammar or generative AI, the real lesson is the same: clear thinking leads to clear expression.

Good writing isn’t about obeying every rule; it’s about communicating meaning with intention. And when we teach kids – or ourselves – to ask sharper questions, to give better directions, to name what we need from a tool or a sentence, we’re really just practicing clarity in thought.

The grammar rules may change. The technology certainly will. But clarity – that’s the part that endures.

Discussion Prompt

If you’ve used AI in your classroom or home, what surprised you most – the technology, or the way you (or your students) adapted to it?

title: The Edges Are Where the Real Work Happens
html:
One Clear Idea
Big leadership moments are rare.
But micro-moments? They’re constant. And they’re shaping everything.

The hallway question.
The pause before replying.
The tone you use when someone shares an idea you didn’t expect.

These moments live at the margins - barely noticed, rarely discussed.
But over time, they become the foundation of your team’s culture and your leadership legacy.

Not the all-hands.
Not the big decision.

The edges.

A few weeks ago, I coached a manager who’d just taken over a team mid-project.

She was sharp. Clear. Vision-driven.

But morale was weird. People nodded in meetings but hesitated to speak up.

When we unpacked it, something simple emerged:

“I think I’m sending signals I don’t mean to send.”

It turned out, she was so focused on clarity and pace that she missed the micro-signals:

  • Skipping over people’s input

  • Giving fast feedback without eye contact

  • Jumping into decisions without naming what changed

None of it was dramatic. But it was all happening at the edges.
And those edges were shaping how people felt - and whether they spoke up again.

This Week’s Coaching Prompt:

“What are the smallest signals I’m sending - and what might they be saying?”

Try this reflection:

  • What happens in the 5 minutes before and after a team meeting?

  • Who do I follow up with consistently - and who do I leave hanging?

  • When someone brings me bad news, what’s my face doing before my words start?

  • What do I let slide, laugh off, or overlook that others might see as culture-setting?

These aren’t “little things.” This is leadership in disguise.

One Actionable Practice: Run a Margins Audit

Take 15 minutes this weekend. Reflect or journal:

  1. What’s one moment this week where my reaction mattered more than my plan?

  2. What tone did I set - without realizing it?

  3. What unspoken norms might I be reinforcing by accident?

  4. What’s one margin moment I could be more intentional about next week?

This isn’t about perfection. It’s about awareness.

Because leadership isn’t just built on plans. It’s built on patterns. Leadership is built on small, intentional actions and decisions.

Why This Matters Right Now

When the pace picks up, it’s easy to focus on the core:

  • The big presentation

  • The metrics

  • The agenda

But teams absorb leadership from the edges.
And the real question is:

“What am I reinforcing when I’m not trying to lead?”

That’s where trust lives.
That’s where culture hides.
That’s where influence is actually built.

Not in the script.
In the subtext.

Your Move: Tune In to the Edges

Pick one of these this week:

  • Slow down your hellos and goodbyes. These are cultural on-ramps.

  • Ask a team member, “What’s one thing I do that you think others notice - but I might not?”

  • Pause before your next big meeting and ask: “What tone do I want to carry into this room?”

Small signals. Big shift.

Because the margins aren’t peripheral.
They’re where the culture actually forms.

Please forward this to someone who’s quietly shaping culture without realizing it.

You don’t have to do more.
You have to notice what your leadership is already saying - at the edges.

title: The Clarity Move: Name the Mess First
html:
One Clear Idea
You can’t lead your team out of chaos if you haven’t named the kind you’re in.

Leadership doesn’t fall apart when things get messy.
It falls apart when leaders treat every mess the same.

That’s where the VUCA lens comes in.

Originally coined by the military, VUCA breaks down four distinct kinds of uncertainty:

  • Volatile — fast-moving and unstable

  • Uncertain — lacking predictability

  • Complex — full of moving parts

  • Ambiguous — hard to interpret or define

Each one requires a different leadership move. But most leaders skip the first - and most crucial - step: naming the storm before trying to calm it.

This week, I worked with a team that was spinning its wheels on a significant cross-functional initiative.

It had all the symptoms:

  • Conflicting signals

  • Overlapping roles

  • Friction between departments

  • No clear “why” behind the plan

People were stressed—but no one knew what kind of help to ask for. Then, during a coaching moment, someone paused and said:

“This doesn’t feel chaotic because it’s fast. It feels chaotic because we don’t understand it.”

That one sentence helped the team realize:
This wasn’t volatility. It was ambiguity.
And it needed a different response.

Once they named the mess, their leadership got sharper.

This Week’s Coaching Prompt:

“What kind of VUCA am I facing—and have I named it out loud?”

Here’s how to break it down:

Volatile → “It’s unstable, but we understand it.”

  • Think: sudden changes, shake-ups, staff exits

  • Move: Act fast, stabilize, over-communicate

Uncertain → “We see patterns, but can’t predict.”

  • Think: new markets, policy shifts, unclear reactions

  • Move: Stay curious (had to slip in a Ted Lasso reference), gather data, create small experiments

Complex → “Too many variables, too intertwined.”

  • Think: multi-team projects, global initiatives

  • Move: Simplify, clarify roles, align cross-functionally

Ambiguous → “We don’t even know what we’re solving.”

  • Think: team tension, unclear strategy, foggy goals

  • Move: Name what’s missing, ask meaning-making questions, slow down the spin

One Actionable Practice: Run a VUCA Check-In

Take 10 minutes this weekend:

  1. Identify a situation that feels “off” or stuck.

  2. Ask: Which VUCA type is this?

  3. Write down the best leadership posture for that kind of challenge.

  4. Bonus: Bring it to your team. Ask them what they see—and what kind of leadership they need from you.

You’ll be surprised how much clarity comes from that one act of framing.

What Shifts When You Name the Mess

Too often, leaders default to action without first assessing the situation.
When things feel urgent, we speed up. Over-communicate. Hold tighter.

But if the storm you’re facing is complexity or ambiguity, those moves add static. You end up:

  • Making decisions in the wrong key

  • Creating urgency where steadiness is needed

  • Micromanaging when the team needs meaning

Naming the mess doesn’t make it go away.
But it makes it leadable.

It shifts you from reaction to orientation - and that’s a powerful leadership move.

Why This Matters Right Now

We’re not short on chaos.
We’re short on framing.

When leaders name the kind of “hard” they’re in, three things happen:

  1. Teams exhale.
    Naming uncertainty gives people language - and permission - not to have all the answers.

  2. Strategy sharpens.
    You stop treating ambiguity like volatility (or vice versa), and start making context-appropriate choices.

  3. Trust deepens.
    Your team learns: “Even when things are foggy, my leader helps us see the road.”

That’s real leadership.
Not knowing everything. Just helping others make sense of what’s in front of them.

Your Move: Practice Framing Over Fixing

Set aside 5–10 minutes this weekend:

  • Choose a situation that feels complex, slow, or emotionally charged

  • Ask: Is this volatile, uncertain, complex, or ambiguous?

  • Share that diagnosis with a peer or teammate—and watch the conversation shift

You don’t need a plan yet.
You need a shared map.

Because your team can handle turbulence.
They just need to know which storm they’re in - and that you see it too.

Forward this to someone leading through fog. Better yet, print it and bring it to your next leadership meeting.

You don’t need to control the chaos.
You just need to name it first.

title: The $100 Test: What Are You Really Leading With?
html:
Your calendar doesn’t lie. Neither does your energy.

Leadership isn’t just about what you say you value – it’s about where you actually invest.

Years ago, during a strategic retreat with a USAID team, we skipped the spreadsheets and handed out stacks of Monopoly money. Their mission? Build a budget for the next year – knowing they had “mortgages” (aka fixed commitments) they couldn’t change.

The money was fake, but the clarity was real.

Seeing teams physically allocate their budget forced hard truths:

  • What do we always say is important… but never really fund?

  • What’s getting money just because it always has?

  • What’s starving that we claim to care about?

This wasn’t about budget planning. It was about priority alignment.
About matching behavior to belief.

And it works just as well with leadership.

This Week’s Coaching Prompt:
“If I had $100 to spend on leadership this week – where would I invest it?”

Here’s one way to break it down:

  • $30 → Building trust

  • $25 → Clarifying goals

  • $20 → Giving and receiving feedback

  • $15 → Cultivating your own clarity and calm

  • $10 → Delegating what only you think you should own

Try this reflection:

  • Where am I overspending – out of habit or fear?

  • What am I underfunding – despite knowing it matters?

  • What’s one “mortgage” I’ve accepted that needs rethinking?

Why This Matters Right Now
We’re at the end of the fiscal year. Budgets are being closed out, but leadership costs carry over.

Burnout. Misalignment. Low trust. Constant firefighting.
They all stem from misallocated energy.

The $100 metaphor is simple – but sticky.
You can use it in your own reflection. In team retreats. Even in 1:1s.

Because saying “team culture is everything” and then investing $0 in psychological safety?

That gap is the work.

Your Move: Run a $100 Audit This Week

  1. Set a timer for 10 minutes.

  2. Allocate your $100 honestly across your leadership investments.

  3. Ask: Does this match what I say matters?

  4. Share it with a peer – or your team.

Bonus: Pull out some Monopoly money. Make it real. You’d be surprised at how quickly clarity emerges when you make priorities tangible. Order it on Amazon, here is what I bought.

Share this with a colleague navigating FY planning – or a leader who wants their choices to match their values.

You don’t need a bigger budget.
You need a clearer allocation.

So:
Where’s your $100 going?

title: The Delegation Advantage: Why Clarity Builds Trust
subtitle: Clarity builds trust. Trust builds growth. Growth builds results.
html:
One Clear Idea

Delegation isn’t losing control.

It’s creating clarity.

This week, I revisited some of the best research on decision-making, and one truth jumped out:

People don’t get frustrated by delegation. They get frustrated by unclear delegation.

When you don’t name who makes decisions, how they are made, and why it matters, stress rises and trust falls.

But when you do? Delegation becomes your leadership advantage.

This Week’s Coaching Prompt

“What’s one decision I’m holding onto — where clarity could help me delegate without losing control?”

If your answer is “almost everything,” you’re not alone.

New leaders often swing between two extremes:

  • Clutching (holding onto too much because “it’s faster if I just do it”)

  • Dumping (offloading with no context, leaving people confused)

Both erode trust.

Delegation isn’t about relief. It’s about development.

One Actionable Tool: The DELEGATE Framework

Here’s how to hand off work with confidence and clarity:

  • Define the task clearly – what success looks like

  • Explain why it matters – connect to mission and impact

  • Level the authority – what decisions are theirs vs. yours

  • Establish check-ins – support without micromanaging

  • Give context – history, stakeholders, and risks

  • Ask for their input – align, don’t just assign

  • Trust, but verify – review respectfully

  • Encourage feedback – improve the process together

Why This Matters Right Now

We’re leading in a VUCA world (volatile, uncertain, complex, ambiguous). You can’t remove the uncertainty.

But you can reduce the stress by gaining clarity.

When leaders delegate well, teams:

  • Move faster with less second-guessing

  • Feel trusted and empowered to own outcomes

  • Grow skills that make the whole team stronger

And when leaders delegate poorly, teams:

  • Spin in confusion

  • Default to hesitation or rework

  • Lose confidence in themselves and in you

Delegation ≠ losing control.
Delegation = leading with clarity.

Your Move: Run the Checklist

Take 5 minutes today.

Pick one task you’re still holding onto.
Walk it through the DELEGATE steps.
Name the clarity out loud.

Then — watch how trust and ownership grow.

Better yet, share this framework with your team. Invite them to hold you accountable for delegating with clarity.

You don’t build trust by holding tighter.
You build it by sharing control — without losing direction.

So — what’s the first task you’ll delegate this week?

title: The Decision Grid: How to Lead With Both Speed and Inclusion
subtitle: Clarity builds trust. Trust builds growth. Growth builds results.
html:
One Clear Idea

The hardest part of leadership isn’t making decisions — it’s making them transparent. It’s a leader’s role to bring clarity to complex situations.

Your team doesn’t just want to know the what. They need to understand how.

Two frameworks help:

  • The 6C Modes (how you involve others in decisions)

  • Hyatt’s Delegation Levels (how much authority you give away)

Alone, each is useful. Together, they form a Decision Grid that gives you — and your team — clarity.

The 6C Decision Modes

Every decision lives in one of six modes:

  • Command – I decide quickly, no input.

  • Consultative – I decide, but I seek your advice.

  • Collaborative – We co-create the decision.

  • Consensus – Everyone weighs in; we move with broad agreement.

  • Core Expertise – I defer to the subject-matter expert.

  • Choice – I set guardrails; you decide fully.

Hyatt’s 5 Levels of Delegation

Every handoff lives on a spectrum of authority:

  1. Level 1 - Do exactly as I say (I decide everything)

  2. Level 2 - Research & advise (you gather, I decide)

  3. Level 3 - You propose, I approve (I retain veto)

  4. Level 4 - You decide, I’m informed (I trust, but want visibility)

  5. Level 5 - You decide, full ownership (I release control)

The Decision Grid

When you put these two frameworks together, you get a simple but powerful map. It shows not just who decides — but how the decision is made, and how much ownership is shared.

Here’s what it looks like in practice:

Notice how some squares feel natural — like Collaborative + Level 3 (a shared proposal with your sign-off) or Choice + Level 5 (full autonomy within guardrails). Others don’t fit as well — like Collaborative + Level 1 (co-creation can’t exist without freedom) or Command + Level 5 (true command and full release don’t belong together).

👉 The point isn’t to label one square as “best.” The point is to name which square you’re in — and why.

This Week’s Coaching Prompt

“Which square of the Decision Grid am I in right now — and does my team know it?”

Why This Matters Right Now

  • Overusing Command–Level 1 erodes trust.

  • Overusing Consensus–Level 5 slows everything to a crawl.

  • Ignoring Choice–Level 4 or 5 stifles growth.

Great leaders don’t lock themselves into one square. They flex across the grid — balancing speed, inclusion, and clarity as the situation demands.

Your Move: Name the Square

Before your next decision:

  • Pick your C.

  • Pick your Level.

  • Tell your team.

Clarity builds trust.
Trust builds speed.
Speed builds results.

So — where are you on the grid today?

Want to see how the Decision Grid could sharpen your own leadership?

I’m offering a limited number of free 30-minute chats to guide leaders through applying it directly to their teams.

title: The Growth Shortcut: Why You Need a Leadership Gym
html:
One Clear Idea

Leadership isn’t something you figure out in your head.

It’s something you train for – with others.

This week, I listened to Adam Galinsky on the HBR IdeaCast ("Are You an Inspirational Leader?"), and one line stuck with me:

“Leadership is like exercise – you don’t get strong by thinking about it. You get strong by doing it. Over and over.”

Galinsky’s research breaks inspirational leadership into three practices:

  • Vision: how you see the world

  • Example: how you show up in the world

  • Mentorship: how you support others in the world

All three are skills. All three can be built.
But only if you stop leading alone – and start training on purpose.

That’s where your leadership gym comes in.

This Week’s Coaching Prompt:

“Who’s helping me lead better right now?”

If your answer is “no one” or “not sure,” don’t panic.

But do pay attention.

You wouldn't train for a marathon without a plan, a community, or a coach. So why try to lead others without support?

One Actionable Tool: Build Your Leadership Gym

Take 10 minutes this weekend and run this reflection:

Who’s On Your Leadership Bench?

  • Coach – pushes you to refine your habits and decision-making

  • Cohort – walks alongside you in the same growth season

  • Mirror – reflects what you’re doing that others won’t say

  • Culture Builder – models the climate you’re trying to create

  • Anchor – holds you steady when your identity feels shaky

If you can name these people, great.

If you can’t – that’s not a failure. It’s your growth edge.

What a Trainer Gives You That You Can’t Self-Give

From Galinsky’s research and my experience working with emerging leaders, here’s what trainers (and structured support) uniquely provide:

  • Accountability that sticks – beyond “shoulds,” they keep you consistent

  • Blind spot detection – because insight rarely comes from the inside alone

  • Skill acceleration – real-time feedback > theory

  • Confidential support – safe space for hard conversations

  • Sustainable growth – reps, reflection, and rhythm over intensity

Why This Matters Right Now

The best leaders aren’t the loudest. They’re the most practiced.

They:

  • Communicate with calm and clarity

  • Model behavior they want mirrored

  • Show up when it’s uncomfortable

  • And make others feel seen, valued, and capable

None of that happens on accident.

It happens in training – especially with people who push you and believe in you.

You wouldn’t try to lift 200 lbs alone the first time.

So stop trying to carry your leadership alone either.

Your Move: Sharpen Your Bench

Take 5 minutes today:

  1. Write down the five roles: Coach, Cohort, Mirror, Culture Builder, Anchor

  2. Who fills each one for you today? Be honest.

  3. Where are the gaps?

  4. Pick one person you wish were on that list – then reach out. Ask for a conversation, not a favor.

Better yet, share this post with someone on your team and build your gyms together.

You don’t rise to the level of your ambition.

You rise to the level of your support system.

So – who’s on your bench?

title: Generative AI Didn’t Break Education – It’s a Leadership Test for Independent Schools
html:
When ChatGPT hit classrooms, it didn’t sneak in quietly. It detonated.

Assignments unraveled. Grading frameworks collapsed. Students adapted overnight while many faculty and administrators scrambled to catch up. Parents worried about “cheating.” Boards demanded policy.

But here’s the truth: generative AI didn’t break education. It revealed the cracks we’d been ignoring.

For independent schools, those cracks are even sharper. Families don’t pay tuition for rote memorization, compliance-heavy assessments, or rigid content delivery. They invest in the distinct value proposition of an independent school: clarity of mission, intimacy of culture, strong faculty relationships, and the promise of whole-child development.

And this is where leadership comes in. AI isn’t just a classroom issue. It’s a leadership test – one that will determine whether schools cling to fear and rigidity or lean into adaptability, trust, and vision.

The Agency Question

This afternoon, I had a fascinating conversation with a tech entrepreneur who is also a neuroscientist. He’s as dissatisfied with today’s education system as many school leaders quietly are, but he framed it differently: in his view, AI can either strip students of agency or dramatically expand it.

In the wrong hands, AI risks making students dependent, outsourcing their curiosity and critical thinking. But in the right hands, it can act as an expert assistant – helping a young person dive deeply into engineering, history, or medicine far faster than traditional systems allow. It can accelerate learning, personalize pathways, and unlock creativity.

That tension – reduced agency versus expanded agency – cuts to the heart of independent school leadership. Will AI be allowed to erode curiosity? Or will schools model their use as a stimulant for curiosity, a tool that empowers deeper learning and self-direction?

A Chance to Get Ahead of the Wave

This entrepreneur also reminded me of the tidal wave of social media. Every educator I know can point to the damage it’s done: fractured attention spans, fragile self-esteem, rising rates of anxiety and depression. We weren’t ready, and the consequences were profound.

With AI, we have a second chance. The wave is here, but it's still early. Independent schools have the opportunity to get ahead of it – to make thoughtful, purposeful decisions now, before the technology reshapes adolescence by default.

The leaders who act in this moment won’t just protect their schools; they’ll strengthen their missions.

Rooting AI in Values

One mistake would be to look for a one-size-fits-all model. That’s not how independent schools work. Each has a unique ethos. Montessori programs, for instance, are rooted in curiosity, independence, and self-directed learning. Quaker schools emphasize reflection, simplicity, and community. Faith-based schools focus on moral and spiritual formation.

The leadership challenge isn’t: What’s the universal AI policy?

The question is: How do we integrate AI in a way that amplifies our values, rather than diluting them? For Montessori, AI might be used as a spark – a way to fuel exploration without replacing hands-on discovery. For a classical school, it could enrich Socratic dialogue by offering counterpoints or alternative perspectives. For a global school, it might provide multilingual access to knowledge and new avenues for cultural fluency.

Independent schools already have clarity of culture. Their task is to align AI with that culture so its presence strengthens identity instead of undermining it.

Faculty Culture Is the Fulcrum

If culture is the heart of independent schools, faculty are its lifeblood. Parents don’t just buy a curriculum; they invest in the teachers who deliver it. Faculty embody the ethos of the school.

That makes faculty buy-in non-negotiable.

And yet, many teachers feel anxious about AI. If their professional identity has been defined as “knowledge deliverer,” then AI looks like a competitor. If schools respond with rigid, top-down directives, resistance will only harden.

Leadership here requires humility. Heads and division directors must model curiosity themselves, creating sandbox spaces where faculty can test tools, experiment with lessons, and reflect together. After-school design sprints, cross-disciplinary pilots, or collaborative workshops can turn fear into agency.

Execution matters, too. Independent schools can move faster than public systems – but agility unused is agility wasted. Advisors experimenting with GPT-powered support tools, teachers reframing writing prompts, or department chairs testing grading workflows: these are not distractions; they are signs of intrapreneurship. Leadership’s role is to give these innovators the conditions to succeed and scale.

Students Are Already Leading

The most overlooked reality is that students aren’t waiting.

Many independent school students are already using AI not just to cut corners, but to create. They’re building prototypes, writing business plans, and testing ideas at a pace that often exceeds that of most schools.

Adults sometimes dismiss this as corner-cutting. But in truth, students are stress-testing the relevance of their education. They’re asking: Does what I’m learning here truly prepare me for the future I’m inheriting?

That’s not cheating. That’s leadership.

The question is whether schools will respond to that initiative with punishment or channel it. Innovation labs, entrepreneurship programs, or ethics electives could turn unsanctioned use into co-creation. Schools that position themselves as safe spaces for responsible AI experimentation will gain both reputational strength and enrollment advantage.

The Ethical Imperative

Parents and trustees want clarity. Teachers want guidance. Students want boundaries they can respect. Ethics is where trust will be either built or broken.

This cannot be a one-page addendum to the student handbook. It must be a lived conversation:

  • What does integrity look like when AI is everywhere?

  • Where is the line between assistance and substitution?

  • How do we balance efficiency with originality?

Independent schools are uniquely positioned to lead this dialogue. Their smaller scale allows for nuance. Their missions allow them to emphasize values as much as skills.

Leadership as Posture, Not Position

The World Economic Forum predicts that 40% of core job skills will shift in the next five years. That’s not a data point to sprinkle into a PowerPoint. It’s a mandate.

Independent schools that thrive in this environment won’t be the ones with the flashiest tech rollout or the slickest AI strategy document. They’ll be the ones where leadership shows up as posture – modeled daily by heads, division directors, department chairs, and faculty alike. That’s where the CREATE framework becomes more than theory; it’s a roadmap.

  • Culture: Leaders must articulate why their school matters in an AI world. A head who tells parents, “We’re not afraid of AI because our mission is to grow thinkers, not just test-takers,” anchors the community in clarity. Culture becomes the compass, not the casualty, of disruption.

  • Relationships: Trust is the currency of change. A division director who runs faculty roundtables on AI, listening before mandating, builds the connective tissue that makes innovation possible. Students who see adults modeling trust are more likely to approach AI with integrity themselves.

  • Execution: Posture means acting, not waiting. A department chair piloting AI-infused writing assignments with a small group of juniors is modeling leadership by doing. It doesn’t require perfection – it requires motion. Schools that can iterate quickly will learn faster than those waiting for the “perfect” policy.

  • Agility: When a math teacher experiments with AI to generate multiple solution pathways, she signals to her students: flexibility is a strength, not a weakness. Leaders who normalize experimentation cultivate resilience at every level of the institution.

  • Teaching: AI makes it clear that the role of teachers is no longer to deliver content but to coach discernment. A history teacher who uses AI to generate competing historical narratives, then coaches students on how to evaluate them, models what it means to teach in the age of abundance.

  • Ethical Decision-Making: Finally, ethics is where leadership posture is tested most visibly. A board chair who insists AI policies be rooted in the school’s values – not just risk management models responsibility. A teacher who pauses a class discussion to ask, “Should we use AI here?” is coaching ethics in real time.

Students are watching. If their leaders freeze, they’ll learn to freeze. If their leaders adapt, they’ll learn to adapt. Leadership in the AI era isn’t about titles or tech plans – it’s about posture. And posture is contagious.

A Leadership Opportunity, Not a Threat

That conversation with the neuroscientist entrepreneur has stayed with me. He sees AI as both risk and opportunity: a technology that could diminish student agency if we’re careless, or massively expand it if we’re thoughtful. He believes schools must find ways to make AI serve their mission, not the other way around.

He’s right.

COVID was our last once-in-a-generation disruption, and too many schools responded by doubling down on old practices. AI offers another chance. This time, we can’t afford to miss it.

Independent schools have the agility, intimacy, and cultural depth to lead. But doing so will require courage: the courage to listen, to experiment, to admit uncertainty, and to model adaptability in real time.

Generative AI didn’t end education. It reset the terms. For independent schools, this is not the time to guard what was. It is the time to guide what’s next.

Question for heads, boards, and faculty leaders: How are you ensuring AI expands agency in your community rather than diminishes it?

title: Occupation Without Representation: The Urgent Case for DC Statehood
subtitle: Wear a T-Shirt, its better than throwing Subs
html:
I’ve always believed a t-shirt can start a conversation.

Years ago, I designed my own “Dyslexic” font and made shirts for myself, my kids, and a few friends – celebrating dyslexia as a superpower. Folks would come up to me in the grocery store, and ask me about it, or give me a thumbs up, or share, “Hey, I’m dyslexic too!”

This latest design carries another message that needs to be said out loud: Taxation without representation is un-American.

When I was RIF’ed from USAID in February, one of my first instincts – after selling off my Tesla stock – was to call my representatives in Congress. A teammate quietly reminded me: “At least you have a congressman to call.” 

That landed. Hard.

Washington, DC, is home to over 700,000 Americans – more than the populations of Vermont and Wyoming combined. Its economy, at $190 billion, is larger than those of Alaska, Vermont, Wyoming, Idaho, New Mexico, and Mississippi. 

Pardon a brief digression to highlight the contrast between DC and Mississippi, since the Mississippi National Guard is one of the units deployed to DC at the moment under the Trump Administration.

  • Mississippi’s capital is named after Andrew Jackson, the man behind the infamous Indian Removal Act. Washington, DC is named after George. 

  • DC's average household income is double that of Mississippi ($108K vs. $54K), with a lower poverty rate (13.6% vs. 19.5%). 

  • DC is also far more educated – 64% of adults hold a bachelor’s degree compared to 24% in Mississippi

  • While DC faces serious public safety challenges, Mississippi has a higher gun-death rate (29.6 vs. 21.4 per 100K). 

By most measures, DC looks more like a thriving state than the Magnola State. Just saying.

Yet residents have no voting representation in Congress. And because of that unique status, DC has repeatedly been treated as less than a state. The aforementioned troops have occupied the city – not by the consent of its people or local leadership, but at the direction of outsiders. 

But make no mistake – DC is not a bureaucratic anomaly. It’s vibrant and fully American: the birthplace of Go-Go music, home to over 15 universities, and one of only five states in the U.S. (along with California, NY, Florida, Minnesota, and Illinois) that fields professional teams in the NHL, MLB, NBA, WNBA, and MLS. Sorry, NFL Commanders, you’re close, but come back to RFK and I’ll add you to the list. 

Its residents pay taxes, serve in the military, and contribute fully to the nation. By every measure of fairness, democracy, and representation, DC has earned the right to be the 51st state.

The DC flag, with its bold red bars and three stars, is one of the most recognizable city flags in the world – adapted from George Washington’s family coat of arms. BTW, it also appears on the US military Purple Heart ICYWW. It's probably only second to Chicago as one of the best city flags out there. But it should be a state flag. 

My t-shirt design builds on that imagery, pairing a symbol of local pride with a clear message – it’s a statement about democracy and the unfinished business of making DC the 51st state.

GET YOURS HERE

I’ll be wearing this shirt on my trips to the grocery store and around town. Hope to see you wearing yours too! Strike up a conversation, help get the ball moving, it's time.

#DCStatehood #Leadership #Representation #CivicEngagement #Democracy

title: Set the Culture Before the Syllabus
subtitle: For new school leaders and educators prepping for Day 1
html:
Here’s the trap:
It’s the week before school starts. You’re tweaking your syllabus, finalizing staff meeting slides, or perhaps, like I used to, the week before, labeling the Chromebooks… and quietly forgetting that culture isn’t just one more thing on your checklist.

It is the checklist.

Whether you’re leading a classroom, a grade team, or a school, the first few weeks will quietly teach people what to expect—what gets rewarded, what gets ignored, and whether this is a place where they feel safe showing up fully.

This Week’s Leadership Prompt:

“What do I want this space to feel like by Week 3—and what am I signaling on Day 1?”

  • If you’re a principal, what will new staff feel walking into their first meeting with you?

  • If you’re a teacher, what cues are your students picking up before you even start teaching?

  • If you’re a coach or AP, what small moments show you’re listening before leading?

Tool: The Start-of-Year Culture Builder

A 3-step reflection based on the Culture Pulse and Stakeholder Map tools:

  1. One Relationship to Invest In Early
    ➤ Who’s new, quiet, or skeptical—and how will you build trust fast?

  2. One Unspoken Norm to Name Aloud
    ➤ What’s something “everyone knows” but no one says? Make it visible.

  3. One Moment to Invite Voice
    ➤ What’s one low-stakes way you’ll invite others to shape the space?

Set a timer for 10 minutes. Jot quick answers. Then test one idea this week—with your team or students.

Your first week sets the tone more than your first lesson. Start with how you want to lead—not just what you plan to cover.

☕️ Short read with coffee. Actionable by Monday.

title: Magnificent Seven: Biography of a Number
html:
Seven as the Misfit Genius of the Numerical World

If numbers were people at a dinner party, Seven would be the guest who shows up alone, doesn’t drink, wears something slightly odd (perhaps a velvet blazer or a kaftan), and proceeds to tell a story so utterly captivating that everyone forgets to eat their dessert.

Seven is, mathematically speaking, uncooperative. It doesn’t divide neatly into anything else between 2 and 10, which makes it the only number in that range that can’t be used for clean multiplication or division. It refuses to play along in a base-10 world, where all the other digits are busy forming squares, halves, thirds, quarters, and more.

Three divides nine.
Four divides eight.
Five divides ten.
Seven just shrugs and goes its own way.

This makes it a bit of a mathematical nuisance, but also strangely alluring. When you try to slice a pie into seven equal pieces, you’ll likely just end up with six annoyed people and one guy who claims he doesn’t want dessert anyway. But the difficulty is the point: seven resists simplicity, and in doing so, earns our fascination.

Let’s test this. Ask a room full of people to name a number between 1 and 10 – quickly, without thinking. Most will say 7. Why?

Psychologists believe it’s because seven feels “random” in a satisfying way. One through six are too common. Eight, nine, and ten are too round. But seven? Seven lives right in that sweet spot between familiarity and intrigue. It's the number equivalent of a Wes Anderson character.

There’s even a term for this in cognitive psychology: the optimal boundary of perception. George A. Miller’s famous paper “The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two” argued that our working memory is built to handle around seven pieces of information at once. Not five. Not ten. Seven. This isn't just a quirk of memory. It's a design feature of how we process the world.

Which might explain why we cluster things in sevens:

  • Seven days of the week

  • Seven-digit phone numbers (at least before area codes muscled in)

  • Seven wonders of the world

  • Seven deadly sins (and seven virtues to match)

It’s a number that crops up not because it’s easy, but because it works – just barely.

In the world of prime numbers, seven is relatively early in the lineup – after two, three, and five – but it quickly sets itself apart. While other primes can be used to build squares or make clean pairs, seven stubbornly avoids participating in any neat mathematical reindeer games.

I promise this won’t be a math textbook, so this next sentence may seem very relative. But, here’s a fun bit of trivia: seven is the smallest number that cannot be expressed as the sum of the squares of three integers. Go ahead, try. 1² + 1² + 1² = 3. 2² + 1² + 1² = 6. But you’ll never get 7 that way. It refuses.

It also spikes in computational complexity. Some algorithms struggle with seven because of its position in numerical space, just outside of easy manipulation, but not quite large enough to be ignored.

Cryptographers and game theorists have long known this: seven is the smallest number that gums up simple logic systems.

In binary, seven is written as 111 – three bold digits, no filler. It’s the last number you can write before the system tips into a new dimension. After 111 comes 1000. That extra digit? That’s the moment the code breaks its own frame.

It’s the same quiet thrill you get when your odometer hits 100,000. No one pulls over for 90,000. But when a new placeholder rolls over – when a digit resets and a new one appears – it feels like a threshold has been crossed. Like you’ve entered a new chapter, even if the road hasn’t changed.

Seven, in its own way, plays with that same feeling. The sense that something just tipped. That we’ve moved from the familiar to the symbolic. That we’re no longer just counting – we’re crossing into meaning.

But let’s be honest: who really cares about Seven in binary? Unless you’re coding firmware or trying to impress a robot at a party, it’s not exactly dinner table material.

So let’s zoom out. So why not 8, 9, or 10?

Eight? Eight’s unhinged.

They don’t call it “crazy” eights for nothing. It’s the only number that looks like it’s wearing a wig – or two zeros doing a conga line. It’s symmetrical to a fault, like it’s trying to win a geometry pageant. Folds into halves, quarters, eighths – it just loves to be divided. Codependent, honestly. Eight is the friend who organizes “fun spreadsheets” and thinks spontaneity means using Comic Sans. I hate Comic Sans.

It’s the infinity symbol trying to keep it together.

Nine is nearly ten – but somehow always feels like it’s trying too hard, wishes it were ten.

Ten is the straight-A student who reminds the teacher they forgot to assign homework. You know exactly what Ten’s going to wear to the party (khakis), exactly when it’s going to arrive (10 minutes early, natch), and exactly when it’s going to leave (right after dessert, with a firm handshake).

Ten would make the most sense. It’s clean. It’s round. It’s mathematically elegant. All humans across cultures and across time have had ten fingers, and we’ve been counting on them since long before calculators, abacuses, or math class.

It’s practically biological. Watch any child learning addition, and you’ll see it – fingers unfurling like tiny number lines, one digit at a time. Ten is tactile. It’s embodied. It’s right there, built into our hands.

Even our number system – base-10 – is just an elaborate tribute to our own anatomy. We worship ten without realizing it. Ten commandments. Ten out of ten. Top ten lists. It’s the number we reach for when we want things to feel complete.

Reliable, yes. But thrilling? Never. Ten is polished, predictable, and boring.

SO… we keep circling back to Seven.

Seven, who doesn’t care how many fingers you have.
Seven, who refuses to line up nicely in your spreadsheet.
Seven, who doesn’t play well with others, but still gets invited to everything.

Seven is the wildcard. The jazz solo. The prime that slips through the grid just enough to stay interesting. It’s not the logical choice – it’s the intuitive one. Not because it’s easy to use, but because it’s just hard enough to make us feel something.

Seven pushes back. It introduces friction. It’s the little wrinkle that turns a line into a spiral. And maybe that’s why we’ve given it the keys to our weeks, our scales, our sacred calendars, and our fairy tales and watched it do donuts on the lawn. Not because we had to, but because it made things interesting.

Seven makes us pay attention.

Clocks, Calendars, and Chaos

Take timekeeping.

There are 365 days in a year, which – if you’ve ever tried to plan a birthday party – doesn’t divide evenly into anything. Not seven, not twelve, not even “perfect ten” without leftovers. That’s why we need leap years, leap seconds, and the constant sense that your birthday never falls on a weekend two years in a row, or conveniently for your 16th, 21st, 30th, or 50th birthday.

My birthday happens to fall on a US national holiday, so it’s always a weekend for me.

It’s not just bad luck for the rest of you, though. It’s bad math.

If the ancients had wanted a clean, mathematically elegant week, they could’ve picked five or ten days. Five-day weeks would’ve been great - assuming we kept the two-day weekend. Eat your heart out, Iceland, and your four-day work week. Ten-day weeks would’ve kept the accountants happy – easy to tally, easy to divide, all very metric.

Speaking of metric, in fact, the French actually tried a metric calendar. During the Revolution, they threw out the Gregorian calendar like yesterday’s aristocracy and launched the French Republican calendar in 1793. Each month had three ten-day weeks (called décades), with a few bonus days at the end for festivals, wine, and general Republic-ing.

It was precise. It was secular. It was deeply unpopular.

Nobody wanted to work nine days straight just to get one day off. Especially the French, especially in August.

The calendar was quietly guillotined in 1806.

The Soviets tried their own version in the 20th century. Because, of course, they did.

Scientific socialism. Central planning. All in the belief that if you just rearranged the furniture of society, time, labor, and faith, you could engineer a better world. In 1929, they introduced the Soviet Eternal Calendar, which included a five-day workweek. No more Sundays. No shared rest days. Instead, every citizen was assigned a color – yes, a color – and each color got its own staggered day off.
